running_heads.HISTORIARVM ET ASTRONOMIÆ STVDIOSO INVES: GREETING TO THE STUDIOUS INVESTIGATOR OF HISTORY AND ASTRONOMY, S.

units.tr: Of Muhamedes
Alfragani
The Arabic Chronological and Astronomical
Elements, taken from the Palatine
library, rendered from old books into Latin,
completed, and polished with scholia.
A commentary has been added,

units.la: qui rationem calendarii Romani, Ægyptiaci, Arabici, Persici, Syriaci & Hebraei explicat, & intervalla præcipuarum ærarum ita declarat, ut ab Olympiadibus & Urbe condita usque ad nostram memoriam, per annos Nabonasari, Iulij Cæsaris & Christi, certa temporum series constare possit:
units.tr: which explains the calendars of the Romans, Egyptians, Arabs, Persians, Syrians and Hebrews, and sets out the intervals of the principal eras so clearly that, from the Olympiads and the founding of the City down to our own time, through the years of Nabonassar, Julius Caesar and Christ, a fixed sequence of dates can be established.

units.la: Autore M. IACOBO CHRISTMANNO Ioannis-bergensi, Inclyta Academia Heidelbergensis Professore.
units.tr: By the author M. Jacob Christmann, of Johannisberg, Professor at the famous Academy of Heidelberg.
Frankfurt,
at the heirs of Andreas Wechel,
for Claude Marnius and Johann Aubrius.
MDXC

units.la: ILLVSTRISSIMO AC FORTISSIMO PRINCIPI, D. IOANNI CASIMIRO, Palatino Rheni, Duci Bauariae, &c. Electoralis Palatinatus Administratori felicissimo, Domino suo clementissimo
units.tr: TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST VALIANT PRINCE, LORD JOHN CASIMIR, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, etc., most fortunate Administrator of the Electoral Palatinate, his most gracious Lord
Greetings.

units.la: CVM ante biennium, Illustrissime Princeps, de chronolo-giae & astronomiae principiis Alfraganū perlegissem; equidem indolui, quod is negligenter versus & pessimè mutilatus in publicum prodiisset. Quamobrem paraphrasin Hebraeam Iacobi Antolii, multis abhinc annis in Alfraganum conscriptam, Lati-nè reddidi; scholiis, quantū fieri potuit, expoliui, totamque calendariorum hi-storiam iusto commentario declaraui.
units.tr: Two years ago, most illustrious Prince, after I had read through Alfraganus on the principles of chronology and astronomy, I was indeed grieved that he had come out in public carelessly translated and very badly mutilated. Therefore I rendered into Latin the Hebrew paraphrase of Jacob Antolius, written on Alfraganus many years ago; I polished it with scholia as far as I could, and I explained the whole history of the calendars with a full commentary.

units.la: Quem sane laborum meorum fructum Celsitudini tuę qua par est, obseruantia, dedico ac consecro: vt is ad instructissimam Palatinorum bibliothecam, ex qua succum omnem & incrementum accepit, quasi postliminio redeat. Magna profecto fama surgit, & bibliothecæ Palatinæ splendor iam Germanis nostris lucere incipit: tibi vero Heroï vt magnanimo, ita singulari studiorum patrono gloriosum est, non modo præciosam supellectilem habere, verum etiam eandem variis voluminibus locupletare. Postquam enim Generosus & Illustris vir Huldrichus Fuggerus libros sibi ingenti pecunia vi comparatos, legas-set Illustrissimo & optimæ spei Principi, D. Friderico IV. Electoralis Palatinatus hæredi: hanc quoque administrationis curam sustinuisti, vt eos veteri bibliothecæ annumerari, atque opera Cl. v. Pauli Melissi[?] Franci in ordinem redigi manumandaris. Quo potißimum nomine gratulabitur sibi posteritas, palam exultabunt lætitia eruditi, & congestum præstantissimorum librorum thesaurū immortalitatis memoria prosequentur. Neque immerito ab omnibus mortalibus prædicandum est, quod Cælsitudini tuæ visum sit, astronomiæ & vniuersæ mathematum scientiæ opem ferre, vt deinceps in promtu sit ratio supputandi motus cœlestes nō tantum compendiosior, verum etiam exactior. Etenim animo ad gratificandum Reipub. maximè propensō, Valentinum Othonem, peritissimum nostri seculi Mathematicum, accersendū, & sumtibus maximo Principe dignis egregios ipsius conatus iuuandos ac promouendos censuisti: vt Canonem triangulorum à Georgio Ioachimo Rhetico inchoatum, tandem absoluat, & absolutum sub nominis tui auspiciis in lucem emittat. Quis verò hic desideret ut ampliores ex artibus Rhetorum locos, laudibus tuis celebrandis conquiram[?]ad id enim virtutu omnium fastigium adscendisti, ut cuncta ista, quæ vel de egregiis Heroïbus exspectantur, vel facunde prædicantur, vita superaueris. Elucet in Celsitudine tua SANCTITAS DOMI, IN ARMIS FORTITVDO, UTROBIQVE PRVDENTIA, in actionibus certe cunctis SINCERITAS & CONSTANTIA: conspicua est summa tua erga studia literarum LIBERALITAS & MVNIFICENTIA. Testimonium nobis locupletissimum præbet collegiu CASIMIRIANVM, adeo eleganter & magnifice sumtibus tuis constructum, ut intuentibus admirationi, Heidelbergensi Academiç honori, totiq; Palatinatui emolumento sit futurum. O felicem diem, quo fundamentum iecisti, & amplissimum hoc Musarum palatium nomine tuo appellasti! lasti/ Factum id est anno Domini & Seruatoris nostri M. D. LXXXVIII. Indictione I. mense Maio, die III Iduum Iulianarum, feria hebdomadis secunda, sesquihora post meridiem. Adstitit Il-lustrissimus & Generosissim⁹ [?] Princeps, Fridericus IV. tuus ex fratre germano Ludouico IV. Elector nepos, tutelae ac patrocinio tuo fideliter commendatus: adfuerunt consiliarii, viri nobilissimi ac prudentissimi: accesserunt Professores celeberrimi, qui fundationis caeremonias nō sine voluptate sunt contemplati. Perge igitur Illustrissime Princeps, de patria & studiis humanioribus optime merèri: maneat tibi animus bibliothecam Palatinam indies magis ac magis exornandi, & viros in omni disciplinarū ac linguarum genere exercitatos fouen-di. Neque mehercule parum dignitatis Academiae accesserit, si cathedram pro-sessionis Arabicae erigas, in eaque cum Philosophiam, tum Medicinam ex suis fontibus doceri permittas. Suppeditat prælum[?] Romanum libros elegantissi-mos: habet bibliotheca Palatina Abil-sedeam cosmographum, Regimen sani-tatis, Takvim uzzihet appellatum, au-tore Aben Gezla, Epitomen Almagesti, Historiam Abul Haffumi[?], quæ ab He-gira usq; ad imperium Ottomannicum res tam Christianorum quam Sarace-norum per septingentos annos gestas, exponit: habet denique alios manuscriptos & insigni eruditione refertos codi-ces. Ex quibus codicibus si Lexicon ali-quod diligenti inquisitione extrahatur, & Grammaticæ institutiones cum me-rhodica Radicum analysi adiungantur; breui futurum est, ut idioma Arabicum penitus innotescat, & multiplex corru-ptissimorum vocabulorum farrago, quæ se in versiones interpretum insinuauit, prorsus exstirpetur. Ad quam rem haud parum fortasse contulerint meditationes a me privatim confectae: quas summi consiliarii non modo viderunt, verum etiam probarunt, & vt abornatissimo viro Abrahamo Colbingero, fidissimo tibi a secretis ministro accepi, editione dignas esse iudicarunt. Quare opportunum esse existimo, vt quae ante complures annos prelo committere decreui, tandem publicae vtilitatis causa pro virili parte promam: & Arabismi non tam proprietatem, quam eiusdem summam cum dialecto Hebraeorum ac Chaldaeorum affinitatem demonstrare pergam. Non enim dubito, quin apud bonos gratiam sim initurus, apud Celsitudinem tuam vero ocii mei rationem redditurus, & apud posteros, cum obtrectationis invidia decesserit, industriç testimonium habiturus. Deus Opt. Max. Celsitudinem tuam clementer tueatur, & Reipub. saluam & incolumem diutissimè conseruet: Datum kalendis Aprilibus, Anno CHRISTI MDXC.
units.tr: I dedicate and consecrate the fruit of these labours to your Highness, with the reverence that is fitting, so that it may return, as if by right of return, to the most splendidly furnished library of the Palatines, from which it has received all its sap and growth. Indeed a great reputation is rising, and the splendour of the Palatine library is now beginning to shine upon our Germans. For you, a hero as magnanimous as you are a singular patron of studies, it is glorious not only to possess a precious store of books but also to enrich the same with various volumes. For when the noble and illustrious man Huldrich Fugger had acquired books at great expense and bequeathed them to the most illustrious and most hopeful Prince, Lord Frederick IV, heir of the Electoral Palatinate, you also undertook this care of administration: that they should be counted among the old library and, by the work of the distinguished Paul Melissus of France, be put in order. For this above all they will congratulate you, and learned men will openly rejoice, and they will honour the collected treasure of most excellent books with the memory of immortality. Nor is it without reason that it must be proclaimed by all mortals that it has pleased your Highness to bring aid to astronomy and to the whole science of mathematics, so that from now on a method of calculating celestial motions will be at hand, not only more compendious but also more exact. For, with your mind most inclined to serve the commonwealth, you thought fit to summon Valentine Otho, the most skilled mathematician of our age, and, with expenditure worthy of a great Prince, to support and advance his outstanding efforts: so that he may at last complete the Canon of Triangles begun by Georg Joachim Rheticus, and, once completed, send it forth into the light under the auspices of your name. But who here would ask for richer commonplaces from the arts of the orators to celebrate your praises? For you have ascended to such a summit of all virtues that you surpass in life all those things which are either expected of excellent heroes or eloquently proclaimed. In your Highness shines HOLINESS AT HOME, FORTITUDE IN ARMS, PRUDENCE EVERYWHERE; in all your actions certainly SINCERITY AND CONSTANCY; conspicuous is your great GENEROSITY AND MUNIFICENCE towards the studies of letters. The college CASIMIRIANUM, so elegantly and magnificently constructed at your expense, gives us a most abundant testimony, and it will be an admiration to onlookers, an honour to the Heidelberg Academy, and a benefit to the whole Palatinate. O fortunate day on which you laid the foundation and named this very ample palace of the Muses after your name! This was done in the year of the Lord and our Saviour 1588, in the first indiction, in the month of May, on the third day before the Ides of July, on the second day of the week, an hour and a half after noon. There stood by the most illustrious and most noble Prince, Frederick IV, your nephew through your full brother Ludwig IV, Elector, faithfully commended to your guardianship and patronage; there were present the councillors, men most noble and most prudent; there came the most celebrated professors, who contemplated the ceremonies of the foundation not without delight. Go on, then, most illustrious Prince, deserving very well of your country and of the humane studies: may you keep the intention of adorning the Palatine library more and more each day, and of fostering men trained in every kind of discipline and language. Indeed, by Hercules, no little dignity will accrue to the Academy if you erect a chair of Arabic teaching, and allow philosophy as well as medicine to be taught in it from its own sources. The Roman press supplies very elegant books; the Palatine library has Abulfeda the cosmographer, the Regimen of Health, called Takvim uzzihet, by Ibn Jazla, an Epitome of the Almagest, and the History of Abu'l-Fida, which sets forth the deeds of both Christians and Saracens from the Hegira down to the Ottoman empire over seven hundred years; finally it has other manuscript codices filled with notable learning. If from these codices some lexicon is extracted by diligent inquiry, and grammatical rules are joined with a methodical analysis of roots, it will soon come about that the Arabic language is thoroughly known, and the manifold farrago of very corrupt words that has crept into the translations of interpreters will be utterly rooted out. To this matter my private meditations, composed by me, may perhaps have contributed not a little: these the most wise councillors not only have seen but have also approved, and, as I received from the most distinguished man Abraham Colbinger, your most trusty secretary, they judged them worthy of publication. Wherefore I think it opportune that what I decided some years ago to commit to the press I now at last bring forth, as far as in me lies, for the public advantage; and I shall go on to show not so much the peculiarity of Arabic as its very great affinity with the dialect of the Hebrews and the Chaldeans. For I do not doubt that I shall win the favour of good men, shall render to your Highness an account of my leisure, and among posterity, when the sting of envy has departed, shall have a witness to my diligence. May God, the best and greatest, graciously protect your Highness and preserve the commonwealth safe and sound for a very long time. Given on the Kalends of April, in the year of Christ 1590.
To your Highness
bound by a perpetual memory of your kindness

units.la: M. Iacobus Christmannus Hebraæ linguæ Professor.
units.tr: M. Jacob Christmann, Professor of the Hebrew language.
Of Paul Melissus of France,
COUNT OF THE SACRED PALATINE AND
KNIGHT, CITIZEN OF ROME.
M E L O S
TO JACOB CHRISTMANN
OF JOHANNISBERG.
Of eternity the last point is not made clear
Time, the part that turns the years in a circle;
the firm clasp and tenacious knot
of the revolving orbs of the wandering stars
of the sliding age. The sun, the eye of the sky,
and the moon, degenerate in countenance, a bastard,
it is fitting that they serve for fixed
measures by continuous motion.
Hence the bright day comes, the giver of light;
hence the dark shadow of night, the mother
of the blackening shades, follows the daily steps
as a dark companion.
Then the dawn, fresh each day,
and the evening star is born from the same source;
and the stars rise and set,
each in its own order, fittingly.

units.la: Cancer caperque est solstitij nota, Nota æquinoctii laniger atque lanx. Ver, æstus, autumnus, geluque Germine, fruge, mero, oliva Stat uber. Ipsi nos & homunculi, Terrestre semen, temporibus statis (Vt quemque cit natura rerum) Exorimur, cadimusque fato Prædestinato consiliis Dei, Mutare mentem & pectora nescij. Arcana in hæc secretiora Si penetrare animum atque sensûs, CHRISTMANNE, fas est; quantula portio Obscuritati per liquidum æthera Demetur? aut quantilla rebus Vela nová retegentur aurâ? Næ, scire nostrum est nil prope; nostraque Plus corda cæca noctis habere amant, Quàm lucis. En, haud secius tu Induis ancipitem bifrontis Iani figuram, lumine metiens Convexa cæli, & menstrua principum
units.tr: Cancer and Capricorn are the mark of the solstice; the mark of the equinox are the Ram and the Scales. Spring, heat, autumn, and frost, the seed-bearing, the fruit, the wine, the olive, stand as the abundance. We ourselves too, little men, earthly seed, at fixed times (as the nature of things moves each), arise and fall by fate, predestined by the counsels of God, not knowing how to change mind or heart. If it is lawful, Christmann, to penetrate with mind and sense these more secret mysteries, how small a portion of obscurity will be taken away through the clear air? Or how few veils will be drawn back by the new breeze of things? Alas, we know almost nothing; and our blind hearts love more to have the darkness of night than the light. Behold, you not less put on the double-faced figure of two-fronted Janus, measuring with light the vaults of heaven, and the monthly conjunctions of the leaders.

units.la: Conventa flam mirum[?] recludens, Præteriti catus ac futuri; Insignis instar Sosigenis, duce Quo Cæsar annis justa repagula, & Intercalares fixit olim Perspicuâ ratione metas. Dehinc catenas irresolubiles Connectis ævi, per rata sæcula; Annisque Christi Juliani Quâ serie numerove quadrent Monstras, receptis non sine calculis Ægyptiorum, deinde Arabum siphris, Fastisque Persarum & Syrorum, Et solitis epochis Hebræum. Omitto quam tu cultior artifex In Alfragáni codice sedulam Navaris operam corrigendo, & In Latium bene transferendo. Omitto quæ tu jam retines domi Ad umbilicos ducta novissimos, Nec nulla partim adfecta, partim (Scæva bona est) avidè inchoata.
units.tr: Opening up the wonderful...; wise both of the past and of the future; remarkable like Sosigenes, by whose guidance Caesar once fixed the just bars of the years and the intercalary limits with clear reasoning. Then you join the indissoluble chains of the age through the fixed centuries; and you show in what order or number the years of Christ agree with the Julian, the calculations of the Egyptians having been received, then the cycles of the Arabs, and the calendars of the Persians and Syrians, and the customary epochs of the Hebrews. I pass over how skilfully, as an artist, you have laboured diligently to correct the codex of Alfraganus and to translate it well into Latin. I pass over what you already keep at home, carried to the final touches, and some things partly finished, partly begun eagerly (the left hand is good).

units.la: Quid his merenti grata laboribus Mercedis ætas postera seu fluens Compensét? aut quæ fortis Heros Præmia digna tibi reponat? Ad me quod optantem attinet, imprecor, Non solum ut ipsum, verùm etiam tuos Cum Sole, cum Lunâ, libellos Vivida perpetuet Perenna.
units.tr: What reward will the following age, flowing on, offer you, grateful for such deserving labours? Or what brave hero will set before you the prizes worthy of you? As far as I am concerned, in praying, I invoke that not only you yourself but also your books, together with the Sun and with the Moon, may be kept alive in lasting vigour.
LIBER

units.la: LIBER ISTE VOCATVR ALFRAGANVS DE NOMINE authoris sui, qui eum succinctè depromsit ex Almagesto, sphærarū motuumq; cœlestium doctrinam, iuxta veterum traditionem explicante. Ego verò Iacobus filiusAntoli transtuli ipsum [Hebraicè] è libro cuiusdam Christiani, eundemq; correxi è codice Arabico: putauiq; me operæprecium facturū, si in gratiā lectoris, summam præscire cupientis, præmitterem triginta duo capita, quæ hîc tractantur.
units.tr: This book is called Alfraganus after the name of its author, who drew it in summary form from the Almagest, explaining the doctrine of the spheres and the motions of the heavenly bodies according to the tradition of the ancients. I, Jacob son of Antolius, translated it into Hebrew from the book of a certain Christian, and I also corrected it from an Arabic manuscript. I thought I would be doing something worthwhile if, for the sake of the reader who wishes to know the substance in advance, I placed before it the thirty-two chapters that are treated here.

units.la: CAput 1 agit de annis, mensibus ac diebus variarum gentium, & quæ in re differant, ostendit.
units.tr: Chapter 1 deals with the years, months and days of various peoples, and shows how they differ in these matters.

units.la: Caput 2 docet cælum sphæricum esse, & circumagere omnes suas stellas orbiculariter.
units.tr: Chapter 2 teaches that the heavens are spherical and that all their stars revolve in circles.

units.la: Caput 3 ostedit terram cum aqua globum con-stituere.
units.tr: Chapter 3 shows that the earth together with the water forms a globe.

units.la: Caput 4 probat terram globum fixum esse in medio cæli instar centri, & habere magnitudinem ad cælum, quam habeat punctum minimum.
units.tr: Chapter 4 proves that the earth is a globe fixed at the centre of the heavens, like a centre point, and that its size relative to the heavens is that of the smallest point.

units.la: Caput 5 declarat solem, lunam, omnesq; reliquas stellas sphæricas esse.
units.tr: Chapter 5 declares that the sun, the moon and all the other stars are spherical.

units.la: Caput 6 agit de duobus motibus primis couer-[?] [?]ionis cœlestis: quorum unus est motus universi, qui die naturali absoluitur ab oriente in occidentem: alter est stellarum, quem videntur habere in orbe signorum ab occasu in ortum.
units.tr: Chapter 6 deals with the two first motions of the heavenly revolution: one is the motion of the whole universe, which is completed in a natural day from east to west; the other is the motion of the stars, which they appear to have in the zodiac from west to east.

units.la: Caput 7 demonstrat quod tantum quarta terræ pars inhabitetur: quid contingat in toto ambitu eius: item quasit diversitas noctium & dierum.
units.tr: Chapter 7 demonstrates that only a quarter of the earth is inhabited: what happens in its whole circuit; likewise it asks about the variation of nights and days.

units.la: Caput 8 tractat de proprietatibus partium in quadrante terræ habitato.
units.tr: Chapter 8 treats the properties of the parts of the inhabited quarter of the earth.

units.la: Caput 9 examinat loca reliqua, quadrantis ni-mirum inhabitabilis, & ostedit quasit proprietas eo-rum, & quid cotingat in illis. Vbi loca recensentur, in quibus per menses aliquot sol cōspicitur, & in qui-bus iterum per menses aliquot nusquam apparet.
units.tr: Chapter 9 examines the remaining places, namely of the uninhabitable quarter, and shows what their properties are and what happens in them. Here the places are listed in which the sun is seen for some months and in which, again, it never appears for some months.

units.la: Caput 10 narrat de mensura terræ, & divisio-ne eius in 7 climata habitabilia secundum longitudines & latitudines.
units.tr: Chapter 10 tells of the measure of the earth and its division into seven inhabitable climates according to longitudes and latitudes.

units.la: Caput 11 recenset nomina locorum in terra cognitorum, & quid accidat in quouis parallelo.
units.tr: Chapter 11 recounts the names of places known on the earth, and what happens on each parallel.

units.la: Caput 12 exponit duodecim esse signa cœlestia, non pauciora nec plura.
units.tr: Chapter 12 sets out that there are twelve heavenly signs, neither fewer nor more.

units.la: Caput 13 proponit ascensiones signorum rectas sub horizonte æquatoris, & obliquas sub horizonte sphæræ inclinatæ.
units.tr: Chapter 13 sets forth the right ascensions of the signs under the horizon of the equator, and the oblique ascensions under the horizon of the inclined sphere.

units.la: Caput 14 ostendit quantitatem noctium & dierum, & docet quodnam sit discrimen inter horas diei naturalis æquales & temporales.
units.tr: Chapter 14 shows the length of nights and days, and teaches what the difference is between equal and temporal hours of the natural day.

units.la: Caput 15 enumerat hypotheses orbium septem planeplanetarum, & stellarum fixarum: quomodo complicentur, quem seruent ordinem, & quam habeat a terra distantiam.
units.tr: Chapter 15 lists the hypotheses of the orbits of the seven planets and of the fixed stars: how they are nested, what order they keep, and how far each is from the earth.

units.la: Caput 16 agit de hypothesibus motuum solis & lunæ, & stellarum fixarum volutatione in orientem & occidentem, secundum motum longitudinis.
units.tr: Chapter 16 deals with the hypotheses of the motions of the sun and moon, and of the revolution of the fixed stars eastward and westward, according to the motion of longitude.

units.la: Caput 17 exponit hypotheses motus quinq; errantium in orbibus suis secundum longitudinem.
units.tr: Chapter 17 sets out the hypotheses of the motion of the five wandering stars in their orbits according to longitude.

units.la: Caput 18 tradit accidetia quinq; errantium, item quis sit motus retrogradationis in Zodiaco.
units.tr: Chapter 18 delivers the accidents of the five wandering stars, and likewise what the motion of retrogradation in the zodiac is.

units.la: Caput 19 perlustrat quantitates orbium planetarum qui vocantur epicycli, & eccentricis imponuntur: & ostendit quæ sit distantia centrorum eccentricorum a centro terræ.
units.tr: Chapter 19 goes through the sizes of the orbits of the planets, which are called epicycles and are placed upon eccentrics, and shows what the distance is of the centres of the eccentrics from the centre of the earth.

units.la: Caput 20 docet revolutiones periodicas planetarum in orbibus suis & in Zodiaco.
units.tr: Chapter 20 teaches the periodic revolutions of the planets in their orbits and in the zodiac.

units.la: Caput 21 ostendit hypotheses motus stellarum declinantium in septentrionem & meridiem secundum motum latitudinis.
units.tr: Chapter 21 shows the hypotheses of the motion of stars declining northward and southward, according to the motion of latitude.

units.la: Caput 22 recenset stellas fixas iuxta magnitudines suas, & enumerat loca, in quibus maxima conspiciantur, quarum sunt quindecim.
units.tr: Chapter 22 recounts the fixed stars according to their magnitudes, and lists the places where the largest are seen; there are fifteen of them.

units.la: Caput 23 refert distantias stellarum fixarum & planetarum a terra.
units.tr: Chapter 23 reports the distances of the fixed stars and planets from the earth.

units.la: Caput 24 proponit quæ sit magnitudo stellarum respectu terræ.
units.tr: Chapter 24 sets out what the size of the stars is in relation to the earth.

units.la: Caput 25 diuersitatem docet, quam habeant stellæ in ascensionibus suis respectu Zodaici, in medio cælo, & in descensionibus suis. Caput 26 tradit ascensionem & descensionem, item occultationem stellarum sub radiis solaribus. Caput 27 explicat phasin lunæ novæ, & rationem incrementi ac decrementi luminis eius. Caput 28 exponit emersionem quinque errantium e radiis solaribus. Caput 29 docet accidentia lunæ & stellarum vicinarum terræ: & quæ sit ratio parallaxeos earū. Caput 30 est de eclipsi lunari. Caput 31 est de eclipsi solari. Caput 32 commemorat, quam breui tempore possit fieri eclipsis lunaris & solaris.
units.tr: Chapter 25 teaches the difference which the stars have in their ascensions relative to the zodiac, in mid-heaven, and in their descensions. Chapter 26 gives the rising and setting of the stars, and likewise their concealment beneath the rays of the sun. Chapter 27 explains the phase of the new moon and the reason for the increase and decrease of its light. Chapter 28 sets out the emergence of the five wandering stars from the sun's rays. Chapter 29 teaches the accidents of the moon and of the stars nearest the earth, and what the ratio of their parallax is. Chapter 30 is on the lunar eclipse. Chapter 31 is on the solar eclipse. Chapter 32 notes in how short a time an eclipse, lunar or solar, can occur.
Scholia of Christmann

units.la: Liber iste vocatur Alfraganus) Hæc verba sunt in-terpretis Hebraei, R. Iacobi Antolii: quibus comme-morat opusculi huius autorem esse Alfraganum, qui id ex Ptolemæi Almagesto compendiose depromtum, in gratiam studiosorum astronomiæ ꝯscripserit. Ve-risimile mihi videtur, ipsum a patria sua Fragana cognominatum fuisse Alfraganum: siquidem in Latina versione bibliothecæ Palatinæ tribuitur illi nomen proprium Ametus, hoc est, Ahmed sive Muhamed: ubi ita scribitur, Incipit liber de aggregationibus scientiæ stellarum & principiis cœlestium, quem Ametus fi-lius Ameti dictus Alfraganus compilauit 30 capitulis. Quo tempore vixerit, ex obseruationibus illius conicere licet: testatur enim cap. 6 suo seculo maximam solis declinationem fuisse 23 graduum & 35 minutorum: & cap. 10 in appendice de umbris, quam He-bræus braeus interpres reiecit ad finem opusculi, ait æquinoctium vernum fuisse die 16 mensis Adar, hoc est, Martii: & cap. 26 profitetur, stellam Canobum fuisse in postremo gradu geminorum. Ex quibus omnibus apparet, Alfraganum vixisse circa annum Christi 950: vt annotaui cap. 26. Quamobrem illi qui exististimant eum fuisse σύνγονον Thebitii, qui primus motum trepidationis obseruauit, falluntur, vt ostendam cap. 6. Sane libellum hunc eruditissimum scripsit de principiis astronomiæ, ex quo fere omnia haustit, quæ in doctrina primi mobilis tradidit Ioannes de sacro bu-sto.
units.tr: "This book is called Alfraganus." These are the words of the Hebrew translator, R. Jacob Antolius, by which he records that the author of this little work is Alfraganus, who wrote it, drawn in compendious form from Ptolemy's Almagest, for the benefit of students of astronomy. It seems probable to me that Alfraganus was so named from his homeland, Fragana. Indeed, in the Latin version in the Palatine library he is given the proper name Ametus, that is, Ahmed or Muhammad, where it is written thus: "The beginning of the book on the collections of the science of the stars and the principles of the heavenly bodies, which Ametus son of Ametus, called Alfraganus, compiled in 30 chapters." The time when he lived may be conjectured from his observations: for in chapter 6 he attests that in his century the greatest declination of the sun was 23 degrees and 35 minutes; and in chapter 10, in the appendix on shadows, which the Hebrew translator put at the end of the work, he says that the vernal equinox fell on the 16th day of the month Adar, that is, March; and in chapter 26 he professes that the star Canopus was in the last degree of Gemini. From all of these it appears that Alfraganus lived around the year of Christ 950, as I noted at chapter 26. Therefore those who think he was a contemporary (σύνγονον) of Thebit, who first observed the motion of trepidation, are mistaken, as I shall show at chapter 6. Certainly he wrote this most learned little book on the principles of astronomy, from which he drew almost everything that John of Sacrobosco delivered in his doctrine of the primum mobile.

units.la: Neque puduit summum mathematicum Ioannem Regiomontanum, vt Alfraganum publice præ-legeret in academia Patauina: est enim autor succinctus, qui non tam primum mobile, quàm theorias planetarum satis perspicuè explicat; sequitur hypothe-ses & placita summorum artificum, Ptolemæi & Muhamedis Aractensis, Albategnii cognominati, Passim enim citat μεγάλην σύνταξιν Ptolemæi, quam vocat Almagestum, hoc est, opus μέγιστον: idem in primo capite vocat canonem Ptolemaicum, dum vult constituere æram annorū Philippicorum. Muhamedis autem Albategnii etsi nominatim non meminerit: tamen totū primum caput, & alia multa ab eo est mutuatus.
units.tr: Nor was John Regiomontanus, the outstanding mathematician, ashamed to lecture publicly on Alfraganus at the University of Padua. For he is a concise author who explains not so much the primum mobile as the theories of the planets with sufficient clarity; he follows the hypotheses and opinions of the great craftsmen, Ptolemy and Muhammad of Aracta, called Albategnius. For he cites everywhere Ptolemy's great syntaxis, which he calls the Almagest, that is, the greatest work [μέγιστον]; in the first chapter he also calls it the Ptolemaic canon, when he wishes to fix the era of the Philippic years. Although he does not name Muhammad Albategnius, he has nonetheless borrowed the whole first chapter and many other things from him.

units.la: Arabicè hanc ifagogen scripsit, quam Ioannes Hispalensis circa annum Christi 1142 in Latinam linguam conuertit: quæ versio vulgata quidem est, sed multis in locis corrupta & mutila. Longè melior & perfectior, incerti tamen authoris, extat in bibliotheca Palatina, cuius paulò ante mentionem feci: quæ translationi Hebraeæ magna ex parte respondet. Ea descripta est à Friderico monacho Ratisponensi, or dinis S.Benedicti, in monasterio S.Emeranni, & absoluta anno Domini 1447 in die Goaris confessoris.
units.tr: He wrote this introduction in Arabic, which John of Seville translated into Latin around the year of Christ 1142. That version is indeed commonly known, but it is corrupt and mutilated in many places. A much better and more perfect version, of uncertain authorship, exists in the Palatine library which I mentioned a little earlier, and it largely agrees with the Hebrew translation. It was copied by Frederick, a Benedictine monk of Regensburg, in the monastery of St Emmeram, and completed in the year of the Lord 1447 on the day of Goar the confessor.

units.la: Quod ad Hebræum interprete attinet, nō immerito inter philosophos celebradus est, quòd operam sua contulerit ad illustranda astronomia, & ad repurgandam Latinam Alfragani versionem, quam Ioanni Hispalensi acceptá referunt. Fuit Arabicæ & Latinæ linguæ peritissimus, & rerum astronomicarū scientissimus: nam ex codice Arabico Alfragani, se versionem vulgatá correxisse testatur cap.10 hisce verbis: in libro Arabico autor plura dicit de his locis ratione umbræ, sicut de aliis climatibus: sed in libro Romanorum (ita vulgatam Latinam IoanisHispalensis versionem vocat) non sunt translata: ideo hic nō adscribemus.
units.tr: As for the Hebrew translator, he is rightly celebrated among philosophers, because he contributed his labour to illuminating astronomy and to purging the Latin version of Alfraganus, which they trace to John of Seville. He was most skilled in the Arabic and Latin languages and very learned in astronomical matters. For from the Arabic manuscript of Alfraganus he attests that he corrected the common version in chapter 10 in these words: "In the Arabic book the author says many things about these places with regard to the shadow, as also about the other climates; but in the book of the Romans" (so he calls the common Latin version of John of Seville) "they have not been translated, so we shall not add them here."

units.la: Ne autem negligens fuisse videretur, qui ea omisisset, quæ ab Alfragano fuerunt tradita, suo quodam consilio, prius omissa fini operis adiecit. In principio cap. 22 primò sequitur translationem exemplaris Romani: deinde ex codice Arabico suam affert interpretationem: quandoquidem in Latino seu Romano pleraque sint corrupta. Capite 23 iterum collationem instituit cum versione Latina, quam se opera cuiusdam Christiani nactum esse hic in proœmio profitetur: quæ omnia non tantum eruditionis, verum etiam summæ fidei & diligentiæ sunt argumenta.
units.tr: Lest he seem negligent in having omitted what Alfraganus had handed down, he added at his own discretion, at the end of the work, the things previously omitted. At the beginning of chapter 22 he first follows the translation of the Roman copy; then from the Arabic manuscript he offers his own rendering, since most things in the Latin or Roman text are corrupt. In chapter 23 he again makes a comparison with the Latin version, which he professes in this preface to have obtained through the work of a certain Christian. All these things are proofs not only of learning but also of the highest faithfulness and diligence.

units.la: Si igitur quod verum est, dicere volumus, interpreti nostro Hebræo debemus, quòd caput primum elegantissimum ac vtilissimum de caledariis & saeris præcipuarum gentium, ad mentem autoris restitutum cernimus: debemus illi multorum numerorum emendationem: debemus illi locorum & stellarum iuxta vsum sermonis Arabici descriptionem: etsi nonnunquam literas Arabicas non ad veram originem Hebræorum reduxerit, cùm magis spectarit popularem rem pronunciationem,quàm communem essentiam literarum. Ne quis autem existimet, translationem Hebraeam a nobis tantum visam [?] esse: sciendū est praestantissimum virum Augustinum Riicium in libro de motu octauae sphaerae, fateri se eam vidisse in Hispania apud praeceptorem suum Abrahamum Zacuthum Iudaeum astronomiae peritissimum. Quid autem sense-ritRicius non tam de opusculo Alfraganico,quàm de Hebraea ipsius translatione, satis apparet ex his verbis, cùm inquit: Hunc etiam accedit Alfraganus, non modica autoritatis vir, quitin [?] cunctis Ptolemaei semitam sequitur, cuiusque libellus epitoma quoddam in Almagestum videtur, capite quintodecimo, iuxta Hebraeorum translationem atque veriorem, licet apud Latinam versionem sit duodecimum, dicit ad literam, quod Ptolemaeus & reliqui sapientes uniuersas sphaeras numero octonario absoluerunt: eosq; affirmasse ait, octauum orbem omnium esse supremum, licet in Latina versione nulla de Ptole-maeo mentio facta sit: in plurimis enim aliis locis illa translatio deficere videtur: unde nihil est mirum etiam hic si nomen Ptolemaei reliquit, Etsi vero Ricius Hebraeam translationem recte praeferat vulgatae Alfragani versioni: non tamen videtur Alfraganus opusculum suum in 32 sed in 30 capita distinxisse: siquidem Latina bibliothecae Palatinae versio totidem agnoscit.
units.tr: If therefore we wish to say what is true, we owe thanks to our Hebrew translator: because we see the first chapter, most elegant and most useful, on the calendars and eras of the principal nations, restored to the mind of the author. We owe him the correction of many numbers; we owe him the description of places and stars according to the usage of Arabic speech; although sometimes he did not reduce the Arabic letters to their true Hebrew origin, since he looked more to the popular pronunciation than to the common essence of the letters. But lest anyone think that we alone have seen the Hebrew translation, it should be known that the most excellent man Augustinus Ricius, in his book on the motion of the eighth sphere, confesses that he saw it in Spain, at the house of his teacher Abraham Zacuth, a Jew most skilled in astronomy. What Ricius thought, not so much of the little work of Alfraganus as of the Hebrew translation itself, sufficiently appears from these words, where he says: "Alfraganus also joins them, a man of no small authority, who follows the path of Ptolemy in all things, and whose little book seems to be a kind of epitome of the Almagest; in the fifteenth chapter, according to the Hebrew and more accurate translation, though in the Latin version it is the twelfth, he says word for word that Ptolemy and the other wise men completed all the spheres in the number eight, and he states that they affirmed the eighth orb to be the highest of all, although in the Latin version there is no mention of Ptolemy at all. For in very many other places that translation seems to fall short; so it is no wonder if here too it has left out the name of Ptolemy." Although Ricius rightly prefers the Hebrew translation to the common Latin version of Alfraganus, nevertheless Alfraganus does not seem to have divided his little work into 32 chapters but into 30; for the Latin version in the Palatine library acknowledges just as many.

units.la: De annis Arabum, Syrorum ac Latinorum, Persarū & Ægyptiorū: itē de mensibus & diebus eorū: & quomodo inter se differant.
units.tr: On the years of the Arabs, Syrians and Latins, Persians and Egyptians; likewise on their months and days, and how they differ from one another.
CHAPTER I.

units.la: MENSES ARABVM sunt Muharam, Safar, Rabie prior, Rabie posterior, Gumadhi prior, Gumadhi posterior, Regab, Schaban, Ramad-han, Schewal, Dhilkahde, Dhilhaga.
units.tr: The months of the Arabs are Muharram, Safar, Rabi I, Rabi II, Jumada I, Jumada II, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah.

units.la: Sunt autem menses quidam 30, nonnulli 29 die-rum: ut annus simplex consistet 354 diebus.
units.tr: Some of these months have 30 days and others 29, so that a simple year consists of 354 days.

units.la: Sed spacio triginta annorum accrescunt unde-cim dies intercalares: ratione vera anni quantita-tis, quae ponitur 354 dierum, & 1/5 & 1/6 diei: si uni lunationi reipsa competant 793 scrupula horaria.
units.tr: But over a span of thirty years eleven intercalary days accumulate, by the true reckoning of the year's length, which is taken as 354 days and 1/5 and 1/6 of a day, if in fact one lunation amounts to 793 hour-scruples.

units.la: Partes 1/5 & 1/6 conficiunt 8 horas, & 864 scru-pula. ² Annus in quo fractiones colliguntur, habet 7 menses plenos, & 5 cavos.
units.tr: The parts 1/5 and 1/6 make 8 hours and 864 scruples. The year in which the fractions are gathered together has 7 full months and 5 hollow ones.

units.la: ³ Menses secundum Ptolemaeum computantur ab una media solis & lunae coniunctione, usque ad alteram: verus autem menses incipit post digressum luminarium, elapso uno die naturali.
units.tr: According to Ptolemy the months are reckoned from one mean conjunction of sun and moon to the next; the true month, however, begins after the luminaries have separated and one natural day has elapsed.

units.la: Menses cui adhibetur intercalatio, semper est 30 dierum: unde annus intercalaris nuncupatur, qui menses Dhilhaga diem adiicit, ut notum est omnibus.
units.tr: A month to which intercalation is applied is always of 30 days, which is why the year is called intercalary: it adds a day to the month Dhilhaga, as is known to everyone.

units.la: Menses Arabum in phasi lunari variant pro luminis additione vel diminutione: ideo recte constitutum est, ut menses alternatim sint pleni & cavi.
units.tr: The Arab months vary in their lunar phase as the light increases or decreases; therefore it was rightly settled that the months should alternate, full and hollow.

units.la: ⁴ Dies Arabum quibus numerantur menses, sunt septem: primus, secundus, tertius, quartus, quintus, dies congregationis, dies sabbathi.
units.tr: The days of the Arabs by which the months are counted are seven: first, second, third, fourth, fifth, the day of assembly, and the day of the sabbath.

units.la: Initium diei sumitur ab occasu solis: exempli gratia, die sabbathi, & extenditur in occasum diei primi: & sic de aliis diebus.
units.tr: The day begins at sunset: for example, the sabbath day, which extends to the sunset of the first day; and so for the other days.

units.la: Voluerunt autem Arabes a vespera diem auspi-cari: cari: quoniam à phasi lunari incipiunt numerare dies mesium. Sed apud reliquos populos principium diei naturalis sumitur ab ortu solis, & extenditur in ortum sequentis diei.
units.tr: The Arabs wished to begin the day from evening, since they begin counting the days of the month from the lunar phase. But among the other peoples the beginning of the natural day is taken from sunrise, and it extends to the sunrise of the following day.

units.la: 5 MENSES SYRORVM sunt Tisrin prior, constans 31 diebus: Tisrin posterior, constas 30 diebus. Canun prior, 31 dierum: 6 cuius 25 nox, vocatur nox natiuitatis: Canun posterior itide 31 dierum est. Sabat tribus annis 28 dies habet, at quarto quouis anno, qui ipsis intercalaris dicitur, habet 29 dies. Adar 31 dies: Nisan 30: Ijar 31 dies: Haziran 30 dies: Tamuz 31 dies: Ab 31: Elul 30 habet dies.
units.tr: THE MONTHS OF THE SYRIANS are: Tisrin prior, of 31 days; Tisrin posterior, of 30 days. Canun prior, of 31 days, on the 25th of which falls the night of the Nativity; Canun posterior likewise has 31 days. Sabat has 28 days in three years, but in every fourth year, which they call intercalary, it has 29 days. Adar 31 days; Nisan 30; Ijar 31 days; Haziran 30 days; Tamuz 31 days; Ab 31; Elul has 30 days.

units.la: Annus communis apud eos est 365 dierum: sed quarto quouis anno intercalatur unus dies: est enim vera anni quantitas 365 dierum, & ¼ diei.
units.tr: The common year among them is 365 days, but one day is intercalated every fourth year, for the true length of the year is 365 days and a quarter of a day.

units.la: MENSES ROMANORVM numero dierum conueniunt cum mensibus Syrorum: nisi quod principium sumant à Ianuario: quem sequitur Februarius constans 28 diebus: quarto vero quouis anno habet 29 dies. Deinceps sequuntur Martius, Aprilis, Maius, Iunius, Iulius, Augustus, September, October, November, December.
units.tr: THE MONTHS OF THE ROMANS agree in the number of days with the months of the Syrians, except that they begin with January. January is followed by February, which has 28 days, but in every fourth year it has 29. Then follow March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, and December.

units.la: Itaque Ianuarius eorum, à quo annum auspicantur, respondet Canun posteriori Syrorum: quo observato in sequentibus mensibus facile quoque erit instituere collationem.
units.tr: Thus January, with which they begin the year, corresponds to the later Canun of the Syrians; by keeping this in mind it will also be easy to draw a comparison for the following months.

units.la: MENSES PERSARVM sunt Afrurdin-meh[?], cuius prima dies est caput anni ipsorum, quod appellant neomeniam. Ardihafchtmeh, Cardimeh, Thirmeh, Merdedmeh, Schaharirmeh, {7}Me-harmeh, in cuius 16 diem incidit Almedgen. Abenmeh, cuius 25 dies initium est 10 dierum, quos vocant Alfrurgen: quorum postremi quinque Abenmeh adiiciuntur infiar appendicis, vt non perti-neant ad numerum mensium. Adarmeh, cuius prima dies est Refeb altofeg. Dimeh, Behenmeh, & Af-firmeh.
units.tr: THE MONTHS OF THE PERSIANS are Afrurdin-meh[?], whose first day is the head of their year, which they call the neomenia; Ardihafchtmeh, Cardimeh, Thirmeh, Merdedmeh, Schaharirmeh, Meharmeh, in whose 16th day falls Almedgen; Abenmeh, whose 25th day begins a period of 10 days which they call Alfrurgen, the last five of which are added after Abenmeh as an appendix, so that they do not belong to the number of months; Adarmeh, whose first day is Refeb altofeg; Dimeh, Behenmeh, and Affirmeh.

units.la: Habent autem singuli menses 30 dies: quibus si post Abenmeh extra ordinem adiiciantur dies quinque appendices, de quibus modo diximus, conflantur totius anni Persici 365 dies. {8}Atque hæc sunt nomina, quibus nominant Persæ dies mensium.
units.tr: Each month has 30 days. If the five appended days, of which we have just spoken, are added after Abenmeh outside the regular order, the whole Persian year makes 365 days. These are the names by which the Persians designate the days of the months.
THE NAMES OF THE EGYPTIAN MONTHS

units.la: nomina hæc sunt, Thoth, qui primus est, Paophi, Athyr, Chiac, Tybi, Mechir, Phamenoth, Pharmuthi, Pachon, Payni, Epiphi, & Mesori: cui adiiciuntur quinque dies, quas appendices appellant.
units.tr: The names are these: Thoth, which is first, Paophi, Athyr, Chiac, Tybi, Mechir, Phamenoth, Pharmuthi, Pachon, Payni, Epiphi, and Mesori. To these are added five days, which they call appendices.

units.la: Habet quilibet mensis 30 dies: & annus habet 365 dies: quot etiam sunt in anno Persico.
units.tr: Each month has 30 days, and the year has 365 days, as also in the Persian year.

units.la: Menses Ægyptiorum respondent mensibus Persarum: verbi gratia, Thoth convenit cum Dimeh, & omnibus eius diebus: & postremus dies Ægyptiorum congruit cum postremo die Adarmeh, vt videre licet in tabulis.
units.tr: The months of the Egyptians correspond to the months of the Persians: for example, Thoth agrees with Dimeh and all its days; and the last day of the Egyptians coincides with the last day of Adarmeh, as may be seen in the tables.

units.la: DIFFERUNT autem menses Coptitarum quos modo vsurpant viri Ægyptii: quatenus ad anni quantitatem ¼ diei adiiciunt. Itaque iuxta rationem Syrorum & Romanorum discrepant mensës eorum a mensibus Persarum: qui tamen collecti tot dies anni producunt, quot etiam habent Romani.
units.tr: THE MONTHS of the Copts, which the Egyptians now use, differ, since they add a quarter of a day to the length of the year. Thus, according to the reckoning of the Syrians and Romans, their months differ from the months of the Persians; yet when these are collected together they produce as many days in the year as the Romans have.

units.la: DIES primus anni Coptitarum incepit a primo die Thoth, qui incidit in 29 Ab.
units.tr: The first day of the Coptic year began on the first day of Thoth, which falls on the 29th of Ab.

units.la: CHARACTER annorū Persicorum 9 a regno Iezdajeris filii Scharedfilii Cosre, est dies tertius.
units.tr: THE EPOCH of the Persian years, from the reign of Iezdajer, son of Schared, son of Cosroes, falls on the third day.

units.la: Character annorum Arabicorum a tempore quo fugit Muhamed ex Mecha, in ciuitatem quæ appellatur Ietrib, est dies quintus.
units.tr: The epoch of the Arab years, from the time when Muhamed fled from Mecca to the city called Jetrib, falls on the fifth day.

units.la: Character annorum Romanorum & Syrorum ab Alexandro 10, est dies secundus.
units.tr: The epoch of the years of the Romans and Syrians, from Alexander, falls on the second day.

units.la: Character annorum Aegyptiorum in libro Almagesti, a regno Nebukadnezaris Babylonii, est dies quartus.
units.tr: The epoch of the years of the Egyptians in the Almagest, from the reign of Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, falls on the fourth day.

units.la: Character annorum Philippi patris Alexandri, iuxta Ptolemæum in libro Canonis, est dies primus.
units.tr: The epoch of the years of Philip, the father of Alexander, according to Ptolemy in the Canon, falls on the first day.

units.la: INTERVALLVM inter Nebukadnezarem & Iezdajerem, est annorum Persicorum 1379. mensium 3.
units.tr: THE INTERVAL between Nebuchadnezzar and Iezdajer is 1379 Persian years and 3 months.

units.la: 11 Interuallum inter Philippum & Iezdajerem est annorum Persicorum 955. mensium 3.
units.tr: The interval between Philip and Iezdajer is 955 Persian years and 3 months.

units.la: Interuallum inter Alexādrum & Iezdajerem est annorum Romanorum 942, dierum 259. Interuallum inter Arabes & Iezdajerem est dierum 3624. 12
units.tr: The interval between Alexander and Iezdajer is 942 Roman years and 259 days. The interval between the Arabs and Iezdajer is 3624 days.

units.la: 13 Hactenus autor absoluit caput de annis, in quo omnium ærarum notas enumerauit. Deprehéditur autem error circa creationem mundi: aliter enim religio & Kabala nostra, quàm Kabala Romanorum docet: sed non libet nunc de eo disputare.
units.tr: Here the author finishes the chapter on years, in which he has listed the epochs of all eras. An error, however, is detected concerning the creation of the world, for our religion and Kabbalah teach differently from the Roman Kabbalah; but I do not wish to dispute that point now.

units.la: 1 Dhilhaga vulgò Zilhitsche appellatur. Est autem postremus mensis: quod cúm aliqui non observant, facile in anni vnius errorem incidunt. 2 Hanc appellationem mensium plenorum & cauorum Arabes acceperunt ab Hebræis:qui appellant menses plenos constantes 30 diebus: & cauos,habentes solummodò 29 dies. Describit Alfraganus hisce verbis annum intercalarem: in quo fractiones siue excessus colligūtur, vt integra dies anno inseratur, habeatque tunc septem menses plenos, & quinque cauos, hoc est,dies 355. Nam in anno communi & simplicitantum sex menses sunt pleni: videlicet Muharam, Rabie prior, Gumadhi prior,Regab, Ramadhan, Dhilkahde: sex reliqui sunt caui,videlicet Safar,Rabie posterior,Gumadhi posterior,Schaban,SchewWal[?],Dhilhaga.In anno vero intercalari adiicitur dies è fractionibus collectus, ad finem mensis Dhilhaga: ita Dhilhaga qui sua natura erat cauus, sit plenus propter intercalationem. 3 Diuidit Alfraganus menses in astronomicos & ciuiles: astronomici incipiunt à media solis & lunæ coniunctione: ciuiles autem vt minimum absoluto die vno naturali, seu elapso spacio 24 horarū post coniunctionem demum incipiūt, quando ludo luna e radiis solaribus emergit, nobisque primam phasin luminis sui ostendit. Quamobrem notandum est, fere semper in diem secudum a coniunctione incidere neomenias Arabicas: cum quibus plerunque conueniunt neomeniae Hebræorum, vel uno tantum die discrepant. 4 Ut Hebræis dies solis est prima septimanæ: ita Arabibus quoque: ita & nobis Christianis. Dies lunæ est secunda, Martis tertia, Mercurii quarta, Iouis quinta, Veneris sexta, Saturni septima & ultima est dies hebdomadis, quam Hebræi & Arabes vocant sabbatum. Diem Veneris Arabes appellant diem congregationis, quod ea die in templis suis ad sacra peragenda congregari soleant. Faciunt autem Arabes cum Hebræis initium diei naturalis a vespera, vel ab occasu solis: quoniam annos & menses suos ciuiles dirigunt ad phases lunares: sed nonnulli populi, ut sunt Syri, Ægyptii & Persæ, diem auspicantur ab ortu solis: sicut astronomi commoditatis gratia diem ordiuntur a sole meridiano. Romani orsi sunt diem a media nocte, teste Censorino. § Ab hoc loco usque ad finem capitis in omnibus vulgatis editionibus, hæc desiderantur: quæ tantum apud Hebræum nostrum interpretem, & in versione manuscripta Latina bibliothecæ Palatinæ extant: ut mirum sit quare Ioannes Hispalensis ea prætermiserit, cum ad chronologiam prorsus sint necessariæ: & meræ sunt fabulæ, dum Hispalensis Alfragano impingit, quasi is voluerit hæc alibi pertractare. Quod enim hæc hoc loco ab Alfragano sint conscriptæ, non tantum versio Hebræa, & Latina manuscripta in bibliotheca Palatina testatur; verum etiam ostendit Author summæ Anglicæ de astronomia & astrologia, qui vixit circa annum Domini 1264, cuiusque liber manuscriptus ex tat in eadem bibliotheca Palatina. Is capite primo de annis,mensibus & diebus Arabum ita scribit : A Domino Jesu Christo saluatore ac creatore nostro Latini suorum annorum principium ducunt: Graci ab Alexandro: Persæ ex principio anni in quo regnauit Iezdagird, & secundum Alfraganum æra Ægyptiorum in libro Almagesti est a principio anni in quo regnauit Nabuchodonosor in Canone vero Ptolemæi fuit æra a principio anni Philippi: Arabes vt dicit Alfraganus primo capitulo libri sui, a primo anno in quo iuit Mahumetus de Mecha ad ciuitatem qua vocatur Jetrib, & fuit principium eius dies quinta. Hæc ille. 6 Alfraganus ex Syris Christianis didicit, Christum natum esse nocte præ-cedente diem 25 Decembris : sed hæc annotatio in codice Hebræo male adiicitur ad Canun posteriorem, cum in Latina bibliothecæ Palatinæ versione recte apponatur ad Canun priorem. 7 In codice Hebræo per negligentiam scribæ, omissus est Mehar-meh, quem ex Albategnio, & Latina bibliothecæ Pal. versione revocaui. 8 Apparet hic aliquè hiatu esse, quem tamen dissimulauit interpres Hebræus. Latinus bibliothecæ Pal. interpres ingenuè fatetur, hic ab Alfragano inserta fuisse nomina singulorum dierum mensis: se autem transferre nō potuisse, nec vidisse in illis vti-litatem, ideoq; præter misisse. Qui autè volet cognoscere, quomodo tricenos dies in vnoquoq; mense appellent Persæ, consulat Iosephum Scaligeru de emendatione temporum. 9 Alfraganus cum vulgo Arabum putat æram Persicam cœpisse à regno Iezdajeris: nos autem eam à morte Iezdajeris initiū sumere, probabimus in commentario. 10 In versione Latina bibl. Pal. hic additur, Et ipse est, quem Arabes appellant habentem duo cornua: quod probè est notandum: nam per æram Alexandri bicornis seu Dhilkarnain Arabes intelligunt principium regni Seleuci Nicanoris, quod incidit elapsis annis Ægyptiis duodecim à morte Alexandri: vt ostendemus in commentario.
units.tr: Dhilhaga is commonly called Zilhitsche. It is the last month, and since some do not observe this, they easily fall into an error of a whole year. The Arabs took this designation of full and hollow months from the Hebrews, who call full those months of 30 days and hollow those having only 29 days. Alfraganus describes the intercalary year in these words: in which the fractions or excesses are gathered together so that a whole day is inserted into the year, and it then has seven full months and five hollow ones, that is, 355 days. For in a common or simple year only six months are full: namely Muharam, Rabie prior, Gumadhi prior, Regab, Ramadhan, and Dhilkahde; the six remaining are hollow: namely Safar, Rabie posterior, Gumadhi posterior, Schaban, Schewal, and Dhilhaga. In the intercalary year a day collected from the fractions is added at the end of the month Dhilhaga, so that Dhilhaga, which by its nature was hollow, becomes full because of the intercalation. Alfraganus divides the months into astronomical and civil. Astronomical months begin at the mean conjunction of sun and moon; civil months begin only when at least one full natural day, or 24 hours, has elapsed after the conjunction, when the moon emerges from the solar rays and shows us the first phase of its light. Therefore it should be noted that the Arab new moons almost always fall on the second day after the conjunction, and the new moons of the Hebrews generally agree with them, differing by only one day. As for the Hebrews the day of the sun is the first of the week, so it is for the Arabs, and so for us Christians. The day of the moon is the second, Mars the third, Mercury the fourth, Jupiter the fifth, Venus the sixth, Saturn the seventh, and the last day of the week, which the Hebrews and Arabs call the sabbath. The Arabs call Friday the day of assembly, because on that day they are accustomed to gather in their temples to perform sacred rites. The Arabs, like the Hebrews, begin the natural day in the evening or at sunset, since they direct their civil years and months to the lunar phases; but some peoples, such as the Syrians, Egyptians and Persians, begin the day at sunrise, just as astronomers, for convenience, begin the day at the sun's meridian. The Romans began the day at midnight, according to Censorinus. From this point to the end of the chapter, the following passage is missing from all the printed editions; it is found only in our Hebrew interpreter and in the Latin manuscript version in the Palatine library. It is strange that John of Seville omitted it, since it is entirely necessary for chronology, and it is pure fable when Hispalensis accuses Alfraganus, as if he had wished to treat these matters elsewhere. That these things were written here by Alfraganus is attested not only by the Hebrew version and the Latin manuscript in the Palatine library, but also by the author of the great English work on astronomy and astrology, who lived about the year of the Lord 1264, and whose manuscript book is likewise in the Palatine library. In the first chapter, on the years, months and days of the Arabs, he writes thus: From our Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour and Creator, the Latins begin the reckoning of their years; the Greeks from Alexander; the Persians from the beginning of the year in which Iezdagird reigned; and according to Alfraganus the era of the Egyptians in the Almagest runs from the beginning of the year in which Nabuchodonosor reigned, but in the Canon of Ptolemy the era ran from the beginning of the year of Philip; the Arabs, as Alfraganus says in the first chapter of his book, from the first year in which Mahumetus went from Mecca to the city called Jetrib, and its first day was the fifth. So he. Alfraganus learned from the Syrian Christians that Christ was born on the night preceding the 25th of December; but this note is wrongly added in the Hebrew codex to the later Canun, whereas in the Latin version of the Palatine library it is rightly placed at the earlier Canun. In the Hebrew codex, through the negligence of the scribe, Meharmeh has been omitted; I have restored it from Albategnius and the Latin version of the Palatine library. Here there seems to be some gap, which the Hebrew interpreter nevertheless conceals. The Latin interpreter of the Palatine library frankly admits that Alfraganus had inserted here the names of the individual days of the month, but that he himself could not translate them nor saw any usefulness in them, and therefore omitted them. Whoever wishes to know how the Persians name the thirty days in each month should consult Joseph Scaliger on the emendation of times. Alfraganus, with the common opinion of the Arabs, thinks the Persian era began with the reign of Iezdajer; but we shall prove in the commentary that it takes its beginning from the death of Iezdajer. In the Latin version of the Palatine library the following is added here: And he is the one whom the Arabs call the two-horned; this is to be carefully noted, for by the era of Alexander the two-horned, or Dhilkarnain, the Arabs understand the beginning of the reign of Seleucus Nicanor, which fell twelve Egyptian years after the death of Alexander, as we shall show in the commentary.

units.la: 11 In codice Hebraeo numeri huius & sequentis interualli sunt corrupti, sed in Latina bibliothecæ Palatinæ versione recte habent.
units.tr: 11 In the Hebrew codex the numbers of this and the following interval are corrupt, but in the Latin version of the Palatine library they are correct.

units.la: 12 In versione Latina bibl.Pal. caput hoc ita concluditur, Prima ergo harum ærarum est æra Nabuchodonosor, deinde æra Philippi: postea æra Alexandri, deinde æra Arabum: postea æra Iezdagird, &c. quæ ideo obseruanda sunt, quòd ostendant Alfraganum chronologiam suam à Nabo-nafaro [?] siue Nabuchodonosore vsque ad æram Persicam supputasse: & hinc nobis eam esse extendendam vsq; ad nostra tempora. Autor summæ Anglicæ de astronomia & astrologia etiâ hanc appendicem cū interuallis ærarum adscribit Alfragano: cum ait, quod est inter æram Nabuchodonosoris & æram Iezdagird sunt anni 1379 Persici, & 3 menses. & id quod est inter æram Philippi & Iezdagird sunt anni Persici 955. & tres menses. & id quod est inter æram Alexandri & Iezdagird sunt anni Romani 942. & 259 dies. & id quod est inter æram Arabum & Iezdagird sunt dies 3614. Prima igitur ærarum est Nabuchodonosoris: deinde æra Philippi: postea Alexandri: postea Arabum: deinde æra Iezdagird. Hæc ille. Sane probabile est, Alfraga-num post declarata ærarum interualla, subiunxisse ordinem quinque vsitatissimarum ærarum: etiamsi ab interprete Hebræo hæc appendix sit prætermissa.
units.tr: 12 In the Latin version of the Palatine library this chapter is concluded thus: The first of these eras is the era of Nebuchadnezzar, then the era of Philip; afterwards the era of Alexander, then the era of the Arabs; after that the era of Yazdegerd, etc. These points are to be noted, because they show that Alfraganus reckoned his chronology from Nabonassar [?], or Nebuchadnezzar, down to the Persian era, and hence that we must extend it to our own times. The author of the English Summa on astronomy and astrology also attaches this appendix, with the intervals between the eras, to Alfraganus, when he says: The interval between the era of Nebuchadnezzar and the era of Yazdegerd is 1379 Persian years and 3 months; and the interval between the era of Philip and Yazdegerd is 955 Persian years and three months; and the interval between the era of Alexander and Yazdegerd is 942 Roman years and 259 days; and the interval between the era of the Arabs and Yazdegerd is 3614 days. The first of the eras, therefore, is that of Nebuchadnezzar; then the era of Philip; afterwards that of Alexander; afterwards that of the Arabs; then the era of Yazdegerd. So he. It is certainly probable that Alfraganus, after declaring the intervals between the eras, added the order of the five most commonly used eras, even though the Hebrew translator has omitted this appendix.

units.la: 13 Hæc adiecta sunt ab interprete Hebræo: quibus indicat Iudæos & Romanos à mundi condito annos deducere: sed eos plurimum inter se discrepare, vt sit dictu difficile, quæ sententia veritati magis sit consentanea[?]. De hoc aliquid dicemus in commentario, quo caput istud chronologicum plene declarare instituimus.
units.tr: 13 These additions were made by the Hebrew translator, by which he indicates that the Jews and the Romans count years from the creation of the world, but that they differ greatly from one another, so that it is difficult to say which opinion is more consistent with the truth. We shall say something about this in the commentary, in which we intend to explain this chronological chapter fully.

units.la: Quod cœlum fit sphæricum & cum omnibus stellis circulariter moueatur.
units.tr: That the heaven is spherical and moves circularly together with all the stars.
CAP. II.

units.la: NUlla est differentia inter sapientes, quod cœlum sit sphæricum & in orbem feratur cum stellis suis, super duobus polis immobilibus, quorum unus in septentrione, alter in meridie existit. Huius rei demonstratio haec est: quia stellae emergunt ab oriente & ascendunt paulatim, ordine uno motus seruato, & manente quantitate corporum, distantiaque ad se invicem eadem: donec attingant culmen cœli, unde iterum descendunt versus occasum. Ex quo apparet eas suo orbi affixas esse, & cum illo æquabiliter rotari.
units.tr: There is no disagreement among the wise that the heaven is spherical and turns with its stars in a circle, about two immovable poles, one of which lies in the north and the other in the south. The demonstration of this is as follows: the stars rise in the east and gradually climb, keeping one fixed order of motion, with the size of the bodies unchanged and their distances from one another the same, until they reach the top of the heaven, from which they then descend towards the west. From this it appears that they are fixed to their sphere and revolve evenly with it.

units.la: Demonstratio altera æque certa est, quod cœlum sit sphæricum: cum videamus stellas quasdam in climatibus septentrionalibus, perpetuo supra terram orbiculariter ferri, ut est Alcheti, quem Romani appellant Herculem, ut sunt Alfarkatan, hoc est, duae stellae lucidiores in ursa mi-nore: ut sunt Beneth As, filia plaustri, hoc est, stellae ursae maioris, & quaecunque hisce propinquae fuerint: quas omnes obseruamus in orbibus parallelis circa idem punctum moueri, ut quo puncto quaeque fuerit vicinior, voluatur in circulo minore, cuius motus tardior apparet: quae autem magis distiterit ab hoc puncto, circumducatur in circulo maiore, cuius motus apparet velocior, pro ratione quantitatis circulorum & distantiae eorum a praedicto puncto, donec perveniatur ad stellas, quae infra terram abscônduntur. Inter has quae vicinior est puncto, supra terram minus moratur: quae vero magis distat, diutius supra terram conspicitur. Unde apparet, omnes stellas aequaliter a se invicem seiunctas circa eadem sphaeram volui. [Sed exemplum proponam tibi satis obvium de bobus triturantibus: figitur in area palus, qui est instar centri: ad quem alligantur boues circa palum oberrantes: horum qui a puncto centri remotior fuerit, velociorem gressum habere cernitur: qui vero propinquior fuerit centro, eius cursus tardior conspicitur: uterque tamen ad eum locum unde digressus fuerat, eodem tepore redit.] Atqui punctum illud, circa quod sphaeram volui videmus, necessario est alteruter polorum: quare ratio evidens est, quod caelum instar sphaerae moveatur. Si enim caelum esset planum, ut opinantur nonnulli, non omnes eius partes eandem inter se servarent distantiam: pars enim vertici nostro incumbens propior esset reliquis omnibus partibus caeli: & quae versus horizontem inclinaret, remotior foret. Ita sol, luna, & reliquae stellae in ortu minores, quam in medio caelo apparerent: hinc descendendo semper minores viderentur, donec circa occasum e conspectu nostro prorsus eriperentur. Sed horum nihil observamus: quin immo quantitate eadem appa-rent in ortu, culmine & occasu: nonnumquam eas in ortu & occasu maiores conspicimus, quam sint in medio cœli. Ita sol circa occasum horizontem attingens, partem priorem corporis sui primo, posteriorem autem postremo abscondit: quod et-iam facit luna. Quod autem tunc luminaria hæc maiora appareant, non ideo fit quasi propinquiora sint nobis, sed quia vapor e terra elevari solitus interponitur inter aspectum nostrum & horizontem: qui ea nobis maiora exhibet, præsertim tempore hyberno, cum aer est humidior, aut alias cum pluviæ sunt frequentes. Simile accidit rei alicui in aquam proiectæ, quæ propter profunditatem suam maior apparet. Eadem causa as-signanda est in reliquis stellis, si in horizonte ma-iores videantur.
units.tr: A second demonstration, equally certain, shows that the heaven is spherical. We see certain stars in the northern climes carried round in circles above the earth without ever setting. Such are Alcheti, which the Romans call Hercules, and Alfarkatan, that is, the two brighter stars in the Little Bear; and Beneth As, the daughter of the wagon, that is, the stars of the Great Bear, and any others near them. We observe that all of these move in parallel circles about the same point, so that the nearer a star is to that point, the smaller the circle it turns in, and its motion appears slower; the farther a star is from that point, the larger the circle it is carried around, and its motion appears faster, in proportion to the size of the circles and their distance from the said point. This continues until we come to the stars that are hidden below the earth. Among these, the one nearer the point stays less time above the earth, while the one farther away is seen above the earth for longer. Hence it appears that all the stars, separated equally from one another, roll about the same sphere. [Let me offer you an example, quite familiar, of oxen treading out grain: a stake is fixed in the threshing floor, serving as a centre, and oxen are tied to it and wander around the stake. Of these, the one farther from the centre is seen to have the faster pace, while the one nearer the centre is seen to move more slowly; yet each returns to the place from which it set out in the same time.] Now that point about which we see the sphere turn must necessarily be one of the poles; hence the evident reason is that the heaven moves like a sphere. For if the heaven were flat, as some suppose, not all its parts would keep the same distance from one another: the part lying over our zenith would be nearer than all the other parts of the heaven, and the part inclining towards the horizon would be farther away. Thus the sun, moon and other stars would appear smaller at their rising than in mid-heaven, and by descending they would always seem smaller, until near their setting they were wholly snatched from our sight. But we observe nothing of this; indeed they appear of the same size at rising, at culmination and at setting. Sometimes we see them larger at rising and setting than they are in mid-heaven. Thus the sun, touching the horizon near its setting, hides first its front part and last of all its hinder part; the moon does the same. That these luminaries then appear larger is not because they are nearer to us, but because a vapour usually rising from the earth lies between our sight and the horizon, and this makes them appear larger to us, especially in winter when the air is more humid, or at other times when rains are frequent. Something similar happens to an object thrown into water, which appears larger because of the depth of the water. The same cause must be assigned for the other stars if they appear larger on the horizon.

units.la: 1 Exemplum hoc, quod adducit interpres He-bræus, non extat in vulgatis editionibus, neque ha-betur in Latina bibliothecæ Palatinæ versione: un-de manifestum est, illud non fuisse ab Alfragano al-latum.
units.tr: 1 This example, which the Hebrew translator adduces, is not found in the printed editions, nor is it contained in the Latin version in the Palatine library; from which it is clear that it was not brought forward by Alfraganus.

units.la: Quod terra cum aqua globum con-stituat.
units.tr: That the earth together with water forms a globe.
CHAP. III.

units.la: Ratio hæc est, quod videamus solem ac lunam, reliquasq; stellas non oriri aut occidere simul
units.tr: The reason is this: we see that the sun, the moon and the other stars do not rise or set at the same time,

units.la: observamus: quin immo quantitate eadem apparent in ortu, culmine & occasu: nonnumquam eas in ortu & occasu maiores conspicimus, quam sint in medio cœli. eodémve tempore : in locis enim orientalibus citius quàm in occidentalibus conspiciuntur. Idmanifeste eclipsis alicuius obseruatio comprobat : si enim duo loca dimidio quadrante distita proponantur, quorum vnum in oriente, alterum verò in occidente habitari contingat : sane si tertia hora vrbi orientali eclipsis appareat, eadem in vrbe occidentali hora nona demum conspicietur. Eadem est aliorum locorum inter ortum & occasum distantium proportio : quanta enim differentia longitudinis reperitur, tanta quoque est sideris alicuius emergentis in tempore discrepantia. Si autem loca inter septentrionem & meridiem distita consideremus : versus polum arcticum stellæ quaedam nobis apparent, & versus antarcticum nonnullæ perpetuo occultantur : quin etiam polus arcticus modo elevatur, modo deprimitur, prout ad eum accedimus, vel ab eo recedimus. Horum omnium accidentium causa nulla alia, præter rotundum aquæ & terræ tumorem excogitari potest : hic enim efficit, vt quod prius apparebat, deinde occultetur ; & quod prius occultabatur, postea in conspectum proferatur : sicut eâdem ratione diei lux noctis tenebris succedit.
units.tr: as we observe. Indeed they appear of the same size at rising, at culmination and at setting, and sometimes we see them larger at rising and setting than when they stand in the middle of the sky. And they are seen at the same time: for they are seen sooner in eastern places than in western ones. The observation of an eclipse clearly confirms this. If two places a quarter of a circle apart are taken, one lying in the east and the other in the west, then if an eclipse appears in the eastern city at the third hour, it will be seen in the western city only at the ninth hour. The same proportion holds for other places separated between rising and setting: as great as the difference of longitude is, so great also is the discrepancy in the time at which a star emerges. If, however, we consider places distant between north and south, some stars appear to us toward the northern pole, while some toward the southern pole are always hidden. Indeed the northern pole is now raised, now lowered, according as we approach it or withdraw from it. No cause for all these phenomena can be devised other than the round swelling of water and earth. For this brings it about that what appeared before is then hidden, and what was hidden before is afterwards brought into view, just as by the same reasoning the light of day follows the darkness of night.

units.la: At si terra esset triangula, quadrangula aut plana : tunc sidera eodem tempore omnibus orirentur, ipsumq; solem orientem aspiceret, quisquis in eodem terræ tractu habitaret : & lumen cum tenebris efficeret figuram triangulam, quadrangulam aut planam. Sed nos videmus tenebras incipere ab ortu, sifolpost occasum stellarum in crepusculo verse-tur: & contra oriente sole in aurora lucem magnam esse, vt tenebrae in occasu oboriatur. Praterea vmbra meridiana, quae breuissima est, magnum nobis argumentum praebet, terram non esse planam: si enim ita esset, nonnunquam in meridie vmbra esset longissima, & horis aliquot ante vel post breuissima: ita nulla sciotericorum ratio constitui posset.]
units.tr: But if the earth were triangular, quadrangular or flat, then the stars would rise at the same time for everyone living in the same tract of the earth, and everyone would see the sun rise at the same moment, and light together with darkness would make a triangular, quadrangular or flat figure. But we see that darkness begins in the east, if it turns to twilight after the stars have set in the west, and conversely, when the sun rises in the dawn, there is great light, so that darkness arises in the west. Moreover, the midday shadow, which is very short, gives us a strong argument that the earth is not flat: for if it were, the shadow at noon would sometimes be very long, and a few hours before or after very short. Thus no science of sundials could be established.]

units.la: 1 Haec quae subsequuntur, apud interpretem Hebraeum tantum extant, neque reperiuntur in prioribus editionibus: ideo paréthesi inclusi, quae deinceps quoque huius rei erit indicium.
units.tr: 1 These things that follow are found only in the Hebrew translator and do not occur in the earlier editions; therefore I have enclosed them in a parenthesis [παρένθεσις], which will also serve as a sign of this matter from now on.

units.la: Quod terra sit centrum vniuersi & sese instar puncti habeat respectu coeli.
units.tr: That the earth is the centre of the universe and, in relation to the heaven, has the nature of a point.
CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Quod terra sit centrum vniuersi probatur obseruatione stellarum, cum in omnibus partibus coeli eadem quantitate appareant: quod si ita est, necessario sequitur, sphaeram aetherea circa terram quasi circa centrum rotari. Si enim centrum terrae diuersum esset a centro vniuersae sphaerae, nunquam dies aequaretur nocti. Postquam itaque terra est in medio coeli, duo hemisphaeria aequalia fiunt, quorum vnum supra, alterum infra terram constituitur: apparet autem perpetuo dimidium caelum, vt sex signa signa supra, & sex signa infra horizontem deprehendatur: ex quo manifeste apparet inter centrum terrae & vniuersi non esse sensibilem differentiam. Si terra non esset in medio coeli, sed in locum vnum magis quam in alterum inclinaret; tunc contingeret vt aliqui pauciora, nonnulli vero plura sex signis possent videre, cuius tamen nullam habemus experientiam: perpetuo enim sex signa apparet. Item si terra declinaret a centro vniuersi; quicunque videret stellas in ortu, maiores cerneret, quam essent in occasu, & qui in partibus occidentalibus easdem conspiceret, putaret se maiores videre, quam essent apud orientales. [Neque terra mouetur: si enim perpetuo descendendo moueretur; tunc res leuis vt stipula aut palea nunquam eam assequeretur, ipsa enim vt pote res grauis citius descenderet: si autem in latera volutaretur, sagitta directo a capite in coelum eiecta, non rediret in eundem locum: nec auis e nido suo egressa, ad eundem redire posset, quoniam terra velocius moueretur. Si aute terra perpetuo ascendendo moueretur, non haberet naturam elementarem, ex frigido, sicco, calido & humido constantem: sed hoc aduersatur placitis antiquorum philosophorum.] Itaque clare ostenditur, terram in medio coelo fixam esse, neque moueri dextrorsum vel sinistrorsum, coelum autem circa eam rotari. Quandoquidem vero minima stella in coelo terrae magnitudinem superat, vt in sequentibus demonstrabimus, & instar puncti est, si cum cœla conferatur: quanto magis corpus terra, quod minus est minima stella, si cum magnitudine cœli conferatur, nullius quantitatis esse æstimabitur? Quare concludimus, terram instar puncti in medio cœli constitutam esse, vt eam aer circumdet, huc autem cœlum sphærice amplectatur: & quantitatem terræ asserimus respectu cœli esse instar pucti in circulo. [At si terra præter ascensionis & descensionis motum, vel ad latera digressionem, diceretur collocata supra cœlos: tunc quicquid e cœlis in terram decideret, necessario ad circumferentiam illius denoluerétur, & qui iter in terra faceret, videretur ex centro versus circumferentiam progredi: quoniam tota terra cœlo obuersa est secundum vnum eundémque longitudinis gradum: atqui ambitus circuli exterioris eandem perpetuo obseruat distantiam, neque centrum illius extra medium esse potest: quare minimè dicendum est, terram supra cœlos positam, aut cœlos supra terram sitos esse: sed cœlum est supra eum qui in terra habitat, & terra est infra eum. Etsi autem hic sit respectus inferioris & superioris loci: tamen ipsa terra est instar puncti, ex quo secundum lineas rectas & æquales stellas aspicimus. Itaque manifestum est, differentiam longitudinis locorum in terra, nullius esse momenti, si ad extimam cœli circumferentiam conferatur: nam qui ambulat in terra, & ex ea ex ea prospectat, in centro ambulare, & ex eodem prospectare putatur.]
units.tr: That the earth is the centre of the universe is proved by observation of the stars, since they appear of the same size in every part of the heavens. If this is so, it necessarily follows that the aethereal sphere revolves around the earth as around its centre. For if the centre of the earth were different from the centre of the whole sphere, day would never be equal to night.
