Since, therefore, the earth is in the middle of the heaven, two equal hemispheres are formed, one above the earth and the other below it; and always half the sky appears, so that six signs signs are seen above and six signs below the horizon. From this it is clear that between the centre of the earth and the centre of the universe there is no perceptible difference. If the earth were not in the middle of the heaven, but leaned toward one place rather than another, then some people would see fewer than six signs and others more; yet we have no experience of this, for always six signs appear. Likewise, if the earth departed from the centre of the universe, whoever saw the stars at their rising would see them larger than when they set, and whoever saw the same stars from the western regions would think he saw them larger than those who are in the east do. [Nor does the earth move: for if it were moving continually downward, then a light thing such as straw or chaff would never reach it, since the earth, being heavy, would fall faster; and if it rolled sideways, an arrow shot straight up from the head into the sky would not return to the same place, nor could a bird flying out of its nest return to it, since the earth would be moving too quickly. If the earth were moving continually upward, it would not have the elemental nature, made up of cold, dry, hot and moist; but this is contrary to the opinions of the ancient philosophers.] Thus it is clearly shown that the earth is fixed in the middle of the heaven, and moves neither to right nor to left, while the heaven revolves around it. Since, indeed, the smallest star in the heaven exceeds the magnitude of the earth, as we shall demonstrate in what follows, and is like a point when compared with the heavens, how much more will the body of the earth, which is smaller than the smallest star, be judged of no quantity when compared with the magnitude of the heaven? Therefore we conclude that the earth, placed in the middle of the heaven, is like a point, surrounded by air, and the heaven embraces it on every side as a sphere; and we assert that the quantity of the earth, relative to the heaven, is like a point in a circle. [But if the earth, besides its motion upward and downward or its departure to the sides, were said to be placed above the heavens, then whatever fell from the heavens would necessarily roll down to the circumference of that sphere, and whoever travelled on the earth would seem to advance from the centre toward the circumference, since the whole earth is turned toward the heaven at one and the same degree of longitude; yet the circumference of the outer circle always keeps the same distance, nor can its centre lie outside the middle. Therefore it must by no means be said that the earth is placed above the heavens, or the heavens above the earth; rather the heaven is above the one who dwells on the earth, and the earth is below him. Although there is here a relation of lower and higher place, nevertheless the earth itself is like a point, from which we see the stars along straight and equal lines. Thus it is evident that the difference of longitude of places on the earth is of no moment when compared with the outermost circumference of the heaven; for one who walks on the earth and looks out from it is thought to walk at the centre and to look out from the same centre.]

units.la: Quòd sol, luna & reliquæ stellæ sint globosæ.
units.tr: That the sun, the moon and the remaining stars are spherical.
CHAPTER V.

units.la: [Ponimus sol-em, lunam & reliquas stellas globosas esse: si enim haberent figuram planam, nullo modo circulum complere deprehenderentur, siue in oriente siue in occasu aspicerentur: sed potius instar scuti apparerent. Ita fieret vt pars eminentior aliqua nobis esset circa verticem, quàm circa horizontem: atqui nihil horum accidit: cùm videamus in omnibus locis circulum perfectum, & corpus sphæricum, vndiquaque æquabile. Hinc satis apparet, quòd sol & luna, & reliquæ stellæ habeant figuram sphæricam: neque opus est plura afferre: siquidem ex his cæteræ intelliguntur. Lu-na autem mutuatur lumen à sole: sicut apparet ex coniunctione: tunc enim pars lunæ nobis obuersa, tenebris est obscurata, altera quæ solem respicit, lumine solari est illustrata: & cùm luna à sole recedit in orientem, quâ solem spectat, lumine suffundi-tur, vt appareat corniculans: quâ verò soli obuertitur, tenebris obscuratur. Sed quando sol est in fi-gno piscium aut arietis, tunc cornua lunæ parallela sunt ferè horizonti: sicut ostendetur cap.27.]
units.tr: We hold that the sun, the moon and the other stars are spherical. For if they had a flat figure, they would not be seen to complete a circle, whether they were viewed in the east or in the west; rather, they would appear like a shield. In that case some part would stand out more prominently above our heads than near the horizon. But none of this happens: we see in every place a perfect circle and a spherical body, equal on every side. From this it sufficiently appears that the sun, the moon and the other stars have a spherical figure, and there is no need to bring forward more; for from these the rest are understood. The moon, moreover, borrows its light from the sun, as appears from conjunction: for then the part of the moon turned toward us is darkened by shadow, while the other part, which faces the sun, is illuminated by solar light; and when the moon recedes from the sun toward the east, the part that looks toward the sun is suffused with light, so that it appears crescent-shaped; but the part turned away from the sun is darkened. But when the sun is in Pisces or Aries, the horns of the moon are nearly parallel to the horizon, as will be shown in chapter 27.

units.la: De duobus motibus primis conuersionis cœ-lestis:quorum vnus est motus vniuersi, qui absoluitur quotidie ab ortu in occasum:al-ter est stellarum ab occasu versus ortum.
units.tr: Concerning the two first motions of the heavenly revolution: of which one is the motion of the whole, which is completed daily from east to west; the other is the motion of the stars from west toward east.
CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Postquam cœli & terræ situm exposuimus, restat vt motus cœlestes cōsideremus. Motus cœlestes, quos in cœlo obseruamus, sunt duo: vnus est à quo mouetur vniuersum spacio diei naturalis: quatenus sol, luna, & reliquæ stellæ ab ortu in occasum se-mel quotidie circumducuntur vno ordine & æquali velocitate, super duobus polis fixis, quos vocant polos primi mobilis: quorum vnus est septentriona-lis, alter meridionalis. Necessario autem stellæ omnes, quæ hoc motu agitantur, in circulis paralle-lis oberrant: ex quibus maximus vocatur æquinoctialis, qui instar cinguli est primi mobilis, quo diui-ditur per medium, vt ab vtroque polo æqualiter di-stet. Nominatur autem æquinoctialis, quia cum sol transierit eum, æquatur nox diei, vbicunque locorum, sicuti postea declarabimus. Alter motus est, qui deprehenditur in sole, luna, & reliquis planetis ab occidente in orientem: hic contrarius est motui primo: nam super aliis duobus polis conficitur, qui appellantur poli Zodiaci. Est autem Zodiacus circulus maximus, qui æqualiter distat à suis polis, estq; instar cinguli secudorum mobilium: quem sol, luna, & quin& quinque erratica stellæ motu suo peculiari ab oc-casu in ortum metiuntur. Diuiditur in 12 partes æquales, quæ appellantur signa: quorum nomina sunt, aries, taurus, gemini, cancer, leo, virgo, libra, scorpius, sagittarius, capricornus, aquarius, pisces. Unumquodque autem signum diuiditur in 30 gra-dus: & quilibet gradus in 60 minuta, omneq; mi-nutum in 60 secunda, & omne secundum in 60 ter-tia, tertium in 60 quarta. Quia vero Zodiacus cir-culus est obliquus, necessario medium eius, quod ecliptica dicitur, secat æquatorem in duobus punctis oppositis, & æqualiter à se inuicem distantibus: & declinat in utramque partem, septentrionalem videlicet & meridionalem, æqualiter. Punctū unum sectionis in æquatore, quod sol transit à meridie meando versus septentrionem, appellatur punctum æquinoctii vernalis, estq; principium arietis: alte-rum quod transit à septetrione meando versus meridiem, appellatur punctum æquinoctii autumna-lis, estq; principium libra. Sex sunt signa septen-trionalia, à principio arietis usque ad finem virgi-nis: & sex signa meridionalia sunt, à principio libra usque ad finem piscium. Fingitur præterea circulus maximus, qui secundum latitudinem transit à se-ptentrione in meridiem, & polos æquatoris & zo-diaci penetrat, secatq; æquatorem & eclipticam in duas æquales partes. Punctum extremum versus septentrionem appellatur solstitium æstiuum, quod est principium cancri: punctum extremum versus meridiem, appellatur solstitium hibernum, quod est principium capricorni. Distantia inter aequatorem & alterutrum horum punctorum, variat pro ratione declinationis eclipticæ ab aequatore: arcus enim ille ex obseruatione sapientis Ptolemæi comprehendit viginti tres gradus, & quinquaginta vnum minuta, quatenus totus circulus diuiditur in 360 partes: sed iuxta Almamonem, & alios, qui eum secuti sunt, sapientes, continet viginti tres gradus, & triginta quinque minuta. [Quomodo autem singulis seculis obseruanda sit summa solis declinatio, in quodam peculia-ri tractatu, si Deus voluerit, ostendam.] Iam ergo patet, planetas motu suo proprio reuolui super polis zodiaci, ab occasu in ortum: voluit autem eos cum reliquis stellis primum mobile, ab oriente in occidentem progrediens. Poli autem æquatoris, circa quos primus motus conspicitur, sunt fixi, neque mouentur: sed poli zodiaci ex motu primo circa polos æquatoris mouentur, quamuis inseparabiles sint ab illo circulo, qui transit polos æquatoris & zodiaci, in quo reperitur motus primus & declinationis.
units.tr: After we have set out the position of heaven and earth, what remains is to consider the celestial motions. We observe two celestial motions in the heavens. One is the motion by which the whole universe is carried round in the space of a natural day: the sun, moon and the other stars are each turned once daily from east to west, in one order and at equal speed, about two fixed poles, which are called the poles of the first mover, one northern and the other southern. All the stars that are carried by this motion necessarily move in parallel circles. The greatest of these is called the equinoctial, which encircles the first mover like a belt and divides it in the middle so that it is equally distant from each pole. It is called the equinoctial because when the sun crosses it, the night becomes equal to the day in every place, as we shall explain later. The other motion is found in the sun, moon, and the five wandering stars, which measure their own peculiar motion from west to east. This motion is contrary to the first, for it is carried out about two other poles, which are called the poles of the zodiac. The zodiac is a great circle, equally distant from its poles, and it lies like a belt around the second movers. Along it the sun, moon, and the five wandering stars measure their course from west to east. It is divided into twelve equal parts, called signs, whose names are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces. Each sign is divided into thirty degrees, each degree into sixty minutes, each minute into sixty seconds, each second into sixty thirds, and each third into sixty fourths. Since the zodiac circle is oblique, its middle line, which is called the ecliptic, necessarily cuts the equator at two opposite points that are equally distant from each other, and it inclines equally to each side, namely north and south. The point of intersection on the equator, which the sun crosses when moving from south to north, is called the point of the vernal equinox, and it is the beginning of Aries. The other point, which the sun crosses when moving from north to south, is called the point of the autumnal equinox, and it is the beginning of Libra. Six signs lie to the north, from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo, and six lie to the south, from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces. Furthermore, a great circle is imagined which runs from north to south through the latitude, passes through the poles of the equator and of the zodiac, and cuts the equator and the ecliptic into two equal parts. The point at the extreme north is called the summer solstice, which is the beginning of Cancer; the point at the extreme south is called the winter solstice, which is the beginning of Capricorn. The distance between the equator and either of these points varies according to the rate at which the ecliptic inclines from the equator. For by the observation of the wise Ptolemy that arc comprises twenty-three degrees and fifty-one minutes, the whole circle being divided into 360 parts; but according to Almamon and the other wise men who followed him, it comprises twenty-three degrees and thirty-five minutes. [How the greatest declination of the sun is to be observed in each age, I shall show, God willing, in a special treatise.] It is therefore now clear that the planets revolve by their own motion about the poles of the zodiac, from west to east, while the first mover, proceeding from east to west, carries them along with the other stars. The poles of the equator, around which the first motion is seen, are fixed and do not move; but the poles of the zodiac move by the first motion about the poles of the equator, although they are inseparable from that circle which passes through the poles of the equator and of the zodiac, in which the first motion and the declination are found.

units.la: 1 Recte asserit Alfraganus, non manere omnibus seculis vnam & eandem solis declinationem: vnde sequitur etiam anni quantitatem variare pro diuersa temporum ratione. Tempore Ptolemæi summa solis declinatio fuit 23 gradus & 51 minut. seculo Almamonis regis Arabum , qui quinquaginta annis vixit ante Albategnium, fuit 23 grad.& 35[?] minut. licut eandem assignauit Albategnius. Arzachel Hispanus inuenit 23 grad.& 34 minuta. Thebitius & Almachon[?] filius Albumafaris inuenit 23 grad. 33 minuta prima, & 30 secunda. Prophatius Iudæus inuenit 23 grad.& 32 minuta. Purbachius & Regiomontanus inuenerunt 23 grad.& 18 minuta. Tempore Copernici iterum coepit accrescere maxima solis declinatio : tunc enim inuenta est 23 graduum, 28 1/3 minutorum : sicut a Wernero deprehensa est 23 graduum, 28 primorum minutorum, & 30 secundorum. Etsi igitur Ptolemæus statuerit, inuariabilem manere maximam solis declinationem; subsequentia tamen secula ostenderunt, illam mutatam fuisse. Copernicus asserit nunquam fuisse maiorem 23 gradibus, & 51 minutis, necvnquam minorem futuram 23 gradibus, & 28 minutis. Qua ratione & quibus instrumentis sit obseruanda, Alfraganus peculiari tractatu ostendit: sed cum is ad manus nostras non peruenerit, consulatur Ptolemæus libro primo Almagesti capite duodecimo. Hic autem notandum est, in omnibus vulgatis editionibus nomen Almamon depravatum esse in Almehon: & legi, fuisse summam solis declinationem 23 grad. & 33 minutorum: cum tamen Hebræus noster interpres, & Latina bibliothecæ Palatinæ versio scribant Almamonem summam solis declinationem obseruasse 23 grad.& 35 minutorum. Quare falluntur, qui putant Alfraganum circa tempora Thebitii vixisse: cum solis summa declinatio effet 23 graduum & 33 minutorum: nam ex libris emendatioribus appa-ret, Alfraganum nostrum post tempora Almamonis & Albategnii claruisse, cùm solis maxima declinatio esset deprehensa 23 grad.& 35 minutorum. Quanta autem est solis in tropicis versantis distantia ab æqua-tore; tantum quoque interuallum est inter polos mundi & zodiaci.
units.tr: 1 Alfraganus rightly asserts that the greatest declination of the sun does not remain one and the same in all ages, and from this it follows that the length of the year also varies according to the changing of the times. In the time of Ptolemy the greatest declination of the sun was 23 degrees and 51 minutes. In the age of Almamon, king of the Arabs, who lived fifty years before Albategnius, it was 23 degrees and 35 [?] minutes, as Albategnius also assigned. Arzachel the Spaniard found 23 degrees and 34 minutes. Thebitius and Almachon, son of Albumasar, found 23 degrees, 33 first minutes and 30 seconds. Profatius the Jew found 23 degrees and 32 minutes. Purbach and Regiomontanus found 23 degrees and 18 minutes. In the time of Copernicus the greatest declination of the sun began to increase again, for then it was found to be 23 degrees and 28 1/3 minutes, as Werner also determined it to be 23 degrees, 28 first minutes and 30 seconds. Although, then, Ptolemy stated that the greatest declination of the sun remains unchanged, the following ages showed that it has changed. Copernicus asserts that it was never greater than 23 degrees and 51 minutes, and that it will never be less than 23 degrees and 28 minutes in the future. By what method and with what instruments it is to be observed, Alfraganus shows in a special treatise; but since that work has not come into our hands, let Ptolemy be consulted, Almagest book 1, chapter 12. Here, however, it must be noted that in all the printed editions the name Almamon has been corrupted into Almehon, and it is read that the sun's greatest declination was 23 degrees and 33 minutes; yet our Hebrew interpreter and the Latin version in the Palatine library write that Almamon observed the sun's greatest declination to be 23 degrees and 35 minutes. Therefore those are mistaken who think that Alfraganus lived around the time of Thebitius, when the sun's greatest declination was 23 degrees and 33 minutes; for from the more correct books it appears that our Alfraganus flourished after the times of Almamon and Albategnius, when the sun's greatest declination had been found to be 23 degrees and 35 minutes. Moreover, as great as the distance of the sun, moving in the tropics, is from the equator, so great also is the interval between the poles of the world and of the zodiac.

units.la: De quadrante terræ habitabilis: quid accidat in quouis parallelo, & quæ sint vicißitudines noctium ac dierum.
units.tr: On the quadrant of the inhabitable earth: what happens in each parallel, and what the alternations of nights and days are.
CHAPTER VII.

units.la: GLobus terræ, quatenus extimo cœlo concentricus est, subiacet plano æquatoris, a quo secatur in duas æquales partes: quarum una vergit ad polum septentrionalem, altera spectat polum meridionalem. Quod attinet ad loca inter æquatorem & septentrionem habitabilia, facile indagari possunt: quæ autem inter extremum orientem & occidentem sunt disita, non excedunt quadratem, hoc est, spacium duodecim horarum æquinoctialium. Quæ vt recte intelligantur, fingendus est in superficie terræ maximus circulus, qui æquatorem secet ad angulos rectos sphæricos: ita fient quatuor quadrates, quorum vnum tantùm inhabitari dicimus. Etsi enim ab oriente in occidetem longitudo sit dimidii circuli, hoc est duorum quadratum, seu 180 graduum, tamen in latitudine summa est angustia, vt inter æquatorem & septentrionem, vbi 66 fere gradus polus supra horizontem eleuatur, postrema sit habitatio. Adhæc horizontis & meridiani in vnounoquoque climate ratio est obseruanda. Horizon est circulus diuidens hemisphærium cœli supra terram conspicuū, ab eo quod latet infra terram; cuius polus est punctum verticis. Diuidit autem horizon cœlum in duas partes æquales: quandoquidem tumor molis terrenæ tantus non est, ut possit de capacitate cœli aliquid subtrahere. Meridianus circulus cuiuscunque loci dicitur, qui transit æquatorem & punctum verticis: ut poli eius sint in horizonte iuxta æquatorem. Diuidit autem hemisphærium quod supra & infra terram est, omnesque alios parallelos æquatori in duas æquales partes. Vt autem generalem dispositionem terræ habitabilis habeamus, incipiamus ab æquatore: hic enim principium est quadrantis habitabilis in latitudine versus meridiem. Qui sub æquatore habitant, iis hic circulus necessariò sit verticalis, ut poli eius incumbât horizonti: propterea æquator in horizonte angulos facit rectos, & declinat sol à vertice eorum versus septentrionem & meridiem æqualiter, ut hiems & æstas parem habeant complexionem: se-catq; horizon omnes parallelos æquatoris in duas æquales partes, cum habeant communes polos cum æquatore, ut tempus ab ortu solis reliquorumq; siderum usque ad occasum supputatum, per totum annum æquale sit tempori ab occasu usque ad ortum numerato: quare ibi perpetuo nox diei æquatur.
units.tr: The globe of the earth, insofar as it is concentric with the outermost heaven, lies beneath the plane of the equator, by which it is cut into two equal parts: one of which tends toward the north pole, while the other faces the south pole. As for the places inhabitable between the equator and the north, they can easily be investigated; but those lying between the furthest east and west do not exceed a quadrant, that is, a space of twelve equinoctial hours. So that these may be rightly understood, we must imagine on the surface of the earth a great circle that cuts the equator at right spherical angles; thus four quadrants are formed, of which we say only one is inhabited. For although the length from east to west is half a circle, that is, two quadrants or 180 degrees, yet in latitude the narrowness is greatest, so that the last habitation is between the equator and the north, where the pole is raised about 66 degrees above the horizon. Moreover, the relation of the horizon and the meridian must be observed in each climate. The horizon is the circle dividing the hemisphere of the heaven visible above the earth from that which lies hidden below the earth; its pole is the point of the zenith. The horizon divides the heaven into two equal parts, since the bulk of the earthly mass is not so great that it could subtract anything from the capacity of the heaven. The meridian of any place is the circle which passes through the equator and the point of the zenith, so that its poles lie on the horizon near the equator. It divides the hemisphere which is above and below the earth, and all the other parallels to the equator, into two equal parts. Now, that we may have a general arrangement of the inhabitable earth, let us begin from the equator, for this is the beginning of the inhabitable quadrant in latitude toward the south. For those who dwell under the equator, this circle must necessarily be vertical, so that its poles rest upon the horizon; therefore the equator makes right angles with the horizon, and the sun declines equally from their zenith toward the north and the south, so that winter and summer have an equal character. The horizon cuts all the parallels of the equator into two equal parts, since they have common poles with the equator, so that the time from the rising of the sun and the other stars until their setting, reckoned over the whole year, is equal to the time counted from setting to rising; hence there night is constantly equal to day.

units.la: {2}Quando vero æquator cum horizonte obliquos facit angulos, vt à vertice capitis in me-ridiem declinet, axisque septentrionalis supra ho-rizontem elevetur iuxta summam solis declina-tionem: tunc arcus inter æquatorem & tropicum cancri æqualis erit altitudini poli supra horizon-tem: & sidera quæ iuxta polum septentrionalem erunt, nunquam occident, quæ iuxta polum an-tarcticum existent, nunquam orientur. Horizon autem solum æquatorem bifariam diuidet, reliquos autem eius parallelos secabit in duas partes inæqua-les, vt arcus diurnus versus septentrionem maior sit futurus arcu nocturno. Contrario modo se ha-bebunt paralleli versus meridiem: ibi enim arcus diurnus minor erit nocturno. Huius rei causa est, quod quantum elevatur polus septentrionalis su-pra horizontem, tantum deprimitur polus meri-dionalis: & quantum elevantur paralleli septen-trionales, vt plus quàm dimidia eorum pars con-spiciatur, tantum deprimuntur meridionales, vt plus quàm dimidia eorum pars occultetur. Quan-to autem magis in climatibus augetur elevatio po-li: tanto magis quoque variant paralleli, cum die-bus æstiuis ac hibernis: quanto enim propinquior est parallelus ipsi polo, tanto quoque maior est ipsius arcus diurnus. Constat itaque ex superioribus in vniuersa terra fieri æquinoctium, quando sol æquatorem permeat, quod fit in principio arietis & librae: nam horizon secat æquatorem cum omnibus eius[?] parallelis in duas aequales partes. In reliquis climatibus, sole peruagante signa septentrionalia, dies prolixior erit nocte: sicut in oppositis signis versus meridiem nox prolixior erit die. Si autem sol maxime ab aequatore declinauerit, ut sit in principio cancri; dies erit prolixissimus, & breuissima nox. Sole peruagante signa meridionalia, dies breuior erit nocte: & quotidie quantitas diei decrescet, donec sol attingat principium capricorni: tunc erit breuissimus dies, & nox longissima. Si duo loca occurrant in duobus ex diametro oppositis parallelis: tunc arcus diurnus vnius loci aequalis erit arcui nocturno alterius, eritque dies vnius aequalis nocti alterius, & nox vnius aequabitur diei alterius: & prolixissimus dies in cancro, aequalis erit longissimae nocti in capricorno. Atque haec in genere accidunt locis habitabilibus terrae.
units.tr: {2}But when the equator makes oblique angles with the horizon, so that it declines from the zenith of the head toward the south, and the northern axis is raised above the horizon according to the greatest declination of the sun, then the arc between the equator and the tropic of Cancer will be equal to the altitude of the pole above the horizon; and the stars that lie near the north pole will never set, while those near the antarctic pole will never rise. The horizon will indeed bisect only the equator, but will cut its other parallels into two unequal parts, so that the diurnal arc toward the north will be greater than the nocturnal arc. The parallels toward the south behave in the opposite way, for there the diurnal arc will be less than the nocturnal. The cause of this is that as much as the north pole is raised above the horizon, so much is the south pole depressed; and as much as the northern parallels are raised, so that more than half of each is visible, so much are the southern parallels depressed, so that more than half of each is hidden. Moreover, the more the elevation of the pole increases in the climates, the more the parallels also vary between summer and winter days; for the nearer a parallel is to the pole itself, the greater is its diurnal arc. It is therefore clear from what has been said above that over the whole earth the equinox occurs when the sun passes the equator, which happens at the beginning of Aries and Libra; for the horizon cuts the equator with all its parallels into two equal parts. In the other climates, as the sun moves through the northern signs, the day will be longer than the night, just as in the opposite signs toward the south the night will be longer than the day. If the sun declines most from the equator, so that it is at the beginning of Cancer, the day will be longest and the night shortest. As the sun moves through the southern signs, the day is shorter than the night, and the length of the day decreases daily until the sun reaches the beginning of Capricorn; then the day will be shortest and the night longest. If two places lie on parallels opposite each other across the diameter, then the diurnal arc of one place will equal the nocturnal arc of the other, and the day of one will equal the night of the other, and the night of one will match the day of the other; and the longest day in Cancer will equal the longest night in Capricorn. These things happen in general to the inhabited places of the earth.

units.la: 1 Vertex capitis dicitur polus horizontis, quem corrupte nominant Zenith, cum Arabes scribant Semith: punctum verticj oppositum appellatur Nathir, quasi dicas punctum simile: est enim illud quasi alter polus horizontis, nobis depressus.
units.tr: 1 The point overhead, the pole of the horizon, which people wrongly call the Zenith, whereas the Arabs write Semith; the point opposite the zenith is called Nathir, as if you were to say "a like point": for it is, as it were, the other pole of the horizon, depressed beneath us.

units.la: 2 Postquam Altraganus per loca aequatori subiecta, naturam sphaerae rectae adumbrauit: incipit declarare situ sphaerae obliquae: in qua cum loca insignia sint, quae subiecta sunt tropico cancri, illorum proprietates prius exponit: quod scilicet in principio cancri solem habeant verticalem, & polus septentrionalis ad 23 [?] gradus & 35 [?]. minuta eleuetur, quanta fit maxima solis declinatio. In reliquis climatibus, quæ magis ad septentrionem vergunt, sol nunquam verticem capitis ascendit.
units.tr: 2 After Alfraganus, by describing places subject to the equator, had sketched the nature of the right sphere, he begins to explain the position of the oblique sphere. Since the notable places here are those lying under the tropic of Cancer, he first sets out their properties: namely, that at the beginning of Cancer they have the sun overhead, and the north pole is raised to 23 [?] degrees and 35 [?] minutes, which is the greatest declination of the sun. In the other climates, which tend more toward the north, the sun never rises to the zenith of the head.

units.la: De proprietatibus partium specialibus, in quadrante terræ habitabilis.
units.tr: On the special properties of the parts, in the quadrant of the inhabitable earth.
CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Ostendemus nunc proprietates locorum, quæ inter æquatorem & extremum quadrantis habitabilis terminum incoluntur. In quibus locis eleuatio poli minor est summa solis ab æquatore declinatione; sol quotannis bis transit punctum verticis: nam antequam perveniat ad principium cancri, sol fit verticalis: & a cancro redeundo iterum verticem conscendit. Vbi autem eleuatio poli æ-qualis est summæ declinationi ecliptice: ibi semel tantum in anno sol fit verticalis, quando nimirum attingit principium cancri. In cæteris locis, in quibus eleuatio poli maior est summa ecliptice de-clinatione, sol nunquam conscendit verticem: sed ad meridiem recedit pro ratione eleuationis poli: ortusq; æstiuus maiori interuallo distat ab ortu hie-mali: quin etiam dies increscit, donec perueniatur ad extrema loca, vbi polus eleuatur 66 gradus, & quartam sextam partem vnius gradus: quanta distantia est inter polum & principium cancri. Atque ibi transit polus ecliptice verticem, & tropicus cancri perpetuo supra terram apparet, tropicus autem capricorni semper infra terram latitat: unde fit ut sole in principio cancri existente, dies fit vi-ginti quatuor horarum continuarum, nulla inter-veniente nocte: & sole existente in principio capricorni, nox fit viginti quatuor horarum continuarum, nullo intercedente die. Quando autem in his locis polus ecliptica vertice trāsit, ipsa ecliptica in-cumbit horizonti, ut principiu arietis fit in orien-te, & principium libra in occidente: & initium ca-pricorni in horizonte meridiano, initiu vero can-cri in horizonte septentrionali. Cumq; ecliptica re-cedit à vertice, secant se orbis signorum & hori-zon per medium, & eleuatur medietas orientalis zodiaci, & deprimitur medietas occidentalis: qua-re ascendunt tunc ex signa subito, in momento quasi temporis, quæ sunt ab initio capricorni usque ad fi-nem geminorum, & similiter occidunt ex reliqua repente.
units.tr: We shall now show the properties of the places that lie between the equator and the outermost limit of the inhabitable quadrant. In those places where the elevation of the pole is less than the sum of the sun's declination from the equator, the sun passes the point of the zenith twice a year. For before it reaches the beginning of Cancer, the sun becomes vertical, and on its return from Cancer it climbs to the zenith again. Where the elevation of the pole equals the sum of the declination of the ecliptic, the sun becomes vertical only once a year, namely when it reaches the beginning of Cancer. In the other places, where the elevation of the pole is greater than the sum of the declination of the ecliptic, the sun never climbs to the zenith but recedes to the south in proportion to the elevation of the pole. The summer rising is at a greater interval from the winter rising. Indeed, the days lengthen until one reaches the extreme places, where the pole is elevated 66 degrees and a sixth part of a degree, which is the distance between the pole and the beginning of Cancer. There the pole of the ecliptic passes the zenith, the tropic of Cancer appears perpetually above the earth, and the tropic of Capricorn always lies hidden below it. Hence, when the sun is at the beginning of Cancer, the day lasts twenty-four continuous hours with no night intervening, and when the sun is at the beginning of Capricorn, the night lasts twenty-four continuous hours with no day intervening. When in these places the pole of the ecliptic is at the zenith, the ecliptic itself lies upon the horizon: the beginning of Aries is in the east, the beginning of Libra in the west, the beginning of Capricorn on the meridian horizon, and the beginning of Cancer on the northern horizon. As the ecliptic recedes from the zenith, the circle of the signs and the horizon cut each other through the middle, the eastern half of the zodiac is raised and the western half is lowered. Therefore the signs from the beginning of Capricorn to the end of Gemini rise suddenly, in what is almost a moment of time, and likewise the rest set all at once.

units.la: De locis reliquis quadrantis, quæ inhabitari nequeunt: quæ sit proprietas eorum, & quid accidat illis.
units.tr: On the remaining places of the quadrant, which cannot be inhabited: what their property is, and what happens to them.
CHAPTER IX.

units.la: In quibus locis polus eleuatur supra horizontem amplius, quàm distet principium cancri à polo: ibi portio, quæ est ab utroque latere principii cancri, & ab æquatore versus septentrionem magis declinat quàm polus à vertice capitis, supra terram semper apparet, & portio opposita versus capricornum perpetuo latet: propterea longitudo diei unius æstiui, quando sol transit gradus istos supra terrā apparetes, æqualis est longitudini noctis unius hiberna. Huiusmodi loca sunt, in quibus polus supra horizontem eleuatur 67 ½ gradus: atq; ibi quod est inter medium geminorum & medium cancri, apparet semper supra terrā, & quod est inter medium sagittarii & medium capricorni, perpetuo occultatur infra terrā: propterea per continuum mensem in astate ibi est dies, ut nulla interueniat nox: in hieme autem per mensem continuum nox est, ut nullus intercedat dies. atq; hic est terminus locorum habitabilium: nō enim probabile est ulterius in septentrione habitatione extendi: itaq; per decem reliquos menses dies & noctes pariter co-stabunt viginti quatuor horis.
units.tr: In those places where the pole is raised above the horizon further than the beginning of Cancer is distant from the pole, the portion lying on either side of the beginning of Cancer, and reaching from the equator toward the north more than the pole is distant from the zenith of the head, always appears above the earth, and the opposite portion toward Capricorn remains perpetually hidden. Therefore the length of one summer day, when the sun passes through those degrees that appear above the earth, equals the length of one winter night. Such are the places where the pole is raised 67½ degrees above the horizon. There, what lies between the middle of Gemini and the middle of Cancer appears above the earth continually, and what lies between the middle of Sagittarius and the middle of Capricorn is perpetually hidden below the earth. Therefore for one unbroken month in summer it is day there, so that no night intervenes; in winter, on the other hand, it is night for one unbroken month, so that no day comes between. This is the limit of the inhabitable regions, for it is not probable that habitation extends further northward. Thus, during the remaining ten months, day and night alike last twenty-four hours each.

units.la: Ubi vero altitudo poli fuerit 69 graduum cum dimidio & quadrante: ibi gemini & cacer[?] perpetuo sunt supra terram, sagittarius autem & capricornus perpetuo occultan-tur: propterea per duos continuos menses in astate est dies, & per duos continuos menses in hieme est nox.
units.tr: Where the altitude of the pole is 69 and a half degrees, Gemini and Cancer are perpetually above the earth, while Sagittarius and Capricorn are perpetually hidden. Therefore for two unbroken months in summer it is day, and for two unbroken months in winter it is night.

units.la: Ubi eleuatur polus 73 ½ gradus: ibi quod est a medio tauri usq; ad medium leonis, supra terram semper apparet, & opposita portio versus capricornum perpe-tuo occultatur: propterea per tres continuos menses in astate dies est, & per tres continuos menses in hie-me nox est.
units.tr: Where the pole is raised 73½ degrees, what lies from the middle of Taurus to the middle of Leo always appears above the earth, and the opposite portion toward Capricorn is perpetually hidden. Therefore for three unbroken months in summer it is day, and for three unbroken months in winter it is night.

units.la: Ubi autem polus eleuatur 78 ½ gra-dus, ibi taurus, gemini, cancer, leo, semper appare-bunt, bunt, & gradus oppositi perpetuo occultabuntur: propterea in æstate per quatuor menses continuos erit dies, & in hieme per quatuor menses continuos erit nox. Vbi polus elevatur 84 gradus, ibi quod est inter medium arietis & inter medium virginis apparet, sicut eius oppositum latet semper: hinc fit ut in æstate per quinq; menses continuos sit dies, & in hieme per quinq; menses continuos sit nox. Sed in his locis quæ commemoravimus accidit, ut polo zo-diaci meridianum versus austrum trafeunte [?], principium arietis in ortu, & libra in occidente collocetur, & signa septentrionalia supra terram semper conspiciantur, meridionalibus infra terrā perpetuo occultatis. Sed aliter signa supra terram ab oriente versus occidentem feruntur, quam fiat in locis habitabilibus: ibi enim oritur taurus ante arietem, & aries ante pisces, pisces ante aquarium: in his autem oppositis locis contrarium euenit. In quo loco polus elevatur 90 gradibus, ut in vertice constituatur: ibi æquator ambit horizontem, & circa eum instar molæ voluitur, & hemisphærium unum cæli supra, alterum infra terram extenditur: quamobrem cum sol est in signis septentrionalibus, perpetuo supra horizontem conspicitur: & maxima eius altitudo tanta est, quanta reperitur summa ecliptica ab æquatore declinatio: cum autem sol peruagatur signa meridionalia, perpetuo infra horizontem latitat: propterea totus annus ibidem constat vna die & vna nocte: quatenus scilicet per sex menses continuos dies est, & per sex reliquos nox.
units.tr: Where the pole is raised 78½ degrees, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer and Leo will always appear, and the opposite signs will be perpetually hidden; therefore in summer there will be day for four unbroken months, and in winter night for four unbroken months. Where the pole is raised 84 degrees, what lies between the middle of Aries and the middle of Virgo appears, while its opposite always lies hidden; hence it comes about that in summer there is day for five unbroken months, and in winter night for five unbroken months. But in the places we have mentioned it happens that, with the zodiac passing toward the south of the meridian, the beginning of Aries is placed at the rising, and Libra at the setting, and the northern signs are always seen above the earth, the southern ones being perpetually hidden below it. But the signs above the earth move from east to west differently than they do in inhabited places; for there Taurus rises before Aries, Aries before Pisces, and Pisces before Aquarius, whereas in these opposite places the contrary happens. In the place where the pole is raised 90 degrees, so that it stands at the zenith, the equator encircles the horizon and turns about it like a millstone, and one hemisphere of the heavens extends above and the other below the earth. Therefore, when the sun is in the northern signs, it is always seen above the horizon, and its greatest altitude is as great as the greatest declination of the ecliptic from the equator; but when the sun wanders through the southern signs, it always lies hidden below the horizon. Consequently the whole year there consists of one day and one night, namely, six unbroken months of day and six remaining months of night.

units.la: De mensura ambitus terrestris, & diuisione eius in septem climata habitabilia ratione longitudinis & latitudinis.
units.tr: On the measurement of the earth's circumference, and its division into seven habitable climates according to longitude and latitude.
CHAPTER X.

units.la: Recensebimus nunc mensuram superficiei terrestris, & ostendemus quid sit sentiendum de climatibus eius habitabilibus secundum longitudinem & latitudinem, quarum utraque sumitur respectu cœli & ambitus terrestris. In superioribus declarauimus, quod centrum sphærae terrestris idem sit cum centro cœli: quare necessarium est, vt ambitus eius vndiquaque respondeat cœlo. Cum enim iter facimus recta secundum lineam meridianam à meridie vel septentrione; augetur vel imminuitur polus septentrionalis supra horizontem pro quantitate itineris nostri: ' & deprehendimus vni gradui cœlesti in terra respondere 56 milliaria, & duas tertias vnius milliaris. Milliare autem habet cubita 4000: prout cubitum accipitur in mensura media. Cubitum habet 6 palmos communes, vt cum Almamone plurimi sapientes testantur.
units.tr: We shall now review the measure of the earth's surface, and show what ought to be thought about its habitable climates, according to longitude and latitude, both of which are reckoned with respect to the heavens and the circumference of the earth. In the earlier chapters we showed that the centre of the earthly sphere is the same as the centre of the heavens, so its circumference must correspond to the heavens on every side. For when we travel in a straight line along the meridian, either south or north, the north pole rises or falls above the horizon in proportion to the distance we have travelled. We find that one degree of the heavens corresponds on earth to 56 and two-thirds miles. A mile contains 4000 cubits, taking the cubit as a middle measure. The cubit has 6 common palms, as many wise men testify with Almamon.

units.la: Si itaque multiplicemus gradum vnum in totum circulum, hoc est, 360 gradus, inueniemus circumferentiam terrestrem continere 20400 milliaria circiter. Si autem diuidatur circumferentia terrestris per 1/3 & 1/7 prodibit diameter terræ, continens fere 6500 milliaria.
units.tr: If, then, we multiply one degree by the whole circle, that is, by 360 degrees, we find that the circumference of the earth contains about 20,400 miles. If the circumference of the earth is divided by 22/7 (one-third and one-seventh), the diameter of the earth results, containing about 6,500 miles.

units.la: Rursus si multiplicemus diametrum in circumferetiam, producetur inde cubica sphæra terrestris area, videlicet 132 millia millium, & 600000, hoc est, milliaria 13260000 cubica: quatenus in vnoquoque quadrati latere milliare vnum continetur.
units.tr: Again, if we multiply the diameter by the circumference, the cubic area of the earthly sphere is produced, namely 132 million million and 600,000; that is, 13,260,000 cubic miles, since one mile is contained along each side of a square.

units.la: Itaque tota terra habitabilis cōtinebit huiusmodi cubica milliaria, 33 millia millium, & 150 millia fere, hoc est, 3315000 milliaria quadrata.
units.tr: Therefore the whole habitable earth will contain such cubic miles: 33 million million and about 150 million, that is, 3,315,000 square miles.

units.la: Summa terræ habitabilis latitudo, vt ex relatione multorum cognouimus, ab æquatore extenditur in septentrionem eovsque, donec polus supra horizontem eleuetur 66 gradus, & 1/4 ac 1/6 vnius gradus: hoc autem interuallum compleƈtitur 3764 milliaria.
units.tr: As we have learned from the report of many people, the greatest breadth of the habitable earth extends northward from the equator until the pole rises above the horizon 66 degrees, and one-quarter and one-sixth of a degree. This interval amounts to 3,764 miles.

units.la: Longitudo maxima tātum spacii occupat, quantum 12 horis reuolutio cœlestis conficit: hoc est, intercipit dimidiam circumferentiam circuli, quæ cōtinet milliaria 10200. Vbi tamen obseruandum est versus septentrionem propter constrictionem sphæræ, extremam longitudinem compleƈtitantum duas quintas circūferentiæ, hoc est, 4080 milliaria.
units.tr: The greatest length occupies as much space as the heavenly revolution accomplishes in 12 hours; that is, it covers half the circumference of the circle, which contains 10,200 miles. It must be noted, however, that towards the north, because of the narrowing of the sphere, the greatest length covers only two-fifths of the circumference, that is, 4,080 miles.

units.la: Loca quadrātus habitabilis diuidūtur in septem climata: quorum primi medium eas transit regiones, in quibus maxima dies est 13 horarum: septimi autem medium in ea incidit loca, vbi maxima dies est 16 horarū. Quicquid enim est versus meridiem ultra terminum primi climatis, fere totum à mari circumdatur, ut non sit magnus locus habitationi: quod autem extenditur supra septimum clima versus septentrionem, exiguum quoque spacium est, in quo pauca civitates nobis sunt cognita.
units.tr: The habitable quadrant is divided into seven climates. The middle of the first passes through those regions in which the longest day is 13 hours; the middle of the seventh falls on those places where the longest day is 16 hours. For whatever lies south beyond the limit of the first climate is almost entirely surrounded by sea, so that there is no large area fit for habitation; and whatever extends beyond the seventh climate towards the north is also a small space, in which few cities are known to us.

units.la: Itaque longitudo omnium climatum ab oriente in occasum spacio 12 horarum à revolutione cœlesti conficitur: latitudo autem climatis unius ab altero discernitur ex prolixitate diei, {2}si dimidiam horam excesserit.
units.tr: Thus the length of all the climates, from east to west, is measured by 12 hours of the heavenly revolution; the breadth of each climate is distinguished from the next by the lengthening of the day, if it exceeds half an hour.

units.la: Primi climatis medium constituitur, ubi prolixis-simus dies est 13 horarum, & polus supra horizontem elevatur 16 gradus, & ⅔ unius. Principium eius est, ubi prolixior dies deprehenditur 12 horarum, cum dimidia & ¼, & polus elevatur 12½ gradus, cum ¼. Finis eius est, ubi prolixior dies habetur 13 horarū, & ¼, & polus elevatur 20 ⅐ gradus. Cotinet hoc clima in latitudine 44 0 milliaria. {3} [In libro Arabico autor plura dicit de his locis ratione umbrae, sicut de aliis climatibus: sed in libro Romanorum non sunt translata: ideo hic non adscribemus.]
units.tr: The middle of the first climate is placed where the longest day is 13 hours and the pole is raised above the horizon 16 and two-thirds degrees. Its beginning is where the longer day is found to be 12 and a half hours, and the pole is raised 12 and a quarter degrees. Its end is where the longer day is 13 and a quarter hours, and the pole is raised 20 and one-seventh degrees. This climate contains 440 miles in breadth. {3} [In the Arabic book the author says more about these places with respect to the shadow, as he does about the other climates; but these were not translated in the Roman book, so we shall not add them here.]

units.la: Secundi climatis medium transit, ubi maxima dies est 13 ½ horarum, & elevatur polus 24 gradus, & decima parte unius. Principium eius sumitur à fine primi climatis. Finis eius extenditur eo usq; ubi prolixior dies habet 13 ½ horas cum ¼, & polus elevatur 27 gradus. Complectitur iter 4 0 0 milliariorum.
units.tr: The middle of the second climate passes where the longest day is 13 and a half hours, and the pole is raised 24 and a tenth of a degree. Its beginning is taken from the end of the first climate. Its end extends as far as where the longer day has 13 and a half hours and a quarter, and the pole is raised 27 degrees. It embraces a journey of 400 miles.

units.la: Tertij climatis medium incidit, vbi dies prolixissimus est 14 horarum, & polus elevatur 30 ½ gradus, cum ⅕. Principium eius sumitur ab extremitate climatis secundi. Finis eius extenditur eo, vbi dies prolixior est 14 horarum, & ¼ & elevatur polus 33 gradus, cum ⅔. Continet 350 milliaria.
units.tr: The middle of the third climate falls where the longest day is 14 hours and the pole is raised 30 and a half degrees and a fifth. Its beginning is taken from the edge of the second climate. Its end extends to where the longer day is 14 hours and a quarter, and the pole is raised 33 and two-thirds degrees. It contains 350 miles.

units.la: Quarti climatis medium transit, vbi longissimus dies est 14 ½ horarum, & elevatur polus 36 gradus, cum ⅖. Principium eius est terminus tertij climatis. Finis eius extenditur eo, vbi prolixior dies est 14 ½ horarum, & ¼, & elevatur polus 39 gradus. Continet spacium 300 milliariorum.
units.tr: The middle of the fourth climate passes where the longest day is 14 and a half hours, and the pole is raised 36 and two-fifths degrees. Its beginning is the limit of the third climate. Its end extends to where the longer day is 14 and a half hours and a quarter, and the pole is raised 39 degrees. It contains a space of 300 miles.

units.la: Quinti climatis medium eo pertingit, vbi prolixior dies est 15 horarū, altitudo autem poli est 41 graduum cum ⅓. Principium eius est terminus climatis quarti. Finis eius eo peruenit, vbi longior dies est 15 horarum, cum ¼, & elevatur polus 43 ½ gradus. Comprehendit hoc spacium 255 milliaria.
units.tr: The middle of the fifth climate reaches where the longer day is 15 hours, and the height of the pole is 41 and one-third degrees. Its beginning is the limit of the fourth climate. Its end arrives where the longer day is 15 hours and a quarter, and the pole is raised 43 and a half degrees. This space comprises 255 miles.

units.la: Sexti climatis medij incidit, vbi prolixissimus dies est 15 ½ horarū, & elevatur polus 45 gradus cū ⅖. Principium eius est terminus quinti climatis. Finis eius eo pertingit, vbi prolixior dies est 15 ½ horarum, cum ¼, & elevatur polus 47 gradus cum ¼. Continet hoc spacium 210 milliaria.
units.tr: The middle of the sixth climate falls where the longest day is 15 and a half hours, and the pole is raised 45 and two-fifths degrees. Its beginning is the limit of the fifth climate. Its end reaches where the longer day is 15 and a half hours and a quarter, and the pole is raised 47 and a quarter degrees. This space contains 210 miles.

units.la: Septimi climatis medij constituitur, vbi prolixissimus dies est 16 horarū, elevatio autē poli reperitur 48 graduum, cum ⅓. Principium eius incidit in extremitatem climatis sexti. Finis eius extenditur
units.tr: The middle of the seventh climate is placed where the longest day is 16 hours, and the elevation of the pole is found to be 48 and one-third degrees. Its beginning falls at the edge of the sixth climate. Its end extends

units.la: eo, vbi longior dies est 16 horarum, cum ⅓ & elevatur polus 50 ½ gradus. Continet hoc clima 185 milliaria.
units.tr: to where the longer day is 16 hours and one-third, and the pole is raised 50 and a half degrees. This climate contains 185 miles.

units.la: Differentia inter initium & finem omnium climatum est 3 ⅓ horarum: & in altitudine poli 38 graduum.
units.tr: The difference between the beginning and the end of all the climates is 3⅓ hours, and in the elevation of the pole it is 38 degrees.

units.la: Summa spaciorum in omnibus climatibus consurgit ad 2140 milliaria.
units.tr: The sum of the distances in all the climates amounts to 2140 miles.

units.la: 1 Vt certo cognoscatur ambitus terrae, necessarium est, habere nos rationem mensurarum geodaeticarum: terram enim metimur stadiis, schoenis aut parasangis, item milliariis. Minima mensura est digitus trasuerus, quem Abilfedea Ismael in geographia sua Arabica, dicit aequari lex granis hordeaceis in longitudinem iuxta se inuicem collatis: cubitum secundum recentiores ait continere viginti quatuor digitos; Alfraganus autem dicit cubitum continere lex communes palmos: ex quo apparet palmum secundum Alfraganum constare quatuor digitis, quod etiam alii autores tradiderunt. Praeterea conuenit Alfraganus cum Abilfedea in mensuratione milliarii: vterque enim adfert, milliare secundum recentiores continere quatuor millia cubitorum. Quid sit parasanga, aut παρασάγγης luculenter ostendit Abilfedea, quando ait, parasangam apud vetustiores & recentiores autores completi tria milliaria. Scribitur hoc vocabulum apud Arabes cum quatuor literis radicalibus, videlicet, Phe, Refch, Sin, & Cheth, & in pronunciatione ante Cheth exprimitur litera n: hinc extitit nomen Pharasanga siue Parasanga: vt annotaui in Institutionibus meis Arabicae & Turcicae linguae, quas me breui editurum esse confido. Significat autem ἔτυμον[?] parasangæ nihil aliud, quàm Persicum schœnum, hoc est, funiculum siue mensuram triginta stadiorum, quæ æquantur tribus milliariis Italicis, seu paruo milliari Germanico. Quòd autem σχοῖνος[?] constet 30 stadiis, ex Marino ostendit Ptolemæus lib. 1 geographiæ, cap. 11 & 12, ubi dicitur 16280 stadia æquari 876 schoe-nis, hoc est parasangis: item 24000 stadia valere 800 schoenos, h.e. parasangas: propterea Herodotus in errore versatur, qui putat σχοῖνον[?] esse sexaginta stadia.
units.tr: 1 To know the circumference of the earth with certainty, we need to take account of geodetic measures, for we measure the earth in stadia, schoenes or parasangs, and likewise in miles. The smallest measure is the transverse finger, which Abilfeda Ismael in his Arabic Geography says equals six barleycorns laid end to end in length. According to more recent writers, a cubit contains twenty-four fingers, but Alfraganus says a cubit contains six common palms. From this it appears that, according to Alfraganus, a palm consists of four fingers, as other authors have also taught. Moreover, Alfraganus agrees with Abilfeda on the measure of the mile, for each states that, according to more recent writers, a mile contains four thousand cubits. What a parasang is, or παρασάγγης [parasanga], Abilfeda clearly shows when he says that among both older and more recent authors a parasang makes three miles. In Arabic this word is written with four radical letters, namely Phe, Reš, Sin and Cheth, and in pronunciation an n is sounded before Cheth; hence arose the name Pharasanga or Parasanga, as I noted in my Institutes of the Arabic and Turkish languages, which I trust I shall soon publish. The etymology [ἔτυμον] of parasang signifies nothing other than the Persian schoenus [σχοῖνος], that is, a cord or measure of thirty stadia, which equals three Italian miles or one small German mile. That the schoenus consists of thirty stadia Ptolemy shows from Marinus in book 1 of his Geography, chapters 11 and 12, where it is said that 16,280 stadia equal 876 schoenes, that is, parasangs; likewise 24,000 stadia are worth 800 schoenes, that is, parasangs. Therefore Herodotus is mistaken, for he thinks the schoenus [σχοῖνον] is sixty stadia.

units.la: Probat autem Alfraganus experientia & autoritate, uni gradui coelesti in terra respondere quinquaginta sex milliaria, cū duabus tertiis unius milliaris. Si enim itinera tam terrestria quàm marina consideremus, manifestum euadit, posse nos intra biduum conficere gradum coelestem, seu quinquaginta sex milliaria, si rectà iter instituamus. quis enim diebus æquino-ctialibus mediocri passu nō peragret quotidie viginti octo milliaria Italica, h.e. septem communia Germanica? quin immò Albategnius cap. 6, asserit ad confi-ciendum unum gradum coelestem requiri iter bidui.
units.tr: Alfraganus, however, proves by experience and authority that one celestial degree corresponds on earth to fifty-six and two-thirds miles. For if we consider journeys both by land and by sea, it becomes plain that we can complete a celestial degree, or fifty-six miles, within two days, if we travel in a straight line. For who on the equinoctial days would not, at an ordinary pace, cover twenty-eight Italian miles a day, that is, seven common German miles? Indeed Albategnius, chapter 6, asserts that two days' journey is required to complete one celestial degree.

units.la: Adhæc adducit Alfraganus autoritatem Almamonis & aliorum Arabum astronomorum, qui tradiderunt uni gradui coelesti in terra respondere quinquaginta sex milliaria, cum ⅓ unius milliaris. Sanè Abilfedea in principio operis sui geographici commemorat præ-cepto Almamonis regis Arabum seu Califæ Babylo-nii quosdam ablegatos fuisse, qui in campis Singar & vicinis maribus iuxta rectum iter & poli situm, ob-seruarent, quot milliaria responderent uni gradui coe-lesti: & deprehensum fuisse ab illis, in uno conficien-do gradu quinquaginta sex milliaria sine fractione ulla, nonnunquam præter quinquaginta sex milliaria tertiam partem milliaris, hoc est 1 3 3 3 ⅓ cubitare-quiri. Et R.Abraham filius Chaia in sphæra sua cap. 9, (vt habet codex manuscriptus in bibliotheca Palatina) fere idem refert, tempore Almamonis amir al-mumanin, h.e. regis Arabum fidelium, compertum esse vni gradui cœlesti responderein terra milliaria 5 6[?] ⅓: quatenus milliare vnum costet 4000 cubitis. Autor theoriarum, qui manuscriptus & cū Summa Anglica compactus extat in bibliotheca Palatina, hæc refert: Experimentauerunt autem Philosophi tempore Maimonis regis & aliorum magnatum quàm plurimum, quòd vnu gradus sphæræ terræ, qui respondet vni gradui cœli, haberet proportionem ad ipsum: & eundem gradum terræ mensurauerunt diligenter: & inuenerunt eum esse milliaria 5 6[?] & duas tertias vnius milliaris: quod milliare est ex cubitis 4000. Cubitum autem sic inuenerunt, posuerunt enim grana 6 hordei contigui in vno ordine: & spacium quod dicta[?] sex grana hordei occupant, appellauerunt pollum: & de 4 pollis fecerunt palmam, & de 4 palmis fecerunt cubitum. Hactenus ille. Ex quibus apparet cum per pollum significare digitum, qui complectatur grana hordei sex: & quatuor digitos vult efficere palmum, & quatuor palmos efficere cubitum. atqui secundum Alfraganū sex palmi efficiunt cubitum. Habeo etiam penes me manuscriptum libru octauum geographiæ Ptolemei, vbi statim à principio annotatur, copertum esse gradu vnū maioris circuli in cœlo valere 5 6 milliaria, & 40 minuta vnius milliaris. Quod ad Ptolemæum attinet, qui stadiamis superficiem terræ metitur, fatetur ille lib. 1 geographiæ cap. 7 & 11, vni gradui cœlesti cóuenire fere quingenta stadia, vt totus ambitus terræ constet 180000 1800000 stadiis: idem asserit lib.7 geographiæ cap.5. Quingenta stadia conficiunt 16 ⅔ parasangas, hoc est milliaria 48 ⅔, quæ vni gradui tribuit Ptolemæus: at Plinius & Strabo gradui cœlesti assignant septingenta stadia, hoc est, 21⅓ parasangas, seu 69 ⅓ milliaria: ex quo apparet Arabes media via ingredi, quando statuunt vni gradui cœlesti respondere 56 ⅔ milliaria Italica, hoc est 14 ⅔ milliaria communia Germanica.
units.tr: Besides, Alfraganus cites the authority of Almamon and other Arab astronomers, who taught that one celestial degree corresponds on earth to fifty-six and a third miles. Indeed Abilfeda, at the beginning of his geographical work, records that by the command of Almamon, king of the Arabs or caliph of Babylon, certain men were sent out who, in the plains of Singar and the neighbouring regions, along a straight route and under the pole's position, were to observe how many miles correspond to one celestial degree; and they found that in completing one degree there were fifty-six miles without any fraction, and sometimes beyond fifty-six miles a third part of a mile, that is, 1333⅓ cubits. And Rabbi Abraham son of Chaia, in his Sphere, chapter 9 (as the manuscript in the Palatine library has it), reports almost the same: in the time of Almamon, amir al-mumanin, that is, king of the faithful Arabs, it was found that one celestial degree corresponds on earth to 56⅓ miles, since one mile costs 4000 cubits. The author of the Theories, which survives in manuscript and bound together with the Summa Anglica in the Palatine library, relates these things: The philosophers in the time of King Maimon and of many other magnates made many experiments, namely that one degree of the earth's sphere, which corresponds to one degree of heaven, has a proportion to it; and they measured that same degree of the earth carefully, and found it to be 56 and two-thirds of a mile, which mile is made of 4000 cubits. They discovered the cubit in this way: they placed six barleycorns touching one another in a single row, and the space which those six grains of barley occupy they called a thumb [pollex]; and from four thumbs they made a palm, and from four palms they made a cubit. So far he. From these things it appears that by thumb he means a finger, which takes in six barleycorns; and he wishes four fingers to make a palm and four palms a cubit. But according to Alfraganus six palms make a cubit. I also have in my possession a manuscript of the eighth book of Ptolemy's Geography, where at the very beginning it is noted that one degree of a great circle in the heavens is worth 56⅔ miles and 40 minutes of a mile. As for Ptolemy, who measures the surface of the earth in stadia, he admits in book 1 of the Geography, chapters 7 and 11, that about five hundred stadia correspond to one celestial degree, so that the whole circumference of the earth amounts to 180,000 (or 1,800,000) stadia; he asserts the same in book 7 of the Geography, chapter 5. Five hundred stadia make 16⅔ parasangs, that is, 48⅔ miles, which Ptolemy assigns to one degree; but Pliny and Strabo assign seven hundred stadia to a celestial degree, that is, 21⅓ parasangs or 69⅓ miles. From this it appears that the Arabs take a middle course when they state that one celestial degree corresponds to 56⅔ Italian miles, that is, 14⅔ common German miles.

units.la: 2 Considerat Alfraganus climata secundù latitudinem dimidiæ horæ: hoc est, inter principium & finem vnius eiusdemque climatis dicit tantum spacii intercedere, vt logissimus dies regionum earum quæ ad finem climatis collocantur, dimidia hora excedat longissimum diem in illis locis, quę ad principium climatis eiusdem collocatur. Sumit autem primi climatis medium ab illis locis, in quibus prolixior dies est tredecim horarum: vt principium illius eo incidat, vbi longior dies habet quadrantem horæ minus; finis autem eius eo pertingat, vbi maximus dies habet quadrante horę plus quàm tredecim horas. idem iudicium est de reliquis climatibus. 3 Quæ hoc loco interpres Hebræus dicit extare in codice Arabico, ipse ad fine huius opusculi reposuit: vt in primis scholiis monui. 4 Nô repetit hic Alfraganus, quot milliaria in terra conti-neat circuferentia maximi circuli, vt loânes Hispalensis in vulgata versione, & Hebræus noster interpres in sua translatione existimarunt, qui hic repetit ambitu terrestrem cótinere 20400 milliaria: sed Alfraganus supputat septem prædictorum climatum spacia: primum enim complectitur 440 milliaria, secundum 400 mill. tertium 350 mill. quartum 300 mill. quintum 255 mill. sextum 210 milliaria, septimum
units.tr: 2 Alfraganus considers the climates according to latitude by half an hour: that is, he says that between the beginning and the end of one and the same climate there lies only so much space that the longest day in the regions placed at the end of the climate exceeds the longest day in those places placed at the beginning of the same climate by half an hour. He takes the middle of the first climate from those places in which the longer day is thirteen hours, so that its beginning falls where the longest day has a quarter of an hour less, and its end reaches where the longest day has a quarter of an hour more than thirteen hours. The same reasoning holds for the other climates. 3 What the Hebrew interpreter says at this point is found in an Arabic codex, but he himself placed it at the end of this little work, as I noted in the first scholia. 4 Here Alfraganus does not repeat how many miles the circumference of the greatest circle contains on earth, as John of Seville in the Vulgate version and our Hebrew interpreter in his translation thought, who here repeats that the earthly circumference contains 20,400 miles; but Alfraganus reckons the spaces of the seven aforesaid climates: the first, for instance, comprises 440 miles, the second 400 miles, the third 350 miles, the fourth 300 miles, the fifth 255 miles, the sixth 210 miles, the seventh

units.la: {y} Suppl. 185 milliaria comprehendit: quæ omnia si addantur, cõsurgit summa 2140 milliariorum, vt recte hic scripficautor versionis Latinæ, quæ manuscripta exstat in bibliotheca Palatina.
units.tr: {y} Supplement: it comprises 185 miles. If all these are added together, the sum comes to 2140 miles, as the author of the Latin version, which survives in manuscript in the Palatine library, rightly writes here.

units.la: De nominibus regionum & ciuitatum in terra notarum, & quem habeant respectum ad climata.
units.tr: On the names of regions and cities known on earth, and the relation they have to the climates.
CHAPTER XI.

units.la: COmmemoremus nunc nomina regionum & ciuitatum, quæ in singulis climatibus sunt nota: & a locis orientalibus incipiamus, vbi declarauerimus quid per longitudinem & latitudinem regionum intelligamus.
units.tr: Let us now recall the names of the regions and cities that are known in each climate, beginning with the eastern places, after explaining what we mean by the longitude and latitude of regions.

units.la: Longitudo cuiusuis ciuitatis, est distantia eius ab extremo oriente vel occidente habitabili, quæ in æquatore numeratur ab vno meridiano ad alterum.
units.tr: The longitude of any city is its distance from the farthest inhabited east or west, reckoned along the equator from one meridian to another.

units.la: Latitudo autem est distantia ciuitatis ab æquatore: quæ semper æquat eleuationem poli supra horizontem.
units.tr: The latitude, however, is the distance of a city from the equator, which always equals the elevation of the pole above the horizon.

units.la: Primum clima in extremo oriente habet regionem Sin, in qua est ciuitas regis Sin versus meridiem: versus summitatem eius est Alfeme: deinde trāsit per littora maris meridionalis in regnum Indiæ: postea peruenit ad insulam Acubil, & secat mare vsque ad insulam Arabum & terram Alimen, in qua ciuitates celebres sunt Ephat, Niuen, Hadromec, Haden, Sencha, Alachin, Mandre, Cubelar, Tafre, Madra & Sabe: deinde pergit versus mare rubrum, & transit in regiones Æthiopum, secatq; Nilum Ægypti: in regno Æthiopum insignes civitates sunt Huma, Dyntala, & multæ aliæ. Hoc idem clima postremo tendit ad occidentem, & per meridionales regiones Barbarorum transit, donec perveniat ad mare occidentale.
units.tr: The first climate, at the farthest east, has the region of Sin, in which lies the city of the king of Sin, toward the south. Toward its northern extent is Alfeme. Then it passes along the shores of the southern sea into the kingdom of India, and afterwards reaches the island of Acubil, and cuts across the sea as far as the island of the Arabs and the land of Alimen. In this land the famous cities are Ephat, Niuen, Hadromec, Haden, Sencha, Alachin, Mandre, Cubelar, Tafre, Madra and Sabe. Then it proceeds toward the Red Sea, passes into the regions of the Ethiopians, and cuts across the Nile of Egypt. In the kingdom of the Ethiopians the notable cities are Huma, Dyntala, and many others. Finally this same climate stretches westward, passes through the southern regions of the Barbarians, until it reaches the western sea.

units.la: Secundum clima incipit ab oriente, & transit per regiones Sin & Indiæ, qua parte civitates sunt Almansoria, Aliabran & Adubil: deinde vadit per combinationes maris viridis & Albasara, & secat infulam Arabum, circa terram Nagoni & Tuema: ubi celebres civitates sunt Aliomenlach[?], Albarahen, Hogor, Vetabh, Alior, Mecha, Acajis & Geda: postea secat mare rubrum, & transit per Sajir Ægypti, secatq; Nilum, qua parte civitates sunt Cabrus, Hacuim, Hansche[?], Astar[?], Azsahe, Afin & Esron: deinde pervenit versus occidentem in regnum Africæ, & transit regiones Barbarorum, donec attingat mare occidentale.
units.tr: The second climate begins in the east and passes through the regions of Sin and India, where the cities are Almansoria, Aliabran and Adubil. Then it goes through the channels of the Green Sea and Albasara, and cuts across the island of the Arabs, around the land of Nagoni and Tuema. There the famous cities are Aliomenlach[?], Albarahen, Hogor, Vetabh, Alior, Mecha, Acajis and Geda. Afterwards it cuts across the Red Sea and passes through the Sajir of Egypt, and cuts across the Nile, where the cities are Cabrus, Hacuim, Hansche[?], Astar[?], Azsahe, Afin and Esron. Then it reaches westward into the kingdom of Africa, crosses the regions of the Barbarians, until it touches the western sea.

units.la: Tertium clima incipit ab oriente, & transit partem septentrionalem regni Sin: deinde pergit ad regiones Kebil, Carmen, Seruasten, & Alexandriam Muhamedanam, Ebroab & Asoceran: postea transit per littora maris Albasara, ubi civitates sunt Astachar, Iothor, Fefe, Sabor, Secren, Siref, Kalbone, Senemir & Maruben: & vadit per diœceses Alguez & Algrath, ubi urbes sunt Albasa, Guaisit, Baged, Ascua, Alenbei, & Sond: postea transit per regiones ⌣Affem[?], id est Syria, vbi ciui-tates sunt ⌣Albar[?], Sulmina, Hummis, Damascus, Sur[?], id est Tyrus, Acim, Tabaria, Cafaria, Amsurf[?], Beit almacdis, hoc est domus sanctificationis, sine Ierusalem, ⌣Alaramti[?], Ascalon, Gaza, Modian & Alkusim[?]: deinde secat inferiora terra Aegypti, vbi vrbes sunt Alforme, Canis, Damiat, Fizarat Aegypti, Alphanun & Alexandria: deinde transit per regiones Barcha, postea per regiones Africa, vbi est ciuitas Alkaharuez: tandem peruenit ad mare occidentale.
units.tr: The third climate begins in the east and passes through the northern part of the kingdom of Sin. Then it goes on to the regions of Kebil, Carmen, Seruasten, and Muhammadan Alexandria, Ebroab and Asoceran. Afterwards it passes along the shores of the Albasara Sea, where the cities are Astachar, Iothor, Fefe, Sabor, Secren, Siref, Kalbone, Senemir and Maruben. It passes through the districts of Alguez and Algrath, where the towns are Albasa, Guaisit, Baged, Ascua, Alenbei and Sond. Afterwards it crosses the regions of Affem, that is Syria, where the cities are Albar[?], Sulmina, Hummis, Damascus, Sur[?], that is Tyre, Acim, Tiberias, Cafaria, Amsurf[?], Beit almacdis, that is the house of sanctification, or Jerusalem, Alaramti[?], Ascalon, Gaza, Modian and Alkusim[?]. Then it cuts through lower Egypt, where the towns are Alforme, Canis, Damiat, Fizarat of Egypt, Alphanun and Alexandria. Then it passes through the regions of Barca, afterwards through the regions of Africa, where there is the city of Alkaharuez. At last it reaches the western sea.

units.la: Quartū clima incipit a parte orientis, & transit per regiones Achebit, deinde per Coraffen & sunt ibi ciuitates Maforia, Afmisema[?], Fragana, Samarcant, Belha, Bochera, Haraba, Hamquena, Magudur, Astrien[?], Saras, Idus, Nisabor, Iurgen, Comis, Cabastren, Dabendimech, Gorduben, Deilen, Arci, Ispatlim, Kem, Heden, Neden, Atenaz[?], Huba, Senroz, Saram, Oce, Almosil, Calbet, Nasabin[?], Euit, Caput fontis, Calicale, Sunzat[?], Hara, Arechah & Kar-kesie: postea transit per partem septentrionalem regionis Affem, id est Syria, vbi ciuitates sunt Belis, Manbet, Ifmisar, Malchana, Zacara, Habeb, Canfirim, An-tiochia, Tripolis, Almafisa[?], Faica, Ecclesia magna, Ozma, Tarsus, Amudia: deinde venit ad mare Affem, id est Syriacu, vbi insulae sunt Cyprus & Rhodus: tandem vergit versus occidentem & transit regione Tange, donec peruenit ad mare occidentale.
units.tr: The fourth climate begins from the side of the east and passes through the regions of Achebit, then through Coraffen. There are the cities Maforia, Afmisema[?], Fragana, Samarcand, Belha, Bochera, Haraba, Hamquena, Magudur, Astrien[?], Saras, Idus, Nisabor, Iurgen, Comis, Cabastren, Dabendimech, Gorduben, Deilen, Arci, Ispatlim, Kem, Heden, Neden, Atenaz[?], Huba, Senroz, Saram, Oce, Almosil, Calbet, Nasabin[?], Euit, Caput fontis, Calicale, Sunzat[?], Hara, Arechah and Karkesie. Afterwards it passes through the northern part of the region of Affem, that is Syria, where the cities are Belis, Manbet, Ifmisar, Malchana, Zacara, Habeb, Canfirim, Antioch, Tripoli, Almafisa[?], Faica, the Great Church, Ozma, Tarsus and Amudia. Then it comes to the sea of Affem, that is the Syrian sea, where the islands are Cyprus and Rhodes. Finally it turns westward and crosses the region of Tange, until it reaches the western sea.

units.la: 𝒬Quintum clima incipit etiam ab oriente in re-gionibus Gog & Magog, deinde transit per partem septentrionalem Chorassen, vbi ciuitates sunt Ale-rez, quod est emporium, Chengebet, Chobarizmue, Aftualno, Alicesce, Alkatabinde, Altabigen, diæce-sis Armeniæ, Barcaha, Nesui, Sciassen[?], Ardon & Chalat: vaditque per regiones Romanorum super Charsana, Cara, & Romam magnam: deinde trā-sit per littora maris Alsemi, id est Syriaci, a parte septentrionis, postea per regiones Hispanorum ince-dit, donec perueniat ad mare occidentale.
units.tr: The fifth climate also begins in the east, in the regions of Gog and Magog, then passes through the northern part of Chorassen, where the cities are Alerez, which is a market town, Chengebet, Chobarizmue, Aftualno, Alicesce, Alkatabinde, Altabigen, the diocese of Armenia, Barcaha, Nesui, Sciassen[?], Ardon and Chalat. It goes through the regions of the Romans above Charsana, Cara, and Great Rome. Then it passes along the shores of the Alsemi Sea, that is the Syrian Sea, on the northern side, afterwards it advances through the regions of the Spaniards, until it reaches the western sea.

units.la: Sextū clima incipit ab oriente & trāsit regiones Gog & Magog, & Alazoh[?], fecatq; medium mare Iurgem usq; ad regiones Romanorum, & trāsit per Iuren, Menese, Eradia, Constatinopolim, & regiones Burgen, & peruenit ad mare occidentale.
units.tr: The sixth climate begins in the east and passes through the regions of Gog and Magog and Alazoh[?], and cuts across the middle sea of Iurgem as far as the regions of the Romans, and passes through Iuren, Menese, Eradia, Constantinople, and the regions of Burgen, and reaches the western sea.

units.la: Septimum clima incipit ab oriente, & a parte septetrionali regionis Gog trāsit per regiones Tur-cia, & littora Iurgen a parte septetrionis: postea secat mare Romanorū, & trāsit per regiones Burgen & Sclauorū, atq; sic peruenit ad mare occidentale.
units.tr: The seventh climate begins in the east, and from the northern part of the region of Gog passes through the regions of Turkey and the shores of Iurgen on the northern side. Afterwards it cuts across the Roman sea and passes through the regions of Burgen and the Slavs, and so reaches the western sea.

units.la: Quod autem est post hoc clima usque ad complementum loci habitabilis, quantum nos nouimus, incipit ab oriente in regionibus Gog, deinde transit per regiones Alleceti & Abmugor, & terra Turcia: postea vadit per regiones Alahin, deinde per Tyr, postea per Fusen, deinde per Sclauos, donec per-veniat ad mare occidentale. Caput hoc,si res ipsas spectes,facillimum est:si au-tem ad nomina regionum & ciuitatum,quae commemorantur,attendas,maximè est perplexum. Nam editiones omnes vulgatae hic corruptissimae sunt:quin etiam interpres noster Hebraeus suo arbitrio vtitur, & à veris appellationibus plurimùm aberrat: sola ver-sio Latina,quae manuscripta, sed nunquam hactenus visa, extat in bibliotheca Palatina,propinquissimè ad mentem Alfragani accedere videtur: propterea hanc in omnibus secutus sum, etsi mihi dubium non sit, multa quoque nomina in ea depravata esse, quae tamen corrigi non possunt, nisi etiam habeatur authenticus, linguaque Arabica conscriptus Alfragani codex.
units.tr: As for what lies beyond this climate, as far as the completion of the inhabited place, so far as we know, it begins in the east in the regions of Gog, then passes through the regions of Alleceti and Abmugor, and the land of Turkey. Afterwards it goes through the regions of Alahin, then through Tyr, afterwards through Fusen, then through the Slavs, until it reaches the western sea. This chapter, if you look at the things themselves, is very easy; but if you attend to the names of the regions and cities that are mentioned, it is most perplexing. For all the printed editions here are most corrupt; indeed our Hebrew translator follows his own judgement and differs very much from the true names. Only the Latin version, which is a manuscript never yet seen but extant in the Palatine library, seems to come closest to the mind of Alfragan; therefore I have followed it in everything, although I do not doubt that many names in it are also corrupted, which cannot be corrected unless the authentic codex of Alfragan, written in the Arabic language, is also available.

units.la: Vt autem vera historia commemoratorum locorum habeatur, plurimum prodest cōsulere Mappam mundi Arabicam, seu typum generalem orbis, qui cum expositione Arabica ante annos aliquot in lucem prodiit: cuiusmodi penes se esse mihi scripsit nobilissimus & clarissimus vir Josephus Scaliger: eiusq; exemplar ego Moguntiae vidi ante bibliothecam Patrum Ignatianorum. Nec minus nos erudire potest geographia Abilfedeae Ismaelis, quae Arabicè scripta extat in bibliotheca Palatina: haec ipsa Geographia est, quà Guilielmus Postellus ex oriente aduexit, & cum aliis quibusdam libris Arabicis, laudatissimae memoriae Principi Palatino, Ottroni Henrico vendidit. De ea Conradus Gesnerus in bibliotheca sua haec scribit:
units.tr: Moreover, to obtain a true account of the places mentioned, it is very helpful to consult the Arabic map of the world, or general figure of the globe, which appeared some years ago with an Arabic explanation. The most noble and distinguished man Joseph Scaliger wrote to me that he had such a map in his possession, and I myself saw a copy of it at Mainz, in front of the library of the Ignatian Fathers. Nor can the geography of Abulfeda, the Ismaelite, teach us less; it is extant in Arabic in the Palatine library. This is that very geography which Guillaume Postel brought from the East, and sold together with certain other Arabic books to the Palatine Prince Otto Henry, of most praiseworthy memory. Conrad Gesner writes of it in his library as follows:

units.la: Abilfedeas cosmographus insignis,& Ptolemaeo par aut superior in describendo orbe Ismaelitis subiectio, cum no-minibus ad nostra tempora aptatis, à Guilielmo Postello ex oriente aduectus est: cuius libri compendium ex sua translatione, Venetiis Postellus D. Rhamnusio ciuireli-quit: quod ut alterum volumen de nouo orbe edere insti-tuisset[?]. tuisset. Fuit autem Abilfedeas princeps Syriæ, Affyria & Persidis, qui ante 300 annos vixit circa Coelen Syriam. Sanè geographiam istam Abilfedeæ vetustam esse ex eo apparet, quòd sit descripta, vt habetur in fine Codicis, anno Hegiræ 721:a quo tempore elapsi sunt ad nostram ætatem anni Arabici 175.
