Huius Abilfedeæ etiam meminit Ortelius in geographico indice, quando exponit Babyloniam Arabibus Baldach appellari.
units.tr: Abulfeda, a distinguished cosmographer, equal or superior to Ptolemy in describing the world, subject to the Ishmaelites, with names adapted to our times, was brought from the East by Guillaume Postel. Postel left an abridgement of this book, from his own translation, at Venice to D. Rhamnusio, with the intention of publishing a second volume on the new world. Abulfeda was prince of Syria, Assyria and Persia, and lived about 300 years ago near Coele Syria. Indeed, that this geography of Abulfeda is old appears from the fact that it was written, as is stated at the end of the codex, in the year of the Hegira 721; since that time 175 Arabic years have elapsed to our age. Ortelius also mentions this Abulfeda in his geographical index, where he explains that Babylon is called Baldach by the Arabs.

units.la: Vtinam verò totam geographiam Abilfedeæ Latinam redditam haberemus, sicut Arabicè extat in bibliotheca Palatina: non dubium esset, quin ex ea geographi nostri magnam vtilitatem essent percepturi, & longitudines ac latitudines regionum rectius assignaturi, & de controuersiis plerisque melius iudicaturi.
units.tr: Indeed, if we had the whole geography of Abulfeda translated into Latin, as it exists in Arabic in the Palatine library, there would be no doubt that our geographers would derive great benefit from it, would assign the longitudes and latitudes of regions more correctly, and would judge better about many controversies.

units.la: Quis enim nescit in geographicis plerisque numerorum notas summè depravatas esse? quis ignorat plurimas & fere inextricabiles existere controuersias?
units.tr: For who does not know that in most geographical tables the notation of the numbers is greatly corrupted? Who is unaware that there are very many and almost inextricable controversies?

units.la: Vrbis Hierosolymitanæ longitudo Prolemæo ponitur 66 graduum, 30 minutorum: Abilfedeæ autem est 56 graduum, 30 minutorum.
units.tr: The longitude of the city of Jerusalem is given by Ptolemy as 66 degrees, 30 minutes; but by Abulfeda it is 56 degrees, 30 minutes.

units.la: Prolemæus Alexandriæ metropoli Ægypti attribuit longitudinem graduum 60, minutorum 30: sed Abilfedea princeps Ifmaelitarum, ex obseruatione summi astronomi Aben Sahid, & autoris geographiæ Græcæ, qui tempore Almamonis in Arabicam linguam versa est, dicit esse graduum 51, minutorum 20: & iuxta canonem Alberuni 52 graduum, 8 minutorum.
units.tr: Ptolemy assigns to Alexandria, the metropolis of Egypt, a longitude of 60 degrees 30 minutes. But Abilfedea, prince of the Ishmaelites, relying on the observation of the greatest astronomer Aben Sahid and on the author of the Greek geography, which was translated into Arabic in the time of Almamon, says that it is 51 degrees 20 minutes. According to the canon of Alberuni, it is 52 degrees 8 minutes.

units.la: Idem Rhodo insulæ, in qua Hipparchus diligentissimus & sagacissimus rerum astronomicarum obseruator floruit, assignat longitudinem 51 graduum, 40 minutorum; cui Ptolemæus tribuit 58 gradus, & 30 minuta. Macha metropolis felicis Arabiæ aliquibus censetur habere in longitudine grad. 71, & 45 minuta: verum Abilfedea tradit eam esse 67 graduum, 31 minutorum: cuius sententiæ adstipulatur Aben Ragel in abaco geographico: idem docet scriptum Saraceni de principiis astronomiæ, cum Meflahala Noribergæ anno 1549 editum: vbi cap. 18 hæc leguntur: Adscien-dum vero rectitudinem meridiei, scias longitudinem Mecha, quæ est sexaginta septem gradus ab occidente, aut sexaginta septem gradus & medietas: & latitudinem ipsius, quæ est vnius & viginti graduum, & medietas, aut duæ tertiæ. Vbi in exemplari pro Mechæ, male excusum est Metre: & decipitur Ioachimus Hel-lerus, qui in annotatione marginali existimat a Saraceno intelligi nomen vrbis Iahen: nam cap. 22 autor ille ait, latitudinem Iahen, esse triginta octo graduum circiter: hic vero tribuit Mechæ latitudinem 21 grad. 30 minutorum: quam etiam ei assignat Abilfedea: nostri autem Geographi dimidio gradu maiorem faciunt. Vt autem nos ex controueriis expediamus, sciendum est duplex dari initium longitudinis: vnum ab insulis fortunatis, alterum a littore citimo oceani occidentalis: præterea tenendum est, interuallum inter insulas fortunatas & littus oceani occidentalis esse decem graduum: quæ duo Abilfedea in geographia sua diligenter inculcat: non enim procul a principio stilo Arabico hæc scribit: Vtique commemoratur quod initium terræ habitatæ ab occidente sit in insulis quæ nominantur fortunatæ, & modo deserta sunt: has insulas quidam faciunt initium longitudinis, quidam vero constituunt littus maris occidentalis initium: est autem differentia decem graduum, in aquatore[?] numeratorum. Sub finem introductionis ante seriem tabularum ita concludit: Quod ad longitudines attinet, quæ enumerantur in hoc libro, sumuntur illa a littoà littore maris occidentalis : itaque ad decem gradus minores sunt longitudinibus illis, quæ capiuntur ab insulis fortunatis. His suppositis dicimus Ptolemæum cum vetustioribus Græcis longitudines capere ab insulis fortunatis: Abilfedea autem cum Arabibus longitudines numerat a termino occidentis noto & insigni, qualis est citimum littus Oceani Hesperii, a columnis Herculis vltrò citroque in austrum & septentrionem exporrectum, & sub vno quasi meridiano gradus latitudinis triginta complectens. Si ergo longitudo Hierofolymitana Ptolemæi coferatur[?] cum ea, quam ponit Abilfedea, præcisè deprehenditur esse[?] discrimen decem graduum. quare utraque recte est assignata: quandoquidem inter insulas fortunatas & litus oceani occidentalis interiacent decem gradus. At si longitudo Alexandrina Ptolemæi conferatur cum ea, quam assignat Abilfedea, discrimen deprehenditur tantùm 9 grad. & 10 minutorum: itaque 50 minuta desiderantur, quo minus recte a Ptolemæo videatur assignata longitudo Alexandrina: cum ex hypothesi Abilfedeæ Alexandria debeat distare ab insulis fortunatis 61 gradus, & 20 minuta. Ad insulam Rhodum quod attinet, manifestum se prodit mendum : siue enim Alexandria ponatur habere ab insulis fortunatis longitudinem 61 gradus, 20 minut. siue 60 gradus & 30 minut. non potest Rhodo assignari longitudo 58 graduū[?], & 30 minut. vt traditur libro 7[?] geographiæ Ptolemaïcæ. Nam Ptolemæus libro quinto Almagesti, capite tertio expressè testatur, Alexandriam & Rhodum eandem longitudinem habere, cum ait, [illegible, ~30 letters] Itaque Abilfedea propius accedit ad rei veritatem: quando à littore oceani occidentalis Alexandriæ tribuit 51 [?] gradus,&c 20 min. &c Rhodo adscribit 51 [?] grad.& 40 minuta:ex quo apparet eum Alexandriam &c Rhodum sub eodem fere meridiano collocare. Neque mirum videri debet, si tabulæ geographicæ Ptolemæi aliquatulum hic aberrare deprehendantur, cum in locis occidetalibus nullam fere proportionem obseruet ad insulas fortunatas. Exemplum sumamus de Corduba,cui Abilfedea tribuit longitudinem a littore maris occidentalis iuxta canonem Alberuni 8 grad. 40 min. sed addit esse 9 grad.&c 20 min. iuxta autorem geographiæ Græcæ: Secundum Aben Sahid autem esse 10 grad.8 min. atque hanc longitudinem præ cæteris elegit Abilfedea.Neque dubitandum est de hac Arabum observatione: cum enim Hispaniam & Mauritaniam non tantum perlustrarint, verum etiam incoluerint: verisimile non est, eos ignorasse quot gradibus Corduba absit à littore maris occidentalis: præsertim cum diligenter recessum maris Hesperii notarint, idque modo hic, modo illic continentem alluere animaduerterint: quo factum est vt diuersos diuersis temporibus limites littori constituerint. Atqui in tabulis Ptolemaicis, quas nos habemus,tribuitur Cordubæ longitudo ab insulis fortunatis 9 grad.&20 minutorum: quæ tamen est 19 grad.&c 20 minutorum:unde appareret, ab ignaro aliquo confusa fuisse diuersa longitudinum initia, & in librum illum geographicum, quem plerique Ptolemæo adscribunt, congesta. Sed librum istum non esse genuinum partum Ptolemæi, non tantum allatæ contradictiones ostendunt: verum etiam locus ille in lib. 1 Almagesti capite 6 satis indicat, ubi sub æquatore exiguam habitationem esse pronunciat, cum tamen in geographia multas regiones & civitates æquatori subiectas cōmemoret. Vt autem clarius elucescat, Arabes consentanea veritati dicere: conferamus inter fe Alexandriam & Cordubam. Al-beruni tribuit Alexandriæ longitudinem 51 grad. 8 min. Cordubæ 8 grad. 40 minuta: subtracta minore à maiore, relinquitur interuallum inter Cordubam & Alexandriam, scilicet 43 grad. & 28 minuta. Aben Sa-hid longitudinem designat Alexandriæ 51 grad. & 20 min. Cordubæ vero 10 grad. & 8 min. subtracta mi-nore à maiore, relinquitur interuallum inter Alexan-driam & Cordubam grad. 41 & 12 min. Autor geo-graphiæ Græcæ tribuit quoque Alexandriæ 51 grad. & 20 minuta: sed Cordubæ assignat 9 grad. & 20 mi-nuta: subtracta longitudine minore à maiore, relin-quitur interuallum inter Alexandriam & Cordubam grad. 42. Cūm autem unū semper sit interuallum inter Alexandriam & Cordubam, opinari quis pos-set, Arabes secum pugnare: at hic obseruandum est, interuallum proprie non mutari, sed littus oceani oc-cidentalis modo accedere, modo recedere, cuius ra-tione interuallum videatur mutari: etsi enim Arabes ab insigni termino longitudines locorum computet: is tamen ratione maris & temporis instabilis est. Un-de intelligitur, limitandum esse pronunciatum Abil-fedæ, quādo ait, inter insulas Fortunatas & littus ma-ris occidentalis intercedere 10 gradus: hoc enim ipsius seculo verum erat, sed aliis temporibus aliter quoque res habere poterit. Quando de longitudine Mechæ quæritur, Arabibus potius vt orientalium regionum diligentissimis perueftigatoribus, quàm nostris geo-graphis credendum est: cùm enim Arabes Mechæ tri-buant longitudinem à littore oceani occidentalis 67 grad. & 31 minutorum: satis intelligitur Mecham à fortunatis infulis distare 77 grad. & 31 minut. sicut id expresse testatur Almagesti Arabici epitome, quę extat in bibliotheca Palatina, vbi ita scribitur: sciendum est lōgitudinem Mecha ab infulis fortunatis esse suptuaginta septem gradus & sextam partem vnius gradus: a littore autem maris occidentalis, sexaginta septem gradus & sextam partem vnius gradus.
units.tr: Ptolemy likewise gives Rhodes, where Hipparchus, the most diligent and acute observer of astronomical matters, flourished, a longitude of 51 degrees 40 minutes, while Ptolemy himself gives it 58 degrees 30 minutes. Some hold that Mecca, the metropolis of Arabia Felix, has a longitude of 71 degrees 45 minutes, but Abilfedea states that it is 67 degrees 31 minutes, and Aben Ragel in his geographical table agrees with him. The same is taught in the Saracen treatise on the principles of astronomy, published at Nuremberg in 1549 with Meflahala, where chapter 18 reads: In order to find the true direction of the meridian, you should know the longitude of Mecha, which is sixty-seven degrees to the west, or sixty-seven and a half degrees, and its latitude, which is twenty-one and a half degrees, or two-thirds. Here, in the printed copy, "Metre" has been wrongly printed for "Mecha", and Joachim Heller is misled, for in a marginal note he thinks the Saracen means the city of Iahen. For the same author says in chapter 22 that the latitude of Iahen is about thirty-eight degrees, whereas here he gives Mecha a latitude of 21 degrees 30 minutes, which Abilfedea also assigns to it; our geographers, however, make it half a degree greater. But that we may extricate ourselves from these disputes, it must be noted that there are two possible starting points for longitude: one from the Fortunate Islands, the other from the nearest shore of the western ocean. Besides, it must be borne in mind that the interval between the Fortunate Islands and the shore of the western ocean is ten degrees. Abilfedea insists on these two points carefully in his geography, for not far from the beginning he writes in Arabic: It is commonly recorded that the beginning of the inhabited earth in the west is in the islands called the Fortunate, which are now deserted. Some make these islands the starting point of longitude, others set the shore of the western sea as the starting point; the difference is ten degrees, counted in the equator. Near the end of the introduction, before the series of tables, he concludes thus: As for the longitudes which are enumerated in this book, they are taken from the coast of the western sea; therefore they are ten degrees less than those which are reckoned from the Fortunate Islands. Given these premises, we say that Ptolemy, with the older Greeks, reckons longitudes from the Fortunate Islands, while Abilfedea, with the Arabs, counts longitudes from a known and conspicuous boundary, namely the nearest shore of the Hesperian ocean, which stretches north and south from the Pillars of Hercules on both sides and, lying under what is almost a single meridian, covers thirty degrees of latitude. If then Ptolemy's longitude of Jerusalem is compared with that which Abilfedea gives, the difference is found to be exactly ten degrees, so both are rightly assigned, since ten degrees lie between the Fortunate Islands and the shore of the western ocean. But if Ptolemy's longitude of Alexandria is compared with that which Abilfedea assigns, the difference is found to be only 9 degrees 10 minutes; so 50 minutes are wanting, and Ptolemy's longitude of Alexandria appears to be not quite correct, since on Abilfedea's hypothesis Alexandria ought to be 61 degrees 20 minutes distant from the Fortunate Islands. As for the island of Rhodes, the error is plain: whether Alexandria is placed at 61 degrees 20 minutes from the Fortunate Islands or at 60 degrees 30 minutes, Rhodes cannot be assigned a longitude of 58 degrees 30 minutes, as is handed down in book 7 of Ptolemy's geography. For Ptolemy, in book 5 of the Almagest, chapter 3, clearly testifies that Alexandria and Rhodes have the same longitude, when he says [illegible, about thirty letters]. So Abilfedea comes closer to the truth, since he assigns Alexandria 51 degrees 20 minutes from the shore of the western ocean and gives Rhodes 51 degrees 40 minutes; from this it appears that he places Alexandria and Rhodes under almost the same meridian. Nor should it seem surprising if Ptolemy's geographical tables are found to stray a little here, since in western places he keeps almost no proportion to the Fortunate Islands. Let us take the example of Cordoba, to which Abilfedea assigns, according to the canon of Alberuni, a longitude from the shore of the western sea of 8 degrees 40 minutes, but he adds that by the Greek geographer it is 9 degrees 20 minutes, and according to Aben Sahid 10 degrees 8 minutes; and Abilfedea chose this longitude above the others. Nor ought we to doubt this observation of the Arabs, for since they not only traversed Spain and Mauritania but also inhabited them, it is not likely that they did not know by how many degrees Cordoba is distant from the shore of the western sea, especially since they carefully noted the recession of the Hesperian sea and observed that it washed the mainland now here, now there; and so it came about that they set different limits to the shore at different times. Yet in the Ptolemaic tables which we have, Cordoba is given a longitude from the Fortunate Islands of 9 degrees 20 minutes, which is in fact 19 degrees 20 minutes; from which it would appear that different starting points of longitude were confused by some ignorant person and gathered into that geographical book which most ascribe to Ptolemy. That this book is not a genuine work of Ptolemy is shown not only by the contradictions cited, but also by the passage in book 1 of the Almagest, chapter 6, which declares that under the equator there is only a small habitable region, although in the geography he mentions many regions and cities subject to the equator. To make it clearer that the Arabs speak in accordance with the truth, let us compare Alexandria and Cordoba with each other. Alberuni assigns Alexandria a longitude of 51 degrees 8 minutes and Cordoba 8 degrees 40 minutes; subtracting the smaller from the larger leaves an interval between Cordoba and Alexandria of 43 degrees 28 minutes. Aben Sahid gives Alexandria 51 degrees 20 minutes and Cordoba 10 degrees 8 minutes; subtracting the smaller from the larger leaves an interval between Alexandria and Cordoba of 41 degrees 12 minutes. The author of the Greek geography also gives Alexandria 51 degrees 20 minutes, but assigns Cordoba 9 degrees 20 minutes; subtracting the smaller longitude from the larger leaves an interval between Alexandria and Cordoba of 42 degrees. Since, however, the interval between Alexandria and Cordoba is always one and the same, someone might suppose that the Arabs contradict themselves; but here it must be observed that the interval itself does not really change, but the shore of the western ocean sometimes advances and sometimes recedes, and by this means the interval seems to change; for although the Arabs reckon the longitudes of places from a conspicuous boundary, that boundary is unstable because of the sea and time. Hence it is understood that Abilfedea's statement, that ten degrees lie between the Fortunate Islands and the shore of the western sea, must be qualified, for this was true in his own age, but at other times things may stand differently. When the longitude of Mecca is in question, the Arabs, as the most diligent investigators of the eastern regions, should be believed rather than our geographers; for since the Arabs assign Mecca a longitude from the shore of the western ocean of 67 degrees 31 minutes, it is sufficiently clear that Mecca is 77 degrees 31 minutes distant from the Fortunate Islands. This is expressly attested by the Arabic epitome of the Almagest which is extant in the Palatine library, where it is written thus: It should be known that the longitude of Mecha from the Fortunate Islands is seventy-seven degrees and a sixth part of one degree, and from the shore of the western sea sixty-seven degrees and a sixth part of one degree.

units.la: In gradibus hic autor prorsus conuenit cum Abilfedea: nisi quod sextam partem vnius gradus, hoc est, decem tantum minuta addiciat, vbi Abilfedea 31 min. ponit: nostri vero geographi, qui Mechae assignant longitudinem ab insulis fortunatis 71 gradus, & 45 minut. fere sex gradibus aberrant.
units.tr: In degrees this author agrees entirely with Abilfeda, except that he adds only a sixth part of one degree, that is, ten minutes, where Abilfeda gives 31 minutes. Our geographers, who assign Mecca a longitude of 71 degrees and 45 minutes from the Fortunate Islands, are out by almost six degrees.

units.la: Porro ut discrimen hoc longitudinum ab infulis fortunatis, & citimo littore oceani occidentalis computatarum, rectius percipiatur, sciendum est, Arabes vocare littus oceani occidentalis, extremitatem orbis versus occidentem habitabilis, vbi sitæ sunt columnæ Herculis: sed infulas fortunatas etiam appellant paradisum, & occidentem medii mundi, hoc est, occidente respectu medii mundi. Medium autem mundi constituitur in civitate Indiae, quae Arim dicitur: hanc dicunt praecise sub aequatore esse siram, ut nullam habeat latitudinem: & quod ad longitudinem praedictae urbis Arim attinet, afferunt eam praecise mediam esse inter extremitatem orbis versus orientem habitabilis, vbi columnas Alexandri erectas esse dicitant, & inter fortunatas insulas: hoc est, distare Arim ab insulis fortunatis 90 gradus, & 90 gradus pariter abesse ab extremo oriente habitabili, in quo regio Sin collocatur. Hoc annotatur in vetustis theoriis planetarum, quae manuscripta extant in bibliotheca Palatina, hisce verbis: Arim distat ab utrisque gadibus, scilicet Alexandri & Herculis æqualiter : distat enim a gadibus Alexandri positus in oriente 90 gradibus, & a gadibus Herculis positis in occidente 90 gradibus, & ab utroque polo 90 gradibus. Si autem Arim conferatur cum litore citimo oceani occidentalis: tunc nequaquam est in medio mundi: à columnis Alexandri quidem distat 90 gradibus, sed ab oceano occidentali, siue columnis Herculis (quas prædictus theoriarū autor male credit sitas esse in insulis fortunaris [?]) abest tantum octoginta gradus, quatenus cum Abilfedea ponimus decedere io gradus, quod interuallum est inter litus oceani occidentalis, & inter fortunatas insulas.
units.tr: Further, so that this difference between the longitudes reckoned from the Fortunate Islands and from the nearest shore of the western ocean may be understood more correctly, it must be noted that the Arabs call the shore of the western ocean the furthest limit of the inhabited world towards the west, where the Pillars of Hercules stand. They also call the Fortunate Islands paradise, and the west of the middle of the world, that is, west with respect to the middle of the world. The middle of the world is placed in an Indian city called Arim. They say it is situated exactly under the equator, so as to have no latitude. As for its longitude, they affirm that Arim lies exactly midway between the furthest limit of the inhabited world towards the east, where they say the Pillars of Alexander stand erected, and the Fortunate Islands. That is, Arim is 90 degrees from the Fortunate Islands, and likewise 90 degrees from the far eastern limit of the inhabited world, where the region of Sin is located. This is noted in the old theories of the planets, which survive in manuscript in the Palatine library, in these words: Arim is equally distant from both Gades, namely that of Alexander and that of Hercules. For it is 90 degrees from the Gades of Alexander placed in the east, 90 degrees from the Gades of Hercules placed in the west, and 90 degrees from each pole. But if Arim is compared with the nearest shore of the western ocean, then it is by no means in the middle of the world. It is indeed 90 degrees from the Pillars of Alexander, but from the western ocean, or the Pillars of Hercules (which the aforesaid author of the theories wrongly believes are situated in the Fortunate Islands [?]), it is only 80 degrees away. This is because, as we place it with Abilfeda, the interval between the shore of the western ocean and the Fortunate Islands is 10 degrees.

units.la: Hic autem obseruandum est, Arabes quosdam ponere interuallum inter litus oceani occidentalis, & inter insulas fortunatas, 17 graduum & 30 minutorum: proinde asserunt Arim distare ab extremitate occidentis habitabilis 72 gradus, & 30 minuta. Ita enim legitur in tabulis Alfonsinis manuscriptis & quibusdam excusis, post catalogum ciuitatum, quarum longitudines computantur à litore oceani occidentalis: Hæ sunt longitudines ciuitatum ab occidente habitato, & latitudines ab æquinoctiali uersus septentrionem.
units.tr: Here, however, it must be observed that some Arabs put the interval between the shore of the western ocean and the Fortunate Islands at 17 degrees and 30 minutes. Accordingly they say that Arim is 72 degrees and 30 minutes from the furthest limit of the inhabited west. This is how it reads in the manuscript Alphonsine tables and in some printed ones, after the catalogue of cities whose longitudes are reckoned from the shore of the western ocean: These are the longitudes of cities from the inhabited west, and the latitudes from the equinoctial towards the north.

units.la: Unde sciendum, quod Astronomi duplicitèr capiunt occidens: uno modo pro eo, quod est extremum uersus occidens habitabile, & ab illo distat Arim per 72 gradus, & 30 minuta, ut ab oriente absit per 90 gradus: secundum illud occidens habitabile solent quædam longitudines regionum assignari, ut sit in tabula supra scripta.
units.tr: Hence it must be understood that astronomers take the west in two ways. In one way it is taken for the furthest point of the inhabited world towards the west, and from it Arim is 72 degrees and 30 minutes distant, so that it is 90 degrees from the east. It is according to this inhabited west that certain longitudes of regions are usually assigned, as in the table written above.

units.la: Alio modo capiunt occidens, prout ab oriente adipsum sunt 180 gradus, quæ est medietas circuli, & tunc Arim est in medio inter oriens & occidens. Unde si quis velit scire longitudines ciuitatum ab occidente vero (id est, ab insulis fortunatis) addat longitudini hic positæ, 17 gradus & 30 minuta. Vice versa, sic[?] a longitudine, cuius initium sumitur ab in-sulis fortunatis, subtrahantur 17 ½ gradus, emergit longitudo earum ab occidente habitabili.
units.tr: In another way they take the west as lying 180 degrees from the east, which is half a circle, and then Arim is in the middle between east and west. Hence, if anyone wishes to know the longitudes of cities from the true west (that is, from the Fortunate Islands), he should add 17 degrees and 30 minutes to the longitude given here. Conversely, if 17 and a half degrees are subtracted from a longitude whose starting point is taken from the Fortunate Islands, the longitude from the inhabited west emerges.

units.la: Geminæ columnæ Herculis fuerunt collocatæ in extremi occidentis orbe habitabili: quas se vidisse ai: Auerroës in commentario lib.1. de cœlo, contextu 111. idem testatur, eas in quodam prælio à Barbaris fuisse destructas, anno à prædicatione Muhamedis quingetesimo tricesimo, hoc est anno Christi millesimo cetesimo tricesimo sexto. Columnæ vero Alexandri sitæ fuerunt in extremo oriente habitabili; quorsum peruenisse dicitur Alexander: unde apud Arabes dictus est Dilkarnain, hoc est bicornis, quod non tantum occidentem, verum etiam totum orientem dominio suo subiecerit. Itaque hoc spacium terræ quod à columnis Herculis usque ad columnas Alexandri extenditur, & in æquatore numeratum conficit 170 gradus, Alfraganus cum Arabibus vocat longitudinem: neque refert sive terminum eius in oriente, sive in occidente habitabili ponamus, modo intelligatur, meridianum cuiuscuiusque ciuitatis in longitudine sibi terminum esse, ut dicatur habere longitudinem eam, quam sectio æquatoris & meridiani ostendit. Atla-titudo vniuscuiusque ciuitatis est arcus meridiani inter æquatorem & verticem capitis interceptus: qui semper æqualis est eleuationi poli supra horizontem, hoc est arcui meridiani ab horizonte septentrionali usque ad polum numerato.
units.tr: The twin Pillars of Hercules were set up at the furthest limit of the inhabited west. Averroes says in his commentary on the first book of On the Heavens, text 111, that he had seen them, and he also testifies that they were destroyed by the Barbarians in a battle in the year 530 after the preaching of Muhammad, that is, in the year 1136 of Christ. The Pillars of Alexander stood at the far eastern limit of the inhabited world, to which Alexander is said to have come; hence among the Arabs he was called Dhu'l-Qarnayn, that is, two-horned, because he subjected to his rule not only the west but the whole east as well. Thus the stretch of land from the Pillars of Hercules to the Pillars of Alexander, which measured along the equator comes to 170 degrees, Alfraganus, with the Arabs, calls the longitude. It makes no difference whether we place its termination in the eastern or in the western inhabited world, provided it is understood that the meridian of each city is its terminus in longitude, so that it is said to have that longitude which the intersection of the equator and the meridian shows. The latitude of each city is the arc of the meridian intercepted between the equator and the zenith of the head, which is always equal to the elevation of the pole above the horizon, that is, to the arc of the meridian measured from the northern horizon up to the pole.

units.la: Porro cum ad ciuitatem Arim, (quæ in mediomu-di sita sub æquatore, distat à columnis Alexandri & fortunatis insulis 90 gradibus) Arabes olim tabulas astronomicas codiderunt, sicut antiquus theoriarum autor ostendit: hinc factum est, ut maluerint reliquarum ciuitatum longitudines referre ad Arim, quàm ad infulas fortunatas, quas incultas & desertas cense-bant, & ad quas nullæ erant factæ tabulæ. Exempla obuia sunt in canonibus Arzachelis, qui pulcherrime in membrana descripti extant in bibliotheca Palati-na: vt cûm dicitur, hos canones reductos esse ad me-ridianum Toleti, cuius longitudo ab Arim comple-ctatur spacium 4 horarum & 1/10 vnius horæ, & latitu-do ab æquinoctiali fit 39 grad.& 54 minutorum. Vni horæ respondent 1 5 gradus, ergo 4 horæ, cum 1/10 co-ficiunt 61 1/6 gradus: quæ est distantia Toleti ab Arim: fi subtrahantur 61 1/6 gradus à 90 gradibus, restant 28 1/2 gradus, quæ est distantia Toleti ab infulis fortu-natis : quam etiam ponit Iudæus quidã in t[?]actatu de astrolabio: fi à 28 1/3 gradibus, auferantur decem gra-dus, tunc iuxta sententiam Abilfedæ remanebunt 18 1/3 gradus: quæ debebat esse distantia Toleti à littore oceani occidentalis. Sed Abilfedea asserit Toletum fecudum Aben Sahid à littore maris occidentalis ab-esse 15 1/2 gradus: quæ sententia veritati magis est con-fentanea. In iisdem Arzachelis canonibus scribitur, vrbem Parisiorum habere longitudinem ab Arim 48 graduum, & 30 minutorum: & à Toleto longitudi-nem habere 10 graduum, altitudinem solis in meri-die, quado sol fit in principio arietis esse 41 grad. & 25 minutorum: hoc est, altitudinem poli esse 48 graduu & 35 minutorum: adiicitur tamen quod ciuitas Pari-fiorum distet à ciuitate Toleti fecundum quosdam 11 gradibus & 30 minutis, hoc est 46 minutis horæ, fe-cundum alios distet 12 gradibus, & 17 minutis, hoc est 49 minutis horæ,& 8 fecundis, fecundum alios 11 gradibus tantum, qui faciunt 44 minuta horæ. Cum autem supia oftenlum fit Toletum ab Arim distare 61 ⅓[?] gradus: & hoc loco afferatur Parilios ab Arim distare 48 ⅓[?] gradus: consequitur hinc interuallum inter Parifios&Toletum fecundum longitudinem ponendum esse 13 graduum: cumq; ex sententia Abilfe-dæ Toletum absit à littore maris occidentalis 15 ⅓[?] gradus, vrbs Parifiorum ab eodem littore aberit 28 ⅓[?] gradus: quibus fi addantur 10 gradus, peruenietur ad infulas fortunatas, eritque interuallum inter Parifios & infulas fortunatas 38 ⅓[?] graduum: atqui tabulæ geographicæ assignant Parifiis longitudinem ab infulis fortunatis 22 gradus: quamobrem differentia est 16 gradum, quod est spacium vnius horæ & paulo amplius. Præterea in tabulis Arzachelis scribitur Tolofam in latitudine habere 42 gradus, & 4 ⅕[?] minuta, & distare ab Arim 5 gradus, & à Toleto 11 grad. & 30 minuta. Sane quia quinquaginta gradibus Tolofa dicitur distare ab Arim, sequitur hinc eam abefle ab infulis fortunatis 40 gradus: atqui tabulæ nostræ tribuunt longitudinem Tolofæ ab infulis fortunatis 10 tantum graduum: quamobrem differentia est 10 graduum, quod est spacium vnius horæ & quadrantis.
units.tr: Now, since the Arabs once compiled astronomical tables for the city of Arim (which, situated in the middle of the world under the equator, is 90 degrees from the Pillars of Alexander and the Fortunate Islands), as the ancient author of the theories shows, it came about that they preferred to refer the longitudes of the other cities to Arim rather than to the Fortunate Islands, which they considered uncultivated and deserted, and for which no tables had been made. Examples are obvious in the canons of Arzachel, which survive in a beautifully written parchment copy in the Palatine library. For instance, it is stated that these canons were reduced to the meridian of Toledo, whose longitude from Arim covers a span of 4 hours and 1/10 of an hour, and whose latitude from the equinoctial is 39 degrees and 54 minutes. One hour corresponds to 15 degrees, so 4 hours with 1/10 make 61 1/6 degrees, which is the distance of Toledo from Arim. If 61 1/6 degrees are subtracted from 90 degrees, 28 1/2 degrees remain, which is the distance of Toledo from the Fortunate Islands. A certain Jew also gives this in his treatise on the astrolabe. If 10 degrees are taken away from 28 1/3 degrees, then according to the opinion of Abilfeda 18 1/3 degrees will remain, which should be the distance of Toledo from the shore of the western ocean. But Abilfeda asserts, following Aben Sahid, that Toledo is 15 1/2 degrees from the shore of the western sea, and this opinion is more consistent with the truth. In the same canons of Arzachel it is written that the city of the Parisians has a longitude of 48 degrees and 30 minutes from Arim, and a longitude of 10 degrees from Toledo, and that the sun's altitude at noon, when the sun is at the beginning of Aries, is 41 degrees and 25 minutes, that is, that the altitude of the pole is 48 degrees and 35 minutes. It is added, however, that according to some the city of the Parisians is 11 degrees and 30 minutes from the city of Toledo, that is 46 minutes of an hour; according to others it is 12 degrees and 17 minutes away, that is 49 minutes of an hour and 8 seconds; and according to others only 11 degrees, which make 44 minutes of an hour. But since it has been shown above that Toledo is 61 1/3 [?] degrees from Arim, and here Paris is said to be 48 1/3 [?] degrees from Arim, it follows that the interval between Paris and Toledo in longitude must be taken as 13 degrees. And since, according to Abilfeda's opinion, Toledo is 15 1/3 [?] degrees from the shore of the western sea, the city of Paris will be 28 1/3 [?] degrees from the same shore. If 10 degrees are added to these, one arrives at the Fortunate Islands, and the interval between Paris and the Fortunate Islands will be 38 1/3 [?] degrees. Yet our geographical tables assign Paris a longitude of only 22 degrees from the Fortunate Islands. Therefore the difference is 16 degrees, which is the span of one hour and a little more. Moreover, in the tables of Arzachel it is written that Toulouse has a latitude of 42 degrees and 4 1/5 [?] minutes, and is 5 degrees from Arim and 11 degrees and 30 minutes from Toledo. Indeed, since Toulouse is said to be 50 degrees from Arim, it follows that it is 40 degrees from the Fortunate Islands. Yet our tables give Toulouse a longitude of only 10 degrees from the Fortunate Islands. Therefore the difference is 10 degrees, which is the span of one hour and a quarter.

units.la: Hactenus ostensum[?] est, qui termini longitudinis ab autoribus soleant aflignari, & quam discrepantes sint sententiæ in interuallis longinquarum regionum no-tandis: profecto longitudinum obseruatio difficilli-maeft, quod raro phænomena cœlestia in diuersis meridianis eodemq; tempore consideremus, & tantum ex itinerum distantia ratiocinemur de longitudi-ne & tempore, quod intercipitur inter ortum stellarum in diuersis & multum à se inuicem dissitis locis. Si conderentur tabulæ motuum cœlestium ad meridianum infularum fortunatarum, possemus facile in omnibus locis ad eas obseruare distantiam: cum autem tabulæ astronomicæ fiant ad meridianū Antuerpiensem, Venetum & Romanum, parum nos iuuare possunt, ut ex illis eruamus longitudines locorum ab infulis fortunatis computatas.
units.tr: Thus far it has been shown which limits of longitude authors are accustomed to assign, and how far their opinions differ regarding the intervals of distant regions that must be noted. Truly, the observation of longitudes is most difficult, because we rarely observe celestial phenomena in different meridians at the same time, and we reason about longitude and time only from the distance of journeys, which is the interval between the rising of the stars in different places, widely separated from one another. If tables of celestial motions were constructed for the meridian of the Fortunate Islands, we could easily observe the distance from it in every place. But since astronomical tables are made for the meridians of Antwerp, Venice and Rome, they can help us little in deriving from them the longitudes of places reckoned from the Fortunate Islands.

units.la: Quòd duodecim sint signa cœlestia, non pauciora neque plura: & quare principium illorum computetur ab ariete.
units.tr: That there are twelve celestial signs, neither fewer nor more; and why their beginning is reckoned from Aries.
CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Sciendum est sapietem Ptolemæum unaquam[?]que cœli costellationem certo nomine appellasse, partem meridionalem distinxisse à septentrionali, & 12 signa zodiaci constituisse, quæ oculis obseruare licet. In hisce 12 signis sol ac luna, itemq; quinque errantes vagatur, neq; amplius excurrunt: vbi enim attigerint sinem geminorum, redeunt & descendunt à septentrione: si peruenerint ad sinem sagittarij, reuertuntur à meridie. Ex quibus intelligimus, quod signa cœlestia, in quibus planetæ oberrant, sint duodecim, non pauciora neque plura. Etsi autem in circulo proprie nullum sit principium; ab ariete tamen zodiacum auspicamur: quod solarie-tem percurrens nouum quodammodo tempus gignat, terram frugiferam reddat, & multis amœnitatibus ornet. Cùm autem taurum ingreditur, auget calorem, quem in geminis admodum inten-dit: neque vllum signum est, in quo nō inducat nō-tabilem supra quemvis horizontem alterationem. Sed diem noctì prius non æquat, quàm fuerit in principio arietis & librae: quantum autem dies incipit augeri supra noctem, tantum quoque nox augetur supra diem. Dies illustrat, nox vero obscurat: idcirco lux diei est tanquam vita, & nox quasi mors, quæ cum ita habeant, non immerito ab illo signo incipitur, in quo sol revolutione sua dies prolixiores noctibus efficere poterit.]
units.tr: It should be known that the wise Ptolemy named each constellation of the heavens with a fixed name, distinguished the southern part from the northern, and set up twelve signs of the zodiac, which the eye can observe. Within these twelve signs the sun and moon, and likewise the five wandering stars, move, and they do not go beyond them: when they reach the end of Gemini they turn back and descend from the north, and when they reach the end of Sagittarius they turn back from the south. From this we understand that the celestial signs, in which the planets wander, are twelve, no fewer and no more. Although in a circle there is properly no beginning, nevertheless we take the start of the zodiac from Aries, because the sun, traversing the Ram, in a way begins a new time, makes the earth fruitful, and adorns it with many delights. When he enters Taurus, he increases the heat, which he intensifies greatly in Gemini; and there is no sign in which he does not bring about a notable change above any horizon. But he does not make day equal to night until he is at the beginning of Aries and Libra; and as day begins to grow longer than night, so night is lengthened beyond day. Day illumines, but night obscures; therefore the light of day is like life, and night like death. Since these things are so, it is not without reason that one begins from that sign in which the sun, by its revolution, can make the days longer than the nights.

units.la: De ascensionibus signorum in sphæra recta & obliqua.
units.tr: On the ascensions of the signs in the right and oblique sphere.
CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: DE ascensionibus signorum rectis & obliquis dicturi, supponimus circulos transeuntes per polos æquatoris, fieri horizontes in illis locis, quæ sub æquinoctiali sunt sita: eosdemque vicem meridianorum habere in singulis climatibus. Horizontes autem in sphæra obliqua, nullo modo transeunt per polos æquatoris, ideoque vicem meridianorum supplere non possunt. Etsi igitur æquatoris ab oriente in occidentem super polis mundi æquabilis sit revolutio, tamen propter zodiaci obliquitatem inæquales sunt in utraque sphæra ascensionum & descensionum spacia. Tempora æqualia æquatoris revolutioni adscribuntur, ut per ea inæquales arcus zodiaci defi-nianniantur: etenim ascensio nihil aliud est, quàm arcus æquatoris, cum dato arcu eclipticæ oriri incipiens & desinens.
units.tr: Speaking of the rising of the signs in the straight and oblique sphere, we suppose that the circles passing through the poles of the equator become the horizons in those places that lie under the equinoctial, and that these same circles take the place of meridians in each climate. But the horizons in the oblique sphere do not pass through the poles of the equator in any way, and so cannot take the place of meridians. Therefore, although the revolution of the equator from east to west about the poles of the world is uniform, the spaces of rising and setting are unequal in each sphere, because of the obliquity of the zodiac. Equal times are assigned to the revolution of the equator, so that by them the unequal arcs of the zodiac may be determined. For the ascension is nothing other than an arc of the equator that begins and ends rising together with a given arc of the ecliptic.

units.la: In sphæra recta æquantur ascensiones quadrantum æquatoris & eclipticæ, qui interiiciuntur inter initium arietis & cacri, item inter principium librae & capricorni.
units.tr: In the straight sphere, the ascensions of the quadrants of the equator and of the ecliptic, which lie between the beginning of Aries and Cancer, and likewise between the beginning of Libra and Capricorn, are equal.

units.la: Partes verò horum quadrantum ascendunt inæqualiter. ut enim bini tantùm oppositi gradus æqualem habent ab æquatore inclinatione, ita ascensiones eorum rectæ æquales quoque sunt. idem accidit in utrisque medietatibus signorum.
units.tr: But the parts of these quadrants rise unequally. For just as two opposite degrees have an equal inclination from the equator, so their right ascensions are also equal. The same happens in both halves of the signs.

units.la: In sphæra obliqua hemicyclia tantùm gemina æquatoris & eclipticæ interposita inter ambo æquinoctialia puncta æqualem habent ascensionem.
units.tr: In the oblique sphere, the two semicircles of the equator and the ecliptic that lie between the two equinoctial points have equal ascension.

units.la: Partes autem horum hemicyclorum inæqualiter ascendunt: nam arcus æquatoris circa signa borea sunt minores, & circa austrina maiores quàm eclipticæ: ea tamen proportione, ut duorum oppositorum & æqualium arcuum ascensiones coniunctæ, æquent ascensiones eorundem in sphæra rectâ.
units.tr: But the parts of these semicircles rise unequally: for the arcs of the equator near the northern signs are smaller, and near the southern signs larger, than those of the ecliptic. Yet in such a proportion that the ascensions of two opposite and equal arcs, taken together, equal the ascensions of the same arcs in the straight sphere.

units.la: Præterea duo signa opposita, quorum ascensiones obliquæ adduntur, habet æquales ascensiones rectas: quorum enim eadem est distantia à principio cancri & capricorni, item ab ariete & libra, æqualem habent ascensionem: idem fit in reliquis gradibus signorum.
units.tr: Furthermore, two opposite signs whose oblique ascensions are added together have equal right ascensions. For those that are equally distant from the beginning of Cancer and Capricorn, and likewise from Aries and Libra, have equal ascension. The same holds for the remaining degrees of the signs.

units.la: At quia ascensio cuiusque gradus zodiaci in
units.tr: But because the ascension of each degree of the zodiac in the

units.la: oriente æquales est descensioni oppositæ in occiden-te: ideo tempus ascensionis uniuscuiusque signi æqua-le est tempori descensionis oppositæ: hoc autem fit in sphæra recta, vbi horizontes transeunt per polos æquatoris.
units.tr: east is equal to the descent of the opposite degree in the west, the time of ascension of each sign is equal to the time of descent of the opposite sign. This happens in the straight sphere, where the horizons pass through the poles of the equator.

units.la: In sphæra autem obliqua, vbi horizontes a polis mundi recedunt, ascensio cuiusque signi differt a descensione oppositæ: quare necesse est, vt tempora quoque ascensionum, diuersa sint a temporibus descensionum: neque erunt tempora ortus & occasus æqualia, nisi duplicentur, vt fit in sphæra recta.
units.tr: In the oblique sphere, however, where the horizons recede from the poles of the world, the ascension of each sign differs from the descent of the opposite sign. Hence the times of ascension must also necessarily differ from the times of descent; nor will the times of rising and setting be equal unless they are doubled, as happens in the straight sphere.

units.la: [Ascensio arietis & piscium in climate quarto, est 19 grad. & 12 minut. Tauri & aquarij 22 grad. 46 minut. Geminorum & capricorni 29 grad. 17 minutorum. Cancri & sagittarij 35 grad. & 15 minutorum. Arietis & scorpij 37 grad. & 3 min. Virginis & libræ 37 grad. & 28 minutorum.
units.tr: [The ascension of Aries and Pisces in the fourth climate is 19 degrees and 12 minutes. Of Taurus and Aquarius, 22 degrees 46 minutes. Of Gemini and Capricorn, 29 degrees 17 minutes. Of Cancer and Sagittarius, 35 degrees 15 minutes. Of Aries and Scorpio, 37 degrees 3 minutes. Of Virgo and Libra, 37 degrees 28 minutes.

units.la: Ascensio arietis & piscium in sphæra recta, est 27 grad. 50 minutorum. Tauri & aquarij 29 grad. 54 minutorum. Geminorum & capricorni 32 grad. & 16 minut. Cancri & sagittarij, æqualis est ascensioni geminorum & capricorni. Arietis & scorpij æqualis est ascensioni tauri & aquarij. Virginis & libræ æqualis est ascensioni arietis & piscium.
units.tr: The ascension of Aries and Pisces in the straight sphere is 27 degrees 50 minutes. Of Taurus and Aquarius, 29 degrees 54 minutes. Of Gemini and Capricorn, 32 degrees 16 minutes. Of Cancer and Sagittarius, it is equal to the ascension of Gemini and Capricorn. Of Aries and Scorpio, it is equal to the ascension of Taurus and Aquarius. Of Virgo and Libra, it is equal to the ascension of Aries and Pisces.

units.la: Si ascensionem arietis & piscium in quarto cli-mate, subtrahamus ab ascensione eorundem signorum in sphæra recta: relinquitur differentia 8 grad. & 38 minutorum: quam si duplicemus, & duplicata per 15 dinudiuidamus, prouenit hora vna, & ²⁄₁₅ horæ, cum 16 minutis: atque hoc incrementum est arietis.
units.tr: If we subtract the ascension of Aries and Pisces in the fourth climate from the ascension of the same signs in the straight sphere, the difference is 8 degrees and 38 minutes. If we double this, and divide the doubled amount by 15, there results one hour and 2/15 of an hour, with 16 minutes; and this is the increment of Aries.

units.la: Eodem modo si ascensionem tauri & aquarij in quarto climate, subtrahamus ab ascensione eorundem signorum in sphæra recta, relinquitur differetia 7 grad. & 8 min. quæ si duplicemus, & duplicatam per 15 diuidamus, prouenit hora dimidia cum ⅓ & 55 scrupulis: atq; hoc est incrementum tauri supra arietē.
units.tr: In the same way, if we subtract the ascension of Taurus and Aquarius in the fourth climate from the ascension of the same signs in the straight sphere, the difference is 7 degrees and 8 minutes. If we double this, and divide the doubled amount by 15, there results half an hour and 1/3, with 55 scruples; and this is the increment of Taurus over Aries.

units.la: Cum autem in quarto climate prolixissimus dies æquinoctialem superet duabus horis cum dimidia, subtrahatur hinc incrementum tauri: proueniet ⅖ vnius horæ, quod est incrementum geminorum.
units.tr: Since in the fourth climate the longest day exceeds the equinoctial day by two and a half hours, subtract from this the increment of Taurus; there results 2/5 of an hour, which is the increment of Gemini.

units.la: Itaq; bina signa vltra & citra æquatorem opposita si considerentur, hac habent inter se proportionem, vt quantum dies in tauro augetur, tantum in scorpio decrescat. idem fit in geminis & sagittario, in cancro & capricorno. Æquinoctium autem contingit in principio libræ & arietis, quem cum sol conficit, res omnes vegetantur, indiesq; magis ac magis perficiuntur: sicut a Deo creatore & conservatore ordinatum est.]
units.tr: Thus, if two signs lying opposite to each other, beyond and on this side of the equator, are considered, they have this relation to one another: as much as the day increases in Taurus, so much does it decrease in Scorpio. The same happens in Gemini and Sagittarius, and in Cancer and Capricorn. The equinox occurs at the beginning of Libra and Aries, and when the sun passes through them, all things are invigorated and day by day are brought more and more to perfection, as ordained by God the Creator and Preserver.]

units.la: De quantitate temporis noctturni & diurni, & diuersitate horarum æqualium & inæqualium. CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: On the length of night and day, and the difference between equal and unequal hours. CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: OStendemus nunc quantitatē noctiu & dierū, item differentia horarū. Primo autem sciendum est, diem naturalem definiri ex motu solis orientis vsque ad ortum eius in diem subsequentem.
units.tr: We now show the length of night and day, and likewise the difference in hours. First, however, it must be understood that the natural day is defined by the motion of the rising sun from one sunrise to the next.

units.la: 1 Mouetur sol in Zodiaco versus orientem contra motum primum, vt spacio diei naturalis anticipet fere gradum vnum, nonnunquam etiam plus: cum enim in quouis anno sol anticipet 36 gradus, totidem etiam dies efficit, & ratione excessus modo quinque, modo sex dies adiicit. Cum autem magna sit variatio ascensionum solarium circa horizontem in sphaera obliqua, astronomi initium diei sumere maluerunt a meridiano, quia hic est instar horizontis in sphaera recta, in qua nulla aut certe perexigua cernitur ortuum solarium discrepantia.
units.tr: 1 The sun moves through the zodiac towards the east, against the primum mobile, so that in the course of a natural day it falls back by almost one degree, and sometimes a little more. For in any year the sun falls back 36 degrees, which also makes that many days; and by the excess it adds now five, now six days. Since the variation of the solar risings about the horizon is great in an oblique sphere, astronomers have preferred to take the beginning of the day from the meridian, because this is like the horizon in a right sphere, in which there is no difference, or certainly only a very slight one, in the risings of the sun.

units.la: Portio circuli, quæ circumducitur ab ortu solis vsque ad occasum illius, appellatur arcus diurnus: quem describit sol motu suo ab oriente in occasum, secundum helicem æquatori feré parallelam. At portio, quæ mouetur ab occasu solis vsque ad ortum, vocatur arcus nocturnus.
units.tr: The part of the circle that is traced from the sun's rising to its setting is called the diurnal arc, which the sun describes by its motion from east to west along a spiral almost parallel to the equator. The part that is traversed from the sun's setting to its rising is called the nocturnal arc.

units.la: 2 Diuiditur autem dies naturalis, hoc est, qui ex die constat & noćte [?], in 24 horas, vt hora quaelibet contineat 15 gradus: excessus enim quisquis fuerit, reputatur pro nihilo. Huiusmodi horæ appellantur æquales: quoniam ipsarum quantitas eadem perpetuo censetur.
units.tr: 2 The natural day, that is, the day consisting of day and night, is divided into 24 hours, so that each hour contains 15 degrees; any excess is counted as nothing. Hours of this kind are called equal, since their length is always regarded as the same.

units.la: Itaque cum diuisus fuerit arcus diurnus per 15, prodibunt horæ diei æquales: similiter si diuisus fuerit arcus nocturnus in quindecim, producentur horæ noctis æquales: quæ sunt complementum 24 horarum.
units.tr: Therefore, when the diurnal arc is divided by 15, the equal hours of the day result; likewise, if the nocturnal arc is divided into fifteen, the equal hours of the night are produced. These make up the 24 hours.

units.la: Horæ inæquales seu temporales diei & noctis perpetuo sunt 12 horarum: quæ modo breues sunt, modo prolixæ, iuxta rationem hiemis aut æstatis. Cum enim dies prolixior fuerit nocte, tunc horæ quoque illius diurnæ prolixiores sunt horis nocturnis: si autem breuior fuerit dies nocte, tunc illius quoque horæ breuiores sunt.
units.tr: The unequal or temporal hours of day and night are always 12 hours each; they are sometimes short, sometimes long, according to the season of winter or summer. For when the day is longer than the night, then the hours of that day are longer than the hours of the night; but if the day is shorter than the night, then its hours are also shorter.

units.la: Itaque cum diuiditur arcus diurnus per 12 ho-ras, prodit quantitas horæ unius inæqualis: & gradus singulis horis diurnis respondentes, vocantur tempora horarum diurna.
units.tr: Therefore, when the diurnal arc is divided by 12 hours, the length of one unequal hour is produced; and the degrees corresponding to the individual daytime hours are called the time of the daytime hours.

units.la: Similiter si diuidatur arcus nocturnus per 12 horas, prodit tempus unius horæ noctis inæqualis: tota autem nox complementum est diei naturalis, quatenus is in 30 partes diuidi potest.
units.tr: Likewise, if the nocturnal arc is divided by 12 hours, the time of one unequal hour of the night is produced; and the whole night is the complement of the natural day, since it can be divided into 30 parts.

units.la: Constat ergo horas æquales eas appellari, quarum tempora sint æqualia, neque vnquam mutentur secundum prolixitatem aut breuitatem dierum: inæquales autem horæ sunt, quarum tempora mutantur, etsi certo numero comprehendantur.
units.tr: It is clear, then, that those hours are called equal whose lengths are equal and never change according to the lengthening or shortening of the days; unequal hours, on the other hand, are those whose lengths change, even though they are comprised of a fixed number.

units.la: [Nunc recensemus quot tempora vni horæ debeantur in singulis signis. Quādo sol ingreditur arietem, tempora horaria sunt 15 gradus. in principio tauri tempora horaria sunt 16½.
units.tr: [We now list how many times belong to one hour in each sign. When the sun enters Aries, the hour-times are 15 degrees. At the beginning of Taurus the hour-times are 16½.]

units.la: Cum autem volueris scire tempora horaria reliquorum dierum, qui interponuntur inter principium arietis & tauri, tunc gradum vnum cum dimidio, hoc est 90 minuta, diuides in 30: productum exhibebit additamentum cuiusque diei quàm proxime. Idem faciendum est in spaciis mediis reliquorum signorum: & unicuique gradui assignandum est tempus 60 minutorum.
units.tr: When you wish to know the hour-times of the remaining days, which fall between the beginning of Aries and Taurus, then divide one and a half degrees, that is 90 minutes, by 30: the product will show the addition for each day as nearly as possible. The same is to be done for the intermediate spaces of the remaining signs, and each degree is to be assigned a time of 60 minutes.

units.la: Si sol fuerit in principio geminorum, tempora horaria sunt 17 ½ & ⅛. In principio cacri [?] 18 ⅛. In principio leonis 17 ½ & ⅛. In principio virginis 16 ½. In principio libræ 15 graduum.
units.tr: If the sun is at the beginning of Gemini, the hour-times are 17½ and ⅛. At the beginning of Cancer 18⅛. At the beginning of Leo 17½ and ⅛. At the beginning of Virgo 16½. At the beginning of Libra 15 degrees.

units.la: In principio scorpij tempus horarium est 13 ½. In principio sagittarij 12 ⅛. In principio capricorni 11 ⅞. In principio aquarij 12 ⅛. In principio piscium 13 ½. Hæc autem inter septem climata quarto tantum conueniunt: si autem ad reliqua climata accommodare velis tempora horaria, oportebit locum solis considerare in binis signis, & iuxta proportionem gradus aliquot addere vel subtrahere, prout ostendet tibi productum e diuisione natum.]
units.tr: At the beginning of Scorpio the hour-time is 13½. At the beginning of Sagittarius 12⅛. At the beginning of Capricorn 11⅞. At the beginning of Aquarius 12⅛. At the beginning of Pisces 13½. These agree only for the fourth of the seven climes; if you wish to adapt the hour-times to the other climes, it will be necessary to consider the sun's place in pairs of signs, and according to the proportion to add or subtract some degrees, as the product of the division shows you.]

units.la: Sicut in superiori capite autor quaedâ adiecit, quæ ascensiones signorum declarant in quarto climate: ita etiam hic ostendit, qualis sit ratio dierum in eodem quarto climate. Ad quartū potissimum clima respicit, quia hoc quasi medii est inter septem comemorata, ex cuius consideratione facile perspicitur, quid in reliquis climatibus fieri possit: vel quartum clima præ-ceteris eligit, quod sub eo patria sua Fragana sit sita, vt ostensum est cap.11, aut quod sub eo collocetur Ara-cta vrbs Syriæ, patria Albategnij, sui in astronomicis studiis antecefloris [?]: etenim Albategnius ipse asserit in Aracta polum eleuari 36 gradus, camq; distare ab infulis fortunatis 73 gradus. Porro vt exactius sciatur, quo in loco sita sit Fragana, vnde sibi cognomen acquisiuit Alfraganus: ante omnia obseruandum est, quod Arabibus Fargana appelletur, quæ nobis Fragana dicitur, quemadmodum Arabes Garnatam nominant, quæ vulgò Granata enunciatur. Tradit autem Abilfedea, Fraganam esse nomen climatis, in quo sint insignes ciuitates & prouinciæ: item nomen esse vrbis nobilissimæ, quæ multorum sapientiū fuerit patria. Logitudinem vtrique assignat à littore maris occidentalis 92 [?] gradus, & latitudinem ab æquatore 41 gradus & 10 min. 1 Obiter demonstrat Alfraganus, quare in anno sint 365 & 366 dies: periodus enim solaris, sicut quæuis aliorum circulorum, complectitur 360 grad. singulis autem diebus sol gradum unum conficit: ergo hinc oriuntur 360 dies. Quia autem sol nonnunquam paulò plus vno gradu conficit, fit vt excessus hic in toto anno quinq; vel sex dies adiiciat. Quomodo vera anni quantitas sit indagada docet Ptolemæus lib. 3. Almagesti cap. 1. Annus duplex est, politicus & astronomicus. Politicus dicitur, qui apud omnes gentes in constitutione calendariorum obseruatur, cuius quantitas est 365 ¼ dierum. Astronomicus iterum duplex est, sidereus & tropicus. Tropicus est qui definitur τροπῶν [?] vel æquinoctiorum [?] interuallo: vt ergo solstitia & æquinoctia mutatur, ita etiam annus tropicus est inæqualis pro diuersa ratione seculorum. Nam Calippus, Aristarchus Samius, & Archimedes Syracusanus dixerunt eum habere 365 ¼ dies, & 6 horas: quæ est quantitas anni politici. Hipparchus obseruauit esse paulò minorem, hoc est continere 365 dies, & trecentesima parte diei. Cuius sententia secutus est Ptol. qui explicauit centesimâ parte diei, esse scrupula diurna 1/14 . 11/48. hoc est, horas quinque, & scrupula horaria 1/55 . 11/12. Albategnius obseruauit suo seculo annum continere 365 dies, quinque horas, scrupula horaria ⁴⁄₆ . ¹¹⁄₁₄ : ut defuerit centesima[?] sexta pars quadra-ti diei. Copernicus deprehendit in anno solari tropi-co, desse quadranti diei centesimam & quintam decimam partem. Annus sidereus est, qui ad aliquam stellam sixam revoluitur: quod accidit iuxta inventu Thebitii Ben Chorae 365 diebus,6 horis, scrup.⁹⁄₁₀ ¹¹⁄₁₀[?]. Copernicus vno duntaxat secundo scrupulo inuenit maiorem, & tertiis decem,ut sit 365 dierum, scrupulorum diurnorum ⁷⁄₅ . ¹¹⁄₄ . ¹¹⁄₁₀ . hoc est, 365 dierum,ho-rarum 6, scrup.horariorum ⁹⁄₄₀ . . Tradit autem in prae-dicto loco Ptolemaeus, conuenientissimum esse ob-seruare interualla solstitiorum & aequinoctiorum, pro indaganda periodo solari: sed a Copernico lib.3 revolutionum cap.13 reprehenditur, quod non obseruauerit annum sidereum: cum is aequalis semper habeatur, neque tot errores in eo assignando committantur. Astronomis quidem necessarium est, ut in calculo suo sequantur exactissimam anni quantitatem: nobis vero sufficit ut attendamus ad quantitatem anni politici, etiam si successu temporis in hac incomoda quaedam observentur, ut suo loco dicetur. ı Dies naturales etiam suam habent inaequalitatem, quae tamen in doctrina sphaerica negligitur: in astronomia autē, ubi opus est calculo exactissimo, semper oportet inaequalitatem dierum naturalium adaequare.
units.tr: As in the preceding chapter the author added certain things which declare the risings of the signs in the fourth clime, so here too he shows what the proportion of days is in that same fourth clime. He looks chiefly to the fourth clime, because it lies roughly in the middle of the seven mentioned, and from its consideration it is easy to see what may be done in the remaining climes. Or he chooses the fourth clime above the others because his own homeland, Fragana, lies beneath it, as was shown in chapter 11; or because beneath it is placed Aracta, a city of Syria, the homeland of Albategnius, his predecessor in astronomical studies. For Albategnius himself asserts that at Aracta the pole is raised 36 degrees, and that it is 73 degrees distant from the Fortunate Isles. Moreover, so that it may be known more exactly where Fragana lies, from which Alfraganus took his surname, it must first be observed that the Arabs call it Fargana, which we call Fragana, just as the Arabs name Garnata, which is commonly pronounced Granata. Abulfeda relates that Fragana is the name of a clime containing notable cities and provinces, and likewise the name of a most noble city, which was the homeland of many wise men. He assigns to both a longitude of 92 degrees from the shore of the western sea, and a latitude of 41 degrees and 10 minutes from the equator. Alfraganus, in passing, demonstrates why the year has 365 and 366 days. The solar period, like any other circle, comprises 360 degrees, and the sun completes one degree each day; hence 360 days arise. But since the sun sometimes completes a little more than one degree, it follows that this excess adds five or six days over the whole year. Ptolemy, in Almagest book 3 chapter 1, teaches how the true length of the year is to be investigated. The year is twofold: civil and astronomical. The civil year is that observed among all peoples in the construction of calendars, and its length is 365¼ days. The astronomical year is again twofold, sidereal and tropical. The tropical year is that defined by the interval between the solstices or equinoxes. Just as the solstices and equinoxes change, so the tropical year is unequal according to the different ages. For Callippus, Aristarchus of Samos, and Archimedes of Syracuse said that it has 365¼ days and 6 hours, which is the length of the civil year. Hipparchus observed it to be a little shorter, that is, to contain 365 days and a three-hundredth part of a day. Ptolemy followed this opinion and, explaining it by the hundredth part of a day, gave the daily minutes as 1/14 and 11/48 [of a minute], that is, five hours and hourly minutes 1/55 and 11/12. Albategnius observed that in his century the year contained 365 days, five hours, and hourly minutes ⁴⁄₆ and ¹¹⁄₁₄, so that the hundredth part, or sixth part, of a quarter of a day was lacking. Copernicus found that in the tropical solar year the hundred-and-fifteenth part of a quarter of a day is lacking. The sidereal year is that which returns to some fixed star; according to the finding of Thebit ben Chora, this occurs in 365 days, 6 hours, and ⁹⁄₁₀ ... of a minute. Copernicus, by one second only, found it longer, and by ten thirds, so that it is 365 days, and in daily minutes ⁷⁄₅, ¹¹⁄₄, ¹¹⁄₁₀; that is, 365 days, 6 hours, and hourly minutes ⁹⁄₄₀. Ptolemy, in the aforementioned place, teaches that it is most suitable to observe the intervals of the solstices and equinoxes in order to investigate the solar period; but Copernicus, in book 3, chapter 13 of the Revolutions, criticises him for not observing the sidereal year, since that is always regarded as equal and does not involve so many errors in its assignment. Astronomers indeed need to follow the most exact length of the year in their calculations; for us it is enough to attend to the length of the civil year, even though in the course of time certain inconveniences are observed in this, as will be said in its place. 1 Natural days also have their own inequality, which is nevertheless neglected in sphaerical doctrine; but in astronomy, where the most exact calculation is needed, the inequality of natural days must always be allowed for.

units.la: De numero orbium coelestium, hypothesi-bus planetarum, eorumq; a terra distantiis.
units.tr: On the number of heavenly spheres, the hypotheses of the planets, and their distances from the earth.
CHAPTER XV.

units.la: POstquam diximus de climatibus, quantitate dierum ac noctium, & aliis quibusdam accidentibus: restat ut de numero orbium coelestium agamus, vestivestigiis insistentes sapientis Ptolemæi, qui tradit septem esse orbes planetarũ, octauū autem omnium esse supremum, in quo stellæ fixæ cum Zodiaco cernantur. Figura horum orbium rotunda est, cuius superficiem conuexam & concauam imaginamur. Infima & propinquissima terræ est sphæra lunæ, secunda mercurij, tertia veneris, quarta solis, quinta martis, sexta iouis, septima saturni, octaua est sphæra stellarum fixarum.
units.tr: Having spoken of the climates, the length of days and nights, and certain other accidents, it remains to treat of the number of the celestial spheres, following in the footsteps of the wise Ptolemy, who teaches that there are seven planetary spheres, and that the eighth, the highest of all, is the one in which the fixed stars are seen together with the Zodiac. The shape of these spheres is round, and we imagine their surface convex and concave. The lowest and nearest to the earth is the sphere of the moon, the second that of Mercury, the third that of Venus, the fourth that of the sun, the fifth that of Mars, the sixth that of Jupiter, the seventh that of Saturn, and the eighth is the sphere of the fixed stars.

units.la: Orbis stellarum fixarum, in quo Zodiacus conspicitur, concentricus est terræ: septem vero planetarum orbes in diuersis partibus cum terra collati sunt eccentrici.
units.tr: The sphere of the fixed stars, in which the Zodiac is seen, is concentric with the earth; but the orbs of the seven planets, compared with the earth, are eccentric in various parts.

units.la: In unoquoque horum octo orbium fingitur circulus, qui secet sphæram in duas æquales partes ab oriente in occidentem: huiusmodi in orbe stellarum fixarum est cingulum signorum, hoc est, ecliptica, ad quam refertur motus inæqualis & verus, quem habent omnes planetæ ab occidente in orientem.
units.tr: In each of these eight spheres a circle is imagined which cuts the sphere into two equal parts from east to west. In the sphere of the fixed stars this is the belt of the signs, that is, the ecliptic, to which is referred the unequal and true motion that all the planets have from west to east.

units.la: Orbes eccentrici sunt hi, in quibus mouetur planetæ medio cursu & æquali ab occidete in orietem.
units.tr: The eccentric orbs are those in which the planet moves with mean motion and uniformly from west to east.

units.la: In his commemoratis septem orbibus eccentricis duo puncta sibi inuicem sunt opposita: quorum vnum est in extrema, alterum in propinqua à terra distantia. Extremum appellatur longitudo maior, apogæum vel aux planetæ: alterum vocatur longitudo minor, perigæum siue oppositum augis.
units.tr: In the seven eccentric orbs just mentioned there are two points opposite to each other: one of them lies at the greatest distance from the earth, the other at the nearest. The farthest point is called the greater longitude, the apogee or aux of the planet; the other is called the lesser longitude, the perigee, or the opposite of the aux.

units.la: Cum autè fuerit planeta in hemicyclo apogæi, motus eius in zodiaco tardior apparet, & minorem habet motum medium, propter summam eius distantiam a terra: si vero fuerit in hemicyclio perigaei; motus eius in signifero velocior est, & maiorem habet motum medium, propter propinquitatem eius ad terram. Medius motus perpetuo idem est, quatenus planeta movetur aequaliter in eccentrico: motus autem verus is est, qui inaequalis apparet in utroque hemicyclio signifseri.
units.tr: When the planet is in the half-circle of the apogee, its motion in the zodiac appears slower and it has a smaller mean motion, on account of its great distance from the earth; but if it is in the half-circle of the perigee, its motion in the zodiac is swifter and it has a greater mean motion, on account of its nearness to the earth. The mean motion is always the same, inasmuch as the planet moves uniformly on the eccentric; the true motion, however, is that which appears unequal in each half of the zodiac.

units.la: Eccentricus deferens corpus solare, cietur motu aequabili: huius orbis eccentrici superficies ita connexa est cum signifero, ut nusquam declinet ab eo.
units.tr: The eccentric carrying the solar body is moved by a uniform motion; the surface of this eccentric orb is so joined to the zodiac that it never departs from it.

units.la: Reliquorum sex planetarum corpora non deferuntur in eccentricis, sed vehuntur in circulis parvis, qui appellantur epicycli, quorum centra implicata sunt eccentricis, ut superficies tam eccentricorum quam epicyclorum declinet a superficie signiferi, hoc est, respectu mundi sit eccentrica. Et centrum epicycli lunaris positum est in praedicto eius eccentrico, veruntamen centrum epicycli aequaliter movetur super centro signiferi. Centra vero epicyclorum in reliquis quinque erraticis stellis posita sunt super aliis eccentricis, qui diversi sunt ab illis prioribus quos commemoravimus; sunt tamen aequales illis in magnitudine, & superficies illorum est eadem. Cum autem centra epicyclorum posita sint in huiusmodi eccentricis, moventur aequaliter ter temporibus æqualibus super centro eccentrico-rum priorum.
units.tr: The bodies of the other six planets are not carried on eccentrics but are borne on small circles, which are called epicycles, whose centres are attached to the eccentrics, so that the surfaces both of the eccentrics and of the epicycles depart from the surface of the zodiac, that is, are eccentric with respect to the world. The centre of the epicycle of the moon is placed on its aforesaid eccentric, yet the centre of the epicycle moves uniformly about the centre of the zodiac. The centres of the epicycles of the remaining five wandering stars are placed upon other eccentrics, which differ from those earlier ones we mentioned; they are, however, equal to them in size, and their surface is the same. And since the centres of the epicycles are placed on eccentrics of this kind, they move uniformly, in equal times, about the centre of the earlier eccentrics.

units.la: Nominatur itaque orbis super quo est centrum epicycli, eccentricus deferens centrum epicycli: orbis autem primus, super cuius centro mouetur centrum epicycli æqualiter, dicitur eccentricus æquans cursum.
units.tr: Therefore the orb on which the centre of the epicycle lies is called the eccentric carrying the centre of the epicycle; the first orb, about whose centre the centre of the epicycle moves uniformly, is called the equating eccentric.

units.la: Vnaquæque autem superficies horum orbium eccentricorum in sex planetis, secat superficiem zodiaci in duo hemicyclia, iuxta duo opposita loca: & declinat ab ea in duabus partibus versus septentrionem & meridiem: & spacium quod ab utraque sectione intercipitur appellatur draco: punctum a quo incipit orbis planetæ declinare ab orbe signorum ad septentrionem, vocatur caput draconis, sine geuzohar, & punctum oppositum dicitur cauda draconis.
units.tr: Now each surface of these eccentric orbs in the six planets cuts the surface of the zodiac into two half-circles at two opposite places, and departs from it on two sides, toward the north and the south; the space intercepted between the two sections is called the dragon. The point from which the orb of the planet begins to decline from the orb of the signs toward the north is called the head of the dragon, or geuzohar, and the opposite point is called the tail of the dragon.

units.la: In luna superficies epicycli est inseparabilis a superficie eccentrici, ut non declinet ab ea: quapropter inest ei in latitudine diuersitas una, propter declinationem eccentrici eius ab orbe signorum.
units.tr: In the moon the surface of the epicycle is inseparable from the surface of the eccentric, so that it does not depart from it; hence it has one variation in latitude, owing to the declination of its eccentric from the orb of the signs.

units.la: Quinque vero reliquorum planetarum epicycli declinant ab eccentricis duplicirter: quare contingunt vnicuique eorum diuersitates duæ, quarum una est propter declinationem eccentrici a signifero, altera accidit propter declinationem epicycli ab eccentrico. Atqhæ sunt hypothesis a sapientibus tradita de sphæris cælestibus.
units.tr: The epicycles of the remaining five planets, however, depart from their eccentrics in two ways; so each of them has two variations in latitude, one of which arises from the declination of the eccentric from the zodiac, the other from the declination of the epicycle from the eccentric. These are the hypotheses handed down by the wise concerning the celestial spheres.

units.la: In vulgatis editionibus huic capiti figurae aliquot inferuntur, vt etiam quaedam apponuntur ad explicationè eclipsium, sub finem huius opusculi: sed Hebraea & Latina bibliothecae Palatinae versio, figuras nullas habet: neque illis vsus est Alfraganus, alias in contextum literas quasdam apposuisset, quibus schemata declarasset: idcirco nos quoque vulgata schemata omisimus.
units.tr: In the common editions several figures are inserted under this chapter, and some are also added at the end of this little work to explain eclipses; but the Hebrew and Latin version of the Palatine library has no figures, nor did Alfraganus use any, for otherwise he would have added certain letters in the text by which he would have explained the diagrams. Therefore we too have omitted the common diagrams.

units.la: Qui autem pleniorem harum hypothe-sium defiderat explicationem, consulat Almageftum Ptolemaei, & neotericorum in planetis theorias: hoc tantum monendum ducimus, vocem aux apud Arabes scribi cum Alef, Vau & Gimel: proinde x more Hispanorum, vt s[?] durum est legendum, quod etiam casus obliqui ostendunt, in quibus x transiit in g literam radicalem.
units.tr: Whoever desires a fuller explanation of these hypotheses should consult the Almagest of Ptolemy and the modern theories of the planets. We think this only needs to be noted: the word aux is written among the Arabs with Alef, Vau and Gimel; therefore, as the Spanish do, the x is to be read as a hard s, as the oblique cases also show, in which x passed into g as the radical letter.

units.la: Alfraganus cum Ptolemęo statuit augem siue apogaeum solis esse immobile: sed Alfonsini mathematici experientia multorum saeculorum edocti, tradiderunt augem solarem paulatim in antecedentia promoueri: propterea tres orbes soli attribuerunt, scilicet eccentricum, qui corpus solare deferat, & duos augem promouentes, quorum vnus mundo sit concentricus, alter eccentricus.
units.tr: Alfraganus, with Ptolemy, held that the aux or apogee of the sun is immovable; but the Alfonsine mathematicians, taught by the experience of many centuries, have taught that the solar aux gradually advances in the direction of the preceding signs. Therefore they assigned three orbs to the sun: the eccentric that carries the solar body, and two that move the aux, of which one is concentric with the world and the other eccentric.

units.la: Quod ad interfectionem draconis attinet, sciendum est, vtrumque nodum seu punctum Arabibus appellari geuzohar, etsi [?]κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν [?] sectio septentrionalis, quo caput draconis pertingere imaginamur, dicatur geuzohar: hinc est quod multa legimus de indagando geuzohar planetarum: nam qui locum capitis draconis nouit, simul etiam cognoscit oppositum geuzohar, hoc est locum caudae draconis. Scribitur autem hoc nomen geuzohar, vt videre licet in epitome Arabica Almagesti, per Gimel, Vau, Zain, He & Refch: vt explodendi sint, qui corrupte scribunt leguntque genzohar.
units.tr: As regards the intersection of the dragon, it must be understood that both nodes, or points, are called geuzohar by the Arabs, although especially [κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν] the northern section, to which we imagine the head of the dragon reaches, is called geuzohar. Hence we read much about investigating the geuzohar of the planets; for whoever knows the place of the head of the dragon at the same time knows the opposite geuzohar, that is, the place of the tail of the dragon. This name is written geuzohar, as may be seen in the Arabic epitome of the Almagest, with Gimel, Vau, Zain, He and Resh; so those who write and read it corruptly as genzohar are to be rejected.

units.la: De motu solis & lunæ, stellarumque fixarum, in duabus partibus orientis & occidentis, qui vocatur motus longitudinis.
units.tr: On the motion of the sun and moon, and of the fixed stars, in the two directions of east and west, which is called the motion of longitude.
CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: POstquam ostendimus rationem orbium cœlestium, incipiamus recesere motum singularum sphærarum: & primo omnium declaremus motum stellarum fixarum, quem communem habent cum erraticis.Sphæra stellarum fixarum mouetur ab occidente in orientem, & rapit secum septem planetarum orbes, super duobus polis zodiaci, vt annis centum gradum vnum promoueatur, fecundum obseruatione Ptolemæi: hinc fit vt auges septe planetarum & geuzohar eorum permutentur fecundum successionem signorum, & gradum vnum quibuslibet centenis annis conficiunt: itaque totus circulus illorum absoluitur spacio 36000 annorum. Nominantur autem stellæ fixæ, quod motus earum pariter æqualis fit ab occidente in ortum, & ad fe invicem eandem perpetuo retineant distantiam.
units.tr: Having shown the arrangement of the heavenly spheres, let us now take up the motion of each sphere. First of all, let us set out the motion of the fixed stars, which they share with the planets. The sphere of the fixed stars moves from west to east and carries with it the orbs of the seven planets, about the two poles of the zodiac, so that it advances by one degree in a hundred years, according to Ptolemy's observation. Hence the apogees of the seven planets and their geuzohar change places according to the order of the signs, and they complete one degree in every hundred years. So the whole circle of these is finished in a space of 36,000 years. The stars are called fixed because their motion is equal from west to east and they keep the same distance from one another at all times.

units.la: Sol itaq; duos habet motus ab occidente in orientem, quorum vnus est illi proprius in eccetrico, quo progreditur omni die naturali 59 [?] fere minuta: alter est motus tardus, quem habet super duobus polis zodiaci æqualem cum motu stellarum fixarum, vt annis centum gradum vnum conficiat. Hos duos motus deprehenditur habere in zodiaco ab occidente in orientem, vt periodum annuam absoluat 365 diebus, & quadrante diei: etsi defit tempus modi-cum quod nullius reputatur quantitatis.
units.tr: The sun, then, has two motions from west to east. One is proper to it on the eccentric, by which it advances about 59 minutes each natural day. The other is a slow motion, which it has about the two poles of the zodiac, equal to the motion of the fixed stars, so that it completes one degree in a hundred years. These two motions are found in the zodiac, from west to east, so that it completes its annual period in 365 days and a quarter of a day, although there is a small amount of time over, which is regarded as of no account.
