units.la: Luna vero habet quinque motus periodicos, vi-delicet motum corporis sui, quo revoluitur in epicy-clo, ab oriente in occasum, cum est in superiore parte epicycli: & ab occidete in orientem, cum est in par-te inferiore epicycli.
units.tr: The moon, however, has five periodic motions. These are: the motion of its body, by which it revolves on the epicycle from east to west when it is in the upper part of the epicycle, and from west to east when it is in the lower part of the epicycle.

units.la: Centrum epicycli eius mouetur in eccentrico ab occidente in orientem: centrum autem eccentrici mouetur in circulo paruo, qui homocentricus est signifero, ab oriente in occidentem, motu scilicet contrario quam est centri epicycli. Luna praeterea habet orbem alium homocentricum zodiaco, cuius superficies secat eclipticam in duo hemicyclia super duobus punctis oppositis, quae vocantur caput & cauda draconis: & declinat ab ecliptica versus septentrionem & meridiem. atque hic orbis homocentricus rapit secum eclipticam super duobus polis zodiaci, ut ambo sectionis loca, quae vocantur caput & cauda draconis, mouentur contra successionem signorum. Habet etiam luna motum tar-dum stellarum fixarum, quo mouetur ab occidente in orientem.
units.tr: The centre of its epicycle moves on the eccentric from west to east. The centre of the eccentric, however, moves in a small circle, which is concentric with the zodiac, from east to west, that is, in a motion contrary to that of the centre of the epicycle. Moreover, the moon has another orb concentric with the zodiac, whose surface cuts the ecliptic into two semicircles at two opposite points, which are called the head and the tail of the dragon, and it inclines from the ecliptic towards the north and south. This concentric orb carries the ecliptic with it about the two poles of the zodiac, so that both points of intersection, called the head and tail of the dragon, move against the order of the signs. The moon also has a slow motion of the fixed stars, by which it moves from west to east.

units.la: Ut autem motus lunares recte intelligatur, eos per exempla specialia explicemus. Dicimus itaque quod luna, cum fuerit in superiori parte epicycli, moueatur in una die per utrosque motus suos. Corpus quidem lunae mouetur in epicyclo versus occi-dendentem 13 gradibus, & 4 minutis, prout hæpar-tes in epicyclo numerantur: sed centrum epicycli mouetur in eccentrico ad orientem, secundum quantitatem orbis cum zodiaco homocentrici, per 24 gradus, & 23 minuta: & centrum eccentrici mouetur in circulo paruo, qui cum zodiaco homocen-tricus est, vt reuoluat longitudinem longiorem in rotunditate etiam ad occidentem 11 gradibus, & 9 minutis. Colligitur itaque motus centri epicycli in orbe cum zodiaco homocentrico versus orietem, in vna die 13 graduum, & 14 minutorum. Ho-mocentricus autem quì rapit secum eclipticam, eam-que secat in prædictis nodis, mouetur versus occi-dentem tribus minutis. Complectitur ergo cursus lunæ in zodiaco, qui ratione epicycli apparet, 13 gradus, & 11 minuta fere, qui est medius motus lunæ. Ex motu corporis lunaris in epicyclo extrahi-tur modicum quid, & additur ad medium eius cur-sum, vel ab eo subtrahitur, vt habeatur verus motus lunæ in zodiaco.
units.tr: So that the lunar motions may be rightly understood, let us explain them by particular examples. We say, then, that when the moon is in the upper part of the epicycle, it moves in one day by both of its motions. The body of the moon moves on the epicycle westward 13 degrees and 4 minutes, as these parts are counted on the epicycle. But the centre of the epicycle moves on the eccentric eastward, according to the extent of the orb concentric with the zodiac, through 24 degrees and 23 minutes. And the centre of the eccentric moves in the small circle, which is concentric with the zodiac, so that it also turns through a longer distance in its circuit, westward by 11 degrees and 9 minutes. Thus the motion of the centre of the epicycle, in its orb concentric with the zodiac, towards the east, is collected as 13 degrees and 14 minutes in one day. The concentric orb which carries the ecliptic with it, and cuts it at the aforesaid nodes, moves westward by three minutes. So the course of the moon in the zodiac, which appears because of the epicycle, comprises about 13 degrees and 11 minutes, which is the mean motion of the moon. From the motion of the lunar body on the epicycle, a small amount is taken away and added to this mean course, or subtracted from it, so that the true motion of the moon in the zodiac is obtained.

units.la: Hinc patet quod motus centri epicycli in ec-centrico est secundum quantitatem duplicatæ dif-ferentiæ, quæ habetur inter medium motum lunæ & solis: si enim à medio lunæ motu, hoc est 13 gra-dib. & 11 fere minutis, subtrahatur medius solis motus, hoc est, 59 minuta, cum aliquot fractioni-bus, remanebit differentia duodecim graduum, 11 ½ minutorum: quæ si duplicata fuerit, summa consurgit 24 graduum, & 23 minutorum, atque hæc quantitas æqualis est motui cetri epicycli. Cùm autem centrum epicycli moueatur in eccentrico se-cundum differentiam duplicatam elongationis fo-lis a luna, vt diximus: necessarium est, vt centrum epicycli secet eccentricum bis in quolibet mense syn-odico. Sphæra præterea lunari continenti hos mo-tus, accidit etiam motus tardus, super duobus polis Zodiaci, quo mouetur versus orientem, in centenis quibuslibet annis gradum vnum, iuxta motus stel-larum fixarum. Iam igitur declaratum est in illis quæ commemorauimus, quod cursus lunæ qui appa-ret in orbe signorum ab occidente versus orientem, fit compositus ex quinque motibus periodicis, scili-cet ex motu corporis lunaris in epicyclo; ex motu centri epicycli in eccentrico; ex motu centri eccen-trici in circulo paruo, qui homocentricus fit cum Zodiaco; ex motu orbis decliuis cum zodiaco, super duobus polis ecliptica, quo defertur caput & cauda draconis cotra successionem signorum; ex motu to-tius sphæra, qui æqualis est motui stellarum fixarum.
units.tr: From this it is clear that the motion of the centre of the epicycle on the eccentric is according to the quantity of the doubled difference which is found between the mean motion of the moon and that of the sun. For if the mean motion of the sun, that is about 59 minutes with some fractions, is subtracted from the mean motion of the moon, that is 13 degrees and about 11 minutes, there remains a difference of 12 degrees and 11½ minutes. If this is doubled, the sum comes to 24 degrees and 23 minutes, and this quantity is equal to the motion of the centre of the epicycle. Since the centre of the epicycle moves on the eccentric according to the doubled difference of the elongation of the sun from the moon, as we have said, it is necessary that the centre of the epicycle cut the eccentric twice in every synodic month. Moreover, to the sphere of the moon, which contains these motions, there also belongs a slow motion about the two poles of the zodiac, by which it moves eastward, one degree in every hundred years, according to the motion of the fixed stars. Now, therefore, it has been made clear from what we have mentioned that the course of the moon, which appears in the orb of the signs from west to east, is compounded of five periodic motions: namely, the motion of the lunar body on the epicycle; the motion of the centre of the epicycle on the eccentric; the motion of the centre of the eccentric in the small circle, which is concentric with the zodiac; the motion of the inclined orb with the zodiac about the two poles of the ecliptic, by which the head and tail of the dragon are carried against the order of the signs; and the motion of the whole sphere, which is equal to the motion of the fixed stars.

units.la: Accidit quoque centro epicycli lunaris, quan-do mouetur in eccentrico, declinatio & reflexio a-liquando ad orientem, nonunquam ad occidentem. hoc autem ideo fit, quia cetro epicycli vere exiften-te in longitudine longiore velpropinquiore eccen-trici; diameter epicycli transiens longitudinem re-motiorem continuatur cum diametro eccentrici transeuntis centrum zodiaci secundum rectitudinem. Cum autem epicyclus transit per duo loca ambarum longitudinum; non fit declinatio diametri eius ad centrum eccentrici, neque ad centrum orbis signorum sed declinat semper ad punctum quod est super diametro eccentrici, a parte longitudinis propinquioris, inter ipsam & centrum signiferi: cuius distantia a centro zodiaci tanta est, quanta deprehenditur centri eccentrici a centro orbis signorum. Quare centrum orbis signorum secat lineam, quae est inter idpunctum, & centrum eccentrici, in duo hemicyclia. Accidit ergo in die motui epicycli reflexio, declinatq; eius longitudo remotior, quae fuit visa, a loco suo, ita differt a longitudine remotiore, quae videtur secundum veritatem ex centro diversorum locorum in epicyclo. Nam cum centrum epicycli procedit a longitudine remotiore ad propinquiorem; tunc longitudo epicycli remotior, quae videtur, etiam antecedit longitudinem priorem ad orientem : cum autem proficiscitur a longitudine propinquiore ad remotiorem; tunc longitudo epicycli remotior, quae videtur, subsequitur longitudinem priorem ad occidentem : sed maxima praecessio vel successio contingit, cum centrum epicycli est prope ambas longitudines medias eccentrici. Longitudo itaque prima remotior epicycli, quae inseparabilis est a puncto praedicto, nominatur longitudo remotior media: illa vero quae videtur ex centro Zodiaci[?], appellatur longitudo æquata. Hactenus absoluimus omnium motuum lunæ commemorationem.
units.tr: It also happens to the centre of the lunar epicycle, when it moves on the eccentric, that it sometimes turns aside and goes back towards the east, and sometimes towards the west. This happens because, when the centre of the epicycle is truly in the farther or nearer longitude of the eccentric, the diameter of the epicycle passing through the more remote longitude is continued in a straight line with the diameter of the eccentric passing through the centre of the zodiac. When the epicycle passes through the two places of both longitudes, its diameter does not incline towards the centre of the eccentric, nor towards the centre of the orb of the signs, but always inclines to a point which lies on the diameter of the eccentric, on the side of the nearer longitude, between that point and the centre of the zodiac. The distance of this point from the centre of the zodiac is as great as the distance of the centre of the eccentric from the centre of the orb of the signs. Therefore the centre of the orb of the signs cuts the line which lies between that point and the centre of the eccentric into two semicircles. Hence on the day of the motion of the epicycle there occurs a reflection, and its more remote longitude, which was seen, is turned aside from its place. So it differs from the more remote longitude which is seen in truth from the centre at different places on the epicycle. For when the centre of the epicycle proceeds from the more remote longitude towards the nearer, then the more remote longitude of the epicycle, which is seen, also goes ahead of the former longitude towards the east. But when it proceeds from the nearer longitude towards the more remote, then the more remote longitude of the epicycle, which is seen, follows the former longitude towards the west. The greatest advance or recession occurs when the centre of the epicycle is near both mean longitudes of the eccentric. Thus the first and more remote longitude of the epicycle, which is inseparable from the aforesaid point, is called the mean more remote longitude; but that which is seen from the centre of the zodiac is called the equated longitude. Thus we have completed the account of all the motions of the moon.

units.la: Cum in decimo quinto capite Alfraganus expo- fuisset, in hoc aspectabili cœlo esse tantum octofphę- ras, inter quas extrema fit stellarum fixarum, quā fequan- tur septem planetarum orbes: iam singularum sphærarum motus proprios incipit declarare. Asserit autem ex Ptolemæi obseruatione, vniuersas stellas fixas spacio cētū annorū, cōtra motū primi mobilis ad orientē promoueri per gradu vnū: Albategnius autē suo tepore notauit, intra annos sexaginta sex, stellas fixas promotas esse gradu vnu: nonnulli intra annos septuaginta tradiderunt stellas fixas gradu vnum progredi, sicut oftedit epitome Arabica Almagefti. Hac diuersitate motuum in firmamento vt saluarent astronomi, primo omnium commenti sunt quoddam cœlum ἀπλανὲς[?] supra octauam sphæram, quod appellarunt primum mobile, motumq; eius æquabilem ab oriente in occasum, qui pertinet spacio 24 horarū, vocauerunt primū seu vniuersale: de quo dictū est cap.6. Cum ergo firmamentum versus orientem quoq; cernamus moueri, existimandum est hunc eius motum esse proprium, etsi septem planetis fit communis. Præter hos duos motus, Thebitius Ben Chorat, in firmamento obseruauit motu trepidationis in septentrione & meridie: ideoq; statuit adhuc vnum cœlum ἀπλανὲς[?], quod ordine decimum effet: hoc putauit esse primum mobile, quòd fimpliciffimo motu circumduceretur ab ortu in occasum, intra spacium 24 horarū: nonam autem, eamq; ἀπλανὲς[?] sphæram credidit duobus motibus agitari, à primo mobili, & suo ipsius proprio impulsu versus orientem cieri: firmamentum à primo mobili, & nona sphæra conuerti, à seipso autem in fe- ptentrio-[?] ptentrionem & meridiem trepidare existimauit. Ve-rum Copernicus cum animaduertisset motum primi mobilis non esse aliu a motu solis per puncta tropica & æquinoctialia meantis: ipfumq; solem autore esse dieru, ac inæqualitatis ipforu, statuit solem in medio Vniuersi immobilem, & circa eum firmamentu motus omnis expers, cuius loco terra fingatur habere triplicem motu. Post expositum motum firmameti, Alfraganus duoru luminariu, hoc est, solis & lunæ epilogifmos declarat: hi enim in vita ciuili maximam habet vtilitatem. Nam ex motu solis, ratio annorum, ex cursu vero lunæ, mensium natura est percipienda.
units.tr: Alfraganus, having set out in the fifteenth chapter that in this visible heaven there are only eight spheres, of which the outermost is that of the fixed stars, followed by the orbs of the seven planets, now begins to explain the proper motions of each sphere. He asserts, on the basis of Ptolemy's observation, that all the fixed stars advance one degree in a hundred years, against the motion of the primum mobile towards the east. Albategnius, however, noted in his own time that the fixed stars had advanced one degree within sixty-six years; some have handed down that the fixed stars advance one degree within seventy years, as the Arabic epitome of the Almagest shows. To save this diversity of motions in the firmament, the astronomers first of all devised a certain unmoving heaven [ἀπλανὲς] above the eighth sphere, which they called the primum mobile, and its uniform motion from east to west, which takes a space of 24 hours, they called the first or universal motion, of which we spoke in chapter 6. Since, then, we also see the firmament moving towards the east, it must be judged that this motion is its own, although it is common to the seven planets. Besides these two motions, Thebit ben Qurra observed in the firmament a motion of trepidation towards the north and south. He therefore established yet another unmoving heaven [ἀπλανὲς], which would be the tenth in order. He thought this was the primum mobile, because it was carried round by the simplest motion from east to west within a space of 24 hours. He believed that the ninth sphere, also unmoving [ἀπλανὲς], was moved by two motions, one from the primum mobile and the other from its own proper impulse towards the east. He held that the firmament was turned by the primum mobile and the ninth sphere, while of itself it trembled towards the north and south. But Copernicus, having observed that the motion of the primum mobile is nothing other than the motion of the sun passing through the tropical and equinoctial points, and that the sun itself is the author of the days and of their inequalities, established the sun immobile in the middle of the universe, and around it the firmament, free of all motion, while the earth is supposed to have a threefold motion in its place. After setting out the motion of the firmament, Alfraganus explains the epilogisms of the two luminaries, that is, of the sun and the moon, for these have the greatest use in civil life. For from the motion of the sun the reckoning of years is to be grasped, and from the course of the moon the nature of months.

units.la: Periodus solis annua coplectitur 365[?] dies, & paulo minus quandrate diei, hoc est, (ex horis: hinc est, quod in annis cetum & triginta quinque pars illa, quæ quadranti diei deest, diem vnum efficiat. Etsi enim in calendariis & ephemeridibus politicis annum definiamus 365 ¼[?] diebus, vt quarto quouis anno bisextum inferamus: hic tamen calculus rationem folarem perat[?], vt solstitiorum & æquinoctiorum puncta, primum in firmamento notata, longo interuallo absint à loco solstitiorum & æquinoctiorum, quæ nostro sæculo contingunt: siquidem experientia comprobauit, quod sol elapsis annis quibuslibet centum & triginta tribus, quatuor aut quinque anteuerterit priscas epochas gradu uno, cui alias reuolutio vna diurna competit. Quod ad mensem, hoc est, periodum lunæ ab vna solis coiunctione vsque ad alteram, attinet, sciendum nos cum Arabibus & Hebræis spacium mensis fynodici definire diebus 29, horis 12, scrupulis horariis 79 3[?], vt Alfraganus innuit capite primo, & nos in commentario luculenter exposuimus.
units.tr: The solar period comprises 365 days and a little less than a quarter of a day, that is, in terms of hours, about six hours less a little. Hence it is that in a hundred and thirty-five years that part which is lacking from a quarter day makes up one whole day. Although in civil calendars and ephemerides we reckon the year as 365 and a quarter days, so that we insert a leap day every fourth year, this reckoning nonetheless disturbs the solar account. The points of the solstices and equinoxes, first noted in the firmament, are at a long interval from the places of the solstices and equinoxes that occur in our century. For experience has confirmed that, after any hundred and thirty-three years, the sun has come back to the ancient epochs by four or five degrees, a thing which otherwise would belong to a single diurnal revolution. As for the month, that is, the period of the moon from one conjunction with the sun to the next, we must understand that, with the Arabs and the Hebrews, we fix the length of the synodic month at 29 days, 12 hours and 793 hour-scruples, as Alfraganus indicates in the first chapter, and as we have set out clearly in our commentary.

units.la: De motu stellarum quinque erraticarum in orbibus suis secundum longitudinem. CAP. XVII.
units.tr: On the motion of the five wandering stars in their orbits according to longitude. CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Quinque autem stellarum erraticarum motus in suis epicyclis diuersi sunt a motu lunæ, & orbes earum discrepant ab orbe lunari, & a se inuicem. Planetæ cum sunt in superiori parte epicycli, mouentur uersus orientem, iuxta reuolutionem centri epicycli in eccentrico. Cuilibet autem eorum sunt duo eccentrici æquales, de quibus supra diximus: quorum unus defert centrum epicycli; alter est, ad quem refertur motus medius cetri epicycli, qui cernitur in temporibus æqualibus abscindere partes æquales. Et ad centrum huius orbis æquantis motum fit declinatio diametri epicycli, & ipsius reflexio.
units.tr: Now the motions of the five wandering stars in their epicycles differ from the motion of the Moon, and their orbs differ from the lunar orb and from one another. When the planets are in the upper part of the epicycle, they move toward the east, following the revolution of the center of the epicycle on the eccentric. Each of them has two equal eccentrics, of which we spoke above: one carries the center of the epicycle; the other is the one to which the mean motion of the center of the epicycle is referred, which is seen to cut off equal arcs in equal times. And at the center of this equant orb there occurs the declination of the diameter of the epicycle and its reflection.

units.la: Vnumquodque autem centrum eccentrici in saturno, ioue, marte, & venere, deferentis centrum epicycli, secat lineam rectam, quæ est inter centrum signiferi & eccentrici æquatis motum, in duas partes æquales inseparabiliter. Sed centrum eccentrici deferentis centrum epicycli in mercurio, non est fixum, sed reuoluitur in circulo paruo, quemadmodum accidit in luna: & centrum huius circuli parui est fixum super linea, quæ transit vtraque centra, & elongatio eius a centro eccentrici fixi est in opposita parte centri signorum: vt circulus iste paruus secet lineam, quæ est inter centrum suum, & centrum signiferi in duo æqualia, super cetro eccentrici fixi.
units.tr: Now the center of the eccentric carrying the center of the epicycle in Saturn, Jupiter, Mars and Venus cuts, inseparably, into two equal parts the straight line that lies between the center of the zodiac and the center of the equant eccentric. But in Mercury the center of the eccentric carrying the center of the epicycle is not fixed; it revolves in a small circle, just as happens with the Moon. And the center of this small circle is fixed upon the line that passes through both centers, and its displacement from the center of the fixed eccentric lies on the opposite side from the center of the signs, so that this small circle cuts in two equal parts the line between its own center and the center of the zodiac, at the center of the fixed eccentric.

units.la: Centrum epicycli utriusque in Venere & mercurio simul iungitur soli per medium motum, quo cietur secundum longitudinem. Oportet ergo ut uterque in longitudine remotiore vel propinquiore existens in epicyclo, sit coniunctus soli per medium motum: at si fuerint in utroque latere super duobus locis duarum linearum contingentium, quae egrediuntur a terra ad ambo latera epicycli, longissime distant a sole. Centrum epicyclorum in hisce tribus, Saturno, Joue & marte, tardius movetur quam in sole: sed cum additur motus corporis planetæ[?] ad motum centri epicycli, producitur summa æqualis medio motui solis. Quare oportet ut centrum epicycli cuiusque horum trium planetarum reuoluatur in tempore æquali ei, quod est a coniunctione eorum cum sole, usque ad reditu eorum ad eundem. Vnus-quisque autem horum cum iungitur soli per medium motum, est in longitudine remotiori epicycli: cum vero opponitur soli, est in longitudine propinquiore epicycli.
units.tr: The center of the epicycle of each of Venus and Mercury is joined to the Sun by the mean motion, by which it is moved in longitude. It follows that each, whether it is in the farther or nearer longitude of the epicycle, is conjoined with the Sun by mean motion; but if they are on either side, at the two points of the two tangent lines that run from the earth to the two sides of the epicycle, they are at their greatest distance from the Sun. In these three, Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, the center of the epicycle moves more slowly than the Sun; but when the motion of the body of the planet is added to the motion of the center of the epicycle, the sum is equal to the mean motion of the Sun. Hence the center of the epicycle of each of these three planets must revolve in a time equal to the interval from its conjunction with the Sun until its return to the same point. Each of them, when it is in conjunction with the Sun by mean motion, is in the farther longitude of the epicycle; when it is in opposition to the Sun, it is in the nearer longitude of the epicycle.

units.la: Sed nunc singulariter commemoremus motus mercurii, cum varii sint & perplexi. Mercurius itaque in superiori parte epicycli consistens mouetur versus orientem, & centrum epicycli trāsit eccentricum deferentem ipsum versus ortum, similiter centrum huius eccentrici deferentis centrum epicycli reuoluitur in circulo paruo, de quo diximus, versus occidentem. habet etiam sphæra mercurii præter hos commemoratos motus, stellarum fixarum motum, quo tarde in orientem promouetur: sed exponemus rem per exempla, vt fecimus in luna.
units.tr: But now let us discuss the motions of Mercury singly, since they are varied and intricate. Mercury, then, standing in the upper part of the epicycle, moves toward the east, and the center of the epicycle passes along the eccentric carrying it toward the east; likewise the center of this eccentric, which carries the center of the epicycle, is revolved in the small circle of which we spoke, toward the west. The sphere of Mercury also has, besides these motions mentioned, the motion of the fixed stars, by which it is slowly carried forward toward the east; but we shall explain the matter by examples, as we did for the Moon.

units.la: Quando mercurius est in superiore parte epicycli, conficit vno die vtrumque suum motum, vt corpus eius revera per epicyclum ad orientem promouetur 3 gradibus, & 6 minutis, prout partes in epicyclo numerantur: monetur autem centrum epicycli eius in eccentrico deferente ipsum versus orientem, secundum quantitatem, quæ est de partibus eccentrici fixi æquantis motum, vt æqualis sit duplicato medio motui solis: cuiusmodi est gradus v-nus, & 58 fere minuta. Centrum eccentrici defe-rentis centrum epicycli, in circulo paruo mouetur, & renoluit longitudinem remotiorem secundum rotunditatem versus occidentem, 59 minutis, vt fit in sole. Est ergo motus centri epicycli ad orietem, de partibus eccentrici fixi, similis medio motui solis, hoc est, 59 minutis.
units.tr: When Mercury is in the upper part of the epicycle, in one day it completes both of its motions: its body, indeed, is carried through the epicycle toward the east by 3 degrees and 6 minutes, as the parts on the epicycle are counted; and the center of its epicycle is moved on the eccentric carrying it toward the east, by the amount that is of the parts of the fixed equant eccentric, so that it equals double the mean motion of the Sun, which is 1 degree and about 58 minutes. The center of the eccentric carrying the center of the epicycle moves in the small circle and revolves the farther longitude, by 59 minutes, toward the west, as happens with the Sun. The motion of the center of the epicycle toward the east, measured on the parts of the fixed eccentric, is therefore similar to the mean motion of the Sun, that is, 59 minutes.

units.la: Quamobrem centru epicycli in mercurio secat eccentricum fixum æquatem motum, in tempore æquali ei, quod requiritur ad annum, in quo sol abscindit eccentricum suum: itaque eodem modo trasibit eccentricus centru deferentis ipsum bis in anno, sicut luna in quolibet mense bis secat eccentricum.
units.tr: Therefore the center of the epicycle in Mercury cuts the fixed equant eccentric in a time equal to that which is required for the year in which the Sun traverses its eccentric; and in the same way the center of the eccentric carrying the center of the epicycle passes across it twice a year, just as the Moon cuts the eccentric twice in each month.

units.la: Præterea eadem sphæra mercurij iuxta motum stellarum fixarum progreditur ad orientem, vt annis quibuslibet centum gradum vnum conficiat.
units.tr: Moreover, the same sphere of Mercury advances toward the east with the motion of the fixed stars, so that in any hundred years it completes one degree.

units.la: Ex his manifestum est, motum mercurij, qui apparet in zodiaco, compositum esse ex quatuor motibus: scilicet ex motu corporis eius in epicyclo, ex motu centri epicycli in eccentrico, item ex motu centri eccentrici deferentis centrum epicycli in circulo parvo contra motum primum, denique ex motu totius sphaerae, qui aequalis est motui stellarum fixarum.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that the motion of Mercury which appears in the zodiac is composed of four motions: namely, the motion of its body in the epicycle, the motion of the center of the epicycle on the eccentric, likewise the motion of the center of the eccentric carrying the center of the epicycle in the small circle, contrary to the first motion, and finally the motion of the whole sphere, which equals the motion of the fixed stars.

units.la: De reliquis quatuor erraticis iam diximus, quod orbes habeant similes, & mutationem centrorum eandem, motumque versus orientem haud discrepantem. Sunt autem haec motuum quantitates: Venus conficit quolibet die in epicyclo 37 minuta, prout numerantur partes in epicyclo, & movetur centrum epicycli in eccentrico aequante motum, iuxta cursum solis & mercurii, scilicet 59 minutis. Saturni vero, Jovis & Martis motus est diversus, ut prius explicavimus: si enim uniuscuiusque motus in epicyclo adiiciatur ad cursum centri epicycli in eccentrico aequante motu, aggregatu aequale est medio solis motui. Movetur itaque Saturnus in uno die per epicyclum 54 minutis: centrum autem epicycli in eccentrico aequante motum progreditur 2 fere minuta. Jupiter movetur in epicyclo, per 57 minuta, & cietur centrum epicycli in eccentrico 5 minutis fere. Mars in epicyclo movetur 28 minutis, & centrum epicycli in eccentrico progreditur 31 minuta fere. Movetur quoque sphaera horum planetarum per gradum unum, quibuslibet centum annis, iuxta motum stellarum fixarum.
units.tr: Concerning the remaining four wanderers we have already said that they have similar orbs, a like change of centers, and a motion toward the east not differing. These are the quantities of their motions: Venus completes in one day 37 minutes in the epicycle, as the parts on the epicycle are counted, and the center of the epicycle is moved on the equant eccentric, following the course of the Sun and Mercury, namely 59 minutes. The motion of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, however, is different, as we explained earlier: for if the motion of each in its epicycle is added to the course of the center of the epicycle on the equant eccentric, the sum is equal to the mean motion of the Sun. Thus Saturn moves in one day through the epicycle 54 minutes, while the center of the epicycle on the equant eccentric advances about 2 minutes. Jupiter moves in the epicycle 57 minutes, and the center of the epicycle is moved on the eccentric by about 5 minutes. Mars moves in the epicycle 28 minutes, and the center of the epicycle on the eccentric advances about 31 minutes. The sphere of these planets also moves through one degree in any hundred years, according to the motion of the fixed stars.

units.la: Ex his omnibus patet, quod motus qui apparet in zodiaco, hisce 4 planetis, excepto mercurio, compositus fit ex tribus motibus tantum, videlicet ex motu planetae in epicyclo, ex motu centri epicycli in eccentrico, & ex motu communi omnium stellarum fixarum.
units.tr: From all this it is evident that the motion which appears in the zodiac in these four planets, Mercury excepted, is composed of only three motions: namely, the motion of the planet in the epicycle, the motion of the center of the epicycle on the eccentric, and the common motion of all the fixed stars.

units.la: Accidit quoque unicuique harum quinque stellarum erraticarum in epicyclo, declinatio & reflexio, quemadmodum accidit lunae: quia diameter epicycli transfiles per longitudinem remotiorem, non transfit per centrum zodiaci, nisi cum vere est in longitudine remotiore & propinquiore eccentrici: cum vero est inter utramque longitudinem, non transit per centrum orbis signorum, nec etiam transfit a parte longitudinis propinquioris, sicut fit in luna, sed insepara biliter inest centro eccentrici aequantis motum. Quapropter in his quinque stellis res ita habet, ut cum centrum epicycli progreditur a longitudine remotiore ad propinquiorem, longitudo remotior aequata epicycli videatur sequi longitudinem mediam versus occidentem, secundum contrarium eius quod fit in luna. Similiter cum procedit motus eius a longitudine propinquiore ad remotiorem, tunc longitudo remotior aequata praevenit longitudinem mediam versus orientem. Hactenus commemorauimus omnes motus stellarum in longitudine.
units.tr: There also befalls each of these five wandering stars in its epicycle a declination and a reflection, just as happens to the Moon: because the diameter of the epicycle, passing through the farther longitude, does not pass through the center of the zodiac, except when the star is truly at the farther and nearer longitude of the eccentric; but when it is between the two longitudes, the diameter does not pass through the center of the orb of the signs, nor does it pass from the side of the nearer longitude, as happens in the Moon, but it lies inseparably in the center of the equant eccentric. Wherefore in these five stars the matter stands thus: when the center of the epicycle advances from the farther longitude to the nearer, the farther longitude, corrected by the epicycle, seems to follow the mean longitude toward the west, the opposite of what happens in the Moon. Similarly, when its motion proceeds from the nearer longitude to the farther, then the corrected farther longitude precedes the mean longitude toward the east. Thus far we have recounted all the motions of the stars in longitude.

units.la: Qua ratione quinque stellis erraticis retrogradatio accidat in zodiaco.
units.tr: By what reason retrogradation occurs in the zodiac for the five wandering stars.
CHAP. XVIII.

units.la: Ostendimus in superioribus, planetam in superiori parte epicycli oberrantem moueri ad orientem, quatenus non tam epicyclus, quàm centrum illius reuoluitur: atque tunc planeta velocior apparet, quia duo motus ad unam partem aggregantur. Cùm verò versatur in inferiori parte epicycli, mouetur versus occidentem contra primum motum. Nunc hoc adiiciamus, quòd cùm planeta est in utroque latere epicycli, procedens ab oriente in occidentem, estq; super duobus locis contactus [?] duarum linearum quæ [?] egrediuntur à terra, ad ambo latera epicycli; non videatur motus eius in epicyclo habere quantitatem manifestam in orbe signorum. Quare quod videtur de cursu eius in zodiaco, est id quod percurrit centrum epicycli tantum. Cùm autem planeta transfit à loco lineæ contingentis epicyclum versus orientem; tunc est principium motus planetæ, quod videtur in epicyclo versus occidentem, tardum, & minus est motu centri epicycli, qui videtur ad orientem: & quanto plus descendit planeta in epicyclo, appropinquando longitudini propiori; tanto tardior videtur motus eius versus occidentem, donec æquetur quantitas, quæ videtur de motu eius in epicyclo, motui cetri epicycli. Cùm ergo æquales fuerint ambo motus in duabus partibus diuersis, non videntur planetæ in orbe signorum progredi aut retrogredi, sed apparent stare. At si augeatur motus planetæ in epicyclo ad occidentem, supra motum alterum qui est ad orientem; tunc videtur planeta retrogradus in zodiaco, quatenus procedit versus occidentem: maxima autem retrogradatio est, cum planeta versatur in propinquitate epicycli: nam cum transiit longitudinem propinquorem ascendendo à parte occidentis, & peruenit ad æqualitatem illius longitudinis, à qua inceperat retrogredi versus orientem, æquantur illi ambo motus tantum, & videtur stare in loco suo, quæ habet in zodiaco, donec pertrasseat illum, & videatur moueri directè ad orientem. Hæsunt causæ retrogradationis circa quinque stellas erraticas.
units.tr: We showed above that a planet wandering in the upper part of its epicycle moves eastward, insofar as it is not so much the epicycle as the centre of that epicycle that revolves; then the planet appears faster, because the two motions add together in one direction. When it is in the lower part of the epicycle, however, it moves westward, against the primary motion. Now let us add this: when the planet is at either side of the epicycle, moving from east to west, and it lies at the two points where the lines that go out from the earth touch the two sides of the epicycle, its motion on the epicycle does not appear to have any clear effect on its course along the zodiac. Therefore what is seen of its course through the zodiac is only what the centre of the epicycle traverses. When the planet passes from the point of the line touching the epicycle toward the east, then the beginning of the planet's motion, which appears westward on the epicycle, is slow and is less than the motion of the centre of the epicycle, which appears eastward. And the further the planet descends on the epicycle, approaching the nearer longitude, the slower its westward motion appears, until the quantity of its motion seen on the epicycle equals the motion of the centre of the epicycle. When both motions in the two different directions are therefore equal, the planets do not appear to advance or retrograde in the zodiac but seem to stand still. But if the motion of the planet on the epicycle toward the west is increased beyond the other motion, which is toward the east, then the planet appears retrograde in the zodiac, insofar as it proceeds toward the west. The greatest retrogradation, however, occurs when the planet is near the epicycle's point of closest approach: for when it has passed the nearer longitude, ascending from the western side, and reaches equality with that longitude from which it had begun to retrograde eastward, only then do the two motions balance, and it seems to stand still in the place it has in the zodiac, until it passes that place and appears to move directly eastward. These are the causes of retrogradation with respect to the five wandering stars.

units.la: Posset hic aliquis quærere, cum luna in epicyclo suo moueatur sicut quinque stellæ erraticæ, quare non accidat ei retrogradatio, cuius ratione possit ad occidentem ferri, cum est in parte superiore epicycli? Causa huius rei est, quod luna, in quacunque epicycli parte consistat, motum exiguum videatur habere in zodiaco, si conferatur cum motu centri epicycli: sed accidit illi propter suum motum in epicyclo, velocitas & tarditas tantum. velocitas quidem in longitudine propinquiore, tarditas vero in longitudine remotiore.
units.tr: Here someone might ask: since the moon moves on its epicycle just as the five wandering stars do, why does it not undergo retrogradation, by which it could be carried westward when it is in the upper part of the epicycle? The cause of this is that the moon, wherever it stands in the part of the epicycle, appears to have only a small motion in the zodiac when compared with the motion of the centre of the epicycle; but it experiences only swiftness and slowness from its motion on the epicycle: swiftness indeed in the nearer longitude, and slowness in the more distant longitude.

units.la: Nunc autem determinemus loca, iuxta quæ fit retrogradatio & directio in epicyclo. cum fuerit longilongitudo planetæ ex longitudine propiori æquata in utroque latere epicycli, tanta aut paulo minor, erit retrogradus: cum vero maior erit, planeta habebit motum directum. Saturno tribuuntur 60 gradus, Iovi 55 gradus, Marti 17 gradus, Veneri 13 gradus, Mercurio 34 gradus. Inter hos duo, Venus sci-licet & Mercurius variant distantiam suam a sole versus orientem & occidentem, quando uterq; est in duabus lineis cotingentibus epicyclum: venus enim distat 48 gradibus, & mercurius 28 gradibus.
units.tr: Now let us determine the places at which retrogradation and direct motion occur on the epicycle. When the planet's longitude, measured from the nearer longitude, is equal on either side of the epicycle to such a quantity, or a little less, it will be retrograde; but when it is greater, the planet will have direct motion. Saturn is assigned 60 degrees, Jupiter 55 degrees, Mars 17 degrees, Venus 13 degrees, Mercury 34 degrees. Of these, Venus and Mercury, namely, vary their distance from the sun toward east and west when each is on the two lines touching the epicycle: for Venus is 48 degrees distant, and Mercury 28 degrees.

units.la: De amplitudine epicyclorum in orbibus eccentricis, & distantiis centrorum eccentricorum à centro terræ.
units.tr: On the amplitude of epicycles in eccentric orbs, and the distances of the eccentric centres from the centre of the earth.
Chapter XIX.

units.la: Describamus itaque in hoc capite longitudines centrorum epicyclorum. De sole quidem iam diximus, quod habeat unum eccentricum, cuius centrum distet à terræ centro, per 2 ½ gradus, quatenus semidiameter eccentrici ponitur 60 graduum, quæ est longitudo solis media à terra: reliquas autem quinque stellas erraticas ostendimus habere duos eccentricos, quorum centra cum centro terræ incidunt in lineam rectam fixam & immobilem, ut longitudines quæ sunt inter ea habeantur æquales.
units.tr: Let us therefore describe in this chapter the longitudes of the centres of the epicycles. We have already said of the sun that it has one eccentric, whose centre is 2½ degrees distant from the centre of the earth, the semidiameter of the eccentric being taken as 60 degrees, which is the sun's mean distance from the earth. We have shown that the remaining five wandering stars have two eccentrics each, whose centres, together with the centre of the earth, fall on a straight line that is fixed and immovable, so that the longitudes between them are taken as equal.

units.la: Ad mercurium quod attinet, habet is centrum tertium, quod mouetur super uno reliquorum duorum centrorum per longitudinem æqualem longitudini centri fixi. De luna quoque diximus, quòd habeat duo centra, quorum vnum est centrum fixum, alterum mouetur super centro terræ fecundum longitudinem æqualem longitudini cetri fixi, quatenus semidiameter eccentrici ponitur 6 o graduum, quæ est distantia media planetarum à terra. Longitudines quæ vnicuique planetæ assignantur sunt hæ : faturno tribuuntur 3 gradus, & ¼ & ½ gradus: jovi 2 ½ gradus, & ¼ gradus: marti 6 gradus: veneri 1 ¼ gradus: mercurio 3 gradus: lunæ tribuuntur 12 ½ gradus.
units.tr: As for Mercury, it has a third centre, which moves upon one of the other two centres through a longitude equal to the longitude of the fixed centre. We have also said of the moon that it has two centres, one of which is the fixed centre, while the other moves about the centre of the earth through a longitude equal to the longitude of the fixed centre, the semidiameter of the eccentric being taken as 60 degrees, which is the mean distance of the planets from the earth. The longitudes assigned to each planet are these: to Saturn, 3 degrees, and ¼ and ½ of a degree; to Jupiter, 2½ degrees and ¼ of a degree; to Mars, 6 degrees; to Venus, 1¼ degrees; to Mercury, 3 degrees; to the moon, 12½ degrees.

units.la: Quantitates vero semidiametrorum in epicyclis, vt etiam fit in semidiametris eccentricorum, ponuntur 60 graduum: iuxta quam rationem saturno debentur 6 ½ gradus: jovi 11 ½ gradus: marti 39 ½ gradus: veneri 43 ¼ gradus : mercurio 22 ¼ gradus: lunæ 6 ⅓ gradus tribuuntur.
units.tr: The magnitudes of the semidiameters of the epicycles, as also of the semidiameters of the eccentrics, are taken as 60 degrees. According to this ratio, Saturn is allotted 6½ degrees, Jupiter 11½ degrees, Mars 39½ degrees, Venus 43¼ degrees, Mercury 22¼ degrees, and the moon 6⅓ degrees.

units.la: De reuolutionibus periodicis planetarum in orbibus suis & zodiaco.
units.tr: On the periodic revolutions of the planets in their orbits and in the zodiac.
CHAPTER XX.

units.la: EXposituri periodicas planetarum reuolutiones, incipiamus ab illis, quæ in epicyclis contingunt. Luna reuoluit epicyclum 27 diebus, & 13 ⅓ horis fere: mercurius 3 mensibus, & 26 diebus fere : venus 1 anno Persico, 7 mefibus, & 9 diebus fere: mars 2 annis, 1 mense, & 20 diebus fere: jupiter 1 anno, 1 mense, & 4 diebus fere: faturnus 1 anno, & 13 diebus fere. Periodi eccentricorum respondent fere reuolutionibus Zodiaci: non enim motus tardus stellarum fixarum adiicit aliquid cursui planetarum in ecce-tricis,quod fit alicuius momenti,nisi in faturno & ioue,propter orbium ipsorum amplitudinem. Luna itaque reuertitur ad idem Zodiaci punctum unde discesserat,27 diebus,7 ½ horis,& ⅕ unius horæ fere. Veneris autem, mercurij & solis periodus absol-uitur 365 diebus,& ¼ diei fere. Martis periodus co-ficitur in anno Persico,10 mensibus, & 22 diebus fere. Iupiter in eccentrico reuoluitur 11 annis,10 mensibus, & 16 diebus fere: in zodiaco autem periodus eius minor est uno die cum dimidio fere. Saturnus in eccentrico reuoluitur,29 annis,5 mensi-bus,& 15 diebus: sed in zodiaco periodus eius minor est 9 fere diebus. Geuzohar lunæ absoluit periodum in Zodiaco,18 annis,7 mensibus,& 16 ½ diebus. Reuolutio stellarum fixarum,& augium septem planetarum, ac geuzohar eorundem conficitur in Zodiaco,spacio 36000 annorum.
units.tr: Intending to set out the periodic revolutions of the planets, let us begin with those that occur in the epicycles. The Moon completes its epicycle in 27 days and about 13⅓ hours; Mercury in 3 months and about 26 days; Venus in 1 Persian year, 7 months and about 9 days; Mars in 2 years, 1 month and about 20 days; Jupiter in 1 year, 1 month and about 4 days; Saturn in 1 year and about 13 days. The periods of the eccentrics roughly correspond to the revolutions of the zodiac, for the slow motion of the fixed stars adds nothing of consequence to the course of the planets in the eccentrics, except in Saturn and Jupiter, on account of the size of their orbits. Thus the Moon returns to the same point of the zodiac from which it had departed in 27 days, 7½ hours and about ⅕ of an hour. The period of Venus, Mercury and the Sun is completed in 365 days and about ¼ of a day. The period of Mars is accomplished in a Persian year, 10 months and about 22 days. Jupiter revolves in its eccentric in 11 years, 10 months and about 16 days, but in the zodiac its period is less by about one and a half days. Saturn revolves in its eccentric in 29 years, 5 months and 15 days, but in the zodiac its period is less by about 9 days. The Moon's geuzohar completes its period in the zodiac in 18 years, 7 months and 16½ days. The revolution of the fixed stars, of the apogees of the seven planets, and of their geuzohar, is completed in the zodiac in a space of 36,000 years.

units.la: Alfraganus in hoc capite triplices ostendit periodos planetarum: quarum vna in epicyclo, altera in eccentrico, tertia vero in zodiaco peragitur. Eccentricus solis, veneris & mercurij absoluitur spacio 365 dierum, & iex fere horarum: atque hæc est quantitas anni solaris politica, de qua diximus cap.14 & 16.Lu-na epicycli motum absoluit 27 diebus,& 13 ½ horis fere: in zodiaco autem periodum coficit 27 diebus,7 ½ horis,& ⅕ unius horæ fere: atque hoc interuallum est mensis periodici. Est etiam periodus synodica lunæ, ab vna solis coniunctione vsque ad alteram, quæ conficitur spacio 29 dierum, 12 horarum, &793 scru-pulorum horariorum, vt ostendimus cap. 16, & hoc interuallum temporis appellatur mensis astronomi-cus: sicut declarat Alfraganus cap. 1. Huic no multum dissimilis est mensis politicus, qui in ephemeridibus variarum gentium vsurpatur: hic enim apud Arabes & Hebræos alternatim habet 29 & 30 dies: apud Ægyptios autem & Persas, habet perpetuo 30 dies: hi enim anno assignant duodecim menses solares æquabiles, hoc est, 360 dies, & adiiciunt quinque dies appendices: vt anni quantitas perpetuo apud eos sit 365 dierum.
units.tr: Alfraganus in this chapter shows three kinds of periods of the planets: one is completed in the epicycle, another in the eccentric, and the third in the zodiac. The eccentric of the Sun, Venus and Mercury is completed in a space of 365 days and about six hours, and this is the length of the civil solar year, of which we spoke in chapters 14 and 16. The Moon completes the motion of its epicycle in 27 days and about 13½ hours; in the zodiac, however, it completes its period in 27 days, 7½ hours and about ⅕ of an hour, and this interval is the periodic month. There is also the synodic period of the Moon, from one conjunction with the Sun to the next, which is completed in a space of 29 days, 12 hours and 793 hour-scruples, as we showed in chapter 16. This interval of time is called the astronomical month, as Alfraganus explains in chapter 1. The civil month, which is used in the calendars of various peoples, is not very different from this. Among the Arabs and Hebrews it alternately has 29 and 30 days; among the Egyptians and Persians, however, it always has 30 days. For these peoples assign to the year twelve equal solar months, that is, 360 days, and add five intercalary days, so that the length of the year among them is always 365 days.

units.la: Alfraganus in hoc capite bis facit mentionem Persi-corum annorum: vt ostedat se periodos planetarum non per annos solares vulgo receptos, sed per annos æquabiles Persarum & Ægyptiorū declarare, in quibus quadrans diei negligitur. quamobrem cum menses nominat, menses quoq; Persicos intelligi vult, quorum singuli constant tricenis diebus. Habet præterea lunæ periodū quandam ratione geuzohar, hoc est, nodorū ascendentiū & descendentiū: ea absoluitur spacio annorū octodecim, mensium septem, & sedecim dierū cum dimidio. huic respondet periodus enneadecaeterica, hoc est, annorum nouendecim solarium, quod est interuallum aurei numeri, de quo in commentario plura dicentur.
units.tr: Alfraganus in this chapter twice mentions Persian years, to show that he sets out the periods of the planets not by the solar years commonly received, but by the equal years of the Persians and Egyptians, in which the quarter of a day is disregarded. Therefore, when he names months, he wishes Persian months to be understood, each of which consists of thirty days. Moreover, he gives a certain period of the Moon in relation to the geuzohar, that is, the ascending and descending nodes; it is completed in a space of eighteen years, seven months and sixteen and a half days. To this corresponds the enneadecaeteris, that is, a period of nineteen solar years, which is the interval of the golden number, about which more will be said in the commentary.

units.la: De motu stellarum declinantium in septentrione & meridie, qui appellatur motus latitudinis. CAP. XXI.
units.tr: On the motion of the stars declining to north and south, which is called the motion of latitude. CHAP. XXI.

units.la: Postquam exposuimus motus stellarum in longi-tudine, restat vt consideremus latitudine earū: quæ nihil aliud est, quàm declinatio in zodiaco ab ecliptica versus septentrionem & meridiem. Si enim imaginemur circulum trāseuntem polos zodiaci & stellam; arcus qui intercipitur inter stellam & ecliptican, appellatur latitudo. Sol expers est omnis latitudinis, ut ex præcedentibus satis intelligitur: ipse enim motu suo ab occidente in orientem, describit Zodiacum, ut superficies eccentrici eius nunquam recedat ab ecliptica: quod non fit in reliquis planetis, ut postea ostendemus. Stellæ fixæ omnes moventur ad orientem super duobus polis zodiaci: quapropter quæ sunt in superficie ecliptica, nullam admittunt declinationem: quæ vero extra superficiem ecliptica positæ sunt versus septentrionem & meridiem, latitudinem quidem habent, pro ratione arcus inter ipsas & ecliptican intercepti, sed eam invariabilem retinet. Quare manifestum est, stellas quasdam fixas nullam habere declinationem: aut si quæ habeat, eam perpetuo unius esse quantitatis. Luna vero & quinque stellæ erraticæ latitudine habet variabile: quia non movetur super polis zodiaci, sed super polis eccentricorum, qui per diametrum secant superficiem ecliptica, & declinat ab ea duobus in locis, scilicet versus septentrionem & meridiem, & latitudinem habent variam ab ecliptica. Superficies quidem eccentrici lunaris secat superficiem ecliptica in duobus punctis capitis & caudæ draconis, & declinat versus septentrionem & meridiem, eiusque declinatio est fixa secundum unam quantitatem, à quâ nunquam recedit, & superficies epicycli eius est in-separabilis a superficie eccentrici, ut non recedat ab ea, quapropter inest ei in latitudine diuersitas una, quae est propter declinationem eccetrici eius ab ecli-ptica. Stellarum vero quinque erraticarum diuersi-tas in latitudine non est una, quoniam eccentrici declinant ab ecliptica, atque epicycli declinant ab eccentricis: orbes namque eccetricorum secant ecli-pticam secundum diametrum, & declinant ab ea versus septentrionem & meridiem. Loca se-ctionum in quinque planetis haec sunt: saturnus quidem se-ctionem suam habet in medio longitudinis media, & utriusque diuersitatis in eccentrico: sed reliqui quatuor planetae sectiones suas habent in longitudi-nibus mediis fere. Declinatio longitudinum remo-tiorum in eccentricis saturni, iouis & martis ver-git ad partem septentrionalem in orbe signorum: longitudines autem propinquiores ad meridiem fi-xae sunt, quemadmodum accidit in luna. Declinatio eccentricorum in venere & mercurio non est fixa, sed mouetur super diametro zodiaci, quae transit utrosque nodos ad septentrionem & meridiem, re-uertitur ad locum principij semel in anno, iuxta motum longitudinis, ut medietas longior eccentri-ci per sex menses sit in parte septentrionali, & me-dietas propinquior similiter per sex menses sit in parte meridionali: & superficies eccentrici incum-bit superficiei zodiaci bis in anno, quando scilicet centrum centrum epicycli in binos nodos incurrit. Cum au-tem centrum epicycli veneris in utroque nodorum fuerit; tunc principium declinationis medietatis quae sequitur ipsum nodum eccentrici, erit versus septentrionem, & medietatis alterius versus meridiem. In mercurio huius contrarium accidit: cum enim centrum epicycli fuerit in utroque nodorum; tunc initium declinationis medie-tatis, quae sequitur illum nodum, erit versus meridiem, & medie-tatis alterius versus septentrionem. Quare neces-sarium est, ut centrum epicycli cuius-que horum pla-netarum duorum sit in superficie zodiaci iuxta utrumque nodum, cumq; fuerit in parte una ab orbe signorum, non declinat ad partem alteram unquam: & centrum epicycli veneris est ad septentrionem semper ab orbe signorum, mercurij vero versus meridiem semper. Manifestum itaque est, quod summa est declinatio eccētrici ab orbe signorum ad septen-trionem & meridiem in venere & mercurio, quando centrum epicycli est in longitudine remotiore vel propinquiore eccētrici.
units.tr: Having set out the motions of the stars in longitude, we must now consider their latitude, which is nothing other than the declination of a star from the ecliptic along the zodiac, towards the north or the south. For if we imagine a circle passing through the poles of the zodiac and the star, the arc intercepted between the star and the ecliptic is called its latitude. The Sun has no latitude at all, as is sufficiently clear from what has gone before: by its own motion from west to east it describes the zodiac, so that the surface of its eccentric never departs from the ecliptic. This does not hold for the other planets, as we shall show later. All the fixed stars move eastward about the two poles of the zodiac. Therefore those that lie in the plane of the ecliptic admit no declination, while those placed outside that plane, towards the north or the south, have a latitude in proportion to the arc intercepted between them and the ecliptic, and they keep this latitude unchanged. Hence it is clear that some fixed stars have no declination, or, if they have one, it is always of one and the same amount. The Moon and the five wandering stars, however, have a variable latitude, because they do not move about the poles of the zodiac but about the poles of their eccentrics, which cut the plane of the ecliptic through its diameter. They deviate from it in two places, namely towards the north and the south, and have varying latitudes from the ecliptic. The surface of the lunar eccentric indeed cuts the plane of the ecliptic at the two points of the head and tail of the Dragon, and inclines towards the north and the south; its declination is fixed at one amount, from which it never departs; and the surface of its epicycle is inseparable from the surface of the eccentric, so that it does not depart from it. Therefore the Moon has one variation in latitude, which arises from the inclination of its eccentric to the ecliptic. The variation in latitude of the five wandering stars, however, is not single, since their eccentrics decline from the ecliptic and their epicycles decline from the eccentrics. For the orbits of the eccentrics cut the ecliptic along a diameter and incline from it towards the north and the south. The places of the sections in the five planets are these: Saturn indeed has its section at the middle of the mean longitude, and at the middle of both variations in the eccentric; but the remaining four planets have their sections at about the mean longitudes. The declination of the more distant longitudes of the eccentrics of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars tends towards the northern part of the zodiac, while the nearer longitudes are fixed towards the south, as happens in the case of the Moon. The declination of the eccentrics in Venus and Mercury is not fixed, but moves about the diameter of the zodiac which passes through both nodes, towards the north and the south. It returns to its starting point once a year, in accordance with the motion of longitude, so that the longer half of the eccentric lies on the northern side for six months and the nearer half likewise lies on the southern side for six months. The surface of the eccentric lies upon the surface of the zodiac twice a year, namely when the centre of the epicycle arrives at the two nodes. When the centre of Venus's epicycle is at either node, then the beginning of the declination of the half that follows the node of the eccentric will be towards the north, and that of the other half towards the south. In Mercury the opposite occurs: when the centre of the epicycle is at either node, then the beginning of the declination of the half that follows that node will be towards the south, and that of the other half towards the north. Hence it is necessary that the centre of the epicycle of each of these two planets lies in the surface of the zodiac at each node, and that, when it is on one side of the zodiac, it never declines to the other side. The centre of Venus's epicycle is always north of the zodiac, and that of Mercury always south of it. It is therefore evident that the greatest declination of the eccentric from the zodiac, towards the north and the south, occurs in Venus and Mercury when the centre of the epicycle is at the more distant or the nearer longitude of the eccentric.

units.la: Declinatio autem epicyclo-rum quinque planetarum mouetur & permutatur, ut reuertatur ad locum principij in anno semel, sic-ut accidit in motu longitudinis.
units.tr: The declination of the epicycles of the five planets, however, moves and changes so as to return to its starting point once in the year, just as happens in the motion of longitude.

units.la: Sed epicyclus cuius-que horum trium planetarum, scilicet Saturni, Iouis & Martis, mouetur super diametro quae trāsit[?] ambas longitudines medias, ut longitudo remotior epicycli sex mensibus sit in parte septentrionali ab eccentrico, & sex mensibus in meridionali: diametet[?] vero quæ transit ambas longitudines medias semper æquidistat superficiei zodiaci, & superficies epicycli perpetuo secat eccetricum: neq; adhæret ei, sed supponitur superficiei zodiaci bis in anno, quod sit cum cētrum eius mouetur in duobus nodis: & principium declinationis epicycli, quam habet longitudo eius remotior & propinquior ab eccetrico, sumitur ex duobus nodis, ut summa declinatio sit apud longitudine remotiorem & propinquiorem. Partes declinationis sic distinguuntur: longitudines propinquæ epicyclorum declinat ab eccentrico, iuxta declinationem eccetricorum à zodiaco, in longitudinibus autè remotioribus huius contrariu accidit: quia declinatio longitudinum propinquiorum epicyclorum, quando sunt in medietatibus septentrionalibus eccentricorū, vergit versus septentrione: & quando sunt in medietatibus meridionalibus, tendit ad meridie. In declinatione autè epicycli cuiusq; horū duorum, scilicet veneris & mercurij, sunt duo motus. quorū unus similis est motui trium reliquorū planetarū, qui accidit propter declinatione longitudinis remotioris & propinquioris epicycli ab eccetrico: alter est propter declinatione ambarum longitudinum & mediarū epicycli, & nominatur hæc declinatio, inuolutio. Principium declinationis longitudinis remotioris & propinquioris epicycli ab eccetrico, est à longitudine remotiore & propinquiore eccentrici, ut summa sit apud utrumq; nodum, ubi supponitur superficies eccentrici, superficiei zodiaci: principium vero duarum longitudinum mediarum epicycli ab eccentrico, est a duobus nodis: summa declinatio est apud longitudinē remotiorem & propinquiore eccentrici, cum etiā est summa declinatio eccentrici a zodiaco. Patet igitur, quod cum unaquaeq; harum duarū declinationū epicycli fuerit summa, nō futurū sit[?] ex declinatione altera quicquam: cuiusq; enim est principium, cum alterius est perfectio. Sed partes declinationis ita habet: cum est centrum epicycli in medietate, quae incipit a longitudine remotiore eccentrici, tunc declinatio superioris partis epicycli ab eccentrico in venere est ad septentrionē, in mercurio vero ad meridiē, erit q; longitudo propinquior contraria longitudini remotiori epicycli: & cum fuerit centrum in medietate altera eccentrici; contrariū quoq; accidet eius, quod narravimus de medietate prima. Manifestum igitur est ex commemoratis, quod in duobus hisce planetis plurima est declinatio apud utrumq; nodū, quādo ambae longitudines mediae epicycli adhaeret superficiei eccentrici, & orbis signorum suppositorum. Partes declinationis inuolutionis ita habet: cum centrum epicycli est in medietate remotiori eccentrici, tunc declinatio longitudinis mediae orietalis ab eccentrico, in venere vergit ad septentrionē, in mercurio ad meridiē, & longitudo media occidentalis mouetur in contrarium partis orientalis: & cum est centrum in medietate propinquiore eccentrici, contrarium accidit illius, quod narrauimus de medietate longiore. Manifestum quoque est, summam involutionem esse apud longitudinem remotiorem & propinquiorem eccentrici, & tunc ambæ longitudines epicycli adhæ-rent superficiei eccentrici.
units.tr: But the epicycle of each of these three planets, namely Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, moves about the diameter that passes through both mean longitudes, so that the more distant longitude of the epicycle lies on the northern side of the eccentric for six months and on the southern side for six months. The diameter passing through both mean longitudes is always parallel to the surface of the zodiac, and the surface of the epicycle perpetually cuts the eccentric. It does not adhere to it, but is placed under the surface of the zodiac twice a year, which happens when its centre moves through the two nodes. The starting point of the declination of the epicycle, which its more distant and nearer longitude has from the eccentric, is taken from the two nodes, so that the greatest declination lies at the more distant and nearer longitude. The parts of the declination are distinguished thus: the nearer longitudes of the epicycles decline from the eccentric in accordance with the declination of the eccentrics from the zodiac, but in the more distant longitudes the reverse occurs, because the declination of the nearer longitudes of the epicycles, when they are in the northern halves of the eccentrics, tends towards the north, and when they are in the southern halves, it tends towards the south. In the declination of the epicycle of each of these two planets, namely Venus and Mercury, there are two motions. One of them is similar to the motion of the other three planets, which arises from the declination of the more distant and nearer longitude of the epicycle from the eccentric. The other arises from the declination of both mean longitudes of the epicycle, and this declination is called involution. The starting point of the declination of the more distant and nearer longitude of the epicycle from the eccentric is taken from the more distant and nearer longitude of the eccentric, so that the greatest declination lies at each node, where the surface of the eccentric is placed under the surface of the zodiac. The starting point of the two mean longitudes of the epicycle from the eccentric is taken from the two nodes, and the greatest declination lies at the more distant and nearer longitude of the eccentric, since this is also the greatest declination of the eccentric from the zodiac. It is therefore plain that when each of these two declinations of the epicycle is at its greatest, the other contributes nothing; for the beginning of the one is the completion of the other. The parts of the declination are arranged thus: when the centre of the epicycle is in the half that begins at the more distant longitude of the eccentric, then the declination of the upper part of the epicycle from the eccentric in Venus is towards the north, and in Mercury towards the south; and the nearer longitude is opposite to the more distant longitude of the epicycle. When the centre is in the other half of the eccentric, the reverse of what we have described for the first half also occurs. It is therefore clear from what has been mentioned that in these two planets the greatest declination lies at each node, when both mean longitudes of the epicycle adhere to the surface of the eccentric and of the zodiac that is assumed. The parts of the declination of the involution are arranged thus: when the centre of the epicycle is in the more distant half of the eccentric, then the declination of the eastern mean longitude from the eccentric in Venus tends towards the north, and in Mercury towards the south, while the western mean longitude moves in the opposite direction to the eastern part. When the centre is in the nearer half of the eccentric, the reverse occurs of what we have described for the longer half. It is also evident that the greatest involution lies at the more distant and nearer longitude of the eccentric, and then both longitudes of the epicycle adhere to the surface of the eccentric.

units.la: Latitudines planetarum versus septentrionem & meridiem ita habent: luna habet 5 gradus, vt numerantur in zodiaco: reliquæ quinque erraticæ stellæ declinant in septentrionem & meridiem plus minusve. Saturno enim tribuuntur 3 gradus, Ioui 2 gradus. Mars in septentrione excurrit per 4 1/3 gradus, & in meridiem 7 gradus: Venus expaciatur per 6 1/3 gradus, vt probat Ptolemæus in Almagesto, etsi alibi ei tribuatur 9 gradus: Mercurius excurrit per 4 gradus. Sic exposuimus motus omnes stellarum secundum latitudinem, Deo auxiliante.
units.tr: The latitudes of the planets towards the north and south are as follows: the Moon has 5 degrees, as they are counted in the zodiac; the other five wandering stars deviate more or less towards the north and south. For Saturn is assigned 3 degrees, and Jupiter 2 degrees. Mars ranges to the north through 4 1/3 degrees, and to the south 7 degrees. Venus extends through 6 1/3 degrees, as Ptolemy proves in the Almagest, although elsewhere 9 degrees are assigned to her. Mercury ranges through 4 degrees. In this way we have set out all the motions of the stars according to latitude, with God's help.
[From the translation of the Roman exemplar.]

units.la: De numero stellarum fixarum, & diversa earundem magnitudine: ubi 15 commemorantur maximè insignes.
units.tr: On the number of the fixed stars, and their differing magnitudes: where 15 of the most conspicuous are mentioned.
CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: CUm in superioribus declaraverimus motus stellarum in longitudine & latitudine; superest ut videamus quis numerus sit stellarum fixarum, quomodo secundum magnitudinem distinguantur à sapientibus, & quæ nomina sint maiorum, item in qua cæli parte hæreant nostro tempore, cum quibuslibet annis centum per gradum vnum promouentur. Dicimus itaque quod sapientes obseruarint vniuersas stellas, quæ instrumentis notari potuerunt vsque ad extrema meridiei loca sub climate tertio: diuiserunt autem magnitudines earum in sex clas-ses, quarum prima est earum, quæ maximæ sunt, vt canis vterque, lyra, cor leonis, & hisce aliæ similes: secunda classis earum est, quæ paulo sunt minores, vt Alfarkathan, hoc est, duæ stellæ lucidiores in vrsa minore, & clariores inter Beneth As, hoc est stellas vrsæ maioris: ita deinceps reliquis stellis magnitudinem suam assignarunt, vt sint progressi ad classem sextam, quæ est minimarum stellarum, prout oculis discerni possunt. Primæ magnitudinis stellas 15 posuerunt: secundæ 45: tertiæ 208: quartæ 474: quintæ 217: sextæ 63. inter quas 9 sunt obscuræ, & 5 nebulosæ, quales habentur in dorso tauri, & naribus leonis. Summa igitur omnium stellarum est 1022: ex quibus in parte septentrionali sunt 360: in constellationibus Zodiaci sunt 346: in parte meridionali sunt 316.
units.tr: Having explained in the preceding chapters the motions of the stars in longitude and latitude, we must now consider how many fixed stars there are, how the wise have divided them by magnitude, what the names of the greater stars are, and in what part of the heavens they now lie, since they advance by one degree every hundred years. The wise, then, observed all the stars that could be noted with instruments, as far as the southernmost places under the third climate. They divided their magnitudes into six classes. The first class contains the largest stars, such as both Dogs, the Lyre, the Heart of the Lion and others like them. The second class contains those that are a little smaller, such as Alfarkathan, that is, the two brighter stars in the Little Bear, and the brighter stars among the Benet As, that is, the stars of the Great Bear. In this way they assigned a magnitude to each of the remaining stars, progressing to the sixth class, which contains the smallest stars that can be discerned by the eye. They counted 15 stars of the first magnitude, 45 of the second, 208 of the third, 474 of the fourth, 217 of the fifth and 63 of the sixth. Among these, 9 are dim and 5 are nebulous, such as those found on the back of the Bull and in the nostrils of the Lion. The sum of all the stars is therefore 1022: of these, 360 are in the northern part of the sky, 346 are in the constellations of the Zodiac, and 316 are in the southern part.

units.la: Stellæ primæ magnitudinis sunt 15: inter has vna est in signo arietis, iuxta extremitatem fluuij, non procul à Sohel: stella russa in tauro, quæ appel-latur oculus tauri, & Aldebaran: stella russa in ge-minis, quæ appellatur Hajok, hoc est capra, quæ ad verticem imminet habitantibus clima quartum: stella quæ est in pede sinistro geminorum, & Aschehre aljemanija, hoc est, canis dexter sive Syrius appella-tur: stella quæ est in humero dextro aurigæ, & ap-pellatur jed[?] algeuze, hoc est manus orionis: stella quæ est in sinistro humero aurigæ, & dicitur rigel algeuze, hoc est, pes orionis: Sohel, hoc est, cano-bus, quæ est in temone nauis: Aschehre assema-lija, hoc est canis sinister, qui est in cancro, & cum Sohel eadem hora cælum mediat: in leone cor leo-nis, quod est prope eclipticam, in qua sol mouetur: cauda leonis, in virgine existens: stella quæ in li-bra est, & dicitur Alramech, hoc est, arcturus: stella quæ est in manu sinistra virginis, & nomina-tur Alahzel sive Asimech, hoc est spica virginis: stella quæ est in summitate dextri pedis centauri, no procul a Sohel distat: stella quæ est in sagittario, & vultur cadens, hoc est, lyra appellatur, & vertici nostro imminere solet: & stella quæ est in ore piscis australis, sub aquario collocata, & mouetur iuxta caudam scorpij. Atque hæ sunt stellæ maximæ in cælo.
units.tr: There are 15 stars of the first magnitude. Among these, one is in the sign of the Ram, near the end of the river, not far from Sohel; the ruddy star in the Bull, called the Eye of the Bull, is Aldebaran; the ruddy star in the Twins, called Hajok, that is, the Goat, hangs over the zenith for those who live in the fourth climate; the star in the left foot of the Twins is called Aschehre aljemanija, that is, the Right Dog, or Sirius; the star in the right shoulder of the Charioteer is called jed algeuze, that is, the Hand of Orion; the star in the left shoulder of the Charioteer is called rigel algeuze, that is, the Foot of Orion; Sohel, that is, Canopus, is in the stern of the ship; Aschehre assemalija, that is, the Left Dog, is in Cancer, and at the same hour as Sohel it culminates; in Leo, the Heart of the Lion, which lies near the ecliptic along which the sun moves; the Tail of the Lion, which exists in Virgo; the star that is in Libra and is called Alramech, that is, Arcturus; the star in the left hand of the Virgin, named Alahzel or Asimech, that is, the Spica of Virgo; the star at the top of the right foot of the Centaur, which is not far from Sohel; the star that is in Sagittarius and is called the Falling Vulture, that is, the Lyre, and which is wont to hang over our zenith; and the star in the mouth of the Southern Fish, placed beneath Aquarius, which moves near the tail of Scorpio. These are the largest stars in the heavens.

units.la: Ad hoc caput 22 interpres Hebreus refert duo capita, videlicet 19, & 20 quæ extant in vulgata editione Latina: quorum illud est de numero stellarum fixarum, hoc vero de mansionibus lunæ. Prius bifariam tradit, primo iuxta exemplar Romanum, deinde iuxta Arabicum: alterum, quod est de mansionibus lunæ, ex codice Arabico tantum enumerat. Quod ad stellas fixas attinet, diligenter eas recensuit Ptolemæus lib.7. & 8 Almagesti: & quæ situm suo seculo habuerint in do-decatemoriis prolixè explicauit: non enim stellæ fixæ inter se mutant distantias, sed tota ipsarū sphæra locū mutat respectu solis & æquinoctiorū. Tempore Ptolemæi, circa annum scilicet Christi 140, spica virginis, quæ est stella primæ magnitudinis, erat in 16 gradu, & 40 minuto sexti dodecatemorii, hoc est, virginis: hodie illa est in 18 gradu septimi dodecatemorij, h.e. librae: ergo a tempore Ptolemæi vsq; ad nostra ætatem stellæ fixæ promotæ sunt per 21 gradus: qui si adiicia-tur longitudinibus Ptolemaicis, habetur loca stellarū correcta ad nostrū seculū. Hinc apparet Ptolemæum rudi quasi minerua docuisse stellas fixas promoueri in centum annis per gradum vnum: cum experientia posteriorum astronomorum sit obseruatum, eas annis quibuslibet sexaginta sex gradu vno progressas es-se. Vt autem loca stellarum primæ magnitudinis, suo seculo accommodata assignaret Alfraganus, mentionem quidem fecit dodecatemoriorum, in quibus illæ conspicerentur, sed gradus in longitudine nullos adiecit, vt hinc no liqueat, quo tempore vixerit. Sane vltima fluuii Eridani stellam, quā Hebrei & Arabes vocat Achar nahar, vulgo Acarnar, hoc est, quæ post fluuium sequitur, dicit locatam esse in signo arietis: oculū tauri in signo tauri: capram in signo geminorum: canem minorem in signo cancri: cor leonis in signo leonis caudam leonis in signo virginis: arcturum in signo librae: lyram in signo sagittarii: eam, quæ est in ore piscis australis, quam Arabes Phom ahauta (pro quo corrupte pleriq; legunt Fomahant) hoc est, os piscis vocat, sitam esse in signo aquarii: vbi dodecatemoria intelligitur, quæ stellæ fixæ mutat pro diuersa ratione seculorum, & anticipatione vera æquinoctiorum. Si enim prædictas stellas ad nostra tempora examinemus, A-char nahar adhuc est in ariete, sed Aldebaran siue oculus tauri non amplius est in signo tauri, sed hęret in geminis. Capra adhuc est in geminis, & canis minor in cancro: item cor leonis adhuc est in leone, vt cauda eius in virgine: sicarcturus adhuc est in libra: sed lyra nō amplius est in sagittario, sed accessit capricornum: ita Phom ahauta non amplius est in aquario, sed adiit principium duodecimi dodecatemorii, hoc est, piscium. Quod ad reliquas notas stellarum attinet, quæ sumuntur ab ipsis sideribus vel constellationibus, nunquam illæ mutantur: nisi quod phrasis peculiaris sit obseruanda, vt cum dicitur canis maior esse in pede sinistro geminorum, idem est ac si dicatur, canem maiorem habere eam longitudinem in zodiaco, quam etiam habeat pes sinistergeminorum: sic jed algeuze, siue manus dextra orionis dicitur esse in humero de-xtro aurigæ, & sinister pes orionis ponitur in sinistro humero aurigæ siue agitatoris. Aliter Sohel dicitur esse in temone nauis, & spica virginis in manu sinistra virginis, & stella primæ magnitudinis in pede dextro centauri, item in ore piscis: hic enim neque dodecatemoria, neque constellationes ad zodiacum compara-tæ intelliguntur, sed tantum indicatur, temonem nauis habere stellam, quæ appelletur Sohel, & virginem in sinistra sua gestare stellam maxime insignem, quæ dicatur spica: & centaurum in coxa dextri pedis, habere lucidissimã stellam, & piscem australem ex ore eiicere stellam, quæ dicitur Phom ahauta. Alfraganus itaque euidenter ostendit, Sohel ab Arabibus appel-lari stellam eam, quæ in clauo nauis fulget: hanc via-tores appellant stellam S.Catharinæ, quod eam sequi & spectare perhibeantur ab vrbe Gaza ad montem Sinai itineribus nocturnis contendentes: hanc R.Io-na in sacris literis putat vocari Chesil, ut refert Dauid Kimchi in radicibus: propterea errant, qui Chesil pro orione interpretantur, cum pro canobo sit accipien-dum: hanc esse Sohel Arabum tribus signis ostendit Alfraganus; quod sit in gubernaculo nauis, quod coe-lum mediet cum cane minore, & quod in eodem fere parallelo circulo moueatur cum Achar nahar, dextro pede centauri, caudaq; scorpij [?]. Constellationem Hais, siue As Kimchi interpretatur pro fidere agni vel arietis septentrionalis, quem alias ursam maiorem vel plaustrū appellamus: hinc Rabbini posteriores stel-las ursae maioris vocant Benoth As, quasi dicas filias feretri: eas Arabes nominant Beneth As: quod postea corruptum fuit in Benenas: hinc apparet interpretes Iobi 9, & 38 capite As siue Has male pro arcturo accipere: arcturus enim apud Hebræos & Arabes dicitur Alramech, vel stella lucidissima Somech haromach, hoc est lanceatoris siue bootis. Indorso tauri sex aut septem obscurae stellae sunt, quae Graecis appellatur pleiades, Hebraeis nominantur Chimah: Iob 38.
units.tr: To this chapter 22 the Hebrew translator refers two chapters, namely 19 and 20, which are found in the Latin Vulgate edition. Of these, the first concerns the number of the fixed stars, the second the mansions of the moon. The former he gives in two ways, first according to the Roman edition and then according to the Arabic. The latter, which concerns the mansions of the moon, he enumerates from the Arabic manuscript only. As far as the fixed stars are concerned, Ptolemy carefully listed them in books 7 and 8 of the Almagest, and he explained at length where they were situated in the twelve signs in his own age. For the fixed stars do not change their distances from one another; rather, their whole sphere changes its place with respect to the sun and the equinoxes. In Ptolemy's time, that is, around the year of Christ 140, the Spica of Virgo, which is a star of the first magnitude, was at the 16th degree and 40th minute of the sixth sign, namely Virgo. Today it is at the 18th degree of the seventh sign, namely Libra. Therefore, from the time of Ptolemy to our age, the fixed stars have advanced by 21 degrees. If this is added to Ptolemy's longitudes, the places of the stars corrected for our century are obtained. From this it appears that Ptolemy, as if taught by a rough intelligence, held that the fixed stars advance by one degree in a hundred years, whereas the experience of later astronomers has observed that they advance by one degree in about every sixty-six years.
