As for Alfraganus, in order to assign the places of the stars of the first magnitude adapted to his own age, he did mention the signs in which they were seen, but he added no degrees of longitude, so that it is not clear from this when he lived. Indeed, he says that the last star of the river Eridanus, which the Hebrews and Arabs call Achar nahar, commonly Acarnar, that is, the one that follows the river, is placed in the sign of the Ram; the Eye of the Bull in the sign of the Bull; the Goat in the sign of the Twins; the Lesser Dog in the sign of Cancer; the Heart of the Lion in the sign of Leo; the Tail of the Lion in the sign of Virgo; Arcturus in the sign of Libra; the Lyre in the sign of Sagittarius; and the star in the mouth of the Southern Fish, which the Arabs call Phom ahauta (for which many read, corruptly, Fomahant), that is, the Mouth of the Fish, in the sign of Aquarius. Here the twelve signs are meant, which the fixed stars change according to the different ages and the true precession of the equinoxes. For if we examine the aforesaid stars in our own times, Achar nahar is still in Aries, but Aldebaran or the Eye of the Bull is no longer in the sign of Taurus, but lies in Gemini. The Goat is still in Gemini, and the Lesser Dog in Cancer; likewise the Heart of the Lion is still in Leo, as its tail is in Virgo; and Arcturus is still in Libra. But the Lyre is no longer in Sagittarius, but has moved into Capricorn; so Phom ahauta is no longer in Aquarius, but has reached the beginning of the twelfth sign, namely Pisces. As for the other names of the stars, which are taken from the stars themselves or from the constellations, these never change, except that a particular manner of speaking must be observed. When it is said that the Greater Dog is in the left foot of the Twins, this is the same as saying that the Greater Dog has in the Zodiac the longitude that the left foot of the Twins also has. Thus jed algeuze, or the right hand of Orion, is said to be in the right shoulder of the Charioteer, and the left foot of Orion is placed in the left shoulder of the Charioteer or driver. Otherwise, Sohel is said to be in the stern of the ship, the Spica of Virgo in the left hand of the Virgin, and the star of the first magnitude in the right foot of the Centaur, and likewise in the mouth of the fish. For here neither the signs nor the constellations compared with the Zodiac are meant; it is only indicated that the stern of the ship has a star called Sohel, that the Virgin carries in her left hand a star most remarkable, called the Spica, that the Centaur has in the thigh of his right foot a most brilliant star, and that the Southern Fish casts out from its mouth a star called Phom ahauta. Alfraganus therefore clearly shows that Sohel is the name given by the Arabs to the star that shines on the helm of the ship. Travellers call this the Star of St Catherine, because they are said to follow and watch it when they journey by night from the city of Gaza to Mount Sinai. R. Jonah thinks that in the sacred writings this star is called Chesil, as David Kimchi reports in his Roots. Therefore those err who interpret Chesil as Orion, since it must be taken for Canopus. Alfraganus shows by three signs that this is the Sohel of the Arabs: that it is on the rudder of the ship, that it culminates together with the Lesser Dog, and that it moves in almost the same parallel circle as Achar nahar, the right foot of the Centaur and the tail of Scorpio. Kimchi interprets the constellation Hais, or As, as the star of the Lamb or the northern Ram, which we elsewhere call the Great Bear or the Wain. Hence the later rabbis call the stars of the Great Bear Benoth As, as if you were to say the daughters of the bier; the Arabs name them Beneth As, which was later corrupted into Benenas. From this it appears that the translators of Job 9 and 38 wrongly take As or Has for Arcturus, for among the Hebrews and Arabs Arcturus is called Alramech, or the most brilliant star Somech haromach, that is, the Lancer or Bootes. In the back of the Bull there are six or seven dim stars, which are called Pleiades by the Greeks and named Chimah by the Hebrews: Job 38.

units.la: [In exemplari Arabico aliter hæc habent vt sequitur.
units.tr: [In the Arabic copy these things read otherwise, as follows.]

units.la: Stellæ fixæ, ut cum Ptolemaeo sapientes in septem climatibus obseruarunt, aliæ sunt septentrionales, aliæ meridionales: nonnullæ in medio harum cernuntur, quæ ad eclipticam & zodiacum referuntur.
units.tr: The fixed stars, as the wise men with Ptolemy observed in the seven climates, are some northern and some southern; some are seen in the middle between these, and these are referred to the ecliptic and the zodiac.

units.la: Quin etiam in ipso Zodiaco, teste Ptolemaeo, pars dimidia stellarum fixarum septentrionalem spectat plagam, & altera dimidia pars vergit ad austrum.
units.tr: Indeed, in the Zodiac itself, according to Ptolemy, half the fixed stars look toward the northern region, and the other half incline toward the south.

units.la: Septentrionales sunt a capite arietis, vsque ad finem virginis, meridionales à libra, usq; ad finem pisciū[?].
units.tr: The northern stars run from the head of Aries to the end of Virgo; the southern from Libra to the end of the Fishes.

units.la: Universæ autem stellæ, quæ in septentrione & meridie, item in zodiaco spectantur, constituunt sidera quadraginta octo: sed primo declarabimus constellationes septentrionales. Ursa minor extenditur inter polum septentrionalem, habet q; stellas septem.
units.tr: The whole number of stars seen in the north, the south, and likewise in the zodiac, make up forty-eight constellations. But first we will set out the northern constellations.

units.la: Ursa maior vergit ad æquatorem, & habet stellas viginti septem. Draco stellis constat triginta una: quarum quatuor illustres in eius capite cernuntur.
units.tr: The Little Bear extends about the north pole and has seven stars. The Great Bear inclines toward the equator and has twenty-seven stars. The Dragon consists of thirty-one stars, of which four bright ones are seen in its head.

units.la: Lyra, seu vultur cadens, cuius caput spectat polum, & pedes vergunt ad æquatorem, habet stellas undecim: iuxta quas sunt duæ stellæ extra figuram.
units.tr: The Lyre, or the falling vulture, whose head faces the pole and whose feet incline toward the equator, has eleven stars; beside them are two stars outside the figure.

units.la: Alchethi, id est, Hercules, cuius caput spectat æquatorem, & pedes eius directi sunt ad polum septentrionalem, stellis constat 28. Corona septentrionalis, stellis micat octo: inter quas est una præcipuè clara. Alsamech alramech, id est, deferens lanceam, siue bootes, stellas habet viginti duas. Auriga stellas habet quatuordecim, inter quas conspicitur Al-haiok. Deferens caput Algol, id est Perseus, cuius caput spectat polum, & pedes eius diriguntur ver-sus æquatorem, stellas habet 26. Domina stellæ, id est, Cassiopea, cuius caput directum est versus æquatorem, & pedes spectant polum septentrionalem, manum erigit vibrantem, & stellas habet trede-cim. Cepheus stellas habet undecim. Vultur volans, id est cygnus, cuius caput spectat occidentem, & cauda vergit versus orientem: ala eius dextra spectat polum septentrionalem, sinistra vero dirigitur ad aequatorem: stellas habet septedecim. Trian-gulum stellas habet quatuor. Famina quae non est experta virum, id est, Andromeda, cuius caput spectat occidentem, & pedes diriguntur in orientem, stellas habet viginti tres. Equus alatus, id est pega-sus, stellas habet viginti. Caput equi minoris, quod Graeci appellat [illegible, ~7 letters] stellas habet quatuor. Del-phinus sive leo marinus, cuius caput vergit ad polum septentrionale, stellis constat decem. Telum ha-bet stellas quinque. Aquila, quae est juxta sagittam, stellis novem est conspicua. Alange sive serpenta-rius, habet stellas viginti quatuor. Serpens stellas habet octodecim. Constellationes ergo septentrio-nales sunt viginti una: quibus si sporades annume-rentur, consurgit summa 360 stellarum.
units.tr: Alchethi, that is Hercules, whose head faces the equator and whose feet are directed toward the north pole, consists of twenty-eight stars. The Northern Crown shines with eight stars, among which one is especially bright. Alsamech Alramech, that is the one bearing the lance, or Bootes, has twenty-two stars. The Charioteer has fourteen stars, among which Al-haiok is seen. The one bearing the head, Algol, that is Perseus, whose head faces the pole and whose feet are directed toward the equator, has twenty-six stars. The Lady of the Chair, that is Cassiopeia, whose head is directed toward the equator and whose feet face the north pole, raises a brandished hand, and has thirteen stars. Cepheus has eleven stars. The flying vulture, that is the Swan, whose head faces the west and whose tail inclines to the east, its right wing faces the north pole, its left wing is directed to the equator; it has seventeen stars. The Triangle has four stars. The woman who has not known a man, that is Andromeda, whose head faces the west and whose feet are directed to the east, has twenty-three stars. The winged horse, that is Pegasus, has twenty stars. The head of the Lesser Horse, which the Greeks call [illegible], has four stars. The Dolphin, or sea-lion, whose head inclines to the north pole, consists of ten stars. The Dart has five stars. The Eagle, which lies beside the arrow, is conspicuous with nine stars. The Serpent-bearer, or Alange, has twenty-four stars. The Serpent has eighteen stars. The northern constellations, therefore, are twenty-one; if the stray stars are added to these, the sum comes to 360 stars.

units.la: Jam recensebimus stellas duodecim signorum coelestium: Aries stellas habet tredecim, in cuius capite tres clariores existunt. Taurus habet stel- las triginta tres, in cuius oculo est Aldebaran, & in dorso eius conspiciuntur pleiades. Gemini stellis splendent octodecim, in quibus luciores sunt, quae ad brachia & pedes collocantur. Cancer habet stellas novem, inter quas est praesepe. Leo stellas obtinet viginti septem: inter quas cor & cauda sunt stellae maximae insignes. Virgo stellas habet viginti sex: inter quas est spica, Alazel appellata. Libra constat stellis octo: inter quas duae in lancibus positæ sunt clariores. Scorpius habet stellas viginti unam: inter eas est cor scorpij secundæ ma-gnitudinis. Sagittarius constat ex stellis triginta una, inter quas, quæ in dextro malleolo conspicitur, lucidior est. Capricornus stellas habet viginti octo. Aquarius stellas posidet quadraginta duas, inter quas fulgentissima est Phomahauta. Pisces habent stellas triginta quatuor: hisce annumeratur funi-culus. Universus zodiacus, quatenus ei annumerantur stellæ extra figuras positæ, complectitur 346 stellas.
units.tr: Now we shall recount the stars of the twelve celestial signs. Aries has thirteen stars, and in its head three are brighter. Taurus has thirty-three stars; in its eye is Aldebaran, and on its back the Pleiades are seen. Gemini shine with eighteen stars, of which the brighter are those placed at the arms and feet. Cancer has nine stars, among which is the Manger. Leo has twenty-seven stars; among them the heart and the tail are very notable large stars. Virgo has twenty-six stars; among them is the Spike, called Alazel. Libra consists of eight stars, of which two placed in the pans are brighter. Scorpio has twenty-one stars; among them is the heart of the Scorpion, of the second magnitude. Sagittarius consists of thirty-one stars, of which the one seen in the right ankle is brighter. Capricorn has twenty-eight stars. Aquarius has forty-two stars, of which the most brilliant is Phomahauta. The Fishes have thirty-four stars; to these is added the cord. The whole zodiac, counting in the stars placed outside the figures, comprises 346 stars.

units.la: Constellationes meridionales, extra zodiacum positæ, hæ sunt: Cetus sive balæna marina, quæ inclinat ventrem à parte australi versus orientem, stellas habet viginti duas. Algibbar, hoc est, Orion qui spectat orientem, stellas habet triginta octo: in pede eius est stella lucida, quæ cotingit fluuium. Alnahar, sive fluuius, constellatio est in modum serpentis inflexa, & caudam habet instar piscis, constat stellis triginta quatuor. Lepus habet stellas duode-cim. Canis maior, qui dicitur Cheleb alechber, insi-gnitus est stellis octodecim. Præterea est Afchahere alsemalija, sive Cheleb alasgar, hoc est canis minor & septentrionalis, positus versus cancrum, stellas habet duas: quarum una est in eius humero prima magnitudinis. Alsephina, id est, navis spectans polum meridionalem inferiori parte, caput eius & medium vergunt ad æquatorem: habet stellas qua-draginta draginta quinque: in eius gubernaculo fulget Sohel. Hinc sequitur Alsigahh, id est hydra, cuius caput spectat occidentem, cauda autem vergit ad orientem, dorsum eius inclinat ad austrum: stellas habet viginti quinque. Patina, crater Græcis dicta, manubrium eius spectat versus polum septentrionalem, fundus autem eius vergit ad austrum, stellas habet septem. Algorab siue corvus rostro spectat occidentem, & pedibus vergit ad orietem, ala eius expanduntur versus septentrionem: stellas habet septem.
units.tr: The southern constellations, placed outside the zodiac, are these. Cetus, or the sea-whale, which bends its belly from the southern side toward the east, has twenty-two stars. Algibbar, that is Orion, which faces the east, has thirty-eight stars; at its foot is a bright star, which touches the river. Alnahar, or the River, is a constellation bent in the manner of a serpent, and has a tail like a fish; it consists of thirty-four stars. The Hare has twelve stars. The Greater Dog, which is called Cheleb alechber, is marked with eighteen stars. Besides there is Afchahere alsemalija, or Cheleb alasgar, that is the Lesser and northern Dog, placed toward the Crab, which has two stars, of which one on its shoulder is of the first magnitude. Alsephina, that is the Ship, which faces the south pole with its lower part, its head and middle incline toward the equator, has forty-five stars; in its rudder shines Sohel. Next follows Alsigahh, that is the Hydra, whose head faces the west, whose tail inclines to the east, and whose back bends toward the south; it has twenty-five stars. The Dish, called Crater by the Greeks, whose handle faces the north pole and whose base inclines to the south, has seven stars. Algorab, or the Crow, faces the west with its beak and inclines toward the east with its feet; its wings are spread toward the north; it has seven stars.

units.la: Præterea est Cetaurus, cuius media pars hominem, & altera media equum refert: pedes eius spectant polum meridionalem, caput eius convertitur ad polum septentrionalem, manu vna gestat scutum, altera transfigit lupum: habet stellas triginta septem. Alsabahh, id est fera siue lupus, incumbit Centauro, cauda eius vergit ad polum meridionalem, caput ad septentrionalem. stellas habet nouendecim. Thuribulum, siue ara, in cuius medio flamma ignis conspicitur, & dirigitur versus polum australem, stellas habet septem. Alachil algenubi, id est corona australis, cuius stellæ in duplicata spira fulgent, stellas habet tredecim. Pisces meridionalis, capite orientem, cauda vero occidentem spectat, aquam ab aquario effusam absorbet, stellas habet vndecim. Ergo quindecim sunt constellationes meridionales, extra zodiacum positæ: in quibus sunt stellæ, sporadibus annumeratis, 316. Summa omnium stellarum fixarum in universo firmamento est 1022.
units.tr: Besides there is the Centaur, whose middle part represents a man and the other middle part a horse; its feet face the south pole, its head is turned toward the north pole; with one hand it carries a shield, with the other it transfixes a wolf. It has thirty-seven stars. Alsabahh, that is the beast or wolf, lies upon the Centaur; its tail inclines to the south pole, its head to the north. It has nineteen stars. The Censer, or altar, in whose middle a flame of fire is seen, and which is directed toward the south pole, has seven stars. Alachil algenubi, that is the Southern Crown, whose stars shine in a double coil, has thirteen stars. The Southern Fish, whose head faces the east and whose tail faces the west, absorbs the water poured out by the Water-bearer, and has eleven stars. Therefore there are fifteen southern constellations placed outside the zodiac, in which, counting the stray stars, there are 316 stars. The sum of all the fixed stars in the whole firmament is 1022.

units.la: In hac appendice enumerantur quadraginta octo afterismi siue constellationes cœlestes: quarum viginti una sunt in septentrione, & copulantur stellas trecentas & sexaginta: duodecim constellationes sunt in zodiaco, quæ suppeditant stellas trecentas & quadraginta sex: in parte meridionali sunt quindecim constellationes, quæ suggerunt stellas trecentas & sedecim. Itaque stellæ totius firmamenti sunt mille & viginti duæ: sicut Ptolemæus tradit, qui eas diligentissime recensuit. Nec est cur hunc numerum stellarum rideamus, quod in sacris literis scribatur, eas esse innumerabiles: non enim dubium est, quin plurimæ fugiant, quæ penitus impressæ sunt sphæræ octauæ. Si vero aliqui plures stellas possint ostendere, quam ab astronomis hactenus sint obseruatæ, magnaipsis gratiam referemus. Epitome Arabica Almagefti hoc ordine, & his nominibus stellas extra zodiacum positas enumerat: in parte septentrionali est dub alalgar, & dub alechber, h.e. vrsa minor, & vrsa maior: tanin, h.e. draco: Cepheus: Alhhava, h.e. vociferator siue bootes: Alpheccha, h.e. corona septentrionalis: Alcheri hale rechabateh, h.e. procidens in genu suum, siue est Hercules: Schaliaf, h.e. lyra: aldigaga, h.e. gallina: Dhath alchursi, h.e. domina sellæ, quæ est Cassiopeia: Chamil ras algol, h.e. deferes caput Algol, hic est Perseus: Memaslich alhanan, h.e. retinens habenas, qui Græcis dicitur Heniochus, siue auriga: Alhhakkab, h.e. aquila: Aldelphin, h.e. delphinus: Alsoham, h.e. telum: Alhava, h.e. serpentarius: Alhaja, h.e. serpens: Kataat alfaras, hoc est [illegible, ~7 letters] ἵππος[?], ut appellat Ptolemæus: Alfaras alathem, h.e. equus maior: Almara al-mefulsela, h.e. fœmina catenata, ea est quæ Androme-dadida dicitur: Almutaleth,h.e.triangulum.Hic autè confiderandu est,quod quædam nomina varient: in vrsa minore tres sunt clariores: quæ in cauda est, appellatur stella polaris: reliquæ duæ, quæ sunt in corpore, dicuntur Alfarkathan.Stellæ vrsæ maioris septem lucidiores,quæ plaustri figuram effingunt, appellantur Beneth As. Inter crura vociferatoris siue lanceatoris micat stella primæ magnitudinis, quæ sporadibus annumeratur,& dicitur Arabibus Alramech, Græcis arcturus.Alcheti hale rechabateh,h.e.procidens in genu suum,Ptolemæo vocatur ὁ ἐν γόνασιν ἀσπασμός[?]: alias Hercules appellatur:nonnunqua simpliciter Alcheti, id est,procidens dicitur,vt habuimus apud Alfraganū cap.2. Vbi lapsus est interpres Hebræus, qui scripsit Algedi,quod nomen capricornū significat, signū scilicet zodiaci: errauit etiã Augustinus Ricius in libello de motu octauæ sphæræ, quãdo asserit Alfraganū fecisse mentione Algedi, h.e. capricorni qui cospiciatur prope polum: nã Alfraganus ibidé nō meminit Algedi,sed Alcheti,h.e.Herculis procubentis in alterū genu.Lyra frequeter dicitur Alvakab,h.e.cadęs,scilicet vultur:& gallina nominatur Altayr,id est,volás,scilicet vultur: Cepheus etiam Alredaf nominatur. Algol Arabes vocat Medufam,caput Medufæ appellant Ras algol,Hebrei vocat id Rosch hassatan,id est,caput diaboli: ergo qui abscidit & defert caput Medufæ gorgonum principis, hic est Perseus,Arabibus dicitur Chamil ras algol. Serpentarius alio nomine vocatur Hazalange: humerus dexter pegasi dicitur Almenkeb, & mulcida in nare illius, appellatur Enif alfaras, hoc est nasus equi. Meridionales costellationes extra zodiacū positas sic enumerat epitome Arabica Almagefti:Cetus: Algibbar,id est orion:Alnahar,h.e.fluuius: Alarnebet, h.e.lepus: Alcheleb alechber,h.e. canis maior: Alcheleb alafgar,h.e.canis minor: Alfephina, h.e.nauis:Alfugahh,h.e.hydra: Albatina,h.e. patina, fiue patera: Algorab,h.e. coruus: Kentaurus: Alfubahh,h.e.fera fiue lupus: Almugamra,h.e. thuribulum:Alaclil algenubi, h.e.corona auftralis: Ahaut algenubi,h.e.pifcis auftralis. In his quoque diuerfa nomina inueniuntur: orion alias dicitur geuze, ficut etiam fignum geminorum in zodiaco,quod fupra orionem collocatur, geuze appellatur. Syrius appellatur Cabbir,fiue ecber hoc eft, canis magnus, vel maior: corrupte Habor dicitur: item canis maior nominatur, Alfahare aliemanija,id eft, canis dexter & meridionalis: canis vero minor dicitur Alfahare alfemalija,id eft canis finifter vel feptentrionalis:nomen alfemalija vulgo depravatum eft in algomeiza. Signa duodecim zodiaci commemorat aftrolabium meum Arabicum,quod ante annos quadringentos pulcherrime in ære cælatum eft: funt autem hæc nomina: alhamel,h.e. aries: Altor,h.e. taurus: algeuze,b.e. gemini: Alfartan,h.e.cancer: Alafcd,h.e.leo: Alfinbala, hoc eft, fpica virginis, κατ' ἐξοχὴν[?]: Almizan, h.e.libra: Alakreb,h.e.fcorpius: Alkus,h.e.fagittarius: Algedi, h.e.capricornus: Aldalu,h.e.aquarius: Alfemcha,h.e. pifcis. Alibi pifces appellantur Alhaut,fiue Ahaut,dissimulata litera 1 articuli, vt in quamplurimis veltotus articulus al, vel prior aut poftrema eius litera in pronunciatione excidere folet:de qua re confulantur Inftitutiones mex linguæ Arabicæ.
units.tr: In this appendix are enumerated forty-eight asterisms, or celestial constellations: of these, twenty-one are in the north, and together they amount to three hundred and sixty stars; twelve constellations are in the zodiac, which supply three hundred and forty-six stars; in the southern part there are fifteen constellations, which yield three hundred and sixteen stars. Thus the stars of the whole firmament are one thousand and twenty-two, as Ptolemy hands down, who recounted them most diligently. Nor is there cause for us to laugh at this number of stars because Holy Scripture writes that they are innumerable; for there is no doubt that very many which are deeply fixed in the eighth sphere escape notice. If indeed anyone can show more stars than have hitherto been observed by the astronomers, we shall render him great thanks. The Arabic Epitome of the Almagest enumerates the stars placed outside the zodiac in this order and with these names. In the northern part there is Dub alalgar and Dub alechber, that is the Little Bear and the Great Bear; Tanin, that is the Dragon; Cepheus; Alhhava, that is the Shouter or Bootes; Alpheccha, that is the Northern Crown; Alcheri hale rechabateh, that is the one falling on its knee, or Hercules; Schaliaf, that is the Lyre; Aldigaga, that is the Hen; Dhath alchursi, that is the Lady of the Chair, which is Cassiopeia; Chamil ras algol, that is the one bearing the head of Algol, this is Perseus; Memaslich alhanan, that is the one holding the reins, which the Greeks call Heniochus, or the Charioteer; Alhhakkab, that is the Eagle; Aldelphin, that is the Dolphin; Alsoham, that is the Dart; Alhava, that is the Serpent-bearer; Alhaja, that is the Serpent; Kataat alfaras, that is [illegible] hippos[?], as Ptolemy calls it; Alfaras alathem, that is the Greater Horse; Almara al-mefulsela, that is the chained woman, which is the one called Andromeda; Almutaleth, that is the Triangle. Here, however, it must be considered that some names vary. In the Little Bear three are brighter: the one in the tail is called the pole star; the remaining two, which are in the body, are called Alfarkathan. The seven brighter stars of the Great Bear, which form the figure of a wagon, are called Beneth As. Between the legs of the Shouter, or Lancer, shines a star of the first magnitude, which is counted among the sporades and is called Alramech by the Arabs, Arcturus by the Greeks. Alcheti hale rechabateh, that is the one falling on its knee, is called by Ptolemy ho en gonasin aspasmos[?]; elsewhere it is called Hercules, and sometimes simply Alcheti, that is, the one who is said to fall, as we had it in Alfraganus, chapter 2, where the Hebrew translator slipped, who wrote Algedi, a name which means the Goat, that is, a sign of the zodiac. Augustinus Ricius also erred in his little book on the motion of the eighth sphere, when he asserts that Alfraganus made mention of Algedi, that is, the Goat which is seen near the pole; for Alfraganus there does not mention Algedi, but Alcheti, that is Hercules falling on the other knee. The Lyre is frequently called Alvakab, that is the falling one, namely the vulture; and the Hen is named Altayr, that is the flying one, namely the vulture. Cepheus is also named Alredaf. The Arabs call Algol Medusa; they call the head of Medusa Ras algol; the Hebrews call it Rosch hassatan, that is the head of the devil. Therefore he who cut off and carries the head of Medusa, the chief of the Gorgons, is Perseus; to the Arabs he is called Chamil ras algol. The Serpent-bearer is called by another name Hazalange. The right shoulder of Pegasus is called Almenkeb, and the bright spot in its nostril is called Enif alfaras, that is the nose of the horse. The Arabic Epitome of the Almagest enumerates the southern constellations placed outside the zodiac thus: Cetus; Algibbar, that is Orion; Alnahar, that is the River; Alarnebet, that is the Hare; Alcheleb alechber, that is the Greater Dog; Alcheleb alafgar, that is the Lesser Dog; Alfephina, that is the Ship; Alfugahh, that is the Hydra; Albatina, that is the Dish or Bowl; Algorab, that is the Crow; the Centaur; Alfubahh, that is the beast or wolf; Almugamra, that is the Censer; Alaclil algenubi, that is the Southern Crown; Ahaut algenubi, that is the Southern Fish. In these too different names are found: Orion is otherwise called Geuze, just as the sign of the Twins in the zodiac, which is placed above Orion, is called Geuze. Sirius is called Cabbir, or Ecber, that is the great or greater dog; it is corruptly called Habor; likewise the Greater Dog is named Alfahare aliemanija, that is the right and southern dog; but the Lesser Dog is called Alfahare alfemalija, that is the left or northern dog; the name alfemalija has been commonly corrupted into algomeiza. My Arabic astrolabe, which four hundred years ago was most beautifully engraved in bronze, records the twelve signs of the zodiac; these names are: Alhamel, that is Aries; Altor, that is Taurus; Algeuze, that is Gemini; Alfartan, that is Cancer; Alafcd, that is Leo; Alfinbala, that is the Spike of Virgo, kat' exochēn[?]; Almizan, that is Libra; Alakreb, that is Scorpio; Alkus, that is Sagittarius; Algedi, that is Capricorn; Aldalu, that is Aquarius; Alfemcha, that is the Fishes. Elsewhere the Fishes are called Alhaut, or Ahaut, the letter 1 of the article being dropped, as happens in very many words where the article al, or its first or last letter, tends to be lost in pronunciation; on this matter the Institutions of the Arabic language may be consulted.

units.la: Hifce fubiungit codex Arabicus, ea quæ commemoratur in exemplari Romano: hæc autem nos cum fuperioribus in vnum caput concontraximus. Sic autem scribunt Romani.]
units.tr: These things the Arabic codex appends, which is mentioned in the Roman copy. We have, however, condensed them together with the above into one chapter. The Romans write thus.

units.la: Stellæ quæ appellantur mansiones lunæ, sunt vi-ginti octo. Hic nos recensebimus mansiones lunæ, nominibus illis, quibus Arabes eas nominant: hæc enim apud plurimos homines sunt notissima. Prima vocatur Aserten[?], & sunt duæ stellæ in capite arietis, lucidæ & separatæ, quarum sinistra sive septentrionalis minor est. Deinde est Albuten, id est venter arietis, & sunt tres stellæ parvæ & propinquæ sibi invicem. Tertia est mansio tauri, in qua sunt sex stellæ parvæ, & invicem aggregatæ, quæ nominantur pleiades. Quarta est Aldebaran, quam nos recensuimus inter stellas primæ magnitudinis, & hæc alias dicitur Arabibus hain altor, id est, oculus tauri: circa eam sunt stellæ parvæ, hyades sive su-culæ dictæ. Quinta est Ras algeuze, id est, caput orionis: sunt tres stellæ parvæ & propinquæ. Sexta est Alhanach: sunt duæ stellæ oppositæ in pedibus geminorum, quarum septentrionalis est lucidior. Septima est Aldirah, brachium sive caput geminorum: sunt duæ stellæ oppositæ. Octava est Anachera, quæ nominatur os leonis: est quasi linteum parvum inter duas stellas nebulosas extensum, quod inter constellationes Ptolemæi refertur ad cacrum[?]. Nona est Altaref, id est, summitas: sunt duæ stellæ parvæ, quas nominat Arabes oculos leonis. Decima est Alzobrach: sunt duæ stellæ lucidæ circa cor leonis, quod nominatur Kebelalased. Undecima est Algubra: sunt duæ stellæ lucidæ, quæ sequuntur post cor leonis, & alias appellantur Alcaraten. Duo-decima est Asampha[?], & stella est, quam diximus appellari caudam leonis. Decima tertia est Al-hanhe: sunt quinque stellæ ad similitudinem literæ Arabicæ Elif collocatæ: quarum quatuor sunt in acie disperse, & una est in reflexione ad occiden-tem: referuntur ad constellationem virginis. Decima quarta est Alazel, id est, spica virginis, stel-la primæ magnitudinis, ut ante diximus. Decima quinta est Algufre: sunt tres parvæ stellæ, quarum duæ tendunt ad Mizan aliemin, id est, li-bram dextram seu meridionalem. Decima sexta est Mizan, id est, duæ lances libræ. Decima se-ptima est Alaclil, id est, corona scorpii: sunt tres stellæ lucidæ in acie posita. Decima octava est cor-scorpii, quæ est stella rubea inter duas lucidas. De-cima nona est Azula, id est, aculeus scorpionis: sunt duæ stellæ, inter quas una est lucida. Vigesi-ma est Anhahin: sunt octo stellæ lucidæ, quarum quatuor sunt in galaxia, & nominantur Afadi-ra, id est, resistentes, & sunt ex stellis arcus sagit-tarij. Vigesima prima est Albendach: est spa-cium parvum cœli in quo non sunt stellæ, sequens post Anhahin. Vigesima secunda est fortuna de-collantis: & sunt duæ stellæ parvæ, quarum septentrionalis obscura est adhærens ei quam Arabes oriens nominant: propterea dicitur fortuna decol-lantis. lantis. Vigesima tertia est fortuna deglutientis, & sunt duae stellae parvae aequalem habentes motum. Vigesima quarta est fortuna fortunarum, & sunt tres stellae quarum una est lucidior. Vigesima quinta est fortuna centurionum, & sunt tres stellae ad formam trianguli disposita, in quarum medio est stella quarta. Vigesima sexta est Arahva, id est, spuma aquarij: sunt duae stellae lucidae, quarum septentrionalis nominatur humerus equi. Vigesima septima est Alfargu, id est, vas ex quo aliquid evacuatur: sunt duae stellae lucidae, divisae, sequentes duas priores. Vigesima octava est pisces septentrionalis, qui extenditur ad cornua arietis.
units.tr: There are twenty-eight stars called the mansions of the moon. Here we shall list the mansions of the moon under the names by which the Arabs call them, since these are best known to most people. The first is called Aserten, and it consists of two stars in the head of the Ram, bright and separate, of which the left or northern one is smaller. Next is Albuten, that is, the belly of the Ram, and it consists of three small stars close to one another. The third is the mansion of the Bull, in which there are six small stars clustered together, which are called the Pleiades. The fourth is Aldebaran, which we counted among the stars of the first magnitude; the Arabs also call it hain altor, that is, the eye of the Bull; around it are small stars called the Hyades or little sows. The fifth is Ras algeuze, that is, the head of Orion; there are three small stars close together. The sixth is Alhanach: there are two opposite stars in the feet of the Twins, of which the northern is the brighter. The seventh is Aldirah, the arm or head of the Twins: there are two opposite stars. The eighth is Anachera, which is named the mouth of the Lion: it is like a small linen cloth stretched between two cloudy stars, and among Ptolemy's constellations it is referred to the ... . The ninth is Altaref, that is, the summit: there are two small stars, which the Arabs call the eyes of the Lion. The tenth is Alzobrach: there are two bright stars around the heart of the Lion, which is called Kebelalased. The eleventh is Algubra: there are two bright stars which follow the heart of the Lion, and which are also called Alcaraten. The twelfth is Asampha, and it is a star which we said is called the tail of the Lion. The thirteenth is Al-hanhe: there are five stars arranged in the likeness of the Arabic letter Elif, of which four are scattered in a line and one is bent back towards the west; they are referred to the constellation of the Virgin. The fourteenth is Alazel, that is, the Spica of the Virgin, a star of the first magnitude, as we said before. The fifteenth is Algufre: there are three small stars, two of which tend towards Mizan aliemin, that is, the right or southern scale of the Balance. The sixteenth is Mizan, that is, the two pans of the Balance. The seventeenth is Alaclil, that is, the crown of the Scorpion: there are three bright stars set in a line. The eighteenth is the heart of the Scorpion, which is a reddish star between two bright ones. The nineteenth is Azula, that is, the sting of the Scorpion: there are two stars, between which is one bright one. The twentieth is Anhahin: there are eight bright stars, four of which lie in the Milky Way and are called Afadira, that is, the resisting ones; they belong to the stars of the Archer's bow. The twenty-first is Albendach: it is a small space of sky with no stars, following Anhahin. The twenty-second is the fortune of the one who decapitates: there are two small stars, of which the northern is obscure and adjoins the one the Arabs call the eastern; for this reason it is called the fortune of the one who decapitates. The twenty-third is the fortune of the one who swallows, and there are two small stars having equal motion. The twenty-fourth is the fortune of fortunes, and there are three stars, one of which is brighter. The twenty-fifth is the fortune of the centurions, and there are three stars arranged in the form of a triangle, with a fourth star in the middle. The twenty-sixth is Arahva, that is, the foam of the Water-carrier: there are two bright stars, of which the northern is called the shoulder of the horse. The twenty-seventh is Alfargu, that is, the vessel from which something is poured out: there are two bright, separate stars, following the two previous ones. The twenty-eighth is the northern Fish, which extends to the horns of the Ram.

units.la: In descriptione mansionum lunarium maximè desidero codicem Arabicum Alfraganii: sine hoc enim nomina corrupta restitui nequeunt. Enumerat autem Alfraganus 18 mansiones lunares, quasi diebus circiter viginti octo totum zodiacum percurrat luna, & quotidie aeris constitutionem immutet, pro temperamento & influxu stellarum, quas adire cernitur. Quae & quanta effecta tribuerint Indi mansionibus lunaribus, videre licet in epitome astrologiae Iohannis Hispalensis capite decimo octavo. Multa etiam de his mansionibus lunae scribuntur apud Abenragelum parte septima librorum ipsius astrologicorum, cap. 101.
units.tr: In the description of the lunar mansions I especially miss the Arabic codex of Alfraganus, for without it the corrupt names cannot be restored. Alfraganus enumerates twenty-eight lunar mansions, since the moon traverses the whole zodiac in about twenty-eight days and each day alters the constitution of the air, according to the temperament and influence of the stars it is seen to approach. What and how great effects the Indians attributed to the lunar mansions may be seen in the epitome of astrology by John of Seville, chapter eighteen. Much is also written about these lunar mansions by Abenragel in the seventh part of his astrological books, chapter 101.

units.la: [Exemplar Romanum.] De distantiis stellarum fixarum & planetarum a terra.
units.tr: [Roman copy.] On the distances of the fixed stars and of the planets from the earth.
CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Postquam commemorauimus numerum stella- rum secundum ordines suos, recenseamus longi- tudinem earum a terra. Sane Ptolemæus in libro suo declarauit solis & lunæ a terra distantiam, sed non legimus eum quicquam dixisse de distantiis re- liquarum stellarum, nisi quod exposuerit longitu- dines centrorum orbium a centro terræ, & quan- titates epicyclorum. Cum ergo posuerimus longitu- dinem remotiorem in ambobus lunæ circulis, scili- cet eccentrico & epicyclo, esse longitudinem pro- pinquiorem mercurÿ: & mercurÿ longitudinem remotiorem esse longitudinem propinquiorem Ve- neris: Venerisq; longitudinem remotiorem in utro- que circulo esse longitudinem propinquiorem solis, sicut demostrauit Ptolemæus: sequitur hinc nullum vacuum esse interiectum inter hos circulos. Si ergo eâdem utamur proportione in reliquis planetis, do- nec perueniamus ad orbem stellarum fixarum, cu- ius centrum est centrum terræ: deprehendemus di- stantias stellarum fixarum a terra æquales esse, ne- que ullam diuersitatem admittere. Ptolemæus & alij sapientes semidiametrum terræ voluerunt esse mensuram, qua distantia a centro terræ examina- rentur: & præsupposuerunt quantitatem molis terrena, ut per eam probarent magnitudinem corpo-rum cælestium. Quod ad mensuram terræ attinet, prius ostendimus, quòd diameter eius contineat 6500 milliaria: itaque semidiameter terræ, qua capiuntur longitudines stellarum continet 3250 milliaria. Secundum hanc rationem distantia lunæ à terra propinquior, semidiametris terræ triginta tribus, cum dimidia, & vigesima eius parte æqualis erit: hoc est, continebit 109037 milliaria: longitudo autem lunæ remotior, quæ est longitudo propinquior mercurij, comprehendet semidiametros terræ sexaginta quatuor, cum sexta eius parte, hoc est, 208541 milliaria. Longitudo remotior mercurij, quæ est longitudo propinquior Veneris, continebit semidiametros terræ centù & sexaginta septem, hoc est, 542750 milliaria. Longitudo remotior Veneris, quæ est longitudo propinquior solis, semidiametros terræ complectetur mille centum & viginti, hoc est, 3640000 milliaria. Longitudo remotior solis, quæ est longitudo propinquior martis, semidiametros terræ comprehendet mille ducentas & viginti, hoc est, 3965000 milliaria. Longitudo remotior martis, quæ est longitudo propinquior Jouis, continebit semidiametros terræ octies mille octingentas & septuaginta sex, hoc est, milliaria 2884700. Longitudo remotior Jouis, quæ est longitudo propinquior Saturni, complectetur semidiametros terræ quatuordecies mille quadringentas & quinque, hoc est, 46816250 milliaria. Longitudo remotior Saturni, quæ est æqualis longitudini stellarum fixarum, continebit semidiametros terræ vicies mille centum & decem, hoc est, 6535750 milliaria: hæc est quantitas semidiametri zodiaci: quæ si duplice-tur, provenit diameter orbis signorum, continens 130715000 milliaria. Diameter si multiplicetur in 1/3 & 1/7, provenit circumferentia circuli signorum, complectens milliaria 410818571: ex quo per diuisionem colligitur unumquemque gradum in circumferentia zodiaci completi 1141162 milliaria.
units.tr: Having set out the number of the stars according to their orders, let us now consider their distances from the earth. Ptolemy, in his book, indeed declared the distance of the sun and moon from the earth. But we do not read that he said anything about the distances of the other stars, except that he set out the distances of the centres of the orbs from the centre of the earth, and the sizes of the epicycles. Since we have placed the farther distance in both lunar circles, namely the eccentric and the epicycle, as the nearer distance of Mercury, and Mercury's farther distance as the nearer distance of Venus, and Venus's farther distance in each circle as the nearer distance of the sun, as Ptolemy demonstrated, it follows that no void lies between these circles. If then we apply the same proportion to the remaining planets, until we reach the orb of the fixed stars, whose centre is the centre of the earth, we shall find that the distances of the fixed stars from the earth are equal and admit no difference. Ptolemy and the other wise men wished the semidiameter of the earth to be the measure by which distance from the centre of the earth is examined, and they presupposed the quantity of the earthly mass so that by it they might prove the size of the heavenly bodies. As for the measure of the earth, we showed earlier that its diameter contains 6500 miles; so the semidiameter of the earth, by which the distances of the stars are taken, contains 3250 miles. According to this reckoning, the nearer distance of the moon from the earth, equal to thirty-three and a half semidiameters of the earth and one twentieth part of it, that is, it contains 109037 miles. The farther distance of the moon, which is the nearer distance of Mercury, comprises sixty-four semidiameters of the earth and a sixth part of one, that is, 208541 miles. The farther distance of Mercury, which is the nearer distance of Venus, contains 167 semidiameters of the earth, that is, 542750 miles. The farther distance of Venus, which is the nearer distance of the sun, embraces 1120 semidiameters of the earth, that is, 3640000 miles. The farther distance of the sun, which is the nearer distance of Mars, comprises 1220 semidiameters of the earth, that is, 3965000 miles. The farther distance of Mars, which is the nearer distance of Jupiter, contains 8876 semidiameters of the earth, that is, 2884700 miles. The farther distance of Jupiter, which is the nearer distance of Saturn, embraces 14405 semidiameters of the earth, that is, 46816250 miles. The farther distance of Saturn, which is equal to the distance of the fixed stars, contains 20110 semidiameters of the earth, that is, 6535750 miles. This is the quantity of the semidiameter of the zodiac; if it is doubled, the diameter of the sphere of the signs results, containing 130715000 miles. If this diameter is multiplied by 1/3 and 1/7, the circumference of the circle of the signs results, comprising 410818571 miles; from this, by division, it is gathered that each degree in the circumference of the completed zodiac is 1141162 miles.

units.la: Quæ sit ratio mensurandæ terræ, dictum est supra cap. 10. Ex ambitu terræ, indagatur diameter & semidiameter terræ: semidiametris terræ postea comparantur reliquarum stellarum distantiæ. Compertum est uni gradui cœlesti respondere in superficie terræ octodecim parasangas, & 2/3. quatenus uni gradui tribuuntur quinquaginta sex milliaria, iuxta recentiores autores: si vero gradus diuidatur in sexaginta sex milliaria, de sententia veteruum, gradus unus in terra continebit parasangas viginti duas. Iuxta hanc rationem si multiplicentur parasangæ cum suis fractionibus in 360 gradus, provenit ambitus terræ, continens octies mille parasangas, sicut Abilfedea & epitome Almagesti Arabici luculenter docent. Atqui octies mille parasangæ conficiunt 24000 milliaria: Alfraganus autem cum præsuppositis uni gradui assignanda esse milliaria 56 2/3, recte concludit circumferentiam terrestrem continere 20400 milliaria. Si parafangæ octies mille diuidantur in ⅓ & ⅐; prouenit diameter terræ continens 2 5 4 5 ⅐ parasangas fere: itaq; semidiameter erit 1 2 7 3 parasangarum fere: quæ efficiunt milliaria 3 8 1 9: Alfraganus autem in hoc capite asserit semidiametrum terræ copleċti milliaria 3 2 5 0: non enim iuxta antiquiores tribuit vni gradui 6 6 milliaria, sed iuxta recentiorum Arabum obseruata assignat vni gradui 5 6 milliaria. Si diameter terræ, quatenus copleditur 2 5 4 5 ⅐ parasangas, multiplicetur in circumferentiam maximi circuli, proueniet tota superficies terræ, habens 2 0 3 6 0 0 0 0 ⅐ parasangas, quæ efficiunt 6 1 0 8 0 0 0 0 milliaria: sed Alfraganus nostercap. 10 aream sphæræ terrestris dixit cotinere 1 3 2 6 0 0 0 0 milliaria quadrata: quæ iuxta hypothesin ipsius sunt accipienda.
units.tr: The method of measuring the earth was explained above in chapter 10. From the circumference of the earth the diameter and semidiameter of the earth are sought; the distances of the other stars are then compared with the semidiameters of the earth. It is established that one celestial degree corresponds on the surface of the earth to eighteen and two-thirds parasangs, since according to recent authors one degree is assigned fifty-six and two-thirds miles. But if the degree is divided into sixty-six miles, according to the opinion of the ancients, one degree on earth will contain twenty-two parasangs. According to this reckoning, if the parasangs with their fractions are multiplied by the 360 degrees, the circumference of the earth results, containing eight thousand parasangs, as Abilfeda and the Arabic epitome of the Almagest clearly teach. Yet eight thousand parasangs make 24000 miles, whereas Alfraganus, presupposing that fifty-six and two-thirds miles are to be assigned to one degree, rightly concludes that the earth's circumference contains 20400 miles. If eight thousand parasangs are divided by 1/3 and 1/7, the diameter of the earth results, containing roughly 2545 1/7 parasangs; so the semidiameter will be roughly 1273 parasangs, which make 3819 miles. Alfraganus, however, in this chapter asserts that the semidiameter of the earth comprises 3250 miles; for he did not assign sixty-six miles to one degree, following the ancients, but following the observations of the recent Arabs he assigns fifty-six miles to one degree. If the diameter of the earth, which comprises 2545 1/7 parasangs, is multiplied by the circumference of the greatest circle, the whole surface of the earth results, having 20360000 1/7 parasangs, which make 61080000 miles. But our Alfraganus, in chapter 10, said that the area of the terrestrial sphere contains 13260000 square miles; these figures are to be taken according to his own hypothesis.

units.la: Ne autem excidant mensuræ geodeticæ, de quibus supra dictum est, obseruetur locus in epitome Almagesti Arabici, vbi ita scribitur: Vsitata est parasanga, quia completitur tria milliaria, quodvis autem milliare habet quatuor milia cubitorum: cubitum constat viginti quatuor digitis: digitus mensura est sex granorum hordeaceorum iuxta aequaliter positorum. Vbi obseruandum est, quod dicitur, cubitum constare viginti quatuor digitis: Alfraganus autem cap. 10 pronunciauit cubitum constare sex palmis: quod unum idem est, quia unus palmus habet quatuor digitos. Quæ pertinent ad distantiam, magnitudinem & mutua proportione trium horum corporum, scilicet solis, lunæ & terræ, legatur prolixius apud Ptolemæum: reliquarum stellarum magnitudines & distantiæ, quæ ab Alfragano & Albategnio comemorantur, incertæ sunt, & coniecturis tantum declarantur.
units.tr: Lest the geodetic measures, of which we spoke above, be forgotten, let the passage in the Arabic epitome of the Almagest be noted, where it is written thus: "The parasang in common use is three miles, and each mile has four thousand cubits; the cubit consists of twenty-four digits; the digit is the measure of six barley grains placed side by side." Here it must be observed that what is said, that the cubit consists of twenty-four digits, agrees with Alfraganus, who in chapter 10 declared that the cubit consists of six palms; this is one and the same, since one palm has four digits. Concerning the distance, magnitude and mutual proportion of these three bodies, namely the sun, the moon and the earth, let the reader consult Ptolemy at greater length. The magnitudes and distances of the remaining stars, which are mentioned by Alfraganus and Albategnius, are uncertain and are declared only by conjecture.

units.la: De quantitatibus stellarum iuxta terræ dimensionem. CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: On the magnitudes of the stars according to the dimension of the earth. CHAP. XXIIII.

units.la: Postquam explicatas longitudines stellarum, recensea-mus magnitudinem corporum earum. Ptole-mæus quidem demonstrauit magnitudinem duo-rum corporum, scilicet solis & lunæ: reliqua-rum vero stellarum mensuram haud explicauit: e-ius tamen rei scientia facile ex iis comparatur, quæ de sole & luna sunt demonstrata. De luna ostendi-tur, quod diameter corporis eius, cum est in longin-quitate orbium suorum, sit æqualis diametro appa-renti corporis solaris, hæc autem deprehenditur esse 31 minutorum, & ⅖ unius minuti: diameter lunæ habet partem unam e tribus & ⅖ unius partis ter-ræ. Diameter solis æqualis est diametris terræ quin-que cum dimidia: ergo mensura corporis lunaris est tricesima nona pars terræ, & mensura corporis so-laris est centesima sexagesima sexta parte maior terra: quatenus partes terræ utrinque æquales ac-cipiuntur.
units.tr: Having explained the distances of the stars, we now review the magnitudes of their bodies. Ptolemy demonstrated the magnitudes of two bodies, the sun and the moon, but he did not set out the measure of the other stars. Knowledge of this matter can nevertheless be easily gained from what has been demonstrated about the sun and the moon. It is shown of the moon that the diameter of its body, when it is at the distance of its orbits, equals the apparent diameter of the solar body; this is found to be 31 minutes and 2/5 of a minute. The diameter of the moon is one part out of three and 2/5 of a part of the earth's diameter. The diameter of the sun equals five and a half earth diameters. Therefore the body of the moon is the thirty-ninth part of the earth, and the body of the sun is one hundred and sixty-sixth times larger than the earth, taking the parts of the earth as equal in every direction.

units.la: Sed nos annectamus reliquarum stel-larum magnitudines, quæ apparent in mediis earū distantiis: deinde dicamus, quid sentiendum sit de veris earundem stellarum quantitatibus.
units.tr: But we add the magnitudes of the remaining stars, as they appear at their mean distances. Then we shall say what should be thought of the true magnitudes of these same stars.

units.la: Diameter corporis mercurij apparet esse decima quinta pars diametri solaris, vt sufficienter probatum est: diameter Veneris est pars decima diametri solaris: diameter martis est pars vigesima diametri solaris: diameter Iouis est pars duodecima, & diameter Saturni est pars decima octaua solis: & vnaquæque quindecim stellarum maiorum fixarum est vigesi-ma pars. mapars. Quantitates vero diametrorum illarum ad diametrum terræ ita se habent: diameter corporis mercurij est vigesima octaua pars diametri terræ: diameter martis est similis diametro terræ, sed insuper completitur sextam eius partem: diameter Veneris est pars tertia diametri terræ, & præterea ⅓ unius partis: diameter Jouis continetur in diametro terræ quater cum dimidia, & decima sexta parte unius: diameter Saturni continetur in diametro terræ quater cum dimidia: diameter uniuscuiusque stellarum fixarum primæ magnitudinis æquatur quatuor terræ diametris cum dimidia, & quarta uniusparte. Est ergo mensura corporum harum stellarum talis: corpus mercurij est fere una pars de viginti duabus millibus partibus corporis terrestris: veneris est tricesima nona pars terræ: martis corpus æquale est terræ semel cum dimidia, & octaua eius parte: Jouis æquat terram nonagies quinquies: Saturni æquat terram nonagies semel: stellarum fixarum primæ magnitudinis unaquæque æquat terram centies & septies. Cūm autem stellæ fixæ in sex classes distribuantur, ut supra ostendimus, non difficile erit ex stellis primæ magnitudinis capere mensuram reliquarum classium: continebit ergo unaquæque stella secundi ordinis, terram nonagies: tertij ordinis septuagesies bis: quarti ordinis quinquagies quater: quinti ordinis trigesies sexies: sexti ordinis, hoc est, unaquæque minimarum stellarum, quas obseruare licuit, terram complectetur decies & octies. Hinc manifestum est, quod maximum corpus mundi sit sol: secundo loco occurrunt quin-decim stellæ primæ magnitudinis: tertius in ma-gnitudine est iupiter: quartus saturnus: quintam magnitudinem habent reliquæ stellæ fixæ se-cundum ordines suos: sexto loco est mars: septimo terra: octauo venus: nono luna: decimo mer-curius.
units.tr: The diameter of the body of Mercury appears to be the fifteenth part of the solar diameter, as has been sufficiently proved. The diameter of Venus is the tenth part of the solar diameter; the diameter of Mars is the twentieth part; the diameter of Jupiter is the twelfth part; and the diameter of Saturn is the eighteenth part of the sun's. Each of the fifteen greater fixed stars is the twentieth part. The magnitudes of these diameters, compared with the diameter of the earth, stand thus: the diameter of the body of Mercury is the twenty-eighth part of the earth's diameter; the diameter of Mars is similar to the earth's diameter, but exceeds it by a sixth part of that diameter; the diameter of Venus is a third part of the earth's diameter and a further third of a part; the diameter of Jupiter is contained in the earth's diameter four and a half times and a sixteenth part of one more; the diameter of Saturn is contained in the earth's diameter four and a half times; the diameter of each fixed star of the first magnitude equals four and a half earth diameters and a quarter of one part. Thus the measure of the bodies of these stars is as follows: the body of Mercury is about one part in twenty-two thousand parts of the terrestrial body; the body of Venus is the thirty-ninth part of the earth; the body of Mars equals the earth once and a half and its eighth part; the body of Jupiter equals the earth ninety-five times; the body of Saturn equals the earth ninety-one times; each fixed star of the first magnitude equals the earth one hundred and seven times. Since the fixed stars are distributed into six classes, as we showed above, it will not be difficult to derive the measure of the remaining classes from the stars of the first magnitude. Each star of the second order will therefore contain the earth ninety times; of the third order, seventy-two times; of the fourth order, fifty-four times; of the fifth order, thirty-six times; and of the sixth order, that is, each of the smallest stars that can be observed, it will embrace the earth eighteen times. From this it is clear that the largest body in the world is the sun. In second place come the fifteen stars of the first magnitude; third in size is Jupiter; fourth is Saturn; the remaining fixed stars hold the fifth place according to their orders; in sixth place is Mars; seventh is the earth; eighth is Venus; ninth is the moon; tenth is Mercury.

units.la: De diuersitate quæ accidit stellis & gradibus earum in zodiaco, cùm fuerint in medio cœli, item in ortu & occasu.
units.tr: On the diversity that befalls the stars and their degrees in the zodiac, when they are in mid-heaven, and likewise at rising and setting.
CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Ostendemus nunc diuersitate, quæ accidit cùm stella meridianum attingit, ipsaq; assequitur gradum suum in longitudine ecliptica: non enim necessarium est in omnibus locis, vt stella transeat meridianum, quando gradus illius eundem transit: sed nonnunquam eum attingit cù gradu profectio-nis circuli magni, qui transit stellam & polum æqua-toris: aliàs gradus longitudinis ille dicitur, quæ osten-dit circulus magnus transiens stellam & polos zodiaci. Cùm ergo stella fuerit in principio cancri vel capricorni, gradus profectionis incidit in gradum longitudinis zodiaci: quia circulus profectionis & longitudinis in duobus istis locis concurrunt, siquidem vterque describitur per polos æquatoris & zo-diaci. Cùm autem stella fuerit extra hæc loca, dif-fert fert gradus profectionis à gradu longitudinis: si enim fuerit stella septentrionalis zodiaci, constituta in medietate, quæ est à principio capricorni usque ad finem geminorum; tunc stella transeunte meridianum, polus zodiaci septentrionalis vergit versus occidentem, & polus australis versus orientem, & peruenit ad medium cælum, antequam id gradus eius attingat: & stella opposita versus meridiē in zodiaco attingit medium cælum, postquam id attigit gradus eius. Si stella fuerit septentrionalis, constituta in medietate, quæ est à principio cancri usque ad finem sagittarij; tunc ipsa transeunte meridianum, polus zodiaci septentrionalis spectat orientem, meridionalis vero occidentem: & attingit stella medium cœli, postquam attigit ipsum gradus eius, & stella opposita versus meridiem peruenit ad meridianum, antequam eum assequatur gradus ipsius.
units.tr: We shall now show the difference that arises when a star reaches the meridian and at the same time attains its degree in the ecliptic longitude. For it is not necessary in all places that a star should cross the meridian when its degree crosses it. Sometimes it reaches the meridian together with the degree of right ascension of a great circle, which passes through the star and the pole of the equator. Otherwise the degree is called the degree of longitude, which is shown by the great circle passing through the star and the poles of the zodiac. So when the star is at the beginning of Cancer or Capricorn, the degree of right ascension falls on the degree of longitude of the zodiac, because the circle of right ascension and the circle of longitude coincide at these two points, since both are described through the poles of the equator and of the zodiac. When, however, the star lies outside these points, the degree of right ascension differs from the degree of longitude. If the star is north of the zodiac and lies in the half from the beginning of Capricorn to the end of Gemini, then when the star crosses the meridian the north pole of the zodiac inclines toward the west and the south pole toward the east, and the star reaches midheaven before its degree reaches it. The opposite star, in the south, reaches midheaven after its degree has reached it. If the star is north and lies in the half from the beginning of Cancer to the end of Sagittarius, then when it crosses the meridian the north pole of the zodiac faces the east and the south pole the west. The star reaches midheaven after its degree has reached it, and the opposite star in the south arrives at the meridian before its degree attains it.

units.la: Maxima igitur diuersitas est in stellis propinquis initio arietis & librae. In ortu quoq; & occasu similiter discrepat gradus longitudinis, exceptis locis illis, de quibus iam dicemus. In illo enim loco, qui transit medii climatis secundi ad septentrionē diuersitas est qualis contingit in gradu profectionis, quoniam polus zodiaci in his climatibus semper apparet supra terram. Quapropter stella septentrionalis zodiaci in quocunq; loco orbis sui fuerit, orietur ante gradum suum, & occidet post occasum gradus sui: sicut stella ei opposita ad meridiem orietur post gradum suum, & occidet ante ipsum. Hinc conspicitur maximam diuersitatem ascensionis illis stellis esse, quae vicinae sunt ortui arietis, & descensionis plurimam discrepantiam esse illis, quae propinquae sunt occasui librae. Si autem stella fuerit in principio cancri aut capricorni, tunc ambae diuersitates in ortu & occasu aequales erunt. In illo vero loco, qui est inter aequatorem vsque ad medium climatis secundi, duplex contingit diuersitas, quoniam polus zodiaci septētrionalis non apparet semper, sed oritur & occidit: vt videre licet sub aequatore, vbi oritur & occidit cum principio capricorni. At in locis vltra aequatorem fitis stellarum ortus contingit ante ortum initi capricorni, & occasus earum accidit ante occasum eius: & distantia ab vtrisq; punctis ortus & occasus in principio capricorni, vnius est quantitatis. Propter hoc igitur in his locis stellae quae oriuntur, polo zodiaci supra terram apparente, sicut narrauimus de aliis climatibus, si sunt septentrionales, oriuntur ante ortum gradus sui; si sunt meridionales, oriuntur post ipsum: & similiter quaecunque occidunt, si sunt septentrionales, occidunt post gradum suum; si sunt meridionales, occidunt ante ipsum. Quaecunque vero stellae oriuntur, polo zodiaci sub terra latente, contrario modo habent: quae enim sunt septentrionales, oriuntur post gradum suum, & quae sunt meridionales, oriuntur ante ipsum: similiter quae occidunt, si sunt septentrionales, occidunt ante gra-dum dum suum; si sunt meridionales, occidunt post ipsum. Si ortus stellae contingat cum ortu poli, quod esse non potest, nisi in illis quae sunt inter principium librae & finem sagittarij, tunc gradus ortus est gradus longitudinis: similiter si occasus stellae contingat cum occasu poli, quod fieri non potest nisi in illis quae sunt inter initium capricorni & finem piscium, tunc gradus occasus est gradus longitudinis, quoniam horizon in his tribus dispositionibus trafit polos zodiaci & stellam.
units.tr: The greatest difference therefore occurs in stars near the beginning of Aries and Libra. Likewise the degree of longitude differs in rising and setting, except in those places which we shall now discuss. In the place that crosses the middle of the second clime toward the north, the difference is of the same kind as occurs at the degree of right ascension, since the pole of the zodiac always appears above the earth in these climes. Hence a star north of the zodiac, wherever it is in its own circle, rises before its degree and sets after its degree sets, while the star opposite it toward the south rises after its degree and sets before it. From this it is seen that the greatest difference of ascension belongs to those stars that are near the rising of Aries, and the greatest discrepancy of descent to those near the setting of Libra. If, however, the star is at the beginning of Cancer or Capricorn, then both differences, in rising and in setting, are equal. In the place between the equator and the middle of the second clime there is a double difference, because the north pole of the zodiac does not always appear but rises and sets. This can be seen under the equator, where it rises and sets together with the beginning of Capricorn. But in places situated beyond the equator, the rising of the stars occurs before the rising of the beginning of Capricorn, and their setting occurs before its setting; and the distance from the two points of rising and setting at the beginning of Capricorn is of one quantity. For this reason, in these places, the stars that rise, while the pole of the zodiac is above the earth, rise before the rising of their degree if they are north, and after it if they are south, as we have said of the other climes. Likewise, whichever stars set, if they are north they set after their degree, and if south they set before it. But whatever stars rise while the pole of the zodiac lies hidden beneath the earth have the opposite arrangement: stars that are north rise after their degree, and those that are south rise before it. Similarly, those that set, if north, set before their degree, and if south, set after it. If the rising of a star coincides with the rising of the pole, which cannot happen except in those stars lying between the beginning of Libra and the end of Sagittarius, then the degree of rising is the degree of longitude. Likewise, if the setting of a star coincides with the setting of the pole, which cannot happen except in those lying between the beginning of Capricorn and the end of Pisces, then the degree of setting is the degree of longitude, since in these three arrangements the horizon passes through the poles of the zodiac and the star.

units.la: De ascensione & descensione stellarum, item de occultatione earum sub radiis solaribus.
units.tr: On the rising and setting of the stars, and likewise on their concealment beneath the rays of the sun.
CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: SCiendum est, saturnum, jovem & martem cursu tardiores esse sole. Cum ergo aliquis eorum solem antecedit, tunc ad eum appropinquat, & apparet in occidente vesperi, nominatur q; occidentalis[?], donec cooperiatur radiis solaribus: quando vero motu suo solem transiit, & ex radiis illius egressus mane apparet in oriente, vocatur orientalis: quare unusquisque horum planetarum habet occasum vespertinum, & ortum matutinum. Venus autem & mercurius habent ortum & occasum vespertinum, & ortum occasum matutinum: quod ideo fit, quia ambo habent motum velociorem sole. Cum itaque unus eorum soli est conjunctus, & motu directo progreditur; tunc anteverti solem, & emergit e radiis
units.tr: It must be known that Saturn, Jupiter and Mars are slower in motion than the sun. Therefore, when any one of them precedes the sun, then it approaches him and appears in the west in the evening; it is called occidental, until it is covered by the rays of the sun. But when it has passed the sun by its motion, and, having come out from his rays, appears in the morning in the east, it is called oriental. Hence each of these planets has an evening setting and a morning rising. Venus and Mercury, however, have an evening rising and setting, and a morning rising and setting; this happens because both have a motion swifter than the sun. Therefore, when one of them is joined to the sun and proceeds by direct motion, then it goes before the sun and emerges from his rays, so as to rise in the evening in the west, until it reaches its greatest distance from the sun. Then its motion is diminished, and it returns under the solar rays, so as to set in the evening in the west. But when it is separated from the sun and comes out of his rays, it rises in the morning in the east, until it reaches its greatest distance from the sun. Then again it moves more swiftly, until it overtakes the sun, so as to set in the east in the morning. The moon has a swifter course than the sun, and does not return to him by retrogradation; therefore it overtakes the sun, so that it sets in the east in the morning, and, having left him, rises in the evening in the west.

units.la: illius, ut oriatur vesperi in occidente, donec perue-niat ad maximam a sole distantiam: deinde minui-tur motus eius, & redit sub radios solares, ut vespe-ri occidat in occidente: quando vero a sole separatur, egrediturq́ e radiis eius; mane oritur in oriente, donec perueniat ad maximam a sole distantiam: deinde iterum velocius mouetur, donec assequatur solem, ut occidat in oriente mane. Luna habet cursum velociorem solem, neq; reuertitur ad ipsum per retrogradatione: propterea assequitur solem, ut mane occidat in oriente, & eo relicto oriatur vesperi in occidente. De stellis fixis, quæ vicinæ sunt polo septentrionali, sub initium huius libri diximus, quod scilicet non occidant in climatibus septentrionalibus: & quanto plus clima aliquod exporrigatur in septentrionem, tanto magis eleuetur polus supra horizontem: hinc fit ut in huiusmodi climate stellæ quaedam nunquam occidant, ut sunt Alcheti, idest, hercules, Alpharkathan, hoc est, duæ stellæ luci-diores in vrsa minore, & Beneth As, idest, stellæ vrsæ maioris, in climate quarto: & quæ hisce oppositæ sunt versus polum australem, nunquam oriuntur. Quacunque autem stellæ occidunt vltra clima secundum, & maxime declinant a zodiaco in septentrionem; illæ nunquam occultantur sub radiis solaribus, quia diutius supra terram commorantur: & cum sol in gradibus earum versatur, oriuntur ante eum, & occidunt post eum. Si autem stella est prope initium cancri aut capricorni, tem-pus quo ascendit ante solem, est æquale tempori, quo descendit post eum. Stella fixæ, quæ sunt in ecli-ptica, aut propinquæ illi, ex utroque latere; habent descensionem sub radiis solaribus vesperi in occi-dente, & ascensionem mane in oriente, sicut appa-ret in Saturno, joue, & Marte: & tempus occulta-tionis earum sub radiis solaribus, habet se secun-dum quantitatem magnitudinis corporum earum, & diuersitatem latitudinum. Si enim latitudo est septentrionalis, abbreuiatur tempus occultationis: si est meridionalis, prolongatur: & quanto quæ-que magis recedit a zodiaco versus meridiem, tan-to minus supra terram commoratur: cumq; fuerit sol in gradu eius, oritur post ipsum, & occidit ante eum, ut ortum & occasum habeat interdiu, qui videri nequit. Quanto autem plus stella recedit ab orbe signorum versus meridiem, tanto prolixius est spacium occultationis eius, ut accidit in stella, quæ appellatur Sohel: hæc enim in principio climatis quarti occultatur infra solem quinque mensibus quotannis, ex quo tempore oritur & occidit inter-diu, ut nusquam appareat. Si stella est prope ini-tium cancri vel capricorni; tempus quo succedit so-li in ortu, æquale est tempori quo præcedit eum in occasu, ut accidit in Sohel, quæ est in fine gemino-rum. Mansiones lunæ habent in oriente & oc-cidente ascensionem & descensionem: ascensionem, quatenus stella emergit e radiis solaribus, & ascendit in oriente mane ante solem: descensionem, quatenus stella ei, quae mane oritur, opposita occidit in occidente eadem hora. Prima itaque mansio, quae Afartan nominatur, tredecim postremis diebus ex mense Aprili ascendit, ut opposita illi mansio, quae Algufre appellatur, descendat: ita deinceps post elapsos quoslibet tredecim dies alia mansio oritur, ut illi opposita occidat: atque hoc continenter fit, usque ad finem anni.
units.tr: Concerning the fixed stars which are near the north pole, we said at the beginning of this book that they do not set in the northern climates; and the more a climate extends northward, the higher the pole is raised above the horizon. Hence it comes about that in such a climate certain stars never set, such as the Alcheti, that is, Hercules, and Alpharkathan, that is, the two brighter stars in the Little Bear, and Beneth As, that is, the stars of the Great Bear, in the fourth climate; and those stars opposite to these towards the south pole never rise. However, whatever stars set beyond the second climate, and especially those which deviate most from the zodiac to the north, these are never hidden under the solar rays, because they remain longer above the earth; and when the sun is in their degrees, they rise before him and set after him. If, however, a star is near the beginning of Cancer or Capricorn, the time in which it rises before the sun is equal to the time in which it sets after him. Fixed stars which lie in the ecliptic, or near it, on either side, have their descent under the solar rays in the evening in the west, and their ascent in the morning in the east, as appears in Saturn, Jupiter and Mars; and the time of their concealment under the solar rays depends on the magnitude of their bodies and the diversity of their latitudes. For if the latitude is northern, the time of concealment is shortened; if it is southern, it is lengthened; and the more any star withdraws from the zodiac towards the south, the less time it remains above the earth; and when the sun is in its degree, it rises after him and sets before him, so that its rising and setting take place by day, when it cannot be seen. But the farther a star withdraws from the circle of the signs towards the south, the longer is the space of its concealment, as happens with the star called Sohel: for this star, at the beginning of the fourth climate, is hidden below the sun for five months every year, from which time it rises and sets by day, so that it never appears. If a star is near the beginning of Cancer or Capricorn, the time in which it follows the sun in rising is equal to the time in which it precedes him in setting, as happens with Sohel, which is at the end of Gemini. The mansions of the moon have their ascent and descent in the east and west: the ascent, insofar as a star emerges from the solar rays and rises in the east in the morning before the sun; the descent, insofar as a star opposite to the one that rises in the morning sets in the west at the same hour. Therefore the first mansion, which is called Afartan, rises during the last thirteen days of April, so that the mansion opposite to it, which is called Algufre, sets; thus, after any thirteen days have elapsed, another mansion rises, so that the one opposite to it sets; and this continues without interruption until the end of the year.

units.la: De stella Sohel dictum est cap. 21, quod ea fit in temone nauis, & communiter Canobus appelletur. Hic autem accurate illud notadum est, quod affirmet Alfraganus suo seculo Canobum fuisse in fine geminorum: cum enim nostro tempore haec stella haereat in octauo gradu cancri, indicium est eam ab Alfraganni aetate usq; ad nostram memoriam per nouem gradus esse progressam. Si vnicuique gradui iuxta medium motum tribuamus septuaginta annos, colligitur Alfraganum ante annos fexcentos & triginta vixisse, circa annum domini scilicet 950, hoc est, post Albategnium annis quinquaginta. Cui coniecturæ suffragatur maxima solis declinatio, quæ illis temporibus deprehensa est 2 3 graduum, & 3 5 minutorum, ut dictu est cap. 6. Huc accedit, quod circa postremos dies mensis Aprilis tunc solita sint oriri cornua arietis, quæ Afartan appellantur, & primam mansionem lunæ constituunt. Cur autem singulis mansionibus lunaribus Alfraganus attribuerit tredecim dies, causa est, quod in vniuersum sint viginti octo mansiones lunæ: quæ fi in totum annum distribuantur, singulis mansionibus bus competunt tredecim dies: quandoquidem tre-decim in viginti octo ducta, efficiunt 364 dies, qui fere absoluunt anni quantitatem.
units.tr: Concerning the star Sohel, it was said in chapter 21 that it is in the helm of the ship, and is commonly called Canopus. Here, however, it must be carefully noted that Alfraganus affirms that in his century Canopus was at the end of Gemini; for since in our time this star stands in the eighth degree of Cancer, it is an indication that it has advanced nine degrees since the age of Alfraganus until our memory. If we assign to each degree, according to the mean motion, seventy years, it is gathered that Alfraganus lived six hundred and thirty years ago, that is, about the year of the Lord 950, namely fifty years after Albategnius. The greatest declination of the sun, which was observed in those times as 23 degrees and 35 minutes, as was said in chapter 6, supports this conjecture. Add to this that about the last days of April the horns of the Ram, which are called Afartan and constitute the first mansion of the moon, were then wont to rise. Why Alfraganus assigned thirteen days to each lunar mansion is because there are in all twenty-eight lunar mansions; if these are distributed over the whole year, thirteen days fall to each mansion, since thirteen multiplied by twenty-eight makes 364 days, which nearly complete the length of the year.

units.la: De ortu nouæ lunæ, & augmento ac decremento luminis eius.
units.tr: Concerning the rising of the new moon, and the increase and decrease of its light.
CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: POstquam ostendimus ascensionem & descensionem stellarum, dicamus de ortu novae lunae, & emersione quinque erraticarum e radiis solaribus. Sed prius loquamur de luna. hac a lumine solari, quod in eam incidit, illustratur, ut dimidia superficies corporis ipsius, quae solem respicit, fulgeat; quae vero a sole auersa est, tenebris sit obducta: quia luna inter solem & terram mouetur. Cum itaque emergit e radiis solaribus, ut solem antecedat in oriente, suo motu paulatim acquirit lumen a parte occidentali, quod reflectitur ad nos instar arcus. Sed quando sol perambulat duo signa, arietis scilicet & piscium, ambo cornua arcus lunaris sunt fere aequidistantia horizonti, quia Zodiacus tunc rectà incum-bit horizonti: sicut sole versante in virgine & libra, conspicitur noua luna cornibus directis, quia Zodiacus maxime declinat ab horizonte. Et quanto plus recedit luna a sole, tanto magis augetur lumen eius, donec opponatur soli: tunc enim dimidia pars eius, quae nobis est exposita, illustratur, quia terra est inter solem & lunam. Facta oppositione incipit appro-pinquare soli ex parte orientali, & dimidia pars eius, quæ tenebris erat obducta, ad nos paulatim co-[?]vertitur à parte occidentali, donec coiungatur soli: tunc enim in oriente prorsus obscuratur. Facta coniunctione solem iterum anteuertit, & in occidente corniculans apparere incipit. Cùm autem luna latitudine habet septentrionalem, velocius mouetur, & parum sub radiis solaribus commoratur: vt ea cerni possit sub fine mensis mane in oriente, & die sequenti in occidente forma habens corniculantem: quod plerunque accidit, cùm versatur in signis, quæ tardam habet ascensionem in sphæra rectâ, cuiusmodi sunt gemini, cancer, sagittarius & capricornus: si enim colligatur tempus ortus & occasus horum signorum in climatibus septentrionalibus, superabit tempus ortus & occasus reliquorum signorum. Sed cùm luna habet latitudinem meridionalem, tardius mouetur, & diutius sub radiis solaribus commoratur, vt totum triduum in tenebris lateat, & demum quarto die corniculans appareat: quod plurimum accidit, cùm luna versatur in signis, quæ velociorem habent ascensionem in sphæra rectâ, cuiusmodi sunt aries, pisces, virgo & libra: si enim tempus ortus & occasus horum signorum in climatibus septentrionalibus colligatur, minus illud erit tempore ortus & occasus reliquorum signorum. At si tempus ortus & occasus horum quatuor signorum, videlicet tauri, leonis, scorpij & aquarij, colligatur, æquale illud erit gradibus eorum in zodiaco. Quàtitas distantiæ lunæ à sole apparet iuxta mediocrem ratioitem, qua utuntur autores Canonū in climate quar-to: aliquando enim inter ipsam & solem interiici-tur quatitas 12 graduum e circuferētia æquatoris, fieri autē potest, vt aliquando ex minori vel maiori interuallo cōspiciatur. Ex minore sanē distantia videtur, quando est in signis habentibus velociorem ortu & occasum, quia tunc maxima eius est distantia à sole in gradibus zodiaci, & maius in corpore illius lumen apparet, videturq; in distātia minore 12 gradibus. Ex maiore distantia videtur, quando est in signis habentibus tardiorem ortum & occasum, quia tunc parua eius est distantia à sole, ideoq; cernitur in distātia maiore 12 gradibus. Vt hoc ostendatur, proponamus exemplū: cum luna apparet corniculans in climate quarto, & in ecliptica versatur, vt inter eam & solem in occasu interiiciantur 12 gradus ex circuferentia æquatoris; tunc inter solem & ipsam, si sit in libra, sunt 18 gradus ex renolutione Zodiaci: si sit in ariete, 10 [?] interiiciuntur gradus, & æquantur ambæ distantiæ in mora temporis, vt diuersitas luminis in corpore lunari sit ferè dupla. Accidit etiam vt reuolutio 12 graduum æquatoris efficiat distantiam, quæ est inter solem & horizontem prope arietem & libram, maiorem quàm sit prope cancrum vel capricornum, propter angu-stiam graduum reuolutionis in hisce duobus locis, scilicet cancro & capricorno, & propter tarditatem motus solaris in illis.
units.tr: Having shown the rising and setting of the stars, let us now speak of the birth of the new moon and the emergence of the five planets from the rays of the sun. But first let us say something about the moon. The moon is lit by the light of the sun falling upon it, so that the half of its body that faces the sun shines, while the half turned away from the sun is covered in darkness, because the moon moves between the sun and the earth. When it therefore emerges from the solar rays and goes ahead of the sun in the east, its motion gradually gains light on its western side, and this light is reflected to us in the form of an arc. When the sun passes through the two signs, Aries and Pisces, both horns of the lunar arc are nearly parallel to the horizon, because the zodiac then lies almost straight across the horizon. Likewise, when the sun is in Virgo and Libra, the new moon appears with its horns pointing upright, because the zodiac then inclines most steeply from the horizon. The further the moon recedes from the sun, the more its light increases, until it stands opposite the sun.
