For then the half of it that is turned toward us is illuminated, because the earth lies between the sun and the moon. After opposition it begins to approach the sun from the eastern side, and the half that had been covered in darkness is gradually turned toward us from the western side, until it joins the sun; then it is wholly obscured in the east. After conjunction it again goes ahead of the sun and begins to appear in the west as a crescent. When the moon has north latitude, it moves more swiftly and remains only briefly beneath the solar rays, so that it can be seen at the end of the month in the morning in the east, and on the following day in the west in the form of a crescent. This happens most often when it is in those signs whose ascension in the right sphere is slow, such as Gemini, Cancer, Sagittarius and Capricorn: for if the times of rising and setting of these signs are summed in the northern climates, they exceed the times of rising and setting of the other signs. But when the moon has south latitude, it moves more slowly and remains longer beneath the solar rays, so that it lies hidden in darkness for the whole three days and finally appears as a crescent on the fourth day. This happens chiefly when the moon is in those signs whose ascension in the right sphere is quicker, such as Aries, Pisces, Virgo and Libra: for if the times of rising and setting of these signs are summed in the northern climates, that total will be less than the times of rising and setting of the other signs. But if the times of rising and setting of these four signs, namely Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius, are summed, that total will equal their degrees in the zodiac. The quantity of the moon's distance from the sun appears, according to the moderate reckoning used by the authors of the Canons in the fourth climate, as twelve degrees of the circumference of the equator lying between it and the sun; yet it may happen that it is seen at a smaller or greater interval. It is seen at a smaller distance when it is in signs with quicker rising and setting, because then its greatest distance from the sun, in degrees of the zodiac, is greater, and a larger light appears in its body, and it appears at a distance of less than twelve degrees. It is seen at a greater distance when it is in signs with slower rising and setting, because then its distance from the sun is small, and therefore it is perceived at a distance of more than twelve degrees. To show this, let us take an example: when the moon appears as a crescent in the fourth climate, and lies in the ecliptic, so that twelve degrees of the circumference of the equator lie between it and the sun at sunset; then, if it is in Libra, there are eighteen degrees of revolution of the zodiac between the sun and itself; if it is in Aries, ten degrees lie between them; and both distances are equalized in the lapse of time, so that the difference of light in the body of the moon is nearly double. It also happens that the revolution of twelve degrees of the equator produces a distance between the sun and the horizon near Aries and Libra that is greater than it is near Cancer or Capricorn, on account of the narrowness of the degrees of revolution in those two places, namely Cancer and Capricorn, and on account of the slowness of the sun's motion there.

units.la: De emerfione quinque stellarum erraticarum e radiis folaribus.
units.tr: On the emergence of the five wandering stars from the rays of the sun.

units.la: INter quinque stellas erraticas tres superiores, vt delirent Saturnus, Iupiter & Mars iunguntur foli, cum sint in suprema parte suorum epicyclorum: atque tunc motus eorum, & quantitates corporum eorum habent exiguam diuersitatem, licet sub radiis folaribus occultentur modo longiore, modo breuiore tempore, prout est diuersa ascensio signorum, & latitudo planetarum in zodiaco. Verum Mercurius & Venus quando iunguntur foli in superiori parte epicycli, semel est directa; & cum est in inferiori parte epicycli, semel est retrograda: quapropter multiplex est diuersitas mora eorum sub radiis folaribus, prout est diuersa ascensio signorum, & latitudo eorum, item in motu planetarum, & magnitudine corporum eorum discrepantia. Venus diuersitatem habet in orbe signorum, & latitudine tantum, neque particeps est duarum reliquarum diuersitatum: summa latitudo eius est, vt demonstrauit Ptolemaeus in Almagefto, sex graduum, & ⅓ vnius: & cum retrograda est in piscibus sub climate quarto, tegitur radiis folaribus per biduum tantum, donec perueniat ad gradum foli, & videatur eadem die in oriente, cum fit coniuncta foli.
units.tr: Among the five wandering stars, the three upper ones, Saturn, Jupiter and Mars, when they are joined to the sun (as the astrologers rave) are in the highest part of their epicycles. Then their motion and the sizes of their bodies differ only slightly, although they are hidden under the solar rays for a longer or shorter time, according as the ascension of the signs differs and as the planets' latitude in the zodiac differs. But Mercury and Venus, when they are joined to the sun, are direct once when they are in the upper part of the epicycle, and retrograde once when they are in the lower part of the epicycle. Therefore their time under the solar rays varies in many ways: according to the differing ascension of the signs, their latitude, the motion of the planets, and the difference in the magnitude of their bodies. Venus has a difference only in the orbit of the signs and in latitude, and does not share in the other two differences. Its greatest latitude, as Ptolemy showed in the Almagest, is six and one-third degrees. When it is retrograde in Pisces under the fourth clime, it is covered by the solar rays for only two days, until it reaches the degree of the sun and is seen on the same day in the east, being conjoined with the sun.

units.la: Quando autem est in virgine, moratur sub radiis folaribus, donec appareat in oriente, elapsis sedecim diebus. Mercurius curius quoq; habet duas has diuersitates: cum enim remotissime distat a sole, versans in linea cotingen-te epicyclum, non videtur penitus: & nominatur hæc linea ecliptica: longitudo autem ecliptice vesper-tina cotingit in scorpione, & matutina in tauro.
units.tr: When, however, it is in Virgo, it remains under the solar rays until it appears in the east, after sixteen days have passed. Mercury too has these two differences. For when it is at its greatest distance from the sun, moving along the line touching the epicycle, it is not seen at all; this line is called the ecliptic. The longitude of the evening ecliptic touches Scorpio, and that of the morning ecliptic Taurus.

units.la: Longitudines visionis mediæ, quas usurpant Canonum autores, quaq; sunt inter solem & stellam orien-tem & occidentem in revolutione æquatoris, ut etiam in nova luna assignantur, sunt hæ: saturno tri-buuntur quindecim gradus, jovi undecim gradus, martiseptendecim gradus, Veneri septem gradus, mercurio tredecim gradus.
units.tr: The longitudes of mean visibility, which the authors of the Canons use, that is, the intervals between the sun and the star rising or setting in the revolution of the equator, and which are likewise assigned at new moon, are these: Saturn is allotted fifteen degrees, Jupiter eleven degrees, Mars seventeen degrees, Venus seven degrees, and Mercury thirteen degrees.

units.la: Secundum Ptolemæum autem hæc de luna non demonstrantur, quia ipse considerat visiones quæ sunt inter solem & horizon-tem, quo tempore planetæ horizontem transeunt: quoniam hæc longitudo tantum ponitur cum lumi-ne solari circa horizontem, & tempus id quod est sub initium noctis vocatur crepusculum, quod autem est sub initium diei, dicitur diluculum, & in omnibus partibus signorum eiusdem est quantitatis.
units.tr: According to Ptolemy, however, these things are not demonstrated concerning the moon, because he considers the visibilities that lie between the sun and the horizon, at the time when the planets cross the horizon. For this longitude is posited only with the solar light near the horizon. The time at the beginning of night is called twilight (crepusculum), and that at the beginning of day is called dawn (diluculum). In all parts of the signs it is of the same extent.

units.la: Si in climate medio, hoc est, quarto, & in decli-natione media zodiaci iuxta horizontem, tum etiam in geminis & cancro, aere puro & subtili exi-stente, considerentur visiones hæ longitudinum; tunc saturnus deprehenditur habere undecim gra-dus, jupiter decem gradus, mars undecim gradus & dimidium, Venus quinque gradus, & mercurius decem gradus.
units.tr: If these longitudes of visibility are considered in the middle clime, that is, the fourth, and at the middle declination of the zodiac near the horizon, and also in Gemini and Cancer, with the air being clear and thin, then Saturn is found to have eleven degrees, Jupiter ten degrees, Mars eleven and a half degrees, Venus five degrees, and Mercury ten degrees.
Now then we have sufficiently explained which

units.la: Sit diuersitas ortus planetarum e radiis solaribus.
units.tr: Let there be a difference in the rising of the planets from the solar rays.

units.la: De diuersitate aspectus seu parallaxi, quam habet luna cum aliis planetis propinquis terrae. CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: On the difference of aspect, or parallax, which the Moon has with the other planets nearest the earth. CHAP. XXIX.

units.la: NVnc declarabimus iuxta methodum superiorum, quid accidat soli, & reliquis infra eum positis stellis, propter diuersitatem aspectus, quam habent in zodiaco. Primo autem omnium imaginamur lineam rectam, egredientem ex centro terrae, quod est centrum zodiaci, ad centrum corporis lunaris aut reliquorum planetarum: haec linea verum locum ostendit stellae in zodiaco secundum latitudinem & longitudinem, si extendatur ad punctum illud, in quo stella haeret. Siita, planeta sit verticalis; tunc linea ista est prorsus eadem cum linea qua egreditur ab aspectu nostro, in superficie terrae sito, ad centrum planetae: quamobrem utraque ostendit verum locum stellae in zodiaco. Si autem planeta non sit verticalis; tunc istae duae lineae differunt, & se invicem secant, neque concurrunt in centro planetae: itaque linea quae egreditur de aspectu nostro ad planetam, locum tantum nobis apparentem ostendit, cum non sit verus locus in zodiaco. Quamobrem diuersitas aspectus appellatur arcus circuli maximi, quem efficiunt ambae lineae in circulo altitudinis, inter punctum verticis & planetam: itaque planeta propter di-versitaversitatem aspectus plus videtur distare a puncto verticis, quàm revera distet. Hinc liquet diversitatem aspectus principium habere a puncto verticis, eamq; maximam esse in planeta iuxta horizontem consistente: quoniam angulus reflexionis tunc est maior, quàm sit in reliquis locis cœli. Planetæ qui sunt supra solem non habent diversitatem aspectus sensibilem: quandoquidem etiam hæc in sole non animadvertitur, sed extrahitur ex distantia eius a terra, & cùm prope horizontem maxima est, deprehenditur tantùm trium minutorum. In Venere autem, mercurio & luna sensibilis est reflexio, præsertim in luna, cuius diversitas aspectus prope horizontem, cùm est in longitudine propinquiore orbium suorum, efficit gradum unum & 44 minuta: cùm autem est in longitudine remotiore orbium suorum, habet minuta 54: in eclipsibus maxima eius diversitas colligitur gradus unus & quatuor minuta. Commemoremus etiam quæ diversitas aspectus dicatur in longitudine & latitudine. Cùm zodiacus transiit punctum capitis, quo tempore aspicitur stella in climate aliquo, ubi id fieri potest, ut stella ipsa sit in ecliptica, tunc Zodiacus est in circulo altitudinis, arcusq; reflexionis est arcus zodiaci, & diversitas tota est in longitudine, neque cadit quicquam ex ea in latitudinem, & declinat pars reflexionis a loco vero ad partem in qua est stella. Nam si est versus orientem, videmus eam antecedere locum suum verum: si est in occidente, videmus eam subsequi locum suum. Si autem zodiacus non ita situs sit, ut narravimus, sed circulus qui transit polos zodiaci & planetam, fuerit is qui transit verticem capitis in hora cum aspicitur planeta; tunc arcus reflexionis est etiam arcus huius circuli, quoniam est in circulo altitudinis: quare reflexio tota est in latitudine, neque cadit aliquid de ea in longitudinem, vergitq; [?] pars huius reflexionis in latitudine etiam ad partem, in qua est stella. nam si est a parte septentrionis iuxta punctum verticis, cernimus eam septentrionalem in loco suo vero: si est a parte meridiei versus punctum verticis, videmus eam meridionalem in loco suo certissimo. Si autem unus ex his duobus circulis, videlicet zodiaco, & circulo transeunte polos eius, non est in puncto verticis, ea hora qua stella aspicitur; tunc reflexionis pars una erit secundum latitudinem, & pars altera secundum longitudinem: erit q; pars reflexionis in longitudine versus partem, ad quam declinat circulus transiens polos zodiaci a puncto verticis in oriente & occidente, & pars reflexionis in latitudine erit versus partem, ad quam declinat zodiacus a puncto verticis in septentrione & meridie. Atque hæc sunt, quæ eveniunt ratione diversitatis aspectus.
units.tr: Now, following the method of the earlier chapters, we will explain what happens to the sun and to the other stars placed below it, because of the difference of aspect they have in the zodiac. First of all, let us imagine a straight line running from the centre of the earth, which is the centre of the zodiac, to the centre of the body of the moon or of the other planets. This line shows the true place of the star in the zodiac, in latitude and longitude, if it is extended to the point where the star is fixed. If so, the planet is overhead, and then this line is exactly the same as the line that runs from our eye, situated on the surface of the earth, to the centre of the planet, so both show the true place of the star in the zodiac. If, however, the planet is not overhead, then these two lines differ and cut each other, and do not meet at the centre of the planet. The line that runs from our eye to the planet therefore shows only the place that appears to us, not the true place in the zodiac. Hence the difference of aspect is called the arc of a great circle which the two lines make on the circle of altitude, between the point overhead and the planet. So the planet seems, because of the difference of aspect, to be farther from the point overhead than it really is. From this it is clear that the difference of aspect has its beginning at the point overhead, and that it is greatest for a planet lying near the horizon, since the angle of reflection is then greater than it is in the other parts of the heavens. The planets that are above the sun do not have a noticeable difference of aspect, since this is not observed even in the sun, but is deduced from its distance from the earth; and when it is greatest near the horizon, it is detected as only three minutes. In Venus, Mercury and the moon, however, the reflection is noticeable, especially in the moon, whose difference of aspect near the horizon, when it is at the closer distance of its orbits, amounts to one degree and 44 minutes; when it is at the more remote distance of its orbits, it is 54 minutes; in eclipses its greatest difference is found to be one degree and four minutes. Let us also recall what is meant by the difference of aspect in longitude and in latitude. When the zodiac passes the point of the head, at the time when the star is seen in some climate, where this can happen so that the star itself is on the ecliptic, then the zodiac is on the circle of altitude, the arc of reflection is an arc of the zodiac, and the whole difference is in longitude, and nothing of it falls into latitude; and the part of the reflection departs from the true place toward the side on which the star is. For if it is toward the east, we see it running ahead of its true place; if it is in the west, we see it lagging behind its true place. If, however, the zodiac is not situated as we have described, but the circle which passes through the poles of the zodiac and the planet is the one that passes through the vertex of the head at the hour when the planet is seen, then the arc of reflection is also an arc of this circle, since it lies on the circle of altitude; so the whole reflection is in latitude, and nothing of it falls into longitude; and part of this reflection in latitude also tends toward the side on which the star is. For if it is on the northern side near the point overhead, we see it north of its true place; if it is on the southern side toward the point overhead, we see it south of its true place. If, however, one of these two circles, namely the zodiac and the circle passing through its poles, is not at the point overhead at the hour when the star is seen, then one part of the reflection will be in latitude and the other part in longitude. The part of the reflection in longitude will tend toward the side to which the circle passing through the poles of the zodiac inclines from the point overhead, toward east and west; and the part of the reflection in latitude will tend toward the side to which the zodiac inclines from the point overhead, toward north and south. These are the effects that come about by reason of the difference of aspect.
On the eclipse of the moon. CHAP. XXX.

units.la: Ostendimus in superioribus, quod luna illustre-tur a splendore solis, ut dimidia superficies corporis eius in coniunctione nobis exposita, tenebris involvatur, in oppositione autem dimidia superfi-cies eius, quam nos aspicimus, lumine solari fulgeat. Nunc etiam adiicimus hoc, quòd sol similiter illu-stret dimidiam superficiem terrae: idcirco lumen in superficie terrae renolvitur cum renolutione solis ab oriente in occidentem: eodem modo tenebrae in ea renolvuntur. Quoniam autem sol maior est terra, oportet ut umbra terrae extendatur in aere ad simi-litudinem coni, & paulatim in rotunditate minuatur atq; reddatur subtilior, donec tota deficiat, manente tamen linea perpendiculari ipsius umbrae tornatilis in superficie Zodiaci, quae opponitur gra-dui solis diametraliter. Umbrae vero longitudo, quae à superficie terrae eò usque extenditur, donec deficiat, secundùm probationem Ptolemaei aequat semi-diametros terrae ducetas & sexaginta octo: & dia-meter rotunditatis umbrae in loco transitus lunae, quo tempore opponitur soli, aequat diametrum cor-poris lunaris bis cum tribus quintis unius. Cùm ergo luna est in oppositione solis, & appropinquat capiti vel caudae draconis; nò habet latitudinem, qua egrediatur ab umbra terrae ad septentrionem vel meridiem: ideò necessariò incurrit in umbram ter-rae, quae subtrahit illi splendorem solis. ita videtur luna pati eclipsin, donec transeat umbram: siqui-dem umbra sequitur motum solis, quem cùm luna vincit, egreditur à parte orietali, quâ lumine solari illustratur. Si autem tempore oppositionis luna praecise fuerit in puncto capitis vel caudae draconis, neque habuerit ullam latitudinem; tunc motus cen-tri corporis lunaris fit super centro rotunditatis umbrae, ideo maxima & prolixissima accidit eclipsis: at si luna tempore oppositionis habuerit latitudinem, non erit eclipsis eius maxima. Si enim eius latitudo habuerit quantitatem aequalem excessui se-midiametri umbrae supra semidiametrum lunae; tunc transit corpus eius circulum umbrae, eumque intrinsecus cotingit ut tota obscuretur, & sine mora in umbra lateat. Si vero latitudo eius fuerit aequalis semidiametro umbrae, tunc centrum corporis eius progreditur tangens circulum umbrae, & dimidium eius obscuratur, illudq; quod in opposita eius parte obscuratur, est eius latitudo. Si autem eius latitudo fuerit aequalis utriq; semidiametro, scilicet lunae & umbrae, tunc transit corpus eius, & extrin-secus umbram contingit, ut non obscuretur. Hae er-go sunt causae eclipsis lunaris.
units.tr: We showed above that the moon is lit by the brilliance of the sun, so that the half of its body exposed to us at conjunction is wrapped in darkness, while at opposition the half of its surface that we see shines with the light of the sun, and it is lit from the eastern part by solar light. We now add that the sun likewise lights up half the surface of the earth. So the light on the earth's surface revolves with the sun's motion from east to west, and the darkness revolves across it in the same way. Since the sun is larger than the earth, the earth's shadow must extend into the air in the shape of a cone, gradually narrowing as it becomes rounder and finer, until it disappears altogether. The line perpendicular to that shadow, however, stays fixed on the surface of the zodiac, opposite the sun's degree in a diametrical line. According to Ptolemy's proof, the length of the shadow, from the earth's surface to the point where it fails, equals sixty-eight semi-diameters of the earth. The diameter of the shadow's circle at the place where the moon passes, at the time it is opposite the sun, equals twice and three fifths of the diameter of the lunar body. So when the moon is in opposition to the sun and approaches the head or tail of the dragon, and has no latitude by which it could leave the earth's shadow to the north or south, it necessarily enters the earth's shadow, which takes away the sunlight from it. Thus the moon seems to suffer an eclipse until it passes out of the shadow, for the shadow follows the sun's motion, and when the moon overtakes it, the moon emerges from the eastern side, where it is lit by solar light. But if at the time of opposition the moon is exactly at the point of the head or tail of the dragon and has no latitude at all, then the motion of the centre of the lunar body takes place directly over the centre of the shadow's circle, and so the eclipse is greatest and longest. If, however, the moon has latitude at the time of opposition, its eclipse will not be greatest. For if its latitude equals the excess of the shadow's semi-diameter over the moon's semi-diameter, then its body crosses the circle of the shadow, touching it on the inside, so that it is wholly darkened and immediately lies hidden in the shadow. If its latitude equals the semi-diameter of the shadow, then the centre of its body advances touching the circle of the shadow, and half of it is darkened; and the part darkened on the opposite side is its latitude. But if its latitude equals both semi-diameters, that is of the moon and of the shadow, then its body passes and touches the shadow from outside, so that it is not darkened. These, then, are the causes of a lunar eclipse.
On the eclipse of the sun. Chapter 31.

units.la: Solis autem eclipsis contingit, quando luna cum sole coiungitur, & propinqua est capiti vel caudae draconis, neque habet latitudinem, qua declinare possit ab ecliptica: tunc enim ipsa interiicitur inter aspectum nostrum & solem. quare eius lumen nobis aufert, ut eum eclipsin pati cernamus. De-clareclaremus autem nunc, quid eueniat ratione diuersitatis aspectus: sane si coniunctio solis & lunæ fuerit præcisè in capite aut cauda draconis, & supra punctum verticis nostri; tunc centrum utriusque sphæræ incidit in lineam, quæ egreditur de loco aspectus ad ambo luminaria, neque luna tunc vllam habet diuersitatem aspectus: quamobrem necessarium est, vt luna obscuret totum corpus solis. Si autem coniunctio non sit præcisè in capite aut cauda draconis, & directè supra punctum verticis nostri; tunc illud quod diximus non eueniet, sed erit diuersitas aspectus secundum tres modos. Erit enim reflexio in longitudine tantum, ideoque differet coniunctio apparens à coniunctione vera, & latitudo lunæ apparens diuersa erit à latitudine eius vera: aut erit reflexio in latitudine tantum, tunc erit coniunctio apparens eadem cum coniunctione vera, sed latitudo lunæ apparens discrepabit à latitudine vera: aut erit reflexio in longitudine & latitudine simul, tunc coniunctio & latitudo apparens diuersa erit à coniunctione & latitudine vera. Si autem coniunctio sit apparens, & luna latitudinem habeat ab ecliptica, vt eius latitudinis reflexio fiat in diuersam partem, sitque æqualis latitudo & reflexio in duabus diuersis partibus; tunc nulla omnino erit latitudo apparens, & incidet centrum lunæ & solis in lineam, quæ egreditur de loco aspectus, & obscurabit luna totum corpus solis. Si vero circulus,qui transfit polos zodiaci & lunam, etiam transierit punctum verticis; tunc in hac dif-positione coniunctio apparens eadem erit cum coniunctione vera: at fi circulus iste, non fuerit ita dif-positus, vt diximus; tunc coniunctio apparens diuersa erit a coniunctione vera, supponetur q; luna foli vere ante & post horam coniunctionis. Si enim fuerit longitudinis reflexio versus orientem, tunc apparet coniunctio antecedet veram: fi fuerit versus occidentem, eam sequetur. Si vero latitudo & reflexio latitudinis no fuerint æquales, excessus qui est inter eas, erit latitudo lunæ apparens. Similiter fi fuerit latitudo & reflexio in parte vna; quicquid colligitur ex vtraque, erit latitudo lunæ apparens.
units.tr: A solar eclipse happens when the moon is joined with the sun and is near the head or tail of the dragon, and has no latitude by which it could deviate from the ecliptic. For then it is interposed between our sight and the sun, and so takes its light away from us, so that we see the sun suffer an eclipse. Now let us explain what follows from the diversity of aspect. Indeed, if the conjunction of sun and moon is exactly at the head or tail of the dragon and directly above the point of our zenith, then the centres of both spheres fall on the line that runs from the place of observation to both luminaries, and the moon then has no diversity of aspect at all. Therefore the moon necessarily obscures the whole body of the sun. But if the conjunction is not exactly at the head or tail of the dragon and not directly above the point of our zenith, then what we have said will not happen, but there will be a diversity of aspect in three ways. For there will be a reflection in longitude alone, and so the apparent conjunction will differ from the true conjunction, and the apparent latitude of the moon will differ from its true latitude. Or there will be a reflection in latitude alone, and then the apparent conjunction will be the same as the true conjunction, but the apparent latitude of the moon will differ from its true latitude. Or there will be a reflection in longitude and latitude together, and then the apparent conjunction and latitude will differ from the true conjunction and latitude. But if the circle which passes through the poles of the zodiac and the moon also passes through the point of our zenith, then in this arrangement the apparent conjunction will be the same as the true conjunction. But if that circle is not arranged as we have said, then the apparent conjunction will differ from the true conjunction, and it must be supposed that the moon is before or after the sun at the true hour of conjunction. For if the reflection in longitude is towards the east, the apparent conjunction comes before the true one; if it is towards the west, the apparent conjunction follows it. But if the latitude and the reflection of latitude are not equal, the excess of one over the other will be the apparent latitude of the moon. Similarly, if the latitude and the reflection are on one side, whatever is gathered from both will be the apparent latitude of the moon. Again, if the moon has latitude from the ecliptic, and its reflection of latitude falls in the opposite direction, and the latitude and reflection are equal in two opposite parts, then there is no apparent latitude at all. The centres of moon and sun fall on the line that runs from the place of observation, and the moon obscures the whole body of the sun.

units.la: Quod fi latitudo apparés fuerit minor femidiame-trisfolis & lunæ simul iunctis, tunc luna obscurabit partem solis, erit q; id, quod obscurabitur ex eo, se-cundùm quantitatem, qua minuitur latitudo de me-dietate vtriusque diametri, & continget eclipsis in corpore solis ex ea parte, qua fuerit latitudo appa-rens: at si latitudo æqualis fuerit medietati vtriusque diametri; tunc luna transibit, solem tantum co-tingens, neque obscurabit quicquam ex eo. Cùm au-tem totus sol fuerit obscuratus, non commoratur in tenebris sicut luna: quia secundùm aspectum pro-pè est eadem magnitudo corporis lunaris & solaris. Hinc apparet, quod luna eclipsin passa, cernatur ab vniuersis hominibus eodem modo, in quacunque terræ terrae parte eam aspexerint, & quantacunq; etiam sit eclipsis & mora illius: sed in eclipsi solis res aliter habet, quoniam diuersitas aspectus incidit ratione diuersorum locorum & climatum, ex quibus videtur. {1}
units.tr: But if the apparent latitude is less than the half-diameters of the sun and moon taken together, then the moon will obscure part of the sun. The amount obscured will correspond to how far the latitude falls short of the half of both diameters together, and the eclipse will fall on the body of the sun on that side where the apparent latitude lies. But if the latitude is equal to the half of both diameters together, then the moon will pass by, just touching the sun, and will obscure nothing of it. When the whole sun has been obscured, it does not linger in darkness as the moon does, because according to our aspect the bodies of the moon and the sun are nearly equal in size. Hence it is clear that the eclipsed moon is seen by all men in the same way, in whatever part of the earth they look at it, and however great the eclipse and its duration may be. But in a solar eclipse the matter is otherwise, since the diversity of aspect arises from the different places and climates from which it is seen. {1}

units.la: Quod autem reliqui quoque planetae eclipsin patiatur, manifestum est ex iis, quae supra de ordinibus orbium ipsorum diximus: quin immo fieri potest, vt luna obscuret omnes stellas, quae sunt vicinae zodiaco, cum ipsa sit propinquissima terrae. Neque septem tantum planetae incidere possunt in eclipsin: verum etiam singuli eorum possunt obscurare stellas fixas, quae sunt propinquae zodiaco.
units.tr: That the other planets also suffer eclipse is clear from what we said above about the orders of their spheres. Indeed it can happen that the moon obscures all the stars that lie near the zodiac, since it is the nearest of all to the earth. Nor can only the seven planets fall into eclipse; each of them can also obscure fixed stars that lie near the zodiac.

units.la: {1} Sicut luna & sol per excellentiam appellatur φω- σφόρος[?] siue luminaria, cum reliquae quinque stellae erraticae Ptolemaeo dicantur planetae: ita etiam eclipses horum luminarium κατ' ἐξοχὴν[?] accipiuntur, licet quinque stellae erraticae inter se, & a luna & sole obscurentur. Stellae etiam fixae, quae sunt in zodiaco, obscurari possunt ab inferioribus omnibus planetis: huiusmodi autem planetarum, & stellarum fixarum coniunctiones & obscurationes minus obseruantur, vt nomen eclipsium vix mereantur. Appendix haec de eclipsibus reliquarum stellarum, non extat in vulgatis editionibus, reperitur autem in codice Latino manuscripto, & in Hebraea translatione bibliothecae Palatinae: unde manifestum est, haec ab Alfragano consignata esse.
units.tr: Just as the moon and sun are called, by preeminence, the luminaries [φωστῆρες], while the other five wandering stars are called planets by Ptolemy, so too the eclipses of these two luminaries are taken as eclipses [κατ' ἐξοχήν] in the proper sense, although the five wandering stars are also obscured by one another, and by the moon and the sun. Fixed stars that lie in the zodiac can also be obscured by all the lower planets. But such conjunctions and obscurations of planets and fixed stars are observed so little that they scarcely deserve the name of eclipses. This appendix on the eclipses of the other stars is not found in the printed editions, but it is found in a Latin manuscript codex and in the Hebrew translation in the Palatine library. From this it is clear that these things were written down by Alfraganus.

units.la: Similis locus extat in astronomia Messahalae cap. vn-decimo.
units.tr: A similar passage is found in the astronomy of Messahala, chapter eleven.

units.la: Quod autem dicit Alfraganus stellas fixas propinquas orbi signorum seu zodiaco eclipsin pati ab inferioribus planetis, id accipiendum est de stellis quae propinquae sunt medio zodiaco seu ecliptice, hoc est, quae sunt in universa latitudine zodiaci: ita enim καταχρηστικῶς[?] zodiacus ab Arabibus subinde accipitur pro medio zodiaci, quod illi communiter cingulum signorum appellant. De congressu planetarum inter se & cum stellis fixis loquitur etiam Aristoteles lib. 1 meteorologicorum, cap. 6.
units.tr: But when Alfraganus says that fixed stars near the sphere of the signs, or zodiac, suffer eclipse from the lower planets, this must be understood of stars that lie near the middle of the zodiac or ecliptic, that is, stars that lie within the whole latitude of the zodiac. For the Arabs often take the zodiac in this catachrestic sense [καταχρηστικῶς] for the middle of the zodiac, which they commonly call the girdle of the signs. Aristotle too speaks of the meetings of the planets with one another and with the fixed stars in the first book of the Meteorology, chapter 6.

units.la: Quàm breui tempore possit fieri eclipsis lunaris & solaris. Cap. XXXII.
units.tr: How quickly a lunar and a solar eclipse can occur. Chapter 32.

units.la: NEcessarium est vt exponamus quanto tempore contingere possit eclipsis secundum medium motum: minimum sane temporis interuallum inter duas eclipses lunares, possunt esse sex menses lunares: contingit tamen quandoque, vt sint inter duas eclipses solares aut lunares interiecti quinq; menses maiores, quales sunt cum sol versatur in lateribus longitudinis propinquioris orbis sui, secundum velocio-rem suum motum: & cum luna tarde mouetur, in quamcunque partem ab orbe signorum declinet, quod sit in eclipsi lunari. Sed in eclipsi solari requiritur, vt sit latitudo lunae in ambabus eclipsibus simul in septentrionem: nam secundum hunc modum, causis scilicet hisce ita coniunctis, fieri potest vt inter duas eclipses interiiciantur quinq; menses lunares. Si vero sint inter duas eclipses septem menses minores, quales sunt cum sol versatur in vtroq; latere longitudinis remotioris orbis sui, secundum tardiorem suum motum, & cum luna velocius mouetur; tunc illud fieri non potest in eclipsibus duabus lunaribus, sed contincontingit in duabus eclipsibus solaribus sub climate quarto, & in illis quae sunt post illud versus septentrionem, ita ut latitudo lunae in utraque eclipsi sit septentrionalis. Dicimus etiam, quod fieri non possit, ut sol obscuretur bis in mense, & uno in loco, neque in duobus diuersis climatibus septentrionalibus unquam: fieri autem illud potest in duobus locis diuersis ab aequatore, quorum unus sit in climatibus septentrionalibus, alter vero in parte meridionali. Iam ergo declaravimus rationem eclipsium solarium & lunarium, prout sufficit intelligenti.
units.tr: It is necessary that we set out how much time may elapse between eclipses according to the mean motion. The least possible interval between two lunar eclipses is six lunar months. Yet it sometimes happens that between two solar or lunar eclipses there intervene five months, which is longer, namely when the sun is situated at the sides of the longitude of its nearer orbit, that is, moving with its faster motion; and since the moon moves slowly, it may decline in whichever direction from the zodiac's orbit, and this produces a lunar eclipse. But for a solar eclipse it is required that the latitude of the moon in both eclipses be to the north at the same time; for in this way, with these causes so conjoined, it can happen that five lunar months intervene between two eclipses. If, however, between two eclipses there are seven months, which is less, namely when the sun is situated on either side of the longitude of its more remote orbit, moving with its slower motion, and when the moon moves more swiftly, then this cannot happen in two lunar eclipses, but it does happen in two solar eclipses under the fourth climate, and in those that lie beyond it toward the north, so that the latitude of the moon in each eclipse is northern. We also say that it cannot happen that the sun is obscured twice in one month and in one place, nor ever in two different northern climates; but that can happen in two different places away from the equator, of which one is in the northern climates and the other in the southern part. Now, then, we have explained the reason for solar and lunar eclipses, as is sufficient for the intelligent reader.

units.la: Explicit Alfraganus de aggregatione scientiae stellarum, felicibus astris.
units.tr: Here ends Alfraganus on the compendium of the science of the stars, with favourable stars.

units.la: APPENDIX QVAM SAPIENS philosophus Rabbi Iacob, Hebraeus Alfragani interpres, superioribus adiecit, postquam Latinam versionem, quae inter Christianos corrupta habetur, consuluisset, eamque e codice Arabico emendasset.
units.tr: APPENDIX: Rabbi Jacob, the Hebrew philosopher and translator of Alfraganus, added the following to the foregoing work, after consulting the Latin version, which is held to be corrupt among the Christians, and after emending it from an Arabic manuscript.

units.la: De diuersitate dierum & noctium in locis habitabilibus: de quantitatibus & anticipatione eorum iuxta diuersitatem temporum & locorum.
units.tr: On the diversity of days and nights in inhabited places, and on their lengths and anticipation according to the diversity of times and places.

units.la: Dicamus primo quod in locis sub aequatore sitis noctes & dies perpetuo sint aequales, neque vlla admittat diuersitate, nisi quae accidit ratione anticipationis: etenim in loco orientali oritur perpetuo sol & occidit, antequam oriatur aut occidat in loco occidentali. Quantitas autem huius anticipationis æstimatur ex interuallo longitudinis, quod est inter duo loca: atque hæc quantitas perpetua est in ortu& occasu solis. In reliquis locis habitabilibus uersus septentrionem diuersitas magna est in quantitatibus & anticipatione illorum, prout tempora discrepant & loca secundum longitudinem aut latitudinem, aut secundum longitudinem & latitudinem simul. Quæ enim loca latitudinem habent eandem, & differunt in longitudine, illa sunt sub uno circulo æquatori parallelo, & duos habent meridianos. id cum accidit, perpetuo differentia est in anticipatione ortus & occasus solaris: quoniam locus orientalis semper habet solem orientem & occidentem ante locum occidentalem, pro ratione longitudinis interiectæ: sed quantitas diei & noctis in ambobus locis eadem est, neque tamen unquam dies fit æqualis noctí, quia neuter illorum locorum est sub æquatore, exceptis duobus anni temporibus, cum scilicet sol fuerit in principio arietis, quod est tempus Tekuphæ Nisan, & cum transierit initiũ librę, quod est tempus Tekuphæ Tisri. Quouis autem tempore, quo sol versabitur in signis septentrionalibus, scilicet in arietę, tauro, geminis, cancro, leone, & virgine: superabit dies noctem in ambobus locis, sicut etiam in omnibus climatibus septentrionalibus dies increscit iuxta ingressum solis in arietem, taurum & gemi-nos: in fine autem geminorum summa diei prolixitas est, atque hoc est tempus Tekuphæ Tamuz. Cum au-tem solis transierit in cancrum, leonem & virginem; paulatim dies decrescit, donec attigerit principium librae, ubi dies æquatur noctis: inde nox paulatim ac-crescit, & fit prolixior die, dum sol peragrat libram, scorpium & sagittarium, donec attingat principium capricorni, ubi prolixissima est nox, atque hoc tem-pus est Tekuphæ Tebeth: cum vero sol transit capri-cornum, aquariū & pisces; paulatim decrescit nox, donec æquetur diei, sole principium arietis attin-gente. Verum si duo loca differant in latitudine, & unam habeant longitudinem, quod accidit dum sunt sub eodem meridiano, & duobus circulis æqua-tori parallelis; tunc numquam etiā dies noctis æqua-tur, exceptis duobus prædictis temporibus, quibus per universam terram contingit æquinoctium: sed in reliquis anni temporibus quantitas diei diuersa est a quantitate noctis: cum enim sol fuerit in signis septentrionalibus, dies superabit noctem; si autem fuerit in signis meridionalibus, nox superabit diem, quemadmodum perpetuo accidit in climatibus sep-tentrionalibus, & duobus locis, quæ diuersam ha-bent quantitatem diei & noctis. Est etiam in an-ticipatione illorum differentia. si enim sol transierit signa septentrionalia; locus qui maiorem habet lati-tudinem, id est, qui magis distat ab æquatore, diem habet prolixiorem, quàm ille locus, qui vicinior est æquatori. Vt autem dies in vno loco increscit, ita nox in altero decrescit: & dividitur incrementum hoc in duas partes, ratione anticipationis ortus solaris, & retardationis occasus eius. Ortus enim illius anticipat in loco vno, & retardatur occasus eius, vt simul anticipet collectionem diurnam, & retardet exitum eius: in loco autem altero anticipat collectio nocturna, & retardatur exitus eius. Si sol fuerit in signis meridionalibus, diversum accidet: etenim locus qui propinquus est æquatori, diem habet prolixiorem, quàm habeat alter locus, qui remotior est ab illo: in nocte autem contrarium huius accidit: & dies colligitur primùm, & exit postea in loco propinquiore, vt nox colligatur primùm, & exeat postea in loco remotiore. Anticipatio autem collectionum illarum & retardatio exitus earum vnius est quantitatis: qui enim excessus est vnius loci ab altero, dividitur in duas partes, ratione collectionis & exitus. Si fuerit duorum locorum differentia in latitudine & longitudine, vt sint in duobus circulis æquatori parallelis, habeatq; duos meridianos; illud accidit duobus modis. Vt locus vnus, qui maiorem habet longitudinem, propinquior sit orienti, quàm alter: vel sit remotior, sole peruagante signa septentrionalia: tunc locus ille qui maiorem habet latitudinem, dies habet prolixiores, quàm alter: noctes autem in altero sunt prolixiores. Si sol tranfeat signa meridionalia, contrarium euenit: at diuersitas anticipationis diuersis modis contingit. Si enim locus vnus, qui habuerit maiore[?] latitudinem propinquior fuerit orienti quàm alter, tunc depre-hendetur diuersitas anticipationis istis modis: sci-licet sol fuerit in æquatore, solaris ortus & occasus præueniet in loco orientali: si verò sol fuerit in signis septentrionalibus, anticipabit ortus solaris in oriente perpetuo, sed occasus eius tribus modis accidet: si-nim maior fuerit latitudo quàm longitudo, retar-dabitur occasus solis in loco orientali: at si deprehen-datur interualla longitudinis & latitudinis æqua-lia, occidet sol in duobus locis tempore vno: cùm au-tem longitudo maior est latitudine, præueniet occa-sus solis in loco orientali. Si sol versetur in signis me-ridionalibus; contrarium accidet, quia in loco oc-cidentali ortus solaris triplex erit: si enim depre-hendatur latitudo maior longitudine, anticipa-bit ortus solis in loco occidentali: si fuerint inter-ualla longitudinis & latitudinis paria, orietur sol in duobus locis simul: & cùm longitudo superaue-rit latitudinem; anticipabit sol in loco orientali. sed occasus solis retardabitur perpetuo in loco oc-cidentali, si fuerit sol in signis meridionalibus: quemadmodum præuenit ortus solis in loco orien-tali, si sol fuerit in signis septentrionalibus. cuius rei ratio est, quòd meridianus loci orientalis præue-niat meridianū loci occidétalis. Si locus vnus fuerit orienti parum propinquior altero, inter utrumque diversitas anticipationis erit etiam secundum tres distinctos modos, sicut prius commemoratum est: id accidet, cum sol versabitur in æquatore, tunc enim similiter in loco orientali anticipatio erit diei & noctis: si sol fuerit in signis meridionalibus, tunc ortus solaris perpetuo præveniet, sed occasus illius triplex erit: si enim deprehendatur latitudo maior longitudine, retardabitur occasus solaris in loco orientali: si inveniantur intervalla latitudinis & longitudinis æqualia, occidet sol in duobus locis simul: at si fuerit longitudo maior gradibus latitudinis, præveniet occasus solis in loco orientali. Si autem sol traicerit signa septentrionalia, cõtrarium accidet, quia in loco occidentali ortus solis triplex erit. Si enim latitudo maior fuerit longitudine, præveniet ortus solaris in loco occidentali: si deprehendantur intervalla latitudinis & longitudinis æqualia, ortus ibidem erit simul: si vero longitudo excesserit latitudinem, anticipabit ortus solis in loco orientali.
units.tr: First, let us say that in places under the equator, nights and days are always equal, and admit no variation except that which arises from anticipation. For in the eastern place the sun always rises and sets before it rises or sets in the western place. The amount of this anticipation is measured by the interval of longitude between the two places, and this amount is constant for sunrise and sunset. In the other inhabited places towards the north, there is great variation in their lengths and anticipation, as the times differ and the places differ in longitude, or in latitude, or in both together. Those places which have the same latitude but differ in longitude lie under one circle parallel to the equator and have two meridians. When this happens, there is always a difference in the anticipation of sunrise and sunset, since the eastern place always has the sun rising and setting earlier than the western place, in proportion to the intervening longitude. But the length of day and night is the same in both places, and yet the day never becomes equal to the night, because neither of those places lies under the equator, except at two times of the year: namely when the sun is at the beginning of Aries, which is the time of the Tekuphah of Nisan, and when it has passed the beginning of Libra, which is the time of the Tekuphah of Tishri. At whatever time the sun moves through the northern signs, namely Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo and Virgo, the day exceeds the night in both places, just as in all northern climates the day grows longer as the sun enters Aries, Taurus and Gemini. At the end of Gemini the greatest length of day occurs, and this is the time of the Tekuphah of Tammuz. When the sun has passed into Cancer, Leo and Virgo, the day gradually shortens until it reaches the beginning of Libra, where day and night are equal. Then the night gradually increases and becomes longer than the day, while the sun traverses Libra, Scorpio and Sagittarius, until it reaches the beginning of Capricorn, where the night is longest, and this is the time of the Tekuphah of Tevet. When the sun passes Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces, the night gradually shortens until it equals the day, when the sun reaches the beginning of Aries. But if two places differ in latitude and have one longitude, which happens when they lie under the same meridian and on two circles parallel to the equator, then the day and night are never equal, except at the two aforementioned times, when the equinox occurs throughout the whole earth. At the other times of the year, the length of day differs from the length of night: when the sun is in the northern signs, the day exceeds the night; but if it is in the southern signs, the night exceeds the day, just as always happens in the northern climates, and in two places which have a different length of day and night. There is also a difference in the anticipation of these. For if the sun passes through the northern signs, the place which has the greater latitude, that is, which is farther from the equator, has a longer day than the place which is nearer the equator. As the day increases in one place, so the night decreases in the other; and this increase is divided into two parts, by reason of the anticipation of the sunrise and the delay of its setting. For its rising is anticipated in one place and its setting is delayed, so that it anticipates the daily gathering of light and delays its departure; but in the other place the nightly gathering is anticipated and its departure is delayed. If the sun is in the southern signs, the reverse happens: the place nearer the equator has a longer day than the other place, which is more remote from it; and the reverse occurs in the night. The day gathers first and departs later in the nearer place, while the night gathers first and departs later in the more remote place. The anticipation of these gatherings and the delay of their departure are of one and the same amount, for the excess of one place over the other is divided into two parts, by reason of gathering and departure. If two places differ in both latitude and longitude, so that they lie on two circles parallel to the equator and have two meridians, this occurs in two ways. Either the place which has the greater longitude is nearer the east than the other, or it is farther away, while the sun moves through the northern signs. Then the place which has the greater latitude has longer days than the other, while the nights are longer in the other place. If the sun passes through the southern signs, the opposite happens; yet the variation in anticipation occurs in different ways. For if the one place, which has the greater latitude, is nearer the east than the other, then the difference in anticipation will be detected in these ways: namely, when the sun is on the equator, the rising and setting of the sun will anticipate in the eastern place; but if the sun is in the northern signs, the rising of the sun will always be anticipated in the east, while its setting will happen in three ways: if the latitude is greater than the longitude, the setting of the sun will be delayed in the eastern place; but if the intervals of longitude and latitude are found to be equal, the sun will set in two places at one time; and when the longitude is greater than the latitude, the setting of the sun will be anticipated in the eastern place. If the sun is in the southern signs, the opposite happens, because in the western place the rising of the sun will be threefold: for if the latitude is found to be greater than the longitude, the rising of the sun will be anticipated in the western place; if the intervals of latitude and longitude are equal, the sun will rise in both places at once; and when the longitude exceeds the latitude, the sun will anticipate in the eastern place. But the setting of the sun will always be delayed in the western place if the sun is in the southern signs, just as the rising of the sun is anticipated in the eastern place if the sun is in the northern signs. The reason for this is that the meridian of the eastern place anticipates the meridian of the western place. If one place is slightly nearer the east than the other, there will also be a difference of anticipation between the two in three distinct ways, as was mentioned earlier. This happens when the sun is on the equator, for then likewise the anticipation of day and night will occur in the eastern place. If the sun is in the southern signs, the rising of the sun will always be anticipated, but its setting will be threefold: for if the latitude is found to be greater than the longitude, the setting of the sun will be delayed in the eastern place; if the intervals of latitude and longitude are found to be equal, the sun will set in two places at once; but if the longitude exceeds the latitude by degrees, the setting of the sun will be anticipated in the eastern place. If, however, the sun passes through the northern signs, the opposite will happen, because the rising of the sun in the western place will be threefold. For if the latitude is greater than the longitude, the rising of the sun will be anticipated in the western place; if the intervals of latitude and longitude are equal, the rising will be simultaneous there; but if the longitude exceeds the latitude, the rising of the sun will be anticipated in the eastern place.

units.la: Hæ sunt umbræ singulorum climatum, quarum tractationem ex capite decimo sumtam, huc reiecimus.
units.tr: These are the shadows of the individual climates. Their treatment, taken from the tenth chapter, I have put back here.

units.la: IN principio climatis primi, quando dies æquatur noctí, sub ingressum solis in arietem, umbra habet pedem unum cum dimidio, & duas tertias unius decimæ partis pedis: in fine illius habet 2 ½ pedes, des, cum vna decima: in medio illius habet 2 pedes, cum vna decima. Die 16 Nisan vmbra longitudi-nem habet dimidij pedis, & quatuor quintarum vnius: die secundo. Ijar stilus non proiicit vmbram in meridiano, donec aduenìat dies sextus Ijar, in quo quantitas vmbrae est sexta pars pedis, eaq; cum prius spargeretur in partem septentrionalem, nunc circumducitur ad meridiem: in die 17 illius mensis, vmbra habet sextam partem pedis, cum vna decima. In die 18 Haziran obtinet quinque sextas pe-dis: in 19 Tamuz habet vnam tertiam & vnam decimam. Si aduenerit dies tertius mensis Ab, ite-rum abscinditur vmbra, neque proiicitur in meri-diano: die septimo mensis Ab vmbra meridiana ha-bet sextam partem pedis, & extenditur in septen-trionem, sicut prius vergebat versus meridiem: die 19 illius mensis habet pedem & quatuor quintas, sed 19 mensis Elul longitudinem habet duorum pe-dum, cum dimidia decima. Die 18 Tisrin prioris habet 3 ½ pedes, cum quarta parte. Die 17 Tisrin posteriorıs habet 4 ½ pedes, cum quarta parte. Die 17 Canun prioris habet quinq̃[?] pedes cum quadrante. Die 14 Canun posterioris habet 4 ½ pedes, cum quarta parte. Die 13 Sabat habet 3 ½ pedes, cum quarta parte. Hæc est vmbra media climatis, prout polus eleuatur in principio & fine illius.
units.tr: At the beginning of the first climate, when day equals night, at the sun's entry into Aries, the shadow is one and a half feet and two thirds of one tenth of a foot long; at its end it is 2½ feet with one tenth; in its middle it is 2 feet with one tenth. On 16 Nisan the shadow is half a foot and four fifths of one tenth long. On 2 Iyar the gnomon casts no shadow at noon until the sixth day of Iyar, when the shadow is a sixth of a foot. Although before this it was cast toward the north, it now swings round toward the south. On 17 Iyar the shadow is a sixth of a foot with one tenth. On 18 Sivan it is five sixths of a foot. On 19 Tammuz it is one third and one tenth. If the third day of Av arrives, the shadow is again cut off and is not cast at noon. On the seventh day of Av the midday shadow is a sixth of a foot and stretches toward the north, as before it had inclined toward the south. On 19 Av it is a foot and four fifths. On 19 Elul the shadow is two feet with half a tenth. On 18 Tishri (the earlier) it is 3½ feet with a quarter. On 17 Tishri (the later) it is 4½ feet with a quarter. On 17 Kislev (the earlier) it is five feet with a quarter. On 14 Kislev (the later) it is 4½ feet with a quarter. On 13 Shevat it is 3½ feet with a quarter. This is the middle shadow of the climate, according as the pole is elevated at its beginning and its end.

units.la: In fine climatis secundi, sole transitum faciente in arietem, vmbra habet 3 ½ pedes, cum vna decima: in medio habet duos pedes & tres quintas, in principio 2 ½ pedes, & tres decimas, quanta est umbrae longitudo in fine primi climatis, ut ante dixi-mus. In omni enim climate umbra spectatur vel in principio, vel in fine, aut in medio illius, per totum annum: ut principium unius fit finis alterius, quemadmodum discipulus ex diuisione singulorum climatum observare potest. Umbra media die 16 Ni-san habet 1 ½ pedem, cum dimidia decima. Die 16 mensis Iiar obtinet dimidium pedem. Die 18 mensis Haziran habet duas tertias decimae partis pedis. Die 19 mensis Tamuz habet dimidium pedem. Die 19 mensis Ab obtinet pedem unum, cum dimidia decima. Die 19 Elul habet tres pedes & decimam. Die 18 Tisrin prioris habet quinque pedes. Die 17 Tisrin posterioris habet 6 ½ pedes, cum una tertia. Die 16 Canun prioris habet septem pedes, & duas tertias. Die 15 Canun posterioris habet 6 ½ pedes, cum quadrante. Die 13 Sabat habet quinque pedes, cum quinta decima.
units.tr: At the end of the second climate, with the sun passing into Aries, the shadow is 3½ feet with one tenth; in the middle it is two feet and three fifths; at the beginning 2½ feet and three tenths, which is the length of the shadow at the end of the first climate, as I said before. For in every climate the shadow is observed either at the beginning, or at the end, or in the middle of it, throughout the year; so that the beginning of one climate becomes the end of another, as the student can observe from the division of the individual climates. The middle shadow on 16 Nisan is 1½ feet with half a tenth. On 16 Iyar it is half a foot. On 18 Sivan it is two thirds of a tenth of a foot. On 19 Tammuz it is half a foot. On 19 Av it is one foot with half a tenth. On 19 Elul it is three feet and a tenth. On 18 Tishri (the earlier) it is five feet. On 17 Tishri (the later) it is 6½ feet with one third. On 16 Kislev (the earlier) it is seven feet and two thirds. On 15 Kislev (the later) it is 6½ feet with a quarter. On 13 Shevat it is five feet with a fifth of a tenth.

units.la: In principio climatis tertii, sole arietem adeunte, die 16 mensis Adar umbra habet 3 ½ pedes, cum una decima, & sexta parte decimae: in fine eius, quando umbra aequalis est, habet 4 ½ pedes, cum una decima, & tertia parte decimae: in medio eius eadem die umbra habet 4 pedes, & sextam partem. Die 16 Nisan habet duos pedes, cum una tertia, & una decima. Die 16 Ijar habet pedem, cum quaquadrante. Die 18 Haziran habet quinquefextas pedis, cum dimidia decima. Die 19 Tamuz obti-net pedem.& quadrantem,cum vna tertia,&vna decima. Die 19 Ab habet duos pedes,cum tertia decima parte. Die 19 Elul habet quatuor pedes, cum sexta parte. Die 18 Octobris habet sex pedes , cum duabus quintis. Die 17 Nouembris habet octo pedes cum dimidio, & vna decima. Die 16 Canun prioris habet nouem pedes & duas tertias , cum dimidia decima. Die 17 Canun poste-rioris habet octo pedes, cum vna tertia , & vna quinta. Die 13 Sabat habet sex pedes cum duabus quintis vnius pedis. Vmbra huius climatis , sicut aliorum quae sequuntur, spargitur versus plagam sep-tentrionalem.
units.tr: At the beginning of the third climate, when the sun enters Aries, on 16 Adar the shadow is 3½ feet with one tenth and a sixth of a tenth; at its end, when the shadow is equal, it is 4½ feet with one tenth and a third of a tenth; in its middle, on the same day, the shadow is 4 feet and a sixth part. On 16 Nisan it is two feet with one third and one tenth. On 16 Iyar it is a foot with a quarter. On 18 Sivan it is five sixths of a foot with half a tenth. On 19 Tammuz it is a foot and a quarter, with one third and one tenth. On 19 Av it is two feet with a third of a tenth. On 19 Elul it is four feet with a sixth. On 18 October it is six feet with two fifths. On 17 November it is eight and a half feet with one tenth. On 16 Kislev (the earlier) it is nine feet and two thirds with half a tenth. On 17 Kislev (the later) it is eight feet with one third and one fifth. On 13 Shevat it is six feet with two fifths of a foot. The shadow of this climate, like the others that follow, is cast toward the northern quarter.

units.la: In principio climatis quarti, sole introitum faciente in arietem, die 16 Adar, umbra habet quatuor pedes & tres quintas cum vna sexta: in fine illius habet quinque pedes: & umbra in medio illius similis est illi, quae in principio eius spargitur. Die 19 Nisan habet tres pedes cum quadrante. Die 16 Iar habet duos pedes & duas tertias unius decimae. Die 18 Haziran obtinet duos pedes cu duabus quintis. Die 19 Tamuz habet duos pedes & tres decimas. Die 19 Ab habet tres pedes cum quadrante. Die 19 Elul habet quatuor pedes cum duabus quintis. Die 18 Octobris habet 7 ½ pedes, cum quadrante. Die 17 Nouembris habet decem pedes cu duabus tertiis. Die 17 Decembris habet duodecim pedes cum vna decima. Die 15 Ianuarii obtinet decem pedes cum duabus tertiis. Die 13 Sabat habet 8 ½ pedes cum quadrante.
units.tr: At the beginning of the fourth climate, when the sun enters Aries, on 16 Adar the shadow is four feet and three fifths with one sixth; at its end it is five feet; and the shadow in its middle is like that which is cast at its beginning. On 19 Nisan it is three feet with a quarter. On 16 Iyar it is two feet and two thirds of a tenth. On 18 Sivan it is two feet with two thirds. On 19 Tammuz it is two feet and three tenths. On 19 Av it is three feet with a quarter. On 19 Elul it is four feet with two fifths. On 18 October it is 7½ feet with a quarter. On 17 November it is ten feet with two thirds. On 17 December it is twelve feet with one tenth. On 15 January it is ten feet with two thirds. On 13 Shevat it is 8½ feet with a quarter.

units.la: In principio climatis quinti, sole peragrante æ-quatorem, vmbra habet quinq; pedes & tres quin-tas cum vna sexta: in fine illius obtinet 6 ½ pedes cum vna decima: in medio illius vmbra eodem die habet 6 pedes cum vna sexta. Die 16 Nisan habet quatuor pedes. Die 16 Iiar habet duos pedes cum duabus tertiis. Die 19 Ab habet quatuor pedes. Die 19 Elul habet quatuor pedes cum vna sexta. Die 17 Nouembris habet 13 pedes. Die 17 Decembris habet 14 pedes, cum duabus decimis vnius pedis. Die 15 Ianuarii habet 13 pedes. Die 13 Sabat habet 9 pedes cum vna sexta.
units.tr: At the beginning of the fifth climate, when the sun traverses the equator, the shadow is five feet and three fifths with one sixth; at its end it has 6½ feet with one tenth; in its middle, on the same day, the shadow is six feet with one sixth. On 16 Nisan it is four feet. On 16 Iyar it is two feet and two thirds. On 19 Av it is four feet. On 19 Elul it is four feet with one sixth. On 17 November it is 13 feet. On 17 December it is 14 feet with two tenths of a foot. On 15 January it is 13 feet. On 13 Shevat it is nine feet with one sixth.

units.la: In principio sexti climatis, quando dies æquatur noƈti, vmbra habet septem pedes cum sex decimis: in fine quoque illius habet septem pedes & sex decimas, etsi pes vnus adiici possit, qui non est in principio eius: in medio illius habet septem pedes, cum vna decima pedis. Die 17 Iiar habet tres pedes, cum vna sexta & vna decima. Die 19 Ab habet quatuor pedes cum dimidio, & quinta parte. Die 19 Elul habet septem pedes cum vna decima. Die 18 Tifrin prioris habet 10 ½ pedes cum quadrante. Die 17 Tifrin posterioris habet 15 ½ pedes. Die 19 Canun prioris habet vndecim pedes cum vna quinta. Die 15 Canun posterioris habet 15 1/2 pedes. Die 13 Sabat habet 10 1/2 pedes cum quadrante.
units.tr: At the beginning of the sixth climate, when day equals night, the shadow is seven feet with six tenths; at its end too it is seven feet and six tenths, although one foot could be added, which is not in its beginning; in its middle it is seven feet with one tenth of a foot. On 17 Iyar it is three feet with one sixth and one tenth. On 19 Av it is four and a half feet with a fifth part. On 19 Elul it is seven feet with one tenth. On 18 Tishri (the earlier) it is 10½ feet with a quarter. On 17 Tishri (the later) it is 15½ feet. On 19 Kislev (the earlier) it is eleven feet with one fifth. On 15 Kislev (the later) it is 15½ feet. On 13 Shevat it is 10½ feet with a quarter.

units.la: In principio climatis septimi, quo tempore sol ingreditur arietem, & contingit æquinoctium, die decimo sexto mensis Adar, umbra habet 7 1/2 pedes cum una decima, & sexta decimæ, quemadmodum est in fine climatis sexti, quandoquidem finis cuiusque climatis est principium alterius: & umbra posterior eodem die in æquatore habet 8 1/2 pedes, cum dimidia decima unius pedis: sed umbra medii climatis eodem die habet octo pedes, cum una tertia decimæ. Die 16 Nisan habet quinque pedes, cum una quinta & sexta. Die 16 Ijar habet tres pedes cum dimidio & una tertia. Die 13 Haziran habet tres pedes cum una tertia. Die 19 Ab obtinet quinque pedes cum una quinta & sexta. Die 13 Elul habet octo pedes cum tertia unius decimæ. Die 18 Octobris habet 12 pedes cum quadrante & decima. Die 17 Nouembris habet 18 pedes cum duabus quintis. Die 17 Decembris habet 21 pedes & una tertiam & unam decimam. Die 15 Ianuarii habet 18 pedes cum duabus quintis. Die 13 Sabat habet duodecim pedes cum una tertia.
units.tr: At the beginning of the seventh climate, when the sun enters Aries and the equinox occurs, on the sixteenth day of Adar, the shadow is 7½ feet with one tenth and a sixth of a tenth, just as it is at the end of the sixth climate, since the end of each climate is the beginning of the next; and the later shadow on the same day at the equator is 8½ feet with half a tenth of a foot; but the shadow of the middle of the climate on the same day is eight feet with one third of a tenth. On 16 Nisan it is five feet with one fifth and a sixth. On 16 Iyar it is three and a half feet with one third. On 13 Sivan it is three feet with one third. On 19 Av it is five feet with one fifth and a sixth. On 13 Elul it is eight feet with a third of a tenth. On 18 October it is 12 feet with a quarter and a tenth. On 17 November it is 18 feet with two fifths. On 17 December it is 21 feet and one third and one tenth. On 15 January it is 18 feet with two fifths. On 13 Shevat it is twelve feet with one third.

units.la: Finiunt umbræ climatum, & definitotus hic liber: laus sit Deo.
units.tr: The shadows of the climates end here, and this book is finished. Praise be to God.

units.la: Caput hoc de noctium & dierum diuersitate, item de quantitatibus & anticipatione eorum, scriptum alicubi inuenit Hebræus Alfragani interpres, & id dignum iudicauit, quod cum superioribus coniungerectur. In eo autem obseruetur distinctio Tekuphoth, hoc est, punctorum æquinoctialium & solstitialium. æquinoctiū vernum appellatur Tekupha Nisan, sicut æquinoctium autumnale dicitur Tekupha Tisri: & solstitium æstiuum dicitur Tekupha Tamuz, sicut hibernum appellatur Tekupha Tebeth. Et cum anni solaris quantitas apud Hebræos ponatur esse 365 1/4 dierum: sequitur hinc vnamquamq; Tekupham habere dies 91,& 7 1/2 horas. Tractatus de vmbris septe climatum, scriptus est ab ipso Alfragano, & pertinet ad caput decimum, in quo agitur de ambitu terræ, & diuisione septem climatum secundum longitudinem & latitudinem: & inferendus est in eo loco, vbi interpres Hebræus sic loquitur, In libro Arabico autor plura dicit de his locis ratione vmbrae, sicut de aliis climatibus: sed in libro Romanorum non sunt translata: ideo hic non adscribemus. Etsi autem codex manuscriptus versionis Latinæ in bibliotheca Palatina, non habeat hoc tractatum de vmbris: credendum tamen est interpreti Hebræo, qui ait eum extare in codice Arabico, & ab Alfragano esse conscriptum. Cuius rei manifestissimum est indicium, quod in eo ter asseritur, æquinoctium vernum fuisse in decimo sexto die mensis Adar, hoc est, Martii: hæc enim obseruatio exacte conuenit cum maxima solis declinatione, quam Alfraganus ex Albategnio sumtam retinuit, & statuit esse 23 graduum, & triginta quinque minutorum: sicut eandem obseruauit Almamon rex Arabum, studiosissimus mathematum, qui paulo ante Albategnium vixit, vel certe illi fuit συγχρονος, si credamus R. Abrahamo Chajain libro de sphæra mundi: cuius editionem Sebastianus stianus Musterus & Erasmus Schreckenfuchsius no-bis benigne procurarunt. Huius exemplar Hebræum manuscriptum extat in bibliotheca Palatina, ex quo restitui potest, quicquid in editione vulgari est depra-vatum. Conuenit etiam huius æquinoctii verni, ab Alfragano in 16 die Martii obseruati notatio, cum lo-cis stellarum fixarum, in quibus hæserunt tempore Alfragani: sicut ex Sohel siue Canobo stella primæ magnitudinis, quæ erat in postremo gradu geminorum, animadvertere licet. Etsi igitur Alfraganus in hoc libello videatur nullas habere observationes: tres tamen præcipuas enumerauit, quæ astronomis omni-bus quouis seculo debent esse notissimæ: huiusmodi sunt maxima solis declinatio, situs æquinoctii verni aut autumnalis in calendario vulgari, & locus stellarum fixarum, secundum comparationem itineris so-laris.
units.tr: Alfragan's Hebrew translator found somewhere a chapter on the difference between nights and days, and likewise on their lengths and their anticipation. He thought it worth adding to the preceding material. In it is noted the distinction of the Tekuphoth, that is, of the equinoctial and solstitial points. The vernal equinox is called Tekupha Nisan, and the autumnal equinox is called Tekupha Tisri. The summer solstice is called Tekupha Tamuz, and the winter solstice is called Tekupha Tebeth. Since the Hebrews put the length of the solar year at 365 1/4 days, it follows that each Tekupha has 91 days and 7 1/2 hours. A treatise on the shadows of the seven climates was written by Alfragan himself, and belongs to the tenth chapter, which deals with the circumference of the earth and the division of the seven climates by longitude and latitude. It should be inserted in the place where the Hebrew translator says: In the Arabic book the author says many things about these places with respect to the shadow, as he does about the other climates; but these have not been translated in the book of the Romans, so we shall not add them here. Although the manuscript Latin version in the Palatine library does not contain this treatise on shadows, we must believe the Hebrew translator, who says that it exists in the Arabic codex and was written by Alfragan. The clearest sign of this is that it three times asserts that the vernal equinox fell on the sixteenth day of the month Adar, that is, March. This observation agrees exactly with the greatest declination of the sun, which Alfragan took from Albategnius and set at 23 degrees and 35 minutes. The same value was observed by Almamon, king of the Arabs, a most diligent student of mathematics, who lived a little before Albategnius, or was certainly his contemporary, if we believe R. Abraham Chajain in his book on the sphere of the world. Sebastian Münster and Erasmus Schreckenfuchs kindly arranged its edition for us. A manuscript Hebrew copy of this work is in the Palatine library, from which whatever is corrupted in the printed edition can be restored. The record of this vernal equinox, observed by Alfragan on 16 March, also agrees with the positions of the fixed stars in which they stood in Alfragan's time, as can be seen from Sohel, or Canopus, a star of the first magnitude, which was at the last degree of Gemini. So although Alfragan seems to have no observations in this little book, he has listed three principal ones, which should be well known to all astronomers in every age: these are the greatest declination of the sun, the position of the vernal or autumnal equinox in the common calendar, and the place of the fixed stars, according to their relation to the path of the sun.

units.la: Quando Alfraganus dicit fuisse æquinoctium vernum in die decimo sexto Adar: intelligit mesem Romanum, qui Martius appellatur: ipse enim ad imitationem Albategnii Ara[?]chelis Syrorum vsurpat calendarium, qui menses duodecim Iulianos nominibus Romanis vel Syriacis exprimunt. Nomina Syriaca duodecim mensium hæc sunt: 1 Adar: 2 Nisan: 3 Ijar: 4 Haziran: 5 Tamuz: 6 Ab: 7 Elul: 8 Tisrin prior: 9 Tisrin posterior: 10 Canun prior: 11 Canun posterior: 12 Sabat. Hisce respondent nomina Romana: 1 Martius: 2 Aprilis: 3 Maius: 4 Iunius: 5 Iulius: 6 Augustus: 7 September: 8 October: 9 November: 10 December: 11 Ianuarius: 12 Februa-rius. Quod autem paulo ante enumerata nomina sint genuina Syrorum, non tantum Alfraganus in primo statim capite, & appendice decimi capitis ostendit: verum etiam commonstrat autor versionis Arabicæ lib. 2 de orthodoxa fide Ioanis Damascēni, qui extat in bibliotheca Palatina. Neque dubium est, hanc esse veram nominum Syriacorum & Romanorum in mensibus Iulianis comparationem: Alfraganus enim in primo capite expresse asserit, Ianuarium Romanum respondere Canun posteriori Syrorum, & Februarium Romanum esse Sabat Syrorum: quod etiam probari potest ex numero dierum, qui singulis mensibus assignatur. Idcirco in hac appendice Alfraganus nominat Octobrem & Nouembrem, quos paulo ante Syriacè appellauerat Tisrin priorem & posteriorem: item vocat Decembrem & Ianuarium, quos prius Canun priorem & posteriorem Syriacè nominauerat. Nihil autem interest, an menses Iuliani Syriacis vel Romanis nominibus appellentur: est enim utriusque genti commune calendarium, cuius initium ducitur ab æra Alexandri Dhilkarnain, seu ab imperio Seleuci Nicanoris, quorum utrumque Arabes agnoscut pro primis Reipub. Romanæ monarchis.
units.tr: When Alfragan says that the vernal equinox fell on the sixteenth day of Adar, he means the Roman month called March. For, in imitation of Albategnius, he follows the calendar of the Syrians, who express the twelve Julian months by Roman or Syriac names. The Syriac names of the twelve months are these: (1) Adar; (2) Nisan; (3) Ijar; (4) Haziran; (5) Tamuz; (6) Ab; (7) Elul; (8) Tisrin prior; (9) Tisrin posterior; (10) Canun prior; (11) Canun posterior; (12) Sabat. The Roman names corresponding to these are: (1) March; (2) April; (3) May; (4) June; (5) July; (6) August; (7) September; (8) October; (9) November; (10) December; (11) January; (12) February. That the names just listed are genuinely Syriac is shown not only by Alfragan at the very start of his first chapter and in the appendix to the tenth chapter, but also by the author of the Arabic version of the second book of John of Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith, which is in the Palatine library. There is no doubt that this is the true comparison of the Syriac and Roman names for the Julian months. Alfragan clearly asserts in his first chapter that January corresponds to the Syrian Canun posterior and February to the Syrian Sabat. This can also be proved from the number of days assigned to each month. For this reason, in this appendix Alfragan names October and November, which he had just called Tisrin prior and posterior in Syriac, and he calls December and January, which he had first named Canun prior and posterior in Syriac. It makes no difference whether the Julian months are called by Syriac or Roman names, for there is one calendar common to both peoples. It begins from the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain, or from the reign of Seleucus Nicator, both of whom the Arabs recognise as the first monarchs of the Roman state.

units.la: Cum autem æquinoctium vernum tempore Alfragani hæserit in decimo sexto die Martii, ex umbrarum declaratione apparet, quando sol fuerit ingressus in reliqua signa zodiaci: quod nimirum 16 Aprilis tau-rū, 16 Maii geminos, 18 Iunii cancrum, 19 Iulii leonem, 19 Augusti Virginem, 19 Septembris libram adierit, ibique æquinoctium autumnale fecerit: sicut in eodem die deprehensum est ab Albategnio. item quod sol die 18 Octobris transfierit in scorpium, die 17 Nouembris in sagittarium, die 16 Decembris in capricornum, die 17 Ianuarii in aquarium, & 13 Februarii in pisces. De proportione gnomonis ad suas umbras cō-sulatur Ptolemaeus lib. 2 Almagesti cap. 5. Hacte-nus Alfraganum ex Hebraea interpretatione exposui, cum manuscripto Latino codice contuli, aliosque autores adhibui, qui lucem aliquam afferre possent: mihi ipsi tamen non satisfeci, cum multa in contextu Alfragani obscura & ambigua transfilire sim coactus, quod deesset exemplar Arabicum. Id si ex Italicis vel Hispanicis bibliothecis eruerint, suoque prælo divulgarint, qui iam Romae libris Arabicis imprimedis occupantur: maximo beneficio Rempub.literariam affecerint, & ingeniis præstatioribus occasionem prae-buerint, quo deinceps terfiorem & absolutiorem fi-mus habituri Alfraganum. Cæterum quia totum pri-mum caput Alfragani est chronologicum, & ratio-nem præcipuorum calendariorum cum suis epochis declarat, breuiter tamen & sine annorum ad nostra tempora continuatione:placet subiungere commentarium, in quo prolixius demonstrationes calendariorum excutiantur, & anni ab Olympiadibus & urbe condita usq; ad nostram memoriam certa serie extendantur. Deus opt.max.faxit, ut omnia illius honori, Ecclesiarum fa-luti, & Scholarum conserua-tioni inseruiant.
units.tr: Since the vernal equinox in Alfragan's time fell on 16 March, the declarations of the shadows show when the sun entered the remaining signs of the zodiac. Evidently, on 16 April it entered Taurus, on 16 May Gemini, on 18 June Cancer, on 19 July Leo, on 19 August Virgo, and on 19 September Libra, and there it made the autumnal equinox. The same day was observed by Albategnius. Likewise the sun passed into Scorpio on 18 October, into Sagittarius on 17 November, into Capricorn on 16 December, into Aquarius on 17 January, and into Pisces on 13 February. For the proportion of the gnomon to its shadows, consult Ptolemy, Almagest, book 2, chapter 5. I have thus far explained Alfragan from the Hebrew translation, compared it with the manuscript Latin codex, and consulted other authors who might throw some light on it. Yet I am not satisfied myself, since I have been forced to pass over many obscure and ambiguous points in Alfragan's text, because the Arabic exemplar is lacking. If those who are now busy printing Arabic books in Rome should dig it out of the Italian or Spanish libraries and publish it with their press, they would confer the greatest benefit on the republic of letters and give better minds the opportunity to make Alfragan cleaner and more complete. Moreover, since the whole first chapter of Alfragan is chronological, and sets out the principal calendars with their epochs, though briefly and without continuing the years down to our own time, I think it fitting to add a commentary. In it the demonstrations of the calendars will be examined at greater length, and the years from the Olympiads and the founding of the city down to our memory will be extended in a fixed sequence. May God, most good and great, grant that all of it serve his honour, the salvation of the churches, and the preservation of the schools.
THE END.

units.la: Syriacum & Hebraum cum suis epochis demonstratur: & ab Olympiadibus Vrbeq[?] condita vsque ad no-stram memoriam certissima annorum connexio ex obseruationibus astronomorum & probatis scriptoribus indicatur:
