of Johannisberg.

units.la: HISTORIARVM ET ASTRONOMIÆ STVDIOSO INVESTIGATORI S.
units.tr: To the Studious Investigator of History and Astronomy, Greetings

units.la: SVccinctam calendariorum historiam tradit nobis Alfraganus: vt cognoscere liceat, quomodo anni tám lunares quàm solares a certis epochis in multas centurias & myriades possint extendi. Quæ si diligenter expendantur, ad obseruationes astronomicas maximum afferunt adiumentum: si vero negligantur, totam rerum cœlestium contemplationem reddunt inutilem & odiosam. Non enim luminarium vel planetarum periodi sine mensium annorumve spaciis definiuntur: nec sine his canones temporum supputandorum apud diuersos populos extruuntur. Accedit huc, quod ad motus cœlestes indagandos plurimorum seculorum experientia requiratur: quæ certè mente comprehendi nò potest, nisi dierum interiestorum numerus sit exploratus. Quamobrem prudenter fecit Alfraganus, qui statim ab initio præcipuarum ararum interualla cum characteribus hebdomadicis recensuit, & à Nabonasaro vsq; ad Iezdagird regis Persarum obitum, indubitatam annorum, mensium, dierumq; connexionem declarauit. Vtinam verò scepum & methodum Alfragani Arabis perspicacissimi omnes intelligerent & sequerentur, qui astronomiam ex fundamentis illustrare, & diuina Ptolemæi scripta publicè interpretari aggrediuntur: optime studiis mathematicis foret consultum, neque tanta esset confusio & temporum ignorantia. Cur enim Almagestum in scholis iacere, & à plerisque contemni videmus, nisi quòd pauci inueniantur, legitimam annorum Nabonasari continuationem è fide dignissimis authoribus ostendentes? Sic Albategnii præclaras de motibus stellarum obseruationes in tenebris delitescere necesse est, nisi calendarium Syrorum explicetur, & anni Alexadri Dilkarnain ad Ægyptiorū, Arabum, & Persarum calculū revocentur. Ex quibus manifestū est, astronomiā in exquisitissima historiarū cœlestium consideratione versari, & tēporibus notandis aptissimū vehiculum prabere. Ut autem revolutionū atherearum utilitas conspiceretur, & chronologiæ universalis ratio apud omnes innotesceret, commentarium hunc non sine magnis laboribus a me congestum in lucem prodire volui: præsertim cum optimus & doctissimus vir, M. Georgius Limnæus, alias Wirn cognominatus, mathematum in Academia Ienensi Professor, illum nostro seculo gratissimum fore indicasset. Ordinem tractationis ab Alfragano institutū non seruaui: is enim a calendario Arabico utpote genti suæ notissimo est exorsus, deinde Syrorū, Romanorum, Persarū, Ægyptiorū & Coptitarum computum est persecutus. Ego calendarium Romanū primo omnium explicaui, quod ad annorū (hristi[?] nobis usitatorum perceptionem maximè sit necessariū: cui subiunxi Ægyptiorum, Arabicorū, Persicorū, & Syriacorum annalium comemorationem. De calendario Hebraeorū nihil habet Alfraganus: id tamen consilio Iacobi Antolii interpretis adiciendum putaui, quod magnam cū Arabico & Syriaco cognationem agnoscat. Quia vero horum calendariorum epochæ, vel alia insignium temporum intervalla, animo comprehendi nequeunt, nisi ab Olympiadibus usque ad nostram ætatem, certa annorum continuatio demonstretur: visum est tabulas chronologicas contexere, easq; observationibus astronomorum & probatissimorum historicorum testimoniis stabilire. Tuum est, studiose lector, lucubrationes meas boni consulere, bene inventis gratiam habere, & leuioribus erratis veniam dare.
units.tr: Alfraganus gives us a brief history of calendars, so that we may learn how both lunar and solar years can be extended from fixed epochs over many centuries and myriads of years. If these matters are studied carefully, they are a very great help to astronomical observation. If they are neglected, they make the whole contemplation of the heavenly bodies useless and tedious. For the periods of the luminaries and planets cannot be defined without the spans of months and years, and without these, the tables for reckoning time among different peoples cannot be constructed. Moreover, to investigate celestial motions requires the experience of many centuries, and this certainly cannot be grasped by the mind unless the number of days between events has been established. So Alfraganus acted wisely, since from the very beginning he listed the intervals of the principal eras together with the weekly cycles, and from Nabonassar down to the death of Yazdegerd, king of the Persians, he set out the certain connection of years, months and days. I wish that all who undertake to explain astronomy from its foundations, and to publicly interpret the divine writings of Ptolemy, would understand and follow the plan and method of Alfraganus, the most perceptive Arab. Mathematical studies would be served best, and there would not be such great confusion and ignorance of chronology. For why do we see the Almagest lying neglected in the schools and despised by most people, unless it is because few can be found who demonstrate the legitimate continuation of the years of Nabonassar from the most trustworthy authors? Likewise, the outstanding observations of Albategnius on the motions of the stars must remain hidden in darkness, unless the calendar of the Syrians is explained and the years of Alexander Dhu'l-Qarnayn are brought back to the reckoning of the Egyptians, Arabs and Persians. From these things it is clear that astronomy consists in the most exact consideration of celestial histories, and provides a most suitable vehicle for marking times. But so that the usefulness of the heavenly revolutions might be seen, and the principle of universal chronology might become known to everyone, I wished to bring this commentary, gathered by me with no small labour, into the light. This was especially so because the very excellent and learned man, M. Georgius Limnaeus, otherwise called Wirn, Professor of Mathematics in the University of Jena, had indicated that it would be most welcome to our age. I have not kept the order of treatment followed by Alfraganus. He began with the Arabic calendar, as being best known to his own people, and then pursued the reckoning of the Syrians, Romans, Persians, Egyptians and Copts. I explained the Roman calendar first of all, since it is most necessary for understanding the years of Christ in common use among us. To this I added a commemoration of the Egyptian, Arabic, Persian and Syriac annals. Alfraganus has nothing on the Hebrew calendar. Nevertheless, on the advice of Jacob Antolius, the translator, I thought it should be added, since it shows a great kinship with the Arabic and Syriac. But because the epochs of these calendars, or other intervals of notable times, cannot be grasped by the mind unless a certain continuous sequence of years is shown from the Olympiads down to our own age, I judged it right to compose chronological tables and to establish them by the observations of astronomers and the testimonies of the most approved historians. It is for you, studious reader, to take my labours kindly, to be grateful for what is well done, and to pardon the lesser errors.
THE ROMAN CALENDAR.

units.la: BVrbe condita vsquead ordinatio-nem Diui Iulii Cæsaris, primi Roma-norum Imperatoris, varia fuit anno-rum supputandorum ratio: sed duo præcipuè calendaria extiterunt, Ro-muli scilicet & Numæ Pompilii, iuxta quæ tempora notari solebant, ex motu solis lunæque inter se ex-æquato.
units.tr: From the founding of the city until the ordinance of the divine Julius Caesar, the first Emperor of the Romans, the method of counting years varied. Two calendars in particular existed, namely that of Romulus and that of Numa Pompilius, by which times were customarily marked, with the motion of the sun and moon matched against each other.

units.la: Romulus vrbis conditor, primusque Romanorum Rex, anno decem menses attribuit, qui 304 dies effi-ciebant. Mensium ordo, & numerus dierum hic est:
units.tr: Romulus, the founder of the city and first King of the Romans, assigned ten months to the year, which made 304 days. The order of the months and the number of days is as follows:
1 March, 31 days. | 6 Sextilis, 30 days.
2 April, 30 days. | 7 September, 30 days.
3 May, 31 days. | 8 October, 31 days.
4 June, 30 days. | 9 November, 30 days.
5 Quintilis, 31 days. | 10 December, 30 days.

units.la: Id expresse testatur Censorinus, cùm ait, Annum vertentem Romæ Licinius quidem Macer & postea Fe-nestella statim ab initio duodecim mensium fuisse scri-serunt: sed magis Iunio Gracchano & Fulvio & Var-roni & Suetonio aliisq; credendum, qui decem mensium putauerunt fuisse: horum quatuor maiores pleni, cæteri sex caui vocabantur. Ex quibus verbis animaduerte-re licet, quatuor menses, scilicet Martium, Maium, Quintilem & Octobrem, plenos fuisse appellatos, quòd haberent singuli triginta vnum dies: sex verò reliquos, videlicet, Aprilem, Iunium, Sextilem, Septem-brem, Nouembrem & Decembrem, nominatos suis-se cauos, quòd constarent tantùm triginta diebus. Ex ordinatione itaq; Romuli Martius erat primus men-sis, Aprilis secundus, Maius tertius, Iunius quartus: reliqui à numero appellabantur Quintilis, Sextilis, September, October, November, December. Vbi obseruandum est, Martium incidisse in principium veris: & durasse hanc rationem mensium annos 38[?]: quot Romulus regnauit, vt testatur Aurelius Caffiodorus. Etsi autem annus lunaris tunc esset imperfe-ctus, habens 304 dies: tamen intercalatione quinquaginta & vnius dierum fuit exaequatus ad annum integrum lunarem.
units.tr: Censorinus expressly testifies to this when he says: "Licinius Macer and afterwards Fenestella wrote that the year at Rome had twelve months from the very beginning; but more credence should be given to Junius Gracchanus, Fulvius, Varro, Suetonius and others, who thought there were ten months. Of these, four were called the full months, the other six the hollow." From these words it may be noted that four months, namely March, May, Quintilis and October, were called full, because each had thirty-one days; and the six others, namely April, June, Sextilis, September, November and December, were named hollow, because they consisted of only thirty days. So in Romulus's ordering March was the first month, April the second, May the third and June the fourth; the rest were called by their numbers: Quintilis, Sextilis, September, October, November, December. Here it should be observed that March fell at the beginning of spring, and this reckoning of months lasted for as many years as Romulus reigned (38, as Aurelius Cassiodorus testifies). Although the lunar year was then imperfect, having 304 days, nevertheless by an intercalation of fifty-one days it was made equal to a full lunar year.

units.la: Numa Pompilius fecundus Romanorum Rex, ad annum Romuli adiecit vnum & quinquaginta dies (teste Censorino:) qui quia menses duos non implerent, sex illis cauis mensibus dies sunt singuli detracti, & adeos additi, faftiq; sunt dies quinquaginta septem: & ex his duo menses Ianuarius vndetriginta dierum, Februarius duodetriginta, atq; ita omnes menses pleni & impari dierum numero esse coeperunt, excepto Februario, qui solus cauus & ob hoc caeteris infauftior est habitus. Ex quibus intelligitur, calendarium Pompilii habuisse duodecim menses, qui 355 dies efficiebant. Mensium ordo & numerus dierum hic est:
units.tr: Numa Pompilius, the second King of the Romans, added fifty-one days to the year of Romulus (according to Censorinus). Since these did not fill two months, a single day was taken from each of the six hollow months and added to the others, and so fifty-seven days were made. From these, two months were formed: January of twenty-nine days and February of twenty-eight. Thus all the months began to be full and of an odd number of days, except February, which alone was hollow and for this reason was considered more unlucky than the others. From this it is understood that the calendar of Pompilius had twelve months, which made 355 days. The order of the months and the number of days is as follows:
1 January, 29 days.
2 February, 28 days.
3 March, 31 days.
4 April, 29 days.
5 May, 31 days.
6 June, 29 days.
7 Quintilis, 31 days.
8 Sextilis, 29 days.
9 September, 29 days.
10 October, 31 days.
11 November, 29 days.
12 December, 29 days.

units.la: Fuisse hanc dispositionem mensium Pompilianorum, ex citatis verbis Censorini manifestissime appa-ret. Si enim Numa in calendario Romuli, (sex cauis me-nsibus subtraxit dies singulos; vtique Aprilem, Iunium, Sextilem, Septembrem, Nouembrem & Decebrem dierum fecit viginti nouem. Diebus illis sex ad vnum & quinquaginta adiectis, expleuit Ianuarium 29, &c.
units.tr: That this arrangement of the Pompilian months existed is quite clear from the cited words of Censorinus. For if Numa, in the calendar of Romulus, took one day from each of the six hollow months, namely April, June, Sextilis, September, November and December, he made them twenty-nine days each. With those six days added to the fifty-one, he filled out January to twenty-nine, and so on.

units.la: Februarium 28 diebus costantem: in quatuor autem mensibus plenis priscum numerum dicrum[?] obseruauit, & Martio, Maio, Quintili & Octobri reliquit dies triginta vnum.
units.tr: February, consisting of twenty-eight days. But in the four full months he kept the ancient number of days, and left March, May, Quintilis and October with thirty-one days.

units.la: Posset hic aliquis quærere, quare Pompilius ad annum Romuli adiiciendos putarit vnum & quinquaginta dies? respondendum est, annum Romuli nec ad solem nec ad lunam habuisse menses dispositos, & iusto breuiore fuisse. Etsi enim intercalatione quinquaginta & vnius dierum ad motum lunarem fuerit redactus: non tamen intercalatio illa congruit ad periodum solarem, quo minus menses ab epocha sua recederent. Quamobrem ne Martius a principio veris multum dimoueretur, aut anni ab vrbe condita incertis legibus numerarentur; visum est Pompilio integram rationem anni lunaris instituere, eumque intercalatione Mercedonii ad annum solarem reuocare.
units.tr: Someone might ask here why Pompilius thought fit to add fifty-one days to the year of Romulus. The answer is that the year of Romulus had its months arranged neither by the sun nor by the moon, and was far too short. For although by an intercalation of fifty-one days it had been brought back to the motion of the moon, that intercalation did not agree with the solar period, so the months would drift from their starting point. Therefore, lest March be moved far from the beginning of spring, or the years from the founding of the city be counted by uncertain rules, Pompilius decided to establish a complete reckoning of the lunar year and to bring it back to the solar year by the intercalation of the Mercedonius.

units.la: Cum ergo dicimus Numam Pompilium anno veteri adiecisse quinquaginta & vnum dies, volumus ipsum ex 51[?] diebus intercalari solitis, duos menses ordinarios conflasse, nimirum Ianuarium & Februarium. Vt autem annus lunaris exacte responderet solari, in Februarium intercalari voluit Mercedonium, de quo paulo post plura dicemus. Numa præposuit Ianuariū & Februarium mensibus decem Romuli: hinc factum est, ut Martius, qui antea primus erat, deinceps habitus fit pro mense tertio, Aprilis pro quarto, &c. Hocipsum testatur Macrobius, cum ait, Sequitur Iulius, qui cum secundum Romuli ordinationem, Martio anni tenente principium, Quintilis a numero vocaretur: nihilominus tamen etiam post præpositos a Numa Ianuarium ac Februarium, retinuit nomen, cum non videretur iam quintum esse, sed septimus: sed postea in honorem Iulii Ca-saris faru[?] Dictatoris, legem ferente M. Antonio Marcifilio consule, Iulius appellatus est, quòd hoc mense, ad quartum Idus Quintilis Iulius procreatus fit. De eodem hęc refert Cassiodorus: Numa Pompilius regnauit annis XLI. quì duos menses anno addidit, Ianuarium & Fe-bruarium, cùm ante hunc X tantùm menses apud Romanos fuissent: Capitolium quoque à fundamentis con-struxit. Ex his apparet, annum verè lunarem, con-stantem trecentis & quinquaginta quinque diebus, à Numa Pompilio demum fuisse institutum, & hinc cœpisse kalendas, nonas, & idus mensium, quæ iuxta motum lunæ, seu iuxta novilunia & plenilunia potis-simùm dirigebantur: vt illi fallantur, qui contra histo-riarum fidem, & autoritatem viri præstantissimi Cen-sorini, Licinio Macro & Fenestellæ adstipulantur, as-serentes annum vertentem Romæ statim ab initio fundationis duodecim mensium fuisse. Scribit enim Censorinus, magis Iunio Gracchano & Fuluio & Var-roni & Suetonio aliisque credendum, qui annum à principio Vrbis conditæ decem mensium putauerunt fuisse: nisi enim res ita habuisset, frustra adiecisset Numa Pompilius Ianuarium & Februarium. Quòd autem dicunt mensem intercalarium 22 aut 23 dierum, inter terminalia & regifugium insertum, facere annum tredecim quasi mensibus constare: verum quidem est, sed non probat annos priores Romanorum ab Vrbe condita numeratos, fuisse duodecim mensium: non enim statim à fundatione vrbis locum habuit mensis intercalaris: aliàs Numa Pompilius non suis-set coactus adiicere ad annum Romuli vnum & quin-quaginta dies. Hinc etiam sequitur, festa Romana referenda esse ad ordinationem anni Pompiliani, ita-quecùm Censorinus ex sententia Varronis refert vrbem[?] conditam esse ipsis parilibus siue palilibus; accipiendum id est ex hypothesi, quatenus calendarium Pompilianum extenditur ad fundationem Romuli: alias enim sentiendum est, Romulum a fundatione vrbis suos decem menses numerasse, vt calendas Martias inchoauerit ab ipsa fundatione vrbis, hoc est a phasi lunari quae incurrit post aequinoctium vernum, vt in tabulis chronologicis ostendemus. Durauit hoc calendarium Pompilianum vsque ad Diuum Iulium Caesarem: etsi enim constaret, duodecim horum mensium lunarium periodum non attingere anni solaris quantitatem, tamen intercalatione dierum aliquot iubinde annus lunaris reducebatur ad annum vertentem solis.
units.tr: When we say, therefore, that Numa Pompilius added fifty-one days to the old year, we mean that from the fifty-one days usually intercalated he made up two ordinary months, namely January and February. In order that the lunar year should correspond exactly to the solar, he wished the Mercedonius to be intercalated into February, of which we shall say more shortly. Numa placed January and February before the ten months of Romulus; hence it came about that March, which before was first, was afterwards counted as the third month, April as the fourth, and so on. Macrobius testifies to this very thing when he says: "Julius follows, which, since under Romulus's ordering March held the beginning of the year, was called Quintilis from its number; nevertheless, even after January and February were placed before it by Numa, it kept its name, since it no longer seemed to be fifth but seventh. Afterwards, however, in honour of Julius Caesar the Dictator, when Marcus Antonius was consul and proposed a law, it was called July, because it was in this month, on the fourth day before the Ides of Quintilis, that Julius was born." Cassiodorus relates the same: "Numa Pompilius reigned forty-one years. He added two months to the year, January and February, when before him the Romans had only ten months. He also built the Capitol from the foundations." From these things it appears that the year truly lunar, consisting of 355 days, was finally instituted by Numa Pompilius, and from this the Kalends, Nones and Ides of the months began, which were directed chiefly according to the motion of the moon, that is, according to new moons and full moons. So those are mistaken who, against the testimony of the histories and the authority of the most distinguished Censorinus, side with Licinius Macer and Fenestella, asserting that the year at Rome had twelve months from the very beginning of the foundation. For Censorinus writes that more credence should be given to Junius Gracchanus, Fulvius, Varro, Suetonius and others, who thought that the year from the beginning of the founding of the city had ten months; for unless things had been so, Numa Pompilius would have added January and February in vain. As for what they say about an intercalary month of 22 or 23 days inserted between the Terminalia and the Regifugium, making the year seem to consist of thirteen months: this is true, but it does not prove that the earlier years of the Romans, counted from the founding of the city, had twelve months. For the intercalary month did not have its place from the very foundation of the city; otherwise Numa Pompilius would not have been compelled to add fifty-one days to the year of Romulus. Hence it also follows that the Roman festivals are to be referred to the arrangement of the Pompilian year. So when Censorinus, following the opinion of Varro, relates that the city was founded on the Parilia or Palilia, that must be understood hypothetically, insofar as the Pompilian calendar is extended back to the foundation by Romulus. Otherwise one must think that Romulus counted his ten months from the foundation of the city, so that the Kalends of March began from the foundation itself, that is, from the lunar phase which falls after the vernal equinox, as we shall show in the chronological tables. This Pompilian calendar lasted until the divine Julius Caesar; for although it was agreed that the twelve lunar months did not reach the quantity of the solar year, nevertheless by the intercalation of some days from time to time the lunar year was brought back to the turning solar year.

units.la: Cum autem Iulius Caesar, opera mathematicorum institutus didicisset anno lunari deesse io[?] dies, & quadrantem diei, quo minus periodo solari responderet: decem dies intrusit in menses lunares, vt Ianuario, Sextili & Decembri a fine adiiceret dies binos, quo tres menses isti, qui prius habebant 29 dies, nancisce-rentur singuli 31 dies: quatuor reliquos dies adiecit Aprili, Iunio, Septembri & Nouembri, vt haberent 30 dies, qui prius constabant duntaxat 29 diebus: ita septem mensibus concessit 31 dies: hisce autem quatuor Aprili, Iunio, Septembri & Nouembri assignauit 30 dies: in Martio, Maio, Quintili, Octobri & Februario seruauit pristinum statum, vt illi retinerent 31 dies, solus autem Februarius constaret 28 diebus, quasi inferis & diminutio & par numerus conueniret. Quamobrem ex correctione Iuliana orti sunt duodecim menses solares, complectentes 365 dies. Mensium horum Iulianorum ordo & numerus dierum hic est: 1 | Ianuarius dierum 31. 2 | Februarius d.28. 3 | Martius d.31. 4 | Aprilis d.30. 5 | Maius d.31. 6 | Iunius d.30. 7 | Quintilis d.31. 8 | Sextilis d.31. 9 | September d.30. 10 | October d.31. 11 | November d.30. 12 | December d.31.
units.tr: But when Julius Caesar, instructed by mathematicians, learned that the lunar year lacked ten days and a quarter of a day to agree with the solar period, he inserted ten days into the lunar months: by adding two days at the end of January, Sextilis and December, so that these three months, which before had 29 days, each received 31 days. He added the remaining four days to April, June, September and November, so that they had 30 days, whereas before they had only 29. Thus he granted 31 days to seven months, and assigned 30 days to these four, April, June, September and November. In March, May, Quintilis, October and February he kept the former state, so that those retained 31 days, while February alone consisted of 28 days, as if diminution and an even number were suited to the gods below. Hence from the Julian correction there arose twelve solar months, comprising 365 days. The order of these Julian months and their number of days is as follows: 1 January, 31 days. 2 February, 28 days. 3 March, 31 days. 4 April, 30 days. 5 May, 31 days. 6 June, 30 days. 7 Quintilis, 31 days. 8 Sextilis, 31 days. 9 September, 30 days. 10 October, 31 days. 11 November, 30 days. 12 December, 31 days.

units.la: Fuisse hanc mensium Iulianorum ordinationem, perspicuè docet Censorinus hisce verbis: Nam intercalario mensè sublato, Casar annum eundem ad solis cursum formauit: itaq; diebus trecentis quinquaginta quin-que addidit decem, quos per septem menses, qui dies vn-detricenos habebant, ita distribuit, vt Ianuario & Sextili & Decembri bini accederent, caeterisque singuli: eosq; dies extremis partibus mensium appositi, ne scilicet religiones sui cuiusque mensis a loco summouerentur. Id nō minus clarè testatur Macrobius lib. 1. Saturnalium, cap. 14 cum ait, Dies autem X, quos ab eo additos diximus, hac ordinatione distribuit: in Ianuarium & Sextilem & Decembrem binos dies inseruit. In Aprilem autem, Iunium, Septembrem, Nouembrem singulos. Sed neq; mensi[?] Februario addidit diem, ne Deo infero religio mutaretur: & Martio, Maio, Quintili, Octobri seruauit prisi-num satum[?] quod satis pleno erat numero, id est, dierum singulorum tricenorum q;.
units.tr: That this was the arrangement of the Julian months is plainly taught by Censorinus in these words: For the intercalary month having been abolished, Caesar fixed the year to the course of the sun. So he added ten days to the 365 days and distributed them over seven months, which had thirty-one days each, so that January, Sextilis and December each received two, and the others one each. These days were placed at the ends of the months, so that the observances of each month should not be moved from their place. Macrobius bears witness no less clearly in book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 14, when he says: He distributed the ten days which we said he added in this order. He put two days into January, Sextilis and December, and one each into April, June, September and November. But he did not add a day to February, so that the religious rites of the gods below should not be changed; and he kept the original arrangement for March, May, Quintilis and October, which already had the full number of thirty days each.

units.la: Hinc intelligitur, mensem Sextilem in primo statim ordinationis Iulianae anno habuisse 31 dies, & Februarium constitisse 28 diebus: vt illi fallantur, qui scripserunt, Sextilem habuisse 30 dies, & Februarium 29 dies, quasi anno demum Iuliano tricesimo septi-mo, quo mensis Sextilis in honorem Augusti, dictus est Augustus, fuerit detractus Februario dies, & appositus ad mensem Augustum. Si historias consulamus, inveniemus quidem in calendario Romuli Sextilem habuisse triginta dies: sed Februario a Numa Pōpilio primum fuisse assignatos 18 dies, & hos deinceps fuisse constanter seruatos comperiemus. Faliam[?] autem & absurdam esse hanc opinionem, ostendet in calendario Ægyptiaco Thoth Actiacus, qui anno Iuliano decimo texto incidit in 29[?] Sextilis, feriam primam, quæ erat dies quartus kal. Septembrium. Sed quis erat ille mensis intercalarius, quem Cæsar sustu-lit? Macrobius sanè cum Cesorino testatur, cum suis-se viginti duum vel viginti trium dierum: hic Plutarcho [illegible, ~8 letters] & [illegible, ~8 letters] dicitur, Latinis appellatur Februarius intercalaris. Huiusmodi Mercedonio ute-bantur Romani ante Iulium Cæsarem, ut per eum annos suos lunares aptaret ad solis cursum, qui 365 diebus & quadrante zodiacum conficit. Etsi autem annus lunaris haberet trecentos & quinquaginta quinque dies: ipsi tamen Romani censebant lunam duodecim suis mensibus trecetos quinquaginta quatuor dies explere, ideo excessum anni unius solaris supra lunarem constituebant undecim dierum, qui spacio biennii excrescebat ad 11 dies, & suppeditabat quantitatem mensis intercalarii. Verisimile itaque est, Romanos exacto uno biennio intercalasse 22 dies, altero autem biennio elapso intercalasse 23 dies: siquidem quadriennii circuitu peracto dies una accedebat anno solari. Hæc ratio intercalandi cum sæpius intermitteretur, & ob odium vel gratiam, (quo quis magistratu citius abiret diutiusve fungeretur, aut publici redemptor ex anni magnitudine in lucro damnove esset) multis modis depravaretur: Cæsar mensem Mercedonium, cum omnibus veterum intercalationibus sustulit, menses lunares abrogauit, & pro illis solares substituit, nouumq; modum intercalandi inuenit, ut scilicet pro quadrante diei, qui mensibus folaribus deerat, quarto quoque anno in Februarium dies insereretur: hinc prodiit cyclus bisextorum, vt annis tribus continuis numerarentur 365 dies: quartus autem quisque annus haberet 366 dies.
units.tr: From this it is understood that the month Sextilis had 31 days in the very first year of the Julian reform, and that February consisted of 28 days. Those are mistaken who have written that Sextilis had 30 days and February 29, as if only in the thirty-seventh Julian year, when Sextilis was named Augustus in honour of Augustus, was a day taken from February and added to the month of August. If we consult the histories, we shall indeed find that in the calendar of Romulus Sextilis had thirty days, but that under Numa Pompilius February was assigned 18 days, and that these were afterwards consistently observed. That this opinion is false and absurd is shown by the Egyptian calendar, in which Thoth Actiacus, in the tenth Julian year, fell on the 29th of Sextilis, the first feria, which was the fourth day before the Kalends of September. But what was that intercalary month which Caesar abolished? Macrobius, indeed, together with Censorinus, testifies that it had twenty-two or twenty-three days. Plutarch [illegible, ~8 letters] and [illegible, ~8 letters] call it Mercedonius; by the Latins it is called the intercalary February. The Romans before Julius Caesar used this month, so that by means of it they might fit their lunar years to the course of the sun, which completes the zodiac in 365 days and a quarter. Although the lunar year had 355 days, the Romans themselves reckoned that the moon completed twelve of its months in 354 days; therefore they reckoned the excess of one solar year over a lunar year as eleven days, which, over the span of two years, grew to 22 days and supplied the length of the intercalary month. It is therefore likely that the Romans, after one two-year period had passed, intercalated 22 days, and after the other two-year period had passed, intercalated 23 days, since when the cycle of four years was completed one day was added to the solar year. This method of intercalation, since it was often omitted, and was distorted in many ways through hatred or favour (so that someone might leave office sooner or hold it longer, or so that a contractor for public revenue might gain or lose according to the length of the year), was abolished by Caesar, together with all the old intercalations. He abolished the lunar months, including Mercedonius, and substituted solar months for them. He devised a new method of intercalation, namely that, to make up for the quarter day which was lacking in the solar months, one day should be inserted into February every fourth year. Hence arose the cycle of bissextile years: three consecutive years were to count 365 days, and every fourth year 366 days.

units.la: Hoc modo Iulius Cæsar decem dies obseruationi vete-ri superadiecit, vt annum trecenti & sexaginta quinque dies, quibus sol lustrat zodiacum, efficerent. Et ne quadrans deesset, statuit, vt quarto quoque anno sacerdotes qui curabant, mensibus ac diebus vnum intercalarent diem, eo scilicet mense ac loco, quo etiam apud veteres mensis intercalabatur, id est, ante quinque vltimos Februarii mensis dies: idq; bisextum censuit nominandum, teste Macrobio. De intercalatione Iuliana idem scribit Censorinus, hisce verbis: Praeterea pro quadrante diei, qui annum verum suppleturus videbatur, instituit vt perasto quadriennii circuitu, dies vnus, vbi mensis quondam solebat, post terminalia intercalaretur, quod nunc bisextum vocatur.
units.tr: In this way Julius Caesar added ten days to the old observance, so that the year would have 365 days, in which the sun traverses the zodiac. And so that the quarter day should not be lacking, he decided that every fourth year the priests who had charge of these matters should intercalate one day, in the same month and place where the intercalary month had formerly been inserted, that is, before the last five days of the month of February; and he decided that this day should be called the bissextile. So Macrobius testifies. Censorinus writes the same about the Julian intercalation, in these words: Moreover, in place of the quarter day, which seemed to be needed to complete the true year, he established that when the four-year cycle was complete, one day should be intercalated after the Terminalia, where the month once used to be, and this is now called the bissextile.

units.la: Porrò in calendario Iuliano duplex est obseruan-dum principium: vnum est totius anni, alterum intercalationis. Dum enim Iulius Cæsar annorum suorum initium sumsit à Ianuario; secutus est ordinem mensium veterum, qui à Numa Pompilio fuerat introductus, &annis fere septingentis vsurpatus: quando vero post peractum quadriennium diem vnum intercalari voluit; respexit principium mensium in calendario Romuli designatorū, vt à Martio quadrien-nii circuitum iusserit numerari: nam ante Martium proprius erat intercalationis locus, quem etiam Cæ-sar sibi obseruandum esse putauit. Cum igitur ante principium mensis Martii, in anno confusionis, inter terminalia & regifugium intercalatum esset; voluit Cæsar vt anno quarto Iuliano currente, post vigesimum & tertium diem Februarii,terminalibus scilicet iam peractis, bilextum intercalaretur: quia a veteri intercalatione ad id tempus elapsum erat integrum quadriennium. Verum sacerdotes non recte mentem[?] Cæsaris perceperunt,& anno quarto a veteri interca-latione non peracto, sed incipiente, hoc est anno labente tertio Iuliano,inter 23 & 24 Februarii diem bi-sextum intercalarunt, quod deinceps pluribus erroribus causam præbuit.
units.tr: Furthermore, in the Julian calendar two beginnings must be observed: one of the whole year and the other of the intercalation. For while Julius Caesar began his years from January, he followed the order of the old months, which had been introduced by Numa Pompilius and had been in use for nearly seven hundred years. But when he wished to intercalate one day after the four-year period had been completed, he looked to the beginning of the months as set out in the calendar of Romulus, so that he ordered the four-year cycle to be counted from March. For before March was the proper place of intercalation, which Caesar also thought should be observed. Therefore, since the intercalation had been placed before the beginning of the month of March, in the year of confusion, between the Terminalia and the Regifugium, Caesar wished that in the fourth Julian year, after the twenty-third day of February, when the Terminalia had already been celebrated, the bissextile should be intercalated, because a full four years had passed since the old intercalation up to that time. But the priests did not rightly grasp Caesar's intention. And so, when the fourth year from the old intercalation had not been completed but was just beginning, that is, in the third Julian year as it was ending, they intercalated the bissextile day between the 23rd and 24th of February. This afterwards gave rise to many errors.

units.la: Hic autem operæprecium est cösiderare in quem annum ab vrbe condita, ab initio Olympiadum, & à regno Nabonafari inciderit annus primus Iulianus: & quæ deinceps fuerit annorum Iulianorum ratio vf-que ad emendationem Augusti Octauiani. Annus qui præcessit emendationem Iulianam, telte Sueto-nio habuit menses quindecim: in eum enim incidit Mercedonius 23 dierum , & Cæsar alios duos menses intercalarios dierum sexaginta septem inter Nouembrem & Decembrem interposuit, telte Censorino: quare annus iste tres menses intercalarios habuit, qui effecerunt nonaginta dies, qui adiecti ad annum communem lunarem, constantem 355 diebus, summam gignunt quadringentorum quadra-ginta quinque dierum. Hunc annum confusionis vocat Macrobius, quod in eo Cæsar exordium nouæ ordinationis inituros, dies omnes, qui confusionem adhuc poterant facere, confumferit. Cum enim propter neglectam aut per imprudentiam factam intercalationem menses lunares a priscis sedibus multum recessissent, & in anteriora fuissent nimis prolapsi: Cæsar coactus est præter ordinariam Mercedonii in-tercalationem, quæ tunc forte incidit, insuper sexaginta septem diebus anno lunari inferere: hisce diebus 67[?] intercalariis locum assignauit inter Nouembrem & Decembrem, quo scilicet retraheretur Mercedo-nius cum Martio & reliquis mensibus ad sedem antiquam: unde postea calendarii fixi solaris, & intercalationis Iulianæ initium sumeretur. Fuit hic annus confusionis tertius consulatus Cæsaris, M. Æmylio collega: de quo eleganter hæc scribit Censorinus, Adeoque aberratum est, vt C. Cæsar Pontifex Maximus suo III, & M. Æmylii Lepidi consulatu, quo retro delictum corrigeret, duos menses intercalarios dierum sexaginta septem in menses Nouem-brem & Decembrem interponeret, cum iam mense Februario dies tres & vigintí intercalasset: faceretq; eum annum dierum quadringentorum quadraginta quin-que, simul prouidens in futurum ne iterum erraretur. nam intercalario mense sublato annum ciuilem ad solis cursum formaunt, &c.
units.tr: Here it is worth considering in which year from the founding of the city, from the beginning of the Olympiads, and from the reign of Nabonassar the first Julian year fell, and what the method of the Julian years was after that, down to the reform of Augustus Octavian. According to Suetonius, the year which preceded the Julian reform had fifteen months. For into it fell Mercedonius of 23 days, and Caesar interposed two other intercalary months of sixty-seven days in all between November and December, according to Censorinus. Therefore that year had three intercalary months, which made ninety days. Added to the common lunar year, which consists of 355 days, these make a total of 445 days. Macrobius calls this the year of confusion, because in it Caesar, about to begin the new arrangement, consumed all the days which could still cause confusion. For since, through neglect or carelessness in intercalation, the lunar months had strayed far from their former places and had slipped too far forward, Caesar was compelled, beyond the ordinary Mercedonian intercalation which happened to fall then, to insert sixty-seven days into the lunar year. He assigned these intercalary days a place between November and December, so that Mercedonius, together with March and the remaining months, might be drawn back to its old position, whence afterwards the beginning of the fixed solar calendar and of the Julian intercalation was to be taken. This year of confusion was the third consulship of Caesar, with Marcus Aemilius as colleague. Censorinus writes elegantly about it: There was so great an error that Gaius Caesar, Pontifex Maximus, in his third consulship and that of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, in order to correct the past error, interposed two intercalary months of sixty-seven days between November and December, although he had already intercalated twenty-three days in February; and he made that year 445 days long, at the same time providing for the future so that the error would not occur again. For, the intercalary month having been abolished, they fixed the civil year to the course of the sun, and so on.

units.la: Hunc secutus est annus primus Iulianus, qui sim-plex fuit, sine intercalari die, constans 365 diebus: vt merito[?] explodendi sint illi, qui annum primum Iulianum intercalarem statuunt fuisse. Cum enim annus confusionis non tantum Mercedonium ordi-narium, verum etiam duos extraordinarios admisi-set menses intercalarios; voluit Cæsar vt annus pro-ximus solaris cum reliquis duobus sequentibus, sim-plex esset, quartus autem ordine acciperet nouum bisextum, quod ille veteri intercalationi substitue-rat. Vt autem ita fieret, etiam res ipsa postulabat: nam Cæsar in anno confusionis intercalationem or-dinariam reuocauerat ad locum illum, qui illi ratio-ne conuersionis cœlestis competebat, ita vt prin-cipium Martii incideret in nouilunium, & reliqui nouem menses lunares prisco more neomenias cœ-lestes indicarent: itaque voluit cyclum bisextilem inire mense Februario, ipso anno confusionis, inter terminalia & regifugium, hoc est, inter 23 & 24 Februarii diem, vt Macrobius interpretatur: quo deinceps elapsis decem mensibus lunaribus, inchoaret annum suum solarem, à Ianuario in ipsam quoque neomeniam cœlestem incidente. Cum ergo à veteri intercalatione quadriennium nondum esset elapsum, nequaquam anno primo Iuliano fieri debuit intercalatio. Hic annus primus Iulianus, fuit quartus consulatus Cæsaris, vt ex Censorino animaduertere licet, cum ait, Ex hoc anno ita a Julio Cæsare ordinato cæteri ad nostram memoriam Iuliani appellantur, eiq; confur-gunt ex IIII Cæsaris consulatu. Scribit autem idem Censorinus in annum ducentesimum octogesimum tertium Iulianum incidisse annum ab vrbe condita nongentesimum nonagesimum primum, annum Olympiadicum millesimum & quartum decimum, & annum Nabonasari nongentesimum octogesimum sextum, vnde consequitur in annum primum Iulianum incidisse annum à Roma condita 709, annum Olympiadicum 732, & annum Nabonasari 704, vt annus primus Iulianus à nouo sole, id est, à bruma: annus à Roma condita 709 ab ortu proximè sequenti vergiliarum; annus Olympiadicus 732 ex diebus duntaxat æstiuis, annus autem Nabonasari 704 circa æquinoctium autumnale in anno primo Iuliano cœpisse intelligatur. Quamobrem datis annis Iulianis, facile est inuenire annos ab vrbe condita, & Olympiadicos. Si enim ad datos annos Iulianos labentes adiiciantur anni 708 ab vrbe condita elapsi, vel si adiiciantur anni 731 à prima Olympiade absoluti, habetur tur quaesitum. Sed in annis Nabonasari indagadis res paulo aliter habet: nam ad datos annos Iulianos la- bentes adiiciendi sunt anni Nabonasari 703 comple- ti, donec peruenia tur[?] ad annum Iulianum 985: qui cum habeat geminum Thoth, duobus quoque prin- cipiis annorum Ægyptiacorum respondet, vt necesse sit anno subsequenti Iuliano 986 labenti dato adiice- re annos Nabonasari completos 704: quia in istum annum Iulianum 986 incidit principium anni Na- bonasari 1690: vt suo loco ostendetur. Si ergo anni aliqui Iuliani dentur, qui sunt post annum Iulianum 985; tunc oportet adeos adiicere completos annos Nabonasari 704: alioquin vnius anni error contin- ger.
units.tr: This was followed by the first Julian year, which was a simple year, without an intercalary day, consisting of 365 days. So those are rightly refuted who hold that the first Julian year was an intercalary year. For since the year of confusion had admitted not only the ordinary Mercedonian month but also two extraordinary intercalary months, Caesar wished that the next solar year and the two following ones should be simple, and that the fourth year in order should receive a new bissextile, which he had put in place of the old intercalation. For this to happen, the matter itself also required it. For in the year of confusion Caesar had brought the ordinary intercalation back to the place that was appropriate to it by the rule of the heavenly revolution, so that the beginning of March fell on the new moon, and the remaining nine lunar months, according to the ancient custom, marked the new moons by the heavens. Accordingly, he wished the bissextile cycle to begin in the month of February of the very year of confusion, between the Terminalia and the Regifugium, that is, between the 23rd and 24th of February, as Macrobius explains. Then, after ten lunar months had elapsed, the solar year was to begin from January, falling on the new moon of the heavens itself. Since, therefore, four years had not yet elapsed since the old intercalation, intercalation certainly ought not to have been made in the first Julian year. This first Julian year was the fourth consulship of Caesar, as we may gather from Censorinus when he says: From this year, so ordered by Julius Caesar, the rest down to our memory are called Julian, and they are reckoned from the fourth consulship of Caesar. Censorinus also writes that the year 983 after Julian... [the year] 293 Julian fell in the 991st year from the founding of the city, the 1014th year of the Olympiads, and the 986th year of Nabonassar. From this it follows that the first Julian year fell in the year 709 from the founding of Rome, the Olympiad year 732, and the Nabonassar year 704. The first Julian year began from the new sun, that is, from the winter solstice; the year 709 from the foundation of Rome began from the rising of the Pleiades next following; the Olympiad year 732 began from the summer days alone; and the Nabonassar year 704 is understood to have begun in the first Julian year around the autumn equinox. Therefore, given Julian years, it is easy to find the years from the founding of the city and the Olympiad years. For if the elapsed Julian years are added to the 708 years from the founding of the city that have passed, or if the 731 years completed from the first Olympiad are added, the sought result is obtained. But in finding the years of Nabonassar the matter is somewhat different. For to the given elapsed Julian years must be added the 703 completed years of Nabonassar, until one arrives at the Julian year 985. Since this year has a double Thoth, it corresponds to two beginnings of the Egyptian years; so it is necessary, for the subsequent Julian year 986 which is running, to add to the given year the 704 completed years of Nabonassar, because the beginning of the 1690th year of Nabonassar falls in this Julian year 986, as will be shown in its place. Therefore, if any Julian years are given which are after the Julian year 985, then one must add to them the 704 completed years of Nabonassar; otherwise an error of one year will arise.

units.la: In annum fecundum Iulianum, qui fuit quintus consulatus Caesaris, M. Antonio collega, teste Censorino, incidit annus a Roma condita septingentesimus decimus. eodem anno secundo Iuliano, Idibus Martii interemtus est Iulius Caesar in senatu, cum iam per integrum annum, duos menses, & quatuordecim dies in usu fuisset calendarium Iulianum. At hic dissentiunt autores, vt incertum videatur esse, an caedes Caesaris referenda sit ad annum vrbis conditae septingentesimo nono, vt communis fert opinio: vel ad annum V.C. septingentesimum decimum, vt fasti marmorei Romae effossi indicant: sicut ex antiquitatibus Romanis Onufrius Panuinius ostendit Iulium Caesarem interfectum esse anno V.C. 710, quando fuit dictator IIII. & Cos. V. Sane dubium non est, quin annus vrbis conditae septingentesimus decimus inciderit in annum fecundum Iulianum: hoc enim e Censorino manifestissime colligitur: sed non semper idem initium fuit computatum ab vrbe condita. De sententia Varronis & Cenforini vrbs condita est ipsis Parilibus,hoc est XI kal. Maii: quamobrem fi annorum vrbis conditæ principium inde fumamus, non potuit cædes Cæsaris incidere in annum V.C. 710: sed incidit sub finem anni ab vrbe condita septingentesimi noni, vt opinio vulgaris est accipienda. Si autem à calendis Martiis Romuli, initium annorum vrbis conditæ numeremus, sicut illustres quidam autores Romani fecerunt; tùc cædes Cæsaris incidet in principium anni ab vrbe condita septingentesimi decimi: neque absurdum est, vt vnus idemque locus diuerso respectu habeat rationem principii & finis.
units.tr: In the second Julian year, which was the fifth consulship of Caesar with Marcus Antonius as colleague, according to Censorinus, fell the 710th year from the founding of Rome. In that same second Julian year, on the Ides of March, Julius Caesar was killed in the senate, when the Julian calendar had already been in use for a full year, two months and fourteen days. But authors disagree here, so that it seems uncertain whether Caesar's murder should be referred to the 709th year from the founding of the city, as the common opinion holds, or to the 710th year from the founding (V.C.), as the marble Fasti excavated at Rome indicate. As Onufrius Panvinius shows from Roman antiquities, Julius Caesar was killed in the year 710 A.U.C., when he was dictator for the fourth time and consul for the fifth. Certainly there is no doubt that the 710th year from the founding of Rome fell in the second Julian year; this is most clearly gathered from Censorinus. But the starting point for counting from the founding of the city has not always been the same. According to the view of Varro and Censorinus, the city was founded on the Parilia itself, that is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Therefore, if we take the beginning of the years from the founding of the city in that way, Caesar's murder could not have fallen in the year 710 A.U.C.; it falls near the end of the 709th year from the founding, as the common opinion is to be accepted. But if we count the beginning of the years from the Kalends of March under Romulus, as certain distinguished Roman authors did, then Caesar's murder falls at the beginning of the 710th year from the founding of the city. Nor is it absurd that one and the same time should have the character of an end from one point of view and of a beginning from another.

units.la: In annum tertium Iulianum incidit annus à Roma condita 711, qui ex ordinatione Diui Iulii Cæsaris debuit esse simplex: sed sacerdotes bisextum in eum intruferunt, & deinceps vsque ad annum Iulianum trigesimum septimum, singulis trienniis elapsis intercalarunt: hinc factum est, vt per triginta sex priores annos Iulianos duodecies fit intercalatum, cum ex instituto Cæsaris nouenæ tantum fuissent intercalationes celebrandæ. Testatur id Macrobius lib.1. Saturnalium,cap.14 cum ait, Et huc vsque error stare potuisset, nisi sacerdotes sibi errorem nouum ex ipsa emendatione fecissent. Nam cum oporteret diem, qui ex quadrātibus confit, quarto quoque anno confecto, antequam quintus inciperet, intercalare: illi quarto non perafto, sed incipiente intercalabant. Hic error sex & tringinta annis permansit, quibus annis intercalati sunt dies duodecim, cum debuerint intercalari nouem. Sed hunc quoque errorem fero deprehensum correxit Augustus, qui annos duodecim fine intercalari die trafigi iussit, vt illi tres dies, qui per annos tringinta & sex vitio sacerdotalis festinationis excreuerant, sequentibus annis duodecim, nullo die intercalato, deuorarentur. Post hoc unū diem, secundum ordinationem (asaris[?] quinto quoque incipiente anno, intercalari iussit, & omnem hunc ordinem area ta-bulæ ad æternam custodiam incisione mandauit. Idem affirmat Solinus dicens: Et tunc quoque vitium admissum est per sacerdotes. Nam cum præceptum esset anno quarto vt intercalarent vnum diem: & oporteret confecto anno quarto id obseruari antequam quintus auspi-caretur: illi incipiente quarto intercalarunt, nō definen-te. Sic per annos sex & triginta, cum nouem tantum dies sufficere debuissent, duodecim iunt intercalati. Quod deprehensum Augustus reformauit: iussitque annos 12 sine intercalatione decurrere: vt tres illi dies, qui ultra nouem necessarios, temere fuerant intercalati: hoc modo possent repensari: ex qua disciplina omnium postea temporum fundata ratio est.
units.tr: Into the third Julian year falls the year 711 from the founding of Rome, which by the ordinance of the divine Julius Caesar ought to have been a common year. But the priests inserted a leap year into it, and thereafter, up to the thirty-seventh Julian year, they intercalated at every three-year interval. Hence it happened that during the first thirty-six Julian years the intercalation was made twelve times, whereas by Caesar's arrangement only nine intercalations were to be celebrated. Macrobius attests this in Saturnalia 1.14, when he says: And up to this point the error could have stood, unless the priests had made a new error for themselves out of the correction itself. For when the day made up of quarter-days was to be intercalated, after the fourth year had been completed and before the fifth began, they instead intercalated in the fourth year not when it had ended but when it was beginning. This error persisted for thirty-six years, in which twelve days were intercalated when nine should have been. But this error too, as I report, was detected and corrected by Augustus, who ordered that twelve years pass without an intercalary day, so that those three days which had grown up through the priests' hasty error over thirty-six years might be consumed in the following twelve years, with no day intercalated. After this, according to Caesar's ordinance, he ordered one day to be intercalated at the beginning of every fifth year, and had this whole arrangement engraved on a bronze tablet for eternal keeping. Solinus affirms the same, saying: And then a fault was also committed through the priests. For when it had been ordered that they intercalate one day in the fourth year, and it was to be observed after the fourth year had been completed and before the fifth began, they intercalated at the beginning of the fourth, not at its end. So through thirty-six years, when only nine days should have sufficed, twelve were intercalated. This, once detected, Augustus reformed, ordering the years to run for twelve years without intercalation, so that those three days which had been rashly intercalated beyond the nine necessary could be made up in this way. From this discipline the reckoning of all later times is founded.

units.la: Ex his omnibus apparet annum quinquagesimum secundum Iulianum accepisse bisextum emendatum, secundum ordinationem Cæsaris, quam Augustus Octauianus censuit reuocandam esse. Cum enim Diuus Iulius Cæsar instituisset, vt anno quarto, octauo, duodecimo &c. labere Iuliano intercalaretur: rectissime fecit Augustus, qui in annum 52[?] Iulianum labentem, bisextum immisit: siquidem anni quique quaterni Iuliani intercalares esse debuerunt.
units.tr: From all these things it appears that the fifty-second Julian year received the leap year corrected according to Caesar's ordinance, which Augustus Octavian judged should be restored. For when the divine Julius Caesar had established that intercalation should take place in the fourth, eighth, twelfth and so on Julian year, Augustus acted quite rightly in inserting a leap year into the falling fifty-second Julian year, since every fourth Julian year was to be intercalary.

units.la: Vt autem integram dispositionem annorum 52[?] priorum Iulianorum habeamus: prorsus necessarium est, vt distinctionem feriarum hebdomadicarum adhibeamus, & quibus diebus septimanæ singuli anni inceperint, consideremus. Sane apud Romanos nulla tunc erat distinctio temporis in hebdomades dierum: ea tamen apud Babylonios & Ægyptios statim a regno Nabonasarii in usu fuit, cum septem planetarum nominibus dies septimanæ appellarentur. Proinde si unius anni Nabonasari, qui in hos § [?] 1 annos Julianos incidit, characterem hebdomadicum noscamus, eumq; cum certo die mensis alicuius Juliani conferamus: statim innotescent reliquorum annorum feriæ. Ad hoc autem maxime accommodatus est, Thoth Nabonasari 719, qui juxta Censorinum incidit in annum Julianum decimum sextum: & in diem 19 Sextilis, hoc est, in quartum kal. Septembris, coepitque die solis, ut testatur Hebræus quidam in scripto de æris & interuallis temporum. Is Thoth est Augusti Octaviani Actiacus, à quo Ptolemæus [?] deducit monarchiam Augusti.
units.tr: So that we may have the complete arrangement of the first fifty-two Julian years, it is absolutely necessary that we apply the division into weekly feast-days and consider on which days of the week each year began. Indeed among the Romans there was then no division of time into weeks; yet among the Babylonians and Egyptians it was in use from the reign of Nabonassar onward, when the days of the week were named after the seven planets. Therefore, if we learn the weekly character of one year of Nabonassar, which falls into these § 1 Julian years, and compare it with a certain day of some Julian month, the feriae of the remaining years will at once become known. Thoth of Nabonassar 719 is especially suited to this; according to Censorinus it falls in the sixteenth Julian year, on the 19th day of Sextilis, that is on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and it began on a Sunday, as a certain Hebrew testifies in his writing on the eras and intervals of time. This Thoth is the Actian one of Augustus Octavian, from which Ptolemy dates the monarchy of Augustus.

units.la: Si ergo septem literas hebdomadicas distribuamus in contextum calendarii Juliani, ut prima dies Januarii habeat A. secunda B. tertia C. quarta D. quinta E. sexta F. septima G. octava iterum A. nona iterum B. &c. sicut solet fieri in computo ecclesiastico: tunc ex ordine litera C incidet in 19 mensis Sextilis, cumque is dies fuerit solis, litera C dicitur character Dominicus anni prædicti 16 Juliani: quamobrem etiam tertia dies Januarii eiusdem anni, quæ obtinet literam C. est feria Dominica sive solaris: unde sequitur calendas Januarias anni decimi sexti Juliani, in quas incidit littera A. coepisse die Veneris. Huius anni 16 Juliani inventa dispositione, si retrorsum & antrorsum numeremus, per idem examen hebdomadicum deprehendemus annum primum Julianum coepisse die sabbati: annum vero 51 [?] Julianum, qui accepit bisextum Augustale, etiam coepisse die sabbati, & propter intercalationem bisextum geminas habuisse literas Dominicales B A. quin etiam apparebit quæ fuerit ratio intercalationum & feriarum, ipsorumque characterum Domi-
units.tr: If, then, we distribute the seven weekday letters through the text of the Julian calendar, so that the first day of January has A, the second B, the third C, the fourth D, the fifth E, the sixth F, the seventh G, the eighth again A, the ninth again B, and so on, as is usually done in ecclesiastical computation, then by this order the letter C falls on the 19th of Sextilis. Since that day was a Sunday, the letter C is called the Dominical letter of the aforesaid sixteenth Julian year. Wherefore also the third day of January of that same year, which has the letter C, is a Sunday, or solar day. Whence it follows that the Kalends of January of the sixteenth Julian year, on which the letter A fell, began on a Friday. Having found this arrangement for the sixteenth Julian year, if we count backwards and forwards, we shall by the same weekly test discover that the first Julian year began on a Saturday, and that the fifty-first Julian year, which received the Augustan leap year, also began on a Saturday, and because of the intercalation had two Dominical letters, B and A. Indeed it will also appear what the reason was for the intercalations and the feriae, and for their Dominical characters.
