units.la: Vt autem perfecte intelligamus ordinationem Iulianam, sciendum est Cæsarem in quatuor mensibus, scilicet Martio, Maio, Quintili & Octobri vsurpasse sex nonas, in reliquis quatuor. Præterea Cæsar in singulos menses distribuit octo idus: reliquos dies numero kalendarum designauit.
units.tr: To understand the Julian arrangement perfectly, it must be noted that Caesar used six Nones in four months, namely March, May, Quintilis and October, and four in the remaining months. Moreover, Caesar assigned eight Ides to each month, and he designated the remaining days by counting back from the Kalends.

units.la: Ex duodecim mensibus Iulianis, teste Censorino, duorum tantum nomina sunt immutata. nam qui Quintilisfuit, Iulius cognominatus est, C.Cæsare V. & M. [?]Antonio C o s s. anno Iuliano secundo. (post mortem Cæsaris.) Qui autem Sextilis fuerat, ex S.C. M.Cenforino, & C.Afinio Gallo Coss. in Augusti honorem distus est Augustus anno Augustano XX. qua nomina etiam nunc ad hanc permanent memoriam. Idem testatur Macrobius de Iulio, ut supra retulimus: quin immo lib.1. Saturnalium cap.12 de Augusto hæc scribit, Augustus deinde est, qui Sextilis antea vocabatur, donec honori Augusti daretur ex senatus consulto, cuius verba subieci: Cum imperator Cæsar Augustus mense Sextili, & primum consulatum inierit, & triumphos tres in urbem intulerit, & ex Ianiculo legiones deductæ sint, eius auspicia ac fidem, & Ægyptus hoc mense in potestatem populi Romani redacta sit, finisq; hoc mense bellis civilibus impositus sit, atq; ob has causas hic mensis huic imperio felicissimum sit ac fuerit, placere senatui, ut mensis Augustus appelletur. In quibus verbis tria scitu dignissima notantur. I. Octavianum Cæsarem primum consulatum iniisse mense Sextili, anno scilicet tertio Iuliano: quamvis alii scribant id factum fuisse XIIII. [?] kal. Septembris. II. Ægyptum redactam esse in potestatem populi Romani mense Sextili, anno scilicet Iuliano decimo sexto, die 29 mensis Sextilis, in qua inciderat Thoth Nabonasari 719: qui dicitur Thoth Actiacus, seu Thoth monarchiæ Augusti: a quo deinceps annos Augustales Ægyptii cœperunt numerare. III. Octavianum Cæsarem fuisse appellatum Augustum, postquam de Epiro, Alexandria, & Hispania victa triumphos tres in urbem intulisset: hoc autem biennio accidit, post Actiacam Augusti victoriam, ut Censorinus scribit. Quamobrem triumphus Augustalis, in quo Cæsar Octavianus est appellatus Augustus, apud Romanos celebratus est sub initium anni decimi octavi Iuliani, vt etiam prius ostendimus.
units.tr: Of the twelve Julian months, according to Censorinus, only two names have been changed. For the month that was Quintilis was surnamed Julius, in the consulship of C. Caesar (for the fifth time) and M. [?] Antonius, in the second Julian year. (After the death of Caesar.) But the month that had been Sextilis was named Augustus by decree of the Senate, in honour of Augustus, in the consulship of M. Censorinus and C. Asinius Gallus, in the twentieth Augustan year. These names also remain in memory to this day. Macrobius likewise testifies about Julius, as we related above; indeed, in Saturnalia 1, chapter 12, he writes this about Augustus: Augustus is the name of the month that was formerly called Sextilis, until it was given in honour of Augustus by decree of the Senate. I have appended the words: "Since the emperor Caesar Augustus both entered his first consulship in the month of Sextilis and brought three triumphs into the city, and the legions were led down from the Janiculum, and his auspices and good faith, and Egypt was brought into the power of the Roman people in this month, and an end was put to the civil wars in this month, and for these reasons this month has been and was most fortunate for this empire, the Senate resolves that the month be called Augustus." In these words three most noteworthy points are marked. I. Octavian Caesar entered his first consulship in the month of Sextilis, in the third Julian year, although others write that this happened on the fourteenth(?) day before the Kalends of September. II. Egypt was brought into the power of the Roman people in the month of Sextilis, in the sixteenth Julian year, on the 29th day of Sextilis, the day on which Thoth of Nabonassar 719 fell. This is called Thoth Actiacus, or Thoth of the monarchy of Augustus, and from it the Egyptians began to count the Augustan years. III. Octavian Caesar was called Augustus after he had brought back three triumphs into the city, won over Epirus, Alexandria and Spain; this happened in the second year after Augustus's victory at Actium, as Censorinus writes. Therefore the Augustan triumph, in which Octavian Caesar was called Augustus, was celebrated among the Romans at the beginning of the eighteenth Julian year, as we showed earlier.
On the Egyptian Calendar.

units.la: Calendarium Ægyptiacum duplex est, retse Alfragano: vnum est antiquum, in quo à Nabonasaro per annos æquabiles tempora supputantur: alterum nouum est, in quo ab æra Diocletiani per annos Iulianos tempora numerantur. Nos autem de antiquo Ægyptiorum calędario hic dicemus, alterius tractationem reiecturi in tabulas chronologicas, ad annum Christi 184.
units.tr: There are two Egyptian calendars, as Alfraganus rightly says. The first is the ancient one, in which times are reckoned from Nabonassar by equal years. The second is the newer one, in which times are counted from the era of Diocletian by Julian years. I shall speak here of the ancient Egyptian calendar, and reserve treatment of the other for the chronological tables, down to the year of Christ 184.

units.la: Prisca nomina mesium Ægyptiorum apud Ptolemæum & alios probatos autores hæc legūtur. 1 ϑωθ. 2 ϻαοφι vel φαωφι. 3 αϑυρ. 4 χοιακ. 5 τυβι. 6 μεχιρ vel μεχυρ. 7 φαμενωθ. 8 φαρμουθι. 9 παχων. 10 παυνι. 11 ϵπιφι vel ϵπηφι. 12 μεσορη vel μεσωρη. Hæc labentibus seculis corrupta sunt ab Arabibus & Hebræis: interpres enim Alfragani Hebræus ita nominat, sicut etiamnum in Ægypto appellantur: 1 Thuth. 2 Baba. 3 Hathur. 4 Chihach. 5 Tube. 6 Emsir. 7 Barmahith. 8 Barmude. 9 Bafnes. 10 Bauna. 11 Abib. 12 Mesori. In epitome Regiomontani, quam ex Almagefto veteri Latino cotraxit corruptissime scripta leguntur, in hunc modū: 1 Thus. 2 Baba. 3 Athyr vel Athus. 4 Signach vel Tangut. 5 Tobi, vel Toc, vel Tuni. 6 Mezir, vel Mesir, vel Mesor. 7 Chamant. 8 Bromadi, vel Formiche, vel Formite, vel Formuth. 9 Machir, vel Machur. 10 Ben, vel Tegni, vel Tegus. 11 Achita, vel Achit, vel Athica. 12 Mesre.
units.tr: The ancient names of the Egyptian months, as found in Ptolemy and other approved authors, are these: 1 Thoth [ϑωθ]. 2 Phaophi or Phaophi [ϻαοφι or φαωφι]. 3 Athyr [αϑυρ]. 4 Choiak [χοιακ]. 5 Tybi [τυβι]. 6 Mechir or Mechyr [μεχιρ or μεχυρ]. 7 Phamenoth [φαμενωθ]. 8 Pharmouthi [φαρμουθι]. 9 Pachon [παχων]. 10 Payni [παυνι]. 11 Epiphi or Epeiphi [ϵπιφι or ϵπηφι]. 12 Mesore or Mesoré [μεσορη or μεσωρη]. As the centuries passed, these names were corrupted by the Arabs and the Hebrews. The Hebrew interpreter of Alfraganus names them as they are still called in Egypt: 1 Thuth, 2 Baba, 3 Hathur, 4 Chihach, 5 Tube, 6 Emsir, 7 Barmahith, 8 Barmude, 9 Bafnes, 10 Bauna, 11 Abib, 12 Mesori. In the epitome of Regiomontanus, which he drew from the old Latin Almagest, they are read in a very corrupt form, in this manner: 1 Thus, 2 Baba, 3 Athyr or Athus, 4 Signach or Tangut, 5 Tobi, or Toc, or Tuni, 6 Mezir, or Mesir, or Mesor, 7 Chamant, 8 Bromadi, or Formiche, or Formite, or Formuth, 9 Machir, or Machur, 10 Ben, or Tegni, or Tegus, 11 Achita, or Achit, or Athica, 12 Mesre.

units.la: Singuli meses æqualiter habet dies 30: qui paritef coficiunt 360 dies. Vt aute accedatur ad quaticate anni æquabilis,ad poftremu mefem Mefori,quinq; dies appedices,quasPtolemæus ἐπαγόμεναι vocat,extra ordine adiiciutur: ita quilibet annus Ægyptiorū nanci- scitur 365 dies.Cum aute quadrans diei,h.e.sex horę, ab Ægyptiis veteribus negligatur in quantitate anni solaris definieda, fit vt successu temporis Thoth cum reliquis mensibus totum zodiacum peruagetur.
units.tr: Each month has thirty days alike, and so the twelve months together make 360 days. To bring the year closer to the equal quarter-day, five extra days, which Ptolemy calls epagomenae [ἐπαγόμεναι], are added outside the regular order after the last month, Mesori. Thus every Egyptian year comes to 365 days. But since the ancient Egyptians disregarded the quarter-day, that is six hours, in fixing the length of the solar year, it happens that over time Thoth, together with the other months, travels through the whole zodiac.

units.la: Examen feriarū in annis & mensibus Nabonafari itanecessariu est, vt fine eo chronologiam certa habere non possimus. Quaobrem fatis mirari nequeo, quod de eo etiā præstantissimi historici ne verbulum quidem fecerint. Sane primus Thoth Nabonasari cœpit die Mercurii à sole meridiano: quod nobis primū fundamentū esse debet. Quod principiū annorū Nabonasari incideritin meridie, multis in locis Ptolemæus oftedit:quod vero incurrerit in diem Mercurii,perspicere licet ex historiis Ægyptiorū & Arabum, itemq; ex connexione annorum Nabonasari cum annis Iulianis ad hæc vsque tempora cōtinuata. Cicero lib.3 de natura Deorum refert Mercurium quintum, quē aliqui Trismegistum putat fuisse, Ægyptiis leges & literas tradidisse, & appellatum fuisse Thoth, quo nomine etiam primus anni mensis apud eos vocatur. Hoc vero adiiciendum est,iplam epocham Ægyptiorum à die Thoth,hoc est,Mercurii cœpisse: non enim dubium est tempore Nabonasari fuisse dierum distinctionem in hebdomades: quippe Ægyptii eam hauserat à Chaldæis, qui primi dies hebdomadis nominibus septem planetarum insigniuerunt Iudæos se- cuti,à mundi ipsius conditu dies numero septenario distinguentes. Testantur quoque Arabes post finem lib.3 Almagesti in veteri translatione, æram Nabonasari incurrisse in diem Mercurii, idem docent indices Alfonsini. Quia igitur primus Thoth Nabonasari, hoc est, prima dies primi mensis Ægyptiorum priscorum cœpit die Mercurii seu feria quarta: vtiq; annus secundus Nabonasari cœpit die Jovis: tertius die Veneris: quartus die sabbati: quintus die solis: sextus die lunæ: septimus die martis: octauus die mercurii, &c. quandoquidem omnes anni Ægyptii, sicut anni simplices Juliani in illa feriam definut, à qua incipiut. Quare si primus annus Nabonasari cœpit feria quarta, eademq; est finitus: sequitur ut annus secundus Nabonasari inchoauerit feria quinta. Indicium ergo annorum Nabonasari in charactere hebdomadico certissimum est, quòd omnes juxta seriem una eandemq; hebdomadis incipiat. Hinc colligitur, quomodo cognoscendum sit, à qua feria singuli anni Nabonasari incipiant: cùm enim anno octauo Nabonasari redeatur ad feriam æræ, h.e. ad die septimanæ quartum: diuidatur annus octauus per septenarium: & relinquetur in resi- duo unitas, quæ ostendet annum octauum incipere à die, quæ prima erat annorum Nabonasari: ergo idem de omni bus annis consequentibus secundum eandem proportionem est intelligendum. Ut anno nono per septem diuiso, manet duo: ergo is annus cœpit feria secunda ab æra, h.e. feria quinta. ita anno decimo quarto diuiso per septem, superest nihil, quod indicium est, annum illum incipere feria septima ab æra, hoc est die martis, quæ appellatur feria tertia. Hoc examine deprehendimus annum Nabonasari 425, in cuius principium incidit mors Alexandri seu æra annorum Philippicorum, cœpisse die solis: Thoth Nabonasari 437, qui est primus annus æræ Dhilkarnain, incurrisse in diem Veneris. Annus Nabonasari 719, in cuius principium incidit æra Augusti Actiaca cœpit die solis, quod etiam con-firmat scriptum Hebræi de æris cum Mesfahala[?] edi-tum. Annus Nabonasari 704, qui incidit in annum primum Iulianum, cœpit die sabbati. Annus Nabona-sari 748, qui incidit in annum Iulianum 45[?], quo Christus natus est, cœpit die lunæ. Thoth Nabona-sari 781, qui incurrit in annum Iulianum 78, & pro-ximus fuit paschali Dominicæ, cœpit die sabbati. An-nus Nabonasari 886, qui secundum Ptolemæum & Censorinum incidit in annum secundum imperatoris Antonini Pij, initium habuit die sabbati. Annus Nabonasari 986, qui iuxta Censorinum incurrit in annum Iulianum 283. cœpit die lunæ. Annus Nabonasari 1380, qui incidit in annum Christi vulgarem 632. quo æra Persica cœpit, initium habuit die mercurij. Thoth Nabonasari 2330, qui incurrit in annum Iulianum 1616, hoc est, in annum Christi 1581, si per septem more solito dividatur, in reliquo remanet 6: quod indicium est annum propositum Nabonasari 2330 cœpisse feria sexta ab æra, hoc est, die lunæ: ut rectissime scribat Iosephus Scaliger de emendatione temporum lib. 8. pagina 416, hisce verbis: Et sane verum est annum Nabonasari 2330 cœpisse 24 Iulij, feria secunda, anno Christi superiore 1581. Prædictorum annorum Nabonasari hic mentionem facere volui, ut constaret ad eos potissimum respiciendum esse, cum ex illorum collatione fere omnes temporum scrupuli tolli possint: apponam tamen deinceps singulis annis Nabonasari characterem suum hebdomadicum, quia sine illo certam annorum connexionem habere non possumus. Ut autem anni Iuliani vehiculum sunt & norma annorum vagorum Nabonasari: ita vice versa anni Nabonasari vehiculum sunt hebdomadum in annis Iulianis & solaribus. Nam anni Iuliani aliquoties fuerunt interrupti propter diversam bisexti intercalationem: anni quoq; solares, qui Iulianos antecesserunt, nō habuerunt definitam dierum periodum: vt per illos nullo modo ostendi possit septimanarū connexio: in solis autē Ægyptiorū annis æquabilibus feriarū ordo saluus & incolumis servatur.
units.tr: A reckoning of the days of the week in the years and months of Nabonassar is so necessary that without it we cannot have a sure chronology. For this reason I can hardly wonder that the most distinguished historians have not said even a word about it. Certainly the first Thoth of Nabonassar began on Wednesday, at noon by the sun; this must be our first foundation. That the beginning of the years of Nabonassar fell at noon, Ptolemy shows in many places. That it fell on a Wednesday can be seen from the histories of the Egyptians and the Arabs, and likewise from the connection of the years of Nabonassar with the Julian years, continued down to our own times. Cicero, in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, reports that the fifth Mercury, whom some think to have been Trismegistus, gave the Egyptians their laws and letters, and that he was called Thoth, a name by which the first month of their year is also called. But this must be added: the epoch itself of the Egyptians began from the day Thoth, that is, from Wednesday. For there is no doubt that in the time of Nabonassar the division of days into weeks already existed, since the Egyptians had taken it from the Chaldeans, who first named the days of the week after the seven planets; the Jews followed them, distinguishing the days by a sevenfold number from the creation of the world itself. The Arabs also testify, after the end of book 3 of the Almagest in the old translation, that the era of Nabonassar fell on a Wednesday, and the Alphonsine tables teach the same. Therefore, since the first Thoth of Nabonassar, that is, the first day of the first month of the ancient Egyptians, began on Wednesday, or the fourth day of the week, then the second year of Nabonassar certainly began on Thursday, the third on Friday, the fourth on Saturday, the fifth on Sunday, the sixth on Monday, the seventh on Tuesday, the eighth on Wednesday, and so on. For all Egyptian years, like simple Julian years, end on the same day on which they begin. Hence, if the first year of Nabonassar began on Wednesday and ended on the same day, it follows that the second year of Nabonassar began on Thursday. The weekday character of the years of Nabonassar is therefore most certain, because they all begin, in order, on one and the same day of the week. From this it is gathered how one may know on which day of the week each year of Nabonassar began. For since in the eighth year of Nabonassar one returns to the weekday of the era, that is, to the fourth day of the week, divide the eighth year by seven and one unit remains. This shows that the eighth year began on the day that was the first of the years of Nabonassar. The same is to be understood of all the following years by the same proportion. For example, when the ninth year is divided by seven, two remains; therefore that year began on the second day of the week counted from the era, that is, on Thursday. Likewise, when the fourteenth year is divided by seven, nothing remains; this is the sign that that year began on the seventh day of the week counted from the era, that is, on Tuesday, which is called the third day. By this test we find that the year 425 of Nabonassar, in whose beginning fell the death of Alexander, or the era of the Philippic years, began on Sunday; and that the first Thoth of Nabonassar 437, which is the first year of the era of Dhulkarnain, fell on Friday. The year 719 of Nabonassar, in whose beginning falls the Actian era of Augustus, began on Sunday, which also confirms the Hebrew writing on eras, edited with Mesfahala[?]. The year 704 of Nabonassar, which fell in the first Julian year, began on Saturday. The year 748 of Nabonassar, which falls in the Julian year 45[?], in which Christ was born, began on Monday. The first Thoth of Nabonassar 781, which falls in the Julian year 78, and was nearest to the Lord's Paschal feast, began on Saturday. The year 886 of Nabonassar, which according to Ptolemy and Censorinus falls in the second year of the emperor Antoninus Pius, began on Saturday. The year 986 of Nabonassar, which according to Censorinus falls in the Julian year 283, began on Monday. The year 1380 of Nabonassar, which falls in the common Christian year 632, when the Persian era began, had its beginning on Wednesday. The first Thoth of Nabonassar 2330, which falls in the Julian year 1616, that is, in the year of Christ 1581, if divided by seven as usual, leaves 6 as remainder; this is the sign that the year 2330 of Nabonassar began on the sixth day of the week counted from the era, that is, on Monday. So Joseph Scaliger writes most correctly in his De emendatione temporum, book 8, page 416, in these words: And indeed it is true that the year 2330 of Nabonassar began on 24 July, on the second day of the week, in the year of Christ 1581 before. I wished to mention these years of Nabonassar here so that it would be clear that we must especially attend to them, since almost all the scruples of chronology can be removed by comparing them. Nevertheless, I shall henceforth set against each year of Nabonassar its weekday sign, since without it we cannot have a sure connection of the years. Just as the Julian years are the vehicle and rule of the wandering years of Nabonassar, so conversely the years of Nabonassar are the vehicle of the weeks within the Julian and solar years. For the Julian years were at times interrupted by the differing intercalation of the leap day, and the solar years which preceded the Julian ones had no fixed period of days, so that the connection of the weeks cannot be shown through them in any way. But in the equal years of the Egyptians alone the order of the days of the week is preserved safe and unimpaired.

units.la: Postquàm ostendimus, quomodo character hebdomadicus sit investigandus in principio singulorum annorum Nabonasari; restat ut videamus quomodo idem quærendus sit in principio singulorum mensium. Ut autem hoc cognoscatur, oportet intueri dispositionem mensium, quæ est in primo anno Nabonasari, ut hinc cæterorum dierum characteres sumantur. Quia primus Thoth Nabonasari cœpit feria quarta, Paophi cœpit feria sexta: & cum Paophi cœperit feria sexta, Athyr cœpit feria prima,&c. sicut ex sequenti tabella apparet. Thoth | 4 | Phamenoth | 1 Paophi | 6 | Pharmuthi | 4 Athyr | 1 | Pachon | 6 Chiac | 3 | Payni [?] | 1 Tybi | 5 | Epiphi | 3 Mechir | 7 | Mefori | 5
units.tr: Having shown how the weekday character is to be found at the beginning of each year of Nabonassar, it remains to see how the same is to be sought at the beginning of each month. To learn this, one must look at the arrangement of the months in the first year of Nabonassar, so that from it the weekday signs of the other days may be taken. Since the first Thoth of Nabonassar began on Wednesday, Phaophi began on Friday; and since Phaophi began on Friday, Athyr began on Sunday, and so on, as appears from the following table: Thoth | 4 | Phaophi | 6 | Athyr | 1 | Choiak | 3 | Tybi | 5 | Mechir | 7 | Phamenoth | 1 | Pharmouthi | 4 | Pachon | 6 | Payni | 1 | Epiphi | 3 | Mesori | 5

units.la: Si igitur in aliquo anno Nabonasari scire cupias characterem mensis alicuius, cæterorumq; dierum confer initium anni illius cum charactere hebdomadico ipsius æræ: & quàm ibi invenies differentiam, eam servabis in reliquis mensibus. Exempli gratia, annus Nabonasari 1 330 [?], qui incidit in diem 24 Iulij anno Christi 1581, cœpit feria secunda, vt prius est ostensum: hanc secundam feriam si conferas cum feria quarta ipsius æræ, deprehendes differentiam bidui: quamobrem biduum in reliquis mensibus. subtrahendum est, vt habeatur verus character; sic Paophi anni 2330 Nabonasari incipiet à feria quarta, quæ incidit in 23 Augusti; & Athyr incipiet à feria sexta, quæ incidit in 22 Septembris. Vbi obseruandum est, si subtractio fieri non possit, adiiciendum esse septenarium, vt alias fieri solet. cùm ergo Athyr anni primi Nabonasari cœperit feria prima, à qua non possit subtrahi feria secunda, adiiciuntur septem, sic fiunt octo, à quibus duo demta, relinquunt sex, characterem hebdomadicum mensis Athyr in anno prædicto Nabonasari 2330. Atqj hoc examen est feriarum in annis Nabonasari: quod nisi diebus omnibus Iulianis respondeat, indicium est errorem commissum esse in connexione, aut bisextorum intercalationem alicubi excidisse, vel turbatam fuisse.
units.tr: If, then, in some year of Nabonassar you wish to know the weekday character of a given month and of its other days, compare the beginning of that year with the weekday character of that era. Whatever difference you find there, keep it for the remaining months. For example, year 2330 of Nabonassar, which fell on 24 July in the year of Christ 1581, began on the second feria (Monday), as was shown earlier. If you compare this second feria with the fourth feria of that era, you find a difference of two days. For the remaining months, therefore, two days must be subtracted to obtain the true character. Thus Paophi of year 2330 of Nabonassar will begin on the fourth feria (Wednesday), which falls on 23 August, and Athyr will begin on the sixth feria (Friday), which falls on 22 September. Here it must be noted that if a subtraction cannot be made, seven must be added, as is usually done in other cases. Since Athyr of the first year of Nabonassar began on the first feria (Sunday), and the second feria cannot be subtracted from it, seven is added, making eight; take away two, and six remains, which is the weekday character of the month Athyr in the said year 2330 of Nabonassar. This is the test of the feriae in the years of Nabonassar. If it does not agree with all the Julian days, it is a sign that an error was made in the connection, or that the intercalation of the leap years was lost somewhere or disturbed.
ON THE ARABIC CALENDAR.

units.la: Arabes puros putos habent annos lunares, hoc est, ex duodecim periodis lunaribus confectos: proinde si quantitas vnius periodi sciatur, tota quoque anni Arabici quantitas innotescit. Didicerunt autem Arabes, & qui eorum calendario vtuntur Turcæ, à veteribus Hebræis & Babyloniis; periodum menstruam ab vna solis lunæq; coniunctione vsq; ad alteram, absolui iuxta medium motum, diebus 29, horis 12, scrupulis horariis 793; quorum 1080 integram horam constituunt. Id tempus si in 12 menses distribuatur, cofurgunt dies 354, horæ 8, & scrupula horaria 876; quæ est quantitas anni lunaris Iudaici. Cùm autem apud Alfraganum afferatur, annum Arabicum verè constare diebus 354, horis 8,& scrupulis horariis 864; satis intelligitur, voluisse Arabes de industria recedere à calendario Iudaico, commodioremq; annorum suorum periodum & rationem intercaladi obseruare. Cùm enim annus communis & ordinarius apud Hebræos sit 354 dierum, 8 horarum, & 876 scrupulorum; Arabibus annus constituitur 354 dierum, 8 horarû, & 864 scrupulorum. Nam à spacio menstruo Arabes subtraxerunt vnum scrupulum horariû; vt annus ipsorum minor sit Iudaico 12 scrupulis horariis. Quod discertè testatur R. Abraham filius Chaja in computo motuum cœlestiû, qui Hebraicè extat manuscriptus in bibliotheca Palatina, vbi in hanc sententiâ scribit: Sciás quòd primus mensis Ismaelitarum perpetuò incidit vel in neomeniam mensis Israelitarum, vel in diem precedentem aut subsequentem: quoniam non est inter ipsos & Israelitas in periodo mensis lunaris differentia alia quam vnum scrupulum. quia ipsi numerant in mensibus suis 29 dies, 12 horas, & 792 scrupula: sed nos tribuimus lunationi 29 dies, 12 horas, & 793 scrupula. Constituerunt itaque Arabes periodum lunarem dierû 29, horarum 12, scrupulorum horariorum 792, quod etiam innuere vult Hebræus Alfragani interpres, cùm inquit; etsi vni lunationi reipsa competant 793 scrupula horaria.
units.tr: The Arabs use purely lunar years, that is, years made up of twelve lunar periods. Therefore, if the length of one period is known, the whole length of the Arabic year is known as well. The Arabs, however, and the Turks who use their calendar, learned it from the ancient Hebrews and Babylonians. The monthly period, from one conjunction of sun and moon to the next, is completed according to the mean motion in 29 days, 12 hours and 793 hour-scruples, of which 1080 make one whole hour. If this time is distributed over 12 months, there result 354 days, 8 hours and 876 hour-scruples, which is the length of the Jewish lunar year. But since Alfraganus states that the Arabic year truly consists of 354 days, 8 hours and 864 hour-scruples, it is clear enough that the Arabs deliberately departed from the Jewish calendar, in order to observe a more convenient period of their years and a more convenient rule of intercalation. For the ordinary year among the Hebrews is 354 days, 8 hours and 876 scruples, whereas the Arab year is set at 354 days, 8 hours and 864 scruples. For the Arabs subtracted one hour-scruple from the monthly period, so that their year is shorter than the Jewish by 12 hour-scruples. R. Abraham son of Chaja clearly bears witness to this in his computation of the heavenly motions, which exists in Hebrew in manuscript in the Palatine library, where he writes to this effect: You should know that the first month of the Ishmaelites always falls either on the new moon of the month of the Israelites, or on the day before or after it, since between them and the Israelites there is no difference in the lunar period except one scruple. For they reckon in their months 29 days, 12 hours and 792 scruples; but we assign to the lunation 29 days, 12 hours and 793 scruples. Thus the Arabs fixed the lunar period at 29 days, 12 hours and 792 hour-scruples, which the Hebrew translator of Alfraganus also wishes to indicate, when he says: although in reality 793 hour-scruples belong to one lunation.

units.la: Ex data enim anni Arabici quantitate dierum 354, horarum 8, scrupulorum horariorû 864; emergit vice versa periodus vnius lunationis Arabicæ 29 dierum, 12 horarum, scrupulorû tantum 792, non autem 793, vt exigebat calculus Iudæorum.
units.tr: For from the given length of the Arabic year, 354 days, 8 hours and 864 hour-scruples, there follows conversely the period of one Arabic lunation as 29 days, 12 hours and only 792 scruples, not 793 as the Jewish calculation required.

units.la: Sed obscurum fortassis alicui videbitur, quomodo quantitas anni Arabici ponatur 354 dierum, & [?] & [?] diei; sicut Alfraganus asserit, & id ipsum Albategnius cap. 31. profitetur: verùm si quis cogitet Hebraeum Alfragani interpretem dicere, Partes 1/5 & 1/6 conficere 8 horas, & 864 scrupula: pulcherrimam habebit fractionum praedictarum explicationem: & intelliget vnum idemq; esse, si dicamus, annū Arabicum constare 354 diebus, 8 horis, & 864 scrupulis horarijs: vel habere 354 dies, & 1/6 ac 1/7 diei. Sexta enim pars diei absq; controuersia suppeditat 4 horas: quibus si quinta pars diei, hoc est, horæ 4, & scrupula horaria 864 adiiciantur, summa consurgit 8 horarum, & 864 scrupulorum. Quintam autē partem diei valere horas 4, & scrupula horaria 864 constabit: si integer dies, hoc est, 24 horæ, diuidatur per quinque, proueniunt 4 horæ: & residuum fractionis 4/5 multiplicetur per 1080 partes, quot vnā horam conficiunt; & diuidatur rursum per quinque, vt fieri solet; proueniunt 864 scrupula. Itaq; excessus anni Arabici supra dies 354, est horarum 8, scrupulorum horariorum 864. quod intelligendum est de anno simplici: nam bisextilis supra dies 355 excessum habet 8 horarum, & 864 scrupulorum. Existimo autem interpretis Hebraei esse explicationem, quando vnam quintam & vnam sextam diei, per 8 horas, & 864 scrupula declarat: nam Arabes in computo annorum suorum contexendo, vnam quintam & vnam sextam diei, explicant per vndecim tricesimas; siquidem integrum diem diuidunt in triginta partes. Id ipsum quoq; testatur Petrus de Aliaco in tractatu de vero cyclo lunari secundùm Arabū doctrinam, cùm inquit, Quia vero vltra 354 dies anni prædictos, restant aliquæ fractiones, vt dictum est, videlicet vnam quintam & vnam sextam diei, seu 12 minuta, velvt alii dicunt 11 tricesimæ vnius diei, quodidem est, & va- let let[?] 8 horas,&48 minuta;hora,ideo in 30 annis sunt anni vndecim habentes dies 355,quos nunc secundo nunc tertio anno attribuunt,ita quod in huius restitutionis anno fiunt septem menses perfecti,& quinque imperfecti.
units.tr: Perhaps, however, it will seem obscure to someone how the length of the Arabic year is put at 354 days, and [?] and [?] of a day, as Alfraganus asserts, and Albategnius likewise professes in chapter 31. But if someone considers that the Hebrew translator of Alfraganus says that parts 1/5 and 1/6 make 8 hours and 864 scruples, he will have a most elegant explanation of the said fractions, and will understand that it is one and the same thing whether we say that the Arabic year consists of 354 days, 8 hours and 864 hour-scruples, or that it has 354 days and 1/6 and 1/7 of a day. For the sixth part of a day undoubtedly supplies 4 hours; if to these is added the fifth part of a day, that is 4 hours and 864 hour-scruples, the sum comes to 8 hours and 864 scruples. That the fifth part of a day is worth 4 hours and 864 hour-scruples will be evident if a whole day, that is 24 hours, is divided by five, giving 4 hours; and the remaining fraction 4/5 is multiplied by 1080, the number of parts that make one hour, and divided again by five, as is customary; the result is 864 scruples. Therefore the excess of the Arabic year over 354 days is 8 hours and 864 hour-scruples. This must be understood of the common year; for the leap year has an excess of 8 hours and 864 scruples over 355 days. I think, moreover, that the Hebrew translator's explanation is correct when he expresses one fifth and one sixth of a day as 8 hours and 864 scruples. For the Arabs, in working out their annual reckoning, express one fifth and one sixth of a day as eleven thirtieths, since they divide the whole day into thirty parts. Peter of Ailly also bears witness to the same thing in his treatise on the true lunar cycle according to the doctrine of the Arabs, when he says: Because, beyond the said 354 days of the year, some fractions remain, as has been said, namely one fifth and one sixth of a day, or 12 minutes, or, as others say, eleven thirtieths of one day, which is the same thing and is worth 8 hours and 48 minutes; therefore in 30 years there are eleven years having 355 days, which they assign now in the second, now in the third year, so that in the year of this restitution there are seven complete months and five incomplete.

units.la: Definita anni Arabici, eiusq; excessus quantitate; superest vt ostendamus, obseruare Arabes cyclum annorum triginta; in quo vndecim anni sunt intercalares, videlicet secundus, quintus, septimus, decimus, tredecimus, decimus sextus, decimus octauus, vigesimus primus, vigesimus quartus, vigesimus sex-tus,& vigesimus nonus; sicut Saracenus in scripto suo de principijs astronomiae ostendit. idem cum Iudaeis Alfonsini tradunt; idem testatur Arzachel in canonibus & tabulis motuum coelestium; idem Robertus Episcopus Linconiensis in computo, & Paulus de Middelburgo Episcopus Forosempro-nienfis in suis Paulinis, & Iordanus in praxi astronomiae perspicue docent. Quomodo vero anni praedicti 2.5.7.10.13.16.18.21.24.26.29 fiant intercalares, nunc est dicendum. Ponitur communis singulorum annorum excessus vndecim tricesimarum; vt anni triginta in cyclo Arabico completantur 330 tricesimas; quae conficiunt vndecim dies intercalares, siquidem 30 tricesimae vnā diem constituunt. Ac cum excessus isti inaequaliter in singulos annos dis-tribuantur, expendendum est, qua ratione & quo ordine, ex tricesimarum coaceruatione anni intercalares oriantur. Primo fingendum est ante primum annum cycli relictum fuisse excessum seu epactum communem vnius anni, videlicet vndecim tricesimas, quae annumerandae sunt excessui anni primi. ita conflantur 22 tricesimae, quibus si addatur anni secundi excessus, proueniunt 33 tricesimae, quae die efficiunt, vt redundent tres tricesimæ.Itaque annus secundus cycli intercalaris est, habens dies 355 ,& supersint tres tricesimæ, quibus si anni tertii epacta addatur, prodeunt 14 tricesimę:hisce iterū si adiiciatur quarti anni excessus,cumulantur 25 tricesimæ:his deniq; si aggregetur quinti anni excessus,fiunt 36 tricesimæ: quæ conflant diem,vt supersint sex tricesimæ. Qua-re annus quoq; quintus cycli intercalaris est, rema-nentibus 6 tricesimis:quibus si addatur sexti anni excessus, colliguntur 17 tricesimæ: his iterum si ad-iiciatur excessus anni septimi, fiunt 28 tricesimæ:vt duæ tricesimæ desiderentur,quò minus annus septi-mus cycli videatur esse intercalaris. Sed hic diligen-ter animaduertendum est,Arabes annum septimum cycli intercalarem facere, etsi tricesimæ nondum excreuerint ad integram diem constituendam: si-quidem de excessu anni octaui subtrahunt duas tri-cesimas, easq; ad 28 tricesimas in anno septimo col-lectas aggregant: quò oriantur 30 tricesimæ, diem integram constituentes. Itaque annum septimum intercalarem habent, vt nihil superfit de fractioni-bus: & anno octauo supersint tantum 9 tricesimæ, cum alias superfuisset vndecim tricesimæ. Ita an-num 18,& 26 cycli intercalares faciunt: etsi e frac-tionibus nondum integra dies fit collecta: in anno enim 18 ad 19 tricesimas, assumunt vnam tricesi-mam de excessu anni decimi noni:& anno 26 ad 27 tricesimas, assumunt tres tricesimas de excessu anni vigesimi septimi: vt paulo post luculentius declara-bimus. Hoc fundamentum est totius calendarii Arabici: quo ignorato necesse est nos in errore ver-sari, aut absurda aliqua contra omnem veterum au-toritatem comminisci. Non enim cogitandum est, Arabes annos suos intercalares ordinare, quasi nul-quam intercalent, nisi integra dies e fractionibus emerserit. Cum ergo annus septimus cycli sit intercalaris, nullis relictis fractionibus: & in anno octauo supersint 9 tricesimae; progrediendum est ad sequentes annos, & quae sit ratio fractionū, est examinandum. Si excessum anni noni adiiciamus ad 9 tricesimas, relictas in anno octauo, oriuntur 20 tricesimae: quibus si addatur excessus anni decimi, fiut 31 tricesimae, quae diem efficiunt, & unam tricesimam: itaque annus decimus intercalaris est, & ex eo superest una tricesima: ad quam si adiiciatur excessus anni undecimi, colliguntur 12 tricesimae: hisce si aggregetur epacta anni duodecimi, fiunt 23 tricesimae: quibus si addatur excessus anni decimi tertii, consurgunt 34 tricesimae, quae diem constituunt, & quatuor tricesimas: sic annus decimus tertius bisextilis est; & ex eo supersunt 4 tricesimae; quibus si anni decimi quarti excessus addatur, fiunt 15 tricesimae; his iterum si adiiciatur anni decimi quinti excessus, aggregantur 26 tricesimae; his denique si anni decimi sexti excessus addatur, conflatur 37 tricesimae; quae diem efficiunt, & 7 tricesimas. Ergo annus decimus sextus intercalaris est, & ex eo supersunt septem tricesimae; ad quas si accedat excessus anni decimi septimi, prodeunt 18 tricesimae; quibus si addatur excessus anni decimi octaui, fiunt 29 tricesimae. Licet autem hic desideretur una tricesima, quo minus annus decimus octauus videatur esse intercalaris; tamen Arabes eum intercalarem faciunt, ut prius dictum est, unam tricesimam assumendo de excessu anni decimi noni; ut nulla fractio remaneat anno decimo octauo bisextili; anno autem decimo nono fuperfint decem tricefimæ: ad quas fi addatur exceffus anni vigefimi, producuntur 21 tricefimæ:his iterum fi adiiciatur exceffus anni 21;colliguntur 3 2 tricefimæ, quæ diê[?] efficiunt cum duabus tricefimis. Itaq; annus vigefimus primus bifextilis eft, & ex eo fuperfunt duæ tricefimæ: quibus fi aggregetur exceffus anni vigefimi fecundi, fiunt 13 tricefimæ: atq; his fi addatur exceffus anni vigefimi tertij, oriuntur 24 tricefimæ: his deniq; fi addatur epacta anni vigefimi quarti, prodeunt 35 tricefimæ, quæ conftituunt die, & quinq; tricefimas. Sic annus vigefimus quartus cycli intercalaris eft, vt ex eo fuperfint quinque tricefimæ: quibus fi annumeretur exceffus anni vigefimi quinti, fiunt 16 tricefimæ: hifce fi adiiciatur exceffus anni vigefimi fexti, oriuntur 27 tricefimæ.
units.tr: Having defined the Arabic year and the amount of its excess, it remains to show that the Arabs observe a cycle of thirty years, in which eleven years are intercalary: namely the second, fifth, seventh, tenth, thirteenth, sixteenth, eighteenth, twenty-first, twenty-fourth, twenty-sixth and twenty-ninth. The Saracen shows this in his writing on the principles of astronomy. The Alphonsine tables likewise teach it in agreement with the Jews. Arzachel attests the same in his canons and tables of celestial motions, and Robert, Bishop of Lincoln, in his computus, Paul of Middelburg, Bishop of Fossombrone, in his Paulinae, and Jordanus in his practice of astronomy, teach it clearly. How the aforesaid years 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, 18, 21, 24, 26 and 29 become intercalary must now be explained. The common excess of each year is put at eleven thirtieths, so that the thirty years of the Arabic cycle make up 330 thirtieths, which constitute eleven intercalary days, since thirty thirtieths make one day. Since these excesses are distributed unevenly among the individual years, we must consider by what reasoning and in what order the intercalary years arise from the accumulation of thirtieths. First it must be supposed that before the first year of the cycle there was left over the common excess or epact of one year, namely eleven thirtieths, which must be counted towards the excess of the first year. So 22 thirtieths are made up; if the excess of the second year is added to these, 33 thirtieths result, which make a day, leaving three thirtieths over. Therefore the second year of the cycle is intercalary, having 355 days, and three thirtieths remain. If the epact of the third year is added to these, 14 thirtieths arise; if the excess of the fourth year is added again, 25 thirtieths accumulate; and if finally the excess of the fifth year is added, 36 thirtieths result, which make a day, leaving six thirtieths over. Therefore the fifth year of the cycle is also intercalary, six thirtieths remaining. If the excess of the sixth year is added to these, 17 thirtieths are collected; if the excess of the seventh year is added again, 28 thirtieths result, so that two thirtieths are lacking, which would prevent the seventh year of the cycle from appearing intercalary. But here it must be carefully noted that the Arabs make the seventh year of the cycle intercalary even though the thirtieths have not yet grown to make a full day. For they take two thirtieths away from the excess of the eighth year and add them to the 28 thirtieths gathered in the seventh year, so that 30 thirtieths arise, making one whole day. Thus they make the seventh year intercalary, so that no fraction remains, and in the eighth year only 9 thirtieths remain, whereas otherwise 11 thirtieths would have remained. So they make the eighteenth and twenty-sixth years of the cycle intercalary too, even though a full day has not been gathered from the fractions. In the eighteenth year they take one thirtieth from the excess of the nineteenth year and add it to make 19 thirtieths; in the twenty-sixth year they take three thirtieths from the excess of the twenty-seventh year and add them to make 27 thirtieths; as we shall show more clearly a little later. This is the foundation of the whole Arabic calendar. If it is ignored, we must necessarily go astray, or invent some absurdity contrary to all the authority of the ancients. For we must not suppose that the Arabs arrange their intercalary years as if they never intercalated unless a full day had emerged from the fractions. Since therefore the seventh year of the cycle is intercalary, with no fractions left over, and 9 thirtieths remain in the eighth year, we must proceed to the following years and examine what the reckoning of the fractions is. If we add the excess of the ninth year to the 9 thirtieths left in the eighth year, 20 thirtieths arise; if the excess of the tenth year is added, 31 thirtieths result, which make a day and one thirtieth. Thus the tenth year is intercalary, and one thirtieth remains from it. If the excess of the eleventh year is added to this, 12 thirtieths are collected; if the epact of the twelfth year is added to these, 23 thirtieths result; if the excess of the thirteenth year is added to these, 34 thirtieths arise, which make a day and four thirtieths. So the thirteenth year is bissextile, and 4 thirtieths remain from it. If the excess of the fourteenth year is added to these, 15 thirtieths result; if the excess of the fifteenth year is added again, 26 thirtieths are gathered; and if finally the excess of the sixteenth year is added, 37 thirtieths are formed, which make a day and 7 thirtieths. Therefore the sixteenth year is intercalary, and seven thirtieths remain from it. If the excess of the seventeenth year is added to these, 18 thirtieths result; if the excess of the eighteenth year is added to these, 29 thirtieths result. Although one thirtieth is still wanting, so that the eighteenth year might not appear intercalary, the Arabs nevertheless make it intercalary, as said before, by taking one thirtieth from the excess of the nineteenth year, so that no fraction remains in the bissextile eighteenth year. In the nineteenth year, however, 10 thirtieths remain. If the excess of the twentieth year is added to these, 21 thirtieths result; if the excess of the twenty-first year is added to these, 32 thirtieths are collected, which together with two thirtieths make a day. Thus the twenty-first year is bissextile, and two thirtieths remain from it. If the excess of the twenty-second year is added to these, 13 thirtieths result; if the excess of the twenty-third year is added, 24 thirtieths arise; and finally if the epact of the twenty-fourth year is added, 35 thirtieths result, which make a day and five thirtieths. Thus the twenty-fourth year of the cycle is intercalary, with five thirtieths remaining from it. If the excess of the twenty-fifth year is counted in, 16 thirtieths result; if the excess of the twenty-sixth year is added to these, 27 thirtieths arise.

units.la: Licet autem hic quoq; deficiant tres tricefimæ, quo minus annus vigefimus fextus videatur effe bifextilis: tamen Arabes cum intercalarem faciunt, vt etiam prius monuimus, aflumtis tribus tricefimis de exceffu anni vigefimi feptimi. Sic anno vigefimo fexto intercalari nulla fractio remanet: in anno autem vigefimo feptimo, fuperfunt tantum 8 tricefimæ: ad quas fi accedat exceffus anni vigefimi octavi, prodeunt 19 tricefimæ: his fi adijciatur exceffus anni vigefimi noni, confurgunt 30 tricefimæ, quæ præcife efficiunt diem vnam. Itaq; annus vigefimus nonus cycli intercalaris eft, vt nihil fuperfit de tricefimis: fic annus tricefimus & poftremus cycli communem habet exceffum vndecim tricefimarū: quas diximus æquipollere vni quintæ, & vni fextæ diei.
units.tr: Although here too three thirtieths are lacking, so that the twenty-sixth year might not appear bissextile, the Arabs nevertheless make it intercalary, as we noted before, by taking three thirtieths from the excess of the twenty-seventh year. So in the intercalary twenty-sixth year no fraction remains; but in the twenty-seventh year only 8 thirtieths remain. If the excess of the twenty-eighth year is added to these, 19 thirtieths result; if the excess of the twenty-ninth year is added, 30 thirtieths arise, which make exactly one day. Thus the twenty-ninth year of the cycle is intercalary, so that nothing remains of the thirtieths. So the thirtieth and last year of the cycle has the common excess of eleven thirtieths, which we said is equivalent to one fifth and one sixth of a day.

units.la: Neq; hic audiendi funt, qui præter omnem rationem fcribere audent, fieri apud Arabes commutationem anni vigefimi noni cum anno trigefimo, vt fcilicet annus simplex: atq; hanc cōmutationem dictitant ideo institui, vt annus primus & postremus cycli ab eadem feria incipiat.
units.tr: Nor are those to be heard who presume, against all reason, to write that among the Arabs the twenty-ninth year is exchanged for the thirtieth, so that the twenty-ninth year is made a common year. They claim this exchange was instituted for the reason that the first and last years of the cycle begin on the same weekday.

units.la: annus trigesimus cycli fit intercalaris: vigefimus autem nonus, qui sua natura est intercalaris, habeatur simplex: atq; hanc cōmutationem dictitant ideo institui, vt annus primus & postremus cycli ab eadem feria incipiat. Quis vero Arabum hoc docuit vnqua? sane Arzachel ostendit feriarum in cyclo triacontaeterico Arabum talem feriem,qualem requirunt anni intercalares 2.5[?].7.10.13.16.18.21.24.26.29.quos etiam elegantissimè Iordanus per fractiones annexas bisextiles esse demonstrat: vt ex sequenti tabella videre licet.
units.tr: The thirtieth year of the cycle is intercalary, while the twenty-ninth year, which is intercalary by its nature, is held to be simple. They claim this exchange was instituted so that the first and last years of the cycle begin on the same weekday. But which of the Arabs ever taught this? Certainly Arzachel shows that the sequence of weekdays in the thirty-year Arabic cycle is such as the intercalary years 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, 18, 21, 24, 26 and 29 require. Jordanus also most elegantly demonstrates that these are bissextile by the attached fractions, as can be seen from the following table.

units.la: Litera b vndecies posita indicat annos bisextiles vndecim: primus annus habet 2 2 tricesimas, quia in eo excessus duo congregatur, quorum primus accedit ex precedenti cyclo, alter vero proprius est illius anni.In reliquis annis excessus proprius,qui est vndecim tricesimarum, semper additur ad fractiones residuas, & cum 30 tricesimae colliguntur, interiicitur dies bisextilis: vt antea prolixe explicauimus.
units.tr: The letter b, placed eleven times, marks eleven bissextile years. The first year has 22 thirtieths, because in it two excesses are gathered: the first comes from the preceding cycle, and the second belongs to that year itself. In the remaining years the proper excess, which is eleven thirtieths, is always added to the residual fractions, and when 30 thirtieths have been collected, an intercalary day is inserted, as we explained at length earlier.

units.la: Hic obseruandum est hanc esse commodissimam epactarum lunarium rationem, vt annis triginta lunaribus aequetur cyclus decennouenalis aurei numeri: quamobrem calendarium Gregorianum sequitur Arabum doctrinam, quando in nouiluniis & pleniluniis indagandis adhibet 30 numeros epactales. Totus autem cyclus Arabicus annorum lunarium triginta, coficit annos aequabiles 19, & 46 dies, hoc est, summatim 10631 dies: vt etiam testatur Saracenus, cum ait, Inuenerunt quod dies triginta annorū Arabicorum sunt decem millia & sexcenti, triginta & vnus dies.
units.tr: It must be observed here that this is the most convenient system of lunar epacts, since thirty lunar years are made equal to the nineteen-year cycle of the golden number. For this reason the Gregorian calendar follows the doctrine of the Arabs when, in finding the new and full moons, it uses the 30 epact numbers. The whole Arabic cycle of thirty lunar years makes 19 equal years and 46 days, that is, in sum 10,631 days. Saracenus also bears witness to this when he says: "They have found that thirty Arabic years are ten thousand six hundred and thirty-one days."

units.la: Sed vt scias, quomodo cyclus triacontaetericus Arabum commutandus sit in annos aequabiles, quorum singuli constant 365 diebus: considera subsequentem tabulam ex Arzachele depromtam. units.la: Annus primus cycli cum sit simplex, habet 354 dies: secundus est intercalaris, habens 355 dies: qui ad superiores adiecti conficiunt annum unum aequabilem, & 344 dies. Sic anni tres priores efficiunt annos duos aequabiles, & 333 dies, &c. Anni autem triginta Arabum suppeditant annos aequabiles 29, & 46 dies. Prorsus necessarium est, vt datos annos Arabicos conuertamus in annos aequabiles, quoniam per annos aequabiles Aegyptiorum, examinamus cōtextum annorum Iulianorum: si enim constet, quo in loco Thoth Nabonasari haereat, & quantum sit interuallum temporis in calédario Iuliano, etiam hinc apparet, quot anni aequabiles sint interiecti.
units.tr: The first year of the cycle, being a common year, has 354 days; the second is intercalary, having 355 days. When these are added to the earlier ones, they make one equal year and 344 days. Thus the first three years make two equal years and 333 days, and so on. The thirty Arabic years yield 29 equal years and 46 days. It is absolutely necessary that we convert the given Arabic years into equal years, because by the equal years of the Egyptians we examine the sequence of the Julian years. For if it is established at what point Thoth of Nabonassar falls, and how great the interval of time is in the Julian calendar, it also becomes apparent from this how many equal years have intervened.

units.la: Cyclum suum triacontaëtericum Arabes ordiuntur ab Hegira Muhamedis, h.e. à migratione Pseudoprophetae sui:quae contigit anno Christi 622, decimo sexto Iulii, feria sexta, litera Dominicali existente C. h.e. anno Nabonasari 1370, die 28 mensis Chiac: vt ad aeram Arabicam trafierint anni Nabonasari 1369, & 117 dies, h.e. in vniuersum 499802 dies. Quodau-tem aera Arabica incipiat a tempore, quo Muhamed Pseudopropheta propter insidias hostium e Mecha in ciuitatem letrib[?] fugisse dicitur, testatur in primo capite Alfraganus noster. Sed is cum omnibus astronomis assignat characterem hebdomadicum in annis Arabicis feriam quintam, hoc est, diem Iouis, quae incurrit in 15 Iulii, anno Christi labente 622, sicut testatur Iordanus, cum ait, Anni & Arabum inceperunt anno Domini 622, Idibus Iulii, cum esset C litera dominicalis: per quod patet, quod 5 feria, quam G litera ibi posita significabat, fuit illis initialis. Causa, quod a-stronomi initiu Hegirae sumat a feria quinta, est coniunctio solis & lunae, quae incidit in feria quinta: vt ex enneadecaeteride Iuliana facile colligi potest: nos au-te more politico sumimus initium Hegirae a feria sexta, die scilicet congregationis, quae secuta est neomeniam cœlesté:in qua die Muhamed post recuperata Mecha praedicare coepit, & dogma suum impium promulgari curauit: unde etiam ab interprete Averrois anni Hegirae appellantur anni a praedicatione Muhamedis. Sequimur autem Saracenum, cum facimus initium annorum Hegirae a feria sexta: is enim ita scribit, Quidam incipiunt computationem mensium a nocte quinta feria, & ponunt ibi Almuharam anni repulsionis: & quidam ponunt ipsum a nocte diei Veneris, & secundum illud fixum est ista noster liber: quoniam ista dies fuit initium anni veri, & est magis conveniens ortui novae lunae. Ex quibus verbis perspicere licet, nos Hegiram incipere a phasi lunari, quae incidit in principium feriae sextae, & minimum integro die post coniunctionem mediam solis & lunae in oculos incurrit.
units.tr: The Arabs begin their thirty-year cycle from the Hegira of Muhammad, that is, from the migration of their false prophet. This took place in the year of Christ 622, on the sixteenth of July, a Friday, the Dominical letter being C; that is, in the year 1370 of Nabonassar, on the 28th day of the month Chiac. So when converted to the Arabic era, the years of Nabonassar are 1369 years and 117 days, that is, in all 499,802 days. That the Arabic era begins from the time when Muhammad the false prophet is said to have fled from Mecca to the city of Yathrib, because of the plots of his enemies, is attested by our Alfraganus in the first chapter. But he, with all the astronomers, assigns the weekday mark of the Arabic years to the fifth feria, that is, Thursday, which falls on 15 July in the year of Christ 622, as Jordanus attests when he says: "The years of the Arabs began in the year of the Lord 622, on the Ides of July, when C was the Dominical letter." From this it is clear that the fifth feria, which the letter G there denoted, was for them the initial day. The reason why the astronomers take the beginning of the Hegira from the fifth feria is the conjunction of the sun and moon, which fell on a Thursday, as can easily be gathered from the Julian enneadecaeteris. We, however, following the civil custom, take the beginning of the Hegira from the sixth feria, that is, the day of assembly, which followed the heavenly new moon. On that day, after recovering Mecca, Muhammad began to preach and took care to have his impious dogma promulgated. Hence also the years of the Hegira are called by the interpreter of Averroes the years of the preaching of Muhammad. We follow Saracenus when we make the beginning of the years of the Hegira the sixth feria, for he writes thus: "Some begin the reckoning of months from the night of the fifth feria, and place there Almuharam, the year of repulsion; and some place it from the night of Friday; and our book has fixed on this, since that day was the beginning of the true year and is more suitable to the rising of the new moon." From these words it may be seen that we begin the Hegira from the lunar phase, which falls at the beginning of the sixth feria, and which appears to the eyes at the earliest a full day after the mean conjunction of the sun and moon.

units.la: Cum igitur fixerimus aeram Arabica ex visu politico ad vesperam diei 16 Iulii, feria sexta, annoque Christi currente 622: restat ut in annis expansis & collectis Arabum characteres feriarum exponamus. Antequam autem id peragamus, videndum est, qui characteres sint hebdomadici singulorum mensium in anno primo Hagareno: ut ex illis erui possint feriae mensium reliquorum annorum. Annus primus Hegirae coepit feria sexta, itaque mensis Safar coepit feria prima, Rabie prior, feria secunda, &c. ut ex sequenti tabella apparet. 1 | Muharam | feria | 6 | 30 | 7 | Regab | feria | 1 | 207[?] 2 | Safar | 1 | 59 | 8 | Schaban | 3[?] | 236[?] 3 | Rabie prior | 2 | 89 | 9 | Ramadhan | 4 | 266 4 | Rabie posterior | 4 | 118 | 10 | Schewal | 6 | 295 5 | Gumadhi prior | 5 | 148 | 11 | Dhilkahde | 7 | 325 6 | Gumadhi posterior | 7 | 177 | 12 | Dhilhaga | 1 | 354
units.tr: Therefore, since we have fixed the Arabic era, from the civil viewpoint, at the evening of the sixteenth of July, a Friday, in the current year of Christ 622, it remains for us to set out the weekday marks of the years in the expanded and collected Arabic years. Before we do this, however, we must see what the weekday marks of the individual months are in the first year of the Hegira, so that from them the weekdays of the remaining months of the years may be drawn out. The first year of the Hegira began on a Friday (feria 6), so the month Safar began on feria 1, Rabi I on feria 2, and so on, as appears from the following table. 1 | Muharram | feria 6 | 30 | 7 | Rajab | feria 1 | 207[?] 2 | Safar | feria 1 | 59 | 8 | Shaban | feria 3[?] | 236[?] 3 | Rabi I | feria 2 | 89 | 9 | Ramadan | feria 4 | 266 4 | Rabi II | feria 4 | 118 | 10 | Shawwal | feria 6 | 295 5 | Jumada I | feria 5 | 148 | 11 | Dhu al-Qa'da | feria 7 | 325 6 | Jumada II | feria 7 | 177 | 12 | Dhu al-Hijja | feria 1 | 354

units.la: Adiectos habes in tabula dies, quos habet mensis unus, duo, tres, quatuor, &c. ut duodecim menses continent 354 dies, in anno scilicet communi: siquidem in anno bisextili 12 menses efficiunt 355 dies, quia ad postremũ mensem Dhilhaga vel Dhilhitsche appellatum accedit dies vnus intercalaris. Si ergo alicuius anni Hagareni Muharam non incipiat à feria sexta, sed ab alia quacunque; tunc oportet collationem instituere cum feria ipsius æræ, & differentiam inter vtramque notare: quæ enim proportio est in primo mense, ea deinceps quoq; retinetur in sequentibus. Exempli gratia, annus Hegiræ 990 cœpit feria quinta, noƈte scilicet præcedente diem 25 Ianuarii, anno Christi 1582. si ergo feriam hanc quintam cõferas cum feria sexta ipsius æræ Arabicæ, deprehendes differentiam vnius diei. Quamobrem sicut vnitas à sex subtracta relinquit quinque, characterem Muharam anni 990 Hagareni: ita vnitas subtracta ab vnitate relinquit nihil, quod indicium est mensem Safar anni 990 incipere à feria septima, quæ incurrit in 24 Februarii, anno Christi 1582. Porro cum Idus nouæ Gregorianæ incipiant post IIII Nonas Octobris Iulianas, anno eodem Christi currente 1582: quatenus exempti vel potiùs anticipati sunt decem dies, vt quo die nos secundum veterem stilum assignamus quintum diem Octobris, alii scribant nouo stilo decimum quintum Octobris: non fuerit alienum hoc loco ostendere, in quem diem anni Hagareni & Nabonasari incidat epocha Gregoriana. A vigesima quinta die Ianuarii inclusiuè vsque ad Idus Gregorianas exclusiuè numerãtur 253 dies, qui efficiunt octo menses Arabicos, & 17 dies: atqui Muharam anni Hagareni 990 cœpit feria quinta, ergo Ramadhan eiusdem anni cœpit feria tertia, quæ incurrit in 18 Septembris anno Christi 1582. Itaque dies decima octaua mensis Ramadhan anni 990 Hegiræ, respondet primis idibus Gregorianis: quæ incurrerunt in feriam sextam. Eodem anno Christi 1582 incidit ThothNabonafari 2331, feria tertia, quæ incurrit in 24 diem Iulii: atqui à 24 Iulii inclusiuè vsque ad primas idus Gregorianas exclusiuè numerantur 73 dies, qui efficiunt duos menses Ægyptios, & 13 dies. itaque dies decima quarta mensis Athyr, anni Nabonafari 2331, respondet primis idibus Gregorianis. Sed interuallum inter idus Gregorianas, & vltimam Decembris, à cuius meridie moreaftronomico[?] incipit annus Christi 1583, est 87 dierum.
units.tr: You have in the table the added days, which one, two, three, four, and so on months contain; so that twelve months contain 354 days in a common year. In a bissextile year, however, the twelve months make 355 days, because one intercalary day is added to the last month, called Dhu al-Hijja or Dhilhitsche. If therefore the Muharram of some Hegira year does not begin on a Friday but on some other day, then one must make a comparison with the weekday of that era and note the difference between the two. For whatever proportion holds in the first month, the same is retained in the following ones. For example, the Hegira year 990 began on a Thursday (feria 5), namely on the night preceding the 25th of January in the year of Christ 1582. If you compare this fifth feria with the sixth feria of the Arabic era itself, you will find a difference of one day. Therefore, just as one subtracted from six leaves five, which is the mark of Muharram of the Hegira year 990, so one subtracted from one leaves nothing, which is the sign that the month Safar of the year 990 began on the seventh feria, which fell on 24 February in the year of Christ 1582. Further, since the Gregorian Ides begin after the fourth Nones of October in the Julian reckoning, in the same year of Christ 1582, in so far as ten days were removed, or rather anticipated, so that the day we assign by the old style as the fifth of October, others write in the new style as the fifteenth of October, it will not be out of place to show here on which day the epoch of the Hegira and of Nabonassar falls in the Gregorian reckoning. From the 25th of January inclusive up to the Gregorian Ides exclusive, 253 days are counted, which make eight Arabic months and 17 days. But Muharram of the Hegira year 990 began on a Thursday; therefore Ramadan of the same year began on a Tuesday (feria 3), which fell on 18 September in the year of Christ 1582. Thus the eighteenth day of the month Ramadan of the Hegira year 990 corresponds to the first Gregorian Ides, which fell on a Friday (feria 6). In the same year of Christ 1582, Thoth of Nabonassar 2331 fell on a Tuesday (feria 3), which fell on the 24th of July. Now from 24 July inclusive up to the first Gregorian Ides exclusive, 73 days are counted, which make two Egyptian months and 13 days. Thus the fourteenth day of the month Athyr of the year 2331 of Nabonassar corresponds to the first Gregorian Ides. But the interval between the Gregorian Ides and the last day of December, from whose midday the astronomical reckoning begins the year of Christ 1583, is 87 days.
