units.la: Annus primus cùm simplex fit, constat 354 die-bus: qui fi per septem diuidantur, in residuo relin-quunt quatuor: hæc ad sex characterem radicis adie-cta producunt decem: à quibus fi subtrahantur fep-tem, remanet ternarius, qui character est anni fe-cundi, incipientis feria tertia. Annus autem fecun-dus cùm bisextilis fit, constat 355 diebus: qui efficiunt
units.tr: When the first year is common, it consists of 354 days. If these are divided by seven, four remain. Added to the radical character 6, these make ten; if seven is subtracted from ten, three remains, which is the character of the second year, beginning on Tuesday (feria tertia). When the second year is leap, it consists of 355 days, which make

units.la: so[?] septimanas, & quinque dies: hi quinque dies additi characteri praecedentis anni, producunt octo: à quo septenarius subtractus, relinquit vnitatem, quae character est anni tertii incipientis à feria prima: eodem modo examinare poterimus reliquos characteres feriarum in tabella praescriptos.
units.tr: fifty(?) weeks and five days. These five days, added to the character of the preceding year, produce eight; if seven is subtracted from this, one remains, which is the character of the third year, beginning on Sunday (feria prima). In the same way we can examine the remaining weekday characters prescribed in the table.

units.la: Si autem exquiras ferias in principio singulorum cyclorum, vt inde reliquorum annorum characteres elicias; en tibi hanc tabulam proponimus.
units.tr: If you wish to find the weekdays at the beginning of each cycle, so that from them you may derive the characters of the remaining years, we set before you this table.
Cycles. | Hagarene years. | Weekdays.
Cycles. | Hagarene years. | Weekdays.

units.la: Primus annus primi cycli, vt paulò ante dictum est, coepit feria sexta: secundus cyclus, hoc est, annus Hagarenus trigesimus primus incipit feria quarta: annus 61 inchoat feria secunda, &c. quod facile poterimus probare per 10631 dies, qui in unoquoque cyclo comprehenduntur: si enim eos re-degerimus in 1518 septimanas, remanebunt quinque dies qui ad characterem radicis, videlicet ad 6 adiecti, producunt undecim. a quibus si auferas 7, remanet quaternarius, qui character est anni primi in secundo cyclo: quod si adieceris quinque ad hunc characte-rem, proueniunt 9: a quo septem sublata, relinquunt duo, qui character est anni Hagareni 61, hoc est, anni primi in tertio cyclo. Qui ergo characteres sunt septem cyclorum primorum, ij deinceps suo ordine repetuntur, hoc modo, 6.4.2.7.5.3.1.
units.tr: As was said a little above, the first year of the first cycle began on a Friday; the second cycle, that is, the thirty-first Hagarene year, begins on a Wednesday; year 61 begins on a Monday, and so on. This we can easily prove from the 10631 days contained in each cycle: for if we reduce these days to 1518 weeks, five days remain, which, added to the radical character 6, make eleven. If seven is subtracted from this, four remains, which is the character of the first year of the second cycle; if five is added to this character, nine results, from which if seven is taken away, two remain, which is the character of Hagarene year 61, that is, of the first year of the third cycle. So the characters of the first seven cycles, in their order, repeat as follows: 6.4.2.7.5.3.1.

units.la: Si voles habere initia annorum reliquorum in sin-gulis cyclis, considera, qua feria primus annus cuiuf-que cycli incipiat, eamque confer cum feria anni primi in cyclo primo: quae enim ibi erit differentia, eadem manebit in annis subsequentibus. Exempli gratia, annus Hagarenus 991, hoc est, annus primus cycli trigesimi quarti, incipit feria tertia, quae incurrit in decimam quintam Ianuarii, diem martis, anno Christi labente 1583. Hanc feriam tertiam si conferas cum feria sexta radicis, videbis differentiam esse feriarum trium: ut ergo tria subtracta a sex relinquunt tria, qui character est anni propositi Hagareni 991: ita si tria demantur a characteribus sequentium annorum in cyclo primo positis, relinquuntur veri characteres omnium annorum trigesimi quarti cycli: ut annus secundus primi cycli incipit feria tertia, a qua si auferantur tres feriae, remanet nihil. quod indicium est, annum Hagarenum 992, hoc est, annum secundum cycli trigesimi quarti incipere feria septima: siquidem principium anni illius incurrit in quartam Ianuarii, diem sabbati, labente anno Christi 1584: ut ex diplomate Turcico prolixius osten-demus demus in tabulis chronologicis.
units.tr: If you wish to have the beginnings of the remaining years in each cycle, consider on which weekday the first year of each cycle begins, and compare it with the weekday of the first year of the first cycle; whatever difference there is will remain the same in the following years. For example, Hagarene year 991, that is, the first year of the thirty-fourth cycle, begins on Tuesday, which falls on 15 January, a Tuesday, in the year of Christ 1583 then running. If you compare this Tuesday with the radical Friday, you will see the difference is three weekdays. As three subtracted from six leaves three, which is the character of the proposed Hagarene year 991, so if three is taken from the characters of the following years placed in the first cycle, the true characters of all the years of the thirty-fourth cycle remain. For the second year of the first cycle begins on Tuesday, and if three weekdays are taken from it, nothing remains. This is a sign that Hagarene year 992, that is, the second year of the thirty-fourth cycle, begins on Saturday, since the beginning of that year falls on 4 January, a Saturday, in the year of Christ 1584 then running. We shall show this more fully from a Turkish diploma in the chronological tables.

units.la: Ostendimus haftenus quomodo examen feriatum fit instituendum in annis Arabicis : restat vt dispiciamus quomodo dati anni Christi Arabicis sint applicandi, vel quomodo dati anni Arabum[?] annos Chriftifint conuertendi. Exempli gratia, cupio scire quis dies & annus Arabum respondeat 26 diei Ianuarij, anno Christi 1582: sane ab aera Nabonafari vfq; ad aeram Arabum, transierunt anni aequabiles 1369, & 117 dies: sed ab aera Nabonafari vfq; ad 26 Ianuarij, anni Christi 1581, elapsi sunt anni aequabiles 2329, & 186 dies: sicut ex tabulis chronologicis apparebit. Si ergo minor numerus subtrahatur a maiori, relinquuntur anni aequabiles 960, & 69 dies: quod est interuallum inter aeram Arabum & tempus propositum. Hoc interuallum commutandum est in annos Arabicos, fecundum regulam proportionum hoc modo: anni aequabiles 19, & 46 dies suppeditant 30 annos Arabicos: quot Arabicos suppeditabunt anni aequabiles 960, & 69 dies? vel vt eadem fit denominatio, primumq; cycli proueniant, sic ad quaestionem problema hoc est disponendum: dies 10631 dant cyclum vnum: quot cyclos efficiunt 960 anni aequabiles, & 69 dies, hoc est dies in vniuersum 350469? Si dies 350469 diuidantur per 10631 dies, proueniunt cycli exacti 32, qui efficiunt annos Arabicos 960: sed in residuo remanent 10277 dies, qui suppeditant annos aequabiles 28, & 57 dies, hoc est, annos Arabicos 29: qui fi adiiciantur ad annos 960 Arabicos, producunt summam 989 annorum Arabicorum, qui elapsi sunt ante diem 26 Ianuarij anno Christi 1582. Quamobrem intelligitur Muharam anniHagareni 990 incurrere in 26 Ianuarij eiusdem anni Christi 1582: quod etiam character feriæ fatis indicat: annus enim Hagarenus 990 a feria sexta incipit, ut ex canonibus supra traditis perspicere licet: atqui feria sexta incurrit in 16 [?] Januarij diem, sicut ex ephemeridibus apparet. Hic vero obiter notandum est, omnes ferias naturaliter incipere ab ortu solis: sed Arabes cum Hebræis anticipant initia dierum a præcedenti vespera: & Ægyptij supputant ferias a meridie, quæ sequitur ortum folarem. Quamobrem cum allerimus æram Nabonafari cœpisse feria quarta; volumus eam initium sumsisse a meridie, quæ secuta est ortum solis die quarto: eadem ratione a Nabonafaro vsq; ad æra Arabica statuimus transiisse annos æquabiles 1369, & 117 dies, & 6 horas: quatenus ab occasu solis feriæ quintæ, initium sumimus feriæ sextæ, quæ epocha est annorum Hagarenorum. Sic etiam cum dicimus a Nabonafaro usq; ad 16 Januarij diem, anno Christi 1582 elapsos esse annos æquabiles 2329, & 186 dies: volumus a meridie Nabonafari feriæ quartæ, usq; ad meridiem diei 16 Januarij, feriæ sextæ tot annos & dies præteriisse: sed iuxta Arabum calculum, qui annum Hagarenum 990 incipiunt ab occasu solis feriæ quintæ, a Nabonafaro usque ad annum Hagarenum 990, elapsi tantum sunt anni æquabiles 2329, & 185 dies, cum sex horis.
units.tr: So far we have shown how the weekday reckoning is to be carried out in Arabic years. It remains to see how given years of Christ are to be applied to Arabic years, or how given Arabic years are to be converted into years of Christ. For example, I wish to know what day and year of the Arabs corresponds to 26 January in the year of Christ 1582. Certainly from the era of Nabonassar to the era of the Arabs there passed 1369 mean years and 117 days; but from the era of Nabonassar to 26 January of the year of Christ 1581 there elapsed 2329 mean years and 186 days, as will appear from the chronological tables. If the smaller number is subtracted from the larger, there remain 960 mean years and 69 days, which is the interval between the era of the Arabs and the time proposed. This interval must be converted into Arabic years by the rule of proportion, thus: 19 mean years and 46 days supply 30 Arabic years; how many Arabic years will 960 mean years and 69 days supply? Or, so that the denomination is the same and the cycles come out first, the question is to be set out as a problem thus: 10631 days make one cycle; how many cycles do 960 mean years and 69 days make, that is, how many days in all, 350469? If the 350469 days are divided by 10631 days, 32 exact cycles result, which make 960 Arabic years; but 10277 days remain, which supply 28 mean years and 57 days, that is, 29 Arabic years. If these are added to the 960 Arabic years, they make a sum of 989 Arabic years, which elapsed before 26 January of the year of Christ 1582. Hence it is understood that Muharram of Hagarene year 990 falls on 26 January of that same year of Christ 1582. The character of the weekday also sufficiently indicates this: for the Hagarene year 990 begins on Friday, as may be seen from the canons given above; and Friday falls on 16 January, as appears from the ephemerides. Here, incidentally, it must be noted that all weekdays naturally begin at sunrise, but the Arabs, together with the Hebrews, anticipate the beginnings of days from the preceding evening, and the Egyptians reckon the weekdays from noon, which follows sunrise. Therefore, when we state that the era of Nabonassar began on Wednesday, we mean that it began at noon following sunrise on the fourth day; by the same reasoning we hold that from Nabonassar to the Arabic era there passed 1369 mean years, 117 days and 6 hours, so that we take the beginning of Friday from sunset of Thursday, which is the epoch of the Hagarene years. Likewise, when we say that from Nabonassar to 16 January of the year of Christ 1582 there elapsed 2329 mean years and 186 days, we mean that from noon of Nabonassar's Wednesday to noon of 16 January's Friday so many years and days have passed; but according to the reckoning of the Arabs, who begin the Hagarene year 990 at sunset on Thursday, from Nabonassar to the Hagarene year 990 there have elapsed only 2329 mean years and 185 days, with six hours.

units.la: Si cupiam scire quis dies & annus Christi respondeat primo diei mensis Muharam anni Hagareni 991: cogitandum est a die 16 Julij anno Christi 622, usq; ad annum Hagarenum 991, elapsos esse annos Arabicos 990, qui efficiunt cyclos triginta tres, hoc est, in universum dies 350823, qui per 365 divisi fugerunt annos æquabiles 961, & 58 dies: qui si adiiciantur ad annos Nabonafari 1369[?],& 117 dies,producunt summam annorum Nabonafari 2330, & 175[?] dierum, vsq; ad annum Hagarenum 991 completorum. Ex quo intelligitur diem 26 mensis Mechir,labentis anni Nabonafari 2331 respodere neomeniæ Muharam anni Hagareni 991; atqui annus Nabonafari 2331 incurrit in 24 Iulii, feriam tertiam, anno Christi 1582, vt ex tabulis nostris chronologicis patebit. Si ergo hinc inclusiue numerentur 175 dies,peruenitur ad 15 diem Ianuarii exclusiue, anno Christi 1583. quamobrem dies decima quinta Ianuarii anni Christi 1583 est initium anni Arabici 991. idem comprobat examen feriarum in annis Nabonafari & Hegiræ.
units.tr: If I wish to know which day and year of Christ corresponds to the first day of the month Muharam of the year 991 of the Hegira, I must reckon from 16 July in the year of Christ 622 to the year 991 of the Hegira. The Arabic years that have elapsed are 990, which make thirty-three cycles, that is, 350,823 days in all. Divided by 365, these leave 961 common years and 58 days. If these are added to the years of Nabonassar, 1369[?] and 117 days, they make a sum of 2330 years and 175[?] days of Nabonassar, completed up to the year 991 of the Hegira. From this it is understood that the 26th day of the month Mechir, in the current year 2331 of Nabonassar, corresponds to the new moon of Muharam in the year 991 of the Hegira. Now the year 2331 of Nabonassar falls on 24 July, a Tuesday, in the year of Christ 1582, as will be clear from our chronological tables. If, then, 175 days are counted from here inclusively, we arrive at 15 January exclusive, in the year of Christ 1583. Therefore the fifteenth day of January in the year of Christ 1583 is the beginning of the Arabic year 991. The check of the weekdays in the years of Nabonassar and of the Hegira confirms the same.

units.la: Ex his duobus propositis exemplis satis apparet, quomodo beneficio annorum Iulianorū & Nabonafari anni Arabici sint conferendi cum annis Chri-sti; siquidem nulla alia methodo eos inter se conci-liare possumus. Porro sciendum est Muhamedanos celebrare duplex Pascha; maiusculum & minusculu. maiusculu vocant kurban beirami, hoc est, oblati-onepafchale,idq; celebrant semper neomenia Schewal: minusculum vocant Vrutsch beirami, hoc est, ieiunium paschale, & id peragunt x die mensis Zilhitsche. Interuallum inter vtrumq; est mensiu duo-rum solidorum, & decem dierum. Aliqui vtuntur mensibus Iulianis, vt cum Martio conferant suum Ramadhan, cum Aprili Sche Wal, &c. quod observandum est, ne confundantur characteres feriarum mensium vagorum Hegiræ cum feriarum Iulianarum indiciis.
units.tr: From these two examples set forth, it sufficiently appears how the Arabic years are to be compared with the years of Christ by means of the Julian years and the years of Nabonassar, since we cannot reconcile them with one another by any other method. Furthermore, it must be noted that the Muhammadans celebrate a double Passover: the greater and the lesser. They call the greater kurban beirami, that is, the paschal offering, and they always celebrate it on the new moon of Schewal. The lesser they call Vrutsch beirami, that is, the paschal fast, and they keep it on the tenth day of the month Zilhitsche. The interval between the two is two full months and ten days. Some use Julian months, so that they match their Ramadhan with March, their Schewal with April, and so on. This must be observed, lest the marks of the weekdays of the wandering months of the Hegira be confused with the indications of the Julian weekdays.
On the Persian Calendar.

units.la: PErfæ more Ægyptiorum menfes duodecim constant ex 360 diebus: quibus adiungunt quinq; dies appendices, vt annos habeant perpetuò a qua-biles, constantes 365 diebus. Nomina menfium Perficorum, vt ab Hebraeo noftro interprete scri-buntur, in fine adiunctam habent dictionem Meh vel Mech, quae menfem significat: nam Afrurdn-meh[?], Ardipafchtmeh, Chardimeh, idem eft ac fi dicas Afrurdin menfis, Ardipafcht menfis, Chardi menfis &c, eos fuo ordine in fequenti tabella habes defcriptos.
units.tr: The Persians, like the Egyptians, have twelve months of 360 days each. To these they add five extra days, so that their years are always 365 days long. The names of the Persian months, as our Hebrew interpreter writes them, end in the word Meh or Mech, which means month. Afrurdin-meh, Ardipaschtmeh, Chardimeh are the same as saying the month Afrurdin, the month Ardipascht, the month Chardi, and so on. You have them described in their order in the following table.
1 Afrurdin, days | 30
2 Ardipascht | 30
3 Chardi | 30
4 Thir | 30
5 Merded | 30
6 Schaharir | 30
7 Mahar | 30
8 Aben | 30
9 Adar | 30
11 Behemen | 30
12 Asfirer | 35

units.la: Menfis Asfirer conftat diebus 35, quot etiam habet Mefori Ægyptiorum: adiiciuntur enim quinque dies appendices. Alfraganus cum Albategnio asserit menfem Aben intercalarem effe; fed obferuandum eft Perfas duplici anno uti, ecclefiaftico nimirum & ciuili; in illo menfis Aben cenfetur intercalaris, in hoc vero ad menfem Asfirer quinq; dies intercalares adiiciuntur. Nam anno Chrifti 632 Perfae cum Hebraeis conuenerunt, vt principia Nifan & Di concurrerent circa aequinoctiu vernum, atq; deinceps fingùli menfes in hunc modum opponerentur. Menfes Hebraeorum | Menfes Perfarum Nilan[?] | Di dierum | 30 Ijar | Behemen | 30 Siuan | Asfirer | 30 Tamuz | Afurdin | 30 Ab | Ardipafcht | 30 Elul | Chardi | 30 Tifri | Thir | 30 Marchefwan | Merded | 30 Cisleu | Schaharir | 30 Tebeth | Mahar | 30 Schebet | Aben | 35[?] Adar | Adar | 30
units.tr: The month Asfirer consists of 35 days, as the Egyptian Mesori also does, since five extra days are added to it. Alfraganus, with Albategnius, asserts that the month Aben is intercalary. But it must be noted that the Persians use a double year, ecclesiastical and civil. In the former, the month Aben is counted as intercalary; in the latter, the five intercalary days are added to the month Asfirer. For in the year of Christ 632 the Persians agreed with the Hebrews that the beginnings of Nisan and Di should coincide about the vernal equinox, and that the individual months should then be matched in this way: Hebrew months | Persian months | days: Nisan | Di | 30; Iyar | Behemen | 30; Sivan | Asfirer | 30; Tammuz | Afrurdin | 30; Av | Ardipascht | 30; Elul | Chardi | 30; Tishri | Thir | 30; Marcheshvan | Merded | 30; Kislev | Schaharir | 30; Tevet | Mahar | 30; Shevat | Aben | 35; Adar | Adar | 30.

units.la: Ex qua oppositione apparet menses Mahar, Aben & Adar in anno Ecclesiastico postremos esse; & mensem Aben respondere Hebraeorum Schebet seu Syro Sabat. Ut ergo Syri post Sabat diem unum intercalarem adiiciunt; ita Persae post Aben quinq; dies appendices inserunt; quemadmodum Hebraei integrum mensem 30 diebus constantem intercalant post Schebet seu ante Adar, quando id rationes lunae & solis postulant. Et quemadmodum Hebraei ultimum mensem Adar ieiunio consecrant; ita Persae suum Adar tribuunt ieiunio, quod vocant Refeb altofeg; quamobrem Alfraganus ait in primam diem Adarmeh[?] incidere Refeb altofeg. h. e. festum ieiunii. Ante Adar diebus decem Persae viuunt Bacchanalia, quae Alfrurgen appellant; sicut Hebraei diebus undecim Purim, circa idem anni tempus vacant voluptatibus. Itaq; quinq; dies appendices, & quinque postremae dies in mense Aben constituunt decé dies bacchanalium, quòt etiā numerat Albategnius cap. 32. Quare cum in codice Alfragani Hebraeo (nam in manuscripto latino bibliothecae Palatinae horum festorum nulla fit mentio) & in Albategnio legitur, dierum decem Alfrurgen initiū esse à 16[?] die Aben; mendum est in codicibus; nam legendum est, vigesimam quintam diem mensis Aben initium esse 10 dierum, &c. Hic vero causa explicanda est, propter quam Persæ diebus decem, Hebræi autem diebus undecim genio bacchanali indulgeant. Hebræi ad mensem Adar, qui perpetuo est 29 dierum, ex mense Nisan adiiciunt undecim dies: quo compleatur tempus ieiunii 40 dierum: hos Persæ imitantur, & ex mense Diad Adar, qui ipsis est perpetuo 30 dierum, adiiciunt decem dies, vt expleatur tempus ieiunii 40 dierum. Hinc videre licet supplemento ieiunii respondere dies bacchanalium: Hebræis quidem undecim, sed Persis tantum decem. Feftu Almedgen, vel vt codex Albategnii habet, Almahregen, ait Alfraganus incidere in 16 die mensis Mahar: cum autem huic respondeat mensis Hebræorum Tebeth, in quo Iudæi celebrant neomenia obsessionis Hierofolymitanæ; verisimile est, huic folennitatem Almedgen apud Persas esse substitutam.
units.tr: From this matching it appears that the months Mahar, Aben and Adar are the last in the ecclesiastical year, and that the month Aben corresponds to the Hebrew Shevat, or to the Syrian Sabat. So just as the Syrians add one intercalary day after Sabat, the Persians insert five extra days after Aben, just as the Hebrews intercalate a whole month of 30 days after Shevat, or before Adar, when the reckonings of the moon and the sun require it. And just as the Hebrews consecrate their last month, Adar, to fasting, so the Persians devote their Adar to fasting, which they call Refeb altofeg. For this reason Alfraganus says that the first day of Adarmeh falls on Refeb altofeg, that is, the feast of the fast. Ten days before Adar the Persians hold bacchanalian festivities, which they call Alfrurgen, just as the Hebrews give themselves up to pleasures for eleven days at Purim, around the same time of year. Therefore the five extra days together with the last five days of the month Aben make up the ten days of the bacchanalia, which Albategnius also counts, in chapter 32. Hence, when the Hebrew codex of Alfraganus (for the Latin manuscript in the Palatine library makes no mention of these feasts) and Albategnius read that the ten days of Alfrurgen begin on the 16th day of Aben, the error lies in the copies. For it should be read that the twenty-fifth day of the month Aben is the beginning of the ten days, and so on. Here, however, the reason must be explained why the Persians indulge the bacchanalian spirit for ten days, but the Hebrews for eleven. The Hebrews add eleven days from the month Nisan to the month Adar, which always has 29 days, so that the period of fasting is completed at 40 days. The Persians imitate this, and from the month Di they add ten days to their Adar, which always has 30 days for them, so that the period of fasting is completed at 40 days. From this one can see that the days of the bacchanalia correspond to the supplement of the fast: eleven among the Hebrews, but only ten among the Persians. Alfraganus says that the feast of Almedgen, or as the codex of Albategnius has it, Almahregen, falls on the 16th day of the month Mahar. Since the Hebrew month Tevet corresponds to this, and in it the Jews celebrate the new moon of the siege of Jerusalem, it is likely that the feast of Almedgen was substituted for it among the Persians.

units.la: Vt autem cognoscatur, vnde principium fit æræ Persicæ respectu anni ecclesiastici; sciendum est anno Christi 632 æquinoctiū vernū incurrisse in 18 diem Martii, feriam quartam, in quam incidit Thoth Nabonafari 1380; quod ex Alfragano colligere licet, qui a't menses Aegyptiorum tunc respondisse mensibus Perfarū, vt Thoth Nabonafari 1380 conuenerit cum Dimeh Persico; & postrema dies anni scilicet Nabonafari 1379 inciderit in postremam diem Adarmeh.
units.tr: In order to establish from what point the Persian era begins in relation to the ecclesiastical year, it must be noted that in the year of Christ 632 the vernal equinox fell on 18 March, a Wednesday, the day on which 1 Thoth of Nabonassar 1380 fell. This can be gathered from Alfraganus, who says that the Egyptian months at that time corresponded to the Persian months, so that 1 Thoth of Nabonassar 1380 coincided with 1 Dimeh of the Persians, and the last day of the year, namely of Nabonassar 1379, fell on the last day of Adarmeh.

units.la: Quamobrem facilimū est annos ecclesiasticos Perfarū extendere; exempli gratia, anno Christi 1588 incurrit Thoth Nabonafari 2337 feria fecunda, die 21 Iulii: fi ergo anni 1379 subtrahantur ab annis 2337, remanet annus 958 Perfarū, qui respondet anno Nabonafari 2337. Itaq; neomenia Dimeh Perfici anni nongentesimi quinquagesimi octaui respon-
units.tr: Therefore it is very easy to extend the Persian ecclesiastical years. For example, in the year of Christ 1588, 1 Thoth of Nabonassar 2337 falls on a Monday, 21 July. If, then, 1379 is subtracted from 2337, there remains the 958th year of the Persians, which corresponds to the year 2337 of Nabonassar. Thus the new moon of Dimeh of the 958th year of the Persians responds

units.la: det zz[?] Iulii anno Christi 1588; & neomenia Epiphi anni Nabonalari 2537, quæ stilo veteri incurrit in dominica Pẽtecoftes, die decimo octauo Maii, anno Christi 1589, respondet neomeniæ Aben; qui mensis cum fecundum vsum ecclefiafticu constet 35 diebus, 30 scilicet ordinariis & quinq; appendicibus, finem habet in 21 Iunii, hoc est, in quinto die Mefori anni Nabonalari 2337, quare neomenia Adarmeh perpetuo respondet sexto diei Mefori Ægyptio-rum.
units.tr: to the [?] of July in the year of Christ 1588. And the new moon of Epiphi of the year 2537 of Nabonassar, which in the old style falls on Whit Sunday, 18 May, in the year of Christ 1589, corresponds to the new moon of Aben. Since this month, according to ecclesiastical usage, consists of 35 days, namely 30 ordinary days and 5 appended days, it ends on 21 June, that is, on the fifth day of Mesori in the year 2337 of Nabonassar. Hence the new moon of Adarmeh always corresponds to the sixth day of Mesori of the Egyptians.

units.la: Annum ciuilem ordiuntur Persæ ab Afrurdin, vt quinque dies appendices adiiciant ad mensem Assi-rer. incidit autem principium æræ politicæ in diem decimam sextam Iunii, feriam tertiam, anno Christi 632; & peculiari nomine hæc æra dicitur Iezdagirdica, sicut etiam anni politici Persarum appel-lantur Iezdagirdici, quòd scilicet computentur a morte Iezdagird regis Persarum: hic alias Iezda-jer, Ifdran & Afcaiorth dicitur, quem Haiton Ar-menius in paffagio terræ sanctæ cap. 15, dicit ad op-pidum Marga a Saracenis interfectum esse anno Christi 632. Quo id die factum fuerit ostendit Al-bumafar in libro de magnis coniunctionibus, videli-cet feria Martis, die vigefima fecunda Rabie prioris, (quatenus initiu Hegiræ ducitur a coniunctione solis & lunæ, quæ incidit in decimam quintam Iulii feriam quintam anno Christi 622, vt in calendario Arabico est expositum) vel die vigefima prima Rabie prioris, anno Hagareno vndecimo; prout nos ex vsu politi-co initiu Hegiræ sumimus a feria sexta, quæ incurrit in diem 16 lulii, anno Christi 622. Quod autem æra Iezdagirdica incurrat in 16 Iunii, feriam tertiam anno Christi fexcentefimo trigesimo fecundo, euidenter ostendit Alfraganus, cum ait, ante æram Persicam elapsos esse annos Nabonafari 1379, & tres menses Persicos, hoc est, 90 dies. idem scribitur in translatione veteri Almagesti ad finem libri tertii. Atqui annus Nabonafari 1380 incurrit in 18 diem Martii, feriam quartam, anno Christi 632. Si ergo a die prædicta inclusiue numeremus tres menses Ægyptios seu Persicos, descendimus ad neomeniam Chiac, quæ incidit in feriam tertiam, 16 Iunii, anno Christi 632: a qua initium sumitur æræ Persarum Iezdagirdicæ. Idem probari potest ex interuallo, quod ab autoribus inter æram Arabum & Persarum constituitur: nam Alfraganus noster capite primo, & Alkabitius differetia quarta, in capite de profectionibus signorum, & Alfonsus in canone ærarum ponunt interuallum 3624 dierum. idem absq; dubio reperitur in codice Arabico Albategnii: idem habet Albumafar, qui etiam hoc addit, inter primum annum Alhegiræ & interfectum Iezdagird intercefisse annos Persicos 9, & vndecim menses, & nouem dies: qui in vniuersum efficiunt 3624 dies, iuxta principium Hegiræ astronomicum. Saracenus autē, quem noscum vulgo Arabū Turcorūmve sequimur, sumit initium æræ Arabicæ a feria sexta; ideoq; interuallum inter Arabes & Persas constituit tantum 3623 dierum, vt testatur hisce verbis, Et postquam transierunt de æra Arabum tria mill'a[?] sexcenti viginti tres dies, qui complentur cum consummatione diei secundi, sumserunt Persa diem tertium, qui fuit post ipsum initium regis eorum Iezdajer.
units.tr: The Persians begin their civil year from Afrurdin, so that they add five appended days to the month Assirer. The beginning of the political era falls on 16 June, a Tuesday, in the year of Christ 632. This era is called by the special name Iezdagirdic, just as the Persian political years are called Iezdagirdic, because they are counted from the death of Iezdagird, king of the Persians. He is also called Iezda-jer, Ifdran and Ascaiorth, and Hayton the Armenian, in his Passage of the Holy Land, chapter 15, says that he was killed by the Saracens at the town of Marga in the year of Christ 632. On what day this happened Albumasar shows in his book on the great conjunctions, namely on a Tuesday, the twenty-second day of Rabi I (inasmuch as the beginning of the Hegira is reckoned from the conjunction of sun and moon, which fell on a Thursday, 15 July, in the year of Christ 622, as is set out in the Arabic calendar), or the twenty-first day of Rabi I in the eleventh year of the Hagarenes. We, following political usage, take the beginning of the Hegira from a Friday, which fell on 16 July in the year of Christ 622. That the Iezdagirdic era falls on 16 June, a Tuesday, in the year of Christ 632, Alfraganus clearly shows, when he says that before the Persian era had elapsed the years of Nabonassar 1379 and three Persian months, that is, 90 days. The same is written in the old translation of the Almagest at the end of the third book. And yet the year Nabonassar 1380 falls on 18 March, a Wednesday, in the year of Christ 632. If, then, we count the three Egyptian or Persian months from the aforesaid day, inclusive, we arrive at the new moon of Chiac, which falls on a Tuesday, 16 June, in the year of Christ 632, from which the beginning of the Iezdagirdic era of the Persians is taken. The same can be proved from the interval that the authors fix between the era of the Arabs and that of the Persians. For our Alfraganus, in chapter 1, and Alkabitius, difference 4, in the chapter on the progressions of the signs, and Alfonsus in the canon of eras, put the interval at 3624 days. The same is undoubtedly found in the Arabic codex of Albategnius. Albumasar has the same, and he adds that between the first year of the Hegira and the killing of Iezdagird there elapsed 9 Persian years, 11 months and 9 days, which in total make 3624 days, according to the astronomical beginning of the Hegira. The Saracen, however, whom we commonly follow among the Arabs and Turks, takes the beginning of the Arabic era from a Friday, and therefore fixes the interval between Arabs and Persians at only 3623 days, as he attests in these words: And after three thousand six hundred and twenty-three days had passed from the era of the Arabs, which are completed with the end of the second day, the Persians took the third day, which was after the beginning of their king Iezdajer.

units.la: Cum igitur probatum sit æram Iezdagirdicæ incurrere in primam diem mensis Chiac anno Nabonafari 1380. & constet Saracenos, qui post interfeCum[?] Iezdagird regnū Persidis occuparunt, ad men-sem Affirer sive Alphandar quinque dies appendices adiecisse, ubi in hodiernum usque diem sedem fixam retinent: non difficile fuerit annos Iesdagirdicos in-dagare, & in multas centurias extendere. Nam neomenia Chiac anni Nabonasari 1380 concurrit cum principio annorum Iezdagirdicorum: & neomenia Di Iezdagirdici prima incurrit in neomeniam ἐπαγ-μένων anno Nabonasari 1380: ut sexta dies mensis Di anno primo Iezdagirdico inciderit in principium anni Nabonasari 1381: sexta dies mensis Behemen in neomeniam Paophi, & sexta dies mensis Affirer in neomeniam Athyr, dies vero trigesima quinta Affirer incurrerit in diem ultimam Athyr Ægyptiorum anno currente Nabonasari 1381: itaque annus secundus Iezdagirdicus iterum incepit a neomenia Chiac. Licet ergo propter diversum situm quinque dierum appendicum postremi tres menses Persici non conveniant cum mensibus Ægyptiis: eorum tamen anni perpetuo incipiunt cum Chiac Nabonasari ,! ut hi novem menses Afrurdin, Ardipascht, Chardi,Thir, Merded, Schaharir, Mahara, Aben, Adar per omnes dies praecise respodeant[?] mensibus Ægyptiorū Chiac, Tybi,Mechir,Phamenoth,Pharmuthi,Pachon,Payni,Epiphi,Mesori. Quamobrem si a quocunque anno Nabonasari subtrahamus annos æquabiles 1379 residuum ostendit annum Iezdagirdicum: exempli gratia,si ab anno Nabonasari 1380 subtrahamus annos nos 1379 æquabiles, remanet unitas, quae indicio est annum primum Iesdagirdicum incipere a Chiac anno Nabonasari 1380 labente: ita si ab anno Nabonasari 2337[?] subtrahamus annos 1379 æquabiles;videmus relinqui 958. quod indicium est annum Iezdagirdicum 958 incipere à Chiac anni Nabonasari 2337.
units.tr: Since it has therefore been shown that the Yazdegerdian era falls on the first day of the month Chiac in the year 1380 of Nabonassar, and it is agreed that the Saracens, who seized the kingdom of Persia after Yazdegerd was killed, added five intercalary days to the month Affirer or Alphandar, where they still keep them fixed to this day, it will not be difficult to work out the Yazdegerdian years and extend them over many centuries. For the new moon of Chiac in the year 1380 of Nabonassar coincides with the beginning of the Yazdegerdian years, and the new moon of the first Di of the Yazdegerdian era falls on the new moon of the epagomenae in the year 1380 of Nabonassar. So the sixth day of the month Di in the first Yazdegerdian year falls on the beginning of the year 1381 of Nabonassar; the sixth day of the month Behemen falls on the new moon of Paophi, and the sixth day of the month Affirer on the new moon of Athyr; and the thirty-fifth day of Affirer falls on the last day of Athyr of the Egyptians in the current year 1381 of Nabonassar. Thus the second Yazdegerdian year again began at the new moon of Chiac. Therefore, although because of the differing position of the five intercalary days the last three Persian months do not agree with the Egyptian months, nevertheless their years always begin with Chiac of Nabonassar. Thus these nine months, Afrurdin, Ardipascht, Chardi, Thir, Merded, Schaharir, Mahara, Aben and Adar, correspond exactly, day for day, to the Egyptian months Chiac, Tybi, Mechir, Phamenoth, Pharmuthi, Pachon, Payni, Epiphi and Mesori. Hence, if from any year of Nabonassar we subtract 1379 equal years, the remainder shows the Yazdegerdian year. For example, if from the year 1380 of Nabonassar we subtract 1379 equal years, a unit remains, which indicates that the first Yazdegerdian year began at Chiac in the year 1380 of Nabonassar, that year having run out. Likewise, if from the year 2337 of Nabonassar we subtract 1379 equal years, we see that 958 remains, which indicates that the Yazdegerdian year 958 began at Chiac of the year 2337 of Nabonassar.

units.la: Porro obseruandu eft, Perfas obferuare magnum annum Cynicum, feu periodum annorum Ægyptiorum 1460,quæ prodit ex multiplicatione quadriennii folaris in dies 365, quos habet integer annus Perficus feu Ægyptius. Cum enim quouis quadriennio folari Thoth Nabonafari diem vnu afcendat defcendatve, fit vt totum contextum anni fimplicis peruagetur elapsis annis 1460 Ægyptiis, qui efficiunt annos folares 1461. Quod ex Cenforino intelligere licet,cum ait, Ægyptiorum annus cimilis folos habet dies trecentos fexaginta quinque fine vllo intercalari. Itaq; quadriennium apud eos vno circiter die minus eft quam naturale quadriennium, eoq; fit vt anno millefimo quadringentefimo fexagefimo primo ad idem reuoluatur principium. Exempli gratia, fi Thoth Nabonafari in æquinoctium vernum incidat; poft elapfos annos 1460 redit ad idem æquinoctium, vbi totum contextum anni fimplicis perluftrauit. Hic vero nobis certa opus eft hiftoria, ex qua intelligamus, vnde cyclus magnus Perfarum initium habeat: id nos docet Ifaacus Monachus in explicatione canonum Perficorum, qui extant manuscripti in bibliotheca Palatina. Locus is, quem mihi de authentico codice exfcripfit doctiffimus & humanifimus vir D.Fridericus Sylburgius, ita habet:
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be observed that the Persians keep the great Cynic year, or period of 1460 Egyptian years, which arises from multiplying the solar quadrennium by the 365 days that a full Persian or Egyptian year contains. For since with every solar quadrennium the Thoth of Nabonassar moves forward or back one day, it comes about that the whole cycle of the simple year is run through after 1460 Egyptian years, which make 1461 solar years. This can be understood from Censorinus, when he says: The Egyptian civil year has only 365 days, with no intercalation at all. Therefore their quadrennium is about one day shorter than a natural quadrennium, and so in the 1461st year it returns to the same starting point. For example, if Thoth of Nabonassar falls on the vernal equinox, then after 1460 years it returns to the same equinox, having passed through the whole cycle of the simple year. Here, however, we need a reliable history, from which we may learn where the great cycle of the Persians begins. Isaac the Monk teaches us this in his explanation of the Persian canons, which exist in manuscript in the Palatine library. The passage, which my most learned and kindly friend Frederick Sylburg copied for me from an authentic codex, reads as follows:

Καὶ Περσας ὁ οἱ μῆνες ὀνομαζονται ἵτως· φαρυαρτης, ἀρπιτες, χορτατ, τυρμα, μερτατ, σαχισρ, μισχρμα, ἀ- παρμα, ἀδιρμα, δημα, πεχμαν, ἀσφανδαρηματ, μασιαρ- χα, ὅν φασιν οἱ Ἕλληνες ἐπαγόμενον. Ἐστι δὲ καὶ παρ' αὐτοῖς ὁ ἐνιαυτὸς τξι ἡμερῶν μόνων, ὡςπερ καὶ παρ' Αἰγυπτίοις· ἑκάστῳ μηνὸς παρ' αὐτοῖς λογιζομένου ἡμερῶν λ, καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ ἐπαγόμενου. ὡς συμβαίνει ἐξ αἰδίκης κατὰ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν τῶν Περσῶν ἐνιαυτὸν ἀναμβάνειν τὸν κατὰ Ῥωμαίους, ἡμέρα μία, διὰ τὸ κατὰ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν κατὰ Ῥωμαίους ἡμερῶν γίνεσθαι τξ'ἐν ὅλοις δὲ αὐξ ἐπ- ιν, ὁλοκληρῷ Περσικῷ ἐπὶ, καὶ πάλιν ἅμα τὴν ἀρχὴν τῶν ἐτῶν ποιεῖν Περσας τε καὶ Ῥωμαίος· μετὰ δὲ ἀναμβανομένη ἐνιαυτῷ, αὖθις ἀρχέσθαι τοῖς Πέρσαις ἀναμβανειν ἡμᾶς ἡμέρα α, καὶ ἐξῆς πάλιν ἀκολούθως. Γίγνεται ἡ εἰρημένη διὰ αὐξ ἐπὶ ὑπο- κατάσασις ὑπὸ τινος ἀρχῆς χρόνῳ, ὡς τζ ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς τῆ Ιασδηγέρδου βασιλείας. ὡς ἐκ τούτου πάλιν τῇ χρόνου τὴν ἀρ- χὴν εἰκνφίναι τοῖς Πέρσαις κατὰ δὲ ἐπὶ τὴ ἡμέρα μία ἀναμβά- νειν ἡμᾶς. hoc est, Persicorum canonum composi- tio facta est illic à mathematicis primo anno Iezda- girdi Sarien Mastre regis Persarum, Persicos annos vsurpantibus. Fuit autem is annus sex millesimus centesimus trigesimus nonus à mundi conditu, incipiens à meridie neomeniæ mensis Persarum Pha- ruarti, secundum Tybenæ Persicæ vrbis meridia- num, secundum longitudinem distantis gradus 72 ab Ntzaer chalitat, vt loquuntur Persæ: hoc est, ab extremitate maris occidentalis.
units.tr: The composition of the Persian canons was made there by the mathematicians of the Magi, in the first year of Iezdegerd, king of the Persians, who used the Persian years. That year was the 6139th from the creation of the world, beginning at noon on the new moon of the Persian month Pharuarti, reckoned by the meridian of the Persian city Tybene, which lies 72 degrees of longitude from the so-called Ntzaer chalitat, as the Persians say, that is, from the extremity of the western sea. The Persians name their months thus: Pharuartes, Arpites, Chortat, Thyrma, Mertat, Sachisr, Mischrma, Apārma, Adirma, Dēma, Pechman, Asphandarimat, Masiarcha, which the Greeks call the intercalary month. Among them too the year has only 365 days, as among the Egyptians, each of their months being reckoned as 30 days, with the added days at the end. Thus it happens that every four years the Persian year runs ahead of the Roman year by one day, since in four Roman years there are 366 days; so that after 1460 years the whole cycle of the Persian year has been run ahead and the Persians and Romans again coincide at the beginning of the year. Then, after the quadrennium has run its course, the Persians again begin to run ahead of us by one day, and so on in the same way. The aforesaid revolution of 1460 years was completed at a certain starting point in time, which came 307 years before the beginning of the reign of Iezdegerd, from which time the Persians again began to run ahead of us by one day in each quadrennium. [That is, the Latin gloss:] The Persian canons were composed in the first year of Iezdegerd, king of the Persians; and from that year the Persians have again begun to run ahead of us by one day in each quadrennium.

units.la: Iuxta Persas men- ses nominantur sic. pharuartis, artipeest, chortat, thyrma, mertat, sachriur, mecherma, apanma, aderma, dima, pechman, asphandarimat, masi- archa, quem nominant Græci intercalarem. Est autem apud ipsos annus 365 dierum tantum, sicut etiam apud Ægyptios: quouis mese apud ipsos obtinente 30 dies, accedentibus quinque diebus appendicibus. Itaque necessario accidit ut quouis quadriennio annus Persarum anteuertat annum Romanorum, die una, cum quarto quouis anno apud Romanos oriantur 366 dies, ut annis 1460 elapsis totus contextus anni Persici anteuertatur, & circa principium anni iterum conueniant Persæ & Romani: deinceps verò post quadriennii decursum iterum incipiunt Persæ anteuertere nos die uno, & deinceps similiter. Absoluta autem fuit prædicta annorum 1460 revolutio quodam temporis principio, quod antecessit trecentis & septem annis initium imperii Iezdagirdi: ex quo tempore denuò cœperunt Persæ nos anteuertere die una secundum quadriennii circuitum. Vocat hic Isaacus Monachus æram Iezdagirdicam, principium regni Iezdagirdici, sicut etiam Alfraganus noster existi-mat annos Persarum incipere à regno Iezdajeris: verùm æra Iezdagirdica sumitur à morte Iezdagird, sicut apud Ptolemæum epocha Alexandri dicitur, cuius initium à morte Alexandri computatur. Mortuus autem est Iezdagird rex Persarum anno Christi 632, die decimo sexto Iunii, feria martis, ut ante probavimus: si ergo ab anno Christi 632 auferamus annos 307, quos ante canones Persicos transiisse refert Isaacus, remanet annus Christi 325, quo celebratus, est primus consessus Nicænus, anno scilicet Alexandri Dhilkarnain 636. [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~20 letters] mensis Dæsij die xix, quæ incurrit in decimum tertium diem kalendarum Iulii, Anitio Paulino, Ceionio Iuliano Coss. ut refert Socrates.
units.tr: Isaac the Monk calls the Iezdegerdian era the beginning of Iezdegerd's reign, just as our Alfraganus thinks the Persian years begin from the reign of Yazdajerd. But the Iezdegerdian era is reckoned from the death of Iezdegerd, just as in Ptolemy the epoch of Alexander is spoken of, whose beginning is reckoned from the death of Alexander. Now Iezdegerd, king of the Persians, died in the year of Christ 632, on the sixteenth day of June, a Tuesday, as we showed earlier. If therefore we subtract from the year of Christ 632 the 307 years which Isaac reports had passed before the Persian canons, there remains the year of Christ 325, in which the first Council of Nicaea was held, in the year 636 of Alexander Dhilkarnain. [illegible] [illegible] the day 19 of the month Daesius, which falls on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Anicius Paulinus and Ceionius Julianus, as Socrates reports.

units.la: Ex quibus concluditur cyclum magnum Persarum incipeincipere a primo consessu Nicæni concilii, vt anno Christi sexcentefimo trigesimo secundo ab æquinoctio verno ineat annus 308 magnæ periodi Persarum: quamobrem Isaacus concessum primum Nicænum indicat, quādo ait nouam reuolutionem annorum 1460, coepisse ἀπὸ τίνος ἀρχῆς χρόνου[?], τῆς ἀρχῆς τῆς Ἰαζδηγέρδου βασιλείας[?]. quasi dicat, a notabili & orbi Christiano saluberrimo tempore, elapsis annis 307 ante aeram Iezdagirdicam, seu vsum canonum Persicorum, iniisse cyclum magnum Persarum. Qui cum initium concilii Nicæni exacte nobis ostendat, ad nostram ætatem est continuandus: hæc autem methodus est, ab annis Christi labentibus auferantur anni 324: reliquum ostendet annum cycli magni Persici à concilio Nicæno ineuntis: exempli gratia, si ab anno Christi 325 auferantur 324; relinquitur vnitas, quæ indicat annum Christi 325 fuisse primum cycli Persici: ita si ab anno Christi 632 subtrahantur 324, relinquitur in residuo 308, quod indicium est, annum Christi 632 esse trecentesimum octauum ab inito concilio Nicæno. Eodem modo si 324 subducantur ab anno Christi 1588, relinquitur 1264: ergo annus Christi 1588 est annus millesimus ducentesimus sexagesimus quartus cycli magni Persici. Monet etiam Isaacus æram Persicam cœpisse in neomenia mensis Pharuarti, hoc est, Afrurdin: quod autem nouilunium tunc inciderit, ex enneadecaeteride facilè perspici potest. Notanda quoque est ἀκυρολογία in appellatione mensium Ægyptiorum & Persicorum: nam quinque dies appendices siue intercalares, appellantur mesis, scilicet intercalaris. Hinc est, quòd Ptolomæus primam dierum appendicum vocet ῥαμνίας ἐπαγομένων[?], & Isaacus quinque dies intercalares appel[illegible, ~6 letters] ἐπαγόμενον, quasi tredecim in vniuersum sint menses: duodecim perfecti, quorum singuli cōstant 30 diebus: postremus autem sit imperfectus, solum-modo habens quinque dies, qui Musteraka siue Ma-siarcha dicitur. Nomina mensium Persicorum, quæ recitat Isaacus, non multum discrepant ab illis quæ Alfraganus proponit. Quod autem dicit Isaacus æ-ram Iezdagirdicam incidere elapsis annis à conditu mundi 6139, in eo sequitur peculiarem opinionem, quæ non conuenit cum reliquorum Græcorum, Moscouitarum aut Christianorum Arabum calculo: ex qua diuersitate non obscurum est intelligere, nihil certi nobis constare de æra aut connexione annorum mundi.
units.tr: From these things it follows that the great Persian cycle began at the first session of the Council of Nicaea, so that in the year of Christ 632, from the vernal equinox, the 308th year of the Persian great period begins. Therefore Isaac indicates the first Council of Nicaea, when he says that the new revolution of 1460 years began from a certain starting point in time, the beginning of Iezdegerd's reign; as if to say that from a notable time, most salutary for the Christian world, 307 years before the Iezdegerdian era, or the use of the Persian canons, the great Persian cycle was entered upon. Since this exactly shows us the beginning at the Council of Nicaea, it must be continued down to our own age, and the method is this: from the elapsed years of Christ subtract 324, and the remainder gives the year of the great Persian cycle beginning from the Council of Nicaea. For example, if 324 is subtracted from the year of Christ 325, a unit remains, which shows that the year of Christ 325 was the first of the Persian cycle. Likewise, if 324 is subtracted from the year of Christ 632, 308 remains, which indicates that the year of Christ 632 was the 308th from the beginning of the Council of Nicaea. In the same way, if 324 is subtracted from the year of Christ 1588, 1264 remains: therefore the year of Christ 1588 is the 1264th year of the great Persian cycle. Isaac also notes that the Persian era began at the new moon of the month Pharuarti, that is, Afrurdin; and which new moon fell then can easily be seen from the nineteen-year cycle. The misuse of terms in the names of the Egyptian and Persian months is also to be noted: the five appended or intercalary days are called a month, namely an intercalary month. Hence Ptolemy calls the first of the appended days the epagomenae, and Isaac calls the five intercalary days the epagomenon, as if there were thirteen months in all: twelve complete months, each of which has 30 days, and a last incomplete month having only five days, which is called Musteraka or Masiarcha. The names of the Persian months which Isaac recites do not differ much from those which Alfraganus gives. But when Isaac says that the Iezdegerdian era fell after 6139 years from the creation of the world, he follows a peculiar opinion, which does not agree with the reckoning of the other Greeks, the Muscovites or the Christian Arabs. From this disagreement it is not hard to see that nothing certain is known to us about the era or the connection of the years of the world.
On the Syrian Calendar.

units.la: Quæ sint nomina mensium Syriacorum expositum est in scholiis, quæ adiecimus ad appendicem vltimi capitis Alfragani. Cum autem Syri & Syrogræci cum Romanis annos suos supputent à regno Seleuci Nicanoris, & annis solaribus vtantur, quorum principium est ab autumno, seu prima die Octobris: placet hic ipsorum menses inter se conferre.
units.tr: The names of the Syriac months were set out in the notes we added to the appendix of the last chapter of Alfraganus. Since the Syrians and Syro-Greeks reckon their years from the reign of Seleucus Nicanor, as the Romans do, and use solar years, which begin in autumn, that is, on the first day of October, it is worth comparing their months with one another here.
