units.la: Quæritur hic, cur dicamus Syros cū antiquis Ro-manis manis à regno Seleuci Nicanoris,seu ab æra Alexādri Dhilkarnain, usos fuisse mensibus Iulianis, cūm ante ordinationem Iulii Cæsaris tales nūquam extiterint? & cur Syrogræcos putemus in suis mensibus obser-vasle distinctionem dierum,quę convenit mensibus Iulianis, cūm constet Græcos ab Alexandro vsque ad Actiacam Augusti victoriam vsurpasle menses Macedonicos & Atticos? Non est dubitandum, quòd tempore Actiacæ victoriæ, Ægyptii, Syri, Græci, Hebraei,& quicunq; populi fuerunt sub imperio Romano,acceperint forma calendarii Iuliani:dum autè hoc extenditur ad principium annorum Alexandri, Nabonasari & Olympiadum,ex hypothesi Arabum proceditur, qui id docendi gratia posuerunt. Neque tamen historiæ quicquam decedit, cūm Ptolemæus & Arabes accuratissimè exposuerint, quàtum sit intervallum dierum inter æram Dhilkarnain & Thoth Actiacum, item inter æram Chaldæorum & Actiacam Augusti victoriā: vt perinde sit ac si reuera tales anni & mēses Iuliani in vsu fuissent, cūm ex dato numero dierū huiusmodi anni & menses Iuliani possint cōslari. Quod sanè artificiosissimū & elegantissimum est inuentum: sine quo nō possumus peruenire ad æquinoctiorū vel epocharū lunariū per enneadecaeteridem inuestigationē: nec sine illo dierum cum annis Nabonasari connexionem apprehendere valemus.
units.tr: The question arises here why we say that the Syrians, together with the ancient Romans, used Julian months from the reign of Seleucus Nicanor, or from the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain, when such months never existed before the reform of Julius Caesar. And why do we think the Syro-Greeks observed in their months a division of days that agrees with the Julian months, since it is established that the Greeks, from Alexander down to Augustus's victory at Actium, used Macedonian and Attic months? There is no doubt that at the time of the victory at Actium the Egyptians, Syrians, Greeks, Hebrews, and all other peoples under Roman rule adopted the form of the Julian calendar. But when this is extended back to the beginning of the years of Alexander, Nabonassar, and the Olympiads, we proceed on the hypothesis of the Arabs, who adopted it for the sake of teaching. Nor does history lose anything by this, since Ptolemy and the Arabs have set out with great exactness how many days lie between the era of Dhilkarnain and the Actian Thoth, and likewise between the era of the Chaldeans and Augustus's victory at Actium. So it is just as if such Julian years and months had really been in use, since from a given number of days such Julian years and months can be calculated. This is a most skilful and elegant invention, without which we cannot arrive at the equinoxes or lunar epochs by investigation through the enneadecaeteris, nor grasp the connection of days with the years of Nabonassar.

units.la: Est autē pernecessariū, vt intelligamus tempus æræ Dhilkarnain: hoc enim ignorato multa nos latēr, quæ eleganter ab historicis sunt conscripta. Asserit Saracenus æram Alexādri Dhilkarnain incepisse die lunæ, kalendis Octobris: vt interuallum inter æram Alexandri & Arabum sit 340701 dierum. Sed cūm istud difficilimum sit intelligere; respiciatur annus
units.tr: It is absolutely necessary that we understand the time of the era of Dhilkarnain, for if this is unknown, many things that historians have written elegantly will remain hidden from us. The Saracen asserts that the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain began on a Monday, on the Kalends of October, so that the interval between the era of Alexander and the Arabs is 340,701 days. But since this is very hard to grasp, let us look at

units.la: primus Iulianus,& ab eo exclusiue retrorsum numerentur anni folares ducenti & sexaginta sex, hoc est, exactæ enneadecaeterides quatuordecim, cum tribus mensibus Decembri, Nouembri & Octobri: tuc ascenditur ad æram Dhilkarnain, quæ incurrit in annum folarem habentem literam dominicalem G, & XIX pro aureo numero: in quem incidit Thoth Nabonalari quadringentesimus trigesimus septimus, feria sexta, nono die Nouembris: vt prima Octobris anni prædicti solaris habenda fit pro æra Alexandri Dhilkarnain. Atqui in prima Octobris incurrit dies vigefima septima Epiphi anni Nabonalari quadringentesimi trigesimi septimi sexti: quamobrem concludimus ante æram Dhilkarnain elapsos esse annos Nabonafari quadringentos triginta quinque, cum diebus trecentis viginti sex, hoc est, in vniuersum 1 5 9101 dies.
units.tr: the first Julian year, and count backwards from it, excluding it, 266 solar years, that is, fourteen exact enneadecaeterides, together with the three months December, November, and October. Then we arrive at the era of Dhilkarnain, which falls in a solar year having the dominical letter G and 19 as the golden number, and into which Thoth 437 of Nabonassar fell, on a Friday, the ninth day of November. So the first of October of that aforesaid solar year is to be taken as the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain. Yet on the first of October there falls the twenty-seventh day of Epiphi in the 437th year of Nabonassar. Therefore we conclude that before the era of Dhilkarnain there had elapsed 435 years of Nabonassar, with 326 days, that is, 159,101 days in all.

units.la: Hi fi subtrahantur ab annis Ægyptiis 1369, & 117 diebus, hoc est, à diebus in vniuersum 499802, qui fluxerunt à Nabonafaro vsque ad politicam æram Arabum, relinquuntur 340701 dies, quod est interuallum inter æram Alexandri Dhilkarnain & Arabum, teste Saraceno. Hinc apparet, qua methodo inuestigandi sint anni Alexandri: fi enim ad annos Iulianos adiiciantur anni 267, prouenit principium annorum Dhilkarnain, quod perpetuo incidit in primam Octobris: quare cum tres menses, October scilicet, Nouember & December, cum annis ducentis sexaginta sex, sint elapsi vfq; ad kalendas primas Iulianas, fi adiiciantur nouem primi menses Iuliani, videlicet Ianuarius, Februarius, Martius, Aprilis, Maius, Iunius, Iulius, Augustus & September, completur annus ducentesimus septuagesimus sexagesimus ab æra Dhilkarnain elapsus, vt anno primo Iuliano, kalendis Octobribus incipit ineat annus ducetefimus sexagesimus octauus Alexandri. Sicut ergo 267 anni absoluti fi ad primum annum Iulianum adiiciantur, producunt 268; quod indicium est annum Alexandri ducentesimum sexagesimum octauum incurrere in kalendas Octobres anni primi Iuliani; ita fi ad reliquos annos Iulianos adiiciantur 267 anni completi, semper prouenit principium annorum Alexandri: incurrens in kal. Octobres labentium annorum Iulianorum. Hac ratione intelligitur, quod in annum Iulianum 369, hoc est, in annum Christi 324 incurrat principium anni 636 Alexandri, ipsis scilicet kal. Octobribus. fi enim ad annum labentem Iulianum 369 adiiciamus 267, consurgit annus 636 Alexandri: sub cuius finem, decimo nono scilicet Iunii die, labente anno Christi 325, Socrates scribit celebratum esse primum confessum Nicaenum. Ita fi addatur summa annorum 267 ad annum Iulinanum 924; prouenit annus Dhilkarnain 1191; cuius initium est a kalendis Octobribus. Cum ergo scribit Albategnius, fe obferuaffe anno Alexandri Magni 1191, qui fuerit annus Nabonafari 1627, quod stella inter duos Scorpionis oculos fuerit in 17 gradu & 50 min. Scorpionis; intelligitur eum initio hiemis in anno praedicto 1191 Alexandri obseruationem instituisse. Idem Albategnius asserit fe obferuaffe eclipfin lunae die 23 mensis Tamuz fiue Iulii, anno Dhilkarnain 1194, qui fuerit annus a morte Alexandri 1206, hoc est, Nabonafari 1630: quia vero mentionem nullam facit mensis Aegyptii; incertum est, an per Iulium intelligat eum mensem qui incidit in annum Nabonafari 1630, vel eum qui incurrit in annum 1194 Dhilkaruain. fi enim priorem intelligeret, effet is Iulius anni Iuliani 927, hoc est anni Christi 882[?]: fi posteriorem accipi vellet, eflet is Iulius anni Iuliani 928, fiue anni Christi 883. Sed Albategnius dubitationem hanc soluit, quando eodem anno Nabonafari 1630, cum octauo die mensis Pachon confert decimum nonu diem Elul, hoc est, Septembris: retento eodem anno Dhilkarnain 1194: ex quo intelligitur eum referre Iulium & Septembre ad annum Nabonalari 1630,cuius Thoth incurrit in 15 Ianuarij labente anno Dhilkarnain 1193. Quamobrem obseruandum est dupliciter accipi annos Dhilkarnain: uno modo, ut sint anni vere folares, quorum quartus quifq; accipiat diem intercalarem: altero modo, ut sint perpetuo æquabiles more Ægyptiorum: atq; tunc Thoth Nabonafari 437 initium est æræ Dhilkarna-in:fi itaq; ab annis datis Nabonafari abiiciantur anni Ægyptij 436,consurgunt anni Dhilkarnain:vel fi ad annos Dhilkarnain adiiciantur anni Ægyptij 436, prodeunt anni Nabonafari. Hoc modo Albategnius accipit annos Dhilkarnain: ita quoq; vsurpat Hebræ-us de æris & interuallis temporum, quando ad diem 24 Martij, feriam feprimam, anno Christi 1191 dicit elapsos esse ab Alexandro annos 1501 cum 173 die-bus, vt ostendemus in tabulis chronologicis.
units.tr: If these are subtracted from the Egyptian years, 1369, and 117 days, that is, from the days in all, 499,802, which flowed from Nabonassar down to the civil era of the Arabs, there remain 340,701 days, which is the interval between the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain and the Arabs, according to the testimony of the Saracen. Hence it appears by what method the years of Alexander are to be investigated. For if 267 years are added to the Julian years, the beginning of the years of Dhilkarnain results, which always falls on the first of October. Therefore, since three months, October, November, and December, together with 266 years, have elapsed up to the first Julian Kalends, if the nine first months of the Julian year are added, namely January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, and September, the year 266 from the era of Dhilkarnain is completed, so that in the first Julian year, on the Kalends of October, the 268th year of Alexander begins. Just as 267 completed years added to the first Julian year produce 268, which shows that the 268th year of Alexander falls on the Kalends of October of the first Julian year, so if 267 completed years are added to the other Julian years, the beginning of the years of Alexander always results, falling on the Kalends of October of the passing Julian years. By this reasoning it is understood that the beginning of the 636th year of Alexander falls in the Julian year 369, that is, in the year of Christ 324, on the Kalends of October itself. For if 267 is added to the passing Julian year 369, the 636th year of Alexander arises; towards the end of which, namely on the nineteenth day of June, in the year of Christ 325, Socrates writes that the first Council of Nicaea was celebrated. Thus if 267 is added to the Julian year 924, the Dhilkarnain year 1191 results, whose beginning is the Kalends of October. Therefore when Albategnius writes that he observed in the year 1191 of Alexander the Great, which was the year 1627 of Nabonassar, that a star between the two eyes of Scorpio was at 17 degrees 50 minutes of Scorpio, it is understood that he made the observation at the beginning of winter in the aforesaid year 1191 of Alexander. The same Albategnius asserts that he observed a lunar eclipse on the twenty-third day of the month Tamuz, or July, in the year 1194 of Dhilkarnain, which was the year 1206 from the death of Alexander, that is, 1630 of Nabonassar. But since he makes no mention of an Egyptian month, it is uncertain whether by July he means the month that falls in the year 1630 of Nabonassar, or the one that falls in the year 1194 of Dhilkarnain. For if he meant the former, that July would be July of the Julian year 927, that is, of the year of Christ 882 [?]; if he wished the latter to be understood, that July would be July of the Julian year 928, or of the year of Christ 883. But Albategnius resolves this doubt when, in the same year 1630 of Nabonassar, he compares the eighth day of the month Pachon with the nineteenth day of Elul, that is, of September, keeping the same year 1194 of Dhilkarnain. From this it is understood that he refers July and September to the year 1630 of Nabonassar, whose Thoth falls on the fifteenth of January in the year 1193 of Dhilkarnain. Therefore it must be observed that the years of Dhilkarnain are taken in two ways: in one way, so that they are truly solar years, of which every fourth receives an intercalary day; in the other way, so that they are always equal, after the manner of the Egyptians. Then Thoth 437 of Nabonassar is the beginning of the era of Dhilkarnain. So if 436 Egyptian years are subtracted from the given years of Nabonassar, the years of Dhilkarnain result; or if 436 Egyptian years are added to the years of Dhilkarnain, the years of Nabonassar arise. Albategnius takes the years of Dhilkarnain in this way, and the Hebrew likewise uses this reckoning for the era and the intervals of time, when he says that on the 24th of March, the seventh day of the week, in the year 1191 of Christ, 1501 years with 173 days had elapsed since Alexander; as we shall show in the chronological tables.

units.la: Prioris modi exemplum extat in tabulis astronomicis Humeni Ægyptij, quas Arzachel reduxit ad annos Alexandri Magni, & Magister Iohannes Papienfis eas transtulit ad annos Christi. Harum bina exemplaria in membranis scripta habet bibliotheca Palatina, vbi sic legitur: Fasta fuerunt hæ tabulæ ad certificanda loca planetarù, ad medium diem ciuitatis Antiochia, & incepit tabula Saturni uno mense ante annum Alexandri 1454, & quatuor mensibus ante annum Christi
units.tr: An example of the former method is found in the astronomical tables of Humenus the Egyptian, which Arzachel reduced to the years of Alexander the Great, and Master John of Pavia transferred to the years of Christ. The Palatine library has two copies of these tables written on parchment, where it reads thus: These tables were drawn up for establishing the places of the planets at mid-day in the city of Antioch, and the table of Saturn begins one month before the year of Alexander 1454, and four months before the year of Christ

units.la: Christi 1143. Apparet hinc annum Alexandri 1454[?] à kal. Octobribus inchoatum incidere in annū Iulianum 1187, hoc est, in annum Christi 1421: si enim iuxta traditum canonem anni 167 adiiciantur ad annum currentem Iulianum, millesimum centesimum octogesimū septimū, prodit annus millesimus quadringentesimus quinquagesimus quartus, Alexadri, cuius principium incidit in eundem annum Iulianū 1187, kalend. Octobribus. Notandum autem est, quod Humenus more Ægyptiorum annum incipiat à Septembri, quia æram Diocletiani siue martyrij Sanctorum; & vetus indictionum initium respicit: idem etiam facit Albategnius, quando annos Syrorum non ab Octobri vel Tisrin priore, sed à præcedente Elul, hoc est, Septembri inchoat: idem facit calendarium Syriacum, quod Arabicè descriptum est ad finem librorum de orthodoxa fide Iohannis Damasceni, qui & ipsi Arabicè versi extant in bibliotheca Palatina. Eandem rationem sequitur Arzachel in canonibus, quos elegantissimè in membranis manuscriptos habet bibliotheca Palatina: ibi enim annotatur, ante æram Arabum elapsos esse annos Alexandri 932, menses 9 Ægyptios, & 17 dies. Si itaq; ad annum Iulianum 666, qui est annus Christi 621, adiiciantur anni 267; prodit annus Alexandri 933, cuius principium incurrit kal. Octobribus anno prædicto Iuliano 666: ergo principium annorum Hagarenorum incurrit in 16 Iulij, currente anno Alexandri nongentesimo trigesimo tertio: postquam elapsi essent anni Christi 621, menses sex, & quindecim dies, vt ibidem testatur Arzachel: ex quo non obscurum est intelligere, eum quoq; initium æræ Arabicæ conferre in feriam sextam*.
units.tr: Christ 1143. From this it appears that the year of Alexander 1454 [?], beginning from the kalends of October, falls in the Julian year 1187, that is, in the year of Christ 1421. For if, according to the accepted canon, 167 years are added to the current Julian year 1187, the result is the year 1454 of Alexander, whose beginning falls in the same Julian year 1187, at the kalends of October. It must be noted, however, that Humenus, following the custom of the Egyptians, begins his year in September, because he looks to the era of Diocletian, or of the martyrs, and to the old beginning of the indictions. Albategnius does the same when he begins the years of the Syrians not in October or the earlier Tishri, but in the preceding Elul, that is, in September. The Syriac calendar does the same, which is written in Arabic at the end of the books of John of Damascus on the orthodox faith, and these Arabic translations also exist in the Palatine library. Arzachel follows the same reckoning in his canons, which the Palatine library holds, elegantly written by hand on parchment. There it is noted that before the era of the Arabs there had elapsed 932 years of Alexander, 9 Egyptian months and 17 days. If therefore 267 years are added to the Julian year 666, which is the year 621 of Christ, the result is the year 933 of Alexander, whose beginning falls at the kalends of October in the aforesaid Julian year 666. Therefore the beginning of the years of the Hagarenes falls on 16 July, in the year 933 of Alexander, after there had elapsed from the years of Christ 621 six months and fifteen days, as Arzachel attests in the same place. From this it is not hard to see that he also assigns the beginning of the Arabic era to the sixth day of the week [Friday].

units.la: Quod ad intercalationem & ordinem annorum bisextilium attinet; sciendum est, Syros adiicere diem intercalarem fini Februarij, vt tunc habeat vndetriginta dies, teste Saraceno. Huiusmodi etiam nos in vulgari calendario seruamus consuetudinem, vt annis bisextilibus ad Februarium 29 assignemus dies: non enim more veterum Romanorum post 23 Februarij intercalamus diem, quasi Februarius perpetuo sit 28 dierum. Proinde frustra se torquent, qui bisextas kal. Martias comparant cū 24 die Februarij: nam Romani diem intercalarem ita intruserunt, quasi minime ad numerum ordinariorum dierum in Februario spectaret: si enim Februario attribuissent 29 dies, non opus habuissent geminare vi kal. Martias. Quod autem Dionysius Abbas Romanus geminum F adscripsit, vnum scilicet ad 24, alterum vero ad 25 Februarii diem, locum veteris intercalationis aliquo modo adumbrare voluit. Sed vt in conspectu habeas discrimen vtriusq; intercalationis, considera tabellam subsequentem. Intercalatio Romanorum. | Intercalatio nostra & Syrorum. 23 | vii kal. Martij | 23 | E ◦ | Bisextæ kal. Mart. | 24 | F 24 | vi kal. Mart. | 25 | F 25 | v kal. Mart. | 26 | G 26 | iv kal. Mart. | 27 | A 27 | iii kal. Mart. | 28 | B 28 | Pridie kal. Mart. | 29 | C
units.tr: As regards intercalation and the order of the leap years, it must be known that the Syrians add an intercalary day at the end of February, so that it has twenty-nine days, according to Saracenus. We in the common calendar also keep this custom, assigning the 29th day to February in leap years; for we do not, after the manner of the ancient Romans, intercalate a day after 23 February, as if February always had 28 days. Therefore they labour in vain who compare the bissextile kalends of March with 24 February, for the Romans inserted the intercalary day as if it did not at all belong to the number of the ordinary days in February. For if they had assigned 29 days to February, they would not have needed to double the sixth day before the kalends of March. But that Dionysius the Roman abbot wrote a double F, that is, one at the 24th and another at the 25th day of February, was a way of somehow indicating the place of the old intercalation. But so that you may have before your eyes the difference between the two intercalations, consider the following table. Roman intercalation: 23, vii kal. Martij; 24, F, bissextile kal. Mart.; 25, F, vi kal. Mart.; 26, G, v kal. Mart.; 27, A, iv kal. Mart.; 28, B, iii kal. Mart.; 29, C, pridie kal. Mart. Our intercalation and that of the Syrians: 23, E; 24, F; 25, F... [the remaining entries as in the table above, with the bissextile day falling after 23 February].

units.la: nnos Alexandri Dhilkarnain feruare huncor-d. acm, vt duo primi sint simplices, tertius vero intercalaris, testatur Saracenus hisce verbis: Et connuenerunt in ara Alexandri propter secretum quoddam, quod posuerunt vnumquemq; duorum primorum an-norum norum absolutum absq; bisexto ex trecentis sexaginta quinq; diebus, & posuerunt tertium bisextilem, ex 366 diebus, deinde processerunt a tertio anno, interstitio annorum quaternario bisextum intercalantes. Fasti sunt ergo anni bisextiles apud eos tertius, septimus, vndecimus, decimus quintus, & sic deinceps reliqui anni quadriennali interuallo discreti. Cum ergo Arabes voluerint annum folarem ducentesimum sexagesimum septimum ab ordinatione Iulij Caesaris exclusiue numeratum simplicem esse, eiusq; Kal. Octobres incurrere in feriam fecundam, quae principium effet aerae Alexandri: fatis intelligitur, illius anni characterem dominicum esse literam G. quia A iuxta feriem septimanarum destinata est primo Octobris, vt videre licet in calendario generali, vbi septem literae hebdomadicae a kal. Ianuarij ad finem anni extenduntur. Etsi autem Arabes annum tertium Alexandri voluerint esse intercalarem, quasi bisextilis intrufus fueritin Februario, currente anno solari 164 ante ordinationem Iulianam: ego tamen anno praecedenti, hoc est, anno 165 ante ordinationem bisextum attribui, ideoq; geminam ibi posui literam dominicalem, videlicet ED: cum primus annus ante ordinationem Caesaris bisextilis fingatur; quia etiam ipsi Arabes putant annos Iulianos 4.8.12.16. 20.24.28.32.36.40.44.48. & 52 intercalares fuisse. Sed anni Christi & Alexandri in bisexto demum convenire coeperunt circa annum 509 Iulianum: proinde ab illo tantum tempore vsq; ad nostram aetatem anni praedicti ratione dierum bisextilium recte conferuntur.
units.tr: ... The years of Alexander, Dhilkarnain, keep this order, so that the first two are simple and the third is intercalary, as Saracenus attests in these words: And they met at the altar of Alexander on account of a certain secret, which they established: each of the first two years is complete without a leap year, of 365 days, and they established a third leap year of 366 days; then from the third year they proceeded, intercalating a leap day at an interval of four years. The leap years among them are therefore the third, seventh, eleventh, fifteenth, and so on, the remaining years being separated by a four-yearly interval. Since therefore the Arabs wished the solar year 267, counted from the ordinance of Julius Caesar exclusive, to be simple, and its kalends of October to fall on the second day of the week, which would be the beginning of the era of Alexander, it is well enough understood that the dominical letter of that year is G, since A is assigned by the order of the weekdays to 1 October, as may be seen in the general calendar, where the seven weekday letters run from the kalends of January to the end of the year. Although the Arabs wished the third year of Alexander to be intercalary, as if a leap day had been inserted in February, in the solar year 164 before the Julian ordinance, I nevertheless assigned the leap day to the preceding year, that is, to the year 165 before the ordinance, and therefore placed there the double dominical letter, namely ED. For the first year before Caesar's ordinance is taken to be a leap year, because the Arabs themselves think that the Julian years 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48 and 52 were intercalary. But the years of Christ and of Alexander began to agree in their leap years only about the Julian year 509. Therefore only from that time until our age are the said years rightly compared with respect to the leap days.

units.la: Vt autem aera Alexandri rectius innotescat, eam probatissimorum autorum sententia confirmemus. Alfonsus in canone ærarum numerat inter Alexan-drum & æra Arabū 340700 dies, quatenus æra Ara-bum feria quinta incipit: Saracenus autem ponit in-teruallum 340701 dierum, quatenus æra Arabū in-choatur feria sexta. Albumafar ait, inter duo cornua habentem, id est, Alexandrum Dhilkanain, & primū annum Alhegiræ, intercessisse annos Romanos 932, & 287 dies, qui efficiunt annos Ægyptios 933, & 155 dies, hoc est, in vniuersum 340700 dies: atq; sic cum Alfonso conuenit. Cum autem in exeplari Albumafaris subnectitur, annos Romanos 932 & 287 dies, conficere annos Arabicos 974 & 294 dies. mendum est: faciunt enim annos Arabicos 961, & 154 dies, sicut ex Arabico calendario discere potes. Alfraganus noster asserit inter Alexandru & æra Persicam intercedere annos Romanos nongetos quadraginta duos, & dies ducentos quinquaginta noue, hoc est, dies in vniuersu 344324 à quibus si subtrahatur radix Persica, quæ est 230639 dierū, remanent 1 1368 dies: quod est interuallū inter Alexandru & æra Christi. Adhæc Albumafar scribit, inter Philippum, hoc est, mortem Alexandri & Iezdagird intercessisse 955 annos Ægyptios, & 90 dies: licet in exeplari edito male legatur 950 annos. Idem Alfraganus noster testatur, quod etiā annotatum est in traslatione antiqua Almagesti, sub finem libri tertii. Atqui à Philippo, hoc est, ab æra mortis Alexandri vsq; ad Alexandru Dhilkarnain, siue æram Alexandrinā Seleucidarū, intercesserunt 4341 dies, hoc est, anni Ægyptij vndecim, & 326 dies: qui si subtrahatur ab annis Ægyptiis 955, & 9 odiebus: remanet anni Ægyptii 943, & 129 dies, h.e. anni Romani 942, & 359 dies: vt ex resolutione appa-ret: atq; hoc interuallū est inter Alexandru & mortē lezdajeIezdajetis.IdeAlbumafar fcribit,inter Philippu&Al-hegira intercefliffe annos Ægyptios 945,&116 dies: ficenim legendu eft: tranflatio vetus Almageftiid6 loco citato aflerit,quadointerPhilippu&annosAra-bu dicit intercedere annosÆgyptios 945,tresmeles Ægyptios,&126 dies.Si enim anniÆgyptij945,&116 dies, hoceft,in vniuerfum 345041 diesfubtrahatur ab annisÆgyptijs 955 &90 diebus, quod eft interuallum inter Philippum &ærå Iezdagirdicam,remanent anniÆgyptii 9,&339dies,fiueanni Perfici 9,& 11menfes,&9 dies:hoc eft in vniuerfum 3624 dies, quod interuallu eftinterAlhegiram Arabu &morte Iezdagird,tefte Alfragano. Rabbi Abrahamusfilius Chajain coputo motuu coelcftiu refert,æraAlexandricornuti,h.e.Dhilkarnain,incidiffe in principium anni ludaici 3450,a creatione mudi,die fecudo:cuius fententia nos amplectimur, cum epochæ lunari annisq; ludæorü hodie vfitatis refpodeat: & reiicimus eos,qui exiftimant æram Alexandrinam Seleucidarü incurriffe in prima die menfis Tifri,anno æræ ludaicæ ineunte 3449.Idecofirmat R. AbrahamusLeuita in kabala fua,quacum calendarioHebræo Sebastianus Munfterus edidit, vbifcribitur,ludæosincipere numerum contractuu fuorum ab eo anno,qui fuerit 3450,a creatione: idem clarius affirmatur hifce verbis, Hiftoriographi determinant verba fua ita accurate,vt indubitate dicant,lefum natum effe anno 312. iuxta computationem contractuum, & pofteaanno 33 crucifixum. Vbiobferuandum eft, æramcontractu-um fiue Minjan fchetaroth Hebræis dici æram Ale-xandri,quia inde rationem annorum fuorum luna-rium inire coeperunt, cum prius vfi fuiffent annis fo-laribus & æquabilibus Ægyptiorum. Cùm ergo æra Alexandri inciderit in principium anni 3450, à creatione mundi, iuxta supputationem Iudæorum, & Christus natus sit anno ineunte Alexandri trecentesimo duodecimo: non difficile est videre, quomodo anni mundi cònectendi sint cum annis Christi. Nam ante æram Christi, hoc est, ante annum Iulianum 46, elapsi sunt anni mundi 3760. quia ab Alexandro usque ad æram Christi elapsi sunt anni so-lares trecenti & undecim, ut apparet si anni mundi 3449, usque ad Alexandrum completi, subtrahantur ab annis mundi 3760, usque ad æram Christi elapsis: unde manifestum est, annum primum Christi incurrere in annum mundi 3761. ut annus mundi 3761 ab æquinoctio autumnali, siue à neomenia, quæ proxima est æquinoctio autumnali, anno Iuliano 45 incepisse intelligatur. Quamobrem datis annis Christi si adiiciantur anni mundi 3760, confur-guntanni Iudaici: exempli gratia, anno fundationis Casimiriani, hoc est, anno Christi 1588 si adiiciantur anni mundi 3760, resultat annus Iudaicus 5348, cuius initium est circa æquinoctium autumnale præcedentis anni Christi 1587. Cùm vero principium annorum Iudaicorum, non multum distet à principio annorum Alexandri, haud incommode possumus annos Christi conferre cum annis Alexandri, & deinde cum annis mundi: exempli gratia, in annum Christi 1588 kal. Octobribus incidit annus Alexandri 1900: qui si ad annos mundi 3449 elapsos adiiciatur, prodit annus mundi Iudaicus 5349, cuius neomenia Tishri circa autumnum incidit, die scilicet duodecimo mensis Septembris, feria quinta, ut Pascha subsequens Iudaicum, quod refertur ad annum mundi 5349, incurrat in vigesimam secundam Martii, feriam septimam, labente anno Christi 1589, quod verissimum esse Hebraei nostro tempore testantur. Quare dubitandum non est, nos veram annorum Iudaicorum connexionem ostendisse cum annis Alexandri, Iulianis, & Christi: vt Dei beneficio confirmare possimus, annum passionis Dominicae fuisse trigefimū tertium ætatis Saluatoris nostri, currete anno Iuliano septuagesimo octauo, anno vero æræ Iudaicæ labente 5793, & anno Alexandri trecetefimo quadragesimo quarto ex semisse elapso. Diem autem passionis Dominicæ constituimus feriam sextam, quæ incurrit in tertiu diem mensis Aprilis, vbi plenilunium hæsisse ennea-decaeteris Iuliana ostendit.
units.tr: So that the era of Alexander may be known more correctly, let us confirm it by the opinion of the most approved authors. Alfonso, in his canon of eras, counts 340,700 days between Alexander and the era of the Arabs, since the era of the Arabs begins on the fifth day of the week [Thursday]. Saracenus, however, gives an interval of 340,701 days, since the era of the Arabs begins on the sixth day of the week [Friday]. Albumasar says that between the two horns, that is, Alexander Dhilkarnain and the first year of the Hegira, there intervened 932 Roman years and 287 days, which make 933 Egyptian years and 155 days, that is, in all 340,700 days; and thus he agrees with Alfonso. But where in the copy of Albumasar it is added that 932 Roman years and 287 days make 974 Arabic years and 294 days, this is an error; for they make 961 Arabic years and 154 days, as you may learn from the Arabic calendar. Our Alfraganus asserts that between Alexander and the Persian era there lie 942 Roman years and 259 days, that is, 344,324 days in all. If from these there be subtracted the Persian root, which is 230,639 days, there remain 113,685 days, which is the interval between Alexander and the era of Christ. Moreover, Albumasar writes that between Philip, that is, the death of Alexander, and Yazdegerd there intervened 955 Egyptian years and 90 days, although in the printed copy it is wrongly read as 950 years. Our Alfraganus also attests the same, which is also noted in the old translation of the Almagest, at the end of the third book. But from Philip, that is, from the era of the death of Alexander, to Alexander Dhilkarnain, or the Alexandrian era of the Seleucids, there passed 4,341 days, that is, 11 Egyptian years and 326 days; if this is subtracted from the 955 Egyptian years and 90 days, there remain 943 Egyptian years and 129 days, that is, 942 Roman years and 359 days, as appears from the calculation. And this is the interval between Alexander and the death of Yazdegerd. Albumasar also writes that between Philip and the Hegira there intervened 945 Egyptian years and 116 days; for thus it must be read, since the old translation of the Almagest in the place cited says that between Philip and the Arab years there intervene 945 Egyptian years, three Egyptian months and 126 days. For if 945 Egyptian years and 116 days, that is, 345,041 days in all, are subtracted from the 955 Egyptian years and 90 days, which is the interval between Philip and the Yazdegerdic era, there remain 9 Egyptian years and 339 days, or 9 Persian years, 11 months and 9 days; that is, 3,624 days in all, which is the interval between the Arab Hegira and the death of Yazdegerd, according to Alfraganus. Rabbi Abraham son of Chayyim, in his reckoning of the motions of the heavenly bodies, reports that the era of Alexander the Horned, that is, Dhilkarnain, fell on the beginning of the Jewish year 3450 from the creation of the world, on the second day. We embrace this opinion, since it corresponds to the lunar epoch and to the years of the Jews in use today; and we reject those who think that the Alexandrian era of the Seleucids fell on the first day of the month Tishri, at the beginning of the Jewish year 3449. Rabbi Abraham the Levite likewise confirms this in his Kabbalah, which Sebastian Münster published together with the Hebrew calendar, where it is written that the Jews begin the count of their contracts from the year which was 3450 from the creation. The same is affirmed more clearly in these words: "The historians determine their words so exactly that they indubitably say Jesus was born in the year 312 according to the reckoning of contracts, and afterwards crucified in the year 33." Here it must be observed that the era of contracts, or Minjan schetaroth, is called by the Hebrews the era of Alexander, because from it they began to take the reckoning of their lunar years, whereas before they had used the solar and regular years of the Egyptians. Since therefore the era of Alexander fell at the beginning of the year 3450 from the creation, according to the Jewish computation, and Christ was born in the year 312 of Alexander at its beginning, it is not difficult to see how the years of the world are to be connected with the years of Christ. For before the era of Christ, that is, before the Julian year 46, there had elapsed 3760 years of the world, because from Alexander to the era of Christ there elapsed 311 solar years; as appears if the years of the world, 3449 completed up to Alexander, are subtracted from the 3760 years of the world elapsed up to the era of Christ. Whence it is clear that the first year of Christ falls in the 3761st year of the world, so that the 3761st year of the world is understood to have begun at the autumnal equinox, or at the new moon nearest the autumnal equinox, in the Julian year 45. Therefore, if the years of the world, 3760, are added to the given years of Christ, the Jewish years result: for example, in the year of the founding of Casimir's, that is, in the year of Christ 1588, if 3760 years of the world are added, the Jewish year 5348 results, whose beginning is about the autumnal equinox of the preceding year of Christ, 1587. Since the beginning of the Jewish years does not differ much from the beginning of the years of Alexander, we may without inconvenience compare the years of Christ with the years of Alexander, and then with the years of the world. For example, in the year of Christ 1588, at the kalends of October, falls the year 1900 of Alexander; if this is added to the elapsed years of the world, 3449, there results the Jewish year of the world 5349, whose new moon of Tishri falls about autumn, namely on the twelfth day of September, on the fifth day of the week, so that the Jewish Passover, which is referred to the year of the world 5349, falls on 22 March, on the seventh day of the week, in the course of the year of Christ 1589. The Hebrews of our time testify that this is most true. Hence there is no doubt that we have shown the true connection of the Jewish years with the years of Alexander, the Julian years, and the years of Christ; so that, by God's blessing, we may affirm that the year of the Lord's passion was the thirty-third year of our Saviour's age, in the seventy-eighth Julian year, and in the Jewish era the year 5793, and in the year 344 of Alexander, the half of which had elapsed. We fix the day of the Lord's passion as the sixth day of the week, which falls on the third day of April, where the Julian nineteen-year cycle shows that the full moon was fixed.
ON THE CALENDAR
OF THE HEBREWS

units.la: Si historias tam sacras quam prophanas diligenter expendamus, comperiemus triplicem fuisse annorum Iudaicorum rationem. Nam à mundi conditu per annos 3449, usque ad æram Alexandri, Hebraei usi sunt annis æquabilibus Ægyptiorū, hoc est, duodenis æqualibus mensibus, cū quinq; appendicibus dierum: vt annus Hebraicus in centum & viginti annis nullum embolimum mensem haberet. Cum enim epocham suam ordirentur à libra; nunquam intercalabant, nisi caput anni triginta dies integros superasset, quod fiebat annis elapsis 120. vt pulcherrimè ostendit Iosephus Scaliger de emendatione temporum, lib. 3. Sed ab æra Alexandri usque ad Thalmud congestum, usi sunt annis lunaribus, quos tamen per embolismos reuocarunt ad annos folares Alexandrinorum & Romanorum,beneficio ennea-decaeteridis Metonicæ, in qua septies intercalatur, teste Cenforino,anno scilicet 3.6.8.11.14.17.&19, vt interuallo 19 annorum solarium, [illegible, ~6 letters] (seu interlunia, ad pristinas sedes proxime restituantur, in quo spacio peraguntur 235 fermè lunationes, teste Maurolyco. Æræ Alexandrinæ initium fuit feria fecunda, incurrens in kal.Octobres anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 267, vt in tabulis chronologicis ostendemus. Hæsit tunc æquinoctium autumnale in 26 Septembris, sicut ex obseruationibus Metonis, Euctemonis & Hipparchi euidenter apparet: quamobrem neomenia proxima æquinoctio autumnali assignata fuit initio mensis Tifri, quod incidit quatriduo post æram Alexandri Dhilkarnain. Vt autem neomenia proxima æquinoctio autumnali semper initium fuit mensis Tifri Hebræorum, ita neomenia proxima æquinoctio verno initium fuit mensis Nisan, cuius die decima quinta soliti sunt Iudæi celebrare suum Pascha: in annis tamen intermediis enneadecaeteridis propter intercalationem mensis vnius solaris, subinde neomenia Nisan & Tifri longius distat à sedibus æquinoctiorum. Cum ergo supposuerimus Christum passum esse anno trecentesimo quadragesimo quarto Alexandri, fi is diuidatur per 19, in residuo relinquuntur 2, quod indicium est annum Iudaicum 3793 fuisse fecundum cycli Metonici, quare communis fuit, continens lunationes duodecim. Fuit tunc æquinoctium vernum in 21 Martii, & annus iste Iulianus 78 ex enneadecaeteride Iuliana habuit aureum numerum 2, qui ponitur ad 13 kal. Aprilis in calendario Iuliano, vt significet die 20 Martii incidere nouilunium proximum æqui-noctio noctio verno: si ergo neomenia Nisan figatur in 2o Martii, vtique decima quinta Nisan incurret in 3 A-prilis, feriam sextam, qua Dominus noster crucifi-xus est. Quamobrem Iudaei circa annum Domini 469, quo obsignarunt Thalmud Hierosolymita-num, & circa annum Domini 507, quo obsignatum est Thalmud Babylonium, in odium Christi statuerunt nunquam neomeniam Tishri celebradam esse feria sexta, quod ea die Dominum gloriae crucifi-xistent: & ordinationem annorum praescripserunt, quam adhuc vsurpant, vt scilicet enneadecaeteris non amplius sumatur iuxta cyclum Metonicum, sed iuxta annos mundi supputetur. In duodecim mensibus reti-nuerunt prisicum numerum dierum, vt alternatim sint 30, & 29 dierum, cum vna lunatio ad vsum politicum poscat sibi 29 dies ac dimidium, neglectis scrupulis horariis. Ergo annus communis & ordinarius apud Hebraeos constat trecentis & quinquaginta quatuor diebus: sed nonnunquam ad mensem Marche-fwan dies adiicitur, atque tunc annus habet trecentos & quinquaginta quinque dies, vocaturq; plenus siue abundans: aliquando ex mense Cisleu tollitur dies, & tunc annus completitur trecentos & quinquaginta tres dies, & vocatur deficiens. Annus embolimaeus superat annum communem & ordinarium 30 diebus: quia propter rationes lunares, ante Adar intercalatur mensis dierum 30, qui dicitur Adar embolimaeus: quamobrem annus embolimaeus idemq; ordinatus habet dies trecentos octoginta quatuor: si autem ad mensem Marche-fwan dies adiiciatur propter annum sequentem, tunc annus embolimaeus habet dies trecentos octoginta quinque, & appellatur abundans: fi ex mense Cifleu dematur dies, tunc annus embolimæus constat trecentis octoginta tribus diebus,& dicitur deficiens.
units.tr: If we carefully weigh the histories, both sacred and profane, we will find that the Jewish reckoning of years was of three kinds. From the creation of the world, through 3449 years, down to the era of Alexander, the Hebrews used the equal years of the Egyptians, that is, twelve equal months with five extra days, so that the Hebrew year had no intercalary month in 120 years. For since they began their epoch from Libra, they never intercalated unless the beginning of the year had run ahead by a full thirty days, and this happened every 120 years, as Joseph Scaliger shows very clearly in On the Emendation of Time, book 3. But from the era of Alexander until the Talmud was compiled, they used lunar years, which they nevertheless brought back into line with the solar years of the Alexandrians and Romans by means of the Metonic nineteen-year cycle, in which, according to Censorinus, seven intercalations fall, namely in years 3, 6, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 19. Thus at the end of an interval of 19 solar years, the new moons [illegible] are restored to their former places, and in this span about 235 lunations are completed, according to Maurolycus. The beginning of the Alexandrian era was a Monday, falling on the Kalends of October in the year 267 before the Julian reform, as we will show in the chronological tables. The autumn equinox then fell on 26 September, as is clearly evident from the observations of Meton, Euctemon and Hipparchus. Therefore the new moon nearest the autumn equinox was assigned to the beginning of the month Tishri, which fell four days after the era of Alexander the Dhu'l-Qarnayn. And just as the new moon nearest the autumn equinox was always the beginning of the Hebrew month Tishri, so the new moon nearest the spring equinox was the beginning of the month Nisan, on whose fifteenth day the Jews customarily celebrated their Passover. In the intermediate years of the nineteen-year cycle, however, because of the intercalation of one solar month, the new moons of Nisan and Tishri sometimes lie farther from the seats of the equinoxes. Therefore, since we have supposed that Christ suffered in the 344th year of Alexander, if this is divided by 19, 2 remains, which is a sign that the Jewish year 3793 was, according to the Metonic cycle, a common year, that is, one containing twelve lunations. The spring equinox then fell on 21 March, and that Julian year 78 of the Julian nineteen-year cycle had the golden number 2, which is placed at 13 days before the Kalends of April in the Julian calendar, to signify that the new moon nearest the spring equinox falls on 20 March. If, then, the new moon of Nisan is fixed on 20 March, the fifteenth of Nisan will certainly fall on 3 April, a Friday, on which our Lord was crucified. Wherefore, around the year of the Lord 469, when they sealed the Jerusalem Talmud, and around the year of the Lord 507, when the Babylonian Talmud was sealed, the Jews, out of hatred of Christ, decreed that the new moon of Tishri should never be celebrated on a Friday, because on that day they had crucified the Lord of glory. They also prescribed the ordering of years, which they still use, so that the nineteen-year cycle is no longer reckoned by the Metonic cycle but is calculated according to the years of the world. In the twelve months they retained the ancient number of days, so that they alternate between 30 and 29 days, although for civil use a lunation requires 29 days and a half, the hour-scruples being disregarded. Therefore the common and ordinary year among the Hebrews consists of 354 days. But sometimes a day is added to the month Marheshvan, and then the year has 355 days and is called full or abundant. Sometimes a day is taken from the month Kislev, and then the year is completed in 353 days and is called deficient. An embolismic year exceeds a common and ordinary year by 30 days, because for lunar reasons a month of 30 days is intercalated before Adar, called the embolismic Adar. Therefore an embolismic year that is also ordinary has 384 days. But if a day is added to Marheshvan on account of the following year, then the embolismic year has 385 days and is called abundant. If a day is removed from Kislev, then the embolismic year consists of 383 days and is called deficient.

units.la: Vt autem sciatur, qui anni sint communes, quíve embolimæi habeantur, perpetuo refpiciedum est ad cyclum decennouennalem: in quo duodecim anni fiunt communes,& septem embolimæi. Communes sunt primus,fecudus,quartus,quintus,septimus, nonus,decimus, duodecimus, decimus tertius, decimus quintus, decimus sextus,& decimus octauus: embolimæi sunt tertius, sextus, octauus, vndecimus, decimus quartus,decimus septimus,& decimus nonus. Si ergo datos annos mundi diuidamus per 19: quotiens ostendit,quot enneadecaeterides sint elapsæ;refiduü autem indicat,quotus is annus fit cycli labetis. exempli gratia, annus mundi 5 349 fi diuidatur per 19, in quotiente prouenit 28 1,& residuum est 10. itaque annus mundi 5 349 est decimus cycli decennouennalis, proinde duodecim tantum habet menses: & ante eum elapsæ sunt 281 enneadecaeterides. Cur autem anni prædicti 3.6.8.11.14.17.& 19 sint embolimæi, efficiunt epactæ anni solaris supra annum communem lunarem: nam annus solaris habet 365 dies, & 6 horas: annus vero communis lunaris praeter 354 dies, habet horas 8, & scrupula horaria 876: vt differentia fiue excessus fit 10 dierum, 21 horarum, 204 scrupulorum. Hic excessus triplicatus producit 32 dies,15 horas, & 612 scrupula: ex qua summa anno tertio colligitur mensis intercalaris 30 dierum,& remanent duo dies,quindecim horæ,& 612 scrupula. Si iterum trium annorum excessus coaceruentur, & addatur epacta ex anno tertio relicta: proueniunt 5 dies, 6 horæ & 1124 scrupula, quæ suppeditant menfem intercalarem 30 dierum, & supersunt quinque dies,6 horæ, & 1224 scrupula, hoc est,quinque dies, 7 horæ,& 144 scrupula: quare annus sextus cycli embolimæus quoque est. Ad epactam anni sexti si duorum annorum excessus, hoc est,21 dies, 18 horæ,& 408 scrupula, adiiciatur; prodit summa 27 dierum, horæ vnius,& 5 5 2 scrupulorum [?]: atqui hæc non complent mensem intercalarem, proinde Hebræi de excessu anni noni tres dies adiiciunt, vt annum octauum faciant intercalarem: itaque anno nono de excessu communi restant 7 dies, 21 horæ, 204 scrupula: quibus si addatur residuum,quod in anno octauo supra 27 dies relinquebatur, videlicet hora vna & 5 5 2 scrupula, producuntur 7 dies, 22 horæ, 756 scrupula. Ad quæ si aggregetur duo excessus anni decimi scilicet & vndecimi; colligitur summa 29 dierum,17 horarum,& 84 scrupulorum. desiderantur igitur sex horæ & 996 scrupula,quo minus ad 30 dies consurgat excessus anni vndecimi: itaque de communi epacta anni duodecimi Hebræi auferunt sex horas & 996, scrupula, vt compleant mensem intercalarem, faciatque annum vndecimum cycli embolimæum: quare residuum epactæ anni duodecimi, est 10 dierum, & 14 horarum, & 288 scrupulorum: ad quod si adiiciatur excessus anni decimi tertii & decimi quarti, hoc est, 21 dies, 18 horæ, & 408 scrupula, consurgunt 32 dies, 8 horæ,& 696 scrupula, quæ suppeditant anno decimo quarto mensem embolimæum, & remanent 2 dies,8 horæ,& 696 scrupula. Ad hæc si adiiciatur excessus trium subsequentium annorum, qui est 32 dierum, 15 horarum, & 612 scrupulorum; provenit summa 35 dierum & 228 scrupulorum: quæ anno decimo septimo suppeditat mensem intercallarem, vt remaneant quinq; dies & 218 scrupula. Ad quod residuum fi adiiciatur poltremoru duoru annoru ex-cc[?]flus, videlicet 21 dies,18 hora, & 408 scrupula, proueniut 26 dies,18 horę,& 636 scrupula: atqui haec no coficiunt mensem embolimaeum, vt decimus nonus annus cycli decennouennalis non videatur esse intercalaris: verum Hebraei quatuor dies adiiciunt, ratione annoru abundantiu & deficietium: siquidem propter hos, plerunque quatuor dies enneadecaeteridi accedut. Si enim omnes anni nouendecim tam communes quam intercalares effent ordinarii & mediocres, vt scilicet singuli communes haberent 354 dies, & singuli embolimaei constarent 384 diebus: tunc enneadecaeteris compleƈteretur 6936 dies, atque ita deRderentur quatuor dies ad complendam enneadecaeteridem naturalem fiue Iulianam, quae continet 6940 dies. Huc defectu vt complerent artifices Hebraeorum, voluerunt aliquos annos esse vno die abundantes, aliquos vno die deficientes, & nonnullos ordinario numero dierum decurrentes: ita enneadecaeteris Hebreorum, propter triplex annoru abundantium, ordinarioru & deficientiu diferimen, nonnun-quam habet 6939 dies, aliquando 6940 dies, & non raro 6941 dies comprehendit. Huiusmodi enneadecaeterides vocare licet politicas, ad differentia enneadecaeteridis naturalis & astronomicae: etenim comper-tum est obseruationibus astronomorum, annis no-uendecim solaribus elapsis lunam redire ad pristina loca, vt Ptolemaeus ex Metone oftedit: atqui nouen-decim anni solares suppeditant 6939 dies: quia qua-tuor anni bisextiles, qui sunt in naturali enneadecae-teride efficiunt 1464 dies, reliqui quindecim dant 5475 dies, quorum omnium summa est 6939 dierum. Verum ad periodicam restitutionem lunæ, præter 19 annos solares, hoc est, 6939 dies, requiritur tempus sedecim horarum, & quingentorum nonaginta quinque scrupulorum, prout hora vna continet 1080. scrupula. Quamobrem Metonica enneadecaeteris si absolute sit dierum 6939, nimis breuis est, discedens à iusta periodo horis 16 & 59 scrupulis: si vero æstimetur absolute dierum 6940, tunc iusto prolixior est, horis 7 & 48 scrupulis: hoc est, horis 7. [?] · 56. 40: vt in annis Calippicis siue Iulianis 76 moretur lunæ curriculum diebus vno, horis v. scrupulis 47. 46. 40. & in annis 304, luna anteuertet primam epocha Metonica diebus solidis quinq;. Sed quomodo cū his coēunt q̃b[?] Hebræi dicunt, luna quouis cyclo decennouennali anticipare horam vna & 48 scrupula? id enim expresse scribit Hebræus de æris seu interualli temporum, cum Mesfahala Norinbergæ editus, quando ait, Veruntamen remanebunt nobis semper in omnibus nonendecim annis, inter solares & lunares, vna hora, & 485 minuta, secundum intentionem gentium & plebiscita earum. Respondendum est, Hebræos quidem ex periodo menstrua lunæ eruere tempus enneadecaeteridis, idq; definire 6939 diebus, 16 horis, & 59 scrupulis: verum hoc ipsum interuallum temporis ad mediocritatem quandam reducunt, & statuunt periodicam [illegible, ~8 letters] lunæ fieri elapsis diebus 6939 & octodecim horis, hoc est, peractis 6940 diebus, quatenus 18 horæ pro integro die sumuntur. Vt autem præter 6939 dies, octodecim horæ oriantur, ad 16 horas, & 59 scrupula, adiicienda est hora vna, & 48 scrupula: itaque anticipatio enneadecaeterica Hebræis sumitur ab hora decima octaua seu ortu solis, quatenus secundum astronomos diei initium capitur à meridie: sicfit[?], vt quod interuallum est inter sedecim horas appendices, & 95 scrupula, & inter decimam octauam horam ineuntem, habea-tur pro anticipatione cycli unius decennouennalis. hæc autem differentia est horæ unius, & 48 scrupulorum, fiue horæ unius & I/16. II/56. III/40. si scrupula Iudaica resoluantur in sexagenas.
units.tr: In order to know which years are common and which are embolismic, one must always refer to the nineteen-year cycle, in which twelve years are common and seven embolismic. The common years are the first, second, fourth, fifth, seventh, ninth, tenth, twelfth, thirteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth and eighteenth; the embolismic years are the third, sixth, eighth, eleventh, fourteenth, seventeenth and nineteenth. If, therefore, we divide the given years of the world by 19, the quotient shows how many nineteen-year periods (enneadecaeterides) have elapsed, and the remainder shows which year of the cycle that year is. For example, the year of the world 5349, divided by 19, gives a quotient of 281 and a remainder of 10. So the year of the world 5349 is the tenth year of the nineteen-year cycle and therefore has only twelve months, and 281 enneadecaeterides have elapsed before it. Why the years 3, 6, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 19 are embolismic is shown by the epacts, which arise from the excess of the solar year over the common lunar year. The solar year has 365 days and 6 hours; the common lunar year, besides 354 days, has 8 hours and 876 hour-scruples. The difference or excess is therefore 10 days, 21 hours and 204 scruples. Tripled, this excess gives 32 days, 15 hours and 612 scruples. From this sum, in the third year, an intercalary month of 30 days is gathered, and there remain two days, fifteen hours and 612 scruples. If again the excesses of three years are heaped up and the epact left over from the third year is added, there result 5 days, 6 hours and 1124 scruples, which supply an intercalary month of 30 days, and there remain five days, 6 hours and 1224 scruples, that is, five days, 7 hours and 144 scruples. Wherefore the sixth year of the cycle is also embolismic. If to the epact of the sixth year the excess of two years is added, that is 21 days, 18 hours and 408 scruples, the sum is 27 days, one hour and 552 scruples. But these do not fill the intercalary month, so the Hebrews add three days from the excess of the ninth year to make the eighth year intercalary. Thus in the ninth year 7 days, 21 hours and 204 scruples remain from the common excess. If to these is added the remainder which in the eighth year was left above 27 days, namely one hour and 552 scruples, there result 7 days, 22 hours and 756 scruples. If to these the two excesses of the tenth and eleventh years are added, the sum is 29 days, 17 hours and 84 scruples. There are therefore lacking six hours and 996 scruples, so that the excess of the eleventh year does not reach 30 days. So the Hebrews take six hours and 996 scruples from the common epact of the twelfth year, to fill the intercalary month and make the eleventh year of the cycle embolismic. Wherefore the remainder of the epact of the twelfth year is 10 days, 14 hours and 288 scruples. If to this the excess of the thirteenth and fourteenth years is added, that is 21 days, 18 hours and 408 scruples, there result 32 days, 8 hours and 696 scruples. These supply an embolismic month to the fourteenth year, and there remain 2 days, 8 hours and 696 scruples. If to these the excess of the three following years is added, which is 32 days, 15 hours and 612 scruples, the sum is 35 days and 228 scruples, which supplies an intercalary month to the seventeenth year, so that there remain five days and 218 scruples. If to this remainder the excess of the last two years is added, namely 21 days, 18 hours and 408 scruples, there result 26 days, 18 hours and 636 scruples. But these do not make an embolismic month, so that the nineteenth year of the cycle does not appear to be intercalary. Yet the Hebrews add four days, on account of the abundant and deficient years, since because of these, commonly four days fall to the nineteen-year period. For if all nineteen years, both common and embolismic, were ordinary and average, that is, if each common year had 354 days and each embolismic year 384 days, the nineteen-year period would make 6936 days, and four days would be lacking to complete the natural or Julian nineteen-year period, which contains 6940 days. To make up this deficiency the Hebrew artificers wished some years to be one day longer, some one day shorter, and some to run the ordinary number of days. Thus the Hebrew enneadecaeteris, because of the threefold difference of abundant, ordinary and deficient years, sometimes has 6939 days, sometimes 6940, and not rarely comprehends 6941 days. Such enneadecaeterides may be called political, to distinguish them from the natural and astronomical enneadecaeteris. For it has been established by the observations of astronomers that after nineteen solar years have elapsed the moon returns to its former positions, as Ptolemy showed from Meton. Yet nineteen solar years give 6939 days, for the four leap years which occur in the natural enneadecaeteris make 1464 days, and the remaining fifteen give 5475 days, the sum of all of which is 6939 days. But for the periodic restoration of the moon, beyond the 19 solar years, that is 6939 days, a time of sixteen hours and 595 scruples is required, since one hour contains 1080 scruples. Wherefore the Metonic enneadecaeteris, if taken absolutely as 6939 days, is too short, departing from the true period by 16 hours and 59 scruples; but if taken absolutely as 6940 days, it is too long, by 7 hours and 48 scruples (that is, 7 hours, 56 and 40 in sixtieths). So in 76 Callippic or Julian years the course of the moon lasts one day, five hours, 47, 46 and 40 (in sixtieths), and in 304 years the moon will precede the first Metonic epoch by five full days. But how do these agree with what the Hebrews say, that the moon in every nineteen-year cycle anticipates by one hour and 485 scruples? The Hebrew author writes this expressly about the difference of the years, in the Mesfahala published at Nuremberg, when he says: There will always remain for us in all nineteen years, between solar and lunar, one hour and 485 minutes, according to the intention of the peoples and their plebiscites. The answer is that the Hebrews indeed derive from the monthly period of the moon the length of the enneadecaeteris, and define it as 6939 days, 16 hours and 59 scruples. But they reduce this very interval of time to a certain average, and establish that the periodic return of the moon occurs after 6939 days and eighteen hours, that is, when 6940 days are completed, inasmuch as eighteen hours are taken for a whole day. So that, beyond 6939 days, eighteen hours may arise, one hour and 485 scruples must be added to the 16 hours and 59 scruples. Thus the enneadecaeteric anticipation is taken by the Hebrews from the eighteenth hour, or sunrise, inasmuch as according to the astronomers the day begins at midday. So what is the interval between the sixteen hours with 95 scruples and the eighteenth hour entering is taken as the anticipation of one nineteen-year cycle. This difference is one hour and 485 scruples, or one hour, 1/16, 11/56, 111/40, if the Jewish scruples are resolved into sixtieths.

units.la: Cum iam declaratum sit, qua ratione luna quouis elapso cyclo enneadecaeterico priorem epocham anticipet per horam unam, & 485 scrupula; non dif-ficile est hinc videre, cyclis tredecim enneadecaeteri-cis, hoc est, confectis annis 247 Iudaicis, anticipatio-nem lunarem excrescere ad 18 horas, & 905 scrupula, hoc est, ad integrum diem: nam quotiescunque in ra-tiociniis lunaribus scrupula consurgunt ad octode-cim horas, integra dies computatur. Tredecim cycli in anticipatione suppeditat tredecim horas: at si tre-decim ducantur in scrupula 485, proueniunt 6305, scrupula, quæ efficiunt quinq; horas & 905 scrupu-la: hæc adiecta ad horas tredecim, constituunt in uni-uersum horas 18, & 905 scrupula, quæ habentur pro integro die. Quamobrem satis expedita est ratio in-ueniendi anticipationem lunarem. si enim anni dati solares diuidantur per 147, quotiens ostendet dies anticipatos, ut etiam prius monuimus in calendario Romano.
units.tr: Since it has now been explained by what reasoning the moon, after any nineteen-year cycle has elapsed, advances its earlier epoch by one hour and 485 scruples, it is not difficult to see from this that after thirteen enneadecaeteric cycles, that is, 247 Jewish years completed, the lunar anticipation grows to 18 hours and 905 scruples, that is, to a whole day. For whenever in lunar calculations the scruples rise to eighteen hours, a whole day is counted. Thirteen cycles give thirteen hours of anticipation; but if thirteen is multiplied by 485 scruples, there result 6305 scruples, which make five hours and 905 scruples. These added to the thirteen hours make in all 18 hours and 905 scruples, which are counted as a whole day. Therefore the method of finding the lunar anticipation is quite simple: if the given solar years are divided by 147, the quotient will show the days anticipated, as we also said before in the Roman calendar.

units.la: Periodum menstruam ab una solis lunæq; coniun-ctione vlq;[?] ad alteram Hebraei præsupponunt 19 di-erum, 12 horarum, & 793 scrupulorum, qualium mille & octoginta integram horâ constituunt: scru-pula 793 conficiunt sexagenas 44[?] 3[?] 111/20[?]. Hanc men-lis lunaris quantitatem acceptam referunt cuidā sa-pienti e domo [?] Dauidis: eamq; pro basi calendarii sui substernunt[?], & ubiq; sequuntur. Hinc est, quòd ex ductu 12mensium[?] lunarium procreetur quantitas anni communis lunaris 3 s 4 dierū,8 horarū,&8 76 scrupulorū: & ex multiplicatione 13 mensium lunarium nascitur quantitas anni embolimæi 383 dierum, 21 horarum, & s 89 scrupulorum. Ita si mensis lunaris ducatur in 235 neomenias absolutas, quod completur enneadecaeteris undeviginti annorum; consurgunt 6939 dies, 16 horæ, & s 95 scrupula, qui est modus enneadecaeteridis coelestis seu astronomicæ.
units.tr: The Hebrews presuppose that the monthly period from one conjunction of sun and moon to the next is 19 days, 12 hours and 793 scruples, of which 1080 make up an hour. The 793 scruples make up sixtieths. They attribute this quantity of the lunar month to a certain wise man of the house of David, and they lay it down as the basis of their calendar and follow it everywhere. Hence, from twelve lunar months, the quantity of a common lunar year arises: 354 days, 8 hours and 876 scruples. From the multiplication of thirteen lunar months arises the quantity of an embolismic year: 383 days, 21 hours and 589 scruples. So if a lunar month is multiplied by 235 complete new moons, which completes the enneadecaeteris of nineteen years, there result 6939 days, 16 hours and 595 scruples, which is the measure of the celestial or astronomical enneadecaeteris.

units.la: Porrò cum una enneadecaeteris continet ducentas & triginta quinq; integras lūnationes, non dubium est, quin tredecim enneadecaeterides, quæ conficiūt annos Iudaicos 247, cōtineant 305 s lūnationes: quæ si multiplicentur per mensem lunarem, hoc est, per 29 dies, 12 horas, &793 scrupula, proveniunt 9021 s dies, 23 horæ, & 175 scrupula, quæ æquipollent annis 247 solaribus. Hinc perspicitur, quomodo ex dato interuallo temporis ab æra Iudaica elapsi, ad aliam quamcunq; epocha supputari debeat annus & mensis currens Iudaicus, mod adò calendariū Iulianum fiat comparatio: quia verò tædiosum est, tot dies accumulare, quot ab æra mundi Iudæorum, usq; ad æræ Alexandri vel aliam quamcunq; sunt elapsi, idcirco Hebræi ex diebus omnibus septenarios auferunt, & secundùm characterem hebdomadicum neomenias singulorū annorum mundi indagant, ut tradicem[?] primâ semper adiiciant. Ita mensis lunaris, qui cōstat 29 diebus, 12 horis, & 79 3 scrupulis, characterem hebdomadicum habet unitatem: si enim ex 29 diebus abiicias septenarium, quoties potes, relinquitur unitas: huic unitati si adiiciantur epactæ sive appēdices horarum & scrupulorum, signum mensis est 1.12.79j. quod denotat præter septimanas feria prima, 12 horas, & 793 [?]crupul[?]. Sic annus communis post abiectione [?]one septen riorum characterẽ relinquit 4.8.876. annus vero embolimæus signum habet 5.21.589. Integra enneadecaeteris, quæ collat 12 annis communibus & septem embolimæis, post abiectos septenarios dierum exhibet characterẽ 2.16.595. tredecim vero enneadecaeterides abiectis septem ariis dierum ostendunt characterem hebdomadicum cum adiunctis epactis 6.23. 175. Hic autẽ sciendum est, Hebræos primam radicem lunæ ponere 1.5.204. hoc est, feria secunda, horam quintam, & ducentesimum quartum scrupulum, quo tempore existimant primam lunæ phasin fuisse conspectā.
units.tr: Moreover, since one enneadecaeteris contains 235 whole lunations, there is no doubt that thirteen enneadecaeterides, which make up 247 Jewish years, contain 3055 lunations. If these are multiplied by the lunar month, that is, by 29 days, 12 hours and 793 scruples, there result 90217 days, 23 hours and 175 scruples, which are equal to 247 solar years. From this it is clear how, from a given interval of time elapsed since the Jewish era, the current Jewish year and month can be calculated for any other epoch, and how a comparison can be made with the Julian calendar. But because it is tedious to accumulate as many days as have elapsed from the Jewish era of the world up to the era of Alexander or any other, the Hebrews therefore take away the sevens from all the days, and by the weekly character they find the new moons of each year of the world, always adding the root at the first. Thus the lunar month, which consists of 29 days, 12 hours and 793 scruples, has the weekly character of unity: for if you subtract sevens from 29 days as often as you can, a unity remains. If the epacts, or appendices, of hours and scruples are added to this unity, the sign of the month is 1.12.793, which denotes, besides the weeks, the first day of the week, 12 hours and 793 scruples. Likewise, the common year, after the sevens are subtracted, leaves the character 4.8.876. The embolismic year has the sign 5.21.589. A whole enneadecaeteris, which consists of twelve common years and seven embolismic years, after the sevens of days are subtracted, shows the character 2.16.595. Thirteen enneadecaeterides, with the sevens of days subtracted, show the weekly character, with the epacts added, 6.23.175. Here it must be noted that the Hebrews place the first root of the moon at 1.5.204, that is, the second day of the week, the fifth hour, and the 204th scruple, at which time they think the first phase of the moon was seen.

units.la: dicut enim anno primo creationis, post elapsum hexamerum à prima rerum facie, coniunctione solis & lunæ fuisse circa vesperam diei sabbati: sed proxime subsequente die lunæ, hora quinta, & ducentesimo quarto scrupulo, lunâ conspectâ esse corniculante, indeq; sumendū esse principiū enneadecaeteridis politicæ: ꝑpterea ad quosuis characteres hebdomadicos datos cū appendicibus horarum & scrupulorum, pperuo adiici voluntas adice, hoc est, feria 2, horam 5, & scrupulu 204 quo peruenitur ad primam coniunctionem solis & lunæ, vel potius ad primam phasin lunarem.
units.tr: For they say that in the first year of creation, after six days had elapsed from the first appearance of things, the conjunction of sun and moon took place about the evening of the Sabbath day; but on the following day, the day of the moon, at the fifth hour and the 204th scruple, the moon was seen as a crescent, and from this the beginning of the civil enneadecaeteris must be taken. Therefore, for any given weekly characters with the appendices of hours and scruples, the root is always to be added, that is, the second day, the fifth hour and the 204th scruple, by which one arrives at the first conjunction of sun and moon, or rather at the first lunar phase.

units.la: Si ergo neomenia φᾶσις lunaris prima fuit feria 2, hora quinta, & 204 scrupulo, adiiciatur character mēsis 1.12.79 3.cōsurg tsumma 3.17.997. quæ indicat mēsem primū desinere feria tertia, hora decimaseptima & scrupulo 997, vt ibidem initiū sit mensis alterius.
units.tr: If, therefore, the first new moon, the first phasis [φᾶσις] of the moon, was on the second day, at the fifth hour and the 204th scruple, add the character of the month 1.12.793; the sum is 3.17.997. This indicates that the first month ends on the third day, at the seventeenth hour and the 997th scruple, so that the beginning of the next month falls there.

units.la: Si ergo cognoscere velimus qua feria secundum motum lunæ occurrat neomenia Tisri quouis anno, dispiciendū est, quot anni siue enneadecaeteridis sint ad tempus datum & cum calendario Iuliano coparatum, finis elapse, vt ex tabulis cōuenientes characteres depromantur,quibus depromtis semper radix est adiicien- da: summa ostendet feria neomeniæ[?]. Si epactæ[?] hora- rum & scrupulorum ad 1 8 horas vel supra excrescat; neomenia naturaliter transferenda est in feriam sub- sequente. Hæc fiunt ratione calculi lunaris:ratione autem ordinationis politicæ sæpenumero neomenia non potest locum habere in feria,quâ oftedit motus lunaris,sed transferenda est ulterius p die vnum atq; alterum, ita fit vt annus tam communis quàm intercalaris subinde fit vno die abundans vel deficiens,aut ordinarium obtineat numerum dierum. In ordinatione annorum politicorum statuerunt Hebræi,nunquam celebrandam esse neomeniam Tisri feria prima,quarta, & sexta,sed transferendam esse in ferias proximè sequentes: deinde si incidat neomenia secundum lunam in feriam secundam,& præcedens annus fuerit emboli-mæus,vt appédices sint assecutæ horas 15,& 589 scrupula;tunc quoq; translatione faciendâ esse in sequentem feriâ: tertio si neomenia inciderit in feriâ tertiâ, & appendices superarint horas 9, & 204 scrupula, in anno communi neomeniâ transferendâ esse in feriâ 5.
units.tr: If, therefore, we wish to know on what day of the week, according to the motion of the moon, the new moon of Tishri falls in any given year, one must examine how many years or enneadecaeterides have elapsed up to the given time, compared with the Julian calendar, so that the corresponding characters may be drawn from the tables; once these are drawn, the root is always to be added; the sum shows the day of the new moon. If the epacts of hours and scruples rise to 18 hours or more, the new moon must naturally be transferred to the following day. These things are done by the reckoning of the moon; but by the civil arrangement the new moon can often not fall on the day which the motion of the moon indicates, but must be moved on by one or two days, so that the year, whether common or intercalary, sometimes has one day too many or too few, or keeps the ordinary number of days. In the arrangement of the civil years the Hebrews decided that the new moon of Tishri must never be celebrated on the first, fourth or sixth day of the week, but must be moved to the days immediately following. Next, if the new moon according to the moon falls on the second day, and the preceding year was an embolismic year, so that the appendices have reached 15 hours and 589 scruples, then also the new moon is to be transferred to the following day. Third, if the new moon falls on the third day and the appendices have exceeded 9 hours and 204 scruples, in a common year the new moon is to be transferred to the fifth day.

units.la: Exempli gratia: si cupiâ scire feriâ neomeniæ Tisri anni mûdi 5349; cogitandû est elapsos esse annos 5348, h. e. enneadecaeterides 281, & 9 annos: quibus debetur character adiunctâ radice 4.3.42: itaq; annus mûdi 5349 secundum lunam incipit feria 4, hora 3, scrupulo 42: quia autem politicè ibi locû habere non potest, vt dictû est in canone primo, ideo transfertur in feriam 5, quæ incurrit in 12 Septembris, anno Christi currente 1588.
units.tr: For example: if I wish to know the day of the new moon of Tishri in the year of the world 5349, it must be considered that 5348 years have elapsed, that is, 281 enneadecaeterides and 9 years. To these belongs the character, with the root added, 4.3.42. Thus the year of the world 5349 begins, according to the moon, on the fourth day, at the third hour and the 42nd scruple. But because it cannot have its place there by civil reckoning, as was said in the first canon, it is therefore transferred to the fifth day, which falls on 12 September in the current year of Christ 1588.

units.la: Vt autem tabulas habeas in promtu, ex quibus characteres & appendices tempori elapso conuenientes erue re possis, proponemus hic triplicem tabulam; mensium scilicet lunarium, annorum & cyclorum.
units.tr: So that you may have at hand the tables from which you can draw the characters and appendices corresponding to the elapsed time, we shall set out here a threefold table: namely, of lunar months, of years, and of cycles.

units.la: Omnes hi meses sunt æquales in ratiociniis lunari-bus: alias ex usu politico alternatim complectuntur 30 & 29 dies: sic Adar embolimæus hic intelligitur esse 29 dierum, 12 horarum, & 793 scrupulorum, cum politice comprehendat 30 dies, neglectis horis & scrupulis appendicibus.
units.tr: All these months are equal in lunar calculations. In civil usage, however, they alternate between 30 and 29 days. So the embolismic Adar is understood here to be 29 days, 12 hours and 793 scruples, although civilly it is counted as 30 days, with the hours and scruples of the appendices disregarded.
