units.la: Hisce tabulis præmissis, redeundū nobis est ad pro-positum exemplum, & quomodo characteres hebdomadici cum horis & scrupulis appendicibus sint inuestigandi est consideran-dum. Neomenia Tifri anni mundi 5349 naturaliter cœpit feria quarta hora tertia, scrupulo 542, quod ostenditur ex annis elapsis 5348, qui conficiunt enneadecaeterides 81, & 9 annos: hisce annis oportet ex tabulis depromere conuenientes characteres, eosq; in summa vna [?]contrahere, & tandem Radicem adiicere, vt ex sequnti praxi apparet. Dies. | Hora. | Scrupula. Cycli 200 | 5 | 22 | 20 Cycli 80 | 5 | 4 | 6 [?] Cyclus 1 | 2 | 16 | 95 Anni 9 | 1 | 21 | 53 [?] Radix | 2 | 5 | 04 Summa | 15 | 68 | 522
units.tr: With these tables set out, we must return to the example we proposed and consider how the weekday characters, with their hours and scruples as appendices, are to be found. The new moon of Tisri in the year of the world 5349 naturally began on the fourth day of the week (Wednesday), at the third hour and 542 scruples. This is shown from the elapsed years 5348, which make 81 enneadecaeterides and 9 years. For these years we must take the corresponding characters from the tables, add them together in one sum, and finally add the root, as the following procedure shows. Days | Hours | Scruples. Cycles 200 | 5 | 22 | 20. Cycles 80 | 5 | 4 | 6. Cycle 1 | 2 | 16 | 95. Years 9 | 1 | 21 | 53. Root | 2 | 5 | 04. Sum | 15 | 68 | 522.

units.la: Scrupula 1622 suppeditant horam vnam, remaneant 542 scrupula: hora ista si adiiciatur a[?]68 horas, fiunt 69 horae, quae efficiunt duos dies, & 21 horas: sed ex 21 horis abiiciendae sunt horae pro integro die numerandae, & supersunt 3 horae: quare integrum triduum adiiciendum est ad 1 dies, & consurgit summa octodecim dierum, ex quibus si septenarij abiiciatur, remanet character hebdomadicus, qui est feria quarta: cui si addantur appendices horarum & scrupulorum, ostenditur inde neomeniae Tisri anno mundi 5349, qui est 4.3.542. Simili ratio-ne cognoscitur index neomeniæ Tisri anni 5350, qui est 1.6.338. Verùm neutra istarum neomeniarum, quæ secundùm motum lunæ indicantur, accommodata est ad ordinationem politicam, proinde prior differtur in feriam quintam, posterior verò traiicitur ad feriam secundam, diem videlicet 1 Septembris anno instante Christi 1589. Fixa neomenia anni præce-dentis & subsequentis, videndum est, qua die inter-veniat pascha ludaicum: huius enim sedes ostendit, an præcedens annus sit ordinarius, abundans, aut deficiens: Feria paschalis sine negocio inveniri potest, si à neomenia anni subsequentis duo subtrahantur: cùm enim neomenia Tisri anni sequentis æqualiter distet à præcedenti paschate, diebus scilicet 183: ita ut tertia dies Paschatis in eandem feriam incidat cum neomenia Tisri anni sequentis, satis apparet methodum hanc iustam esse. Ita si à neomenia Tisri anni mundi 5350, quæ est feria secunda, incurrens in 1 Septembris anno Christi labente 1589, duo subtrahantur, remanet nihil, quod indicium est, Pascha ludaicum anni mundi 5349 incurrere in feriam septimam, ita ut tertia dies paschatis, feria nimirum secunda, eadem sit cum feria neomeniæ politicæ anni 5350 mundi. Hoc autem verissimum est, pascha ludaicum anno 5349 mundi, incidisse in feriam septimam, quæ fuit decima quinta Nisan, respondens vigesimo secundo Martii, anno Christi 1589: quatenus principium feriæ septimæ ducitur à vespera præcedente, hoc est, ab occasu solis feriæ sextæ, quæ incurrit in 21 Martii: quamobrem hæc epocha fundamentum nobis debet esse, ad subsequentes annos ludaicos indagandos. Ex fixo paschate ludaico, & neomenia præcedentis Tisri eiusdem anni, intelligitur qualis fit dispositio anni 5 349 mundi : cum enim illius Tifri incipiat feria quinta, quæ fuit dies duodecima mensis Septembris anno Christi 1 5 88, & palcha proximè fubfequensincur-rat in 7 feriam,quæfuit 21 Martij anno Christi 1589: omninò sequitur annum illum esse ordinarium, quatenus menses omnes habent ordinarium numerum dierum. Vt autem ex vtriusque anni, præcedentis scilicet & subsequentis, neomeniis fixis, statim inda-gari possit anni dispositio, Hebræi præcipiunt, vt pri-mo cognoscatur an annus communis fit, vel emboli-mæus, cuius dispositionem quarimus: fi fit commu-nis eiusque feria subtracta à feria anni subsequentis differentiam relinquat quatuor dierum,tunc annum esse ordinatum: fi differetia fit 3 dierum, esse annum deficientem:fi 5 dierum habeatur differentia, annum quoq; esse abundantem. Si annus propositus fit embolimeus,eiusq; feria subtracta à feria anni subsequentis, relinquat differentiam sex dierum , tunc annum esse ordinatum : fi differentia fit quinque dierum, significare annum deficientem: fi verò differentia fit septem dierum, indicium esse anni abundatis. Exempli gratia,neomenia Tifri anni communis 5 349 cœpit feria quinta,anni verò subsequentis 5 350 neomenia Tifri incurrit in feriam fecundam:fi ergo feria prioris anni,scilicet quinta subtrahatur à feria posterioris anni, scilicet fecunda; differentia relinquitur quatuor dierum , quæ ostendit annum communem 5 349 simul esse ordinatum. Vbi obseruandum est, fi fubtra-ctio feriarum duarum propositarum fieri non possit,ad po-fteriore adiiciendum esse septenarium,vt in exeplo allato apparet: cum enim 5 à 2 subtrahi nequat,ad 2 adiicitur septenarius, & fit summa 9 feriarum : à quibus feriæ quinque sublatæ, relinquunt differetiam 4 feriarum.
units.tr: The 1622 scruples supply one hour, leaving 542 scruples. If this hour is added to the 68 hours, there are 69 hours, which make two days and 21 hours. But from the 21 hours we must subtract the hours that are counted as a full day, leaving 3 hours. Therefore a full three days are added to the 1 day, and the sum comes to eighteen days. If seven is subtracted from these, the weekday character remains, which is the fourth day (Wednesday). If the hours and scruples of the appendices are added to this, it shows the new moon of Tisri in the year of the world 5349 as 4.3.542. By a similar method the index of the new moon of Tisri in the year 5350 is found to be 1.6.338. But neither of these new moons, which are indicated according to the motion of the moon, is suited to civil arrangement. Therefore the former is deferred to the fifth day, and the latter is moved forward to the second day, namely 1 September in the current year of Christ 1589. Having fixed the new moons of the preceding and following years, we must see on which day the Jewish Passover falls, for its position shows whether the preceding year is ordinary, abundant or deficient. The Passover weekday can be found without difficulty by subtracting two from the new moon of the following year. For since the new moon of Tisri in the following year is equally distant from the preceding Passover, namely by 183 days, so that the third day of the Passover falls on the same weekday as the new moon of Tisri in the following year, it is clear that this method is sound. So if two is subtracted from the new moon of Tisri in the year of the world 5350, which is the second day and falls on 1 September in the current year of Christ 1589, nothing remains. This indicates that the Jewish Passover of the year of the world 5349 falls on the seventh day, so that the third day of the Passover, namely the second day, is the same weekday as the civil new moon of the year 5350 of the world. This is entirely true: the Jewish Passover of the year 5349 of the world fell on the seventh day, which was the fifteenth of Nisan, corresponding to 22 March in the year of Christ 1589. The day is reckoned from the evening before, that is, from sunset on the sixth day, which falls on 21 March. Therefore this epoch must be the foundation for us in investigating the following Jewish years. From the fixed Jewish Passover and the new moon of the preceding Tisri of the same year, we understand what the arrangement of the year 5349 of the world is. For since its Tisri begins on the fifth day, which was the twelfth day of September in the year of Christ 1588, and the next Passover falls on the seventh day, which was 21 March in the year of Christ 1589, it certainly follows that this year is ordinary, since all its months have the ordinary number of days. So that the arrangement of a year may be found at once from the fixed new moons of both the preceding and following years, the Hebrews prescribe first that one determine whether the year whose arrangement we seek is common or embolismic. If it is common and the weekday of its new moon, subtracted from the weekday of the following year, leaves a difference of four days, then the year is ordinary. If the difference is three days, the year is deficient. If the difference is five days, the year is also abundant. If the year in question is embolismic, and the weekday of its new moon, subtracted from the weekday of the following year, leaves a difference of six days, then the year is ordinary. If the difference is five days, it signifies a deficient year. If the difference is seven days, it is a sign of an abundant year. For example, the new moon of Tisri of the common year 5349 began on the fifth day, and the new moon of Tisri of the following year 5350 fell on the second day. If, then, the weekday of the earlier year, namely the fifth, is subtracted from the weekday of the later year, namely the second, a difference of four days remains. This shows that the common year 5349 is at the same time ordinary. Here it must be observed that if the subtraction of the two given weekdays cannot be made, seven must be added to the later one, as appears in the example given. For since 5 cannot be subtracted from 2, seven is added to 2, and the sum is 9 weekdays. When five weekdays are taken away from these, a difference of four weekdays remains.

units.la: Vides in superiore tabula, in quem diem Iulianum labentibus annis Christi commemoratis incurrant Paschata Hebraeorum, & principia annorum quos illi numerant a conditu mundi: exempli gratia, in anno Christi 1588 die secundo Aprilis, feria tertia incidit Pascha Iudaicum, quod pertinet ad annum mundi 5348: & die 12 Septembris, feria quinta, incipit annus mundi 5349. Quamobrem monendus es, Paschata illa, quae e regione annorum Hebraeorum assignantur, non pertinere ad illos annos consignatos: sed retrahenda esse ad annos proxime praecedentes: sic Pascha quod anno Domini 1589 incidit 12 Martij, feria septima; non est Paschatis anni mundi 5350, sed pertinet ad annum mundi proxime praecedentem 5349: etenim annus mundi 5350 demum incipit die primo Septembris, feria secunda, currente eodem anno Christi 1589.
units.tr: You see in the table above on which Julian day the Hebrew Passovers fall as the years of Christ pass, and the beginnings of the years that the Hebrews count from the creation of the world. For example, in the year of Christ 1588, on 2 April, a Tuesday, the Jewish Passover falls, and it belongs to the year of the world 5348. On 12 September, a Thursday, the year of the world 5349 begins. You must therefore be warned that these Passovers, which are assigned opposite the Hebrew years, do not belong to the years they are listed beside, but must be referred back to the years immediately before. Thus the Passover that falls in the year of the Lord 1589, on 12 March, a Saturday, is not the Passover of the year of the world 5350, but belongs to the immediately preceding year of the world 5349. For the year of the world 5350 begins only on 1 September, a Monday, in the same year of Christ 1589.

units.la: Praeterea diligenter animadvertendum est a Pascha te praecedente inclusive, sumto usque ad principium annorum subsequentium exclusive acceptis, perpetuo intercedere centum & sexaginta tres dies: nam a Pascha usque ad Pentecosten numeratur quinquaginta dies, a Pentecoste vero usque ad initium anni subsequentis semel centum & tredecim dies: qui in universum efficiunt 163 dies. Idem patet ex numero dierum, qui pertinet ad sex menses æstiuos: Nisi enim constat 30 diebus, ipsum verò Pascha Iudaicũ perpetuò celebratur decima quinta Nisan: quare à Pascha te usq; ad finem mesis, die utroq; inclusiue sumto, numerantur dies sedecim: hinc sequitur Ijar costans[?] 29 diebus, Siuan 30, Tamuz 29, Ab 30, Elul 29 habens dies: ut certissimū sit à Paschate usque ad principium anni subsequentis intercipi dies centum & sexaginta tres. Cognito Paschate, si in decimū quintum diem præcedentem ascendatur, occurrit neomenia Nisan, quæ in eadem cum Paschate feria celebratur: verbi gratia, anno Christi 1588[?], die 2 Aprilis, feria 3 incidit Pascha Iudaicum[?]: si igitur ab eo inclusiue ascedamus in decimum quintum diem, occurret neomenia Nisan die 19 Martij, feria tertia. Quamobrem adminiculo tabulæ nostræ quouis anno facilè conferuntur sex menses æstiui Hebræorum cum mesibus Iulianis: sed quia maxima inæqualitas dierū incurrit in semestre hibernum; omninò necessarium est, ut ad singulorum annorū Hebræorum dispositionem attedamus: nam absq; illa nullo modo coparationem instituere possumus cum diebus Iulianis. Dispositio autem annorū in hoc consistit, ut intelligamus, quinam simplices sint vel intercalares, quod ex cyclo decennouenali Hebreorū addiscitur: ire qui anni sint deficientes, mediocres, vel abundantes, quod ex collatione cycli enneadecaeterici & neomeniarū indagatur. Sanè annus mundi 5349 est decimus cycli enneadecaeterici: is autem est simplex siue communis, habes duntaxat duodecim menses: est etiā mediocris siue ordinar[?], quod in eo retineatur numerus usitatus mesiū, ut priùs est declaratū. Hinc intelligitur semisse hibernū anni mundi 5349 constare dieb. centū & septuaginta septe: at si à die 1 Septebris, in quo incurrit principiū anni mundi 5349, usque ad 8 Martij, in quem incidit neomenia Nisan, currente anno Christi 1589, dies interiectos nume-res, totidem invenies: quod indiciu est, dies Hebræo-rum præcisè respondere diebus Iulianis, etsi diversa sint initia mensium. Tifri enim anni mundi 5349 in-cipit a 12 Septembris, currente anno Christi 1588. Marchefwan incidit in 12 Octobris. Cifleu incurrit in 10 Nouembris. Tebet incipit a 10 Decembris. Sche-bet incidit in 8 Ianuarij, currente anno Christi 1589. Adar simplex incipit die 7 Februarij, & definit die 7 Martij: idcirco neomenia Nisan incurrit in octauum diem Martij, & 21 Martii, feria septima, die nimirum decimo quinto Nisan celebratum est Pascha Iudai-cum. Ex hoc exemplo coniicere potes, quomodo ex data anni dispositione, semestre hibernum quodcun-que occurrat, comparare debeas cum interiectis die-bus Iulianis. Sed ne tibi hac quoq; in parte desim, per eosdem annos integram dispositionem adscribam, vt reliqua proprio Marte assequi possis. units.tr: Furthermore, it must be carefully noted that from the Passover preceding you, inclusive, counted up to the beginning of the following year, exclusive, there always intervene 163 days. For from Passover to Pentecost one counts fifty days, and from Pentecost to the beginning of the following year one counts once a hundred and thirteen days; in total these make 163 days. The same appears from the number of days in the six summer months. Unless they make up 30 days, and Passover is always celebrated on the fifteenth of Nisan, then from Passover to the end of the month, counting both days inclusive, sixteen days are reckoned. Hence it follows that Iyar has 29 days, Sivan 30, Tammuz 29, Av 30 and Elul 29, so that it is quite certain that 163 days intervene from Passover to the beginning of the following year. Once Passover is known, if one ascends fifteen days back from it, the new moon of Nisan falls, celebrated on the same weekday as Passover. For example, in the year of Christ 1588, on 2 April, a Tuesday, the Jewish Passover falls; if then we ascend inclusively fifteen days from it, the new moon of Nisan falls on 19 March, a Tuesday. Therefore, with the help of our table, the six summer months of the Hebrews can easily be compared with the Julian months in any year. But because the greatest inequality of days falls in the winter half-year, it is absolutely necessary to attend to the arrangement of each individual Hebrew year, for without it we can in no way make a comparison with the Julian days. The arrangement of a year consists in this: we learn from the nineteen-year cycle of the Hebrews which years are simple or intercalary, and we investigate, by comparing the nineteen-year (enneadecaeteric) cycle with the new moons, which years are deficient, regular or abundant. Now the year of the world 5349 is the tenth of the enneadecaeteric cycle. It is a simple or common year, having only twelve months; it is also regular or ordinary, since the usual number of months is retained in it, as was explained earlier. Hence it is understood that the winter half-year of the year of the world 5349 consists of 177 days. But if you count the intervening days from 1 September, on which the beginning of the year of the world 5349 falls, up to 8 March, on which the new moon of Nisan falls in the current year of Christ 1589, you will find the same number. This is a sign that the Hebrew days correspond exactly to the Julian days, even though the beginnings of the months differ. For Tishri of the year of the world 5349 begins on 12 September in the current year of Christ 1588. Marheshvan falls on 12 October. Kislev falls on 10 November. Tevet begins on 10 December. Shevat falls on 8 January in the current year of Christ 1589. Simple Adar begins on 7 February and ends on 7 March; hence the new moon of Nisan falls on the eighth day of March, and on 21 March, a Saturday, namely on the fifteenth of Nisan, the Jewish Passover was celebrated. From this example you may gather how, given the arrangement of the year, whatever winter half-year occurs, you ought to compare it with the intervening Julian days. But lest I fail you in this part too, I will set out the complete arrangement for these same years, so that you can work out the rest by your own effort. units.la: Tabulæ huius hic est usus: si ex præcedentibus constet, ubi principium sit alicuius anni, & ubi hære-at subsequens neomenia Nisan: tunc interuallum illud numeretur in diebus Iulianis, & ad id accom-modentur dies, quos dispositio anni Hebræi requi-rit. Exempli gratia, annus mundi 5350 incipit die pri-mo Septembris, currente anno Christi 1589: subse-quens autem neomenia Nisan incurrit in 26 Martij, labente anno Christi 1590, quia Pascha Hebræu[?] incidit die 9 Aprilis: at si a primo Septembris usque ad 26 Martij descendas, videbis interiectos esse dies ducentos & sex: quot etiam requirit anni Hebræi 5350 dispositio: est enim is annus embolimæus deficiens: unde sequitur in semestri hiberno ante simplicem Adar, inseri embolimæum Adar, qui perpetuo habet 30 dies: sequitur etiam diem unum subtrahendum esse mensi Cisleu. Atqui semestre illud ordinarie habet centum & septuaginta septem dies: si unus ex Cis-leu dematur, relinquuntur centum & septuaginta sex dies, quibus si 30 dies intercalares addantur, oritur summa ducentorum & sex dierum. Hisce perspe-ctis, singulorum mensium initia facile indagantur: nam Tisri anni mundi 5350 incurrit in primum Septembris, currente anno Christi 1589. Marcheswan incidit in kal. Octobris. Cisleu incipit 30 Octobris, & definit 27 Nouembris, cum habeat dies tantum 29. Tebet incurrit in 28 Nouembris. Schebet occu-pat 27 Decembris. Adar embolimæus transfertur ad 26 Ianuarij, currente anno Christi 1590: sed Adar ordinarius transfit ad 25 Februarij, ut finem habeat in 15 [?] Martij.quamobrem neomenia Nisan occurrit die sequenti, hoc est, 26 Martij, cum ipsum Pascha celebretur 9 Aprilis. Exemplū aliud sumamus: annus mundi 5366 incipit die tertio Septembris, feria tertia, currente anno Christi millesimo sexcentesimo quinto: subsequens autem neomenia Nisan cadit in diem 29 Martii, feriam septimam, currente anno Christi millesimo sexcentesimo sexto, quia Pascha Hebraeum incidit die 12 Aprilis, feria septima: sed a tertio Septembris usque ad 29 Martii in contextu Iuliano intercipiuntur ducenti & septem dies, quot etiam postulat anni Hebraei 5366 dispositio: is enim annus est embolimaeus & mediocris, siue ordinatus: quare semestre hibernum praeter dies 177, admittit 30 dies intercalares, quorum omnium summa excrescit in 207 dies. Hisce cognitis, singulorum mensium initia facile percipiuntur: nam Tishri anni mundi 5366 respondet 3 Septembris, labente anno Christi 1605. Marcheshwan incurrit in 3 Octobris. Cisleu incidit in kal. Novembris. Tebet figitur in kal. Decembris. Schebet incurrit in 30 Decembris. Adar embolimaeus incipit 29 Ianuarij, currente anno Christi 1606. Adar communis recidit in 18 Februarij, & definit 18 Martij: quamobrem neomenia Nisan occupat 19 Martij, & dies decima quinta Nisan, in qua Pascha agitur, respondet 12 Aprilis. Ex his omnibus apparet, calendarium Hebraeorum elegantissimum quidem esse, sed contumacissimum, vt non facile in gratiam redeat cum anno Iuliano: oportet enim illud a certa epocha deduci, consideratis omnibus hypothesibus & circumstantiis: quarum si vel vna negligeretur, tota series annorum luxaretur: vt mirum sit quare nonnulli annos Hebraeorum nunc vsitatos ad principium mundi extendat, quasi certa in illis essèt cum annis Iulianis comparatio. Quomodo enim annì Hebraeorum æqualiter conferri possent cum annis Iulianis, si quidem nullus cyclus datur, qui exæquationem illam præstare possit? notissimum quidem est, enneadecaeteridè Iulianam constare 6940 diebus, sedHebraeorum enneadecaeteris politica inæqualis est, vt habeat 6940 dies, modò cotineat 6939 dies, nonnunquam completatur 6941 dies: eadem etiam ratione cyclus magnus Hebraeorum, qui continet tredecim inæquales enneadecaeterides, hoc est annos solares 247, necessario inæqualis est. Quare nec per enneadecaeterides, nec per cyclos magnos Hebraeorum comparatione vllam cum annis Iulianis instituere possumus. Sane annus mundi Hebraeorum 5 3 5 o [?] incipit a primo Septembris, currete anno Christi 1589: cum autem is sit embolimaeus & deficiens, vtiq; habet trecentos octoginta tres dies, qui absoluuntur 18 Septebris, labete anno Christi 1590: vt annus mundi 5351 incipiat a 19 Septembris: sed is est communis & abundans, idcirco dies habet trecentos & quinquaginta quinq;, qui absoluuntur 8 Septembris, currente anno Christi 1591: vt annus mundi 5352 incurrat in 9 Septembris, &c. Ita vides, quomodo a certa epocha anni Hebraeorum elegantissimè deducantur in contextum annorum Iulianorum vsitatum & æquabilem: quòd si is contextus mutaretur & inæqualis fieret, quemadmodum accidit in ordinatione Gregoriana, non amplius eadem esset ratio collationis. Quare in deductione temporum tam antecedentium quàm consequentium, non tantùm epocham certissimam esse oportet, verùm etiam requiritur, vt norma per quam exæquationem facimus, fit æquabilis, vel saltem in maximo interuallo temporis habeat certissimum numerum dierum.
units.tr: The use of this table is as follows. If it is established from the preceding data when the beginning of a given year falls, and when the following new moon of Nisan falls, then that interval is counted in Julian days, and to it are fitted the days that the arrangement of the Hebrew year requires. For example, the year of the world 5350 began on the first day of September in the current year of Christ 1589, and the following new moon of Nisan fell on 26 March in the year of Christ 1590, since the Hebrew Passover fell on 9 April. If you count from 1 September to 26 March, you will see that there are 206 days between them, which is also what the arrangement of the Hebrew year 5350 requires. For that year is an embolismic deficient year, whence it follows that in the winter half-year an embolismic Adar is inserted before the ordinary Adar, which always has 30 days. It also follows that one day must be subtracted from the month Cisleu. The winter half-year ordinarily has 177 days; if one day is removed from Cisleu, 176 days remain, and if 30 intercalary days are added to these, the sum is 206 days. With these points clearly understood, the beginnings of the individual months are easily found. Tishri of the year of the world 5350 falls on 1 September in the current year of Christ 1589. Marcheshwan falls on 1 October. Cisleu begins on 30 October and ends on 27 November, since it has only 29 days. Tebet falls on 28 November. Shebat occupies 27 December. The embolismic Adar is transferred to 26 January in the current year of Christ 1590, but the ordinary Adar passes to 25 February, so as to end on 15 March [?]. Therefore the new moon of Nisan occurs on the following day, that is, 26 March, while the Passover itself is celebrated on 9 April. Let us take another example. The year of the world 5366 began on the third day of September, a Tuesday, in the current year of Christ 1605. The following new moon of Nisan fell on 29 March, a Saturday, in the current year of Christ 1606, since the Hebrew Passover fell on 12 April, a Saturday. But from 3 September to 29 March, in the Julian sequence, there intervene 207 days, which is also what the arrangement of the Hebrew year 5366 requires. For that year is embolismic and ordinary, or regular. Therefore the winter half-year, besides its 177 days, admits 30 intercalary days, and the sum of all of these comes to 207 days. With these facts known, the beginnings of the individual months are easily perceived. Tishri of the year of the world 5366 corresponds to 3 September in the year of Christ 1605. Marcheshwan falls on 3 October. Cisleu falls on 1 November. Tebet is fixed on 1 December. Shebat falls on 30 December. The embolismic Adar begins on 29 January in the current year of Christ 1606. The ordinary Adar falls back to 18 February and ends on 18 March; therefore the new moon of Nisan occupies 19 March, and the fifteenth day of Nisan, on which the Passover is kept, corresponds to 12 April. From all these things it appears that the Hebrew calendar is indeed most elegant, but so obstinate that it does not easily come into harmony with the Julian year. For it must be derived from a fixed epoch, with all the hypotheses and circumstances taken into account; if even one of these were neglected, the whole series of years would be thrown out of joint. So it is a wonder why some extend the years of the Hebrews now in use back to the beginning of the world, as if there were a sure comparison of those years with the Julian years. For how could the years of the Hebrews be equally compared with the Julian years, since no cycle exists that could effect that equation? It is indeed well known that the Julian nineteen-year cycle consists of 6940 days, but the Hebrew nineteen-year cycle is irregular by convention: it sometimes has 6940 days, sometimes 6939, and sometimes it is completed with 6941 days. In the same way the Hebrews' great cycle, which contains thirteen unequal nineteen-year cycles, that is 247 solar years, is necessarily irregular. Therefore we can make no comparison with the Julian years either through the nineteen-year cycles or through the great cycles of the Hebrews. Certainly the year of the world 5350 of the Hebrews begins on 1 September in the current year of Christ 1589. But since it is embolismic and deficient, it certainly has 383 days, which end on 18 September in the year of Christ 1590, so that the year of the world 5351 begins on 19 September. But that year is ordinary and abundant, and therefore has 355 days, which end on 8 September in the current year of Christ 1591, so that the year of the world 5352 falls on 9 September, and so on. You see, then, how the years of the Hebrews are most elegantly derived from a fixed epoch into the usual and uniform sequence of Julian years. But if that sequence were altered and made irregular, as happened in the Gregorian reform, the same basis of comparison would no longer hold. Therefore, in the deduction of times both earlier and later, not only must the epoch be most certain, but it is also required that the standard by which we make the equation be uniform, or at least that over the largest interval of time it have a most certain number of days.

units.la: Quæ cum Ptolemæus diligentissime consideraf-set, noluit antiquiore æram vlurpare, quàm eam quæ deducitur à Nabonasaro: quia incerta sit, qualis ante Nabonasarum fuerit temporum ratio. Ita enim scribit lib. 3 Almagesti, cap. 1: ὅσ(ται) αὐτάρκεις ... νομίζο-μεν ... [?] hoc est, Vnde satis conuenire existimamus, si quantum interiectum tempus inter nos & illos quorum habemus vetustas simul & accuratas obseruationes, poterit vt proximè accommodari ad periodicas hypotheses, tantum etiam nos tentemus cō ferre, ne studio negligamus competentem inquisiti-onem. Totius autem mundi æras, aut alius multipli-cis temporis obseruationes consideware, putamus alicnum esse ab iis qui discedi & veri cognoscendi studio ducuntur. Quibus verbis Ptolemæus indicat, satius esse certa temporum interualla examinare, & ad hypotheses astronomicas deducere, quàm ad mundi conditum aut alias remotissimas epochas, in quibus tamen nihil sit certi, deuenire.
units.tr: Since Ptolemy had considered these matters most diligently, he was unwilling to adopt an era older than that derived from Nabonassar, because the nature of the reckoning of times before Nabonassar is uncertain. For he writes thus in book 3 of the Almagest, chapter 1: Thence we think it sufficiently suitable, if as much of the interval of time as lies between us and those whose ancient and accurate observations we have, can be closely fitted to the periodic hypotheses; so we also try to make this comparison, so that we do not neglect through indifference a suitable inquiry. But to consider the era of the whole world, or other observations of a manifold time, we judge to be alien to those who are led by the desire to know the truth. [ὅσται αὐτάρκεις ... νομίζομεν ...] In these words Ptolemy indicates that it is better to examine fixed intervals of time and reduce them to astronomical hypotheses, than to arrive at the creation of the world or other most remote epochs, in which nothing certain is to be found.

units.la: Censorinus ex Varronis sententia testatur, tria esse temporum discrimina. primum ab hominum princi- pio ad cataclysmum priore, quod propter ignorantia vocatur ἀ̃ψηλον: secundum à cataclysmo priore ad Olympiadem, quod quia in eo multa fabulosa referuntur, μωσικὸν[?] nominatur: tertium a prima Olympi-ade ad nos, quod dicitur ἱστορικὸν[?], quia res in eo gestæ veris historiis cotinentur. Primum tempus quot annorum sit non potest comprehendi: secundum non plane quidem scitur, sed tamen ad mille circiter & sexcentos annos esse creditur: de tertio autem tempore fuit quidem aliqua inter autores dissensio in sex septemve tantummodo annis versata: sed hoc quodcunque caliginis Varro discussit, & pro cæteris lua sagacitate nunc diuersarum ciuitatum conferens tempora, nūc defectus eorumq; interualla retro dinumerans eruit verum, lucemq; ostendit, per quam numerus certus non annorum modo, sed & dierum perspici possit. Ex quibus verbis videre licet, quā ob causam Cenforinus æram Olympiadibus antiquiorem noluerit vsurpare: quia scilicet ante Olympiades nihil certi de connexione annorum est conscriptum. Eadē ratione nos mouemur, vt tabulas nostras chronologicas ab Olympiadibus incipiamus, & vfq; ad annum Christi millesimum & septingentesimum extendamus: cum in eo interuallo temporis certissimas habeamus rerum gestarum historias. Quod enim ad annos à creatione mundi attinet, quos Græci Latiniq; scriptores hactenus fuint secuti, tanta in illis est discrepantia & confusio, vt inde nullam temporum feriem colligere possimus, nisi aliæ circumstantiæ exprimantur. Certum quidem est, computationem annorum mundi apud multos populos & longo tempore in vsu fuisse: attamen sæpissime fuit intermissa: & licet subinde reuocaretur, saltem nouis hypothesibus annorum ordo fuit luxatus.
units.tr: Censorinus, following Varro, testifies that there are three divisions of time. The first, from the beginning of humankind to the earlier cataclysm, is called obscure [ἀ̃ψηλον] on account of ignorance. The second, from the earlier cataclysm to the first Olympiad, because many fabulous things are related in it, is called mythical [μωσικὸν]. The third, from the first Olympiad down to us, is called historical [ἱστορικὸν], because the events done in it are contained in true histories. The number of years in the first period cannot be determined; the second is not known exactly, but is believed to be about sixteen hundred years; as for the third period, there was indeed some disagreement among authors, concerning only six or seven years. But Varro dispelled whatever darkness there was in this matter, and, by his acumen, comparing now the chronologies of different states and now counting back their lapses and intervals, brought out the truth and showed the light by which a certain number not only of years but also of days can be perceived. From these words we may see why Censorinus was unwilling to use an era older than the Olympiads: namely, because nothing certain about the connection of years had been recorded before the Olympiads. By the same reasoning we are moved to begin our chronological tables from the Olympiads and extend them down to the year of Christ 1700, since in that interval of time we have the most certain histories of events. As for the years from the creation of the world, which Greek and Latin writers have hitherto followed, there is such discrepancy and confusion in them that we cannot gather from them any sequence of times, unless other circumstances are brought in. It is certain that the reckoning of the years of the world was in use among many peoples and for a long time, yet it was very often interrupted; and although it was sometimes restored, the order of the years was at least disturbed by new hypotheses.

units.la: Exfexto & septimo capite Genefeos intelligitur diluuium incidisse in annum mundi millesimum fexcentesicentesimum & quinquagesimum septimum: quot autem inde vsque ad primam Olympiadem, Vrbem conditam vel Nabonasarum anni sint elapsi, autores tam sacri quam profani minime consentiunt. Censorinus a cataclysmo priore vsq; ad Olympiades numerat annos circiter mille & sexcentos: qui si adiiciantur ad annos 1656 ante diluuium elapsos, conflatur summa 3 2 5 6 annorum, qui a condita mundi vsq; ad primam Olympiadem fuissent praeteriti: iuxta quam rationem annus Christi 1588 esset a mundi creatione quinquies millesimus quingentesimus nonagesimus septimus. Alfonsus inter diluuium & Nabonasarum putat transfiisse annos bis mille trecentos & quinquaginta quinque: qui si addatur ad annos 1656 ante diluuium translatos, prouenit summa 4011 annorum, qui a creatione mundi vsque ad Nabonasarum translatos: itaque annus Christi 1588 esset a conditu mundi sexies millesimus trecentesimus septuagesimus quartus. Nostri chronologi a diluuio ad promulgatam legem seu primum Pascha numerant 797 annos, inde ad excidium Troiae 327 annos, inde ad primam Olympiadem 403 annos: quorum omnium summa est 1527 annorum: hi additi ad annos 1656, qui a creatione mundi vsque ad diluuium sunt praeteriti, conficiunt annos 3173, qui ab initio mundi vsque ad primam Olympiadem effent elapsi: itaque annus Christi 1588 foret a conditu mundi quinquies millesimus quingentesimus trigesimus sextus. Graeci aliqui scribunt a conditu mundi vsque ad aeram Iezdagirdicam elapsos fuisse annos 6139, vt indicatum est in calendario Persico: iuxta hanc hypothesin annus Christi 1588 esset a creatione mundi septies millesimus nonagesimus sextus. Hebræi dictitat à mundo condito vsq; ad æram Alexandri Dhilkarnain effluxisse annos 3449[?], vt ostensum est in calendario Syriaco: iuxta quā ratione annus mundi 5349[?] incurrit in annū Christi 1588. Hæ sunt insigniores de creatione mundi autorum sententiæ, quas nullo modo conciliare licet. Hebræusno-stri Alfragani interpres sub finem capitis primi, animaduertit dissensionem esse inter Christianos & Iudæos in æra mundi constituenda, sed de ea nihil definire voluit: probabile tamen est, ipsum in numeratione annorum mundi suæ genti adhæsisse[?], &contrariā opinione reiecisse. Inter nostros chronologos sunt aliqui, qui existimant æram Iudaicam cœpisse, cum a principio mundi elapsæ essent decē enneadecaeterides, h.e. anni centū & nonaginta: secundum hanc rationem annus mundi 5539 incurreret in annū Christi 1588. Quod autem æquinoctium autumnale tempore creationis mundi confectū fuerit die 28 Octobris, anticipatio in annis Iulianis satis indicat: nostro enim seculo Tekupha Tisri statuitur in xiiii Octobris. Atq; inter 14 & 28 Octobris dies interiecti sunt quatuordecim, cū tamen anni mundi elapsi 5539 requirant dies anticipatos 44: quatenus ad anticipationem diei vnius assumuntur anni centu. Sed dicendum est ab Hebreis TekuphăTisri nostro tempore collocari in xiiii Octobris, in quo hesit ætate Mosis cum primū Pascha celebraretur, currente anno æræ Iudaicæ 2264: alias si verū æquinoctium autumni respiciatur, quod iam coficitur 14 Septebris, vtiq; inter illud & priscum creationis mundi æquinoctiū autumnale dies sunt interiecti 44. Hactenus ratione præcipuorum calendariorum exposuimus, simulq; ostendimus a quibus epochis in multas annorum centurias continuari debeant. Cum autem hæc omnia sine iusta annorum ab Olympiadibus & Vrbe condita vsque ad nostram ætatem connexione percipi nequeant, restat vt tabulas chronologicas subiungamus, & in illis seriem omnem declaremus.
units.tr: In the seventh and eighth chapters of Genesis it is understood that the Flood fell in the year of the world 1657. How many years have elapsed from there to the first Olympiad, the founding of the City, or the Nabonassar era, however, sacred and profane authors by no means agree. Censorinus counts about 1,600 years from the earlier cataclysm to the Olympiads. If these are added to the 1656 years that passed from the creation of the world to the Flood, the sum is 3256 years that would have passed from the beginning of the world to the first Olympiad. On this reckoning the year of Christ 1588 would be the 5597th year from the creation of the world. Alfonsus holds that 2355 years passed between the Flood and Nabonassar. If these are added to the 1656 years before the Flood, the sum is 4011 years from creation to Nabonassar, so the year of Christ 1588 would be the 6374th year from the founding of the world. Our chronologers count 797 years from the Flood to the promulgation of the law, or the first Passover; from there to the fall of Troy 327 years; and from there to the first Olympiad 403 years. The sum of all these is 1527 years. Added to the 1656 years that passed from the creation of the world to the Flood, they make 3173 years, which would have elapsed from the beginning of the world to the first Olympiad. So the year of Christ 1588 would be the 5536th year from the creation of the world. Some Greeks write that 6139 years elapsed from the creation of the world to the Iezdegerdic era, as indicated in the Persian calendar. On this hypothesis the year of Christ 1588 would be the 7096th year from the creation of the world. The Hebrews assert that 3449[?] years passed from the founding of the world to the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain, as shown in the Syriac calendar. On this reckoning the year of the world 5349[?] falls in the year of Christ 1588. These are the more notable opinions of authors about the creation of the world, and they cannot be reconciled in any way. The Hebrew translator of our Alfraganus, near the end of the first chapter, notes that there is disagreement between Christians and Jews over fixing the era of the world, but he chose not to decide the matter. It is nonetheless probable that he adhered to his own people's way of counting the years of the world and rejected the opposing view. Among our chronologers there are some who think the Jewish era began when ten enneadecaeterides, that is 190 years, had elapsed from the beginning of the world. On this reckoning the year 5539 of the world would fall in the year of Christ 1588. That the autumnal equinox at the time of the creation of the world fell on 28 October is sufficiently indicated by the Julian anticipation: in our century the Tekuphah of Tishri is set on 14 October. Between 14 and 28 October there are fourteen days, yet the 5539 elapsed years of the world require 44 days of anticipation, since one day of anticipation is reckoned for every hundred years. But it must be said that the Hebrews place the Tekuphah of Tishri in our time on 14 October, in which, in the age of Moses, when the Passover was first celebrated, in the year 2264 of the Jewish era. Otherwise, if the true autumnal equinox is considered, which now falls on 14 September, then between it and the ancient autumnal equinox at the creation of the world there are 44 days. So far we have set out, by reference to the principal calendars, and we have also shown from which epochs they ought to be continued over many centuries of years. Since all of this cannot be grasped without a sound connection of the years from the Olympiads and the founding of the City down to our own age, it remains for us to append chronological tables and to set out the whole sequence in them.

units.la: TABVLÆ CHRONOLOGICÆ AB OLYMPIADIBVS ET VRBE conditæ vsque ad nostram ætatem annorum connexionem verissimè indicantes.
units.tr: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLES, MOST ACCURATELY SHOWING THE CONNECTION OF YEARS FROM THE OLYMPIADS AND THE FOUNDING OF THE CITY DOWN TO OUR OWN AGE.

Hinc sequitur principium Olympiadum incidere circa solstitium, currente anno se-ptingentesimo trigesimo primo ante ordinationem Iulianam, aureo numero Iulij Cæsaris designato XI. & litera dominicali existete F. quatenus annu primu ante ordinatione Iulianam fingimus bisextilem suis-se, literis dominicalibus existentibus DC. & assigna-to aureo numero Iulij Cæsaris XIX. Quamobrem ante ordinatione Iulianam ab Olympiade prima elapsi sunt menses sex, & septingenti triginta anni solares: quod etiam ex cyclis enneadecaëtericis manifestissi-me apparet:nam principium aurei numeri,quod incurrit in annum septingetesimum vigesimum secun-dum ante ordinationem Iuliana, incipit trigesimam octauam enneadecaëteridem: itaque si annos undecim unius enneadecaëteridis ducamus in 3 8 enneadecaëterides ante ordinationem Iulianam elapsas, proueniunt anni 722, à solstitio astiuo ineuntis anni Olympiadici decimi, usq; ad solstitium idem ante ordinationem Iulij Cæsaris elapsi: quibus si annumerentur anni novem ex trigesima nona enneadecaeteride consummati; prodit annus septingentesimus trigesimus primus ante ordinationem Iulianam labens: is fi à kal.Ianuariis more Romano initium fumat, oftendit primam Olympiadem incurre-re circa kalendas Iulias, vbi folftitium æftiuum hæ-fiffe ex Ptolemæo euidenter probari poteft. Hæc eft veriffima epocha Olympiadum : quam nifi exacte notauerimus, nunquam rationem temporum affe-quemur, quæ nobis Græci in fuis faftis defcripferunt. Eufebius Cæfarienfis in chronicis ait, A captiuitate Troiæ vfque ad Olympiadem primam elapfi anni 405. Æfchyli Athenienfium iudicis fecundo anno prima Olympias acta, quo erat Agon gymnicus, in quo Chorœbus Elienfis extitit victor. Elij agunt quinquennale certamen, quatuor annis in medio expletis, in quibus principes annui conftituuntur quatuor,quam Olympiadem Iphitus filius Praxonidæ fiue Æmonis primus conftituit. Ab hoc tempore Græca de temporibus hiftoria vera creditur: nam ante hoc vt cuique vifum eft diuerfas fententias protulerunt. Vult Eufebius annum primum Olympiadicum effe quadringentefimum fextum ab excidio Troiæ: fiquidem etiam Ephorus teftatur Ilium captum effe circa folftitium : verum hic character fatis obfcurus eft, nifi ad annos Iulianos & Chrifti referatur. Itaque nos dicimus à prima Olympiade circa folftitium æftiuum celebrata, vfque ad ordinationem Iulianam die octauo poft brumam incuntem elapfos effe menfes fex, & feptingentos trigin-ta annos folares: ab ordinatione vero Iuliana vfq; ad principium annorum Chrifti vfitatorum effluxiffe annos Iulianos quadraginta quinque: unde fequitur à prima Olympiade vfq; ad principium annorum Chrifti vfitatorum elapfos effe fex menfes & feptingentos & feptuaginta quinque annos folares. Agon quidem Olympicus ante excidium Troiæ ab Hercule eft instítutus, sed negligentia posterorum fuit intermif-sus, donec Iphitus eum instauraret, & Olympiadicorum annorum vsum introduceret. Ludicrum Olympicum committebatur plenilunio siue die decima quinta mesis Hecatombæonis, cuius neomenia proxime sequebatur, ut Scholiastes Pindari in Olympiis, [illegible, ~20 letters] ὁ ὁ- λυμπικὸς ἀγὼν ἀγέτω, [illegible, ~30 letters] κρίσις, hoc est, quoniam in plenilunio Olympiacum certamen committitur, & die decima sexta mensis iudicium fertur de victoria. Olympias continet quatuor annos solares, unde etiam πενταετηρίς[?] dicitur, at quia quinto quoque anno redeunte secundum Athenienses novilunium ad epocham suam recurrebat, & plenilunio subsequenti certamen Olympicum committebatur, Olympias dicta est πενταετηρίς[?], teste Censorino, cum inquit: Quare agon & in Elide Ioui Olympio & Romæ Capitolino quinto quoq; anno redeun-te celebratur. & alibi expressius, Et tetraeterida fecerunt, sed eam quod quinto quoq; anno redibat, pen-taeterida nominabant.
units.tr: Years before the Julian reform | Golden number | Olympiad years | Dominical letters 731 | XI | α 1 | A F 730 | XII | β 2 | E 729 | XIII | γ 3 | DC 728 | XIV | δ 4 | B 727 | XV | α 5 | B A 726 | XVI | β 6 | G 725 | XVII | γ 7 | FE 724 | XVIII | δ 8 | D 723 | XIX | α 9 | Γ C 722 | 38—I[?] | β 10 | B 721 | II | γ 11 | AG 720 | III | δ 12 | F 719 | IV | α 13 | Δ E 718 | V | β 14 | D 717 | VI | γ 15 | CB 716 | VII | δ 16 | A 715 | VIII | α 17 | E G 714 | IX | β 18 | F 713 | X | γ 19 | ED 712 | XI | δ 20 | C 711 | XII | α 21 | Z B 710 | XIII | β 22 | A 709 | XIV | γ 23 | GF 708 | XV | δ 24 | E ——I The city of Rome was founded by Romulus on the Kalends of March, which fell on the new moon nearest the equinox, at the end of the twenty-third Olympiad year, three months before the fourth year of the sixth Olympiad began, which began at the new moon nearest after the solstice. Therefore the twenty-fourth Olympiad year of Iphitus, that is the fourth year of the sixth Olympiad, falls around the solstice, the year 708 before the Julian reform having run out, with the golden number of Julius Caesar designated as 15 and the dominical letter being E. From this it follows that the beginning of the Olympiads falls around the solstice, in the year 731 before the Julian reform, with the golden number of Julius Caesar designated as 11 and the dominical letter being F; for we suppose that the first year before the Julian reform was a leap year, with the dominical letters DC, and the golden number of Julius Caesar assigned as 19. Accordingly, before the Julian reform there had elapsed from the first Olympiad six months and 730 solar years, which is also very clearly apparent from the enneadecaeteric cycles. For the beginning of the golden number, which falls in the year 722 before the Julian reform, begins the thirty-eighth enneadecaeteris. So if we multiply eleven years of one enneadecaeteris by the 38 enneadecaeterides elapsed before the Julian reform, there result 722 years, from the summer solstice on which the tenth Olympiad year began, to the same solstice before the Julian reform of Julius Caesar. If nine years completed from the thirty-ninth enneadecaeteris are added to these, the year 731 before the Julian reform results, which is running out. If this year is taken to begin on 1 January in the Roman manner, it shows that the first Olympiad falls around 1 July, where the summer solstice is clearly shown from Ptolemy to have been. This is the most accurate epoch of the Olympiads; unless we note it exactly, we will never grasp the reckoning of the times that the Greeks described for us in their annals. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Chronicle, says that 405 years elapsed from the captivity of Troy to the first Olympiad. In the second year of Aeschylus, the Athenian magistrate, the first Olympiad was held, in which the gymnastic contest took place, in which Coroebus of Elis was victor. The Eleans hold a quinquennial contest, with four years completed in between, in which four annual magistrates are appointed; this Olympiad Iphitus, son of Praxonides or of Aemon, first established. From this time Greek history of the times is believed to be true; for before this, each writer advanced different opinions as he saw fit. Eusebius holds that the first Olympiad year was the 406th year after the fall of Troy, since Ephorus also testifies that Ilium was taken around the solstice. But this statement is rather obscure unless it is referred to the Julian and Christian years. Accordingly, we say that from the first Olympiad, celebrated around the summer solstice, until the Julian reform, on the eighth day after the incoming winter solstice, six months and 730 solar years had elapsed; and from the Julian reform until the beginning of the customary years of Christ, forty-five Julian years had run out. Hence it follows that from the first Olympiad until the beginning of the customary years of Christ six months and 775 solar years had elapsed. The Olympic games were indeed instituted by Hercules before the fall of Troy, but through the negligence of later generations they were discontinued, until Iphitus restored them and introduced the custom of counting years by Olympiads. The Olympic festival was held at the full moon, or on the fifteenth day of the month Hekatombaion, and the new moon immediately preceded it, as the scholiast of Pindar on the Olympian odes says: [illegible] "let the Olympic contest be held" [ὁ ὁλυμπικὸς ἀγὼν ἀγέτω], [illegible] "judgment" [κρίσις]; that is, since the Olympic contest is held at the full moon, and on the sixteenth day of the month judgment is given concerning the victory. An Olympiad contains four solar years, whence it is also called a pentaeteris [πενταετηρίς]; but because, at the return of every fifth year, according to the Athenians the new moon returned to its epoch, and the Olympic contest was held at the full moon following, the Olympiad was called a pentaeteris [πενταετηρίς], as Censorinus attests when he says: "Therefore the contest is also celebrated in Elis for Olympian Zeus and at Rome for the Capitoline god, at every fifth year's return." And elsewhere more expressly: "They also made the tetraeteris, but because it returned in every fifth year, they called it the pentaeteris."

units.la: Ita octaeteris dicitur spacium octo annorum: quae etiam enneaeteris vocitata est, quia periodus illius nono quoque anno redibat. Sic biennium vocatum est, [illegible, ~8 letters] & [illegible, ~8 letters], quod tertio quoque anno ineunte periodus illius inciperet. Ita enneadecaeteridem Metonicam eam dicimus, quae complectitur annos nouendecim solares, in quibus absoluuntur lunationes ducentæ triginta quinque: quam etiam [illegible, ~12 letters] possumus appellare, quia periodus cycli Metonici redit anno quoque vigesimo ineunte, hoc est numeratur à ducentesima trigesima sexta quaq; redeunte lunatione. Facile resoluuntur Olympiades in simplices annos Olympiadicos, & anni Olympiadici quoque sine negocio rediguntur ad Olympiades. si enim elapsæ Olympiades per quatuor multiplicetur, proueniunt anni Olympiadici absoluti: at si anni Olympiadici elapsi per quatuor diuidantur; confur-gunt Olympiades elapsæ, & si quid in residuo relin-quitur, ostendit annum currentis Olympiadis. Verbi gratia, in annum septingentesimum octauum ante ordinationem Iulianam, circa solstitium æstiuum incidit annus Olympiadicus incipiens vigesimus quartus: ergo tunc elapsi sunt anni Olympiadici viginti tres, qui per 4 diuisi, ostendunt elapsas Olympiades quinque, & relinquunt in residuo 3. quod indicium est annum vigesimum tertium Olympiadicum, esse tertium sextæ Olympiadis currentis. Hæc vt indicarem, singulis quadriennis Olympiadicis adscripsi literas Græcorum α, β, γ, δ[?], & maiusculis numerorum notis initia sex priorum Olympiadum designaui, vt sciretur in subsequentibus annis eandem rationem obseruandam esse. Statuimus igitur Vrbem a Romu-lo conditam esse tribus mensibus ante initium anni Olympiadici vigesimi quarti, hoc est anno Olympiadico 23 ad finem labente, seu quod idem est, anno tertio sextæ Olympiadis ad finem currente, sicut verissimè scribit Onufrius Panuinius. Idem probari potest ex Velleio Paterculo, asserente Romam conditam esse, sexta Olympiade, post duos & viginti annos. quibus verbis indicat, Vrbem conditam esse, labente anno Olympiadico vigesimo tertio, postquam a prima Olympiade anni viginti duo fuissent cofum-mati[?]. Hanc sententiam confirmat Paterculus consulatu M. Vinicij, ante quem ait elapsos fuisse annos ab vrbe condita 782, & ab Olympiorum initio annos exactos 804: quasi dicere velit, M. Vinicium consu-latum iniisse anno Vrbis conditæ 783, & anno Olympiadico 805: quod verissimum esse nō tantum ostendit Onufrius, verum etiam indicat annus Iulianus 75, in quem ab æquinoctio verno incurrit annus Vrbis conditæ 783, & à solstitio sequenti incipit annus Olympiadicus 806. Eandē ratione sequitur Censorinus acerrimus temporum vindex, quæ optimo iure sequuntur omnes chronologi de connexione annorum diligentissime differentes: is scribit in annū Iulianum ducentesimum octogesimum tertium, circa æquinoctium vernum incurrisse annum Vrbis conditæ nongentesimum nonagesimum primum, & circa solstitium æstiuum incidisse annum Olympiadicum millesimum & quartum decimum. Si enim ad annum 991 ab vrbe condita labentem adiiciamus 23 annos Olympiadicos, qui à principio Olympiadum vsq; ad iacta fundamenta vrbis Romanæ fere elapsi fuerant, prodit annus 1014 Olympiadicus. Hinc intelligitur, quomodo datis annis ab vrbe condita sint comparandi anni Olympiadici: Si enim ad annos ab vrbe condita labentes, adiiciamus 23 annos à prima Olympiade fere elapsos, prodeunt respondentes anni Olympiadici, quorum initium sequitur fere quadrante anni lunaris post initium annorum ab vrbe condita supputatorum. Exempli gratia, in annum septingentesimum tertium ante ordinationem Iulianam, circa æquinoctium vernum incurrit principium anni sexti ab vrbe condita: Si ergo anni 23 Olympiadici adiiciantur, resultat annus Olympiadicus vigesimus nonus, cuius principium circa solstitium incidit, labente anno eodem 703 ante ordinationem Iulianam. E contrario, si anni Olympiadici proponantur mantur,&c ab illis subtrahantur 23 anni,prodeunt an- ni ab vrbe condita labentes. verbi gratia, si ab anno Olympiadico 19, qui ex diebus æstiuis[?] incurrit in annum 703 ante ordinationem Iulianam, subtrahamus 23 annos; relinquitur sextus annus ab vrbe condita, qui respondet anno vigesimo nono Olympiadico. Porrò diligenter obseruandum est, annos triginta octo priores ab vrbe condita fuisse decimestres, vt ex Censorino retulimus in calendario Romano: verùm singuli intercalatione 5 1[?] dierum fuerunt reuocati ad integros annos lunares. Etsi verò intercalatione aliqua decem menses lunares fuerint exæquati ad duodecim menses solares: tamen ex ordinatione Numæ Pompilij constat, anno lunari defuisse quinquaginta vnum dies, quo minùs occuparet prisc[?]as sedes[?] a Romulo constitutas. Ex quo sequitur diem XI kal.Maij ex ordinatione Numæ Pompilij, qui duodecim primùm introduxit menses lunares, & interualla certa inter kalendas, Nonas & Idus constituit, necnon religionibus & festis suum locum assignauit, incurrisse in kal.Martias secundum constitutionem Romuli: si enim in calendario Romuli a kalend.Martiis numerentur quinquaginta & vnus dies, quos Numa adiecit, recte Censorino, peruenitur ad diem XI kalend.Maij. Quare pro principio certissimo hoc tenendum est, vnum & eundem locum in zodiaco respondisse kalend.Martii iuxta calendarium Romuli, & diei XI kalend.Maij, iuxta calendarium Numæ Pompilij: nam vterque dies incidit in neomeniam proximam post æquinoctium. Quare cùm nos dicimus, Romulum vrbis fundamenta iecisse kalendis Martiis; annum, vt tunc erat constitutus, decimestrem intelligimus, cui defuerunt quinquaginta unus dies, quos deinde Romulus adiecit. Censorinus autem cum Varrone tradit urbem conditam esse ipsis Parilibus sive Palilibus, hoc est, die XI kal. Maij. Sed istud accipiendum est ex hypothesi, 'quasi anni a Romulo introducti fuissent duodecim mensium lunarium, in quibus solis ratio ordinaria festorum locum habuit: quod ex ordinatione Iulij Caesaris evidentissime conspicitur. Is enim cum a maioribus suis accepisset annum Numae Pompilij, in quo per duodecim menses lunares singula festa erant disposita, & iam multo tempore usurpata: decem dies adiecit anno lunari, quos extremis partibus mensium[?] apposuit, ne scilicet religiones suo cuiusque mensis a loco summouerentur, teste Censorino. units.tr: So the octaeteris denotes a span of eight years, and it is also called the enneaeteris, because its cycle returns in every ninth year. So the biennium was so called, [illegible] and [illegible], because its period began at the start of every third year. Likewise we call the Metonic enneadecaeteris the span of nineteen solar years, in which two hundred thirty-five lunations are completed. This too we can call [illegible], because the period of the Metonic cycle returns at the beginning of every twentieth year; that is, it is counted from the two hundred thirty-sixth returning lunation. Olympiads are easily resolved into single Olympiad years, and Olympiad years are just as easily reduced to Olympiads. If the Olympiads elapsed are multiplied by four, the complete Olympiad years result; but if the Olympiad years elapsed are divided by four, the Olympiads elapsed emerge, and whatever is left over shows the year of the current Olympiad. For example, in the seven hundred and eighth year before the Julian reform, around the summer solstice, there fell the Olympiad year beginning as the twenty-fourth. Therefore twenty-three Olympiad years had then elapsed; divided by four, these show five Olympiads elapsed and leave three as a remainder, which indicates that the twenty-third Olympiad year is the third year of the current sixth Olympiad. So that I might make this clear, I have added to each four-year Olympiad the Greek letters α, β, γ, δ, and with capital numerals I have marked the beginnings of the first six Olympiads, so that it may be known that the same method is to be observed in the following years. We therefore establish that the City was founded by Romulus three months before the beginning of the twenty-fourth Olympiad year, that is, when the twenty-third Olympiad year was drawing to its close; or, what is the same, in the third year of the sixth Olympiad, as Onufrius Panvinius writes most truly. The same can be proved from Velleius Paterculus, who asserts that Rome was founded in the sixth Olympiad, twenty-two years after [the first]. By these words he indicates that the City was founded as the Olympiad year twenty-three was ending, after twenty-two years had been completed from the first Olympiad. Paterculus confirms this opinion in the consulship of M. Vinicius, before which he says that 782 years had elapsed from the founding of the city and 804 full years from the beginning of the Olympics. It is as if he wished to say that M. Vinicius entered upon his consulship in the year 783 from the founding of the City and in the Olympiad year 805. That this is most true is shown not only by Onufrius, but also by the Julian year 75, into which the year 783 from the founding of the City falls from the vernal equinox, and from the following solstice the Olympiad year 806 begins. Censorinus, a most keen champion of chronology, follows the same method, and all chronologists rightly follow him in the most careful discussion of the connection of years. He writes that in the Julian year 283, around the vernal equinox, the year 991 from the founding of the City fell, and around the summer solstice the Olympiad year 1014 fell. For if to the year 991 from the founding of the City, now elapsing, we add 23 Olympiad years, which had nearly elapsed from the beginning of the Olympiads to the laying of the foundations of the Roman city, the Olympiad year 1014 results. From this it is understood how, given years from the founding of the City, the Olympiad years are to be matched: for if to the years from the founding of the City now elapsing we add the 23 Olympiad years that had nearly elapsed from the first Olympiad, the corresponding Olympiad years result, whose beginning follows about a quarter of a lunar year after the beginning of the years reckoned from the founding of the City. For example, in the seven hundred and third year before the Julian reform, around the vernal equinox, the beginning of the sixth year from the founding of the City fell. If therefore the 23 Olympiad years are added, the twenty-ninth Olympiad year results, whose beginning falls around the solstice, the same year 703 before the Julian reform now elapsing. Conversely, if Olympiad years are given and 23 years are subtracted from them, the years from the founding of the City now elapsing result. For example, if from the Olympiad year 19, which in the summer falls in the year 703 before the Julian reform, we subtract 23 years, the sixth year from the founding of the City remains, which corresponds to the twenty-ninth Olympiad year. Moreover, it must be carefully observed that the first thirty-eight years from the founding of the City were of ten months, as we reported from Censorinus in the Roman calendar; but each of them was brought back to full lunar years by an intercalation of 51 days. Although by some intercalation ten lunar months were made equal to twelve solar months, nevertheless from the ordinance of Numa Pompilius it is established that the lunar year lacked fifty-one days, which prevented it from occupying the ancient seats established by Romulus. From this it follows that the 11th day before the Kalends of May, according to the ordinance of Numa Pompilius, who first introduced twelve lunar months and fixed definite intervals between the Kalends, Nones and Ides, and also assigned their place to religious observances and festivals, fell on the Kalends of March according to the arrangement of Romulus. For if in the calendar of Romulus we count from the Kalends of March fifty-one days, which Numa added, we rightly arrive, as Censorinus says, at the 11th day before the Kalends of May. Hence this must be held as a most certain principle: that the Kalends of March according to the calendar of Romulus, and the 11th day before the Kalends of May according to the calendar of Numa Pompilius, corresponded to one and the same place in the zodiac; for both days fell on the next new moon after the equinox. Therefore when we say that Romulus laid the foundations of the City on the Kalends of March, we understand the year, as it was then constituted, to have been one of ten months, which lacked fifty-one days that Romulus afterwards added. Censorinus, however, with Varro, relates that the City was founded on the Parilia or Palilia itself, that is, on the 11th day before the Kalends of May. But this must be taken as a hypothesis, as if the years introduced by Romulus had been of twelve lunar months, in which the ordinary solar reckoning governed the place of the festivals; which is most clearly seen from the ordinance of Julius Caesar. For when he had received from his ancestors the year of Numa Pompilius, in which each festival had been arranged over the twelve lunar months, and had been used for a long time, he added ten days to the lunar year, which he placed at the end of the months, so that the religious observances of each month should not be removed from their place, as Censorinus testifies.
