units.la: In annum septingentesimum secundum ante ordinationem Iulianam, aureo numero assignato II. & litera dominicali existente E. die vigesima sexta Februarii, feria quarta, ipso meridie Thoth sive Mercurij incurrit principium annorum Nabonasari. Atqui eodem anno 702 ante ordinationem Iulianam circa aequinoctium vernum incidit annus septimus ab urbe condita: unde sequitur principium annorum Nabonasari incurrere sub finem anni sexti ab urbe con-dita. Praeterea eodem anno 702 ante ordinationem Iulianam circa solstitium aestivum incipit annus Olympiadicus trigesimus, labente anno septimo ab urbe condita: & si solstitium ponamus in kal. Iulias, sequitur a 26 Februarii vsq; ad kal. Iulias, quibus init annus trigesimus Olympiadicus, intercedere centum & viginti quinq; dies, qui pertinent ad annum Olympia-dicum vigesimum nonum, cuius complementu est 240 dierum. Quare a prima Olympiade solstitio aestiuo ineunte, vsq; ad principium annorum Nabona-fari elapsi sunt anni Aegyptii viginti octo, & 247 dies, hoc est, anni Iuliani viginti octo & ducenti quadraginta dies. Quod autem aera Nabonafari ponenda sit in 26 Februarii, ostendunt connexiones annorum ante ordinationem Iulianam, & post eam vsq; ad annum 283 Iulianum, quo Thoth Nabonafari 986 incurrit in die 25 Iunii, teste locupletissimo Censorino. Scribit Ptolemaeus lib. 3 Almagesti, sub fine capitis octavi, in principio annorum Nabonafari solem secundum medium motum occupasse 4 [?]5 minuta pr. mi gradus Piscium: si ergo ascendamus a 26 Februarii per duo signa, animaduertemus brumam fuisse pridie kal. Ianuarii: si vero a 26 Februarii per vnum signum coelestes descendamus, perueniemus ad 27 Martii, in quo fuit aequinoctium vernum: hinc si iterum per tria signa descendamus, accedimus ad diem pridie kal. Iulias: vbi solstitium haesisse verisimile est: si quidem Meton annis trecentis post obseruauit solstitium in die 28 Iunii. Quod ad epocham lunarem attinet in principio annorum Nabonafari, scribit Ptolemaeus lib. 4 Almagesti, cap. 8, lunam secundum medium motum fuisse in gradu vndecimo, & 21 minuto Tauri: ergo luna a sole distabat 70 gradus, & 37 minuta, quod etiam annotatum est in versione Arabica. Ex quo sequitur coniunctionem praecedentem solis & lunae contigisse 21 Februarii, cum sol occuparet vigesimu quintum gradum Aquarij, in ficta neomenia μηνῶν[?], hoc est, die quinto ante primum Thoth Nabonasari. Hoc ipsum confirmat enneadecaeteris Julia-na: annus enim 702 ante ordinationem Julianam, habet aureum numerum II, qui in calendario Julia-no ponitur ad XII kal. Martij, sed propter anticipationem lunarem triduo serius neomenia coelestis occurrit, videlicet 21 Februarij: vt hinc appareat nos epocham nouilunij recte cotulisse in kal. primas Julianas, veramque annorum Nabonasari cum annis Julianis connexionem autore Censorino tradidisse, quod deinceps etiam multis aliis exemplis comprobabimus.
units.tr: In the seven hundred and second year before the Julian reform, with the golden number assigned as II and the dominical letter being E, on the twenty-sixth day of February, a Wednesday, at noon on Thoth, or Mercury's day, the beginning of the years of Nabonassar falls. Yet in that same year 702 before the Julian reform, around the vernal equinox, the seventh year from the founding of the City fell; from which it follows that the beginning of the years of Nabonassar falls at the end of the sixth year from the founding of the City. Moreover, in that same year 702 before the Julian reform, around the summer solstice, the thirtieth Olympiad year begins, the seventh year from the founding of the City having elapsed. And if we place the solstice on the Kalends of July, there lie between 26 February and the Kalends of July, on which the thirtieth Olympiad year begins, 125 days, which belong to the twenty-ninth Olympiad year, whose total is 240 days. Therefore from the first Olympiad, at the beginning of the summer solstice, to the beginning of the years of Nabonassar, twenty-eight Egyptian years and 247 days have elapsed; that is, twenty-eight Julian years and two hundred forty-seven days. That the era of Nabonassar must be placed on 26 February is shown by the connections of years before the Julian reform, and after it up to the Julian year 283, in which Thoth of Nabonassar 986 falls on 25 June, according to the most learned Censorinus. Ptolemy writes in book 3 of the Almagest, near the end of chapter 8, that at the beginning of the years of Nabonassar the sun, according to mean motion, occupied 4[?]5 minutes of the first degree of Pisces. If therefore we ascend from 26 February through two signs, we notice that the winter solstice was the day before the Kalends of January; but if from 26 February we descend through one sign, we reach 27 March, on which the vernal equinox fell; and if again we descend through three signs, we come to the day before the Kalends of July, where the solstice most probably stood, since Meton observed the solstice on 28 June three hundred years later. As for the lunar epoch at the beginning of the years of Nabonassar, Ptolemy writes in book 4 of the Almagest, chapter 8, that the moon, according to mean motion, was in the eleventh degree and 21st minute of Taurus. Therefore the moon was 70 degrees and 37 minutes distant from the sun, which is also noted in the Arabic version. From this it follows that the preceding conjunction of sun and moon happened on 21 February, when the sun occupied the twenty-fifth degree of Aquarius, at the feigned new moon [μηνῶν], that is, five days before the first Thoth of Nabonassar. This very thing is confirmed by the Julian enneadecaeteris: for the year 702 before the Julian reform has the golden number II, which in the Julian calendar is placed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March; but because of the lunar anticipation the celestial new moon occurs two days later, namely on 21 February. From this it appears that we have rightly placed the epoch of the new moon on the first Kalends of Julian, and that Censorinus has handed down the true connection of the years of Nabonassar with the Julian years, as we shall further prove by many other examples.

units.la: De anticipatione autem lunari hoc notum est, quod annis elapsis 247 solaribus luna praeuertat die vno enneadecaeteridem: quare vt post ordinati-onem Julianam elapsis quibuslibet 247 annis solaribus epocha enneadecaeteridis die vno serius nouilu-nia ostendit, vt per diem vnam sit ascendendum, ita ante ordinationem Julianam elapsis quibuslibet 247 annis solaribus epocha enneadecaeteridis die vno citius nouilunia ostendit, vt per diem vna sit descendendum, quo habeatur verus nouiluniorum situs.
units.tr: Concerning the lunar anticipation, it is known that after 247 solar years the moon runs ahead by one day in the nineteen-year cycle. So after the Julian reform, after any 247 solar years the epoch of the nineteen-year cycle shows the new moons one day later, so one must move forward by one day. Likewise, before the Julian reform, after any 247 solar years the epoch shows the new moons one day earlier, so one must move back by one day, in order to obtain the true position of the new moons.

units.la: Quis vero fuerit Nabonasarus, a cuius imperio coeperit epocha apud Ptolemaeum & Censorinum celeberrima, non prorsus nobis est perspectum. Arabes & Hebraei propter solam nominum affinitatem Nabonasarum vocant Nabuchodonosore siue Nebukadnezarem Babylonium. quod autem nequaquam sit magnus Nabuchodonosor, patet ex indubitato interuallo annorum Aegyptiorum quadringentorum viginti quatuor, qui inter imperium Nabonasari & mortem Alexandri fuerunt absoluti. Si historiam sacram cum observationibus Ptolemaicis conferamus, deprehendemus Nabuchodonosorem magnum coepisse[?] imperare anno decimo nono Nabopollasari: Nabopollasarum vero regnasse annos octodecim.
units.tr: Who Nabonassar was, from whose reign the epoch famous in Ptolemy and Censorinus began, is not entirely clear to us. The Arabs and Hebrews, on the strength of the mere similarity of names, call Nabonassar Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian. That he is by no means the great Nebuchadnezzar is clear from the undoubted interval of 424 Egyptian years that elapsed between the reign of Nabonassar and the death of Alexander. If we compare sacred history with the Ptolemaic observations, we find that Nebuchadnezzar the Great began to reign in the nineteenth year of Nabopolassar, and that Nabopolassar reigned eighteen years.

units.la: Nam Ezechiel propheta a principio primi capitis scribit annum trigesimum, scilicet Nabopollasari, patris Nabuchodonosoris, esse quintum capti Ioiachin: ex quo sequitur primum annum capti Ioiachin incidere in annum vigesimum sextum Nabopollasari. Atqui primus annus capti Ioiachin fuit octavus imperii Nabuchodonosoris: ex quo intelligitur annum decimum nonum Nabopollasari fuisse primum imperii Nabuchodonosoris, hoc est, annum Nabonasari centesimum quadragesimum primum, quatenus annum 1 Nabopollasari Ptolemaeus refert ad annum cetesimum vigesimum tertium Nabonasari. Itaq; inter Nabonasarum Ptolemaei & Censorini, & inter Nabuchodonosorem magnum sunt interiecti anni centum & quadraginta: unde evidens est, non posse esse eundem Nabonasarum & Nabuchodonosorem. Nabonasaro successit Mardokempadus, ut refert Ptolemaeus. Atq; Mardokempadus Esaiae 39 dicitur filius Bel-adan, cuius nomen proprium fuerit Merodac, qui libro secundo Regum cap. 20 appellatur Berodac: ex quo apparet, Bel-adan patre Merodachi coferri posse cum nostro Nabonasaro. Haec si displiceant, possumus dicere Nabonasarum esse nomen generale regum Chaldaeorum sive Babyloniorum, aeramq; Nabonasari eam appellari, unde Aegyptii annales suos ad motuū coelestium observationes coeperint supputare: quod Ptolemaeus cum Censorino affirmat accidisse, elapsis annis Aegyptiis quadringentis & 24 ante mortem Alexandri. Hac ratione Ptolemaeus & Censorinus per Nabonasarum videtur voluisse indicare certum Babyloniorum regem, cuius tunc nomen ꝓpriū fuerit incognitum.
units.tr: For the prophet Ezekiel writes at the beginning of his first chapter that the thirtieth year, that is, of Nabopolassar, the father of Nebuchadnezzar, was the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin. From this it follows that the first year of the captivity of Jehoiachin fell in the twenty-sixth year of Nabopolassar. Yet the first year of the captivity of Jehoiachin was the eighth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. From this it is understood that the nineteenth year of Nabopolassar was the first year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, that is, the hundred and forty-first year of Nabonassar, since Ptolemy refers the first year of Nabopolassar to the hundred and twenty-third year of Nabonassar. Therefore between the Nabonassar of Ptolemy and Censorinus and the great Nebuchadnezzar there lie one hundred and forty years, whence it is evident that Nabonassar and Nebuchadnezzar cannot be the same person. Nabonassar was succeeded by Mardokempadus, as Ptolemy reports. And Mardokempadus is called in Isaiah 39 the son of Baladan, whose proper name was Merodach, who in the second book of Kings chapter 20 is called Berodach; from this it appears that the father of Merodach, Baladan, can be compared with our Nabonassar. If these points are unwelcome, we may say that Nabonassar is the general name of the kings of the Chaldeans or Babylonians, and that the era is called the era of Nabonassar, from which the Egyptians began to compute their annals by observations of the heavenly motions; this Ptolemy together with Censorinus affirms happened 424 Egyptian years before the death of Alexander. In this way Ptolemy and Censorinus seem to have wished to indicate by Nabonassar a certain king of the Babylonians, whose proper name was then unknown.

units.la: Porro in annis Nabonasari duo maxime necessaria sunt obseruanda: quorum primum pertinet ad collationem annorum bisextilium, alterū vero spectat ad comparationem annorum æquabilium Nabonasari cum annis folaribus Olympiadū, vrbis conditæ,Iulii Cæsaris,&Christi.Cum enim ex hypothesi ab anno primo Iuliano retrorsum numeremus vsq; ad principium Olympiadum, annos folares 731, vt quartus quisq; eorum bisextilis sit, ac literæ dominicales iuxta ordinarium cyclum 28 annorum solarium fe subsequantur: fit vt propter bisextum interiectum, Thoth Nabonasari semper diem vnum anticipet, etsi dies ille anticipatus diuersum situ obtineat. Exempli gratia,primus Thoth Nabonasari fixus fuit in 26 Februarii, feria quarta,currente anno 702 ante ordinationem Iuliana,litera dominicali existente E: itaq; anno sequenti bisextili, qui est annus 701 ante ordinationem Iulianā,literis dominicis existentibus DC. Thoth secundi anni Nabonasari traducitur ad 25 diem Februarii, feriam quintam, cum bisextu inferatur inter 23 & 24 Februarii diem. In 25 Februarii die manet annis subsequentibus, licet feriarum situ mutet, donec anno sexto Nabonasari, qui incurrit in annum 697 ante ordinationem Iulianam, bisextile, & habentem literas dominicales FE, propter bisextum proxime interiectum transfeat ad 24 Februarii, feriā secundā: & in 24 Februarii subsistit, donec anno vndecimo Nabonasari, qui incurrit in annum 692 ante ordinationem Iulianam, simplicem, & literam dominicalem habentem F, Thoth peruenit ad 23 Februarii, feriam septimam, quod anno decimo praecedenti Nabonasari, qui incurrit in annum 693 ante ordinationem Iulianam, bisextilem, & literas dominicales AG habentem, interiectum fuerit bisextum ante Februarii diem:hoc est,quòd Thoth Nabonafari decimus inciderit in ipsum bisextum. Eadem est ratio anticipationis dierum in annis subsequentibus: cùm enim Thoth Nabonafari anteuerterit fedé intercalationis Romanæ,non amplius adscribitur annis bisextilibus dies anticipatus, sed annis communibus proximè subsequentibus, donec perueniatur ad annum 477 ante ordinationem Iuliana, qui bisextilis est,literis dominicalibus existentibus DC: in cuius kal.Ianuarias,feria quinta incurrit principium anni Nabonafari 226:&in diem postremam anni illius bisextilis, h.e. in 31 Decembris, feria sexta,incidit principium anni Nabonafari 227. Anno ducentesimo trigesimo primo Nabonafari,qui incurrit in annu folarem 473 ante ordinationem Iuliana,bisextile, literas dominicales habentem FE, Thoth transfertur ad 30 Decembris,feriam tertiam.Ita deinceps annis bisextilibus assignatur dies à Thoth Ægyptiorū anticipatus, quia proximè interiectum fuit bifextu ante 24 Februarii diem : donec perueniatur ad annum Iulianum 769,hoc est,ad annu Christi 724. qui licet bisextilis fit,literis dominicalibus existentibus BA;non tamè accipit notâ anticipationis,cùm Thoth Nabonafari iam cœperit anteuertere fedé intercalationis Romanæ. Itaq; anno subsequenti Iuliano 770 simplici,cuius litera dominicalis est G, Thoth Nabonafari 1473 transit ad 23 Februarii,feriam sexta:atq;sic annis simplicibus, qui proximè fequùtur post bisextiles, dies anticipatus assignatur, donec perueniatur ad annu Iulianu 98 ʃ,qui bisextilis est,literis dominicalibus existentibus ED.In cuius kal. Ianuarias, feria quarta, incurrit principium anni Nabonafari 1688, &in eiusdem anni finem, hoc est,in 31 Decembris, feriam quintam, incidit principium anni Nabonafari 1689. Anno Iuliano 989[?], hoc est, anno Christi 944, qui bisextilis est, literis dominicalibus existentibus GF. Thoth Nabonafari 1693 transfertur ad 30 diem Decembris, feria secunda, quod proxime interiectum fuerit bisextum. Itaque deinceps usq; ad nostra tempora dies anticipatus iterum adscribitur annis bisextilibus. Haec summa est collatio annorum Nabonafari cum annis solaribus ante Iulium Cæsarem excogitatis, & post ordinationem Iulianam reuera elapsis: in qua pulcherrime sibi respondent characteres feriarum, qui annis Ægyptiis & solaribus attribuuntur: simul etiam perspicitur, an dies bisextiles referendi sint ad annos Nabonafari labentes, vel ad præteritos.
units.tr: Furthermore, in the years of Nabonassar two things are chiefly to be observed: the first concerns the collation of the leap years, and the second concerns the comparison of the equal years of Nabonassar with the solar years of the Olympiads, the founding of the city, Julius Caesar and Christ. For when, on the hypothesis, we count backwards from the first Julian year to the beginning of the Olympiads, 731 solar years, so that every fourth of them is a leap year, and the dominical letters follow one another according to the ordinary cycle of 28 solar years, it comes about that, because of the intercalated leap day, the Thoth of Nabonassar always anticipates by one day, although that anticipated day holds a different position in the week. For example, the first Thoth of Nabonassar was fixed on 26 February, a Wednesday, in the year 702 before the Julian reform, the dominical letter being E. Therefore in the following year, a leap year, which is the year 701 before the Julian reform, with the dominical letters DC, the Thoth of the second year of Nabonassar is carried over to 25 February, a Thursday, since the leap day is inserted between 23 and 24 February. The Thoth remains on 25 February in the following years, although its place in the week changes, until in the sixth year of Nabonassar, which falls in the year 697 before the Julian reform, a leap year with the dominical letters FE, it is moved, because of the leap day lying just before, to 24 February, a Monday; and it stays on 24 February until the eleventh year of Nabonassar, which falls in the year 692 before the Julian reform, a common year with the dominical letter F, when the Thoth comes to 23 February, a Saturday. This happens because in the tenth preceding year of Nabonassar, which falls in the year 693 before the Julian reform, a leap year with the dominical letters AG, the leap day was inserted before 24 February; that is, the tenth Thoth of Nabonassar fell upon the leap day itself. The reason for the anticipation of days is the same in the following years: since the Thoth of Nabonassar has anticipated the seat of the Roman intercalation, the anticipated day is no longer added to the leap years, but to the common years immediately following, until we come to the year 477 before the Julian reform, which is a leap year with the dominical letters DC. On its first of January, a Thursday, falls the beginning of the 226th year of Nabonassar, and on the last day of that leap year, that is 31 December, a Friday, falls the beginning of the 227th year of Nabonassar. In the 231st year of Nabonassar, which falls in the solar year 473 before the Julian reform, a leap year with the dominical letters FE, the Thoth is transferred to 30 December, a Tuesday. Thus in succession the day anticipated by the Egyptian Thoth is assigned to the leap years, because the leap day was inserted just before 24 February; until we come to the Julian year 769, that is, the year 724 of Christ. Although this is a leap year with the dominical letters BA, it does not receive the mark of anticipation, since the Thoth of Nabonassar had by then begun to anticipate the seat of the Roman intercalation. Therefore in the following Julian year 770, a common year whose dominical letter is G, the Thoth of Nabonassar 1473 passes to 23 February, a Friday; and so the anticipated day is assigned to the common years which immediately follow the leap years, until we come to the Julian year 98?, which is a leap year with the dominical letters ED. On its first of January, a Wednesday, falls the beginning of the 1688th year of Nabonassar, and at the end of that year, that is on 31 December, a Thursday, falls the beginning of the 1689th year of Nabonassar. In the Julian year 989?, that is the year 944 of Christ, a leap year with the dominical letters GF, the Thoth of Nabonassar 1693 is transferred to 30 December, a Monday, since the leap day has been inserted just before. And so from then on, down to our own times, the anticipated day is again assigned to the leap years. This is the sum of the collation of the years of Nabonassar with the solar years devised before Julius Caesar and actually elapsed after the Julian reform; in it the marks of the weekdays, which are attributed to the Egyptian years and the solar years, agree most beautifully; at the same time it is also seen whether the leap days are to be referred to the Nabonassar years that are passing or to those that have passed.

units.la: Quod ad comparationem attinet annorum Nabonafari cum annis Olympiadicis, Urbis conditæ, Iulii Cæsaris, & Christi: circumspectione magna opus est, ne in anni unius vel duorum errorem incidamus. Si enim singulis annis solaribus, quales sunt Olympiadici, Urbis conditæ, Iulii Cæsaris, & Christi, prout in quouis quadriennio continentur 1461 dies, responderent singuli anni Nabonafari, res esset expeditissima: sed haud necessario tot sunt anni Olympiadici, Urbis conditæ, Iulii Cæsaris, & Christi, quot sunt anni Nabonafari: siquidem quadriennii quoduis Nabonafari complectitur tantum 1460 dies. Idcirco contingit ut in unicum annum solarem & naturale, si bisextilis est ex aggregatione quatuor quadrantum diei, incurrant principia duorum annorum Nabonafari, quorum unum in kal. Ianuariis, alterum in fine Decembris eiusdem anni bisextilis constituitur: cuius rei exemplum extat in anno 477 ante ordinationem Iulianam, item in anno Iuliano 985. Hunc scrupulum
units.tr: As regards the comparison of the years of Nabonassar with the years of the Olympiads, of the founding of the city, of Julius Caesar and of Christ, great care is needed lest we fall into an error of one or two years. For if each solar year of the Olympiads, of the founding of the city, of Julius Caesar and of Christ, as they are contained in any four-year period, namely 1461 days, corresponded to each year of Nabonassar, the matter would be most easily settled. But the years of the Olympiads, of the founding of the city, of Julius Caesar and of Christ are not necessarily as many as the years of Nabonassar, since any four-year period of Nabonassar comprises only 1460 days. Hence it happens that, into a single solar and natural year, if it is a leap year, from the sum of four quarters of a day, the beginnings of two years of Nabonassar fall, one of which is placed on the first of January and the other at the end of December of that same leap year; an example of this occurs in the year 477 before the Julian reform, and likewise in the Julian year 985.

units.la: {*} Annus vigesimus septimus Nabonafari incurrit in annum sexcentesimum septuagesimum sextum ante ordinationem Iulianam, die 19 Februarij, feria secunda: is est annus primus Mardokempadi apud Ptolemęum, quo dicit fuisse eclipsin lunare die 19 Thoth, sole occupante 14 gradu Piscium, ut videre licet lib.4 Almagesti, cap.6. Si a 19 Februarij, in quam incidit prima dies Thoth, numeremus dies 19, peruenimus ad 20 Martij, quando cospecta est in Babylonia eclipsis in oppositione luminariu: ergo diebus quindecim ante, sexta nimirum die Martij nouiluniu fuit, quod etiam probat enneadecaeteris Iuliana. Annus enim 676 ante ordinationem Iuliana habet aureu numerum IX, qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad quintu nonarum Martij: hinc si in triduum subsequens propter anticipationem lunare descendatur, neomenia coelestis ostenditur die secundo Nonarum.
units.tr: The twenty-seventh year of Nabonassar falls in the year 676 before the Julian reform, on 19 February, a Monday. This is the first year of Mardokempad according to Ptolemy, in which he says there was a lunar eclipse on the 19th of Thoth, with the sun in the 14th degree of Pisces, as can be seen in Almagest book 4, chapter 6. If we count 19 days from 19 February, the day on which the first day of Thoth fell, we arrive at 20 March, when the eclipse at the opposition of the luminaries was observed in Babylon. Therefore fifteen days earlier, namely on the sixth of March, there was a new moon, which the Julian nineteen-year cycle also confirms. For the year 676 before the Julian reform has golden number IX, which in the Julian calendar is placed at the fifth of the Nones of March. Hence, if we go down the following three days on account of the lunar anticipation, the heavenly new moon is shown to fall on the second of the Nones.

units.la: b Anno secundo Mardokempadi, hoc est, anno Nabonasari 28, refert Ptolemęus in Babylone iterum conspectam eclipsin lunare, die 18 Thoth, sole occupante 13 gradu Piscium. atqui Thoth Nabonasari 28 incidit in 19 Februarij, feriam tertiam, currente anno 675 ante ordinationem Iulianam. Si ergo a 19 Februarij numeremus dies 18, descendimus ad 9 Martij, quo fuit eclipsis in oppositione luminariu: hinc si quindecim dies antrorsum numeremus, peruenimus ad 24 Februarij diem, in quo nouilunium fuisse etiam enneadecaeteris Iuliana ostendit: annus enim 675 ante ordinationem Iulianam numerum aureu habet X, qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad decimum kal. Martij. hinc si in triduum subsequens descendatur propter anticipationem lunare, neomenia coelestis ostenditur circa die 7 kal. Martij. Eodem anno secundo Mardokempadi, hoc est, vigesimo octavo Nabonasari, scribit Ptolemæus conspectam esse tertiam eclipsin lunæ, transacto decimo quinto die Phamenoth, sole occupante tertium gradum Virginis. Si itaque à 19 Februarij numeremus sex menses Ægyptios,&quin-decim dies; descendimus ad secundam Septembris, qua visa est eclipsis in oppositione luminarium: hinc si retrorsum numeremus dies quindecim, peruenimus ad 18 Augusti, quo nouilunium fuisse etiam neadecaeteris Iuliana indicat: etenim numerus aureus X in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 12 kal.Maij, & recurrit circa 15 Augusti diem, sed triduo serius neomenia cótigit propter anticipationem lunarem.
units.tr: In the second year of Mardokempad, that is, the twenty-eighth year of Nabonassar, Ptolemy reports that a lunar eclipse was again observed at Babylon, on the 18th of Thoth, with the sun in the 13th degree of Pisces. Now Thoth of Nabonassar 28 fell on 19 February, a Tuesday, in the year 675 before the Julian reform. If, then, we count 18 days from 19 February, we come down to 9 March, when the eclipse occurred at the opposition of the luminaries. Hence, if we count fifteen days forward, we arrive at 24 February, on which the new moon also occurred, as the Julian nineteen-year cycle shows. For the year 675 before the Julian reform has golden number X, which in the Julian calendar is placed at the tenth of the Kalends of March. Hence, if we go down the following three days on account of the lunar anticipation, the heavenly new moon is shown to fall about the seventh of the Kalends of March. In the same second year of Mardokempad, that is, the twenty-eighth of Nabonassar, Ptolemy writes that a third lunar eclipse was observed, after the fifteenth day of Phamenoth had passed, with the sun in the third degree of Virgo. So if from 19 February we count six Egyptian months and fifteen days, we come down to 2 September, when the eclipse was seen at the opposition of the luminaries. Hence, if we count fifteen days backward, we arrive at 18 August, on which the new moon also occurred, as the Julian nineteen-year cycle indicates. For the golden number X is placed in the Julian calendar at the twelfth of the Kalends of May, and recurs about 15 August; but the new moon fell three days later on account of the lunar anticipation.

units.la: Has tres eclipses lunares Ptolemæus ponit pro fundamento suarum obseruationum, ex quibus etiam nos nouiluniorum situm optima ratione demonstrare possumus. Quòd autem annus secundus Mardokempadi sit 28 Nabonasari, indicat Ptolemæus lib.4. Almagefti cap.7,quando inter eclipsin priorem, quæ contigit anno secundo Mardokempadi,transacto 18 die Thoth,& inter eclipsin, quam ipse obseruauit anno decimo nono Adriani Imperatoris, elapso die secundo Chiac, dicit intercessisse annos Ægyptios 854, &73 dies:quasi velit dicere,à se obseruata esse eclipsin anno 855 currente ab anno secundo Mardokempadi. Si ergo annos 27 Nabonasari, qui elapsi sunt ante secundum annum Mardokempadi, adiiciamus ad annum 855 labentem ;producitur annus Nabonasari 882,qui respondet[?] anno decimo nono Adriani:quod etiam patet ex lib.5 Almagefti,cap.13,vbi Ptolemæus diserte asserit annum vigesimum Adriani esse 883[?] Nabonasari: ex quo sequitur annum decimum nonum Adriani esse 882 Nabonasari. Præterea fatetur Ptolemæus se defectionem lunæ obseruasse anno nono Adriani Imperatoris, tranfactio die 17 menfi& Pachon, & ab epocha Nabonafari vfque ad tempus obferuationis propofitum tranfiiffe 871 annos, & 56 dies: vt videre licet lib.4 Almagefti cap.9:ex quo manifeftiffime apparet,Ptolemaeum coniungere annum nonum Adriani cum anno 871 Nabonafari. Verum hic animaduertendum eft, in editione Graeca Almagefti mendu effe in numero:legitur enim ibi: [illegible, ~60 letters] [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: Ptolemy uses these three lunar eclipses as the foundation of his observations, and from them we too can demonstrate the position of the new moons by the best method. That the second year of Mardokempad is the twenty-eighth of Nabonassar, Ptolemy indicates in Almagest book 4, chapter 7, where he says that between the earlier eclipse, which occurred in the second year of Mardokempad, after the 18th day of Thoth had passed, and the eclipse which he himself observed in the nineteenth year of the Emperor Hadrian, after the second day of Choiak had elapsed, there were 854 Egyptian years and 73 days. He seems to mean that he observed the eclipse in the year 855 counting from the second year of Mardokempad. So if we add the 27 years of Nabonassar that passed before the second year of Mardokempad to the current year 855, we get the year 882 of Nabonassar, which corresponds to the nineteenth year of Hadrian. This is also clear from Almagest book 5, chapter 13, where Ptolemy expressly asserts that the twentieth year of Hadrian is the 883rd of Nabonassar, from which it follows that the nineteenth year of Hadrian is the 882nd of Nabonassar. Moreover, Ptolemy confesses that he observed an eclipse of the moon in the ninth year of the Emperor Hadrian, on the 17th of the month Pachon, and that from the epoch of Nabonassar to the time of the proposed observation 871 years and 56 days had passed, as can be seen in Almagest book 4, chapter 9. From this it appears most plainly that Ptolemy connects the ninth year of Hadrian with the year 871 of Nabonassar. But here it must be noted that there is an error in the number in the Greek edition of the Almagest, for it reads there: [illegible in the scan] [illegible in the scan]

units.la: vt ex collatione reliquorum locorum appa-ret: fic etiam verfio habet Arabica, cum in editione Lichteftenij fcribatur, Secunda autem eclipfis confideratio fuit in Alexandria, quae fuit in nono annorum Adriani. Et tranflatio Panormitana, facta tempore Rogerij regis Siciliae de Graeco in Latinum, quae manufcripta extat in fex prioribus libros Almagefti in bibliotheca Palatina, ita habet, Secundam autem obferuatam in Alexandria, IX. anno Adriani fecundum Aegyptios Pachon XVII. Iofephus Scaliger eandem emendationem agnofcit lib. 5 de emendatione temporum, pag.244. Sed quid opus eft pluribus argumentis? citato capite exprefse fatetur Ptolemaeus annum fecundum Mardokempadi, quo cotigit eclipfis die 18 Thoth, effe annum Nabonafari 18, quia dicit ante eclipfin illam a Nabonafaro elapfos effe 17 annos Aegyptios, & 17 dies. Indicauimus fupra Mardokempadum in facris literis appellari Merodac, fiue Berodac, qui fuerit filius Bel-adan. Hunc Mardokempadum Arabes in fua tranflatione vocat Mardochaeum, quo modo etiam appellatur in Epitome Regiomontani. Anni ante Aur. ord. units.tr: As the comparison of the other passages shows, the Arabic version also has it, where Lichtenstein's edition reads: "The second observation of an eclipse was in Alexandria, which was in the ninth year of Hadrian." The Palermo translation, made from Greek into Latin in the time of King Roger of Sicily, survives in manuscript in the first six books of the Almagest in the Palatine Library, and it reads: "The second observed in Alexandria, in the ninth year of Hadrian according to the Egyptians, Pachon 17." Joseph Scaliger also accepts this same emendation in book 5 of De emendatione temporum, p. 244. But why need more arguments? In the chapter cited, Ptolemy expressly states that the second year of Mardokempad, in which the eclipse fell on 18 Thoth, was the eighteenth year of Nabonassar, because he says that before that eclipse 17 Egyptian years and 17 days had passed since Nabonassar. We have shown above that Mardokempad is called Merodach or Berodach in the sacred letters, and was the son of Bel-adan. The Arabs in their translation call this Mardokempad "Mardochaeus," as he is also called in the Epitome of Regiomontanus. units.la: a AnnusNabonafari centesimus vigesimus tertius est annus primus imperij Nabopollasari, teste Ptole-maeo lib. 5 Almagesti cap. 14, vbi dicit, annum quin-tum Nabopollasari, esse annum Nabonafari centesi-mum vigesimum septimum. Fuit Nabopollasarus pa-ter magni Nabuchodonosoris, vt testatur Berosus a-pud Iosephum & Eusebium, qui totius Syriae & Asiae imperium obtinuit: vnde factum est, vt ab initio im-perij eius æra fit instituta, qua vtitur Ezechiel propheta: cum enim scribit annum quintum capti Ioiachin fuisse annum trigesimum, intelligendum id est de an-no trigesimo Nabopollasari, vt ex collatione histotiarum fatis apparet. {b}Hic annus centesimus vigesimus septimus Nabonasari, est annus quintus Nabopolassari, quo Ptolemaeus scribit fuisse lunae eclipsin in Babylone, die 27 Athyr, sole constituto in 27 gradu Arietis. Thoth Nabonasari 127 incurrit in 25 Ianuarij, feriam quartam: si hinc numerentur duo menses Ægyptij & 27 dies, descenditur ad 22 Aprilis, currente anno 576 ante ordinationem Iulianam, quo tempore fuit eclipsis in oppositione luminarium: ergo decimo quinto die ante, hoc est, octauo die Aprilis nouilunium fuit, quod etiam ostendit en-neadecaeteris Iuliana. Etenim anno 576 ante ordinationem Iulianam aureus numerus fuit XIV. qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 8 Iduum Aprilis: sed propter anticipationem lunarem descendendum est in triduum subsequens, hoc est, in 8 Aprilis, quia nouilunium fuisse euidenter apparet. units.tr: The year 123 of Nabonassar is the first year of the reign of Nabopolassar, according to Ptolemy, Almagest book 5, chapter 14, where he says that the fifth year of Nabopolassar is the 127th year of Nabonassar. Nabopolassar was the father of the great Nebuchadnezzar, as Berosus testifies in Josephus and Eusebius. He obtained rule over all of Syria and Asia. Hence it came about that the era was instituted from the beginning of his reign, the era which the prophet Ezekiel uses. When he writes that the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin was the thirtieth year, this must be understood of the thirtieth year of Nabopolassar, as the comparison of the histories makes plain. {b} This 127th year of Nabonassar is the fifth year of Nabopolassar, in which Ptolemy writes that there was a lunar eclipse at Babylon on the 27th of Athyr, with the sun placed at the 27th degree of Aries. Thoth 127 of Nabonassar falls on 25 January, a Wednesday. If from this we count two Egyptian months and 27 days, we come down to 22 April in the year 576 before the Julian reform, when the eclipse occurred at the opposition of the luminaries. Therefore the new moon was fifteen days earlier, that is, on the 8th day of April; this is also shown by the Julian enneadecaeteris. For in the year 576 before the Julian reform the golden number was XIV, which in the Julian calendar is placed on the 8th day before the Ides of April. But because of the lunar anticipation, one must go down to the three days following, that is, to 8 April, since it is clearly evident that the new moon fell then. units.la: {a} Annus Nabonafari 141 est decimus nonus Nabopollafari, & primus imperii Nabuchodonosoris magni. {b} Annus Nabonafari 148 est vigesimus sextus Nabopollafari, & octauus imperii Nabuchodonosoris magni, ite primus captiuitatis Iechoniae filiae Ioiachin. {c} Annus Nabonafari 15 est trigesimus Nabopollafari, & duodecimus imperii Nabuchodonosoris magni, & quintus captiuitatis Ioiachin, teste Ezechiele cap. 1. {d} Annus Nabonafari 184 est sexagesimus fecundus Nabopollafari, & trigesimus septimus captiuitatis Ioiachin, item primus imperii Euilmerodachi filii Nabuchodonosoris magni: ex quo colligitur, Nabuchodonosore annos 43 solidos imperasse, autore Berofo Chaldaeo apud Iofephum & Eusebium. {e} Annus 189 Nabonafari est primus Cyri: quia apud Ciceronem in libris de diuinatione Cyrus dicitur xxx annos vertentes imperasse. Si igitur 30 anni Aegyptii numerentur ab anno 189 Nabonafari inclusiue sumto, descenditur ad annum 219 Nabonafari, qui primus est imperii Cambysis, teste Ptolemaeo. {f} Hic annus ducentesimus decimus nonus Nabonafari est primus imperii Cambysis, quia Ptolemaeus annum ducentesimum vigesimum quintum Nabonafari confert cum anno septimo Cambysis, ut videre licet lib. 5 Almagesti, cap. 14. {g} Hoc anno Nabonafari 225, die 17 Phamenoth, in Babylone fuit eclipsis lunae, sole occupate 18 gradu cancri, ut refert Ptolemaeus lib. 5 Almagesti, cap. 14. Thoth Nabonafari 225 incurrit in anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 478, prima die Ianuarii, feria quarta, quo tempore sol fuit in primo gradu capricorni: si ergo a prima Ianuarii deorsum numeremus sex menses Aegyptios, & 16 dies elapsos, peruenimus ad Iulii, quo die contigit eclipsis in oppositione luminarium: itaq; nonilunium antecessit die secunda Iulii, quod etiam ostendit enneadecaeteris Iuliana: siquidem anno 478 ante ordinationem Iulianam aureus numerus est XVII. qui ponitur in calendario Iuliano ad 3 Nonarum Aprilis, & recurrit die vltimo Iunii, sed propter anticipationem lunare triduo post nouilunium coeleste accidit. * Hic annus Nabonafari ducentesimus vigesimus septimus incurrit in postremam diem Decembris, labente anno 477 ante ordinationem Iulianā bisextili, literis dominicalibus existentibus DC. Est autem hic annus Nabonafari 217, primus imperii Darii magni, filii Hystaspis, qui successit Cambysi: nā Ptolemaeus ait lib. 4 Almagesti, cap. 9, annum vigesimum Darii fuisse annū Nabonafari 246, annumq; trigesimum primum Darii primi, & successoris Cambysis fuisse annum Nabonafari 257: quod non abhorret ab historia Herodoti, qui Cambysi annos 7 & menses attribuit: quia 219 anno Nabonafari computati, desinunt in 226 annum Nabonafari.
units.tr: Year 141 of Nabonassar is the nineteenth year of Nabopolassar and the first year of Nebuchadnezzar the Great. {b} Year 148 of Nabonassar is the twenty-sixth year of Nabopolassar and the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar the Great, and also the first year of the captivity of Jeconiah, daughter of Jehoiachin. {c} Year 15 of Nabonassar is the thirtieth year of Nabopolassar, the twelfth year of Nebuchadnezzar the Great, and the fifth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, as Ezekiel attests in chapter 1. {d} Year 184 of Nabonassar is the sixty-second year of Nabopolassar, the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, and likewise the first year of Evil-Merodach, son of Nebuchadnezzar the Great. From this it is gathered that Nebuchadnezzar reigned a full 43 years, on the authority of the Chaldean Berosus as cited by Josephus and Eusebius. {e} Year 189 of Nabonassar is the first year of Cyrus, because in Cicero's books on divination Cyrus is said to have reigned thirty years and more. If, then, thirty Egyptian years are counted from year 189 of Nabonassar, counting that year inclusively, one comes down to year 219 of Nabonassar, which is the first year of the reign of Cambyses, according to Ptolemy. {f} This year, the 219th of Nabonassar, is the first year of the reign of Cambyses, because Ptolemy compares the 225th year of Nabonassar with the seventh year of Cambyses, as can be seen in book 5 of the Almagest, chapter 14. {g} In this year 225 of Nabonassar, on the 17th of Phamenoth, there was a lunar eclipse at Babylon, with the moon obscured in the 18th degree of Cancer, as Ptolemy reports in book 5 of the Almagest, chapter 14. Thoth 1 of year 225 of Nabonassar falls in the year 478 before the Julian reform, on the first day of January, a Wednesday, when the sun was in the first degree of Capricorn. If, then, we count downward from the first of January six Egyptian months and 16 elapsed days, we arrive at July, on which day the eclipse occurred at the opposition of the luminaries. Thus the new moon preceded it by the second of July, which the Julian nineteen-year cycle also shows: for in the year 478 before the Julian reform the golden number is 17, which is placed in the Julian calendar on 3 Nones of April, and recurs on the last day of June; but because of the anticipation of the lunar cycle, the heavenly event happened three days after the new moon. * This year 227 of Nabonassar falls on the last day of December, in the leap year 477 before the Julian reform, the dominical letters being DC. This year, moreover, is the 217th year of Nabonassar, the first year of Darius the Great, son of Hystaspes, who succeeded Cambyses. For Ptolemy says in book 4 of the Almagest, chapter 9, that the twentieth year of Darius was the year 246 of Nabonassar, and the thirty-first year of Darius I, successor of Cambyses, was the year 257 of Nabonassar. This does not disagree with the account of Herodotus, who assigns Cambyses seven years and some months, since the years counted from 219 of Nabonassar end in the 226th year of Nabonassar.

units.la: Hoc anno Nabonafari 246, qui fuit annus vigesimus primi Darii, contigit eclipsis lunae in Babylone, die 18 Epiphi, vt ex Hipparcho recitat Ptolemaeus lib. 4 Almagesti cap. 9. Hanc eclipsin Ptolemaeus confert cum illa, quam obseruauit Alexandriae nono anno Adriani, die 17 Pachon: & ex interuallo dato colligit lunam tunc abfuisse a nodo descendente nouem gradibus & 21 minutis: proinde in die assignato non potuisse contingere eclipsin, ideoque mendum esse in numeris Hipparchicis. Hunc etiam errorem detegit enneadecaeteris Iuliana: nam Thoth Nabonafari 246 incurrit in annū 458 ante ordinationem [?] lulianam, 17 Decembris, feria quarta. quamobrem si hinc numeremus menses decem Aegyptios, & 17 dies praeteritos, descendimus ad 18 Nouembris, currente anno 457 ante ordinationem Iulianam, bisextili, literis dominicalibus existentibus GF. & aureo numero assignato XIX. qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 3 Idus Aprilis, & recurrit die quarto Nouembris, sed propter anticipationem lunarem neomenia coelestis triduo serius, hoc est sexto Nouembris est conspecta: ergo die decimo quinto post, videlicet 20 Nouembris, fuit oppositio luminarium: quae secundum relationem Hipparchi fuisset 18 Nouembris: itaque concluditur eclipsin illa fuisse die ultimo Epiphi, seu potius die primo Mesori, luna occupante caudam draconis. ɩ[?] Hoc anno Nabonafari 257, qui fuit annus trigesimus primus Darii primi, cötigit eclipsis lunae, die 3 Tybi, ut loco citato ex Hipparcho recitat Ptolemaeus. Sed non immerito relationem Hipparchi suspectam habet Ptolemaeus, cum ait, ἐμετρήθη δὲ ἐκ τῶν ὡσεικτημένων [?] ἐν τῇ Ἱππάρχῳ ὑπὸ ἐκ μέσων παρα[?] ἀων, ἐν τῷ πρὸς τῷ χρόνῳ ἐκ ὅλας ἐπικρίσεις μείζης ι καὶ ἐξήκοντα ἑξ[?] ς'. hoc est, Deficiunt autem ex supra positis Hipparchi hypotheses mediorum motuum in tato tempore ad integras restitutiones gradus x. & sexagenae ad proximum duae. Fieri enim non potuit ut oppositio luminarium esset, quo tempore Hipparchus ea tradit fuisse: nam Thoth Nabonafari 257 incurrit in annu 447 ante ordinationem Iulianam, die 24 Decembris, feria prima: hinc si numeremus quatuor menses Aegyptios, & 2 dies praeteritos, peruenimus ad 15 Aprilis, quo eclipsis fuisset in oppositione luminarium, iuxta traditionem Hipparchi. Quod autem tunc nulla fuerit oppositio, etiam ostendit ennecaenneadecaeteris luliana: in anno enim 447 ante ordinationem Iulianam aureus numerus est X. qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 12 kal. Maij: sed propter anticipationem lunarem intelligimus novilunium fuisse in 25 Maij die: itaque die decimo sexto ante, die scilicet septima Maij fuit luminarium oppositio: hanc autem Hipparchus dicit fuisse 25 Aprilis, ergo plus quam decem dies deficiunt: unde colligitur mendum esse in numeris Hipparchicis, quos ex tabulis aequalium motuum corrigendos esse asserit [?] Ptolemaeus. Quod autem de tempore duarum harum eclipsium Ptolemaeus dubitarit, indicium illud est, quod in neutra locum solis designarit. An ante. Aur. An. Olym- Anni Vrb. Lit.dom. Nabo- Feriæ· ord. units.tr: In the year 246 of Nabonassar, which was the twentieth year of Darius I, a lunar eclipse occurred at Babylon on the 18th of Epiphi, as Ptolemy reports from Hipparchus in Almagest 4, ch. 9. Ptolemy compares this eclipse with one he observed at Alexandria in the ninth year of Hadrian, on the 17th of Pachon. From the interval between them he concludes that the moon was then 9 degrees and 21 minutes from the descending node, and so no eclipse could have occurred on the date assigned. He therefore judges that there is an error in Hipparchus's figures. The Enneadecaeteris of Julian also exposes this error. Thoth of Nabonassar 246 falls in the year 458 before the Julian reform, on 17 December, a Wednesday. If we count back ten Egyptian months and 17 days from there, we arrive at 18 November in the year 457 before the Julian reform, a bissextile year, with dominical letters GF and golden number XIX. In the Julian calendar that golden number is placed at 3 Ides of April and recurs on 4 November. But because of the lunar anticipation, the heavenly new moon was seen three days later, that is, on 6 November. Fifteen days after that, on 20 November, the conjunction of the luminaries occurred. According to Hipparchus's account it should have been on 18 November. It follows that the eclipse fell on the last day of Epiphi, or rather on the first day of Mesori, when the moon was in the tail of the dragon. In the year 257 of Nabonassar, which was the thirty-first year of Darius I, a lunar eclipse occurred on the 3rd of Tybi, as Ptolemy also reports from Hipparchus in the passage cited. Yet Ptolemy rightly holds Hipparchus's account under suspicion, when he says: "The hypotheses of Hipparchus, set out above, for the mean motions fall short over that whole period, by 10 degrees and 2 sixtieths, when restored to whole units" [ἐμετρήθη δὲ ἐκ τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἐν τῇ Ἱππάρχου ὑποθέσει τῶν μέσων κινήσεων ... μοιρῶν ι καὶ ἐξηκοστῶν β]. For the conjunction of the luminaries could not have happened at the time Hipparchus gives. Thoth of Nabonassar 257 falls in the year 447 before the Julian reform, on 24 December, a Sunday. If we count back four Egyptian months and two days from there, we come to 15 April, when the eclipse would have been at conjunction according to Hipparchus's tradition. That there was then no conjunction at all is also shown by the Julian Enneadecaeteris. In the year 447 before the Julian reform the golden number is X, which in the Julian calendar is placed at 12 Kalends of May. But because of the lunar anticipation we understand that the new moon fell on 25 May. Sixteen days before that, that is on 7 May, was the conjunction of the luminaries. Hipparchus, however, says it was 25 April, so more than ten days are missing. From this it is concluded that there is an error in Hipparchus's figures, which Ptolemy asserts must be corrected from the tables of mean motions. That Ptolemy doubted the dates of these two eclipses is shown by the fact that in neither case did he specify the position of the sun. units.la: 4 Hoc anno 316 Nabonasari, die 21 Phamenoth, solstitium æstiuum obseruauit Meton Atheniensis, Paulaniæ filius, insignis geometra & astronomus, vt refert Ptolemæus lib. 3 Almagesti cap 1. Erst autem Ptolemæus non exprimat, an is fuerit annus 316 Nabonasari: id tamen ex subsequentibus intelligitur, quando ait Aristarchum solstitium æstiuum obseruasse anno quinquagesimo primæ periodi Calippicæ, qui fuerit annus 44 a morte Alexandri, hoc est, annus Nabonasari 468, & ab obseruatione Metonis vsque ad obseruationem Aristarchi ait elapsos esse anno Ægyptios 152, quod etiam Hipparchus testetur. Si itaque ab anno Nabonasari 468 abiiciamus annos 152, superest annus Nabonasari 316, in cuius 21 die Phamenoth solstitium seu ingressum solis in cancrum notauit Meton. Sane annus Nabonasari 316 coepit labente anno 388 ante ordinationem Iulianam, die 9 Decembris, feria quarta: hinc si numeremus sex menses Ægyptios, & 21 dies, descendimus ad 28 Iunii, currente anno 387 ante ordinationem Iulianam, quo solstitium fuit & oppositio luminarium, si anticipationem lunarem negligamus: quamobrem die 13 Iunii, siue [illegible, ~10 letters] nouilunium fuit, sub finem currente anno quarto Olympiadis 86, hoc est, anno Olympiadico 344, vbi enneadecaeteridis principium posuit, vt refert Diodorus Siculus lib. 12. A nouilunio itaque antecedente solstitium æstiuum Meton exorsus est suam enneadecaeteridem, & deprehendit intra annos 19 solares absolui 235 lunationes, itaque ab anno vigesimo ineunte solari nouilunium conspiciatur ducentesimum trigesimum sextum.
units.tr: 4 In this year 316 of Nabonassar, on the 21st of Phamenoth, Meton of Athens, son of Pausanias, a distinguished geometer and astronomer, observed the summer solstice, as Ptolemy reports in book 3, chapter 1, of the Almagest. Ptolemy does not state outright that this was the year 316 of Nabonassar, but it is understood from what follows, where he says that Aristarchus observed the summer solstice in the fiftieth year of the first Callippic period, which was the 44th year after the death of Alexander, that is, year 468 of Nabonassar. He also says that 152 Egyptian years elapsed from Meton's observation to Aristarchus's, as Hipparchus likewise attests. If we subtract 152 years from year 468 of Nabonassar, year 316 of Nabonassar remains, and on its 21st day of Phamenoth Meton noted the solstice, that is, the sun's entry into Cancer. Indeed, year 316 of Nabonassar began, with the year 388 before the Julian reform nearly over, on 9 December, a Wednesday. If we count six Egyptian months and 21 days from there, we come down to 28 June in the year 387 before the Julian reform. That was the solstice and the opposition of the luminaries, if we neglect the lunar anticipation. Therefore, on 13 June, or [illegible] was the new moon, near the end of the fourth year of the 86th Olympiad, that is, Olympiad year 344, where he set the beginning of the enneadecaeteris, as Diodorus Siculus reports in book 12. Meton therefore began his nineteen-year cycle from the new moon preceding the summer solstice, and he found that 235 lunations are completed within 19 solar years. Thus, from the twentieth solar year beginning, the 236th new moon is seen.

units.la: Hanc obseruationem veriffimam effe oftendit Hip-parchus apud Ptolemaeum lib. 3 Almagesti cap. 1. hifce verbis, ἡμεῖς δὲ μηνὸς μὲν ὅλως ἐνεληλυθὼς περιεχόμενον [?] ἐν τοῖς ιθ' ἐτῶν [illegible, ~12 letters], hoc eft, Nos vero deprehendimus integrarum lunationum periodos (fcilicet 235) abfol-ui 19 annis, ficut & illi obferuarunt, fcilicet Meton & Euctemon. Quod autem Meton cyclum fuum 19 annorum coeperit a neomenia proxima folftitio, indicat Feftus Auienus pulcherrimis hifce verfi-bus:
units.tr: Hipparchus, quoted by Ptolemy in book 3, chapter 1, of the Almagest, shows that this observation is most accurate, in these words: ἡμεῖς δὲ μηνὸς μὲν ὅλως ἐνεληλυθὼς περιεχόμενον [?] ἐν τοῖς ιθ' ἐτῶν ("But we have found that the periods of whole lunations (namely 235) are completed in 19 years, just as they too observed, namely Meton and Euctemon"). Hipparchus adds that Meton began his nineteen-year cycle from the new moon nearest the solstice; this is indicated by Festus Avienus in these very fine verses:

units.la: Sed primaua Meton exordia fumfit ab anno, Torreret rutilo cum Phoebus fidere cancrum, Cingula cum veheret pelagus procul Orionis, Et cum caruleo flagraret Sirius aftro.
units.tr: Sed primaua Meton exordia fumsit ab anno, Torreret rutilo cum Phoebus sidere cancrum, Cingula cum veheret pelagus procul Orionis, Et cum caeruleo flagraret Sirius astro. ("But Meton made his first beginnings from the year when Phoebus, with his ruddy star, was scorching the Crab, when the Belt of Orion was carrying the sea far off, and when Sirius was blazing with its blue star.")

units.la: Duodecim enneadecaeterides fuppeditant annos 228, quo interuallo fingulianni lunares redeunt ad priftinas fedes: anni autem 28 folares fi multiplicen-tur in nouendecim annos enneadecaeteridis, prodit cyclus magnus annorum 532, quo vfus eft Dionyfius Exiguus Abbas Romanus. Pulcherrimum hoc inuentum eft enneadecaeteridis: in quo hoc obferuandum eft; lunam elapfis annis folaribus 19 non praecise redire ad idem punctum, fed anticipare horam vnam, & 48 fcrupula Hebraica: vnde fit vt tranfactis annis 247 folaribus luna diem vnum afcendat vel defcendat. Itaque intra annos 247 ennea-decaeteris nouilunia fatis praecise indicat, vt error notabilis non appareat: fed in annis 484 luna a prio-re epocha biduum afcendit vel defcendit, qui error nifi noua fixione epochae emendetur, statim a vulgo deprehenditur. In annis autem 741 luna anticipat epocham per triduum, in annis 988 anticipat per quatriduum. triduum, in annis 12 3 5 [?] ascendit descenditve in quintum diem. qui error prorsus est intolerabilis, quam obrem noua correctione prorsus est opus. units.tr: Twelve enneadecaeterides supply 228 years, at the end of which the individual lunar years return to their former places. If the 28 solar years are multiplied by the 19 years of the enneadecaeteris, the great cycle of 532 years results, which Dionysius Exiguus, the Roman abbot, used. This discovery of the enneadecaeteris is most excellent, but in it one must observe that after 19 solar years the moon does not return exactly to the same point, but runs ahead by one hour and 48 Hebrew scruples. Hence it happens that after 247 solar years the moon gains or loses one day. So within 247 years the enneadecaeteris indicates new moons quite precisely, so that no notable error appears. But in 484 years the moon gains or loses two days from the earlier epoch, and this error is at once detected by the common people unless it is corrected by a new fixing of the epoch. In 741 years the moon anticipates the epoch by three days, and in 988 years by four days. In [1235] years it gains or loses the fifth day. This error is wholly intolerable, so a new correction is entirely needed. units.la: 4 Hoc anno Nabonasari 366, die 26 Thoth, in Babylone conspecta est eclipsis lunaris, sole occupante 28 gradum Sagittarii, ut ex traditione Hipparchi refert Ptolemaeus lib. 4 Almagesti, capite 11, Thoth Nabonasari 366 incurrit in 27 Nouembris, feriam quintam, labente anno 358 ante ordinationem Iulianam: itaque dies 26 Thoth incidit in 22 Decembris, feriam secundam, qua fuit eclipsis in oppositione luminarium. Hinc sequitur decimo quinto die ante, nimirum 8 Decembris fuisse nouilunium: quod etiam ostendit enneadecaeteris Iuliana. Aureus enim numerus anni 338 ante ordinationem Iulianam est v. qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 17 kal. Maij, & recurrit die 7 Decembris: quia vero ab epocha Iuliani nouilunii elapsis annis 338 facta est anticipatio lunaris per diem unum, intelligi-tur notur nouilunium fuisse in 8 Decembris. Alias si hanc exiguam anticipationem lunarem velimus negligere pollumus dicere die 7 Decembris incurrisse coniunctionem solis & lunæ: quemadmodum ante annos quinquaginta nouilunium Metonicum etiam considerauimus sine vlla anticipatione lunari. In principio autem Olympiadum, Vrbis conditæ, Nabonasari, & antiquissimarum eclipsium obseruatione, anticipatio lunaris ab epocha Iuliana per totum biduum fuerat prolapsa: quamobrem bidui illius necessario fuit ratio habenda. Eodem anno Nabonasari 366, die 24 Phamenoth, sole fere occupante 22 gradum Geminorum, altera contigit eclipsis lunæ. Si itaque a 27 Nouembris, currente anno 338 ante ordinationem Iulianam, numeremus sex menses Ægyptios, & 23 dies elapsos, descendimus ad 17 Iunij, currente anno bisextili 337 ante ordinationem Iulianam: quo tempore fuit eclipsis in oppositione luminarium. Ergo decimo quinto die ante præcessit nouilunium, sicut id ostendit enneadecaeteris Iuliana: anno enim 337 ante ordinationem Iulianam aureus numerus est VI. qui ponitur in calendario Iuliano pridie Nonarum Aprilis, & recurrit die secundo Iunij, vbi nouilunium ostendit sine vlla anticipatione lunari.
units.tr: In this year of Nabonassar 366, on 26 Thoth, a lunar eclipse was observed at Babylon, with the sun in the 28th degree of Sagittarius, as Ptolemy reports from the tradition of Hipparchus in Almagest book 4, chapter 11. Thoth 1 of Nabonassar 366 falls on 27 November, a Thursday, in the year 358 before the Julian reform. So 26 Thoth fell on 22 December, a Monday, when the eclipse occurred at the opposition of the luminaries. It follows that the new moon was fifteen days earlier, namely on 8 December; the Julian enneadecaeteris also shows this. For the golden number of the year 338 before the Julian reform is 5, which stands in the Julian calendar at 17 kal. May and recurs on 7 December. But since the lunar anticipation has advanced by one day in the 338 years elapsed from the Julian epoch of the new moon, the new moon is understood to have fallen on 8 December. Otherwise, if we wish to disregard this slight lunar anticipation, we may say that the conjunction of sun and moon occurred on 7 December, just as we earlier considered the Metonic new moon fifty years ago without any lunar anticipation. At the beginning of the Olympiads, of the founding of Rome, of Nabonassar, and of the observations of the most ancient eclipses, the lunar anticipation from the Julian epoch had slipped by a full two days, so that this two-day interval must necessarily be taken into account. In the same year of Nabonassar 366, on 24 Phamenoth, with the sun at about the 22nd degree of Gemini, another lunar eclipse occurred. If therefore we count six Egyptian months and 23 days from 27 November in the year 338 before the Julian reform, we come down to 17 June in the bissextile year 337 before the Julian reform; at that time there was an eclipse at the opposition of the luminaries. So the new moon preceded it by fifteen days, as the Julian enneadecaeteris shows: in the year 337 before the Julian reform the golden number is 6, which stands in the Julian calendar on the day before the Nones of April and recurs on 2 June, where it shows the new moon without any lunar anticipation.

units.la: b Anno Nabonasari 367, die 16 Thoth, sole occupante 17 gradum Sagittarij, vt loco citato refert Ptolemæus, in Babylone conspecta est eclipsis lunæ. Thoth Nabonasari 367 incurrit in 26 Nouembris, feriam sextam, currente anno 337 ante ordinationem Iulianam: itaque 16 dies Thoth incidit in 11 Decembris, quo eclipsis fuit in oppositione luminarium: ex quo sequitur 15 die ante nouilunium fuisse, quod etiam enneadecaeteris Iuliana ostendit: quippe annus 337 ante ordinationem Iulianam habet aureu numerum VI, qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur pridie nonarum Aprilis, & recurrit 17 Nouembris, vbi nouilunium haesisse euidenter apparet. Hilce tribus expositis eclipsibus Ptolemaeus adiicit indices mensium Atheniensium: nam refert anno Nabona-sari 366, die 26 Thoth, ἀρχοντος Ἀθήνησι Φανοστράτου, ποσιδεῶνος μηνός, hoc est, magistratum gerente Athenis Phanostrato, Posideone mense, id est, Decembri obseruatam esse eclipsin lunae. Eodem anno Nabonasari, Phamenoth 14. σκιροφοριῶνος μηνός, hoc est, mense Iunio, idem sidus defecisse ait. Anno sequenti Nabonasari 367, die 16 Thoth, ἀρχοντος Ἀθήνησιν Εὐανδρου, μηνὸς ποσιδεῶνος ὑστέρου, hoc est, magistratum Athenis gerente Euandro, mense Posideone priore, id est, Decembri priore lunam defecisse. Si ergo a solstitio incipiamus, mensium Atticorum nomina haec sunt, ἑκατομβαιῶν, μεταγειτνιῶν, βοηδρομιῶν, πυανεψιῶν, μαιμακτηριῶν, ποσιδεῶν, γαμηλιῶν, ἀνθεστηριῶν, ἐλαφηβολιῶν, μουνυχιῶν, θαργηλιῶν, σκιροφοριῶν, qui respondent mensibus Iulianis, Iulio, Augusto, Septebri, Octobri, Nouembri, Decembri, Ianuario, Februario, Martio, Aprili, Maio, Iunio. Hoc modo si mensis intercalaris ante solstitium aestiuum interiiciatur, duplex oritur Scirrhophorion: si vero inferatur ante brumam, vt Ptolemaei tempore factum esse apparet, oritur duplex Posideon. Respondere autem dicimus menses Atticos mensibus Iulianis, non quod prorsus conueniant, nam Iuliani sunt solares, & per bisextum figuntur ad signa zodiaci & periodum solarem: Attici autem sunt lunares, & beneficio Mercedonij adfixos menses solares reuocantur. Praeterea sicut solstitium mutat locum in calendario Iuliano, ita etiam menses Attici pro diuturfa-ra-
units.tr: b In the year of Nabonassar 367, on 16 Thoth, with the sun in the 17th degree of Sagittarius, as Ptolemy reports in the passage cited, a lunar eclipse was observed at Babylon. Thoth 1 of Nabonassar 367 falls on 26 November, a Friday, in the year 337 before the Julian reform. So 16 Thoth falls on 11 December, when the eclipse occurred at the opposition of the luminaries. From this it follows that the new moon was fifteen days earlier, which the Julian enneadecaeteris also shows: the year 337 before the Julian reform has the golden number 6, which stands in the Julian calendar on the day before the Nones of April and recurs on 17 November, where the new moon is clearly seen to have stuck. Having set out these three eclipses, Ptolemy adds the indications of the Athenian months. For he reports that in the year 366 of Nabonassar, on 26 Thoth, when Phanostratos was archon at Athens, in the month Posideon (that is, December), the lunar eclipse was observed. In the same year of Nabonassar, on 14 Phamenoth, in the month Skirophorion (that is, June), he says the same body was eclipsed. In the following year of Nabonassar 367, on 16 Thoth, when Euandros was archon at Athens, in the later Posideon (that is, the earlier December), the moon was eclipsed. So if we begin from the solstice, the names of the Attic months are these: (1) Hekatombaion [ἑκατομβαιῶν]; (2) Metageitnion [μεταγειτνιῶν]; (3) Boedromion [βοηδρομιῶν]; (4) Pyanepsion [πυανεψιῶν]; (5) Maimakterion [μαιμακτηριῶν]; (6) Posideon [ποσιδεῶν]; (7) Gamelion [γαμηλιῶν]; (8) Anthesterion [ἀνθεστηριῶν]; (9) Elaphebolion [ἐλαφηβολιῶν]; (10) Mounychion [μουνυχιῶν]; (11) Thargelion [θαργηλιῶν]; (12) Skirophorion [σκιροφοριῶν]. These correspond to the Julian months July, August, September, October, November, December, January, February, March, April, May and June. In this way, if an intercalary month is inserted before the summer solstice, a double Skirophorion arises; if it is inserted before the winter solstice, as seems to have happened in Ptolemy's time, a double Posideon arises. We say that the Attic months correspond to the Julian months, not because they agree exactly: the Julian months are solar and, by means of the bissextile, are fixed to the signs of the zodiac and the solar period, whereas the Attic months are lunar, and are brought back to the solar months by the help of the Mercedonian intercalation. Moreover, just as the solstice changes its place in the Julian calendar, so too the Attic months, on account of the lapse of time, correspond to different Julian months.
