units.la: {a} Annus Olympiadicus 446 circa solstitium æstiuum cœpit, & ab æquinoctio verno præcedente incurrit annus vrbis conditæ 423, labente anno 286 ante ordinationem Iulianam, cuius initium fuit à præcedente bruma seu kalend.Ianuariis. Hoc anno Olympiadico 446, nocte quæ secuta est 20 diem Septembris, fuit eclipsis in oppositione luminarium: vndecima vero die post illam defectionem lunæ, hoc est, kal.Octobris, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 286 copiæ Macedonum & Persarum in conspectum sese [?] dederunt, & acriter pugnatum est ad Gaugamela, vel vt alij volunt ad ArbeArbela, donec Darius vltimus ab Alexandro Magno caederetur. Ergo victoria Alexandri in currit in kal. Octobris currente anno 286 ante ordinationem Iulianam: porro Darius à Bcflo[?] interfectus est altero anno post cladem in Arbelis acceptam, Plutarcho & Diodoro testibus, anno scilicet labente Olympiadico 447: siquidem Eusebius Cæsariensis in chronicis affirmat, Alexandrum obtinuisse Babylonem interfecto Dario, in quo Persarum regnū destructum est, anno tertio Olympiadis cerefimae & duodecimae, hoc est anno Olympiadico 447: ex quo sequitur cladem Darij, victoriamque Alexandri quae anno vno praecessit necem Darij, incurrisse in annum Olympiadicum 446.
units.tr: The Olympiad year 446 began around the summer solstice. From the preceding spring equinox it runs into the year 423 from the founding of the city, with the year 286 before the Julian reform having run out. The Julian reform began at the preceding winter solstice, or the Kalends of January. In this Olympiad year 446, on the night following 20 September, there was an eclipse with the luminaries in opposition. On the eleventh day after that eclipse of the moon, that is on the Kalends of October, in the year 286 before the Julian reform, the armies of the Macedonians and the Persians came into view of one another, and a fierce battle was fought at Gaugamela, or, as others prefer, at Arbela, until Darius the Last was slain by Alexander the Great. So Alexander's victory fell on the Kalends of October in the year 286 before the Julian reform. Moreover, Darius was killed by Bessus a year after the defeat at Arbela, according to the testimony of Plutarch and Diodorus, namely in the passing Olympiad year 447. Eusebius of Caesarea affirms in his Chronicle that Alexander took Babylon after Darius was killed, and that the kingdom of the Persians was destroyed there in the third year of the 112th Olympiad, that is, in Olympiad year 447. From this it follows that the defeat of Darius and Alexander's victory, which came one year before Darius's death, fell in Olympiad year 446.

units.la: Quòd autem hoc anno 446 Olympiadico eclipsis lunae fuerit nocte quae secuta est 2o diem Septembris, quodque cladem magnam acceperit Darius ad Gaugamela, kal. Octobribus, hoc est, die vndecima post defectionem, ex Plutarcho euidenter probari potest. Is enim ita scribit: τὴν δὲ μεγάλην μάχην Δαρεῖον ἐν Ἀρβήλοις, ὥσπερ οἱ πολλοὶ γράφουσιν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν Γαυγαμήλοις [?] συμβεβηκέναι [?], & paulo post: ἡ μὲν ἐν σελήνῃ τῆς βοηδρομιῶνος [?] τὴν περὶ τὰ μυστήρια [?] Ἀθήνησιν ἀρχήν. ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς ἡλιακῆς σκιᾶς [?] &c. hoc est, Magnam pugnam aduersus Darium, non in Arbelis, quemadmodum multi scribunt, sed in Gaugamelis accidisse.
units.tr: That in this Olympiad year 446 there was an eclipse of the moon on the night following 20 September, and that Darius suffered a great defeat at Gaugamela on the Kalends of October, that is, on the eleventh day after the eclipse, can clearly be proved from Plutarch. For he writes thus: the great battle was fought against Darius not at Arbela, as most writers have it, but at Gaugamela [τὴν δὲ μεγάλην μάχην Δαρεῖον ἐν Ἀρβήλοις, ὥσπερ οἱ πολλοὶ γράφουσιν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐν Γαυγαμήλοις συμβεβηκέναι], and a little later: the moon was eclipsed in Boedromion, around the start of the mysteries; and at the beginning of the solar shadow [ἡ μὲν ἐν σελήνῃ τῆς βοηδρομιῶνος τὴν περὶ τὰ μυστήρια Ἀθήνησιν ἀρχήν. ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς ἡλιακῆς σκιᾶς] etc. That is, the great battle against Darius happened not at Arbela, as many write, but at Gaugamela.

units.la: (& paulo post) Defecit autem luna mense Boedromione circa initium mysteriorum Athenis peragi solitorum. Vndecima vero post eclipsin nocte, exercitibus in conspectum prodeuntibus, &c. Constat autem μυστήρια celebrari solita τῆς ἐκάστης βοηδρομιῶνος, vt ipse Plutarchus autor est in Camillo & Phocione: vnde sequitur vigefimam Boedromionis comparari cum 2o Septembris, & noctefequenti fuisse eclipfin lunæ in oppofitione luminarium, ita vt decimo quinto die ante, hoc est, die 6 Septembris inciderit noui-lunium: quod etiam ostendit enneadecaeteris lulia-na. Annus enim 186 ante ordinationem Iulianam numerum aureum habet XIX, qui in calendario luliano ponitur ad 3 [?] Idus Aprilis, & recurrit 6 die Septembris, vbi nouilunium indicat: quare nocte quæ secuta est 2o Septembris, fuit eclipsis lunæ in oppofitione luminarium, & die vndecima post defectionem lunarem Darius magna clade accepta ab Alexandro, fugatus est cum reliquo suo exercitu, kalendis scilicet Octobribus. Vnde Macedones occasionem fumfe-runt, vt suos annos deinceps ordirentur à kal. Oct. quibus suum Hyperberetæum accomodarunt: quod etiam Syri & Arabes postea sunt secuti in annis Alexandri Dhilkarnain consignandis. {b}Hoc anno Olympiadico ineunte 447 Darius vltimus à Beffo interfectus est, & Babylonis imperium cessit Alexandro Magno, teste Eusebio in chronicis. In cuius rei memoriam Calippus Cyzicenus mathematicus periodum 76 annorum instituit, quæ aggregata erat ex quatuor cyclis Metonicis (seu enneadecaeteridis) : vt enim posteris innotesceret tempus destructionis regni Perfici, & ad Græcos translati, voluit Calippus vt ab Olympiadico anno 447, numerarentur quatuor enneadecaeterides, hoc est, anni 76 folares: & his elapsis periodum 76 annorum repetere iussit. Itaque fecunda periodus Calippi iniit ab anno Olympiadico 52[?]1, tertia coepit ab anno Olympiadico 59[?]9, quarta initium habuit ab anno Olympiadico 67[?]7. Quod autem Calippus periodum suam 76 annorum, quam ProlePtolemaeus lib. 6 Almagesti, cap. 3 vocat [illegible, ~10 letters] [illegible, ~8 letters], à solstitio incepisse, hoc ipsum indicat, quod secutus fit Metone, qui suam enneadecaeteridem quoque à solstitio est exorsus, vt principio annorum Olympiadicorum responderet. Idem ex Ptolemaeo colligere licet: iis enim scribit lib. 3 Almagesti, cap. 1. observationem solstitii ab Aristarcho factam incurrisse in annum quinquagesimum primæ periodi Calippicæ iam definentem. Verùm Hipparchus & Ptolemaeus, vt esset æquabilis annorum Calippicorum cum annis Nabonasari comparatio, sumserunt primæ periodi Calippicæ principium à proximè subsequenti Thoth Nabonasari 419, & deinde cum singulis annis Nabonasari singulos annos Calippicos contulerunt: itaque secunda periodus Calippi incurrit in annum Nabonasari 495, tertia incidit in annum Nabonasari 571, quarta incipit cum anno Nabonasari 647. quod probè notandum est, propter obseruationes quas in has tres & quatuor periodos priores Calippi inciderunt. Ex his colligitur primam periodum Calippicam coepisse anno ineunte sexto ante mortem Alexandri: quod etiam Copernicus indicat lib. 3 Revolutionum cap. 2, quando ex Almagesti Ptolemaei lib. 7 cap. 3, refert Timocharin obseruasse spicam Virginis anno 36 primæ 76 annorum secundum Calippum periodi, qui fuerit annus ab excessu Alexandri Magni trigesimus, hoc est, Nabonasari 454: ergo annus primus primæ periodi Calippicæ est annus Nabonasari 419. c Annus Nabonasari 425 principium æræ est, quæ à morte Alexandri deducitur: testatur id Ptolemaeus lib. 3 Almagesti, cap. 8, quando dicit, inter Nabonasarium & mortem Alexandri intercessisse annos Ægyptios quadringentos & viginti quatuor. Totidem annos Arabes ponunt inter Nabonasarum & aeram Philippicam, sicut ex Alfragano euidenter apparet. is enim inter Nabonasarum (quem Nabuchodonosorem siue Nebukadnezarem Babylonii cum Albategnio & toto Arabum collegio appellat) & inter Iezdajerem regem Persarum dicit elapsos esse annos Aegyptios seu Persicos 1379, & tres menses: inter Philippum autem & Iezdajerem ait elapsos esse annos Aegyptios 955, & tres menses: quare si minor numerus a maiore subtrahatur, relinquuntur anni 424 Aegyptii, qui a Nabonasaro vsq; ad aeram Philippicam sunt elapsi. Ergo Thoth Nabonasari 425 [?] est initium annorum Philippicorum: is autem coepit die solis, vt ostendit Alfraganus: quod etiam comprobat examen feriarum. Hinc colligere licet, Arabes aeram Philippicam eam vocare, quae Ptolemaeo a morte Alexandri dicitur: cuius rei etiam signum est, quod afferunt Ptolemaeum in canone Almagesti ab aera Philippica tempora supputare, cum tamen Ptolemaeus nusquam meminerit epochae Philippicae, sed tantum epocharum a morte Alexandri computatarum mentione faciat. Neq; soli Arabes, verum etiam Graeci & Latini annos a morte Alexandri computatos vocant annos Philippicos. Testis est Kabasilla interpres Graecus Ptolemaei, commentario sexto:quando annos τῆς Ἀλεξάνδρου τελευτῆς, vocat ἀπὸ Φιλίππου ἔτη [?]. Ipse quoq; Censorinus scrupulorum chronologicorum summus conciliator, annos ab excessu Alexandri appellat annos Philippi: cuius rei causa haec est, quod viuente Alexandro Macedones adhuc tempora numerarent ab imperio Philippi patris Alexandri. Quod cum Arabes ignorassent, factum est, vt existimarint Philippum coepisse regnare, quando Ptolemaeus Alexandrum scribit esse mortuum: utque Alexandrum demum regnasse crediderint, quo tempore historiae tradunt Seleucum Nicanore Asiae & Syriae gubernacula tractas-se. Quare aera Alexandri simpliciter dicta, iuxta Arabes, nihil aliud est, quàm aera Alexandrina Seleucidarum, quæ ab æra Philippica seu à morte Alexandri distat annis Ægyptiis 12, & 325 diebus: cum incidat in primam Octobris, feria secunda, litera dominicali existente G, currente anno ante ordinationem Iuliana 267, hoc est, cum incidat in 17 diem mensis Epiphi anno Nabonasari labente 436: ut paulo post luculentius ostendetur. Ut autem tempus mortis Alexandri exacte intelligatur, sciendum est Eusebium Caesariensem in chronicis asserere, Alexandrum XXXIIII ætatis suæ anno mortuum esse in Babylone anno primo Olympiadis centesimæ decimæ quartæ, hoc est anno Olympiadico 453. Mortuu autem eum esse in principio anni Olympiadici 453 à solstitio æstiuo incuntis, constat ex Plutarcho, qui eum scribit obiisse [illegible, ~20 letters] hoc est circa 23 Iunii die, iuxta calendarium Syrorum. atqui tunc solstitium hæsit in 27 Iunii, quandoquidem ante annos centum & octo à Metone fuerat deprehensum in 28 Iunii die: itaque Alexander excessit triduo ante solstitium, currente anno 279 ante ordinationem Iulianam. Sed ut esse æquabilis annorum à morte Alexandri cum annis Nabonasari comparatio, Ægyptii annos mortis Alexandri à subsequenti Thoth Nabonasari 425, qui incidit in 12 Nouembris, feriam primam, cœperunt computare. Quod autem Thoth Nabonasari 425 inciderit in 12 Nouembris cum Arabibus etiam fatetur Paulus Crusius in libello de epochis: neque rem aliter posse habere indicat epocha Nabonasari, quam cum
units.tr: (And a little later.) The moon was eclipsed in the month of Boedromion, around the beginning of the mysteries that were customarily celebrated at Athens. On the eleventh night after the eclipse, when the armies came into view, etc. It is established that the mysteries [μυστήρια] were customarily celebrated on the twentieth of each Boedromion [τῆς ἐκάστης βοηδρομιῶνος], as Plutarch himself states in his Life of Camillus and Phocion. Hence it follows that the twentieth of Boedromion corresponds to 2 September, and that on the night following it there was an eclipse of the moon at opposition of the luminaries; so that the new moon fell fifteen days earlier, that is on 6 September. This is also shown by the nineteen-year cycle of the Julian calendar. For the year 186 before the Julian reform has the golden number 19, which in the Julian calendar is placed at the 3rd of the Ides of April, and it recurs on 6 September, where it indicates the new moon. Therefore on the night following 20 September there was an eclipse of the moon at opposition of the luminaries; and on the eleventh day after the lunar eclipse, namely on the Kalends of October, Darius was routed by Alexander with a great defeat and fled with the rest of his army. The Macedonians then took the opportunity to begin their years from the Kalends of October, to which they adapted their Hyperberetaeus; Syrians and Arabs afterwards followed this in dating the years of Alexander Dhilkarnain. {b} In the early part of this Olympiad year 447, Darius the Last was killed by Bessus, and the rule of Babylon passed to Alexander the Great, according to Eusebius in the Chronicle. In memory of this event, Callippus of Cyzicus, a mathematician, established a period of 76 years, which was made up of four Metonic cycles (or nineteen-year cycles). For Callippus wished that posterity should know the time of the destruction of the Persian kingdom, and that it should be transferred to the Greeks; so he willed that four nineteen-year cycles be counted from the Olympiad year 447, that is, 76 solar years, and when these had elapsed, that the 76-year period be repeated. Thus the second period of Callippus began in Olympiad year 521, the third began from Olympiad year 599, and the fourth had its beginning from Olympiad year 677. That Callippus began his 76-year period from the solstice, which Ptolemy calls the period in Book 6, chapter 3 of the Almagest, is indicated by the fact that he followed Meton, who also began his nineteen-year cycle from the solstice, so that it would correspond to the beginning of the Olympiad years. This may also be gathered from Ptolemy, for he writes in Book 3, chapter 1 of the Almagest that the solstice observation made by Aristarchus fell in the fiftieth year of the first Callippic period, which was then ending. But Hipparchus and Ptolemy, so that the comparison of Callippic years with the years of Nabonassar would be uniform, took the beginning of the first Callippic period from the next Thoth of Nabonassar 419, and then compared each Callippic year with each year of Nabonassar. Thus the second Callippic period falls in the year 495 of Nabonassar, the third falls in the year 571 of Nabonassar, and the fourth begins with the year 647 of Nabonassar. This must be carefully noted on account of the observations which fell in these first three and four periods of Callippus. From these things it is gathered that the first Callippic period began in the sixth year before the death of Alexander, which Copernicus also indicates in Book 3, chapter 2 of his Revolutions, where, from Book 7, chapter 3 of Ptolemy's Almagest, he reports that Timocharis observed the spike of Virgo in the 36th year of the first 76-year period according to Callippus, which was the thirtieth year after the departure of Alexander the Great, that is, Nabonassar 454. Therefore the first year of the first Callippic period is the year 419 of Nabonassar. {c} The year 425 of Nabonassar is the beginning of the era which is reckoned from the death of Alexander; Ptolemy attests this in Book 3, chapter 8 of the Almagest, where he says that between Nabonassar and the death of Alexander there lay 424 Egyptian years. The Arabs assign the same number of years between Nabonassar and the Philippic era, as is clear from Alfraganus. For he says that between Nabonassar (whom the Babylonians, with Albategnius and the whole company of the Arabs, call Nabuchodonosor or Nebuchadnezzar) and Yazdegerd, king of the Persians, there elapsed 1379 Egyptian or Persian years and three months; and between Philip and Yazdegerd he says there elapsed 955 Egyptian years and three months. So if the smaller number is subtracted from the larger, there remain 424 Egyptian years which have elapsed from Nabonassar to the Philippic era. Therefore the Thoth of Nabonassar 425 is the beginning of the Philippic years; and that began on a Sunday, as Alfraganus shows, which the examination of the weekdays also confirms. From this it may be gathered that the Arabs call the era that Ptolemy dates from the death of Alexander the Philippic era. A sign of this is that they say Ptolemy in the Almagest's canon reckons times from the Philippic era, although Ptolemy nowhere mentions a Philippic epoch, but only mentions epochs reckoned from the death of Alexander. Nor do only the Arabs, but also the Greeks and Latins, call the years reckoned from the death of Alexander the years of Philip. Kabasilas, the Greek interpreter of Ptolemy, is a witness to this in his sixth commentary, where he calls the years of the death of Alexander years from Philip [ἀπὸ Φιλίππου ἔτη]. Censorinus too, the greatest reconciler of chronological scruples, calls the years from the departure of Alexander the years of Philip. The reason for this is that while Alexander was alive the Macedonians still counted time from the reign of Philip, the father of Alexander. Since the Arabs were unaware of this, it came about that they thought Philip had begun to reign when Ptolemy writes that Alexander had died, and they believed that Alexander had at last reigned at the time when the histories say that Seleucus Nicanor took up the government of Asia and Syria. Hence the era of Alexander, simply so called, according to the Arabs, is nothing other than the Alexandrine era of the Seleucids, which is distant from the Philippic era, or from the death of Alexander, by 12 Egyptian years and 325 days; it falls on 1 October, a Monday, when the dominical letter is G, in the year 267 before the Julian reform, that is, it falls on the 17th day of the month Epiphi in the year 436 of Nabonassar, as will be shown more clearly a little later. In order to understand exactly the time of Alexander's death, it must be known that Eusebius of Caesarea asserts in the Chronicle that Alexander died at Babylon in the 34th year of his age, in the first year of the 114th Olympiad, that is, Olympiad year 453. That he died at the beginning of the Olympiad year 453, which begins at the summer solstice, is established from Plutarch, who writes that he died [illegible], that is, around 23 June, according to the Syrian calendar. But at that time the solstice fell on 27 June, since 108 years earlier it had been detected by Meton on 28 June. So Alexander died three days before the solstice, in the year 279 before the Julian reform. But so that the comparison of years from the death of Alexander with the years of Nabonassar would be uniform, the Egyptians began to count the years of Alexander's death from the following Thoth of Nabonassar 425, which fell on 12 November, a Sunday. That the Thoth of Nabonassar 425 fell on 12 November is also admitted by Paulus Crusius with the Arabs in his little book on epochs; and the epoch of Nabonassar indicates that the matter cannot be otherwise, than when we placed it with the Arabs on 26 February, a Wednesday. Indeed the Actian epoch of the Egyptians, which falls on Thoth of Nabonassar 719, a Sunday, in the sixteenth Julian year, confirms the same.

units.la: a In annum ducentesimum sexagesimum septimum ante ordinationem Iulianam, kalendis Octobris bus, feria secunda, incurrit æra Alexandri Dhilkar-nain, secundum annos Iulianos computata. Sed Albategnius & alii quidam Arabes, qui eum sunt secuti, ut æquabilis sit comparatio annorum Alc-xandri cum annis Nabonafari, æram Dhilkarnain, auspicantur à sequenti Thoth Nabonafari 437, qui incurrit in 9 Nouembris feriam sextam, labente eo-dem anno 167 ante ordinationem Iulianam: de quibus prolixius dictum est in calendario Syro-rum. Quid nomen Dhilkarnain significet, non est obscurum: karnain siue alkarnain adiecto articulo, dicuntur bina cornua, iuxta Arabismum & Chal-daismum: accedente autem particula Dhu vel Dhi, dicitur Dhulkarnain vel Dhilkarnain, vel, ut vulgo pronunciatur, Zilkarnain, is qui habet duo cornua. Ita dictus fuit Alexander Magnus, filius Philippi re-gis Macedonum, ut ex Saraceno & Alfragano ani-maduertere licet: quod imperium tenuerit in totum orientem & occidentem, seu quod à columnis Her-culis regnum Græcorum propagarit in extremam Indiam: in cuius rei signum erectæ[?] fuerunt columnæ Alexandri, ut ostendimus in scholiis, cap. undecimo. Itaque per duo cornua cum Arabibus intelligimus columnas Herculis & Alexandri, intra quas regnum Græcorum erat extensum. Possumus etiam dicere, æram Alexandrinam Seleucidarum, post mortem Alexandri elapsis annis duodecim, fuisse dictam Dhilkarnain, quod tunc regnum Græcorum fuerit bipertitum in Asiam & Syriam: siquidem hi anni in libris Machabæorum & aliis historicis tam ecclesia-sticis quam profanis, a tempore Seleuci Nicanoris diligenter commemorantur. Quamobrem fallun-tur, qui existimant, Alexandrum dictum esse Ail-karnain. karnain ,hoc est, arietem bicornem , de quo scribit Daniel cap. 8. non enim Arabes arietem vocant Ail, vt Hebraei, sed Hamel, vt Germani: quin imo perpetuo apud Arabes Alexander appellatur Dhilkarnain, quasi dicas Αλ[?]ξάνδρος ὁ ὢν κερ[?]άστης, seu Alexander habes duo cornua, id est duo regna. Testis est Abul Haffumi Historicus Arabs, qui est in bibliotheca Palatina: ibi enim aliquoties fit mentio aerae Alexandri Dhil-karnain. Neque mihi dubium est ita etiam scriptum reperiri hoc nomen in codice Arabico Albategnii: cuius fi fecerint nobis copiam, qui Romae libris Ara-bicis imprimendis occupantur, praeclare de studiis astronomicis apud omnes posteros merebuntur.
units.tr: a In the year 267 before the Julian reform, on 1 October, a Monday, the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain begins, reckoned by Julian years. But Albategnius and certain other Arabs who followed him, so that the comparison of the years of Alexander with the years of Nabonassar may be even, begin the era of Dhilkarnain from the following Thoth of Nabonassar 437, which falls on 9 November, a Friday, in the same year, which is 167 before the Julian reform. These matters are treated at greater length in the calendar of the Syrians. What the name Dhilkarnain means is not obscure: karnain, or alkarnain with the article added, means "two horns," in the Arabic and Chaldean usage. With the particle Dhu or Dhi prefixed, it becomes Dhulkarnain or Dhilkarnain, or, as it is commonly pronounced, Zilkarnain, that is, "the one who has two horns." Thus Alexander the Great, son of Philip king of the Macedonians, was so called, as may be gathered from Saracenus and Alfraganus, because he held rule over the whole East and West, or because he extended the kingdom of the Greeks from the Pillars of Hercules to farthest India. As a sign of this, the pillars of Alexander were set up, as we have shown in the scholia, chapter eleven. Accordingly, by the two horns the Arabs understand the pillars of Hercules and of Alexander, within which the kingdom of the Greeks was extended. We may also say that the Seleucid era of Alexander, reckoned from twelve years after his death, was called Dhilkarnain because the kingdom of the Greeks was then divided into Asia and Syria; for these years are carefully recorded in the books of the Maccabees and in other historians, both ecclesiastical and profane, from the time of Seleucus Nicanor. Therefore those are mistaken who think Alexander was called Ail-karnain, that is, the two-horned ram, of which Daniel writes in chapter 8. For the Arabs do not call a ram Ail, as the Hebrews do, but Hamel, as the Germans do. Indeed, among the Arabs Alexander is always called Dhilkarnain, as if you were to say Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ ὢν κεράστης [Alexandros ho ōn kerastēs], or Alexander having two horns, that is, two kingdoms. The Arab historian Abul Haffum, who is in the Palatine library, is a witness: for mention is made there several times of the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain. Nor am I in doubt that this name is also found written thus in an Arabic manuscript of Albategnius. If those who are engaged in printing Arabic books at Rome would make a copy of it available to us, they would deserve well of astronomical studies among all posterity.

units.la: Porrò obseruandum est Syros adkal. Octobris, in quibus aeraDhilkarnain haeret, fixisse fuu Tifrin prio-rem, & Hebraeos ibidem collocaffe initium mensis Tifri anni ineuntis 3 4 5 0 a creatione mundi: ex quibus manifestum est, Hebraeos etiam tunc annis mere folaribus vel aequabilibus Aegyptiorum esse vsos.
units.tr: Moreover, it should be observed that the Syrians fixed their first month, Tifri, at the kalends of October, the date to which the era of Dhilkarnain is attached, and that the Hebrews placed the beginning of the month Tifri of the year 3450 from the creation of the world on the same day. From this it is clear that at that time the Hebrews too used solar or fixed years, like the Egyptians.

units.la: Si enim mensis iste Tifri lunaris fuisset, vtique incurrisset in nouilunium: atqui nouilunium fuit quinto Octobris, sicut ostendit enneadecaeteris Iuliana: anno enim 267 ante ordinationem Iulianam currente, aureus numerus est XIX, quii in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 3 Idus Aprilis, & recurrit quinto Octobris, feria sexta. Cum autem anni Iuliani & menses non fuerint in vsu: & probabile fit aeram Alexandri coepisse a neomenia proxima post aequinoctiu autumnale, vnde etiam initium habuerit annus Iudaicus lunaris 3 4 5 0 a creatione mundi: fatis euidenter hinc colligere licet, Arabes qui autores fuerunt istarum hypothesium, quod scilicet aera Dhilkarnain inciderit in primam diem Octobris, quodq; æra contraductu Hebræorum eodem tempore incurrerit in nouiluniu, in epocha lunari deceptos (se quatriduo, quia non considerarunt anticipationem lunarem. Si enim anno 167 ante ordinationem Iulianam ponamus nouilunium in quintum Octobris, & descendamus ad quintum Octobris currente anno Christi 612 quo æram suam inierunt Arabes, nouilunium deprehendemus circa diem 10 Octobris: quod indicium est, lunam a primo nouilunio Alexandreo vsque ad nouilunium anni 933 Alexandri, quod incurrit circa decimum Octobris, anticipasse dies quatuor: quos cum Arabes neglexissent, dictarunt primum nouilunium Alexandri & Tifri Iudaici incurrisse in primam Octobris currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 167: cum reuera nouilunium fuerit circa quintam Octobris. Hac ratione statuerunt Arabes in translatione Almagesti, quæ liberalitate Almamonis regis Saracenorum est facta, inter Alexandrum & principium annorum Arabicorum intercessisse annos 932, nouem menses, & quindecim dies: si menses lunares Aegyptiorum sumamus, sunt dies sexdecim. Vide appendicem Arabum ad librum 5 Almagesti. Ex quibus apparet Arabes æram Alexandri Dhilkarnain transtulisse ad primam Octobris, suam autem inchoasse 1 Iulii, currente anno Alexandri 932. Quod ad sedem æquinoctii autumnalis attinet, diximus antea in calendario Hebræorum, fuisse illud in 26 Septembris: quamobrem neomenia proxima post æquinoctium autumnale fuit in die quinto Octobris, licet Arabes & Hebræi propter neglectam anticipationem lunarem, eam putarint præcise incidisse in kal. Octobres, unde factum est vt æram Dhilkarnain & contractuum à kal. fictitiis Octobrib. auspicaretur. b Prolcmeus regnum Chaldaeorum à Seleuco Nicanore institutum orditur ab anno Nabonasari 438: quamobrea morte Alexandri vsq; ad principium regni Chaldaeorum statuit elapsos annos Aegyptios tredecim. Nam lib. 11 Almagesti, cap.7, annum Chaldaeorum 82 coniungit cum anno Nabonasari 519, & lib.9 Almagesti cap.7, annum 75 Chaldaeorum copulat cum anno 512 Nabonasari. annum vero 67 Chaldaeorum coniungit cum anno 504 Nabonasari: ex quib. omnibus apparet, Ptolemaeum initium æræ Chaldaeorum deducere ab anno 438 Nabonasari. c Annus Nabonasari 454 incurrit in annum trigesimum sextum primæ periodi Calippicæ, teste Ptolemaeo lib.7 Almagesti, cap.3. d Annus Nabonasari 464 est principium regni Ptolemaei Philadelphi regis Aegyptiorum, à quo Dionysius astronomus annos suos computauit secundum menses cœlestes.
units.tr: For if this month Tifri had been lunar, it would certainly have fallen on the new moon. But the new moon fell on the fifth of October, as the nineteen-year cycle shows: in the year 267 before the Julian reform, the golden number is 19, which in the Julian calendar is placed on the 3rd of the Ides of April, and it recurs on the fifth of October, a Friday. Since Julian years and months were not in use then, and it is probable that the era of Alexander began at the first new moon after the autumnal equinox, whence the Jewish lunar year 3450 from the creation of the world also had its beginning, we can fairly clearly conclude from this that the Arabs, who were the authors of these hypotheses, were deceived about the lunar epoch by four days, because they did not take the lunar anticipation into account. That is, they supposed that the era of Dhilkarnain fell on the first of October, and that the era of contracts, reckoned from the fictitious kalends of October, coincided with the new moon at the same time. For if we place the new moon of the year 167 before the Julian reform on the fifth of October, and descend to the fifth of October in the year of Christ 612, when the Arabs began their era, we find the new moon about the 10th of October. This is evidence that the moon, from the first new moon of the Alexandrian era up to the new moon of the year 933 of Alexander, which falls about the tenth of October, had anticipated by four days; the Arabs, neglecting these days, asserted that the first new moon of Alexander and of the Jewish Tishri fell on the first of October in the year 167 before the Julian reform, whereas in truth the new moon was about the fifth of October. By this reasoning the Arabs, in the translation of the Almagest made at the generosity of Almamon, king of the Saracens, established that between Alexander and the beginning of the Arab years there lay 932 years, nine months and fifteen days; if we take the lunar months of the Egyptians, these are sixteen days. See the Arab appendix to the fifth book of the Almagest. From these things it appears that the Arabs transferred the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain to the first of October, and began their own on the first of July in the year 932 of Alexander. As for the position of the autumnal equinox, we said earlier, in the discussion of the Hebrew calendar, that it fell on the 26th of September; therefore the first new moon after the autumnal equinox was on the fifth of October, although the Arabs and the Hebrews, on account of the neglected lunar anticipation, thought it fell exactly on the kalends of October; whence it came about that the era of Dhilkarnain and of the contracts was reckoned from the fictitious kalends of October. b Ptolemy begins the kingdom of the Chaldeans, established by Seleucus Nicanor, from the year 438 of Nabonassar; therefore he reckons that 13 Egyptian years elapsed from the death of Alexander to the beginning of the kingdom of the Chaldeans. For in the eleventh book of the Almagest, chapter 7, he joins the 82nd year of the Chaldeans with the 519th year of Nabonassar, and in the ninth book of the Almagest, chapter 7, he couples the 75th year of the Chaldeans with the 512th year of Nabonassar, and joins the 67th year of the Chaldeans with the 504th year of Nabonassar. From all of these it appears that Ptolemy derives the beginning of the era of the Chaldeans from the year 438 of Nabonassar. c The year 454 of Nabonassar falls in the thirty-sixth year of the first Calippic period, as Ptolemy testifies in the seventh book of the Almagest, chapter 3. d The year 464 of Nabonassar is the beginning of the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of the Egyptians, from which Dionysius the astronomer reckoned his years according to the celestial months.

units.la: Iraq; epocha Dionysii & Philadelphi est vna & eadem: nam Ptolemaeus annum decimum tertium Philadelphi comparat cum anno Nabonasari 476, lib.10 Almagesti, cap.4. & eundem annum Nabonasari 476 dicit esse decimum tertium Dionysii, libro eodem, cap.9, & lib.9 Almagesti cap.10, ait annum 21 Dionysii esse annum Nabonasari 484. & cap.7 dicit annum 23 Dionysii esse 486 Nabonasari: item annum 28 Dionysii esse 491 Nabonasari. Idem Ptolemaeus scribit lib.11 Almagesti, cap.3, quod annus 45 secundum Dionysium, sit annus a morte Alexandri octogesimus tertius, hoc est, a Nabonasaro quingentesimus septimus. Ex quibus apparet æram Philadelphi coniiciendam esse in annum Nabonasari 464, qui incurrit in annum Olympiadicum 492, hoc est in annum quartum Olympiadis 123: etsi Eusebius Cæsariensis in chronicis regnum Ptolemęi Philadelphi conferat in principium Olympiadis 124. Hic Ptolemæus Philadelphus ex Hebraeo in Græcum sermonem per LXX interpretes curauit transferri sacra biblia: vt Eusebius indicat hisce verbis: Ptolemaeus Philadelphus Iudaeos qui in Aegypto erant, liberos esse permisit: & vasa Eleazaro Pontifici Hierofolymarū votiua transmittens, diuinam scripturam in vocem Græcam ex Hebraea lingua per LXX interpretes transferre curauit, quam sibi ex omni genere literatura comparauerat. e Annus Nabonafari 465 incurrit in annum 47 primæ periodi Calippicæ vt testatur Ptolemaeus lib.7 Almagesti cap.5. quo anno die 19 Athyr occupante sole septimum gradum Aquarii, Luna vero possidente vigefimum minutū primi gradus Tauri, hoc est, distante ab æquinoctio verno gradibus 30, & 20 minutis, Timocharis Alexandriæ obseruauit coniunctionem lunæ cum pleiadibus. Thoth Nabonafari 465 incidit in fecun-dam Nouembris, feriam sextam, currente anno 239 ante ordinationem Iulianam: itaq; dies 19 Athyr incurrit in 19 Ianuarii, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 238: atqui die illa sol occupauit gradum septimum Aquarii: ex quo sequitur æquinoctium vernum fuisse in 24 die Martii, & autumnale in 26 Septembris. f Hunc annū Nabonafari 466 Ptolemaeus comparat cum anno 48 primæ periodi Calippicæ, lib.7 Almagesti cap.3. g Hic annus Nabonafari 468 est quinquagesimus primæ periodi Calippicæ, quo definente Ptolemaeus fatetur Ariftarchum solstitium obferuaffe: vt videre licet lib.3 Almagesti cap.1. Sed obseruandum est, duplex esse principium annorum Calippicorum: vnum quod sumitur 419 Thoth Nabonasari, & deinceps singulis annis Aegyptiorum respodet: alterum vero est, quod sumitur a principio annorum Olympiadicorum circa solstitium aestiuum ineuntium, qua ratione annus Olympiadicus 496 est annus quinquagesimus primae periodi Calippicae, quo circa solstitium definente, & incipiente anno Olympiadico 497, currente anno 135[?] ante ordinationem Iulianam, Aristarchus observavit solstitium, diebus scilicet 93 ante aequinoctium autumnale quod haerebat in 26 Septembris, quae erat dies 36 ante Thoth Nabonasari 469 ineuntem primo Nouembris, feria tertia. Eadem ratione annus quinquagesimus tertiae periodi Calippicae incipit ab anno Olympiadico 648, qui incurrit in annum 84 ante ordinationem Iulianam: quamobrem solstitium anni ineuntis Olympiadici 648, & quinquagesimi tertiae periodi Calippicae incidit in annum Nabonasari 619, a quo usque ad solstitium incidens in annum primum Antonini Pii, hoc est, in annum Nabonasari 885: Ptolemaeus vult elapsos esse annos solares 265, sicut videre licet lib. 7 Almagesti, cap. 2. Sic annus trigesimus secundae tertiae periodi Calippicae incipit ab anno Olympiadico 630, qui incurrit in annum 102 ante ordinationem Iulianam: quamobrem solstitium anni ineuntis Olympiadici 630 fiue anni trigesimi secundi tertiae periodi Calippicae, incidit in annum Nabonasari sexcentesimum primum, diebus scilicet 93 ante aequinoctium autumnale, quod haerebat circa 26 Septembris, quae erat dies tertia ante Thoth Nabonasari 602 ineuntem 29 Septembris, feria tertia. Aequinoctium quidem illud autumnale incurrit in annum 32 tertiae periodi Calippicae, quatenus is intelligitur incipere a proxime praecedenti solstitio circa initium anni Olympiadici 630: sed incidit circa finem anni sexcentesimi primi Nabonasari, die scilicet tertia [illegible, ~9 letters]: à quo autumnali æquinoctio vsq; ad æquinoctium autumnale incidens in annum quadringentesimum sexagesimum tertium à morte Alexandri, hoc est, in annum Nabonasari 887, qui fuit annus tertius Antonini Pii, Ptolemæus dicit elapsos esse annos solares 28 s[?], vt videre licet lib. 3 Almagesti cap. 1. Vt aurem intelligatur hæc verissima esse intervalla, sumatur[?] annus Nabonasari 619, in quem incidit solstitium inquem euntis anni quinquagesimi tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, & ad eum adiiciantur 265 anni, qui elapsi sunt vsq; ad solstitium incurrens in annum Nabonasari 885. proveniunt anni 884 à Nabonasaro elapsi vsque ad solstitium incurrens in annum 885 Nabonasari. Ita si ad annū Nabonasari 601, in quem incurrit æquinoctiu autumnale, adiiciantur anni 285, qui elapsi sunt vsq; ad æquinoctium autumnale, quod incidit in annum Nabonasari 887,proveniunt anni 886 à Nabonasaro absoluti vsq; ad æquinoctium autumnale incurrens in annum Nabonasari 887.
units.tr: The epoch of Dionysius and of Philadelphus is one and the same. For Ptolemy compares the thirteenth year of Philadelphus with the 476th year of Nabonassar, in the tenth book of the Almagest, chapter 4, and in the same book, chapter 9, he says that the same 476th year of Nabonassar is the thirteenth of Dionysius; and in the ninth book of the Almagest, chapter 10, he says that the 21st year of Dionysius is the 484th year of Nabonassar; and in chapter 7 he says that the 23rd year of Dionysius is the 486th year of Nabonassar; likewise that the 28th year of Dionysius is the 491st year of Nabonassar. The same Ptolemy writes in the eleventh book of the Almagest, chapter 3, that the 45th year according to Dionysius is the 83rd year from the death of Alexander, that is, the 507th from Nabonassar. From these things it appears that the era of Philadelphus must be placed in the year 464 of Nabonassar, which falls in the Olympiad year 492, that is, in the fourth year of the 123rd Olympiad; although Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Chronicle, places the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus at the beginning of the 124th Olympiad. This Ptolemy Philadelphus had the Holy Bible translated from Hebrew into Greek by the Seventy interpreters, as Eusebius indicates in these words: Ptolemy Philadelphus allowed the Jews who were in Egypt to be free; and, sending votive vessels to Eleazar, the High Priest of Jerusalem, he had the divine Scripture translated from the Hebrew language into the Greek tongue by the Seventy interpreters, which he had obtained for himself from every kind of literature. e The year 465 of Nabonassar falls in the 47th year of the first Calippic period, as Ptolemy testifies in the seventh book of the Almagest, chapter 5. In that year, on the 19th of Athyr, when the sun occupied the seventh degree of Aquarius and the moon the twentieth minute of the first degree of Taurus, that is, distant from the vernal equinox by 30 degrees and 20 minutes, Timocharis at Alexandria observed the conjunction of the moon with the Pleiades. Thoth of the year 465 of Nabonassar fell on the 2nd of November, a Friday, in the year 239 before the Julian reform; therefore the 19th of Athyr falls on the 19th of January in the year 238 before the Julian reform; but on that day the sun occupied the seventh degree of Aquarius; from which it follows that the vernal equinox was on the 24th of March and the autumnal on the 26th of September. f Ptolemy compares this year 466 of Nabonassar with the 48th year of the first Calippic period, in the seventh book of the Almagest, chapter 3. g This year 468 of Nabonassar is the fiftieth of the first Calippic period, at the end of which Ptolemy admits that Aristarchus observed the solstice, as may be seen in the third book of the Almagest, chapter 1. But it must be observed that the Calippic years have a double beginning: one, taken from 1 Thoth of Nabonassar, which corresponds to the Egyptian years year by year; the other, taken from the beginning of the Olympiad years, which begin about the summer solstice; in this way the Olympiad year 496 is the fiftieth year of the first Calippic period, at the end of which, about the solstice, and at the beginning of the Olympiad year 497, in the year 135 [?] before the Julian reform, Aristarchus observed the solstice, namely 93 days before the autumnal equinox, which stood on the 26th of September, which was the 36th day before Thoth of the year 469 of Nabonassar, beginning on the first of November, a Tuesday. By the same reasoning the fiftieth year of the third Calippic period begins from the Olympiad year 648, which falls in the year 84 before the Julian reform; therefore the solstice at the beginning of the Olympiad year 648, and of the fiftieth year of the third Calippic period, fell in the year 619 of Nabonassar, from which, up to the solstice falling in the first year of Antoninus Pius, that is, in the year 885 of Nabonassar, Ptolemy wishes 265 solar years to have elapsed, as may be seen in the seventh book of the Almagest, chapter 2. Thus the 32nd year of the third Calippic period begins from the Olympiad year 630, which falls in the year 102 before the Julian reform; therefore the solstice at the beginning of the Olympiad year 630, or of the 32nd year of the third Calippic period, fell in the 601st year of Nabonassar, namely 93 days before the autumnal equinox, which stood about the 26th of September, which was the third day before Thoth of the year 602 of Nabonassar, beginning on the 29th of September, a Tuesday. That autumnal equinox falls in the 32nd year of the third Calippic period, inasmuch as that period is understood to begin from the solstice immediately preceding, about the beginning of the Olympiad year 630; but it falls near the end of the 601st year of Nabonassar, namely on the third day [illegible, about nine letters]. From this autumnal equinox up to the autumnal equinox falling in the 463rd year from the death of Alexander, that is, in the year 887 of Nabonassar, which was the third year of Antoninus Pius, Ptolemy says that 285 solar years elapsed, as may be seen in the third book of the Almagest, chapter 1. And so that these intervals may be understood to be most accurate, let us take the year 619 of Nabonassar, in which the solstice falls at the beginning of the fiftieth year of the third Calippic period, and add to it the 265 years which elapsed up to the solstice falling in the year 885 of Nabonassar: there result 884 years elapsed from Nabonassar up to the solstice falling in the year 885 of Nabonassar. Likewise, if to the year 601 of Nabonassar, in which the autumnal equinox falls, we add the 285 years which elapsed up to the autumnal equinox, which falls in the year 887 of Nabonassar, there result 886 years completed from Nabonassar up to the autumnal equinox falling in the year 887 of Nabonassar.

units.la: Quod ad meles cœlestes Dionysii Astronomi atti-net, sciendum est annum cœlestem expleri 365 ¼ diebus, qui constat ex quatuor quadrantibus inæqualibus. Possumus auté[?] annum cœlestem ordiri vel ab æquinoctiis, vel à solstitiis. si à solstitio auspicemur, deprehendemus semissem æstiuum, qui recipit hos sex menses Carcinonem, Leontoné, Parthenonem, Zygonem, Scorpionem & Toxonem, habere 182 dies: semissem aut hibernū, qui recipit hos sex menses Ægonem, Hydronem, Ichthyone, Crione, Tauronem, & Didymoné, cotinerei 83 dies: & si dies bisextilis quarto quouis anno ante solstitium interiiciatur, habere eũ i 84 dies Si aute annũ cœleste ordiamur ab æquinoctiis, deprehendemus arcũ vernũ, qui cõpleƥtitur hos sex meses Crionem, Tauronem, Didymone, Carcinone, Leontone, & Parthenone, continere 187 dies arcũ vero autumnale, qui completitur hos menses sex Zygonem, Scorpionem, Toxone, Ægonem, Hydrone, & Ichthyone, habere in anno communi 178 dies: &si dies bisextilis quarto quouis anno inferatur ante æquinoctium vernale, habere eum 179 dies. Si itaq; semisses anni cœlestis sumantur à solstitiis, tunc vno & altero tantum die se inuice excedut: si vero à punctis æquinoctiorum stimentur, tunc octo vel nouem diebus se mutuo excedunt. Quod autê arcus vernalis completatur centũ octoginta septem dies, & arcus autumnalis habeat centũ septuaginta octo dies, manifestũ fiet ex obseruationibus Hipparchi, de quibus dicemus circa annum Nabonasari 602. Idem intelligi potest ex quadrantibus anni cœlestis: nã Hipparchus & Ptolemæus, vt videre licet lib. 3 Almagesti cap. 4, ab æquinoctio verno vsq; ad solstitiũ æstiuũ inuenerut 94 ½ dies: à solstitio verò æstiuo ad æquinoctiũ autumnale inuenerunt 92 ½ dies. Ergo iuxta eorũ obseruationes arcus vernalis completitur 187 dies, vt scilicet vtrumq; æquinoctiũ in eũ incurrat: nam Arabes arcum vernale ponunt 186 dierũ, quatenus in illũ vnũ tantũ æquinoctiũ incurrit, sicut videre licet in astrolabio meo Arabico. Hunc annũ cœleste pulcherrimè describit Varro de re rustica lib. 1 cap. 28, hilce verbis: Dies primus est verũ in Aquario, astatiũ in Tauro, autumnũ in Leone, hiemis in Scorpione. Cũm vnuscuiusq; horũ quatuor signorum dies tertius & vicesimus, quatuor temporum sit primus, efficitur ut ver dies habeat XCI, æstas XCIV, autumnus XCIX hiems XXCIX. Qua redacta ad dies ciuiles nostros qui nunc sunt primi veris temporis, ex a.d. VII. Februarii. Aestiui ex a. d. VII. Id. Maii. autumnales ex a. d. VII. Id. Sextilis. hiberni ex a. d. IV. Id. Nouembris. subtilius discretis temporibus obseruanda quaedam sunt, eaque in partes VIII diuiduntur. Primum a Fauonio ad aequinoctium vernum dies XL: hinc ad Vergiliarum exortum dies XLIV: ab hoc ad solstitium dies XLIIX: inde ad Caniculae signum dies XXIX: dein ad aequinoctium autumnale dies LXVII: exin ad Vergiliarum occasum dies XXXII: ab hoc ad brumam dies LVII: inde ad Fauonium dies XLV. Ex quibus apparet Varronem arcum vernalem e duobus quadrantibus conflatum ponere dierum 185, ut die vno absit a calculo Arabum: cum autem arcum autumnalem e duobus quoq; quadrantibus constitutum facit dierum tantum 170, manifestum est, eum intelligere annum lunarem 355 diebus constantem: si enim ad dies 185 adiiciamus dies 170, consurgit anni lunaris quantitas, quae est 355 dierum, iuxta constitutionem Numae Pompilii. Hinc sequitur Varronem quoq; intelligere menses lunares, quando aiet arcus vernalis initium computari a 23 gradu Aquarii, qui incurrat in VII Id. Februarii, &c. annum tamen lunarem per octo temporum interualla redigit ad annum solarem: si enim dies nominati colligantur, consurgit summa 362 dierum, quae est quantitas anni solaris Attici ciuilis, quam Romani ab Atheniensibus acceperunt, & per certas intercalationes ad annum solis naturalem, cuius periodus est 365 1/4 dierum, renocarunt, teste Macrobio. Annus certe caelestis siue sit lunaris siue solaris, maximum usum præstat historicis & astronomis : ut silentio minimè sit prætereundus. De mensibus cœlestibus ita scribit Censorinus: Qui sunt cœlestes, siue solis seu luna, neque peraque inter se pares sunt, nec dies habent totos. quippe sol in aquario moratur circiter undetriginta, in pisce fere triginta, in ariete unum & triginta, in geminis prope triginta & duos: & sic in cæteris inæquabiliter: sed usque adeo non totos dies in singulis, ut annum suum, id est, dies trecentos sexaginta quinque, & portionem nescio quam adhuc astrologis inexploratam, in duodecim suos dimidat menses. Luna autem singulos suos menses conficit diebus undetriginta circiter & dimidiato, sed & hos inter se dispares, alias longiores, alias breviores. Quem mensem Aquarii vocat Censo-rinus, eum Dionysius appellat Hydronem, Piscium Ichthyonem, Arietis Crionem, Geminorum Didy-monem: tribuit etiam iisdem mensibus cœlestibus tot ferè dies Dionysius, quot eis assignauit Censorinus. Sed quantum ex scriptis Ptolemaicis coniice-re possumus, hi sunt menses Dionysii, in quibus nu-merus dierum adscriptus habetur. units.tr: As to the celestial months of Dionysius the astronomer, it must be noted that the celestial year is completed in 365¼ days, and that it consists of four unequal quadrants. We may begin the celestial year either from the equinoxes or from the solstices. If we begin from the solstice, we find that the summer half-year, which contains the six months Carcinon, Leonton, Parthenon, Zygon, Scorpion and Toxon, has 182 days; and the winter half-year, which contains the six months Aegon, Hydron, Ichthyon, Crion, Tauron and Didymon, has 183 days; and if an intercalary day is inserted before the solstice every fourth year, the former has 184 days. If, however, we begin the celestial year from the equinoxes, we find that the spring arc, which is completed by the six months Crion, Tauron, Didymon, Carcinon, Leonton and Parthenon, contains 187 days; and the autumnal arc, which is completed by the six months Zygon, Scorpion, Toxon, Aegon, Hydron and Ichthyon, has 178 days in a common year; and if an intercalary day is inserted before the vernal equinox every fourth year, the latter has 179 days. Thus, if the halves of the celestial year are reckoned from the solstices, they exceed one another by only one or two days; but if they are measured from the points of the equinoxes, they exceed one another by eight or nine days. That the vernal arc is completed in 187 days, and the autumnal arc has 178 days, will become clear from the observations of Hipparchus, of which we shall speak around the year 602 of Nabonassar. The same can be understood from the quadrants of the celestial year. For Hipparchus and Ptolemy, as may be seen in book 3 of the Almagest, chapter 4, found that from the vernal equinox to the summer solstice there are 94½ days, and from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox they found 92½ days. Therefore, according to their observations, the vernal arc is completed in 187 days, so that both equinoxes fall within it; for the Arabs make the vernal arc 186 days, since only one equinox falls within it, as may be seen in my Arabic astrolabe. Varro, in book 1, chapter 28 of On Agriculture, describes this celestial year most elegantly in these words: "The first day of spring is in Aquarius, of summer in Taurus, of autumn in Leo, of winter in Scorpio. Since the third and twentieth day of each of these four signs is the first of the quarter-seasons, it comes about that spring has 91 days, summer 94, autumn 99, and winter 99 [as printed]. These, reduced to our civil days, which are now the first days of the seasons of the year: spring from the 7th day before the Kalends of February, summer from the 7th day before the Ides of May, autumn from the 7th day before the Ides of August, and winter from the 4th day before the Ides of November. More finely distinguished seasons must be observed, and these are divided into eight parts. First, from the Favonius to the vernal equinox, 40 days; from there to the rising of the Pleiades, 44 days; from this to the solstice, 48 days; then to the sign of the Dog Star, 29 days; then to the autumnal equinox, 67 days; thereafter to the setting of the Pleiades, 32 days; from this to the winter solstice, 57 days; and from there to the Favonius, 45 days." From these things it appears that Varro takes the vernal arc, made up of two quadrants, as 185 days, so that it is one day short of the Arabs' reckoning; but when he makes the autumnal arc, likewise made up of two quadrants, only 170 days, it is clear that he has in mind a lunar year of 355 days, according to the arrangement of Numa Pompilius. For if we add the 170 days to the 185 days, the sum is the quantity of a lunar year, which is 355 days. From this it follows that Varro also means lunar months, when he says that the vernal arc is reckoned from the 23rd degree of Aquarius, which falls on the 7th day before the Ides of February, and so on. Yet he reduces the lunar year by eight intervals of the seasons to the solar year; for if the named days are added together, the sum is 362 days, which is the length of the civil Attic solar year, which the Romans received from the Athenians and afterwards, through certain intercalations, restored to the natural solar year, whose period is 365¼ days, as Macrobius testifies. Certainly the celestial year, whether it is lunar or solar, is of the greatest use to historians and astronomers, so that it must by no means be passed over in silence. Concerning the celestial months Censorinus writes thus: "Those that are celestial, whether solar or lunar, are neither all equal among themselves nor have whole days. For the sun remains in Aquarius about 29 days, in Pisces about 30, in Aries 31, in Gemini nearly 32; and so on in the rest, unequally. But they do not have whole days in each case to such an extent that it divides its year, that is 365 days and some portion not yet explored by astrologers, into twelve of its months. The moon, however, completes each of its months in about 29½ days, and these too are unequal among themselves, some longer, some shorter." The month which Censorinus calls of Aquarius, Dionysius calls Hydron; of Pisces, Ichthyon; of Aries, Crion; of Gemini, Didymon. Dionysius also assigns to these celestial months about as many days as Censorinus assigned to them. But as far as we can conjecture from the Ptolemaic writings, these are the months of Dionysius, with the number of days ascribed to each: Krion [Κριῶν] 31 days; Tauron [Ταύρων] 31 days; Didymon [Αἰδυμῶν] 32 days; Carcinon [Καρκινῶν] 31 days; Leonton [Λεοντῶν] 31 days; Parthenon [Παρθενῶν] 31 days; Zygon [Ζυγῶν] 30 days; Scorpion [Σκορπιῶν] 30 days; Toxon [Τοξῶν] 29 days; Aegon [Αἰγῶν] 29 days; Hydron [Ὑδρῶν] 30 days; Ichthyon [Ἰχθυῶν] 30 days.

units.la: Hi duodecim menses cœlestes conficiunt 365 [?] dies: quibus quarto quoq; anno ex quadrantis diei accessione, dies unus adiicitur: cum compertum sit, quadrante diei annum æquabilem Ægyptiorum excedi ab anno naturali solis, quem omnes
units.tr: These twelve celestial months make up 365 [?] days, to which one day is added every fourth year from the accumulation of a quarter of a day; for it has been ascertained that the Egyptians' equal year exceeds the natural solar year, which all have found to consist of 365¼ days, plus or minus.
