units.la: a Ab hoc anno Nabonasari 495 secundum Ægyptios incipit secunda periodus Calippi, die videlicet 25 Octobris, feria prima, currente anno ducentesimo nono ante ordinationem Iulianam: at secundum Græcos iuxta institutionem Calippi, secunda periodus Calippica, hoc est, annus 77 ab interfecto Dario ultimo, incipit a præcedenti solstitio æstiuo, hoc est ab anno Olympiadico quingentesimo vigesimo tertio.
units.tr: a From this year of Nabonassar, 495, the second period of Callippus begins according to the Egyptians, namely on 25 October, a Sunday, in the 209th year before the Julian reform. But according to the Greeks, following the institution of Callippus, the second Callippic period, that is, the 77th year from the death of the last Darius, begins from the preceding summer solstice, that is, from the 523rd year of the Olympiad.

units.la: b Ab hoc anno Nabonasari 571 secundum Ægyptios incipit tertia periodus Calippica, die videlicet 6 Octobris, feria septima, currente anno centesimo trigesimo tertio ante ordinationem Iulianam: at secundum Græcos iuxta institutionem Calippi tertia periodus Calippica, hoc est, annus 153 ab interfecto Dario ultimo, incipit a præcedenti solstitio æstiuo, hoc est, ab anno Olympiadico quingentesimo nonagesimo nono.
units.tr: b From this year of Nabonassar, 571, the third Callippic period begins according to the Egyptians, namely on 6 October, a Saturday, in the 133rd year before the Julian reform. But according to the Greeks, following the institution of Callippus, the third Callippic period, that is, the 153rd year from the death of the last Darius, begins from the preceding summer solstice, that is, from the 599th year of the Olympiad.

units.la: In istis duabus periodis præstantissimæ obseruationes conscriptæ sunt apud Ptolemæum, quæ diligenter sunt considerandæ: cum per eas primum nouilunium ab ordinatione Iuliana confirmetur, & annorum Iulianorum cum annis Olympiadicis, Urbis conditæ, Actiacæ[?] victoriæ, & Christi, connexio iustissima comprobetur.
units.tr: In these two periods, the most excellent observations are recorded in Ptolemy, which must be carefully considered, since through them the first new moon after the Julian reform is confirmed, and the most exact correspondence of Julian years with Olympiad years, years from the foundation of the city, the Actian victory, and Christ is demonstrated.

units.la: * Hoc anno Nabonasari 547 ad finem currente, videlicet die 16 Mesori eclipsis lunæ conspecta est Alexandriæ, ut refert HipparHipparchus apud Ptolemæum lib.4 Almagesti, cap. 11. Sanè Thoth Nabonasari 547 incurrit in 12 Octobris, feriam quartam, currente anno centesimo quinquagesimo septimo ante ordinationem Iulianam: hinc si numerentur menses Ægyptii undecim, & 15 dies elapsi, hoc est, in universum 345 dies, descenditur ad 24 Septembris, currente anno 156 ante ordinationem Iulianam: fuit tunc eclipsis lunæ in oppositione luminarium, sole occupante 26 gradum Virginis, luna vero tenete 16 gradum Piscium, teste Ptolemaeo: ergo die nono Septembris praecessit novilunium, quod etiam ostendit enneadecaeteris Iuliana: anno enim 156 ante ordinationem Iulianam adscribitur aureus numerus XVI. qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 17 kal.Februarij, & recurrit die nono Septembris.
units.tr: * In this year 547 of Nabonassar, at its end, namely on 16 Mesori, a lunar eclipse was observed at Alexandria, as Hipparchus reports in Ptolemy, Almagest book 4, chapter 11. Now Thoth of Nabonassar 547 falls on 12 October, a Wednesday, in the 157th year before the Julian reform. Hence, if the Egyptian months are counted, eleven months and fifteen days having elapsed, that is, 345 days in all, one arrives at 24 September, in the 156th year before the Julian reform. There was then a lunar eclipse at opposition of the luminaries, the sun occupying the 26th degree of Virgo and the moon the 16th degree of Pisces, according to Ptolemy. Therefore the new moon preceded on 9 September, which the Julian enneadecaeteris also shows: for to the 156th year before the Julian reform is assigned the golden number XVI, which in the Julian calendar is placed at 17 kalends of February, and it recurs on 9 September.

units.la: Scribit autè Ptolemaeus ex relatione Hipparchi eclipsin istam incurrisse in annum quinquagesimum quartum secundæ periodi Calippicæ: quod more Graecorum accipiendum est, quatenus annus quinquagesimus quartus secundæ periodi Calippicæ incipit ab anno Olympiadico 576, cuius initium est circa solstitium æstivum, currente anno 156 ante ordinationem Iulianam. Si enim more Ægyptiorum annos Calippicos conferamus cum annis æquabilibus Nabonasari, ut alias solet facere Hipparchus & Ptolemaeus; tunc annus 54 secundæ periodi Calippicæ respondet anno Nabonasari 548, quo eclipsis commemorata non contigit. Observandum hic est mendum in editione Graeca: ibi enim scribitur fuisse hanc eclipsin [illegible, ~6 letters] ἔτει, τῆς [illegible, ~8 letters] Καλλίππου [illegible, ~8 letters]: cum scribi debeat, [illegible, ~6 letters] ut subsequens locus statim indicat de eclipsi quæ facta est anno eodem secundæ periodi Calippicæ, & 548 anno Nabonasari, die nona Mechir: idem etiam apparet ex collatione annorum Calippi-corum,de quibus dicitur lib.7 Almagesti,cap.5.Prae-terea Almagestum Latinum manuscriptum,quod est in bibliotheca Palatina, habet annum 54[?] fecundae periodi Calippi: licet Almagestum a Lichtenstenio editum corruptissime scribat annu 24 fecundę periodi Calippi. Adhaec versio Panormitana, quae in sex priores libros Almagesti manuscripta extat in bibliotheca Palatina,rectissime hic scribit annu 54[?] fecundae periodi secundum Calippum: eandem emendationem agnoscit Iosephus Scaliger de emendatione temporum pag.67. Porro eodem anno quinquagesimo quarto fecundae periodi Calippicae,h.e. anno Nabonasari 548, eclipsis lunaris altera fuit die nona Mechir,sole occupante 16 gradum Piscium,luna vero tenente 16 gradu Virginis.Annus 548 Nabonasari coepit feria quinta,die 12 Octobris,currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 156: hinc si numerentur quinque menses Aegyptiorum, & octo dies elapsi, hoc est in vniuersum 158 dies,peruenitur ad 19 Martij currente anno 155 ante ordinationem Iulianam: fuit tunc eclipsis in oppositione luminarium. itaque diebus quindecim praeceßit nouilunium,die quinto Martij,vt etiam ostendit enneadecaeteris Iuliana: anno enim 155 ante ordinationem Iulianam adscribitur aureus numerus XVII, qui in calendario Iuliano apponitur ad Nonas Ianuarij, & recurrit tertio Nonarum Martij.
units.tr: Ptolemy, however, writes on Hipparchus's report that this eclipse fell in the fifty-fourth year of the second Callippic period. This must be understood in the Greek manner, insofar as the fifty-fourth year of the second Callippic period begins from the Olympiad year 576, whose beginning is about the summer solstice, in the 156th year before the Julian reform. For if we compare the Callippic years according to the custom of the Egyptians with the equal years of Nabonassar, as Hipparchus and Ptolemy are accustomed to do elsewhere, then the fifty-fourth year of the second Callippic period corresponds to the 548th year of Nabonassar, in which the aforementioned eclipse did not occur. Here a fault must be noted in the Greek edition: there it is written that this eclipse occurred [ἔτει, τῆς ... Καλλίππου ...] [partly illegible], whereas it ought to be written [illegible], as the following passage immediately indicates, concerning the eclipse which took place in the same year of the second Callippic period and the 548th year of Nabonassar, on the ninth day of Mechir. The same also appears from a comparison of the Callippic years, which are discussed in Almagest book 7, chapter 5. Moreover, the manuscript Latin Almagest, which is in the Palatine library, has the 54th[?] year of the second period of Callippus, although the Almagest edited by Lichtenstein very corruptly writes the 24th year of the second period of Callippus. Besides, the Panormitan version, which survives in manuscript in the Palatine library for the first six books of the Almagest, rightly writes here the 54th[?] year of the second period according to Callippus. Joseph Scaliger also recognises this same emendation in his De emendatione temporum, p. 67. Furthermore, in that same fifty-fourth year of the second Callippic period, that is, in the 548th year of Nabonassar, there was a second lunar eclipse, on the ninth day of Mechir, the sun occupying the 16th degree of Pisces and the moon the 16th degree of Virgo. The 548th year of Nabonassar began on Thursday, 12 October, in the 156th year before the Julian reform. Hence, if five Egyptian months and eight days are counted, that is 158 days in all, one arrives at 19 March, in the 155th year before the Julian reform. There was then an eclipse at opposition of the luminaries. Thus the new moon preceded by fifteen days, on 5 March, as the Julian enneadecaeteris also shows: for to the 155th year before the Julian reform is assigned the golden number XVII, which in the Julian calendar is placed at the Nones of January, and it recurs on the third day before the Nones of March.

units.la: Tertia eclipsis contigit eodem anno Nabonasari 548, die quinto Mesori, sole occupante 15 gradum Virginis, luna vero tenente gradum 15 Piscium, vt ibidem recenset Ptolemaeus. Si ergo a 12 Octobris, qui incurrit in annum 156 ante ordinationem Iulianam, numerentur vndecim menses Aegyptiorum, & quatuor dies elapsi,hoc est,in vniuersum 334 dies;per-[?] uenitur ad vndecimum diem Septembris, currente anno 155[?] ante ordinationem Iulianam: tunc eclipsis conspecta est in oppofitione luminarium. ergo quindecim diebus ante, nimirum 29 Augusti die prxcessit nouilunium. quod etiam ostendit enneadecaeteris Iuliana: nam ibi aureus numerus XVII secundum ordinem lunationum recurrit. Quod autem Ptolemæus dicit eclipsin hanc contigisse anno quinquagesimo quinto periodi Calippicæ secundæ; verum est, quatenus annus 55 secundæ periodi Calippicæ initium sumit ab anno Olympiadico 77[?],h.e.a solstitio quod antecesserit annum Nabonasari 549: hinc sequitur priorem eclipsin, quæ contigit anno Nabonasari 548, die nona Mechir incurrisse in annum 54 secundæ periodi Calippicæ, non autem in annum 55 secundæ periodi Calippicæ, vtiliās exemplaria omnia constanter asserunt. Quamobrem in Græca editione ita legendum est, τὴν δὲ ἐξῆς ἔκλειψιν φησὶ γίγνεσθαι τῇ αὐτῇ [?] ... ἐπὶ τῆς ... καὶ Αἰγυπτίως μεσορὶ [?] ϑ. τὴν δὲ τρίτην φησὶν ἔκλειψιν γίγνεσθαι τῆς ... ἐπὶ τῆς δευτέρας περιόδου, τῆς ... καὶ Αἰγυπτίως μεσορὶ [?] α. hoc est, Sequentem eclipsin ait fuisse eodem 54 anno eiusdem periodi, secundùm Ægyptios die nona Mechir. tertiam verò eclipsin ait fuisse anno 55, secundæ periodi, secundùm Ægyptios die quinto Mefori. Certissimum enim est annum 54 secundæ periodi Calippicæ secundum Græcos incipere ab anno 576 Olympiadico, cùm annus primus Calippicus cœperit ab anno 447 Olympiadico: nam si ab anno 576 Olympiadico subtrahamus annum 447 Olympiadicum, remanent anni 129, qui elapsi sunt à primo anno Calippico vsq; ad annū 54 Calippicum: itaque si anni 129 elapsi adiiciantur ad annos 446 Olympiadicos elapsos ante primam periodum Calippi;
units.tr: A third eclipse occurred in the same year, Nabonassar 548, on the fifth day of Mesori, with the sun at 15 degrees of Virgo and the moon at 15 degrees of Pisces, as Ptolemy recounts in the same place. If we count from 12 October, which falls in the year 156 before the Julian reform, through eleven Egyptian months and four elapsed days, that is 334 days in all, we arrive at the eleventh day of September in the year 155 before the Julian reform. Then the eclipse was observed at the opposition of the luminaries. So fifteen days earlier, namely on 29 August, the new moon had preceded it. The Julian enneadecaeteris also shows this, for there the golden number XVII recurs in the order of the lunations. As for Ptolemy's statement that this eclipse happened in the fifty-fifth year of the second Calippic period, that is true, insofar as the fifty-fifth year of the second Calippic period begins from the solstice that preceded the year Nabonassar 549, in Olympiad year 77. From this it follows that the earlier eclipse, which occurred in the year Nabonassar 548 on the ninth day of Mechir, fell in the fifty-fourth year of the second Calippic period, not the fifty-fifth, as all the copies consistently assert. Therefore the Greek edition must be read thus: [τὴν δὲ ἐξῆς ἔκλειψιν φησὶ γίγνεσθαι τῇ αὐτῇ [?] ... ἐπὶ τῆς ... καὶ Αἰγυπτίως μεσορὶ [?] ϑ. τὴν δὲ τρίτην φησὶν ἔκλειψιν γίγνεσθαι τῆς ... ἐπὶ τῆς δευτέρας περιόδου, τῆς ... καὶ Αἰγυπτίως μεσορὶ [?] α.] That is: he says the following eclipse took place in the same fifty-fourth year of that period, according to the Egyptians on the ninth day of Mechir; and he says the third eclipse took place in the fifty-fifth year of the second period, according to the Egyptians on the fifth day of Mesori. For it is most certain that the fifty-fourth year of the second Calippic period, according to the Greeks, begins from Olympiad year 576, since the first Calippic year began from Olympiad year 447. If we subtract Olympiad year 447 from Olympiad year 576, 129 years remain, which have elapsed from the first Calippic year up to the fifty-fourth Calippic year. Thus, if these 129 elapsed years are added to the 446 Olympiad years that elapsed before the first Calippic period,

units.la: Note on the Greek: the Greek letters and accents are read from a small, damaged scan; uncertain letters are marked [?]. oritur summa 575 annorum Olympiadicorum, quos manifeste apparet ante initium anni 4 secundæ periodi Calippicæ,hoc est,ante annum Olympiadicum 576 elapsos. Si placet annos Calippicos conferre cum annis Nabonassari, eadem est ratio: exempli gratia, ante annum Nabonassari 548, qui secundum Ægyptios est annus 4 secundæ periodi Calippicæ, elapsi sunt anni Nabonassari 547; atque ante annum Nabonassari 419, in quo secundum Ægyptios incurrit primus annus Calippicus, elapsi sunt anni Nabonassari 418: si itaque annus 418 subtrahitur ab anno 547, remanet anni 129 elapsi ante annum Nabonassari 548. Ita annus Nabonassari 549 secundum Ægyptios est 5 secundæ periodi Calippicæ, etsi secundum Græcos inceperit à præcedente solstitio, h.e. ab anno Olympiadico 577. Hac collatione qui non diligenter expendit, nunquam veram seriem annorum Calippicorum habere potuit, neque etiam quicquam de emendatione numerorum depravatorum rorum pronunciare audet. Hoc anno Nabonassari 586 fere desinente, die 30 Mesori, Hipparchus invest igavit æquinoctiū autumnale: dicit autem tempus illud incurrisse in annū 17 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, quod verum est constat: quoniam secundum Græcos incipit ab anno Olympiadico 615 circa solstitium inchoante, labente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 117. Thoth Nabonassari 586 cœpit die 3 Octobris, feria prima, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam centesimo decimo octavo: itaque trigesima dies Mesori incurrit in 26 Septembris, quo æquinoctium est deprehensum, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam bisextili centesimo decimo septimo. Hoc anno Nabonassari 589, eodem die 30 Mesori, quæ incurrit in 26 Septembris, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam cætesimo decimo quarto, idé æquinoctiũ autumnale obseruauit Hipparchus, & ait incidisse in annum vigesimum tertiæ periodi Calippicæ: quod omnino verum esse ex eo intelligimus, cum annus is cœperit à solstitio, ineunte anno Olympiadico 618. {e} Hoc anno Nabonasari 590 eodé die 30 Msori, quæ respódet 25 Septembris, currete anno ante ordinationé Iulianam cætesimo decimo tertio, idé æquinoctiũ autumnale obseruauit Hipparchus, & ait incidisse in vigesimũ primũ annũ tertiæ periodi Calippicæ: quod certũ esse cõstat, siquidem annus ille iuxta Græcos incipit ab anno Olympiadico 619. {f} Hoc anno Nabonasari 601 die quarta ἐπιγινομένων seu appendicũ, quæ respódet 26 Septembris, currente anno ante ordinationé Iulianam centesimo (secundo?) decimo secundo, idem æquinoctium autumnale obseruauit Hipparchus, & ait illud incurrisse in annum trigesimum secundum tertiæ periodi Calippicæ: quod verissimum esse inde apparet, cũ annus iste 31 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ cœperit ab anno 630 Olympiadico circa solstitiũ ineunte. {g} Hoc anno Nabonasari 603, die quarta ἐπιγινομένων, quæ respódet 26 Septembris, currete anno ante ordinationem Iulianam centesimo, idem æquinoctium autumnale obseruauit Hipparchus, & ait illud incidisse in annum 34 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ: quod certum esse ex eo liquet, cũ annus iste cœperit à solstitio, ineunte anno 632 Olympiadico. {h} Hoc anno Nabonasari 605, die quarta ἐπιγινομένων, quæ respódet 26 Septembris, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam nonagesimo octauo, idem æquinoctium autumnale obseruauit Hipparchus, & ait illud incidisse in annum 36 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, quod verum esse arguit annus 634 Olympiadicus, unde secundum Græcos incipit annus 36 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ. Hæ sunt sex obseruationes Hipparchi de æquinoctio autumnali, ex quibus deprehendit annum solarem superare annum æquabilem Ægyptiorum fere sex horis.
units.tr: the sum of 575 Olympiad years arises, which clearly have elapsed before the beginning of the fourth year of the second Calippic period, that is, before Olympiad year 576. If it pleases us to compare Calippic years with years of Nabonassar, the reasoning is the same. For example, before the year Nabonassar 548, which according to the Egyptians is the fourth year of the second Calippic period, the years Nabonassar 1 to 547 have elapsed; and before the year Nabonassar 419, in which according to the Egyptians the first Calippic year falls, the years up to 418 have elapsed. If, then, 418 is subtracted from 547, 129 years remain, elapsed before the year Nabonassar 548. Thus the year Nabonassar 549 is, according to the Egyptians, the fifth year of the second Calippic period, although according to the Greeks it began at the preceding solstice, that is, in Olympiad year 577. Whoever does not weigh this comparison carefully can never have had the true sequence of Calippic years, nor dare to pronounce anything on the emendation of corrupted numbers. In the year Nabonassar 586, nearly at its end, on the thirtieth day of Mesori, Hipparchus investigated the autumnal equinox. He says that this time fell in the seventeenth year of the third Calippic period, and this is certainly true, since according to the Greeks that period begins from Olympiad year 615, at the start of the solstice, the year being 117 years before the Julian reform. The first of Thoth in Nabonassar 586 began on 3 October, a Sunday, in the year 118 before the Julian reform. So the thirtieth day of Mesori falls on 26 September, when the equinox was detected, in the leap year 117 before the Julian reform. In the year Nabonassar 589, on the same thirtieth day of Mesori, which falls on 26 September, in the year 114 before the Julian reform, Hipparchus again observed the autumnal equinox, and he says it fell in the twenty-third year of the third Calippic period. This is entirely true, as we understand from the fact that this year began at the solstice, at the start of Olympiad year 618. {e} In the year Nabonassar 590, on the same thirtieth day of Mesori, which corresponds to 25 September, in the year 113 before the Julian reform, Hipparchus again observed the autumnal equinox, and he says it fell in the twenty-first year of the third Calippic period. That this is certain is established, since that year, according to the Greeks, begins from Olympiad year 619. {f} In the year Nabonassar 601, on the fourth epagomenal day [ἐπιγινομένων], or added days, which corresponds to 26 September, in the year 112 before the Julian reform, Hipparchus again observed the autumnal equinox, and he says it fell in the thirty-second year of the third Calippic period. That this is most true is clear from the fact that this thirty-first year of the third Calippic period began from Olympiad year 630 at the start of the solstice. {g} In the year Nabonassar 603, on the fourth epagomenal day [ἐπιγινομένων], which corresponds to 26 September, in the year 100 before the Julian reform, Hipparchus again observed the autumnal equinox, and he says it fell in the thirty-fourth year of the third Calippic period. That this is certain is clear, since that year began at the solstice, at the start of Olympiad year 632. {h} In the year Nabonassar 605, on the fourth epagomenal day [ἐπιγινομένων], which corresponds to 26 September, in the year 98 before the Julian reform, Hipparchus again observed the autumnal equinox, and he says it fell in the thirty-sixth year of the third Calippic period. That this is true is shown by Olympiad year 634, whence, according to the Greeks, the thirty-sixth year of the third Calippic period begins. These are the six observations of Hipparchus on the autumnal equinox, from which he concluded that the solar year exceeds the Egyptians' equal year by about six hours.

units.la: {α} Hoc anno Nabonasari 602, qui incurrit in annum 32 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, die 17 Mechir æquinoctiû vernum obseruauit Hipparchus. Sane Thoth Nabonasari 602 incurrit in 19 Septembris, feriam tertiam, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam centesimo secundo: hinc si numerentur quinque menses Ægyptiorum, & 26 dies ex mense Mechir elapsi, peruenitur ad 2 Martij, in quo deprehensum est æquinoctium vernum, currente anno bisextili ante ordinationem Iulianam centesimo primo. Atqui ante semestre, sub finem anni Nabonasari 601, die tertia ὑπαγρμένῳ[?] Hipparchus obseruauerat æquinoctium autumnale in 16 Septembris, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam centesimo secundo: quamobrem interuallum inter ambo hæc æquinoctia fuit dierum 178. Restabant enim ex anno Nabonasari 601 duæ postremæ dies, quibus si adiiciantur dies 16 ex mense Mechir elapsi, proueniunt 18 dies[?]: hi cum quinque mensibus Ægyptiorum efficiunt summam centum & septuaginta octo dierum: qui ab anno communi constante 365 diebus subtracti, relinquunt quantitatem arcus vernalis 187 dierum.
units.tr: {α} In the year Nabonassar 602, which falls in the thirty-second year of the third Calippic period, Hipparchus observed the vernal equinox on the seventeenth day of Mechir. Now, the first of Thoth in Nabonassar 602 falls on 19 September, a Tuesday, in the year 102 before the Julian reform. Hence, if five Egyptian months and 26 days of Mechir are counted, we arrive at 2 March, on which the vernal equinox was detected, in the leap year 101 before the Julian reform. Yet half a year earlier, at the end of the year Nabonassar 601, on the third day [ὑπαγρμένῳ[?]], Hipparchus had observed the autumnal equinox on 16 September, in the year 102 before the Julian reform. So the interval between these two equinoxes was 178 days. For there remained from the year Nabonassar 601 two final days, and if 16 elapsed days of Mechir are added to them, there result 18 days; these, together with five Egyptian months, make a sum of 178 days. When this is subtracted from the common year of 365 days, there remains the length of the vernal arc, 187 days.

units.la: {β} hoc anno Nabonasari 613, die 29 Mechir, qui incurrit in annum 43 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, idem æquinoctiû vernum obseruauit Hipparchus. Thoth Nabonasari 613 cœpit 26 Septembris, feria septima, in quam incurrit æquinoctium autumnale, currente anno 91 ante ordinationem Iulianam: hinc si numerentur rentur menses quinque Ægyptij, & 28 dies elapsi, peruenitur iterum ad 23 Martij, in quo fuit æquinoctium vernum, currente anno 90 ante ordinationem Iulianam.
units.tr: {β} In the year Nabonassar 613, on the 29th day of Mechir, which falls in the forty-third year of the third Calippic period, Hipparchus observed the same vernal equinox. The first of Thoth in Nabonassar 613 began on 26 September, a Saturday, the day on which the autumnal equinox fell, in the year 91 before the Julian reform. Hence, if five Egyptian months and 28 elapsed days are counted, we arrive again at 23 March, on which the vernal equinox fell, in the year 90 before the Julian reform.

units.la: γ Hoc anno Nabonafari 620, die primo Phamenoth, qui incurrit in annum 50 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, idem æquinoctium vernum obseruauit Hipparchus. Thoth Nabonafari 620 incurrit in 24 Septembris, feriam septimam, currente anno 84 ante ordinationem Iulianam: si ergo hinc numerentur sex menses Ægyptij, desce nditur ad 23 Martij, currente anno 83 ante ordinationem Iulianam: vbi hæsit æquinoctium vernum.
units.tr: (3) In this year, Nabonassar 620, on the first day of Phamenoth, which falls in the 50th year of the third Callippic period, Hipparchus observed the vernal equinox at the same time. Thoth of Nabonassar 620 falls on 24 September, a Saturday, in the 84th year before the Julian reform. If six Egyptian months are then counted from this date, one arrives at 23 March in the 83rd year before the Julian reform, where the vernal equinox stuck fast.

units.la: Hæ sunt tres obseruationes Hipparchi de æquinoctio vernali: in quibus anni Calippici diligenter sunt annotadi. Nam primum æquinoctium vernum incidit in annum 32 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ, vt Hipparchus & Ptolemæus testatur: si-quidem is annus incipit a solstitio, ineunte anno Olympiadico 630, vt sæpius diximus: idemq; æquinoctium vernum incurrit in annum 602 Nabonafari, diem 27 Mechir: si enim ad annum Nabonafari 418 elapsum ante annum Nabonafari 419, a quo secundum Ægyptios incipit annus primus Calippicus, adiiciamus annos Calippicos 184, h.e. duas periodos Calippicas, cū an-nis 32 e tertia periodo sumtis, prodit annus Nabonafari 602, qui respondet anno 32 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ. Idem probat interuallū, quod Ptolemæus lib. 3 Almagesti, c. 1. ponit inter æquinoctiū vernū ab Hipparcho anno Nabonafari 602, die 27 Mechir obseruatum, & inter suum æquinoctium vernum anno Nabonafari 887, die 7 Pachon notatum: expresse enim ait inter ambas has obseruationes interiectos esse annos 285 solares. Eadem ratione secundū æquinoctiū vernum incidit in annum 43 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ: cum is secundum Græcos cœperit ab anno Olympiadico 641: secundum Ægyptios verò ab anno Nabonasari 613, in cuius 29 Mechir secunda vice obseruatum est æquinoctium vernum. Ita tertium æquinoctium vernum incidit in annum quinquagesimū tertiæ periodi Calippicæ: cum is secundum Græcos cœperit ab anno Olympiadico 648, secundum Ægyptios verò ab an-no Nabonasari 620, in cuius prima die Phamenoth tertia vice obseruatum est æquinoctium vernum.
units.tr: These are the three observations of Hipparchus on the vernal equinox, and the years of the Callippic cycle must be carefully noted in them. For the first vernal equinox fell in the 32nd year of the third Callippic period, as Hipparchus and Ptolemy testify, since that year begins at the solstice, at the start of the Olympic year 630, as we have said often. The same vernal equinox also falls in the 602nd year of Nabonassar, on the 27th of Mechir. For if we add 184 Callippic years to the year 418 of Nabonassar, which had elapsed before the 419th year of Nabonassar (from which, according to the Egyptians, the first Callippic year begins), that is, two Callippic periods together with the 32 years taken from the third period, we get the year 602 of Nabonassar, which corresponds to the 32nd year of the third Callippic period. The same interval is confirmed by what Ptolemy, in book 3 of the Almagest, chapter 1, gives between the vernal equinox observed by Hipparchus in the year 602 of Nabonassar, on the 27th of Mechir, and his own vernal equinox noted in the year 887 of Nabonassar, on the 7th of Pachon. For he expressly says that 285 solar years lay between these two observations. By the same reckoning, the second vernal equinox falls in the 43rd year of the third Callippic period, since according to the Greeks that period began in the Olympic year 641, and according to the Egyptians in the year 613 of Nabonassar, in whose 29th of Mechir the vernal equinox was observed a second time. Thus the third vernal equinox falls in the 53rd year of the third Callippic period, since according to the Greeks that period began in the Olympic year 648, and according to the Egyptians in the year 620 of Nabonassar, on whose first day of Phamenoth the vernal equinox was observed a third time.

units.la: Vt autem pulcherrimam istam historiam de æquinoctiis tam autumnalibus quàm vernalibus integram habeamus, & ab omni deprauatione numerorum correctam, placet hūc totum locū ex primo cap. lib. 3 Almagesti transscribere, vbi sic ait Ptolemæus:
units.tr: Now, so that we may have that most beautiful account of the equinoxes, both autumnal and vernal, complete and cleansed of every corruption of the numbers, I have decided to transcribe this whole passage from the first chapter of book 3 of the Almagest, where Ptolemy speaks thus:

units.la: Ἐκθέμενος γὰρ τὸ τῶν ἐν τῇ μεταπτώσει τῶν προτέρων σημείων, τὰς ἀκριβεῖς αὐτῶν ἀκεραίως καὶ ἐφεξῆς τηρήσεις τὰς τε χειμερινὰς καὶ θερινὰς τροπάς, ὁμολογεῖ καὶ αὐτὸς (Ἵππαρχος) μὴ πάσῃ τῶν ἐν αὐταῖς εἶναι τὸ διαφωνον, ὥστε δὲ αὐτὰς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐνιαυσίων χρόνων [?] ἀποκαταστῆναι τὰ ἐνιαυσία χρόνων. Φησὶ γὰρ αὐτὰς ὥστε· Ἐκ μὲν οὖν τούτων τῶν τηρήσεων, σμικρὰ πανταπασι γίνονται ἀφ' ὧν ἑκάστη διαφορά· ἀλλ' ὅτι μὲν τῶν προτέρων, καὶ ἐν τῇ τηρήσει, καὶ ἐν τῷ συλλογισμῷ, διαμαρτάνειν, καὶ ἕως πέντε ἡμέρας· ἀκριβῶς δὲ δυνατὸν καταφανεῖ καὶ ἄνωμαλία τῶν ἐνιαυσίων χρόνων, ἐκ τῆς τετρημένων δὲ τὰ ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ κυμένου χαλκῆ κεχωρισμένῃ ... ἐν τῇ πεντηκοστῇ ... ἡμέρας, ὡς δοκεῖ διαμεμενηκέναι τὴν ἰσημερινὴν ἡμέραν, ἐν ᾗ καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἑτέρας μέρους ἀρχὴν τὸν κόσμον ἐπιφανεῖαν φωτίζειν, εἶτα ... ἐπὶ τῆς τρίτης Κάλιππον ... τὸ μεσηλ... τὴν δύσιν τὰ ἡλίου μετὰ δὲ γ' ἐπὶ ἐν τῇ χ... ἐπὶ τὴν νεομηνίαν ... ἐπαγρυπνῶν, ὠσπερ ἐπιφανὲς ... ἀνοίας ... ἡμέ-ρας.
units.tr: For after setting out, in the transition of the earlier signs, the exact and continuous observations of the winter and summer solstices, Hipparchus himself admits that there is no discrepancy in them at all, so that the years could be restored from the solstices [Ἐκθέμενος γὰρ τὸ τῶν ἐν τῇ μεταπτώσει τῶν προτέρων σημείων, τὰς ἀκριβεῖς αὐτῶν ἀκεραίως καὶ ἐφεξῆς τηρήσεις τὰς τε χειμερινὰς καὶ θερινὰς τροπάς, ὁμολογεῖ καὶ αὐτὸς (Ἵππαρχος) μὴ πάσῃ τῶν ἐν αὐταῖς εἶναι τὸ διαφωνον, ὥστε δὲ αὐτὰς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐνιαυσίων χρόνων [?] ἀποκαταστῆναι τὰ ἐνιαυσία χρόνων. Φησὶ γὰρ αὐτὰς ὥστε· Ἐκ μὲν οὖν τούτων τῶν τηρήσεων, σμικρὰ πανταπασι γίνονται ἀφ' ὧν ἑκάστη διαφορά· ἀλλ' ὅτι μὲν τῶν προτέρων, καὶ ἐν τῇ τηρήσει, καὶ ἐν τῷ συλλογισμῷ, διαμαρτάνειν, καὶ ἕως πέντε ἡμέρας· ἀκριβῶς δὲ δυνατὸν καταφανεῖ καὶ ἄνωμαλία τῶν ἐνιαυσίων χρόνων, ἐκ τῆς τετρημένων δὲ τὰ ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ κυμένου χαλκῆ κεχωρισμένῃ ... ἐν τῇ πεντηκοστῇ ... ἡμέρας, ὡς δοκεῖ διαμεμενηκέναι τὴν ἰσημερινὴν ἡμέραν, ἐν ᾗ καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἑτέρας μέρους ἀρχὴν τὸν κόσμον ἐπιφανεῖαν φωτίζειν, εἶτα ... ἐπὶ τῆς τρίτης Κάλιππον ... τὸ μεσηλ... τὴν δύσιν τὰ ἡλίου μετὰ δὲ γ' ἐπὶ ἐν τῇ χ... ἐπὶ τὴν νεομηνίαν ... ἐπαγρυπνῶν, ὠσπερ ἐπιφανὲς ... ἀνοίας ... ἡμέ-ρας.]

units.la: [?]ἔας. μετὰ δὲ ἐνιαυτὸν ἐν τῷ κα ἐπὶ ὥρας ς, ὅπερ καὶ ἦν ἀκόλουθον τῇ ὥρᾳ αὐτῆς τυρήσει. μετὰ δὲ ια ἔτη, τῷ λβ ἐπὶ, τὴν ἐπαγρμένων εἰς τὴν δ τὴν μεσονυκτίαν, ἢ ὥσπερ τῷ δ παλιν διαπεφωνηκέναι. μετὰ δὲ ἐνιαυτὸν ἕνα, τῷ λδ ἐνιαυτοῦ τὴν γ τὴ ἐπαγρμένων, ὥσπερ ὅπερ ἦν ἀκόλουθον τῇ ὥρᾳ αὐτῆς τυρήσει. μετὰ δὲ γ ἔτη τῷ λς ἐπὶ, τὴν πτῶρτην τῆς ἐπαγρμένων, ἑκάτερα, δἰον τὴν μεσονυκτίαν, ὡς τῷ δ μόνῳ παλιν διαπεφωνηκέναι. μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ὁπὸ τῷ ὁμοίως ἀκεριβῶς πεπυρημένα, ἑαρινὰς ἰσημερίας.
units.tr: [...]ἔας. After one year, in the 21st, at the sixth hour, which also followed from the hour of its own observation. After eleven years, in the 32nd, on the third of the days that follow, near midnight, or as before it differed again. After one more year, in the 34th year, on the third of the following days, as was consistent with the hour of its own observation. After three years, in the 36th, on the fourth of the following days, at both times, that is at midnight, so that it again differed only by one day. After these, the vernal equinoxes were similarly observed inexactly [ἔας. μετὰ δὲ ἐνιαυτὸν ἐν τῷ κα ἐπὶ ὥρας ς, ὅπερ καὶ ἦν ἀκόλουθον τῇ ὥρᾳ αὐτῆς τυρήσει. μετὰ δὲ ια ἔτη, τῷ λβ ἐπὶ, τὴν ἐπαγρμένων εἰς τὴν δ τὴν μεσονυκτίαν, ἢ ὥσπερ τῷ δ παλιν διαπεφωνηκέναι. μετὰ δὲ ἐνιαυτὸν ἕνα, τῷ λδ ἐνιαυτοῦ τὴν γ τὴ ἐπαγρμένων, ὥσπερ ὅπερ ἦν ἀκόλουθον τῇ ὥρᾳ αὐτῆς τυρήσει. μετὰ δὲ γ ἔτη τῷ λς ἐπὶ, τὴν πτῶρτην τῆς ἐπαγρμένων, ἑκάτερα, δἰον τὴν μεσονυκτίαν, ὡς τῷ δ μόνῳ παλιν διαπεφωνηκέναι. μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ὁπὸ τῷ ὁμοίως ἀκεριβῶς πεπυρημένα, ἑαρινὰς ἰσημερίας.]

units.la: [?]ἐν μὲν τῷ λβ ἐπὶ τῆς τρίτης κϝ Καλίππου ᾧ εἰόδν, μεχρὶρ κξ, ὥρας, καὶ ὁ κεῖνος δὲ φησιν ὁ ἐν Αλεξανδρεία ἴσον ἐξ ἑκατέρᾳ μέρης παρηνυκόθη ὥς ἐ ὥραν, ὥσπερ ἦδη καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἰσημεία διαφόρως πεπυρημένην ἐ ὥρας ἐγίσα διενεγκῶν. καὶ τὰς ἐφεξῆς δὲ φησι μέχει τῷ λζ ἴτης συμπεφωνηκέναι τὴ ὥρας τὸ δ ἐπησία. μετὰ δὲ ια ἔτη, τῷ μ καὶ τρίτωπι, τῷ μεχρὶρ τὴ κβ, μετὰ τὸ μεσονυκτιον τὸ εἰς τὴν λ, ἥμεσθαι φησι τὴν ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅπερ καὶ ἀκόλουθον ἦν τῇ ὁ τῷ λβ ἐπὶ τυρήσι, καὶ συμφωνεῖν φησι πάλιν καὶ ὥρας τὰς ὧν πὶς ἐχομένοις ἔτσι τυρήσις, μέχει τῇ γ ἔτης. ἐγίνετο δὲ τὸ φαμενῶθ τὴ ὥρα τῇ δύσιν ἡλίω, μετὰ μίαν ἡμέραν καὶ ς καὶ δ ἐγίσα ἀπὸ τῆς ὧν τῷ μγ ἐ-πι, ὅπερ καὶ διπλασίμει πὶς μεταξὺ ζ ἔτσιν. ὁ δ᾽ ὧν ταῦταις αρα ταῖς τυρήσεσι γίγνεται πρὸς ἀξιόλογος διαφορά, καὶ πὶ διωατὰ ὄντες, ἢ μόνον ὥσπερ τὰς προπικὰς τυρήσις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥσπερ τὰς ἰσημερινὰς γίνεσθαι π παρ αὐτὰς διαμάρτημα, καὶ μέχει δ᾽ μιᾶς ἡμέραι. καὶ νῦν δὲ τῷ γ καὶ χ μόνῳ μέρει τὴ δι᾽ τὴν πόλων τὸ ἰσημερινὸς κύκλω ὥσπερ ἀλλαξίν τῆς ἀκεριβείας ἢ ἔσις, ἢ καὶ διαίρεσις τῆς ὀρᾳ-ων, τὴν ποσαύτην ἡ πλάτης ὥσπερ χώρησιν ὁ ἥλιος διορθῆται ὥσπερ τῆς ἰσημερινοῖς τμήμασι δ μιᾶς μοιρᾶς, ἡ μῆκος δὲ τὸ λο-ξῶ κύκλω κινηθεὶς, ὥστε καὶ τὴν διαφωνίαν μέχει δ μιᾶς ἡμέρας ἐγίσα διενεγκῶν.
units.tr: [...]In the 32nd year of the third Callippic period, on the 17th of Mechir, the equinox was observed in the morning, and the circle in Alexandria was illuminated equally on both sides at about the fifth hour, so that this same equinox, observed differently, was off by five hours from the nearest [ἐν μὲν τῷ λβ ἐπὶ τῆς τρίτης κϝ Καλίππου ᾧ εἰόδν, μεχρὶρ κξ, ὥρας, καὶ ὁ κεῖνος δὲ φησιν ὁ ἐν Αλεξανδρεία ἴσον ἐξ ἑκατέρᾳ μέρης παρηνυκόθη ὥς ἐ ὥραν, ὥσπερ ἦδη καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἰσημεία διαφόρως πεπυρημένην ἐ ὥρας ἐγίσα διενεγκῶν. καὶ τὰς ἐφεξῆς δὲ φησι μέχει τῷ λζ ἴτης συμπεφωνηκέναι τὴ ὥρας τὸ δ ἐπησία. μετὰ δὲ ια ἔτη, τῷ μ καὶ τρίτωπι, τῷ μεχρὶρ τὴ κβ, μετὰ τὸ μεσονυκτιον τὸ εἰς τὴν λ, ἥμεσθαι φησι τὴν ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅπερ καὶ ἀκόλουθον ἦν τῇ ὁ τῷ λβ ἐπὶ τυρήσι, καὶ συμφωνεῖν φησι πάλιν καὶ ὥρας τὰς ὧν πὶς ἐχομένοις ἔτσι τυρήσις, μέχει τῇ γ ἔτης. ἐγίνετο δὲ τὸ φαμενῶθ τὴ ὥρα τῇ δύσιν ἡλίω, μετὰ μίαν ἡμέραν καὶ ς καὶ δ ἐγίσα ἀπὸ τῆς ὧν τῷ μγ ἐ-πι, ὅπερ καὶ διπλασίμει πὶς μεταξὺ ζ ἔτσιν. ὁ δ᾽ ὧν ταῦταις αρα ταῖς τυρήσεσι γίγνεται πρὸς ἀξιόλογος διαφορά, καὶ πὶ διωατὰ ὄντες, ἢ μόνον ὥσπερ τὰς προπικὰς τυρήσις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥσπερ τὰς ἰσημερινὰς γίνεσθαι π παρ αὐτὰς διαμάρτημα, καὶ μέχει δ᾽ μιᾶς ἡμέραι. καὶ νῦν δὲ τῷ γ καὶ χ μόνῳ μέρει τὴ δι᾽ τὴν πόλων τὸ ἰσημερινὸς κύκλω ὥσπερ ἀλλαξίν τῆς ἀκεριβείας ἢ ἔσις, ἢ καὶ διαίρεσις τῆς ὀρᾳ-ων, τὴν ποσαύτην ἡ πλάτης ὥσπερ χώρησιν ὁ ἥλιος διορθῆται ὥσπερ τῆς ἰσημερινοῖς τμήμασι δ μιᾶς μοιρᾶς, ἡ μῆκος δὲ τὸ λο-ξῶ κύκλω κινηθεὶς, ὥστε καὶ τὴν διαφωνίαν μέχει δ μιᾶς ἡμέρας ἐγίσα διενεγκῶν.]

units.la: hoc est, Exponens enim primo in libro de anticipatione solstitialium & aequinoctialium punctorum, visas à se accuratè & deinceps obseruatas aestiuas & hibernas conuersiones, fatetur etiam ipse, (Hipparchus) non tantam in ipsis esse discrepantiam, vt propter illas inæqualitas aliqua cognoscatur an-nui temporis. de illis enim sic pronunciat: Ex his igitur obseruationibus manifestum est, quòd exiguæ omnino fuerint annorum differentiæ. quod ad sol-stitia attinet, non dubito quin nos & Archimedes in obseruatione, & ratiocinatione tantum quarta parte diei discrepemus. Accuratè autem poterit notari inæqualitas annuorum temporum ex obseruatis æneo circo, posito Alexandriæ, in quadrata vocata Stoa, qui videtur indicare æquinoctialem diem, qua ex vtraque parte incipit cauam superficiem illu-strare. Deinde adiicit primum autumnalium æquinoctiorum tempus, quasi accuratissimè obseruatorum in 17 anno, tertiæ secundùm Calippum perio-di, die 30 Mesori circa occasum solis. Post tres vero annos æquinoctium contigisse anno 20, neomenia ἐπιγρ[?]μένων, mane, cùm oportuisset illud accidere ipsa meridie, vt differentia fuerit quadrans vnius diei. Anno subsequenti 21 accidisse æquinoctium hora sexta, quod etiam consequens erat ad præce-dentem obseruationem. Post annos vero vndecim [?], videlicet anno trigesimo secundo, die tertia ἐπιγρ[?]μένων, quæ vergit ad diem quartam, fuisse æquinoctium media nocte, cùm oportuisset illud mane accidere, vt differentia iterum fuerit quadrans diei. Post annum vero elapsum, videlicet trigesimo quarto anno, die tertia ἐπιγρ[?]μένων, fuisse æquinoctium mane, quod etiam erat consequens ad præceden-tem obseruationem. Anno dehinc tertio, nimirum anno trigesimo sexto, die quarta ἐπιγρ[?]μένων, fuisse æquinoctium vesperi, cùm oportuisset illud incidere media nocte, vt differentia iterum fuerit quadrans diei. Post hæc similiter exponit æquinoctia verna exacte obseruata : ait enim vnum fuisse anno trigesimo secundo tertiae secundum Calippi periodi, die 17 Mechir, mane, & circus, inquit, in Alexandria aequaliter ex utraque parte illuminatus est circa quintam horam, vt etiam id ipsum aequinoctium differenter obseruatum quinque horis quàm proximè discreparit. quin etiam ait subsequentes obseruationes vsque ad annum trigesimum septimum conuenisse in quadrantis excessu. Anno vndeci-mo post, nimirum quadragesimo tertio anno, die 29 Mechir, post mediam noctem quae vergit in diem trigesimum, fuisse ait vernum aequinoctium, quod etiam consequens erat ad obseruationem factam anno trigesimo secundo, & iterum conuenisse ait hanc obseruationem cum illis, quae sequentibus annis fuerint habitae, vsq; ad quinquagesimum annum. In illo enim aequinoctium contigisse ait, die prima Phamenoth circa occasum solis, post vnam horam cum dimidia & quadrante propinquissime, ab eo quod fuerat obseruatum anno quadragesimo tertio, quem excessum etiam adiicit annis septem interiectis. In hisce igitur obseruationibus non fuit differentia alicuius momenti: quamuis fieri potuit, vt non tantum circa solstitiorum obseruationes, verum etiam circa aequinoctiales incidere potuit aliquis praeter illas errores, & vsque ad quadrantem vnius diei. Si enim tertia & sexcentesima[?] solummodo parte circuli per polos aequinoctialis transeuntis varietate accurationis situs, aut etiam diuisione instrumentorum, tantam secundum latitudinem digressionem sol corrigit iuxta aequinoctiales sectiones quadrante vnius gradus, secundum longitudinem in obliquo circulo circumuectus, vt etiam differentia quàm proximè se extendat ad qua-drātem vnius diei. Hæc Ptolemæus refert ex libro Hipparchi, quem scripserat de anni quantitate, & anticipatione punctorum solstitialium & æquinoctialium. Vbi notanda est descriptio circi Alexandrini ex ære conflati, quo Ptolemæus & Hipparchus ad observanda æquinoctia & solstitia vtebantur. Fuit is circus armilla ænea amplissimæ capacitatis, in quam ex utraque parte radius solaris immittebatur, vt altitudo centri solis meridiana deprehenderetur, quod hodie per quadrantem circuli expedimus. Collocatus fuit Alexandriæ in Stoa seu porticu quadrata, sumtibusque vt coniicere licet Ptolemæorum regum constructus: ad quem se recipiebant astronomiæ artifices e longinquis locis confluentes, vt certas æquinoctiorum ac solstitiorum observationes colligerent, ex iisq; anni quantitatem, sine qua cæteri motus cœlestes considerari nequeunt, eruerent. Hoc modo probabile est Hipparchum cum Archimede quodam, vel vt translatio Panormitana habet, cum Archimenide Rhodo Alexandriam professum esse, vt æneo circo obseruaret, sequeinpalæstra astronomica exerceret.
units.tr: That is: For Ptolemy, setting out first in his book on the anticipation of the solstitial and equinoctial points, the summer and winter turnings that Hipparchus himself observed exactly and in unbroken sequence, admits that there is no such discrepancy among them that the inequality of the year can be known from them. For he pronounces on them thus: "From these observations, therefore, it is clear that the differences among the years were altogether small. As for the solstices, I do not doubt that Archimedes and I differ from one another in observation and reasoning by only a quarter of a day. But the inequality of the seasons can be accurately noted from the observations taken with the bronze circle set up at Alexandria, in the square portico called the Stoa, which seems to show the equinoctial day, when light begins to fall on the hollow surface equally from either side. Then he adds the time of the first autumnal equinox, as observed most accurately in the 17th year of the third period according to Callippus, on the 30th of Mesori, near sunset. But after three years the equinox fell in the 20th year, on the first of the following days, in the morning, when it ought to have happened exactly at midday, so that the difference was a quarter of one day. In the following year, the 21st, the equinox happened at the sixth hour, which also agreed with the preceding observation. But after eleven years, that is in the 32nd year, on the third of the following days, which tends toward the fourth, the equinox was at midnight, when it ought to have happened in the morning, so that the difference was again a quarter of a day. But after a year had passed, that is in the 34th year, on the third of the following days, the equinox was in the morning, which also agreed with the preceding observation. After three years, in the 36th year, on the fourth of the following days, the equinox was in the evening, when it ought to have fallen at midnight, so that the difference was again a quarter of a day. After these, he similarly sets out the vernal equinoxes exactly observed. He says that one fell in the 32nd year of the third Callippic period, on the 17th of Mechir, in the morning, and he says the circle in Alexandria was illuminated equally on both sides at about the fifth hour, so that this same equinox, observed in a different way, differed by about five hours from the nearest. Indeed, he says the following observations agreed with one another up to the 37th year, in an excess of a quarter. Eleven years later, that is in the 43rd year, on the 29th of Mechir, after midnight, which tends toward the 30th day, he says there was the vernal equinox, which also followed from the observation made in the 32nd year; and he says this observation again agreed with those made in the following years, up to the 50th year. For he says the equinox fell on the first day of Phamenoth, near sunset, after one and a half hours, very nearly, from what had been observed in the 43rd year, an excess which he also adds for the seven years intervening. In these observations, therefore, there was no difference of any importance; yet it is possible that, not only in the solstice observations but also in the equinoctial ones, some errors may have occurred beyond these, up to a quarter of one day. For if the sun corrects by only a third part of six hundred of the circle passing through the poles of the equinoctial, by variation in the exactness of the position, or even by the division of the instruments, so great a departure in latitude, along the equinoctial sections, by a quarter of one degree, and in longitude, moved around the oblique circle, so that the difference may extend up to a quarter of one day. Ptolemy reports these things from the book of Hipparchus, which he had written on the quantity of the year and the anticipation of the solstitial and equinoctial points. Here the description of the Alexandrian circle cast in bronze, which Ptolemy and Hipparchus used to observe the equinoxes and solstices, deserves notice. It was a bronze ring of very large capacity, into which a ray of sunlight was admitted from either side, so that the meridian altitude of the sun's centre could be determined, which today we accomplish by means of a quadrant. It was set up at Alexandria in the square Stoa or portico, and was built, as one may conjecture, at the expense of the Ptolemaic kings. To it the astronomers came together from distant places, to gather certain observations of the equinoxes and solstices and from these to work out the length of the year, without which the other heavenly motions cannot be considered. In this way it is probable that Hipparchus went to Alexandria with a certain Archimedes, or, as the Panormitan translation has it, with Archimenides of Rhodes, to observe at the bronze circle and to exercise himself in the astronomical arena."

units.la: Has enim observationes ab Hipparcho Alexandriæ institutas esse etiam Copernicus ex Ptolemæo elicit, quando lib.3 Revolutionum cap.13 ait, Assumit enim (Ptolemæus) autumni æquinoctium, quàm accuratissimè ab illo (Hipparcho) observatum Alexandriæ, post excessum Alexandri Magni, anno CLXXVI. intercalarium diem secundum Ægyptios in media nocte, quàm sequebatur quartum intercalarium. & cap.18 inquit: Accepimus illud autumni æquinoctium, quod ab Hipparcho observatum erat Alexandriæ, tertia Calippi periodo, anno eius XXXI. qui erat a morte Alexandri Mandri[?] annus, vt supra recitatum est, centesimus feptua-gefimus septimus, post diem tertium quinq;[?] intercalarium in media nocte, quam sequebatur dies quartus. Quod autem Hipparchus ait, non tantum obseruationes, verum etiam ratiocinationem requiri ad designanda æquinoctia & solstitia; probè est notandum. Etsi enim beneficio circi æneī Hipparchus cepérit altitudinem solis meridianam; non tamen ex eo statim patuit æquinoctiorum locus, cum illis horis, quibus æquinoctium incidisse affirmat, sæpenumero non potuerit videre solem. Itaq; probabile est eū ante imminens & post elapsum æquinoctium excepisse radios folares in meridiano, & tandem adhibita ratiocinatione per tabulas sinuum & triangulorum tempus incidentium æquinoctiorum eruisse: quem modum inuestigandorum æquinoctiorum & solstitiorum etiam hodie obseruant artifices astronomiæ: de quo breuiter & perspicuè quædam tradit Nicolaus Reymarus Vrsus in fundamento astronomico. Porro in prædictis Hipparchi obseruationibus illud diligenter animadvertendum est, in annum 3 ½[?] tertiæ periodi Calippicæ incidisse ambo æquinoctia, autumnale scilicet die tertia intercalarium, & vernale die 27 Mechir obferuarum: atqui annus 3 ½[?] tertiæ periodi Calippicæ incipit ab anno Olympiadico 630 circa solstitium incunte, currente anno 102 ante ordinationem Iulianam: eodemq; anno, die 29 Septembris incidit annus Nabonafari 602, triduo post æquinoctium autumnale: unde sequitur æquinoctium autumnale, die 26 Septembris ab Hipparcho obseruatum incidisse sub finem anni Nabonafari 601. Vt cum Hipparchus dicit, æquinoctium illud autumnale fuisse die tertia [illegible, ~6 letters] necessario fit intelligendum de anno Nabonafari 601, hoc est, de anno post mortem Alexandri centesimo septuagesimo septimo, vt verissimè asserit Copernicus in duobus locis paulò ante citatis. Sequitur etiam hinc æquinoctium vernale, die 27 Mechir, hoc est, die 23 Martii, currente anno bisextili ante ordinationem Iulianam centesimo primo ab Hipparcho obseruatum incidisse in annum Nabonasari 602, b.e. in annū à morte Alexandri 178, sicut Ptolemaeus declarat: proinde cum Hipparchus scribit, æquinoctiū illud vernale labente anno 3 tertiæ periodi Calippicæ fuisse die 27 Mechir; necessariò intelligendum est de anno Nabonasari 602: etsi enim Hipparchus annorum Calippicorum initiū sumat à solstitio, mensib⁹ tamen Nabonasari vtitur. Ex quo euidens est, non posse intelligi rationem horum mensiū Ægyptiorū, nisi etiā anni Nabonasari conferantur in contextu calendarii Iuliani cū annis Calippicis siue Olympiadicis. Vt aut intelligat quomodo hæc Ptolemæus ex verbis Hipparchi allatis eliciat, age consideremus interpretationem Ptolemæi, quæ extat lib. 3 Almagesti c. 1. vbi sic ait,
units.tr: For that Hipparchus made these observations at Alexandria, Copernicus also draws from Ptolemy, when in book 3 of the Revolutions, chapter 13, he says: For Ptolemy takes the autumnal equinox, observed by Hipparchus at Alexandria as accurately as possible, in the year 176 after the departure of Alexander the Great, on the intercalary day, according to the Egyptians, at midnight, which was followed by the fourth intercalary day. And in chapter 18 he says: We have received that autumnal equinox, which was observed by Hipparchus at Alexandria in the thirty-first year of the third Callippic period, which was the year 177 from the death of Alexander, as was recited above, after the third intercalary day, at midnight, which was followed by the fourth day. That Hipparchus says that not only observations but also calculation are required to determine the equinoxes and solstices should be carefully noted. For although Hipparchus, with the help of the bronze circle, took the sun's meridian altitude, the position of the equinoxes did not become clear from this alone, since the sun often could not be seen at the very hours when he says the equinox occurred. It is therefore probable that he took the sun's rays on the meridian both before the approaching and after the passing of the equinox, and then, by applying calculation through tables of sines and triangles, worked out the time when the equinoxes fell. Astronomers even today follow this method of finding the equinoxes and solstices, on which Nicolaus Reymarus Ursus briefly and clearly gives some account in his Fundamentum astronomicum. Furthermore, in the aforesaid observations of Hipparchus we must carefully note that both equinoxes fell in the year 3½ of the third Callippic period, namely the autumnal equinox on the third intercalary day and the vernal equinox on the 27th of Mechir. Now the year 3½ of the third Callippic period begins from the Olympiad year 630, around the incoming of the solstice, in the year 102 before the Julian reform; and in that same year, on 29 September, the year 602 of Nabonassar fell, three days after the autumnal equinox. Hence it follows that the autumnal equinox observed by Hipparchus, on 26 September, fell at the end of the year 601 of Nabonassar. So when Hipparchus says that this autumnal equinox was on the third day [illegible], it must necessarily be understood of the year 601 of Nabonassar, that is, of the year 177 after the death of Alexander, as Copernicus most truly asserts in the two places cited shortly before. It also follows from this that the vernal equinox, on the 27th of Mechir, that is, on 23 March, in the hundred and first year before the Julian reform, a leap year, observed by Hipparchus, fell in the year 602 of Nabonassar, that is, in the 178th year after the death of Alexander, as Ptolemy declares. Therefore, when Hipparchus writes that this vernal equinox, in the course of the third year of the third Callippic period, was on the 27th of Mechir, it must necessarily be understood of the year 602 of Nabonassar. For although Hipparchus takes the beginning of the Callippic years from the solstice, he nevertheless uses the months of Nabonassar. From this it is evident that the reckoning of these Egyptian months cannot be understood unless the years of Nabonassar are also compared, in the context of the Julian calendar, with the Callippic or Olympiad years. But to see how Ptolemy deduces these things from the words of Hipparchus just quoted, let us consider Ptolemy's own account, which is found in book 3 of the Almagest, chapter 1, where he speaks thus:

units.tr: The confusion of the equinoctial observations, and the exactness undertaken, as the most secure things taken up by them, or the beginning of the arrangement having been indicated, but rather from those things which we find to the others... the days before the equinox ... to the day ... up to the year ... but to the month following, Hipparchus, noting it as most accurately observed, and reckoning it, says that it occurred on the eighth day at midnight...

Several words are doubtful and are marked [?].] Ἰππαρχος, ὡς ἀκριβέστατα τετηρημένην, καὶ ἐπιλογιζόμενος φησὶν αὐτὴν γενομένην τῇ η̄ τῶν ἐπαρομένων τῷ μεσονυκτίῳ, τῷ εἰς τὴν η̄ τὴν φέροντος[?]: καὶ ἔτι τὸ ἔτος ρπζ ἀπὸ τῆς Αλεξάνδρου τελευτῆς. μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ἐτῇ τῷ γ' ἔτει Αντωνίνῳ, ὃ δὴ ὑπὸ τῆς Αλεξάνδρου τελευτῆς, ἡμεῖς ἐτηρήσαμεν ἀσφαλέστατα πάλιν τὴν μετοπωρινὴν ἰσημερίαν γενομένην τῇ θ' τῆς Αθὺρ, μετὰ μίαν ὥραν ἐγγὺς τῆς τῶν ἡλίου ἀνατολῆς[?]. ἐπελάβεν ἀρα ἡ ὑποκατάστασις ἐφ' ὅλοις Αἰγυπτίοις ὅτι ἐπέσει[?], τοῦτ' ἔστι τοὺς ἀνὰ τὰς ἡμέρας τὰς πάσας ὁ χρόνος δ' καὶ χ' ἐγγὺς μιᾶς ἡμέρας, ἀντὶ τῆς κατὰ τὴν τῆς δ' ἐπισιᾶν, ἐμβαλλουσῶν τοῖς προκειμένοις ἔτεσιν ἡμερῶν οα δ'. ὥστε πρότερον γενομένη ὑποκατάστασις τῆς ὧν τὸ δ' ἐπισίας ἡμέρα α, λειπούσῃ τὸ ἡ μέρος ἐγγύς. ὡσαύτως δὲ παλινοῦμεν Ἰππαρχος φησι τὴν ἐν τῷ προκειμένῳ βῳ ἔτει, τῆς γ' ἢ κατὰ Καλίππου περιόδου, ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν ἀκριβέστατα τηρηθεῖσαν, γενομένην τῇ κζ τῶ μεχείρ[?], ὡρῶν ἀρ[?]: καὶ δὴ τὸ ἔτος τὸ ρον ἀπὸ τῆς Αλεξάνδρου τελευτῆς. ἡμεῖς δὲ τὴν μετὰ τὰ σ' ἔτη, τῷ νξ' ἀπὸ τῆς Αλεξάνδρου τελευτῆς, ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν εὑρίσκομεν γενομένην τῇ ζ' τῶ παχῶν[?], μετὰ μίαν ὥραν ἐγγὺς τῆς μεσημβρίας, ὡς καὶ ταύτην τὴν περιόδου ἐπεὶ ἀνεφέναι[?] τὰς ἴσας ἡμέρας ὁ καὶ δ' καὶ χ' ἐγγὺς, ἀντὶ τοῦ ὀφθαλμοῦ[?] ἐπιβαλλουσῶν τοῖς σ' ἔτεσιν, ἡμερῶν οα δ'. πρότερον ἄρα ἡ ταύτη γένοιτο ἂν ἡ τῆς ἐαρινῆς ἰσημερίας ὑποκατάστασις τῆς τῷ δ' ἐπισίας, ἡμέρα μία, λειπούσῃ τὸ κ' μέρος.[?]
units.tr: Hipparchus, reckoning it as most accurately observed, says that it occurred on the eighth day of the month at midnight, in the year 127 from the death of Alexander. Afterwards, in the third year of Antoninus, which was the 1st year (?) after the death of Alexander, we ourselves most securely observed the autumnal equinox again, occurring on the ninth of Athyr, about one hour after sunrise. Therefore the restoration to the same position, for all Egyptians, was that the time which elapses over all the days, about 4 and 60 [quarter-days], nearly one day, in place of the fourth-part reckoning, which adds 1 day 4 parts to the given years. So the restoration that occurred earlier was one day of the fourth-part, leaving a small part. Likewise Hipparchus says that in the year 3 of the third Callippic period, the vernal equinox, most accurately observed, occurred on the 27th of Mechir, at about the hour ...; and this was the 150th year from the death of Alexander. We, after 6 years, in the 156th year from the death of Alexander, find the vernal equinox occurred on the 7th of Pachon, about one hour before midday, so that in this period also the equal days, about 4 and 60 [quarter-days] nearly, in place of ... fall in with the six years, 1 day 4 parts. Thus the restoration of the vernal equinox would be one day earlier in the fourth-part reckoning, leaving a 20th part.

units.la: hoc est, Usi autem fumus ad propositam comparationem æquinoctiorum obseruationibus, idq; propter harum accurationem, & iis quæ ab Hipparcho maxime sunt notatæ, tanquam certissime ab ipso exploratis, & à nobis ipsis per instrumenta quam diligentissime applicata, quorum constructionem docuimus circa principiu Almagesti. Ex quibus deprehendimus in 300 quàm proximè annis una die anticipata fuisse solstitia & æquinoctia, fecundum periodum anni solaris, quæ complectitur 365 dies cum excessu quadrantis. Etenim in 31 anno tertiæ fecundum Calippum periodi, notauit maxime autumnale æquinoctium Hipparchus, tanquà accuratissimè obseruatum, &ait fe ratiocinando deprehendisse, quod inciderit in diem tertiam appendicum intercalariu, quæ vergebat in diem quartam: est autem hic annus 177 à morte Alexandri. Post annos 185, videlicet anno tertio Antonini, qui est 463 ab Alexandri obitu, nos obseruauimus certissimè iterum autumnale æquinoctium contigisse die 9 Athyr, hora vna quàm proximè post ortum solis. Accepit ergo restitutio in integris Ægyptiacis 185 annis, quatenus fingguli constant 365 diebus, præterea 70 dies, & quadrantem, & vigefimam quàm proximè partem vnius diei: cum debuisset accipere 71 dies cum quadrante, fi annis propositis fuisset integer quadrans annumerandus. Itaq; anticipauit restitutio quadrantis excessum die vno, deficiente parte 20 quàm proximè. Similiter autem rursus Hipparchus dicit, quòd in proposito 31 anno tertiæ fecundùm Calippum periodi, vernū æquinoctium accuratissimè obseruatum, inciderit die 17 Mechir, mane: est autem hic annus 178 ab Alexandri morte. Nos post 185 annos, videlicet eodem dem anno 463 à morte Alexandri, vernum æquinoctium deprehendimus fuisse,die 7 Pachon,hora vna quàm proximè post meridiem, ut etiam hæc periodus receperit æquales dies 70& quadrante,&vigesimam quàm proximè partem diei, cùm recipere debuisset dies 71 cum quadrante, si integer quadrans annis singulis 18 s fuisset annumerandus. Anticipavit ergo etiam hic vernalis æquinoctii restitutio excessum quadrantis,die vno, deficiente vigesima parte. Hic primò observandū est,in editione Græca mendū esse,cum scribitur,æquinoctiū autumnale ab Hipparcho observatum anno 32 periodi tertiæ Calippicæ, die tertia appendicum intercalatium, incidisse in annum a morte Alexandri 178; cùm is fuerit annus à morte Alexandri 177, hoc est annus Nabonasari 601 iam defituru. Neq; illud mendum quisquam interpretum Arabum & Latinorum animadvertit,aut emendare cupiuit:solus Copernicus vidit, & constanter asseruit, æquinoctium autumnale ab Hipparcho anno 32 tertiæ secundùm Calippum periodi,incidisse sub finem anni clxxxvii,post excessum Alexandri Magni,ut apparet ex duobus locis supra citatis. Quòd autè res ita habeat,evidenter monstrat interuallum inter observationem Hipparchi & Ptolemæi duplicem: nam inter æquinoctium autumnale Hipparchi & Ptolemæi intercesserunt anni Ægyptii 185, & 70 dies: quippe ex anno 177 post mortem Alexandri reliqui tantum erat duo dies:qui si adiiciantur ad duos menses Ægyptios & octo dies ex Athyrante observationem Ptolemaicā in anno 463 post mortem Alexandri elapsos, oritur summa 70 dierū,qui ab observationeHipparchi usq; ad Ptolemæi considerationem præter annos integros 28 s sunt elapsi. Quòd autem inter ambas obseruationes elapsi sint anni integri Aegyptiorum 285, hinc facile colligere licet, quòd ante obseruationem Ptolemaei absoluti fuerint anni à morte Alexandri 462, sed ante obseruationem Hipparchi adiectis tantùm duobus diebus, praeterierunt anni à morte Alexandri 177. quare si numerus minor à maiore auferatur, differentia relinquitur 185 annorum. Idem fuit interuallum inter alteram obseruationem Hipparchi & Ptolemaei de aequinoctio verno: nam Hipparchus eodem anno 32 tertiae periodi Calippicae, die 27 Mechir, currente anno à morte Alexandri 178, hoc est, anno Nabonasari 602, aequinoctium vernum obseruauit: Ptolemaeus autem id deprehendit eodem anno 463 à morte Alexandri, hoc est, anno Nabonasari 887, die 7 Pachon. Sane à 27 Mechir inclusiue sumta, vsque ad 7 Pachon exclusiue summam sunt 70 dies: qui praeter annos integros 185 Aegyptiorum sunt elapsi. Hoc interuallum certissimum est, licet obscuris verbis à Ptolemaeo declaretur: quod enim ille ait, Accepit ergo restitutio in integris Aegyptiacis 185 annis, quatenus singuli constant 365 diebus, praeterea 70 dies, &c. idem est ac si dixisset, interuallum inter ambas obseruationes fuisse 185 annorum Aegyptiorum, & 70 dicrum: nam per restitutionem siue ἀποκατάστασιν [?] interuallum indicat, quasi velit dicere, interuallum habere praeter 185 annos Aegyptios, insuper 70 dies. Cùm autem praecisius ipsum interuallum iupputat, quòd praeter 70 dies habeat quadrantem diei, hoc est, sex horas, & vigesimam ferè partem vnius diei, illi propositum est elicere anni quantitatem, & ostendere eam paulo minorem esse quadrante diei cum diebus: quod ex anticipatione ostendit. Si enim annus exactissime contineret 365 dies, cum integro quadrante diei: tunc vtique interuallum inter ambas obseruationes fuisset 28 annorum Aegyptiorum, & 71 dierum, cum quadrante diei: atqui ex certissimis illis obseruationibus constat, interuallum fuisse 28 annorum Aegyptiorum, & 70 tantum dierum, cum quadrante diei, & vigesima parte diei. Vbi regula generalis obseruanda est, omnem anticipationem indicare periodum maiorem esse vel poni, quàm esse seu poni debebat. Sic in anni Iuliani ordinatione Caesar anni quantitatem constituit 365 dierum, & quadrantis, hoc est, sex horarum, quas quater repetitas bisextum efficere credidit: sed aequinoctiorum & solstitiorum anticipationes, quae ab ordinatione Iuliana vsque ad nostra tempora duodecim diebus in anteriora prolapsae sunt, satis indicant, anni quantitatem a Iulio Caesare definitam iusto maiore esse, vt ei non exacte respondeat τροπικῶν ὑπὸ καταστάσεως [?] solis. Ita enneadecaeteridem Iulius Caesar posuit absolui annis 19 Iulianis: sed obseruationes quouis seculo docuerunt, lunam non redire praecise ad eundem locum post annos nouemdecim elapsos Iulianos seu solares, quatenus singuli intelligantur constare 365 diebus, cum integro quadrante: quin immo deprehensum est, annis 247 solaribus elapsis lunam diem vnam anticipare: ex quo intelligitur enneadecaeteridem vulgarem, quatenus completi censetur 6940 dies, iusto maiorem esse. Ptolemaeus itaque ex suis & Hipparchi obseruationibus ostendit annum tropicum constare 365 diebus, & quadrante, cui deest pars 3 0 0 diei. Illius verba & mente dilucide exponit Regiomontanus in epitome Almagesti, lib. 3. propositione 2, cum ait: Interuallum aute inter ambas obseruationes fuit 28ʃ [?] anni Ægy-ptii, 70 dies, & quarta, & vicesima diei. Quia itaq; in hoc intervallo fuerunt 28ʃ [?] reuolutiones solis, & sic annus constitutus ex 36ʃ [?] diebus, & quarta vnius, oportuit ipsum interuallum fuisse 28 anni Ægyptii, 71 dies, & quarta vnius: sed non fuit interuallum nisi 185 [?] anni, 70 dies, 7 horæ, & quinta vnius. Ergo minor quantitas anni est 365 diebus, & sex horis. Differentia vero inter hæc interualla est 23 horæ, & quatuor quintæ vnius, quæ sunt 19 vicesimæ vnius diei. Proportio autem 19 ad 20 est velut 28 anno-rum ad 300 annos: quare coclusit Ptolemæus quòd in 300 annis solaribus deficiat vnus dies à numero dierum quæ facerent 300 anni, si annus ex 365 diebus & quarta vnius constaret: ideoq; veram anni quantitatem colligare dicebat ex 365 diebus, & quarta vnius, minus 300 parte diei. Hactenus de obseruationis æquinoctiorum. Hic autem duæ sunt considerandæ eclipses, quarum prior contigit anno septimo Ptolemæi Philometoris, hoc est, anno Nabonasari quingente-simo septuagesimo quarto, die 27 Phamenoth: altera fuit anno 37 tertiæ secundum Calippum periodi, anno scilicet Nabonasari 607, die secunda Tybi, vt refert Ptolemæus lib. 6 Almagesti, cap. 5. Si annus septimus Philometoris fuit 574 Nabonasari, constat initium Philometoris incurrisse in annum Nabonasari 568, hoc est, in annum Olympiadicum 596, vel in annum quartum Olympiadis 149: quamuis Eusebius Cæsariensis referat initium Philometoris in annum primum Olympiadis 150. Regiomontanus in epitome Almagesti lib. 6, propositione 6, Philometorem ex translatione Arabum vocat Naboth: mendum tamen est in illius codice, fuisse annum octauum Naboth, hoc est, Philometoris, asserente; cum prior contingeret eclipsis, anno scilicet 574 Nabonasari, die 27 Phamenoth: Ptolemaeus enim dicit eum annum fuisse septimum Philometoris, ita etiam omnia alia habent exemplaria. Sane annus Nabonasari 574 incurrit in 6 Octobris, feria tertia, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 130. Hinc si numeren ur sex menses Aegyptii, & 26 dies, ex Phamenoth elapsi, hoc est in universum 206 dies, descendicur ad 29 Aprilis, currente anno bisextili ante ordinationem Iulianam 129, quo aureus numerus fuit V, qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 17 kal. Maii: ubi novilunium ostendit sub fine 16 diei Aprilis: ergo die decimo quinto post, sub fine scilicet diei 19 Aprilis oppositio fuit luminarium, in qua observata est eclipsis lunae, sole tenente textum gradum Tauri, luna vero occupante textum gradum Scorpii, ut ibidem recenset Ptolemaeus. Altera eclipsis contigit anno Nabonasari 607, die secunda Tybi.
units.tr: That is, we have used, for the proposed comparison of the equinoxes, the observations that are most exact, and especially those that Hipparchus noted most carefully and that are regarded as most certainly established by him, and which we ourselves have applied with the greatest diligence by means of instruments, the construction of which we explained at the beginning of the Almagest. From these we have found that, in about 300 years, the solstices and equinoxes had been anticipated by one day, according to the period of the solar year, which contains 365 days with an excess of a quarter of a day. For in the 31st year of the third Calippic period, Hipparchus noted the autumnal equinox as observed with the greatest accuracy, and he says that by calculation he found that it fell on the third day of the intercalary days, which was tending toward the fourth day. This year is the 177th from the death of Alexander. After 185 years, namely in the third year of Antoninus, which is the 463rd from the death of Alexander, we have observed with the greatest certainty that the autumnal equinox again occurred on the 9th of Athyr, about one hour after sunrise. The restitution [ἀποκατάστασιν] therefore received, in the 185 Egyptian years, each of which has 365 days, an additional 70 days, a quarter of a day, and very nearly a twentieth part of a day. Yet it ought to have received 71 days with a quarter, if a whole quarter day had been added for each of the years in question. So the restitution anticipated the excess of a quarter by one day, falling short by very nearly a twentieth part. Likewise, Hipparchus again says that in the same 31st year of the third Calippic period, the vernal equinox, observed with the greatest accuracy, fell on the 17th of Mechir, in the morning. This year is the 178th from the death of Alexander. We, after 185 years, namely in the same year, the 463rd from the death of Alexander, found the vernal equinox to have occurred on the 7th of Pachon, about one hour after noon. So this period also received 70 and a quarter days, and very nearly a twentieth part of a day, whereas it ought to have received 71 days with a quarter, if a whole quarter for each of the 185 years had been added. The restitution of the vernal equinox therefore also anticipated the excess of a quarter by one day, falling short by a twentieth part. Here it must first be observed that there is an error in the Greek edition, where it is written that the autumnal equinox observed by Hipparchus in the 32nd year of the third Calippic period, on the third day of the intercalary days, fell in the 178th year from the death of Alexander; whereas that was the 177th year from the death of Alexander, that is, the 601st year of Nabonassar, which was about to end. No interpreter, Arab or Latin, has noticed this error or wished to correct it. Only Copernicus saw it and consistently asserted that the autumnal equinox observed by Hipparchus in the 32nd year of the third Calippic period fell near the end of the 187th year after the death of Alexander the Great, as appears from the two passages cited above. That this is so is clearly shown by the double interval between the observations of Hipparchus and Ptolemy. For between the autumnal equinox of Hipparchus and that of Ptolemy there intervened 185 Egyptian years and 70 days. Indeed, from the 177th year after the death of Alexander only two days remained. If these are added to the two Egyptian months and eight days elapsed from Athyr to the Ptolemaic observation in the 463rd year after the death of Alexander, the sum is 70 days, which elapsed from Hipparchus's observation until Ptolemy's consideration, beyond 285 whole years. That whole Egyptian years, 285 in number, elapsed between the two observations can easily be inferred from this: before Ptolemy's observation, 462 years from the death of Alexander had been completed, but before Hipparchus's observation, with only two days added, 177 years from the death of Alexander had passed. So if the smaller number is subtracted from the larger, the difference left is 185 years. The same interval lay between the second observation of Hipparchus and that of Ptolemy concerning the vernal equinox. For Hipparchus observed the vernal equinox in the same 32nd year of the third Calippic period, on the 27th of Mechir, the year being the 178th from the death of Alexander, that is, the 602nd year of Nabonassar. Ptolemy, however, found it in the same 463rd year from the death of Alexander, that is, the 887th year of Nabonassar, on the 7th of Pachon. Indeed, if one counts from the 27th of Mechir inclusive up to the 7th of Pachon exclusive, the sum is 70 days, which elapsed beyond 185 whole Egyptian years. This interval is most certain, although Ptolemy states it in obscure words. For when he says: "The restitution therefore received, in 185 whole Egyptian years, each of which has 365 days, an additional 70 days, etc.," it is the same as if he had said that the interval between the two observations was 185 Egyptian years and 70 days. For by "restitution" [ἀποκατάστασιν] he indicates the interval, as if he wished to say that the interval consists of 185 Egyptian years and, over and above that, 70 days. But when he reckons the interval more precisely, saying that besides the 70 days it has a quarter of a day, that is six hours, and very nearly a twentieth part of a day, he purposes to elicit the quantity of the year and to show that it is a little less than a quarter day beyond the full days, which he shows from the anticipation. For if the year contained exactly 365 days with a full quarter day, then the interval between the two observations would have been 28 Egyptian years and 71 days with a quarter day. But from those most certain observations it is established that the interval was 28 Egyptian years and only 70 days, with a quarter day and a twentieth part of a day. Here a general rule must be observed: every anticipation indicates that the period is taken, or set, as greater than it ought to be or to be set. Thus in the arrangement of the Julian year, Caesar fixed the length of the year at 365 days and a quarter, that is six hours, which he believed, when repeated four times, made a leap year. But the anticipations of the equinoxes and solstices, which since the Julian arrangement down to our own times have slipped backward by twelve days, sufficiently show that the length of the year defined by Julius Caesar is too great by a little, so that it does not exactly correspond to the tropical [τροπικῶν] station of the sun [ὑπὸ καταστάσεως]. So Julius Caesar posited that the nineteen-year cycle is completed in 19 Julian years. But observations in every century have taught that the moon does not return precisely to the same place after nineteen elapsed Julian or solar years, taking each year to consist of 365 days with a full quarter. Indeed, it has been found that after 247 solar years the moon anticipates by one day. From this it is understood that the common nineteen-year cycle, in which 6940 days are reckoned as completed, is too great by a little. Ptolemy therefore, from his own and Hipparchus's observations, shows that the tropical year consists of 365 days and a quarter, from which is lacking a part of 1/300 of a day. Regiomontanus, in his epitome of the Almagest, book 3, proposition 2, clearly sets out both his words and his meaning, when he says: "The interval between the two observations was 28 Egyptian years, 70 days, and a quarter and a twentieth of a day. Since, therefore, in this interval there were 28 revolutions of the sun, and thus the year was constituted of 365 days and a quarter of one day, the interval itself ought to have been 28 Egyptian years, 71 days, and a quarter of one day; but the interval was only 185 years, 70 days, 7 hours, and a fifth of one day." Therefore the smaller quantity of the year is 365 days and six hours. The difference between these intervals is 23 hours and four fifths of one hour, which are 19 twentieths of one day. Now 19 is to 20 as 28 years is to 300 years. Therefore Ptolemy concluded that in 300 solar years one day is lacking from the number of days that 300 years would make if the year consisted of 365 days and a quarter of one day; and so he said that the true length of the year is to be gathered as 365 days and a quarter of one day, minus a 300th part of a day. So far concerning the observation of the equinoxes. Here, however, two eclipses are to be considered. The first occurred in the seventh year of Ptolemy Philometor, that is, in the 574th year of Nabonassar, on the 27th of Phamenoth. The other was in the 37th year of the third Calippic period, namely in the 607th year of Nabonassar, on the second of Tybi, as Ptolemy reports in book 6 of the Almagest, chapter 5. If the seventh year of Philometor was the 574th of Nabonassar, it is established that the beginning of Philometor fell in the 568th year of Nabonassar, that is, in the 596th year of the Olympiads, or in the fourth year of the 149th Olympiad, although Eusebius of Caesarea reports the beginning of Philometor as falling in the first year of the 150th Olympiad. Regiomontanus, in his epitome of the Almagest, book 6, proposition 6, calls Philometor "Naboth" on the authority of the Arab translation. There is, however, an error in his manuscript, which asserts that it was the eighth year of Naboth, that is, of Philometor, when the first eclipse occurred, namely in the 574th year of Nabonassar, on the 27th of Phamenoth. For Ptolemy says that it was the seventh year of Philometor, and all the other copies have the same. Indeed, the year 574 of Nabonassar falls on 6 October, a Tuesday, in the year before the Julian arrangement, which was the 130th. Hence, if six Egyptian months and 26 days are counted from Phamenoth, that is 206 days in all, we come down to 29 April, in the leap year before the Julian arrangement, the 129th, in which the golden number was V, which in the Julian calendar is placed at 17 days before the Kalends of May. There the new moon is shown near the end of the 16th day of April. Therefore on the fifteenth day after it, that is, near the end of 19 April, there was an opposition of the luminaries, in which a lunar eclipse was observed, the sun occupying the tenth degree of Taurus and the moon occupying the tenth degree of Scorpio, as Ptolemy recounts in the same place. The other eclipse occurred in the 607th year of Nabonassar, on the second of Tybi.

units.la: Atqui Thoth Nabonasari 607 coepit 17 Septembris, feria prima, currente anno bisextili ante ordinationem Iulianam nonagesimo septimo, numero aureo existente XVIII, & literis dominicalibus signatis ED: si ergo hinc numerentur quatuor menses Aegyptii, & unus dies ex Tybi elapsus, hoc est, in universum 121 dies, perveniitur ad 26 Ianuarii, currente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 96, quando confecta est eclipsis in oppositione luminarium: itaq; die decimo quinto ante, videlicet die 13 Ianuarii fuit novilunium: quod etiam ostendit ennea decaeteris Iuliana. Anno enim nonagesimo sexto ante ordinationem Iulianam numerus aureus assignatur XIX, qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad Idus Ianuarias, hoc est, ad 13 diem Ianuarii, in quo fuit coniunctio luminarium: itaq; die decimo quinto post, hoc est, 27 Ianuarii fuit eclipsis lunæ, sole occupante quintu gradu Aquarii, luna vero tenente quintum gradum Leonis, vt ibidem testatur Ptolemæus. Hæc eclipsis diligentissime obseruanda est, quia proxima fuit ordinationi Iulianæ, vt ex ea certissime elici possit epocha solis & lunæ ineunte anno primo Iuliano: si enim die 27 Ianuarii, currente anno 96 ante ordinationem, sol tenuit quintu gradum Aquarii, vt iq; die 25 Ianuarii obtinuit primum gradum Aquarii & fine Capricorni: vnde sequitur calendas Ianuarii anni 96 ante ordinationem Iulianam ineuntis incurrisse in octauum gradum Capricorni: ex quo iterum hoc manifestum est, kalendas quoq; primas Iulianas incidisse in gradum octauum Capricorni, quia per annos 96 non potuit anticipatio solaris a-scenderead[?] diem vnum: sequitur etiam hinc anno primo ante ordinationem Iulianam brumam fuisse in 27 Decembris, sole adeunte principium Capricorni, sicut rectissime persuaserat Iulio Cæsari Sosigenes mathematicus: vnde etiam à nobis creditur, sub natiuitatem Christi, currente anno 4 s Iuliano brumam hæsisse in 25 & 24 Decembris. Hæc qui ignorat, nunquam annorum Iulianorum cum annis Nabonasari connexionem cernere potest. Anni ante ord. Iul. | Aureus num. | An. Olympiadici. | An. units.tr: Yet Thoth of Nabonassar 607 began on 17 September, a Sunday (feria prima), in a bissextile year, the ninety-seventh before the Julian reform, with golden number 18 and dominical letters ED. If we count from there four Egyptian months and one elapsed day of Tybi, that is 121 days in all, which brings us to 26 January in the year 96 before the Julian reform, when the eclipse occurred at the opposition of the luminaries. Therefore fifteen days earlier, that is 13 January, there was a new moon. The Julian nineteen-year cycle (ennea decaeteris) also shows this. In the year 96 before the Julian reform the golden number is given as 19, and in the Julian calendar it is placed at the Ides of January, that is, on 13 January, when the luminaries were in conjunction. Therefore fifteen days later, that is 27 January, there was a lunar eclipse, with the sun occupying the fifth degree of Aquarius and the moon the fifth degree of Leo, as Ptolemy testifies in the same place. This eclipse must be observed with the greatest care, because it was the nearest to the Julian reform, so that from it the epoch of the sun and moon at the beginning of the first Julian year can be most certainly drawn out. For if on 27 January, in the year 96 before the reform, the sun held the fifth degree of Aquarius, then on 25 January it was at the first degree of Aquarius and the end of Capricorn. From this it follows that the first day of January in the year 96 before the Julian reform fell on the eighth degree of Capricorn. From this again it is clear that the first Julian calendar day also fell on the eighth degree of Capricorn, since over 96 years the solar anticipation could not have advanced by one day. It follows also that in the first year before the Julian reform the winter solstice was on 27 December, when the sun entered the beginning of Capricorn, as the mathematician Sosigenes most correctly persuaded Julius Caesar. Hence we also believe that around the birth of Christ, in the year 4 of the Julian reckoning, the solstice fell on 25 and 24 December. Whoever does not know this can never perceive the connection between the Julian years and the years of Nabonassar.
