units.la: {*}Ab hoc anno Nabonasari 647 secundū Ægyptios incipit quarta periodus Calippica, quæ secundum Græcos initium habet à præcedenti solstitio, hoc est ab anno Olympiadico 675,qui incurrit in annum quinquagesimum septimū ante o dinationem Iulianam: ex quo concluditur annum primum Iulianum incurrisse in annum quinquagesimum octa-uum quartæ periodi Calippicæ, cuius initium sumebatur secundum Græcos ab anno 731 Olympiadico à solstitio ineunte, labente anno primo ante ordinationem Iulianam. Verum hic obiter sciendum est, periodos Calippicas finem habuisse post introductos annos Iulianos: non enim in historicis legimus eas post institutam enneadecaeteridem Iulianam amplius in usu fuisse: cum ex Dione & Xiphilino appareat Iulium Cæsarem ab astronomis Alexandrinis accepisse rationem anni solaris figendi, vt quarto quoque anno bissextum intercalaretur, & enneadecaeteridis principium sumeretur à primis kalendis Iulianis: quam rationem deinceps usque ad concilium Nicænum constanter observatam esse, fidem faciunt auctores grauissimi.
units.tr: From this year, Nabonassar 647, according to the Egyptians, the fourth Callippic period begins. According to the Greeks it begins at the preceding solstice, that is, in Olympiad year 675, which falls in the fifty-seventh year before the Julian reform. From this it follows that the first Julian year fell in the fifty-eighth year of the fourth Callippic period. The Greeks took its beginning from Olympiad year 731, at the solstice that opens the year, the first year before the Julian reform having already lapsed. But here it must be noted in passing that the Callippic periods ceased to be used after the Julian years were introduced. We do not read in the historians that they remained in use once the Julian nineteen-year cycle had been instituted. For from Dio and Xiphilinus it appears that Julius Caesar received from the Alexandrian astronomers the method of fixing the solar year, so that a leap year was intercalated every fourth year, and the nineteen-year cycle was counted from the first Julian kalends. Reliable authors bear witness that this method was steadily observed from then until the Council of Nicaea.

units.la: {b}Hunc autem Olympiadicum septingentesimum vndecimum recte coniungit Copernicus cum anno Nabonasari 683, seu cum anno a morte Alexandri 259, vt videre licet lib. 3 Reuoluti-onum capite 22. Thoth quidem Nabonasari 683 cœpit 8 Septembris, feria septima, currente anno bissextili, & vigesimo primo ante ordinationem Iulianam: sed annus 711 Olympiadicus, hoc est, annus tertius Olympiadis CLXXVIII, exorius est à præcedente solstitio. Vnde apparet Copernicum in applicatione annorum Olympiadicorum ad annos Nabonasari lapsum esse, quando lib. 3. Reuolutionum cap. 11. scripsit,à prima Olympiade ineunte à meridie primæ diei mensis Hecatombæonis Græcorum, ad Nabo-nafarū ac meridiem primæ diei mensis Thoth, fecundum Ægyptios elaplos fuisse annos viginti septe, & dies 147:cum debuisset dicere,elapsos fuisse annos Ægyptios viginti octo,& 247 dies.nos enim in principio tabularum nostrarum chronologicarum demonstrauimus, vrbem conditam esse ineunte vere atq; æquinoctio verno,sub finem anni vigefimi tertii Olympiadici, hocefst, sub finem anni tertii sextæ Olympiadis labentis, quod cuidenter apparet ex Cenforino,Eutropio,Onufrio, & aliis fide dignißimis historicis. Sed error Copernico obrepere potuit,quia nö expendit in vnum annü solare, si bisextilis sit, incidere posse duo principia annorū Nabonafari: quod nos supra demonstrauimus de anno 477 ante ordinationem Iulianam.Hoc autem loco ex Hipparchicis obseruationibus colligit Copernicus locum apogæi solis fuisse in 5 ½[?] gradu Geminorū, hoc est, ab æquinoctio verno grad.1 x v.s.quæanno Christi M.D.x vi deprehendit in 6 gradu,& duab.tertiis Cancri: ex qua collatione multa alia ad motus cœlestes spectatia eruit[?]
units.tr: Copernicus rightly links this Olympiad year 711 with Nabonassar 683, or with year 259 from the death of Alexander, as may be seen in book 3 of the Revolutions, chapter 22. Thoth of Nabonassar 683 began on 8 September, a Saturday, in a leap year and in the twenty-first year before the Julian reform. But Olympiad year 711, that is, the third year of Olympiad 178, arose from the preceding solstice. Hence it is clear that Copernicus slipped in applying the Olympiad years to the years of Nabonassar. In book 3 of the Revolutions, chapter 11, he wrote that from the beginning of the first Olympiad, from noon on the first day of the Greek month Hecatombaeon, to Nabonassar, that is, noon on the first day of the Egyptian month Thoth, there had elapsed twenty-seven years and 147 days. He should have said twenty-eight Egyptian years and 247 days. For at the beginning of our chronological tables we demonstrated that the city was founded at the beginning of spring, at the vernal equinox, toward the end of the twenty-third year of the Olympiad, that is, toward the end of the third year of the sixth Olympiad that had passed. This clearly appears from Censorinus, Eutropius, Onuphrius and other most trustworthy historians. But the error could creep into Copernicus because he did not consider that, if a solar year is a leap year, two beginnings of the Nabonassar years can fall within it. We demonstrated this above concerning the year 477 before the Julian reform. Here, from Hipparchus's observations, Copernicus gathers that the apogee of the sun lay at 5½ degrees of Gemini, that is, 1 degree 15 minutes from the vernal equinox. In the year of Christ 1516 he found it at 6⅔ degrees of Cancer. From this comparison he draws out many other points bearing on the heavenly motions.

units.la: Hoc anno fecundo ante ordinationem Iulianam,die 14 Octobris iniit annus Confusionis, qui teste Cenforino habuit 445 dies: locum enim habuit eo anno ordinaria intercalatio Mercedonii viginti trium dierum,praeter quos Iulius Cæsar adiecit 67 dies, vt in vniuersum annus Confusionis completeretur dies intercalares 90, qui conficiunt tres menses Ægyptiorum: vt recte dictum fit a Suetonio, annum Confusionis habuisse quindecim menses. Itaque kal. Ianuariæ anni lunaris a Numa Pompilio introducti occuparunt diem 14 Octobris, las[?] [?]bente anno ante ordinationem Iulianam 1, sub initium anni Confusionis: hinc si numerentur 29[?] dies, quot sunt in Ianuario lunari, peruenitur ad 12 Nouembris, vbi locum habent kalend. Februarii lunaris, cuius dies 23, hoc est dies Terminaliorum incurrit in 4 Decembris, post quem intercalatus fuit Mercedonius impar 23 dierum, teste Cenforino, qui desiit in 27 Decembris: hinc si adhuc quinque dies numerentur, qui absoluunt Februarium lunarem per intercalationem abruptum, descenditur ad kalend. Ianuarias ineuntis anni primi ante ordinationem Iulianam, in quibus desiit Februarius lunaris. Ergo kalend. Martiae lunares in anno Confusionis inciderunt in secundam Ianuarii diem, labente anno primo ante ordinationem Iulianam. A kalend. Martiis lunaribus usque ad exitum Nouembris lunaris computantur 269 dies, qui desinunt in 27 Septembris: hinc sequuntur 67 dies, quos Caesar peculiari ratione inter Nouembre & Decembrem menses lunares intercalauit, teste Cenforino. Si igitur ad 27 Septebris, adiciantur dies intercalarii Iulii Caesaris 67, peruenit ad tertiu Decebris, quo init Deceber lunaris: iscum habuerit 29 dies, desiit in 31 Decebris. Haec fuit anni Confusionis dispositio: quam nullo modo intelligere possumus, nisi fingam{9} annos ante ordinationem Iulianam praecedetes solares fuisse, & secundum meses Iulianos decurrisse. Sed hic operaepreciu est considerare, quamobre Caesar in anno Confusionis post ordinariam Mercedonii intercalationem voluerit praeterea intercalare 67 dies. Vidit Caesar post oi dinaria Mercedonii intercalationem, kalend. Martias lunares post ie reliquisse duobus mensibus Ægyptiacis fede[?] æquinoctii verni, in quod merito incidere debuif-fent, iuxta tempus fundationis Vrbis a Romulo defignatum:idcirco adiecit 60 dies,vt Marriu·n cum præ-cedente Mercedonio retraheret ad locu naturalem, quo iusto interuallo abesset a bruma subsequenti. At quia Cæsar non præcise ab ipsa bruma, hoc est, ingrediIu iolis in Capricornum, qui contingebat die 1 Decembris, currente anno primo ante ordinationem Iulianam, ded ab octauo demum die subsequente, in quem noui unium incurrit, voluit epocham suam exordiri, præterea adiecit 7 dies: quiad 60 priores additi, summam intercalationis Iulianæ efficiunt 67 dierum. Quæ vtrecitius intelligantur, cogitetur, Cæsarem intercalalle iuos 67 dies post finem Decembris lunaris, ita vt posit 27 Septembris, currente anno primo ante ordinationem Iulianam, fingatur statim subsecutus fuisse December lunaris, qui desierit in 16 Octobris, labente anno eodem primo ante ordinationem Iulianam: itaq; a 27 Octobris, kal. Ianuarij lunares iterum fuissent inchoandi; sed animaduertit Cæsar hac ratione kal. Ianuarias lunares anticipaturas brumam 60 diebus, & præcedentes ante nouilunium a bruma proximum diebus 67: quare coactus est inserere 67 dies, quo kal. suas primas Ianuarias figeret in nouilunio proximo brumæ, quod incurrebat in mediam noctem, ineunte secundum Romanos die octauo post brumam. Hinc colligitur annum confusionis definentem 31 Decembris incurrisse in diem septimum a bruma: ordinationem vero ipsam annorum & mensium Iulianorum incurrisse in diem octauum post brumam, hoc est in octauum gradum Capri-corni. units.tr: In the second year before the Julian reform, on 14 October, the Year of Confusion began. According to Censorinus it had 445 days. In that year the ordinary intercalation of Mercedonius, of twenty-three days, took place, and in addition Julius Caesar inserted 67 days, so that the Year of Confusion as a whole came to 90 intercalary days, which make up the three months of the Egyptians. Hence Suetonius rightly says that the Year of Confusion had fifteen months. Thus the kalends of January of the lunar year introduced by Numa Pompilius fell on 14 October, at the beginning of the Year of Confusion, while the first year before the Julian reform was running out. If we count forward 29 days, the number of days in lunar January, we arrive at 12 November, where the kalends of lunar February fall, and this has 23 days. That is the day of the Terminalia, and it falls on 4 December. After it, according to Censorinus, Mercedonius was intercalated, an odd month of 23 days, which ended on 27 December. If five more days are now counted, which complete the lunar February cut short by the intercalation, we come down to the kalends of January at the start of the first year before the Julian reform, on which lunar February ended. Therefore the lunar kalends of March in the Year of Confusion fell on the second day of January, while the first year before the Julian reform was running out. From the lunar kalends of March to the end of lunar November there are counted 269 days, which end on 27 September. Then follow the 67 days which Caesar, for a special reason, intercalated between the months of November and December, according to Censorinus. So if the 67 intercalary days of Julius Caesar are added to 27 September, we arrive at 3 December, on which lunar December begins. Since it had 29 days, it ended on 31 December. This was the arrangement of the Year of Confusion, which we cannot understand at all unless I suppose that the years before the Julian reform were solar and ran according to the Julian months. But here it is worth considering why Caesar, in the Year of Confusion, after the ordinary intercalation of Mercedonius, wished to intercalate a further 67 days. Caesar saw that, after the ordinary intercalation of Mercedonius, the lunar kalends of March had fallen back two Egyptian months from the spring equinox, on which they ought rightly to have fallen according to the time of the founding of the City designated by Romulus. He therefore added 60 days, so that by means of them, together with the preceding Mercedonius, he might bring March back to its natural place, from which it would be at the proper interval from the following winter solstice. But because Caesar wished to begin his epoch not exactly at the winter solstice itself, that is, at the sun's entry into Capricorn, which fell on 1 December in the first year before the Julian reform, but only from the eighth day after it, on which the new moon fell, he added 7 more days. These, added to the earlier 60, make the total of the Julian intercalation, 67 days. To understand this more clearly, let us imagine that Caesar intercalated his 67 days after the end of lunar December, so that after 27 September in the first year before the Julian reform, lunar December immediately followed, ending on 16 October in that same first year before the Julian reform. Then from 27 October the lunar kalends of January would again have had to begin. But Caesar noticed that in this way the lunar kalends of January would anticipate the winter solstice by 60 days, and the preceding months would fall short of the new moon nearest the solstice by 67 days. He was therefore compelled to insert 67 days, so that he might fix his first kalends of January at the new moon nearest the solstice, which fell at midnight on the eighth day after the solstice, reckoned in the Roman manner. From this it is gathered that the Year of Confusion, ending on 31 December, fell on the seventh day after the solstice, while the very beginning of the Julian years and months fell on the eighth day after the solstice, that is, on the eighth degree of Capricorn.

units.la: * Hic est annus primus ordinationis Iulianæ, in quem à solstitio incurrit annus Olympiadicus septin-gentesimus trigesimus secundus, ab æquinoctio autem verno incidit annus Vrbis conditæ septingentesimus nonus; at 3 Septembris, feria septima incipit annus Nabonasari septingentesimus quartus. De quibus omnibus prolixè dictum est in calendario Iuliano.
units.tr: This is the first year of the Julian ordination. From the solstice it falls in the 732nd year of the Olympiads, and from the spring equinox in the 709th year from the founding of the City. But on 3 September, a Saturday, begins the 704th year of Nabonassar. All of these matters were treated at length in the Julian calendar.

units.la: Porrò vt certius nobis constet de epocha Iuliana ab editione calendarij Romani, quod etiam num in vsu est, sciendum est, eam incurrisse in annum Nabonasari 705, inquè meridie primum Tybi, feriâ septimam: Thoth enim Nabonasari 705 incidit in 3 Septembris, feriam sextam, currente anno primo ante ordinationem Iulianam: inde si numeremus quatuor menses Ægyptios, perueniemus ad primâ Tybi, feriam septimam, in qua fuerunt kal. primæ Iulianæ. Iosephus Scaliger de emendatione temporum pag. 231, ait, Proinde kal. Ianuarij Iuliani inciderunt in annum Nabonasari currentem 705. Cuius neomenia Thoth fuit IIII Septembris, feria VI. Itaq; à meridie Nabonasari ad primam kal. Iulianas. Iulianas, anni sunt Aegyptiaci 702, dies 120. Recte scribit Thoth Nabonasari 703 coepisse feria sexta: eam tamen haud bene ad IIII Septembris die accomodat. Inter Thoth Nabonasari 703, & inter primas kal. Ian. Iulianas idem nobiscum intervallum statuit, scilicet 120 dierum: quatenus scilicet a meridie diei Sabbati more astronomico initium sumitur annorum Iulij Caesaris: si vero a media nocte praecedenti more Romano epocha Iuliana deducatur, unde anni a se constituti Caesar fecit principium, tunc a Nabonasaro usque ad epocham Iulianam elapsi fuerint 702 anni Aegyptiorum & 119 1/2 dies, qua ratione epocha Iuliana incurrit in feriam sextam, sive [illegible, ~8 letters], vt etiam sentit Paulus Middelburgensis, idemque Episcopus Forosemproniensis.
units.tr: Furthermore, so that we may be more certain about the Julian epoch, consider the edition of the Roman calendar, which is still in use. It must be known that the epoch fell in the 705th year of Nabonassar, at noon on the first of Tybi, a Saturday. For Thoth of Nabonassar 705 fell on 3 September, a Friday, the year running being the first before the Julian ordination. If we count four Egyptian months from there, we arrive at the first of Tybi, a Saturday, on which were the kalends of the first Julian year. Joseph Scaliger, in de emendatione temporum, p. 231, says: Therefore the Kalends of January of the Julian year fell in the current year 705 of Nabonassar. Its new moon, Thoth, was 4 September, a Friday. So from noon of Nabonassar to the first Julian Kalends are 702 Egyptian years and 120 days. He rightly writes that Thoth of Nabonassar 703 began on a Friday, yet he does not fit it well to 4 September. Between Thoth of Nabonassar 703 and the first Julian Kalends of January he sets the same interval as we do, namely 120 days. That is, the years of Julius Caesar begin astronomically from noon of the Saturday. But if the Julian epoch is deduced from midnight before, in the Roman manner, from which Caesar made the beginning of the years he established, then the years elapsed from Nabonassar to the Julian epoch are 702 Egyptian years and 119½ days. By this reckoning the Julian epoch falls on a Friday, or [illegible], as Paulus Middelburgensis also thinks, and the same man was bishop of Forosempronium.

units.la: Quod autem epocha Iuliana inciderit in neomeniam Tybi, aperte ostendit calendarium fixum Alexandrinorum: hi enim statim a principio ordinationis Iulianae acceperunt menses Iulianos, hoc est nomina mensium Aegyptiacorum accomodarunt ad menses Iulianos, atque tot illis dies tribuerunt, quot eis erat assignaret a Iulio Caesare. Huius calendarij exemplum est apud Nicolaum Myrepsum Alexandrinum antidoto 371, & in epigrammatis Graecis: quod diligenter observandum est, ne confundamus menses Aegyptiorum Iulianos cum mensibus Diocletiani. Sed haec est collatio mensium Alexandrinorum & Iulianorum: Ianuarius, Tybi | 31 d. | Iulius, Epiphi | 31 d. Februarius, Mechir | 28 d. | Augustus, Mesori | 31 d. Martius, Phamenoth | 31 d. | September, Thoth | 30 d. Aprilis, Pharmuthi | 30 d. | October, Paophi | 31 d. Maius, Pachon | 31 d. | November, Athyr | 30 d. Iunius, Payni | 30 d. | December, Chiac | 31 d.
units.tr: That the Julian epoch fell on the new moon of Tybi is clearly shown by the fixed calendar of the Alexandrians. From the very beginning of the Julian ordination they took Julian months: that is, they fitted the names of the Egyptian months to the Julian months and assigned to them as many days as Julius Caesar had assigned. An example of this calendar is found in Nicolaus Myrepsus of Alexandria, antidote 371, and in the Greek epigrams. This must be carefully observed, lest we confuse the Julian months of the Egyptians with the months of Diocletian. This is the comparison of Alexandrian and Julian months: January, Tybi, 31 days; February, Mechir, 28 days; March, Phamenoth, 31 days; April, Pharmuthi, 30 days; May, Pachon, 31 days; June, Payni, 30 days; July, Epiphi, 31 days; August, Mesori, 31 days; September, Thoth, 30 days; October, Paophi, 31 days; November, Athyr, 30 days; December, Chiac, 31 days.

units.la: Cum autem Alexandrini cum finitimis Syris & Graecis epocham annorum suorum deducerent ab aera Alexandri Dhilkarnain, sciendum est annum primum ordinationis Lulianæ incurrisse in annum ducentesimum sexagesimum sextum Alexandri: etenim anno primo ante ordinationem Lulianam kal. Octobribus iniit annus Alexandri 266: ut annus subsequens æræ Alexandri Dhilkarnain 267 incurreret in annum primum Lulianum, kal. Octobribus: quod etiam cum illis consentit, quæ diximus in calendario Syriaco. Si enim Christus natus est anno ineunte Alexandri trecentesimo duodecimo, hoc est, anno Iuliano 4[?] ad finem labente: utque annus Alexandri 267 incurrit in annum primum Iuliani, kal. Oct. & annus 312 Alexandri cœpit tribus elapsis mefibus ante initium annorum Christi vsitatorum, quod incurrit in kal. Ianuarias anni 46 Iuliani. Præterea annos ordinationis Lulianæ statim vfurpurunt Antiocheni: sicut id ex Eusebio diserte comprobari potest. Is enim in Chronicis annum fecundum Probi dicit esse 321 iuxta Antiochenos, eumque confert cum anno Christi 280, & persecutionem Christianam fuisse ait anno 351 fecundum Antiochenos, quem comparat cum anno Christi 306. Ex quo est manifestum, Eusebium Cæfarienfem annum primum Christi comparare cum anno Antiocheno 46, hoc est, cum anno Iuliano 46, quod etiam nos facimus secuti præstantissimos historicos & astronomos. Si enim ab anno Antiocheno 321 subtrahamus annum Christi 280, item fi ab anno Antiocheno 351 abiiciamus annum Christi 306, relinquitur differentia annorum 45, quantum scilicet interuallum est inter editionem calendarij, & inter primum annum Christi. Itaque constanter afferimus, annum primum Iuliani fuisse quintum ante primum annum Christi, hoc est, elapsos fuisse quadragesimum quintum annum ante primum annum Christi, hoc est, elapsos fuisse annos 45 Iulianos ante aeram Christianam seu ante principium annorum Christi vsitatorum: quod etiam abundè probauimus in calendario Romano. Hinc sequitur, si ad annos ante ordinationem Iulianam adiiciantur anni 45, summam ostendere annos ante Christum: exempli gratia, ostendimus principium Olympiadum iuxta solstitium incurrere in annum 731 ante ordinationem Iulianam, cui si adiiciantur quadraginta quinque anni, fit summa 776 annorum, quod indicium est, Olympiades incipere a solstitio aestiuo, quod incurrit in annum 776 ante Christum. Hac ratione deprehenditur Vrbem Romanam conditam esse ineunte vere, labente anno 753 ante Christum, & coepisse annum primum Nabonasari, die 26 Februarij, feria quarta, labente anno 747 ante Christum. Etsi autem Eusebius in historia ecclesiastica verissimè dixerit, Christum natum fuisse anno 42 imperij Augusti, & 28 Actiaco secundum Romanos; satis tamen indicat, se epocham Christi non praecisè deducere a natali Christi ἐνσαρκῷ, qui incidit, ut testatur chronologia Nicephori Archiepiscopi Constantinopolitani, in 25 Decembris: sed a kal. proximè sequentibus Ianuarij, hoc est, ab ineunte anno Iuliano 46, qui fuit annus Actiacæ victoriæ secundum Romanos 29, & 43 ab imperio Augusti: quia annum 46 Antiochenum facit initium annorum Christi vsitatorum. Idem secuti sunt omnes astronomi, quando aeram Christi scripserunt deduci ab anno 46 Iuliano: idem statuit Maximus monachus in cōputo, cum ait,
units.tr: When the Alexandrians and their neighbours the Syrians and Greeks deduced the epoch of their years from the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain, it must be known that the first year of the Julian ordination fell in the 266th year of Alexander. For in the year before the Julian ordination, on 1 October, the year 266 of Alexander began. So the following year, 267 of the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain, fell on the first Julian year, on 1 October. This agrees with what we said in the Syriac calendar. If Christ was born in the beginning of the 312th year of Alexander, that is, near the end of Julian year 4[?], and if the 267th year of Alexander fell on the first year of Julius, on 1 October, then the 312th year of Alexander began three months before the start of the commonly used years of Christ, which falls on 1 January of the 46th Julian year. Moreover, the Antiochenes at once adopted the years of the Julian ordination, as can be clearly proved from Eusebius. For in his Chronicle he says that the second year of Probus is 321 according to the Antiochenes, and he compares it with the year of Christ 280. He says the Christian persecution took place in the year 351 according to the Antiochenes, which he compares with the year of Christ 306. From this it is plain that Eusebius of Caesarea compares the first year of Christ with the Antiochene year 46, that is, with the Julian year 46. We also do this, following the most eminent historians and astronomers. For if we subtract the year of Christ 280 from the Antiochene year 321, and likewise subtract the year of Christ 306 from the Antiochene year 351, the difference of years is 45. That is exactly the interval between the publication of the calendar and the first year of Christ. Therefore we firmly assert that the first year of Julius was the fifth year before the first year of Christ. That is, 45 Julian years had elapsed before the Christian era, or before the beginning of the commonly used years of Christ. We have amply proved this also in the Roman calendar. From this it follows that if we add the 45 years to the years before the Julian ordination, the sum shows the years before Christ. For example, we showed that the beginning of the Olympiads at the solstice falls in the year 731 before the Julian ordination. If we add forty-five years to this, the sum is 776 years. This is evidence that the Olympiads begin at the summer solstice, which falls in the year 776 before Christ. By this reckoning it is established that the City of Rome was founded at the beginning of spring, in the year 753 before Christ, and that the first year of Nabonassar began on 26 February, a Wednesday, in the year 747 before Christ. Although Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History rightly said that Christ was born in the 42nd year of Augustus, and in the 28th year after Actium according to the Romans, he nonetheless makes it clear that he does not deduce the epoch of Christ exactly from the Nativity of Christ in the flesh. According to the chronology of Nicephorus, Archbishop of Constantinople, that Nativity fell on 25 December. Rather, he deduces it from the Kalends of the following January, that is, from the beginning of the Julian year 46. That was the 29th year of the Actian victory according to the Romans, and the 43rd from the reign of Augustus, because the Antiochene year 46 is the starting point of the commonly used years of Christ. All the astronomers followed the same practice when they wrote that the era of Christ is reckoned from the Julian year 46. Maximus the monk also states this in his computus, when he says:

units.la: ἐν ἔτει μὲν Αὐγούστῳ Καίσαρος γεννᾶται κατὰ ἡμᾶς ὁ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς μονογενὴς τῆς πατρὸς υἱός, Ἰησοῦς Χριστός, καὶ φύσει γίνεται δὲ ἡμᾶς τέλειος ἄνθρωπος, φύσει τέλειος δὲ ἑαυτὸν ὑπάρχων Θεός. [?]
units.tr: ἐν ἔτει μὲν Αὐγούστῳ Καίσαρος γεννᾶται κατὰ ἡμᾶς ὁ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς μονογενὴς τῆς πατρὸς υἱός, Ἰησοῦς Χριστός, καὶ φύσει γίνεται δὲ ἡμᾶς τέλειος ἄνθρωπος, φύσει τέλειος δὲ ἑαυτὸν ὑπάρχων Θεός. [?]

units.la: h.e. anno 43 Augusti Cæsaris nascitur secundum nos, qui supra nos est unigenitus patris filius, Iesus Christus,& natura sit propter nos perfectus homo, natura perfectus per seipsum existens Deus. Ult dicere, annum primum Christi secundum nos incipere ab anno 43 imperij Augusti,hoc est,ab anno 46 ineunte Iuliano: eumq; appellari annum Nativitatis Christi, licet octiduo ante, sub finem scilicet anni 42 imperij Augusti Christus natus perhibeatur. Eadem ratione scribit Iosephus Scaliger de emendatione temporum pag.106,Dionysium Exiguum Abbatem Romanum fecisse initium annorum a natali Christi usitatorum, ab anno 29 Actiaco, scilicet secundum Romanos,hoc est ab anno incipiete Iuliano 46, qui fuit 29 atrium-pho Augustali, & 31 ab ipsamet Augusti Actiaca victoria secundum Aegyptios, quae incurrit in 29 mensis Sextilis currente anno Iuliano decimo sexto. Itaque ne anno uno aberremus circa epocham Christi designanda, distinguedus est annus nativitatis Christi,a principio annorum Christi usitatorum,quod Arabes & astronomi aeram Christi appellant: nativitas enim Christi incurrit in contextum anni Iuliani 45, sive statuamus Christum natum esse in sine illius anni, quemadmodum Dionysius cum tota ecclesia hactenus persuasum habuit, sive etiam asseramus Christum natum esse circa aequinoctium autumnale currente eodem anno 45 Iuliano, quemadmodum viri quidam docti ex circumstantiis in historia Euangelica expressis coiiciunt. Sed initium annorum Christi usitatorum incurrit in contextum anni 46 Iuliani ineuntis,ut si a datis annis Iulianis abiiciamus annos 45, qui usque ad aeram Christi sunt praeteriti, semper habeamus annos Christi usitatos: & contra si ad annos Christi usitatos adiiciamus annos 45,proveniat anni Iuliani. Cùm itaque intellexerimus annum primum Christi esse 46 Iulianum & Antiochenum; sequitur annum Christi 238, esse annum Iulianum & Antiochenum 283, in quo Censorinus nobis ostendit veram connexionem annorum Olympiadicorum, Vrbis conditæ, Nabonasari, mortis Alexandri, & Actiacæ Augusti victoriæ. Ex quo intelligitur annorum Iulianorum maximam esse habendam rationem, quippe fine illis[?] nec annos Actiacos percipere, neque hos ad annos Christi accommodare possumus. Quis ve-ro inter omnes autores annos Iulianos diligentius Censorino & Eusebio Cæsariensi consignauit? quibus merito fides habenda est, cum ipsorum seculo in recenti adhuc fuerit memoria tempus ordinationis Iulianæ. Profecto nisi anni Iuliani vehiculum nobis præberent, incerta esset omnis chronologia.
units.tr: That is, in the 43rd year of Augustus Caesar, there is born for us, who is above us, the only-begotten Son of the Father, Jesus Christ, and by nature he becomes for us a perfect man, being by nature perfect God in himself. Hence it follows that the first year of Christ according to us begins in the 43rd year of Augustus, that is, in the year 46 beginning Julian. It is called the year of the Nativity of Christ, although Christ is said to have been born eight days before, namely near the end of the 42nd year of Augustus. In the same way Joseph Scaliger writes in de emendatione temporum, p. 106, that Dionysius Exiguus, the Roman abbot, made the beginning of the commonly used years from the birth of Christ, from the Actian year 29, that is, according to the Romans, from the beginning Julian year 46. That was the 29th year of Augustus's triumph, and the 31st from Augustus's own Actian victory according to the Egyptians, which fell on the 29th of Sextilis in the current Julian year 16. So that we do not go wrong by one year in fixing the epoch of Christ, the year of Christ's Nativity must be distinguished from the beginning of the commonly used years of Christ, which the Arabs and astronomers call the era of Christ. The Nativity of Christ falls within Julian year 45, whether we hold that Christ was born at the end of that year, as Dionysius and the whole Church have hitherto believed, or we maintain that Christ was born about the autumnal equinox of that same Julian year 45, as certain learned men conjecture from circumstances stated in the Gospel history. But the beginning of the commonly used years of Christ falls within the beginning of Julian year 46. So if we subtract 45 from the given Julian years, which have passed up to the era of Christ, we always have the usual years of Christ. Conversely, if we add 45 to the usual years of Christ, we get the Julian years. Since we have therefore understood the first year of Christ to be Julian and Antiochene 46, it follows that the year 238 of Christ is Julian and Antiochene 283. In that year Censorinus shows us the true connection of the Olympiad years, the years from the founding of the City, the years of Nabonassar, the death of Alexander, and the Actian victory of Augustus. From this it is understood that the greatest account must be taken of the Julian years, since without them we can neither perceive the Actian years nor fit these to the years of Christ. Indeed, who among all authors recorded the Julian years more carefully than Censorinus and Eusebius of Caesarea? They deserve to be trusted, since in their own century the memory of the time of the Julian ordination was still fresh. Truly, unless the Julian years provided us with a vehicle, all chronology would be uncertain.

units.la: a Hic annus octauus Iulianus est primus æræ Hispanicæ, quā Alfonsus vocat æram Cæsaris, quòd eo demum anno Hispani acceperint calendarium à Iulio Cæsare institutum: Saracenus appellat æram æ-ris, scilicet fisco Romano soluendi, quia fama erat Augustum Octauianum anno octauo Iuliano tributum impoſuisse Hispanis, quod deinceps anno 42 sui imperij exegerit ab vniuerso populo Romano, vt videtur indicare historia natiuitatis Christi: Hebræus de æris seu interuallis temporum vocat κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν Æram [?] æræ, h.e. æram Hispanorum celebratissimā. Æræ Hispanicæ designationes extant in cippis copiosis Hispanicæ, sicut Ambrosius Moralis obseruauit, item in tomis conciliorum, & aliis antiquioribus monumentis. Quod autem æra Cæsaris, siue æra Hispanica fit coferenda[?] in annum octauum Iuliani, ex eo manifestum est, quod æra Christi ab omnibus referatur ad annū 46 Iulianum. incipientem, & inter æram Cæsaris & Christi inter- iecti sint anni trigiuta octo Iuliani, sicut ex Saraceno & Alfonso intelligere possumus. Propterea illi hallu- cinantur, qui æram Hispanicam coniiciunt in annum septimum Iulianum, seipsos confundentes, quando annum natiuitatis Christi, hoc est, annum 4s[?] Iulia- num, non distinguunt ab anno æræ Christianæ, hoc est, ab anno Iuliano 46: nam & hi concedunt atque scribunt annum primum Christi esse annum 46 Iulianum, idcirco annum Christi 2 38[?] recte comparant cum anno 285 Iuliano, in quo Censorinus certissimam nobis annorum connexionem ostendit: & tamen idem interuallum annorum scilicet 38 cum Arabibus agnoscunt inter æram Cæsaris & Christi interiectorum: quæ sane nulla ratione conuenire possunt. Si enim æra Christi, cœpit ab anno 46 Iuliano, vt Alfonsus verissime statuit; vtiq; annus primus æræ Hispanicæ incurrit in annum octauum Iulianum, siquidem ab æra Cæsaris vsque ad Christi æram sunt anni præcise triginta octo. Si autem æra Cæsaris coniiceretur[?] in principium anni septimi Iuliani, sequere- tur æram Christi incipiendam esse ab anno 45 Iuliano, quod est absurdissimum: vel interuallum inter æram Cæsaris sixam ad principium anni septimi Iuliani, & inter æram Christi sixam ad principium anni 46 Iuliani, esset annorum triginta nouem, quod æque intolerabile est. Nam Alfonsus Hispaniarum Rex optimè de studiis mathematicis meritus ante annos trecentos Arabum opera adiutus nobis ostedit connexionem annorum Nabonasari cum annis Christi, atque ex certis historiis eruit, æram Hispanicam siue æram Cæsaris præcessisse principium annorum Christi vsitatorum 38 annis, à qua hypothesi nobis nequaquam est discedendum: inde enim intelligitur æram Cæsaris incipere ab anno octauo Iuliano, æram verò Christi inchoare ab anno 46 Iuliano. Hæc res tanti momenti est, ut ab eo qui historiam astronomicam texit, nullo modo possit aut debeat negligi: ego sane libenter fateor, me adminiculo æræ Cæsaris & Chri-fti peruenisse ad characteres hebdomadicos in annis § 2 prioribus Iulianis indicandos, & ad principia annorum Nabonasari, qui incurrunt in hos § 2 priores annos Iulianos, designanda & cum characteribus hebdomadicis conferenda summum praesidium habuisse. Vocabulum æræ Latinum non est, etsi à Latinis scriptoribus, puta Fausto Reginensi, Isidoro, Hildérico Gallo atque aliis sit usurpatum, qui per æram numerum & supputationem intelligunt: Arabes per æram siue Teric chronologiam quamuis siue radicem & epocham insignioris temporis intelligunt, quo in significato etiam nos hodie usurpamus: cum enim Censorinum secuti, coepissent Arabes de connexione annorum disquirere; vocabuli huius usum introduxerunt. Etsi autem tradant ab æra Cæsaris usque ad æramChristi, hoc est, annum 46 Iulianum elapsos esse annos triginta octo; fatentur tamen simul ab anno primo Iuliano usque ad æram Christi, elapsos esse annos 4 §, quod Saracenus indicat, cum air, Extranei dicunt, quod æra Christi, supra quem sit salus, sit post hoc initium (scilicet æra Cæsaris, retro numerando) per annos 7: at secundum primum firmatur noster liber. quasi velit dicere, æram Cæsaris ab Arabibus assignatam septem annis, posteriorem esse anno primo ordinationis Iulianæ. Ne autem dubitari possit de æra Cæsaris & Christi, characteres hebdomadicos & bisextilium exprimit Saracenus: nam annum primum æræ Cæsaris dicit fuisse intercalarem, & coepisse die solis: quod nihil aliud est, quàm fi dixisset, annum primum æræ Cæsaris, h.e. octauum Iulianum literas dominicales habuisse A G. & annum primum æræ Christi dicit coe-piffe die sabbati, vt annus tertius æræ Christi fuerit bisextilis: quod nihil aliud est, quàm fi dixisset annum primum æræ Christi, h.e. annum 46 Iulianum literam dominicalem habuisse B. annum fecundum æræ Christi, hoc est, annum Iulianum 47 literam dominicalem habuisse A. & annum tertium æræ Christi, hoc est, annum Iulianum 48 literas dominicales habuisse G F. & deinceps annum septimum æræ Christi, hoc est, annum 5 1 Iulianum habuisse literas dominicales B A.
units.tr: This eighth Julian year is the first year of the Spanish era, which Alfonso calls the era of Caesar, because it was in that year that the Spaniards at last received the calendar instituted by Julius Caesar. Saracen calls it the era of money, that is, of payment to the Roman treasury, since it was commonly said that Augustus Octavian imposed a tribute on the Spaniards in the eighth Julian year, which he afterwards exacted from the whole Roman people in his forty-second year of rule, as the history of the birth of Christ seems to indicate. The Hebrew writer, speaking of eras or intervals of time, calls it pre-eminently [κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν] the era, that is, the most celebrated era of the Spaniards. Inscriptions of the Spanish era survive in the many tombstones of Spain, as Ambrosius Morales observed, and likewise in the volumes of the councils and in other older monuments. That the era of Caesar, or the Spanish era, is to be referred to the eighth Julian year is clear from the fact that the era of Christ is everywhere referred to the forty-sixth Julian year as its beginning, and that exactly thirty-eight Julian years lie between the era of Caesar and the era of Christ, as we can understand from Saracen and Alfonso. Therefore those are mistaken who place the Spanish era in the seventh Julian year, confusing themselves when they do not distinguish the year of the birth of Christ, that is, the forty-fifth Julian year, from the year of the Christian era, that is, the forty-sixth Julian year. For they too concede and write that the first year of Christ is the forty-sixth Julian year, and so they rightly compare the year 2 of Christ with the 285th Julian year, in which Censorinus shows us a most certain connection of years; and yet they acknowledge the same interval of thirty-eight years between the era of Caesar and that of Christ as the Arabs do, which certainly cannot agree in any way. For if the era of Christ began in the forty-sixth Julian year, as Alfonso most truly holds, then the first year of the Spanish era certainly falls in the eighth Julian year, since from the era of Caesar to the era of Christ there are exactly thirty-eight years. But if the era of Caesar were placed at the beginning of the seventh Julian year, it would follow that the era of Christ must begin in the forty-fifth Julian year, which is most absurd; or the interval between the era of Caesar fixed at the beginning of the seventh Julian year and the era of Christ fixed at the beginning of the forty-sixth Julian year would be thirty-nine years, which is equally intolerable. For Alfonso, king of the Spains, who deserved well of mathematical studies, some three hundred years ago, aided by the work of the Arabs, showed us the connection of the years of Nabonassar with the years of Christ, and from certain histories he worked out that the Spanish era, or era of Caesar, preceded the beginning of the customary years of Christ by thirty-eight years; we must by no means depart from this hypothesis, for from it we understand that the era of Caesar begins in the eighth Julian year, while the era of Christ starts in the forty-sixth Julian year. This matter is of such importance that it cannot and must not be neglected by one who weaves together an astronomical history. I freely confess that with the help of the era of Caesar and of Christ I arrived at indicating the dominical letters for the first 52 Julian years, and that I had the greatest assistance in designating the beginnings of the years of Nabonassar, which fall in these first 52 Julian years, and in comparing them with the dominical letters. The word "era" is not Latin, although it has been used by Latin writers, such as Fastus of Regium, Isidore, Hildericus the Gaul and others, who understand by "era" a number and reckoning; the Arabs understand by "era," or Teric, a chronology, a root, or an epoch of some more notable time, in which sense we too use it today. For when the Arabs, following Censorinus, began to inquire into the connection of years, they introduced the use of this word. Although they hand down that thirty-eight years elapsed from the era of Caesar to the era of Christ, that is, to the forty-sixth Julian year, they also admit that from the first Julian year to the era of Christ there elapsed 4 and a half years [?], which Saracen indicates when he says, "Foreigners say," because the era of Christ, from which salvation is counted, lies after this starting point (namely the era of Caesar, counting backwards) by seven years; but according to the first, our book is confirmed, as if he wished to say that the era of Caesar assigned by the Arabs is seven years later than the first year of the Julian reform. Lest any doubt be possible about the era of Caesar and of Christ, Saracen sets out the dominical letters and the bissextile years: for he says that the first year of the era of Caesar was intercalary and began on a Sunday, which is nothing other than if he had said that the first year of the era of Caesar, that is, the eighth Julian year, had the dominical letters A G. And he says that the first year of the era of Christ began on a Saturday, so that the third year of the era of Christ was bissextile; which is nothing other than if he had said that the first year of the era of Christ, that is, the forty-sixth Julian year, had the dominical letter B; the second year of the era of Christ, that is, the forty-seventh Julian year, had the dominical letter A; and the third year of the era of Christ, that is, the forty-eighth Julian year, had the dominical letters G F; and so on, the seventh year of the era of Christ, that is, the fifty-first Julian year, had the dominical letters B A.

units.la: Hinc etiam sequeretur annum quartum Iulianum fuisse bisextilem, literis dominicalibus existentibus F E, annumque primum Iulianum, literam dominicalem habuisse B. Atqui nos in anno tantum primo Iuliano, & quinquagesimo fecundo Iuliano eosdem cum Arabibus characteres hebdomadicos agnosci-mus, in cæteris autem annis interiectis aliam demo-strauimus fuisse dispositionem: nam anni 36 priores Iuliani non fuerunt transacti ordinaria intercalatione à Iulio Cæsare præscripta, deinde ex edicto Augu-fti Octauiani duodecim anni subsequentes fine bi-sexto effluxerunt, donec anno quinquagesimo fecundo Iuliano bisextum primum Augustale intercalaretur, sicut luculenter ostendimus in calendario Romano. Atque hæc vera fuit annorum 5 1 priorum Iulianorum dispositio, quod etiam comprobant anni Nabonafari: sed astronomi Iudæi, Arabes, & Christiani finxerunt annos illos ordinaria & à Iulio Cæsare præ-scripta intercalatione fuisse trafactos: idcirco annum 45 Iulianum, quo Saluator noster est natus, dixerunt fuisse primum à bisextili: & annum 46 Iulianum, unde principium est annorum Christi usitatorum, posfuerunt [?] coepisse die sabbati: & annum tertium Christi, hoc est, 48 Iulianû scripserunt fuisse intercalarem, sicut etiam annû octauum Iulianum, hoc est, annum primum æræ Hispanicæ statuerunt fuisse bisextilem. Proinde in annis 52 prioribus Iulianis secundùm illos hæ fuerunt literæ dominicales. units.tr: From this it would also follow that the fourth Julian year was bissextile, with the dominical letters F E, and that the first Julian year had the dominical letter B. But we recognise the same dominical letters as the Arabs only in the first Julian year and in the fifty-second Julian year, and we have shown that in the other intervening years the arrangement was different. For the first 36 Julian years did not pass with the ordinary intercalation prescribed by Julius Caesar; then, by the edict of Augustus Octavian, the twelve following years passed without a bissextile, until in the fifty-second Julian year the first Augustan bissextile was intercalated, as we have clearly shown in the Roman calendar. And this was the true arrangement of the first 51 Julian years, as the years of Nabonassar also confirm; but the Jewish, Arab and Christian astronomers have imagined that those years passed with the ordinary intercalation prescribed by Julius Caesar. Hence they say that the forty-fifth Julian year, in which our Saviour was born, was the first after a bissextile; and that the forty-sixth Julian year, from which the customary years of Christ begin, began on a Saturday; and they have written that the third year of Christ, that is, the 48th Julian year, was intercalary, and likewise they have stated that the eighth Julian year, that is, the first year of the Spanish era, was bissextile. Accordingly, in the first 52 Julian years, on their reckoning, these were the dominical letters: Jul. year | Dom. letter || Jul. year | Dom. letter || Jul. year | Dom. letter || Jul. year | Dom. letter 1 | B || 13 | A || 25 | G || 37 | F 2 | A || 14 | G || 26 | F || 38 | E 3 | G || 15 | F || 27 | E || 39 | D 4 | F E || 16 | E D || 28 | D C || 40 | C B 5 | D || 17 | C || 29 | B || 41 | A 6 | C || 18 | B || 30 | A || 42 | G 7 | B || 19 | A || 31 | G || 43 | F 8 | A G || 20 | G F || 32 | F E || 44 | E D 9 | F || 21 | E || 33 | D || 45 | C 10 | E || 22 | D || 34 | C || 46 | B 11 | D || 23 | C || 35 | B || 47 | A 12 | C B || 24 | B A || 36 | A G || 48 | G F

units.la: Sic annus 49 Iulianus literam dominicalem habuisset E. annus 50 Iulianus D. annus 51 Iulianus C. & annus 52 Iulianus literas dominicales geminas habuisset B A. ut ostendit consecutio cycli solaris. Etsi autem finxerint annos 52 prædictos Iulianos ordinaria intercalatione fuisse transfactos, nobis tamen figmentum illud minimè curandum est, siquidem ex eo nulla consecutio annorum Nabonasari apparet: quicquid autem boni habet, est illud quòd ponat annum primum Iulianum coepisse die sabbati, litera dominicali existente B: hinc enim sequitur annum primum ante ordinationem Iulianam bisextilem fuisse literis dominicalibus existentibus DC. quatenus scilicet eum annum in dispositione Iuliana accipimus, etsi reuera talis non fuerit: est enim ostensum, quod ante primas kal. Ianuarij Iulianas, praecessertitannus Cofusionis, habens duodecim menses lunares & tres intercalares, hoc est, in universum dies 44[?]. Praeterea figmentum illud de ordinaria intercalatione annorum ƒ 2 priorum Iulianorum, etiam hoc boni habet, quod statuat annum quinquagesimum secundum Iulianum, hoc est, septimum annum Christi fuisse intercalarem, literis dominicalibus existentibus B A: hoc enim convenit cum ipsa historia, quae exponit Octavianum Augustum intrusisse bisextum emendatum in annum Iulianum ƒ 2, ut probavimus in calendario Romano: conveniunt etiam assignatae literae dominicales cum situ Thoth Nabonasari 755[?], qui incurrit in feriam secundam, die 21 Augusti, currente eodem anno Iuliano ƒ 2. Neque hic curandum est, quod aliqui scribant primum bisextum Augustale fuisse iniectum in annum ƒ 3 Iulianum. hic enim error ab illis proficiscitur, qui non recte figunt aeram Caesaris & Christi: hinc statuerunt annum primum Iulianum fuisse bisextilem, quod & rationi & experientiae repugnat. Sed hic queri potest, an interuallum inter principium annorum Iulianorum, & aeram Christi iustum servari possit, si ex hypothesi Arabum statuamus annos 45 praecedentes Iulianos cum ordinaria intercalatione decurrisse? Respondendum est, differentiam tantum esse unius diei: nam a novilunio primo Iuliano quod incurrit in mediam noctem, unde anni a se constituti Caesar principium fecit usque ad mediam noctem quae praecessit kal. Ianuarias aerae Christi, elapsi sunt anni 45 Iuliani, sed inaequales, quorum duodecim tantum bisextiles fuerunt ex sacerdotum Romanorum mādato, qui efficiunt 4392 dies, reliqui triginta tres fuerunt simplices de sententia sa-cerdotū & Octauiani Augusti, qui suppeditant 12045 dies: quorum omnium summa est 16437 dierum, qui conficiunt annos æquabiles Ægyptiorū 45 & 12 dies: quot Copernicus asserit a principio ordinationis Iulianæ vsque ad æram Christi a media nocte inchoatam esse elapsos: vt tunc medius solis motus fuerit 8 gradus, & 11 scrupula Capricorni, vt ostendit lib. 3 Reuolutionum cap. 26. Si autem anni 45 Iuliani fingantur fuisse translacti cum ordinaria intercalatione tunc interuallum illud comprehendit annos 34 simplices, qui efficiunt 12410 dies, & annos intercalares vndecim, qui efficiunt dies 4026: quorum omnium summa est 16436 dierum: ex quo sequitur si æram Christi iuxta hypotheses Arabum deducamus ab anno 46 Iuliano, quasi is cœperit a meridie diei sabbati, diem vnum anticipari, qui tamen ad suum locum restituitur anno tertio Christi, quem ipsi intercalarem faciūt, literis dominicalibus existentibus GF. cum reuera fuerit simplex, litera dominicali sola existente F, quia in eum annum incidit Thoth Nabonasari 751, die 22 Augusti, feria quinta.
units.tr: Thus, if the year 49 Julian had the dominical letter E, the year 50 Julian D, the year 51 Julian C, and the year 52 Julian the double dominical letters B A, as the succession of the solar cycle shows. Although they feign that these 52 Julian years were carried through with ordinary intercalation, we need not concern ourselves at all with that fiction, since no consistent succession of the years of Nabonassar appears from it. Whatever good it has is this: it makes the first Julian year begin on a Saturday, with dominical letter B. For from this it follows that the year before the Julian reform was bissextile, with dominical letters D C, if we take that year as belonging to the Julian arrangement, although in fact it was not such. For it has been shown that before the first Kalends of January of the Julian years there came the year of Confusion, having twelve lunar months and three intercalary months, that is, 44[?] days in all. Moreover, that fiction about the ordinary intercalation of the first 2 Julian years also has this merit: it states that the fifty-second Julian year, that is, the seventh year of Christ, was intercalary, with dominical letters B A. For this agrees with the history itself, which tells that Octavian Augustus inserted the corrected bissextile into the Julian year 2, as we proved in the Roman calendar. The assigned dominical letters also agree with the position of Thoth of Nabonassar 755[?], which fell on Monday, 21 August, in the same Julian year 2. Nor need we heed what some write, that the first Augustan bissextile was inserted into the Julian year 3. This error arises from those who do not fix the era of Caesar and of Christ correctly; hence they have held that the first Julian year was bissextile, which is contrary both to reason and to experience. But here it may be asked whether the interval between the beginning of the Julian years and the era of Christ can be kept exact, if on the hypothesis of the Arabs we suppose that the 45 preceding Julian years ran on with ordinary intercalation. The answer is that the difference is only one day. For from the first new moon of the Julian years, which fell at midnight, from which point Caesar made the beginning of the years he had established, up to the midnight that preceded the Kalends of January of the era of Christ, there elapsed 45 Julian years, but unequal ones. Of these, only twelve were bissextile, by the command of the Roman priests, and these make 4392 days; the remaining thirty-three were simple, by the decision of the priests and of Octavian Augustus, and these supply 12045 days. The sum of all of them is 16437 days, which make 45 equal Egyptian years and 12 days; this, Copernicus asserts, is the number of days that elapsed from the beginning of the Julian arrangement to the era of Christ, begun at midnight, so that the mean motion of the sun was 8 degrees and 11 minutes of Capricorn, as he shows in book 3 of the Revolutions, chapter 26. But if the 45 Julian years are supposed to have been carried through with ordinary intercalation, then that interval comprises 34 simple years, which make 12410 days, and 11 intercalary years, which make 4026 days. The sum of all of them is 16436 days. From this it follows that if we reckon the era of Christ, according to the hypotheses of the Arabs, from the 46th Julian year, as though it began at noon on a Saturday, one day is anticipated; yet this is restored to its place in the third year of Christ, which they make intercalary, with dominical letters G F, whereas in fact it was simple, with the dominical letter F alone, because in that year fell Thoth of Nabonassar 751, on 22 August, a Thursday.

units.la: In hunc annum decimum sextum Iulianum, die vigesima nona mensis Sextilis, feria prima, incurrit Thoth Nabonasari 719, a quo Ptolemæus cum Ægyptiis numerat Augusti Actiacam victoriam: etsi Dion referat prælium Actiacum commissum esse 2 Septembris. Actiaca Augusti victoria, vnde monarchiam Romanam sibi vendicauit AugustusOctauianus, diligentissime est observanda, cum vinculum sit arctissimum, quo apud Ptolemæum anni Imperatorum Romanorum copulantur cum annis Nabonafari,cumq; per eam intelligamus, quomodo anni irri- perij Augufti reuocandi fint ad annos Iulianos & Chrifti. Sed vt magis innotefcat annū decimū fextum Iulianum effe primum annum Actiacum ; ex Cenfo- rino probe notandum eft, Actiacam Augufti victo- riam bienio antiquiore effe triumpho Auguftali, qui incurrit in annū ineuntem 18 Iulianum: vnde colligi- tur Cenforinū biennij illius initiū fupputare à kal. Ia- nuariis ineuntis anni Iuliani decimi fexti, licet poft o- cto demū menfes inciderit Augufti Actiaca victoria, labente anno Olympiadico 747, hoc eft, anno tertio Olympiadis centefimæ octogefimæ feptimæ, quem- admodum etiā recte tradit Eufebius in Chronicis, vbi hifce verbis defcribit Actiacam Augufti victoriam: Cleopatra & Antonium femet interficiunt, & Ægyptus fit Romana provincia, quam primus tenuit Caius Cornelius Gallus, de quo Virgilius scribit in Bucolicis. Quod autem monarchia Augufti coeperit ab Actiaca victoria, indeq; æra tempori s fuerit inftituta, Xiphilinus e Dio- ne recitat hifce verbis, [?]τοιαῦτα μὲν τῆς ἡ ναυμαχία [illegible, ~12 letters] Σεβαστὸς ἐγένετο. τότε δὲ ἐκ ἀλλως [?] [illegible, ~25 letters] ἡμέρας [?] [illegible, ~15 letters] Καίσαρ [illegible, ~20 letters] h.e. tale nauale praeliū inter ipsos comissum fuit die fecunda Septembris. hoc autē aliter nusquam dixi (neq; enim foleo id facere) atq; tūc primum Caesar potentia omnē folus obtinuit, vt inde monarchiæ ipsius anni & præcise ab illa die numerarentur. Cum autem Thoth Actiacus fecundum Ægy- ptios incidisset in 29 Augufti fiue Sextilis iuxta ratio- nem perturbati calendarij, factū deinde est vt primo anno Diocletiani Tyranni, currete anno Chrifti 284 figeretur Thoth Coptitarū ad 29 quoq; Augufti die, feriam sextam: proinde plurimum errant, qui putant æram Diocletiani, siue primum Thoth Coptitarum, & Thoth Actiacum in eandem feriam incurrisse.
units.tr: In this 16th Julian year, on the 29th day of the month of Sextilis, a Monday, fell Thoth of Nabonassar 719, from which Ptolemy, with the Egyptians, counts the Actiac victory of August, although Dio reports that the battle of Actium was fought on 2 September. The Actiac victory of August, by which Augustus Octavian claimed for himself the Roman monarchy, must be observed most carefully, since it is the very close bond by which, in Ptolemy, the years of the Roman emperors are joined to the years of Nabonassar; and through it we understand how the years of the reign of Augustus are to be traced back to the Julian years and to the years of Christ. But so that it may become clearer that the 16th Julian year was the first Actiac year, it must be carefully noted from Censorinus that the Actiac victory of Augustus was two years older than the Augustan triumph, which fell in the year beginning in the 18th Julian year. Hence it is gathered that Censorinus reckons the beginning of that two-year period from the Kalends of January of the beginning Julian year 16, although the Actiac victory of Augustus fell only after eight full months, in the year 747 of the Olympiads, that is, in the third year of the 187th Olympiad, as Eusebius also rightly records in the Chronicle, where in these words he describes the Actiac victory of Augustus: Cleopatra and Antony killed themselves, and Egypt became a Roman province, which Gaius Cornelius Gallus first held, about whom Virgil writes in the Bucolics. That the monarchy of Augustus began with the Actiac victory, and that from it an era for the times was instituted, Xiphilinus recites from Dio in these words: [Greek; the text is partly illegible: "such things indeed of the naval battle ... became Augustus. Then, however, not otherwise ... days ... Caesar ..."] that is, such a naval battle was fought between them on the second day of September. I have said this nowhere else otherwise (for I am not in the habit of doing so), and only then did Caesar alone obtain power over everything, so that the years of his monarchy were counted from that very day. But since Thoth of Actium, according to the Egyptians, had fallen on 29 August, or Sextilis, by the reckoning of the disordered calendar, it then came about that in the first year of the tyrant Diocletian, which was the year 284 of Christ, Thoth of the Copts was fixed on the 29th day of August also, a Friday. Therefore they are greatly mistaken who think that the era of Diocletian, or the first Thoth of the Copts, and Thoth of Actium fell on the same weekday.

units.la: Hoc anno decimo octauo Iuliano celebratus est Romæ triumphus Augustalis, XVI kalend. Febr. teste Censorino ideo anni Actiaci secundum Romanos supputatur a triumpho Augusti, hoc est, ab anno 18 Iuliano, a quo Censorinus sumit initium annorum Augustanorum, cum eo demum anno Octauianus appellatus sit Augustus: idem facit Eusebius in historia ecclesiastica, quando annum 42 imperij Augusti copulat cum anno 28 Actiaco secundum Romanos, hoc est, cum anno Iuliano 45, quo Christum natum esse affirmat.
units.tr: In this eighteenth Julian year the Augustan triumph was celebrated at Rome on the 16th day before the Kalends of February, as Censorinus testifies. For this reason the years of the Actiac era are reckoned by the Romans from the triumph of Augustus, that is, from the 18th Julian year, from which Censorinus takes the beginning of the Augustan years, since it was in that year that Octavian was at last named Augustus. Eusebius does the same in his Ecclesiastical History, when he joins the 42nd year of the reign of Augustus with the 28th Actiac year according to the Romans, that is, with the Julian year 45, in which he affirms that Christ was born.

units.la: † Hic annus trigesimus septimus Iulianus est vigesimus ab appellatione Augustorum, siue a triumpho Augustali post Actiacam victoriam Romæ celebrato, vt testis locupletissimus est Censorinus: eo anno in gratiâ Augusti Octauiani me-fis Sextilis appellatus est Augustus, & Thoth Nabo-nafari 740 incidit in 22 Augusti, feriam primam, cum anno præcedenti bisextili Thoth Nabonafari 739 transfiliet [?] ad 22 Sextilis, feriam septimam. Atque hic annus 37 Iulianus fuit primus illorum duodecim, quos Augustus Octauianus sine intercalatione transigi voluit, vt triduum illud eximeretur, quod per vitiosam sacerdotum intercalationem annis 36 præteritis excreuerat: sicut ostendimus in calendario Romano.
units.tr: † This is the 37th Julian year, the twentieth from the naming of the Augusti, or from the Augustan triumph celebrated at Rome after the Actiac victory, as Censorinus, the most weighty witness, testifies. In that year, in the favour of Augustus Octavian, the month of Sextilis was named August, and Thoth of Nabonassar 740 fell on 22 August, a Sunday; and in the preceding bissextile year, Thoth of Nabonassar 739 passed over to 22 Sextilis, a Saturday. And this 37th Julian year was the first of those twelve which Augustus Octavian wished to be run without intercalation, so that that three-day excess, which had accumulated through the faulty intercalation of the priests in the 36 years past, might be removed, as we have shown in the Roman calendar.

units.la: Anno hoc Iuliano 45 ad finem decurrente natus est Dominus noster Iesus Christus, cum Augustus a primo fuc [?] cosulatu imperasset annos 42, & post triumphum Actiacum fere compleuisset annos 28.
units.tr: In the course of this Julian year 45 our Lord Jesus Christ was born, when Augustus had reigned 42 years from his first consulship and had nearly completed 28 years since the Actian triumph.

units.la: Hic annus 46 Iulianus est primus æræ Christianæ, seu annorum Christi vsitatorum: quemadmodum insuperioribus sufficienter est demonstratum.
units.tr: This Julian year 46 is the first year of the Christian era, or of the customary years of Christ, as has been sufficiently demonstrated above.

units.la: ƒ Hoc anno Iuliano quinquagesimo secundo, qui fuit septimus Christi, bisextum emendatum interiecit Augustus Octavianus, ut Thoth Nabonasari 75 transierit ad 11 Augusti diem, feriam secundam: fuit tunc aureus numerus XIV. & annus Olympiadicus 783 coepit a solstitio, annus vero Urbis conditae 760 incurrit circa proxime precedens vernum aequinoctium, labente eodem anno Iuliano 52, & literis dominicalibus existentibus BA. Sed quia deinceps propter angustiam columnarum impedimur, quo minus haec omnia possimus in tabulis repraesentare, aureum numerum, cum annis Olympiadum, & Urbis conditae omittemus: cum haec omnia ex datis annis Iulianis facile indagari possint, sicut docuimus in calendario Romano: & annos dutaxat Iulianos cum annis Nabonasari & Christi conferemus. units.tr: In this Julian year 52, which was the seventh of Christ, Augustus Octavian inserted the corrected leap year, so that Thoth of Nabonassar 75 passed to 11 August, the second feria. At that time the golden number was 14, the Olympiad year 783 began at the solstice, and the year 760 from the founding of the City fell shortly before the preceding vernal equinox, with this Julian year 52 running on and the dominical letters being BA. But since the narrowness of the columns prevents us from setting out all these things in the tables, we will omit the golden number, along with the years of the Olympiads and of the founding of the City, since all of these can easily be worked out from the given Julian years, as we taught in the Roman calendar. We will compare only the Julian years with the years of Nabonassar and of Christ. units.la: 4 Ab hoc anno quinquagesimo tertio Iuliano incipit cyclus bisextilis secundum ordinationem Augusti Octauiani, vt scilicet anno quoq; quarto deinceps bisextum interiiciatur, & tres quinq; anni interiecti simplices habeantur, quemadmodum ostendit continuatio ordinaria in annis 28 solaribus. Hic autē cyclus solaris interruptus fuit anno Iuliano 708, in quo bisextum ordinarium fuit sublatum, vt dies vnus anticiparetur in gratiam neomeniæ Paschalis, vt suo loco ostendemus.
units.tr: 4 From this fifty-third Julian year the bissextile cycle begins, according to the arrangement of Augustus Octavianus: that is, a leap day is to be inserted every fourth year thereafter, and three five-year intervals are to be kept as common years, as the regular sequence over 28 solar years shows. This solar cycle was interrupted in the Julian year 708, when the ordinary leap day was dropped so that one day was brought forward for the sake of the paschal new moon, as we will show in its place.

units.la: b Hic annus Iulianus septuagesimus octauus est annus Christi trigesimus tertius, in quem incurrit annus ab Vrbe condita septingentesimus octogesimus sextus, XI kal. Maii, & annus Iphiti Olympiadicus octingentesimus nonus, hoc est, annus primus Olympiadis ducentesimæ tertiæ, cuius initium fuit circa solstitium æstiuum, iuxta suppu-tationem Varronis, Censorini, & Phlegontis. Hoc ipso anno Iuliano septuagesimo octauo, tertio die Aprilis, feria sexta, hoc est, die Veneris, litera dominicali existente D, currente anno secundo aurei numeri qui est in cyclo enneadecaeterico Iuliano, & neomenia cœlesti hærete in XIII kal. Aprilis: Christus Domin° & saluator noster acerbissimā mortem sustinuit pro redemtione generis humani. Quamobrem statuimus ab æra Christi vsq; ad passionem Dominicā transactos esse 33 annos, tres menses, & decem dies, sicut cesue-rūt patres Græci, ite Apollinaris Laodicenus & Victor Lemouicensis Episcopi, Petrus Comestor, Marianus Scotus, Rogerius Bacchon, Iohannes de Muris, Nicolaus de Lyra, Paulus Burgensis, & Ioannes Lucidus, qui Christum XXXIII aetatis anno crucifixu scribunt. Idem tradunt Eusebius Caesariensis & Epiphanius, iuxta quos Christus passus est anno decimo octauo Tiberii. Siquidem[?] anno decimo quinto Tiberii à Ioanne in Iordane est baptizatus, cum ingressus fuisset annum trigesimum aetatis, vt testatur historia Evangelica. Vt autem haec intelligantur, sciendum est, quoto anno aetatis suae Augustus Octauianus obierit, vt certi simus de initio annorum Tiberii Caesaris. Suetonius scribit, Augustum Octauianum initium imperii sui, hoc est, triumuiratus coepisse anno aetatis vigesimo.
units.tr: b This Julian year 78 is the thirty-third year of Christ, the year from the founding of the City 786 falls into it, on 21 April, and the 809th year of Iphitus in the Olympiad reckoning, that is, the first year of the 203rd Olympiad, whose beginning fell about the summer solstice, according to the reckoning of Varro, Censorinus and Phlegon. In this same Julian year 78, on the third day of April, a Friday, that is, the day of Venus, with the dominical letter D, in the second year of the golden number in the Julian nineteen-year cycle, and with the heavenly new moon falling on 20 March, Christ our Lord and Saviour underwent a most bitter death for the redemption of the human race. Therefore we determine that 33 years, three months and ten days passed from the age of Christ to the Lord's passion, as the Greek Fathers, namely Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, and Victor, bishop of Lemoges, Peter Comestor, Marianus Scotus, Roger Bacon, John de Muris, Nicholas of Lyra, Paul of Burgos and John Lucidus, have held, who write that Christ was crucified in the thirty-third year of his age. Eusebius of Caesarea and Epiphanius also hand this down, according to whom Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius. For in the fifteenth year of Tiberius he was baptized by John in the Jordan, when he had entered his thirtieth year of age, as the Gospel history testifies. But so that these things may be understood, we must know in what year of his life Augustus Octavianus died, so that we may be certain about the beginning of the years of Tiberius Caesar. Suetonius writes that Augustus Octavianus began his rule, that is, the triumvirate, in the twentieth year of his age.

units.la: Ostendimus autem nos in calendario Romano, quod Augustus Octauianus triumuiratum inierit V Kal. Decembris, sub finem anni tertii Iuliani: quamobrem si annum quartum Iulianum, cui adscribimus initium imperii Augusti, comparemus cum anno vigesimo aetatis Augusti, deprehendemus annum decimum tertium sextum Iulianum, qui est primus annorum Actiacorum secundum Aegyptios, illc annum decimum tertium imperii Augusti, & trigesimum secundum aetatis Augusti: item annum quadragesimum quintum Iulianum, esse 42 imperii Augusti, & sexagesimum aetatis ipsius: item annum sexagesimum Iulianum esse 7 imperii Augusti, & septuagesimum sextum aetatis ipsius, quo moritur Augustus Actiae in Campania, sepelitur Romae in campo Martio, teste Eusebio. Obiit autem Augustus, vt Xiphilinus e Dione refert, die decima nona Augusti, qua etiam primum consulatum fuerat adeptus, cum vixisset septuaginta quinque annos, menses decem, & dies viginti sex, cuq; monarchiam ab Actiaca victoria habuisset annis fere 44, quibus tantum tredecim dies decerant. Verba eius haec sunt: καὶ ὁ μὲν ἔτος τῷ τῆς ἀνικήτου Αὐγούστου[?], ὃς ἡ[?] τὴν πρὸ τῆς Ἀκτιακῆς νίκης[?] μὲν ἔτι ὅ ἐξ[?] ζῶντας μὲν τὴν καὶ ἑξήκοντα ἔτη, μῆνας δέκα καὶ ἡμέρας ἐξ καὶ εἴκοσι. τὴν δὲ περὶ τὴν καὶ εἴκοσι[?] Σεπτεμβρίου ἐγεννήθη, μοναρχήσας δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ χρόνου ἐνίκησε τῷ Ἀκτίῳ νίκῃ, ἔτη τεσσαράκοντα τέσσαρα, ὧν ἐλλείπουσιν ἡμέραι τρεῖς καὶ δέκα[?]. hoc est, Hic autem die decima nona Augusti, qua aliquando primum consulatum inierat, vitam cum morte commutauit, cum vixisset 75 annos, menses 10, & dies 26. etenim vigesima tertia Septembris natus erat. cumque monarcha fuisset a quo tempore ad Actium victor euasisset annos 44, quibus decerat tredecim dies. Hic animaduertere licet Dionem cum Xiphilino Actiacam victoriam referre ad diem secundam Septembris, currente anno decimo sexto Iuliano, vt inter diem obitus Augusti, & diem Actiacae victoriae, vtrinq; exclusiue sumtu, interuallum ponant tredecim dierum: & fingere anno decimo septimo ante ordinationem Iulianam fuisse menses Iulianos, quasi die 23 Septembris ad fine labente, hoc est, incipiente 24 die Septembris a media nocte iuxta Romanam consuetudinem, Octauianus fit natus: itaq; septem dies restabant ex mense Septembri, quibus si adiiciamus nouendecim dies ex mense Augusto, quibus superuixit Augustus, labente anno sexagesimo Iuliano, prodeunt illi viginti sex dies, quos trafegit Augustus praeter annos 75, & 10 menses. At menses illi decem partim specarunt ad annum 17 ante ordinationem Iulianam, partim vero ad annum sexagesimum Iulianum: si enim tres postremi menses anni 17 ante ordinationem Iulianam, adiiciantur ad septem priores menses anni 60 Iuliani; proueniunt illi decem integri menses, quos transegit Augustus praeter 75 annos, & 26 dies. Historiam hanc pulcherrimam qui ignorat, nunquam apprehendere potest tempus Actiacę victorię, neq; etiam determinare audet, qua ratione annus 42 imperii Augusti incidat in annum 45 Iulianum. Recepta sanè opinio est, Christum natum esse circa brumam, labente anno Iuliano 45; ita-que si hypothesis Eusebii Caesariensis sit retinenda, qua asseritur Christū natū anno 42 imperii Augusti, omnino statuendum est annū totum 42 imperii Augusti comparandum esse cum toto anno 45 Iuliano, quemadmodum nos a principio fecimus: alias fieri non posset, ut 25 Decembris, qua Christum auctoritate ecclesiae natum esse credimus, incurreret in contextum anni 42 ab imperio Augusti; quo etiam respexisse videtur Maximus monachus, quando ait natalem Domini, quem octiduo post secura [?] est æra Christiana, incidisse in annum 43 ab imperio Augusti. Aliqui annos imperii Augusti supputarunt ab eius triumuirato, qui incurrit in Vkal. Decembris, anno labente tertio Iuliano, & ut æquabilis esset mensium comparatio, à kal. Decembribus non tam imperium Augusti, quàm annos Christi deduxerunt, sicut apparet ex scripto Hebraei de aeris. Sed præcisissime anni imperii Augusti secundum Dionem computantur à primo Augusti consulatu, qui incurrit in decimam nonam diem Augusti, currente anno tertio Iuliano, quo tempore Augustus inibat annum vigesimum ætatis: hinc illi qui dicunt, Christum natum esse anno 42 imperii Augusti, circa æquinoctium autumnale, currente anno 45 Iuliano; decepti fuisse deprehenduntur, cum exi-stimarent se natiuitatem Christi retulisse ad finem anni 42 ab imperio Augusti: etenim annus 42 ab imperio Augusti iuxta propriam acceptionem coepit die decima nona Augusti, currente anno Iuliano 44, & desiit circa eandem diem 19 Augusti, currente anno Iuliano 45, ita vt aequinoctium subsequens autumnale incidat in contextum anni 43 ab imperio Augusti. Quamobrem si quis vnquam autorum vetustissimorum recte assignauit diem natiuitatis Christi, fuit is D. Epiphanius Episcopus Constantiae Cypri, qui in oratione contra demetes non sufficientes Euangelium Ioannis & Apocalypsin, scribit Christum natum esse anno 42 Augusti, ante diem octauum Iduum Ianuarii: hoc tempus fere incidit in medium annum 42 ab imperio Augusti, & in principium anni 45 Iuliani: idem Epiphanius adiicit fuisse tunc Iudaeis diem decimam tertiam Tebet, unde colligitur decima quinta Thebeth, hoc est die septimo Ianuarii fuisse plenilunium: a quo si quindecim dies numeretur, descendit in 1 Ianuarii, vbi h[?]fit neomenia coelestis, sicut etiam indicat ennea-decaeteris Iuliana: anno enim 45 Iuliano aureus numerus est VII, qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 8 kalend. Februarias, vbi nouilunium triduo serius indicat, quatenus in triduum prolapsum erat calendarium Romanum non obseruata legitima intercalatione a Iuliano Caesare praescripta.
units.tr: We have shown, however, in the Roman calendar, that Augustus Octavianus entered the triumvirate on 27 November, near the end of the third Julian year; therefore if we compare the fourth Julian year, to which we assign the beginning of Augustus's rule, with the twentieth year of Augustus's age, we find that the sixteenth Julian year is the thirteenth year of Augustus's rule, which is the first of the Actian years according to the Egyptians, and the thirty-second year of his age; likewise the forty-fifth Julian year is the forty-second year of Augustus's rule and his sixtieth year of age; likewise the sixtieth Julian year is the seventh year of Augustus's rule and his seventy-sixth year of age, in which Augustus died at Actium in Campania and was buried at Rome in the Campus Martius, according to Eusebius. Augustus died, as Xiphilinus reports from Dio, on the nineteenth day of August, the day on which he had also first attained the consulship, having lived seventy-five years, ten months and twenty-six days, and having held the monarchy from the Actian victory for nearly 44 years, less thirteen days. His words are these: καὶ ὁ μὲν ἔτος τῷ τῆς ἀνικήτου Αὐγούστου [as printed in the Latin; the Greek text is garbled in the scan], that is: "He, however, on the nineteenth day of August, on which he had once entered his first consulship, changed life for death, having lived 75 years, 10 months and 26 days; for he had been born on the twenty-third of September, and having been monarch from the time when he had won the victory at Actium, for 44 years, of which thirteen days are lacking." Here one may notice that Dio and Xiphilinus refer the Actian victory to 2 September in the sixteenth Julian year, so that they place an interval of thirteen days between the day of Augustus's death and the day of the Actian victory, counting both exclusively; and that, in the seventeenth year before the Julian reform, the Julian months were supposed to be such that, with the 23rd of September coming to an end, that is, the 24th of September beginning at midnight according to Roman custom, Octavianus was born. Thus seven days remained of September; if we add to these nineteen days of August, in which Augustus survived, as the sixtieth Julian year was ending, there result those twenty-six days which Augustus lived beyond 75 years and 10 months. But those ten months partly fell in the seventeenth year before the Julian reform, and partly in the sixtieth Julian year: for if the last three months of the seventeenth year before the Julian reform are added to the first seven months of the sixtieth Julian year, there result those ten full months which Augustus lived beyond 75 years and 26 days. Whoever does not know this very beautiful history can never grasp the time of the Actian victory, nor dare to determine by what reckoning the forty-second year of Augustus's rule falls in the forty-fifth Julian year. It is indeed a received opinion that Christ was born about the winter solstice, at the end of the forty-fifth Julian year; therefore, if the hypothesis of Eusebius of Caesarea is to be kept, which asserts that Christ was born in the forty-second year of Augustus's rule, it must be determined without fail that the whole forty-second year of Augustus's rule is to be compared with the whole forty-fifth Julian year, as we have done from the beginning; otherwise it could not happen that 25 December, on which we believe on the authority of the Church that Christ was born, would fall within the course of the forty-second year from Augustus's rule. Maximus the monk seems also to have had this in view when he says that the birthday of the Lord, which eight days after... [text garbled in scan] the Christian era, fell in the forty-third year from the rule of Augustus. Some have reckoned the years of Augustus's rule from his triumvirate, which fell on 27 November in the third Julian year; and, so that the comparison of months might be uniform, from the Kalends of December they have counted not so much the rule of Augustus as the years of Christ, as appears from a writing of the Hebrews concerning the eras. But most precisely, the years of Augustus's rule are reckoned, according to Dio, from his first consulship, which fell on 19 August in the third Julian year, at which time Augustus entered his twentieth year of age. Hence those who say that Christ was born in the forty-second year of Augustus's rule, about the autumn equinox, in the forty-fifth Julian year, are found to be mistaken, since they thought they had referred the birth of Christ to the end of the forty-second year from Augustus's rule: for the forty-second year from Augustus's rule, in its proper reckoning, began on 19 August in the forty-fourth Julian year and ended about the same day, 19 August, in the forty-fifth Julian year, so that the following autumn equinox falls within the course of the forty-third year from Augustus's rule. Therefore, if anyone of the most ancient authors has rightly assigned the day of Christ's birth, it was Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, who, in his work against those who do not accept the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse, writes that Christ was born in the forty-second year of Augustus, before the eighth day before the Ides of January. This time falls roughly in the middle of the forty-second year from Augustus's rule and at the beginning of the forty-fifth Julian year. The same Epiphanius adds that the Jews then had the thirteenth day of Tebet, whence it is inferred that the fifteenth of Thebeth, that is, the seventh of January, was the full moon; if fifteen days are counted back from this, one comes down to 1 January, where the heavenly new moon falls, as the Julian nineteen-year cycle also indicates: for in the forty-fifth Julian year the golden number is 7, which is placed in the Julian calendar at 25 January, where it indicates the new moon three days later, because the Roman calendar had slipped by three days, the lawful intercalation prescribed by Julius Caesar not having been observed.
