units.tr: That is: "For the Saviour is born in the forty-second year of Augustus, king of the Romans, which was the twenty-ninth year, from which time the Jews were brought under the power of the Roman people. Augustus, however, had already reigned thirteen years from his first consulship, before Judea was fully subjected to the Romans." And a little later: "Since he himself was born about the month of January, that is, before the eighth of the Ides of January, which is, according to the Romans, the fifth day of the month of January, etc." To understand this passage, it must be noted that Epiphanius dates the time from the Actian victory of Augustus, when the Jews together with the Egyptians came under the power and dominion of the Roman people, and from there reckons the fourteenth year of Augustus' reign, so that the thirteenth year of the same reign began on 19 August, in the fifteenth year of the Julian calendar. This computation agrees exactly with the account of Dio. Therefore, when he says that the forty-second year of Augustus was the twenty-ninth year in which Judea was brought under the power of the Roman people, he counts the beginning of this period from the fourteenth year of Augustus' reign, which began thirteen days before the Actian victory of Augustus. But how do these things agree with the account of Eusebius and the common opinion, which holds that Christ was born in the forty-first year of Augustus, in the eighteenth year after the Actian victory, on 25 December, near the end of the Julian year 45? We have said that this comparison holds if the first year of Augustus' reign is taken from the entering of the triumvirate, and one month is added, so that it is fixed to the fourth year of the Julian calendar. For in this way it would follow that the forty-first year of Augustus agrees with the forty-fifth Julian year and with the eighteenth Actian year according to the Romans, since the Actian victory is reckoned from the eighteenth Julian year, that is, from the Augustan triumph. Nevertheless we cannot deny that the account of Epiphanius is more consistent with the truth: that Christ was born in the forty-first year of Augustus, and in the twenty-ninth year from the Actian victory of Augustus according to the Egyptians, on the fifth day of January, at the beginning of the Julian year 45. Therefore we judge, saving however the judgment of our elders, that Dionysius the Roman Abbot, who introduced the years of Christ counted from the conception, followed his own hypothesis rather than the history of the event, when he laid down that Christ was born on 25 December, at the very time of the winter solstice, near the end of the Julian year 45. For although he was persuaded that Christ was born in midwinter, which he could gather from Epiphanius, nevertheless he wished to bring his nativity back to the solstice, since Julius Caesar had begun his reform from there. So whether we hold that Christ was born on 5 January, at the beginning of the Julian year 45, or near the autumnal equinox, or on 25 December, near the end of the same Julian year 45, no inconvenience follows, provided we know that the Christian era, or the beginning of the customary years of Christ, falls on the Kalends of January of the beginning Julian year 46, as Eusebius teaches us through the application of the Antiochene years. Thus it is enough if we hold that the nativity of Christ fell within the course of the Julian year 45. For we do not agree with the opinion of Tertullian, who in the book he wrote against the Jews affirms that Christ was born in the forty-first year of Augustus, which opinion Cassiodorus and Marianus Scotus also followed. For Eusebius mentions this opinion only in his Chronicle and does not approve it, since from it, against the authority of Holy Scripture, it follows that Christ suffered in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, when the Gospel history says he was baptized. For after his baptism he preached for a full two years with some months besides, until he was led to the cross to be offered to God the Father for the redemption of the human race, as Eusebius and Epiphanius testify; and the circumstances related in the Gospel history also support this view. But even if we grant that the nativity of Christ fell in the forty-first year of the reign of Augustus, this nonetheless remains a firm and unshaken foundation: that the customary years of Christ are reckoned from the forty-sixth Julian year, and they should not begin earlier, unless we wish to reckon them from the preceding winter solstice, or from the day of the incarnation, that is, the conception of Christ, which according to the common opinion and the hypothesis of Dionysius the Roman Abbot fell on 25 March in the Julian year 45. In the same way, it is established from histories that this reckoning of the years of Christ was once in use in certain provinces. But let us return to where we digressed, and demonstrate that Christ suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. To do this conveniently, it is necessary that we carefully compare the years of Augustus' life with the years that passed before and after the Julian ordination, and apply the beginning of the years of Tiberius to the death of Augustus Octavian. So that you may have all these things before you, consider the following table.

units.la: Natus est Augustus anno decimo septimo ante or-dinationem Iulianam, die 2 3 Septembris: cum itaq; nos annũ primũ ætatis Augusti applicamus ad princi-pium anni 1 6 ante ordinationē Iulianā, anticipan-di sunt menses tres,& septem dies,vt perueniatur ad verũ tempus natiuitatis Augusti: etenim a 2 3 Septe-bris, currente anno ante ordinationē Iulianam decimo septimo,vsq; ad 2 3 Septembris, currente anno 1 6 ante ordinationem Iulianam, intelligitur Augustus annum primum ætatis transegisse: eadem comparatio obseruanda est in annis subsequentibus. Ita applicamus annum vigesimum ætatis Augusti ad principium anni quarti Iuliani, etsi is inceperit die 25 Septem-bris, currente anno tertio Iuliano: nam a 23 Septebris labente anno tertio Iuliano, vsque ad 23 Septembris currente anno quarto Iuliano, Augustus intelligitur transegisse annum vigesimum ætatis. Hinc solui po-test scrupulus, an Augustus Octavianus cum primum consulatum iniret, ingressus fit annum vigesimum ætatis, vel natus fuerit annos vndeuiginti? Consulatum primum iniit Augustus Octavianus anno tertio Iuliano, vt ostendimus in calendario Romano, die decimo nono Augusti, hoc est, XIII[?] kalend. Septembris, vt paulo ante ex Xiphilino retulimus: si ergo a primo consulatu Augusti, quo exercitum in patris interfectores comparauit, deducamus principium imperii Augusti, vt Dio facit, vtique Augustus nondum excesserat annum decimum nonum ætatis, quod ipsemet Augustus fatetur in indice rerum à se gestarum, quem beneficio Augerii Busbekii publicauit Andreas Schottus. In eo enim sic de se scribit Augustus: Annos vndeuiginti natus exercitum priuato consilio, & priuata impensa comparaui &c. quasi velit dicere se primum consulatum adeptum annos fe-re vndeuiginti transegisse. Quot autem dies defuerint, quo minus Augustus tunc attigerit annum vigesimum ætatis, non est obscurum videre: annum enim ætatis vigesimum iniit Augustus anno tertio Iuliano, die 23 Septembris, hoc est IX kal. Octobris: atqui inter 19 Augusti, & 23 Septembris diem vtrinque exclusiue fuerunt interiecti 34 dies: vnde sequitur Augustum Octavianum consulatum inuasisse per vim adacto Senatu, cum ageret annum decimum nonum ætatis, eumque fere expleuisset, deficientibus tantum 34 diebus. Si autem ab inito triumuiratu Augusti Octauiani deducamus principium imperii Augusti, vt Suetonius computare videtur, vtique Augustus iam fuerat ingressus annum vigesimum aetatis: ostendimus enim in calendario Romano Augustum triumuiratum iniisse v kalend. Decembris, hoc est, die 27 Nouembris, currente anno Iuliano tertio: ex quo sequitur Augustum post quam triumuiratu iniisset, transfegisse sexaginta quinque dies ex anno vigesimo aetatis: tot enim dies repetuntur inter 23 Septembris, & 27 Nouembris. Quod si vero placeat dicere, Augustum iniisse annum vigesimum aetatis, cum primum consulatum adipisceretur; animaduertendum est, id fieri ex hypothesi anticipatis scilicet diebus 34. Hac ratione intelligimus Augustum victoriam Actiacam contra Antonium & Cleopatram obtinuisse anno decimo sexto Iuliano, die 2 Septembris, vt Diorefert, vel die 29 Augusti, vt Ptolemaeus computat, quo Actiaca victoria applicetur ad Thoth Nabonasari 719: cum annos 32 fere vixisset, quibus secundum Dionem tantum deerant 10 dies, secundum Ptolemaeum vero 24 dies: & cum monarchiam a primo suo consulatu habuisset fere per tredecim annos, quibus tantum deerant secundum Ptolemaeum dies decem, secundum vero Dionem dies tredecim: vt etiam hic dicere possimus Actiacam Augusti victoriam incurrisse sub initium anni decimi quarti ab imperio Augusti, quod deducitur a primo eius consulatu. Mortuus est Augustus, cum post Actiacam victoriam imperasset fere 44 annos, quibus tantum deerant tredecim dies, licut supra ex Xiphilino explicauimus: cum vixisset Augustus annos 75, menses decem, & dies viginti sex. Unde intelligitur Augustum obiisse anno septuagesimo sexto ætatis suæ, quod etiam testatur Eusebius in Chronicis: atqui annus 76 ætatis Augusti cœpit die 23 Septembris, currente anno quinquagesimo nono Iuliano, & desiit ante 23 Septembris labente anno Iuliano sexagesimo: si enim Augustus adhuc unum mensem cum tredecim diebus vixisset, attigisset diem 23 Septembris, currente anno Iuliano sexagesimo. Quamobrem sine vlla controuersia concludimus Augustum mortuum esse anno Iuliano sexagesimo, die decima nona Augusti, cum post primum consulatum vi a Senatu extortum regnasset præcise annos quinquaginta septem, sicut præclare ostendit Dio. Itaq; falluntur qui imperio Augusti tantum attribuunt 56 annos. Post mortem Augusti successit Tiberius: cuius annum primum imperii nos in supra scripta tabella applicauimus ad initium anni sexagesimi primi Iuliani. Sed vt peruenia tur ad verum initium annorum Tiberii, hoc est, ad mortem Augusti, anticipandi sunt quatuor menses & tredecim dies: nam a decimo nono Augusti die, labente anno Iuliano 60, vsq; ad decimum nonum Augusti diem, currente anno Iuliano 61, intelligitur Tiberius imperasse annum primum: sic a 19 Augusti labente anno 74 Iuliano, vsque 19 Augusti, currente anno Iuliano 75, intelligitur Tiberius imperasse annos quindecim: ita a 19 Augusti labente anno 77 Iuliano, vsq; ad 19 Augusti, currente anno 78 Iuliano, intelligitur Tiberius imperasse annos octodecim. Ex his omnib. videre licet, quanta sit vtilitas in annis Actiacis & Iulianis cognoscendis. nisi enim omnis chronologia ad hos annos reuocetur, nunquam tempus natiuitatis Christi, annorum Christi vsitatorum, & passionis Dominicæ intelligetur. Miror ego sæpius quid in mentem venerit quibusdam, vt afferrent Augu-ftum decessisse anno Iuliano 69[?], die scilicet decima nona Augusti, cum tamen luce meridiana clarius sit Augustum obiisse anno 60[?] Iuliano, die decima nona Augusti. quod quemvis fateri necesse est, qui nobiscum statuit Augustum primum consulatum in-vasisse anno tertio Iuliano, die 19 Augusti, ad finem decurrente anno decimo nono aetatis ipsius, siquidem ei anno absoluendo deerant dies 34, & qui annos imperii Augusti deducit a primo eius consulatu, vt agnoscat ab eo Augustum imperasse annos fere 44, quibus tantum secundum Dionem deerant tredecim dies, donec potiretur Actiaca victoria. Sané mortis Augusti sinistra ad annos Iulianos applicatio viros illos perspicacissimos ita decepit, vt in subsequentium imperatorum Romanorum epochis designandis plurimum aberrarint, & se solos diem passionis Dominicae cognouisse persuasum habuerint, quasi inter baptismum & passionem Dominicam intercesserint quatuor paschata, ita vt Christus quinto paschate, currente anno aetatis ipsius trigesimo quarto, mortem sustinuerit, labente scilicet anno Iuliano 79, die 13 Aprilis. Tiberius post Augustum regnauit annos viginti duos, menses septem & dies septem, vt refert Dio: ex quo colligitur eum decessisse mense Martio, currente anno Iuliano 83, vnde consurgit initium Caligulae, qui interfectus fuit & sensit vindictam Dei, cum regnasset annos tres, menses [?] & viginti octo dies, teste eodem Dione. itaque mortuus est Caligula anno 87 Iuliano, die x kal. Februarii: cui successit Claudius qui veneno interemtus fuit a coniuge Agrippina, cum regnasset annos tredecim, menses octo, & dies viginti. itaque mors [illegible, ~3 letters] incidit in annum Iulianum centesimum, & in diem decimam Octobris, quemadmodum expresse tradatur Dio. A die 13 Octobris, currente anno Iuliano centesimo, Claudio successit Nero, qui seipsum interemit, cum regnasset annos tredecim, & menses octo, teste Dione: ex quo intelligitur Nerone decessisse anno Iuliano centesimo decimo quarto, mense Iunio: huic successit Galba, qui regnavit menses novem & dies tredecim: unde intelligitur Galbam mortuum esse circa finem Martii, currente anno Iuliano centesimo decimo quinto: Galbae successit Otho, qui regnavit 90 dies, hoc est menses fere tres: quamobrem si imperium Othonis numeremus a kal. Aprilis, desiit circa finem Iunii, currente anno Iuliano centesimo decimo quinto. Othonem secutus est Vitellius, homo sumtuosi-[?]simus & luxuriosi-[?]simus, qui regnavit fere annum unum, cui tantum decerant decem dies, teste Dione: ex quo intelligitur, morte Vitellii incidisse circa kalendas Iulias, currente anno Iuliano centesimo decimo sex-to. Etsi autem Vitellius suffragiis populi Romani post mortem Othonis fuerit Imperator nominatus, tamen fato reclamante imperium suscepit, & pessimis moribus statim exosum se reddidit, ut absens Vespasianus in Syria contra Iudaeos pugnans Imperator eligeretur & ab omnibus declararetur. Hinc factum est, ut in chronologia Imperatorum Romanorum nulla habeatur ratio Vitellii, & initium imperii Vespasiani sumatur a morte Othonis, paucis interiectis diebus. Hoc ipsum diligentissime notavit Dio, qui ait inter mortem Neronis, & principium imperii Vespasiani numerari annum unum & viginti duos dies: cum autem Nero mortuus sit anno Iuliano centesimo decimoquarto mense Iunio, intelligitur prinprincipium imperii Vespasiani incurrere in annū centesimum decimum quintū Iulianum, mēse Iulio: hac ratione intelligitur, a morte Neronis ad creationem Vespasiani annū plus minūs interfuisse. Quod autem imperium Vespasiani non fit numerandum a morte Vitellii, sed potius a morte Othonis, siue ab eodem tempore quo etiā Vitellius legitur imperiū suscepisse; pulcherrimè indicat è Dione Xiphilinus, hisce verbis: ἐπειδὴ τὸ ὀ̄ πλεύσει, ἔφη, (Βεσπασιανὸς) Θεὸς ἤδη γενήσομαι. ἔζησε δὲ ἔτη ἐννέα [?] μῆνας ὀκτώ, ἐμονάρ-χησε δὲ ἔτη δέκα [?] ἡμερῶν ἐξ [?], καὶ τότε συμβαίνει αὐτῷ [?] καὶ δύο καὶ εἴκοσιν ἡμέρας ὑπὸ τῆς θανάτου τῆς Νέρωνος μέχρι τῆς Βεσπασιανοῦ ἀρχῆς ἠλθεν. ἐγὼ δὲ τὸ, τὴν μὲν τινὰς ἀπα-ὑπηγγείλαν τὴν ἐξαίρεθμησιν τῷ χρόνῳ τῷ τῆς τὴν ἡγεμονίαν ἔχοντας ποιησάμενοι. ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ διελέξαντο ἀμήλας, ἀλλὰ ζῶντος τε καὶ ἐπ' ἀρχοντος ἐπρύ, ἕκαστος αὐτῶν ὀπὶ [?] Αὐτοκράτωρ, ἀφ' ἧς καὶ ἐς τὸ παρὰ [?] ἱλιν, ἐναυ. δὲ δ' ἡ πάσας σφῶν τὰς ἡμέρας, ὡς καὶ ἐξῆς ἀλλήλαις ἐκ διαδοχῆς γινομέναις, ἀεὶ θμεῖν, ἀλλ' ἐφά-πας ὡς τὴν ἀκρίβειαν τὸ χρόνῳ, καθάπερ εἰρηται μοι, λογί-ζεσθαι. hoc est, Cùm verò sciret sibi moriendum esse, dixit, (Vespasianus) Deus iam fiam. Vixit autem annos sexaginta nouem, & menses octo, cum monarchiam habuisset annis fere decem, quibus tantum deerant sex dies. Atque hinc accidit, vt an-nus vnus & viginti duo dies numerentur pro in-terualllo quod fuit inter mortem Neronis & prin-cipium imperii Vespasiani. Scripsi autem hoc, ne ali-qui deciperentur in supputatione temporis, qui principatum habentes sigillatim enumerarent: isti enim (scilicet Vitellius & Vespasianus) sibi in[?]icem non successerunt, sed potius viuente adhuc principe altero, quilibet ipsorum nouit se Imperatorem esse, à quo tempore saltem obliquè administrationem suscepit. Quare non oportet omnes ipsorum dies, quasi serie continua & secundùm successionem sint elapsi, enumerare, sed potiùs eos simul recensere, quo accurata habeatur temporis designatio, quàdmodum prius à me dictum est. Necessariam hic adiecit Dio de annorum connexione admonitionem, in qua ostendit vel nullam haberi rationem imperii Vitellii, vel cum imperio illius coniungendum esse imperium Vespasiani: quia vterque eodem quasi tempore fuerat designatus imperator: quin immo licet populus Romanus post mortem Othonis Vitellio Imperatore nominasset, diuinitus tamen Vespasiano imperium erat decretum: unde etiam factum est, ut absens Vespasianus exercitu colligeret, eumq; in Urbem Romanam introduceret ad deiiciendum Vitellium, ut in eius vita diligenter recensetur apud Dionem. Itaq; hoc firmissimum esse debet, à morte Neronis usq; ad initium Vespasiani interuenisse annum unum cum diebus viginti duobus: ex quo manifestum est, diem primum Vespasiani cofurgere ex kal. Iulii, currente anno Iuliano centesimo decimo quinto, cum scilicet Tiberius Alexander præfectus Ægypti Alexandrinas legiones primus in Vespasiani verba adegit: qui principatus dies, inquit Suetonius, in posteru obleruatus est. Regnauit Vespasianus annos decem minus sex diebus: itaq; imperium eius desiit circa finem mensis Iunii, currente anno Iuliano centesimo vigesimo quinto. Vespasiano successit Titus, qui teste Dione regnauit annos duos, menses duos, & viginti dies: ex quo intelligi Titu decessisse mense Septembri, currente anno Iuliano centesimo vigesimo septimo. Titu secutus est Domitianus, qui regnauit annos quindecim & quinq; dies, ut testatur Dio: itaq; Domitianus decessit mense Septembri. ptebri, currente anno Iuliano 142. Domitiano fuc-ceffit Nerua, qui regnauit annum vnū, menfes qua-tuor,& dies noue, tefte Dione: ex quo apparet Ner-uam deceffiffe mefe Ianuario, ineunte anno Iuliano centefimo quadragefimo quarto. Neruā fecutus eft Traianus, qui regnauit annos nouendecim, menfes fex, & dies quindecim, tefte Dione. Itaq; Traianus obiit menfe Iulio, currente anno Iuliano centefimo fexagefimo tertio: cui fucceffit Adrianus, qui re-gnauit annos viginti & menfes vndecim, vt teftatur Dio: ex quo intelligitur Adrianum obiiffe menfe Iu-nio,labente anno centefimo octogefimo quarto Iu-liano. Adriano fucceffit Antoninus Pius,qui regnauit annos viginti quatuor,tefte Dione: ex quo fequitur Antoninum Pium deceffiffe menfe Iunio,currente anno Iuliano 208. Antonini Pium fecutus eft Mar-cus Antoninus Philofophus, qui tefte Dione regna-uit nouendecim annos & vndecim dies: ex quo in-telligitur Marcu Antoninum e viuis exceffiffe menfe Iunio, labente anno Iuliano ducentefimo vigefimo feptimo: quanquī fcribat Dio eu obiiffe die decima feptima Martii, fed ipfe interualla menfium quae nos obiter indicauimus,exactiffime fupputauit:propter-ea nos eius relationevt authenticam deinceps feque-mur. Marco Antonino fucceffit filius Commodus, qui tefte Dione regnauit annos duodecim, menfes noue,& dies quatuordecim.fi itaq; a decima feptima Martii die,labente anno Iuliano 227,fumamus initiu imperii Comodi,intelligemus Commodu deceffiffe menfe lanuario, ineunte anno Iuliano ducentefimo quadragefimo. Commodo fucceffit Pertinax qui re-gnauit octoginta fepte dies.hunc fecutus eft Iulianus Didius,qui regnauit fexaginta fex dies,vt refert Dio: itaq; imperium amborum horum Imperatorum du- rauit tantùm centum & quinquaginta tres dies, vt fi à kal. Ianuariis, anno ineunte Iuliano ducente fimo quadragefimo Pertinacis imperium deducamus, Iu- lianus Didius intelligatur mortuus effe fub principiu menfis Iunii: quādo cœpit imperare Seuerus,qui re- gnauit annos fcp,rendecim,&mefes octo,&dies tres, tefte Dione: ex quo intelligitur ipfum obiiffe menfe Februario, currente anno ducentefimo quinquage- fimo octauo Iuliano. Seuero fucceflit Antonin' Ca- racallus, qui regnauit annos fex, & menfes duos, te- fte Dione: vnde intelligitur, Antoninũ Caracallum deceflifle menfe Aprili, currente anno Iuliano ducē- tefimo fexagefimo quarto. Antonino Caracallo fuc- ceflit Macrinus,qui regnauit annũ,&duos fere men- fes,quib°tantum triduũ deerat,tefte Dione:hinc in- telligitur Macrinum deceflifle menfe Iunio, currete anno Iuliano ducentefimo fexagefimo quinto. Poft Macrinũ fecutus eft Pfeudantoninus Sardanapalus, qui regnauit annos tres,menfes nouem,& dies qua- tuor,tefte Dione:ex quo fequitur,Pfeudàtoninũ de- ceflifle menfe Martio,currente anno Iuliano ducen- tefimo fexagefimo nono. Hunc excepit Alexander Mamæx filius,quo imperante hiftoria fuam Roma- nã finiuitDio. Atq; hactenus recefuimus fucceflio- nes Imperatorũ Romanorum,&oftendimus vetiflī- mam connexione annorũ: reftat vt videamus, quo- modo hæc cũ epochis Ptolemaicis conueniant,quas ipfe in annis Domitiani,Traiani,Adriani,&Antoni- ni Pii annotauit. Diximus Titũ deceflifle menfe Se- ptembri,currente anno Iuliano centefimo vigefimo feptimo,quo tépore illi fucceflit Domitianus:at Pto- lemæus principiũ imperiiDomitiani refert ad Thoth NaboNabonasari octingetesimū vigesimū nonum, notatum litera c, qui incurrit in diem tertiā Augusti, feriam sextam, currente anno Iuliano centesimo vigesimo sexto: itaq; Ptolemaeus anno integro citius quam Dio imperiū Domitiani orditur. Nā Ptolemaeus lib.7 Almagesti cap. 3 copulat annū 1 2 Domitiani cū anno Nabonasari 840, ex quo sequitur annū primum Domitiani coniungendū esse cū anno Nabonasari 829.
units.tr: Augustus was born in the seventeenth year before the Julian reform, on 23 September. Since we apply the first year of Augustus's life to the beginning of the year sixteen before the Julian reform, three months and seven days must be advanced to reach the true date of his birth. For from 23 September in the seventeenth year before the Julian reform to 23 September in the sixteenth year before it, Augustus is understood to have completed his first year of life. The same comparison must be observed in the following years. Thus we apply the twentieth year of Augustus's life to the beginning of the fourth Julian year, although that year began on 25 September in the third Julian year. For from 23 September in the course of the third Julian year to 23 September in the fourth Julian year, Augustus is understood to have completed his twentieth year of life. From this a doubt is resolved: when Augustus Octavianus entered upon his first consulship, had he begun his twentieth year of life, or was he then nineteen years old? Augustus Octavianus entered upon his first consulship in the third Julian year, as we have shown in the Roman calendar, on 19 August, that is, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, as we reported a little earlier from Xiphilinus. If, therefore, we date the beginning of Augustus's rule from his first consulship, when he drew up his army against his father's murderers, as Dio does, then Augustus had certainly not yet completed his nineteenth year of life. Augustus himself admits this in his list of the deeds he performed, which Andreas Schottus published thanks to the kindness of Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq. In it Augustus writes of himself: "Being nineteen years old, I raised an army on my own counsel and at my own expense, etc." It is as if he wished to say that he had lived almost nineteen years when he obtained his first consulship. How many days were lacking before Augustus reached the twentieth year of his life at that time is not hard to see. For Augustus entered his twentieth year of life in the third Julian year on 23 September, that is, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. Yet between 19 August and 23 September, both days excluded, there lie 34 days. From this it follows that Augustus Octavianus seized the consulship by force, with the Senate compelled, when he was in his nineteenth year of life and had nearly completed it, lacking only 34 days. If, on the other hand, we date the beginning of Augustus Octavianus's rule from the start of his triumvirate, as Suetonius seems to reckon, then Augustus had certainly already entered his twentieth year of life. For we have shown in the Roman calendar that Augustus entered the triumvirate on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, that is, on 27 November in the third Julian year. From this it follows that after he entered the triumvirate, Augustus had completed sixty-five days of his twentieth year of life, for that many days lie between 23 September and 27 November. But if one prefers to say that Augustus entered his twentieth year of life when he obtained his first consulship, it must be noted that this holds only on the hypothesis of the 34 days being anticipated. In this way we understand that Augustus gained the victory at Actium over Antony and Cleopatra in the sixteenth Julian year, on 2 September, as Dio reports, or on 29 August, as Ptolemy computes, so that the Actian victory falls on Thoth of the 719th year of Nabonassar. Augustus had then lived nearly 32 years, of which, according to Dio, only 10 days were lacking, and according to Ptolemy 24 days. And since he had held the monarchy from his first consulship for nearly thirteen years, of which, according to Ptolemy, only ten days were lacking, but according to Dio thirteen days, we can say here too that Augustus's victory at Actium fell near the beginning of the fourteenth year of his rule, reckoned from his first consulship. Augustus died after he had ruled for nearly 44 years after the Actian victory, of which, as we explained above from Xiphilinus, only thirteen days were lacking. He had lived 75 years, ten months and twenty-six days. From this it is understood that Augustus died in the seventy-sixth year of his life, as Eusebius also testifies in his Chronicle. Yet the seventy-sixth year of Augustus's life began on 23 September in the fifty-ninth Julian year and ended before 23 September in the sixtieth Julian year. For if Augustus had lived one more month and thirteen days, he would have reached 23 September in the sixtieth Julian year. Therefore we conclude without any controversy that Augustus died in the sixtieth Julian year, on 19 August, having reigned after his first consulship, which he obtained by force from the Senate, exactly fifty-seven years, as Dio clearly shows. Hence those are mistaken who attribute only 56 years to Augustus's rule. After Augustus's death Tiberius succeeded. We have applied the first year of his reign in the table above to the beginning of the sixty-first Julian year. But to reach the true beginning of Tiberius's years, that is, the death of Augustus, four months and thirteen days must be advanced. For from 19 August in the course of the sixtieth Julian year to 19 August in the sixty-first Julian year, Tiberius is understood to have completed his first year of rule. Likewise, from 19 August in the course of the seventy-fourth Julian year to 19 August in the seventy-fifth Julian year, Tiberius is understood to have completed fifteen years, and from 19 August in the course of the seventy-seventh Julian year to 19 August in the seventy-eighth Julian year, Tiberius is understood to have completed eighteen years. From all these things one can see how useful it is to know the Actian and Julian years. For unless all chronology is referred to these years, the time of Christ's birth, of the Christian years commonly used, and of the Lord's passion will never be understood. I often marvel what came into the minds of certain men who maintain that Augustus died in the sixty-ninth Julian year, namely on 19 August, when it is clearer than broad daylight that Augustus died in the sixtieth Julian year, on 19 August. Anyone who agrees with us that Augustus seized the first consulship in the third Julian year, on 19 August, at the end of the nineteenth year of his own life, must concede this, since 34 days were lacking to complete that year. And whoever reckons the years of Augustus's rule from his first consulship must admit that Augustus ruled for nearly 44 years, of which, according to Dio, only thirteen days were lacking until he obtained the victory at Actium. Certainly the unlucky application of Augustus's death to the Julian years deceived those most keen-sighted men so much that they went badly wrong in fixing the epochs of the later Roman emperors. They were persuaded that they alone had known the day of the Lord's passion, as if four Passovers had intervened between Christ's baptism and his passion, so that Christ suffered at his fifth Passover, in the thirty-fourth year of his age, that is, in the course of the seventy-ninth Julian year, on 13 April. Tiberius ruled after Augustus for twenty-two years, seven months and seven days, as Dio reports. From this it is gathered that he died in March of the eighty-third Julian year, from which the beginning of Caligula is derived. Caligula was killed and felt God's vengeance, having reigned three years, [? months] and twenty-eight days, on the testimony of the same Dio. And so Caligula died in the eighty-seventh Julian year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February. He was succeeded by Claudius, who was poisoned by his wife Agrippina after reigning thirteen years, eight months and twenty days. Thus the death [illegible, about three letters] fell in the hundredth Julian year and on 10 October, as Dio expressly relates. From 13 October in the course of the hundredth Julian year, Claudius was succeeded by Nero, who took his own life after reigning thirteen years and eight months, on the testimony of Dio. From this it is understood that Nero died in June of the hundred and fourteenth Julian year. He was succeeded by Galba, who reigned nine months and thirteen days. So it is understood that Galba died about the end of March in the course of the hundred and fifteenth Julian year. Galba was succeeded by Otho, who reigned 90 days, that is, nearly three months. Therefore, if we reckon Otho's rule from the Kalends of April, it ended about the end of June in the course of the hundred and fifteenth Julian year. Otho was followed by Vitellius, a most extravagant and most luxurious man, who reigned nearly one year, lacking only ten days, on the testimony of Dio. From this it is understood that Vitellius's death fell about the Kalends of July in the course of the hundred and sixteenth Julian year. Although Vitellius was named emperor by the votes of the Roman people after Otho's death, nevertheless, with fate opposing him, he took up the empire, and by his worst conduct he at once made himself hated, so that Vespasian, fighting against the Jews in Syria while absent, was chosen emperor and proclaimed by all. Hence it came about that in the chronology of the Roman emperors no account is taken of Vitellius, and the beginning of Vespasian's rule is dated from the death of Otho, a few days intervening. Dio noted this very carefully. He says that between the death of Nero and the beginning of Vespasian's rule there is counted a period of one year and twenty-two days. Since Nero died in June of the hundred and fourteenth Julian year, it is understood that the beginning of Vespasian's rule fell in the hundred and fifteenth Julian year, in July. In this way it is understood that about a year passed between Nero's death and Vespasian's accession. That Vespasian's rule should be reckoned not from Vitellius's death but rather from Otho's death, or from the same time at which Vitellius too is read to have taken up the empire, Xiphilinus, from Dio, shows very clearly in these words: "When Vespasian, as he said, perceived that he must die, he said, 'I shall now become a god.' He lived sixty-nine years and eight months, and held the monarchy for nearly ten years, lacking six days. And so it came about that the interval between Nero's death and the beginning of Vespasian's rule amounted to one year and twenty-two days." [ἐπειδὴ τὸ ἀποθανεῖσθαι ᾔσθετο, ἔφη, Θεὸς ἤδη γίγνομαι· ἔζησε δὲ ἔτη ἐνενήκοντα ... μῆνας ὀκτώ, ἐμονάρχησε δὲ ἔτη δέκα ... ἡμερῶν ἕξ· καὶ οὕτως συνέβη αὐτῷ ... ἔτος ἓν καὶ δύο καὶ εἴκοσιν ἡμέρας ἀπὸ τῆς Νέρωνος τελευτῆς μέχρι τῆς Οὐεσπασιανοῦ ἀρχῆς ἠλθεν.] Dio adds: "I have set out the reckoning of the time of those who held the principate in order, but some reckon it differently. For they did not succeed one another, but while the previous emperor was still alive and ruling, each of them proclaimed himself Imperator, from which time he took up the administration, at least obliquely. Therefore one ought not to count all their days as if they had passed in a continuous series and in succession, but rather to recount them together, so that a precise designation of time is kept, as I said before." Dio, in fact, adds here a necessary admonition about the connection of the years, in which he shows either that no account is taken of Vitellius's rule, or that Vespasian's rule must be joined with his: both were, as it were, appointed emperor at the same time. Indeed, although the Roman people had named Vitellius emperor after Otho's death, the empire had been divinely decreed to Vespasian. Hence also it came about that Vespasian, though absent, gathered an army and led it into the city of Rome to overthrow Vitellius, as is carefully recounted in Dio's account of Vitellius's life. So this must be held as most certain: between Nero's death and the beginning of Vespasian's rule there passed one year with twenty-two days. From this it is clear that Vespasian's first day falls on the Kalends of July in the hundred and fifteenth Julian year, when Tiberius Alexander, prefect of Egypt, was the first to bring the Alexandrian legions to swear allegiance to Vespasian. This day of the principate, says Suetonius, was observed afterwards. Vespasian reigned ten years less six days, so his rule ended about the end of June in the hundred and twenty-fifth Julian year. Vespasian was succeeded by Titus, who, on the testimony of Dio, reigned two years, two months and twenty days. From this it is understood that Titus died in September of the hundred and twenty-seventh Julian year. Titus was followed by Domitian, who reigned fifteen years and five days, as Dio attests. So Domitian died in September of the hundred and forty-second Julian year. Domitian was succeeded by Nerva, who reigned one year, four months and nine days, on the testimony of Dio. From this it appears that Nerva died in January, at the beginning of the hundred and forty-fourth Julian year. Nerva was followed by Trajan, who reigned nineteen years, six months and fifteen days, on the testimony of Dio. So Trajan died in July of the hundred and sixty-third Julian year. He was succeeded by Hadrian, who reigned twenty years and eleven months, as Dio testifies. From this it is understood that Hadrian died in June, in the course of the hundred and eighty-fourth Julian year. Hadrian was succeeded by Antoninus Pius, who reigned twenty-four years, on the testimony of Dio. From this it follows that Antoninus Pius died in June, in the course of the 208th Julian year. Antoninus Pius was followed by Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, who, on the testimony of Dio, reigned nineteen years and eleven days. From this it is understood that Marcus Antoninus departed this life in June, in the course of the 227th Julian year. Although Dio writes that he died on the seventeenth day of March, nevertheless Dio himself reckoned the intervals of months, which we have noted in passing, most exactly; therefore we shall follow his account from now on as authentic. Marcus Antoninus was succeeded by his son Commodus, who, on the testimony of Dio, reigned twelve years, nine months and fourteen days. If therefore we take the beginning of Commodus's reign from 17 March in the course of the 227th Julian year, we shall understand that Commodus died in January, at the beginning of the 240th Julian year. Commodus was succeeded by Pertinax, who reigned eighty-seven days. He was followed by Julian Didius, who reigned sixty-six days, as Dio reports. So the rule of these two emperors together lasted only 153 days, so that if we date Pertinax's rule from the Kalends of January in the 240th Julian year, Julian Didius is understood to have died near the beginning of June. Then Severus began to rule, who reigned eighteen years, eight months and three days, on the testimony of Dio. From this it is understood that he died in February, in the course of the 258th Julian year. Severus was succeeded by Antoninus Caracalla, who reigned six years and two months, on the testimony of Dio. Hence it is understood that Antoninus Caracalla died in April, in the course of the 264th Julian year. Antoninus Caracalla was succeeded by Macrinus, who reigned one year and nearly two months, lacking only three days, on the testimony of Dio. From this it is understood that Macrinus died in June, in the course of the 265th Julian year. After Macrinus, Pseudantoninus Sardanapalus followed, who reigned three years, nine months and four days, on the testimony of Dio. From this it follows that Pseudantoninus died in March, in the course of the 269th Julian year. He was succeeded by Alexander Mamaea's son, under whose rule Dio ended his Roman History. Thus far we have traced the successions of the Roman emperors and shown the most ancient connection of the years. It remains to see how these agree with the Ptolemaic epochs, which he himself noted in the years of Domitian, Trajan, Hadrian and Antoninus Pius. We said that Titus died in September, in the course of the 127th Julian year, when Domitian succeeded him. But Ptolemy refers the beginning of Domitian's rule to Thoth of the 829th year of Nabonassar, marked with the letter C, which falls on the third day of August, a Friday, in the course of the 126th Julian year. So Ptolemy begins Domitian's rule a full year earlier than Dio. For Ptolemy, in book 7 of the Almagest, chapter 3, links the twelfth year of Domitian with the 840th year of Nabonassar, from which it follows that the first year of Domitian must be joined with the 829th year of Nabonassar.

units.la: Nerua excessit mēse Ianuario, ineunte anno Iuliano centesimo quadragesimo quarto, quo tēpore imperium suscepit Traianus: at Ptolemaeus principium imperii Traiani confert in Thoth Nabonasari octingetesimum quadragesimum quintum, qui incidit in trigesimā die Iulii, feriam primam, currente anno Iuliano 142: itaq; Ptolemaeus anno uno cum dimidio citius auspicatur epocham Traiani quàm Dio. Traianus decessit mēse Iulio, currente anno Iuliano centesimo sexagesimo tertio, quo tēpore illi successit Adrianus: at Ptolemaeus principium imperii Adriani numerat à Thoth Nabonasari octingetesimo sexagesimo quarto, qui incurrit in 25 Iulii, feriam sextam, currente anno Iuliano centesimo sexagesimo primo: itaq; biennio integro citius quàm Dio numerat Ptolemaeus epocha Adriani. Adrianus obiit mēse Iunio, labente anno Iuliano 184, quo tempore illi successit Antoninus Pius, siue primus: at Ptolemaeus cū Censorino æram Antonini auspicatur à Thoth Nabonasari 88[?]5, qui incurrit in vigesimam diem Iulii, feriam sextam, currente anno Iuliano 882: itaq; etiam hic Ptolemaeus cū Censorino biennio integro citius quàm Dio exorditur epocha Antonini Pii. Sed quæ causa est, quòd tanto interuallo epochæ Ptolemaicæ differant à vera historia Romana, quam exquisitissimè tradidit Dio? Ptolemæus sequitur hypotheses Græcorum & Ægyptiorum, qui annos imperatorum Romanorum æqualiter applicant ad principia annorum Nabonassari, quod etiam Menelaum Geometram Romanum ante Ptolemæum fecisse, videre licet libro 7 Almagesti, cap. 3. Neq; Græci & Ægyptii æqualiter tantum applicant annos imperatorum Romanorum ad annos Nabonassari, verum etiam certa interualla obseruant & principia, in quibus cum Romanis non conueniunt: quod nos perspicue docet Maximus monachus in computo. Si enim annos æquabiles accipiamus, & seriem sequamur à Maximo præscriptam, videbimus summam conuenientiam esse cum relationibus Menelai, Censorini & Ptolemæi: etenim Græci Iulio Cæsari primo Romanorum imperatori quadriennium assignant à primo eius inito consulatu, qui incidit in annum tertium ante ordinationem Iulianam, currente anno Urbis conditæ septingentesimo sexto: Ægyptii autem consulatum primum Cæsaris auspicantur à Thoth Nabonassari septingentesimo primo, qui incurrit in quartam Septembris, currente anno tertio ante ordinationem Iulianam. Augusto Cæsari statim à cæde Iulii Cæsaris Græci assignant quinquaginta septe annos, quorum initium sumunt ab anno secundo Iuliano, & Urbis conditæ septingentesimo decimo: Ægyptii autem à subsequenti Thoth Nabonassari septingentesimo quinto, qui incidit in tertiam Septembris, currente anno secundo Iuliano, deducunt imperium Augusti Octauiani. Quo cognito facile illis possumus respondere, qui quærunt an imperium Augusti Cæsaris sumendum sit statim à cæde Iulii Cæsaris, quæ incurrit in annum secundum Iulianum, an vero deducendum fit a primo Augusti Octauiani consulatu, queminiit die decima nona Augusti, currente anno tertio Iuliano? Sane vtrumq; habet locum. Dio enim Romanus historicus, quem nos hactenus fumus fe- cuti, imperium Augusti Octauiani supputat ab eius primo consulatu: quia inde vfq; ab Actiacam victo- riam dicit intercefliffe annos quadraginta quatuor, minus tredecim diebus. At Graeci cum Aegyptiis im- perium Augusti Octauiani deducunt ab ipsa caede Caesaris, vel a Thoth proxime subsequenti: quam hypothefin etiam Ptolemaeus est secutus. Tiberio Caesari Graeci tribuunt viginti duos annos, quos in- cipiunt ab anno Vrbis conditae feptingetefimo fexa- gefimo septimo, qui incurrit in annum Iulianu quin- quagefimum nonum: Aegyptii autem eosdem inci- piunt a subsequenti Thoth Nabonafari feptingente- fimo sexagesimo fecundo, qui incurrit in vigefimam Augusti, currente anno Iuliano quinquagesimo no- no. Caligulae Graeci tribuunt quadriennium, cuius initium fumum ad anno Vrbis conditae feptingente- fimo octogesimo ...no, qui incurrit in annum octo- gefimum primum Iulianu. Sed Aegyptii quadriennium illud auspicantur a Thoth Nabonafari feptingente- fimo octogesimo quarto, qui incidit ... quarta Augusti, currente anno Iuliano octogesimo primo. Claudio assignat Graeci annos quatuordecim, quorum initiu deducunt ab anno Vrbis conditae feptingente- fimo nonagesimo tertio, qui incurrit in annu Iuliam num octogefimu quintu: sed Aegyptii imperiu Clau- dii numerant a Thoth Nabonafari septingentesimo octogesimo octauo, qui incidit in decimam tertiam Augusti, currente anno octogesimo quinto Iuliano.
units.tr: Nerva died in the month of January, at the beginning of the Julian year 144, when Trajan took up the empire. But Ptolemy dates the beginning of Trajan's reign from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 845, which fell on the thirtieth day of July, a Sunday, in the Julian year 142. So Ptolemy begins Trajan's epoch a year and a half earlier than Dio does. Trajan died in the month of July, in the Julian year 163, when Hadrian succeeded him. But Ptolemy counts the beginning of Hadrian's reign from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 864, which fell on the twenty-fifth of July, a Friday, in the Julian year 161. So Ptolemy dates Hadrian's epoch a full two years earlier than Dio does. Hadrian died in the month of June, in the Julian year 184, when Antoninus Pius, or the First, succeeded him. But Ptolemy, together with Censorinus, begins the era of Antoninus from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 885, which fell on the twentieth day of July, a Friday, in the Julian year 882 (sic; 142 was the year of the era's start, so this reads as the Julian year 882 in the Nabonassar reckoning). So here too Ptolemy, together with Censorinus, begins the epoch of Antoninus Pius a full two years earlier than Dio. But what is the reason that the Ptolemaic epochs differ so much from the true Roman history, which Dio handed down most exactly? Ptolemy follows the hypotheses of the Greeks and Egyptians, who apply the years of the Roman emperors evenly to the beginnings of the years of Nabonassar. That Menelaus the Roman geometer also did this before Ptolemy may be seen in book 7 of the Almagest, chapter 3. Nor do the Greeks and Egyptians merely apply the years of the Roman emperors evenly to the years of Nabonassar; they also observe certain intervals and beginnings in which they do not agree with the Romans. Maximus the monk clearly teaches this in his computation. For if we take the years as equal and follow the sequence prescribed by Maximus, we shall see that there is complete agreement with the reckonings of Menelaus, Censorinus and Ptolemy. The Greeks assign to Julius Caesar, the first Roman emperor, four years counted from his first entry upon the consulship, which fell in the third year before the Julian reform, in the year 706 from the founding of the City. The Egyptians, however, begin Caesar's first consulship from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 701, which fell on the fourth of September, in the third year before the Julian reform. To Augustus Caesar, the Greeks assign fifty-seven years from the murder of Julius Caesar itself, reckoning their beginning from the second Julian year and the 710th year from the founding of the City. The Egyptians, however, reckon from the following Thoth of the Nabonassar era 705, which fell on the third of September, in the second Julian year, as the start of the reign of Octavian Augustus. Knowing this, we can easily answer those who ask whether the reign of Augustus Caesar should be counted from the murder of Julius Caesar, which falls in the second Julian year, or rather be dated from the first consulship of Octavian Augustus, which fell on the nineteenth day of August in the third Julian year. Indeed, both have their place. For Dio the Roman historian, whom we have followed so far, reckons the reign of Octavian Augustus from his first consulship, since from the Actian victory, he says, forty-four years less thirteen days had passed. But the Greeks, with the Egyptians, date the reign of Octavian Augustus from the murder of Caesar itself, or from the Thoth immediately following; Ptolemy too followed this hypothesis. To Tiberius Caesar the Greeks assign twenty-two years, which they begin from the year 767 from the founding of the City, which falls in the fifty-ninth Julian year. The Egyptians, however, begin the same years from the following Thoth of the Nabonassar era 762, which fell on the twentieth of August, in the fifty-ninth Julian year. To Caligula the Greeks assign four years, whose beginning they take from the year 780 from the founding of the City, which falls in the eighty-first Julian year. But the Egyptians begin that four-year period from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 784, which fell on the fourth of August, in the eighty-first Julian year. To Claudius the Greeks assign fourteen years, whose beginning they derive from the year 793 from the founding of the City, which falls in the eighty-fifth Julian year. But the Egyptians count Claudius's reign from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 788, which fell on the thirteenth of August, in the eighty-fifth Julian year.

units.la: Neroni Graeci tribuunt etiam annos quatuordecim, quos auspicantur ab anno Vrbis conditæ octingen-tesimo septimo, qui incurrit in annum nonagesimū Iulianum: verum Ægyptii Neronis imperium dedu-cunt à Thoth Nabonasari octingentesimo secundo, qui incidit in decimā Augusti, currente anno Iuliano nonagesimo nono. Deinceps Galbam & Othonem omittunt Græci cum Ægyptiis, quorū tamen ambo-rum imperium teste Dione durauit integrū annum, & statim Vespasianū subiungunt: ex quo euidens est, ipsos quoq; Vitellium omittere. Sed in eare [?] minime peccarur [?], cum etiā Dio ostendat Vitellium in catalo-go imperatorum Romanorum esse prætereundum, & imperium Vespasiani inchoadum esse ab eo tem-pore, quo Vitellius à populo Romano fuerat impe-rator nominatus. Cum autem Galbam & Othonem Græci cū Ægyptiis omittant, fit vt in annis subsequē-tibus epochæ ipsorum iusto citius assignentur. Sed quod Græci omittat in serie annorum Galba, Otho-nem, & Vitellii, luculenter videre licet in computo Maximi monachi: is enim statim post Neronem assi-gnat Vespasiano annos decem, quorum initium sup-putat ab anno Vrbis conditæ octingentesimo vigesi-mo primo, qui inci-dit in annum Iulianum centesimū decimum: eadem ratione Ægyptii initium Vespasiani referūt ad annum Nabonasari octingen-tesimum decimum sextum, cuius principium incur-rit in diem sextam Augusti, currente anno Iuliano centesimo decimo tertio. Tito assignant Græci tri-ennium, cuius initium deducunt ab anno Vrbis con-dita octingentesimo trigesimo primo, qui incidit in annum Iulianum centesimum vigesimum tertium: Ægyptii autem imperium Titi supputant a Thoth Na-bonasari octingentesimo vigesimo sexto, qui incur-rit die rit die quarta Augusti, currente anno Iuliano cente-simo vigesimo tertio. Domitiano Græci assignant quindecim annos, quorum initiu sumut ab anno Vrbis conditæ octingetesimo trigesimoquarto, qui incidit in annum Iulianum centesimum vigesimum sextum: sed Ægyptii principium imperii Domitiani deducut a Thoth Nabonasari octingetesimo vigesimo nono, qui incidit in diem tertiam Augusti, currente anno Iuliano centesimo vigesimo sexto. Neruæ Græci tri-buunt vnum annum, cuius initium sumunt ab anno Vrbis conditæ octingetesimo quadragesimo nono, qui incurrit in annum Iulianum centesimum quadragesimum primum: sed Ægyptii annum primum Neruæ auspicantur a Thoth Nabonasari octingen-tesimo quadragesimo quarto, qui incidit in diem tri-gesimam Iulii, currente anno centesimo quadrage-simo primo Iuliano: idem intelligitur facere Ptole-mæus, qui ab æra Domitiani vsq; ad æram Traiani interuallum ponit annorum Ægyptiorum sedecim, quod ita accipiendum est, quasi Domitiano tribuat quindecim annos, Neruæ autem assignet annum vnum: vel quod Neruam omittat, & loco illius Do-mitiano assignet sedecim annos. Traiano Græci as-signant nouendecim annos, ersi in computo Maxi-mi librariorum culpa scribantur tantum anni octo-decim: horum nouendecim annorum initiu suppu-tant ab anno Vrbis conditæ octingentesimo quin-quagesimo, qui incurrit in annum Iulianum cente-simum quadragesimum secundum: sed Ægyptii epo-cham Traiani referunt ad Thoth Nabonasari octin-gentesimum quadragesimum quintu, qui incidit in diem trigesimam Iulii, currente anno Iuliano cente-simo quadragesimo secudo. Adriano Græci assignāt annos viginti & unū,quorum initium sumunt ab an-no Urbis conditæ octingentesimo sexagesimo nono, qui incurrit in annum Iulianum centesimū sexagesi-mum primū: sed Ægyptii imperiū Adriani deducunt ab anno Nabonasari octingentesimo sexagesimo quar-to,qui incidit in 1 s Iulii[?], currente anno Iuliano centesimo sexagesimo primo. Antonino Pio Græci tri-buunt annos viginti,quorum initium sumunt ab anno Urbis conditæ octingentesimo nonagesimo,qui in-currit in annum Iulianum centesimū octogesimū se-cundum: sed Ægyptii imperiū Antonini Pii auspican-tur à Thoth Nabonasari octingentesimo octogesimo quinto, qui incidit in die vigesima Iulii,currente anno Iuliano centesimo octogesimo secundo. Hinc appa-ret,qua ratione Ptolemæus & Censorinus in suppu-tandis annis imperatorum Romanorum discrepent à reliquis historicis: quod diligenter animadverten-dum est, ne putemus Ptolemæum & Censorinum malam connexionem annorum tradidisse, ut non-nulli somniant hypothesium ignari.
units.tr: To Nero the Greeks also assign fourteen years, which they count from the year 807 from the founding of the City, which falls in the ninetieth Julian year. But the Egyptians derive Nero's reign from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 802, which fell on the tenth of August, in the ninety-ninth Julian year. After this the Greeks together with the Egyptians omit Galba and Otho, although, according to Dio, the reign of each of them lasted a full year; and they immediately add Vespasian. From this it is evident that they also omit Vitellius. Yet they do not err at all in this, since Dio also shows that Vitellius must be passed over in the catalogue of Roman emperors, and that the reign of Vespasian must be dated from the time when Vitellius had been named emperor by the Roman people. But since the Greeks together with the Egyptians omit Galba, Otho and Vitellius, it follows that in the later years their epochs are assigned too early by just that much. That the Greeks omit Galba, Otho and Vitellius from the sequence of years can be clearly seen in the computation of Maximus the monk. For he immediately after Nero assigns ten years to Vespasian, which he reckons from the year 821 from the founding of the City, which falls in the 110th Julian year. In the same way the Egyptians refer the beginning of Vespasian to the Nabonassar year 816, whose beginning fell on the sixth day of August, in the 113th Julian year. To Titus the Greeks assign three years, whose beginning they derive from the year 831 from the founding of the City, which falls in the 123rd Julian year. But the Egyptians reckon the reign of Titus from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 826, which fell on the fourth of August, in the 123rd Julian year. To Domitian the Greeks assign fifteen years, whose beginning they take from the year 834 from the founding of the City, which falls in the 126th Julian year. But the Egyptians derive the beginning of Domitian's reign from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 829, which fell on the third of August, in the 126th Julian year. To Nerva the Greeks assign one year, whose beginning they take from the year 849 from the founding of the City, which falls in the 141st Julian year. But the Egyptians begin Nerva's first year from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 844, which fell on the thirtieth of July, in the 141st Julian year. The same thing seems to be done by Ptolemy, who places between the era of Domitian and the era of Trajan an interval of sixteen Egyptian years. This must be understood as though he assigns fifteen years to Domitian and one year to Nerva; or else he omits Nerva and assigns sixteen years to Domitian in his place. To Trajan the Greeks assign nineteen years, although in the computation of Maximus the copyists' error has written only eighteen years. They reckon the beginning of these nineteen years from the year 850 from the founding of the City, which falls in the 142nd Julian year. But the Egyptians refer the epoch of Trajan to Thoth of the Nabonassar era 845, which fell on the thirtieth of July, in the 142nd Julian year. To Hadrian the Greeks assign twenty-one years, whose beginning they take from the year 869 from the founding of the City, which falls in the 161st Julian year. But the Egyptians derive Hadrian's reign from the Nabonassar year 864, which fell on the twenty-fifth of July, in the 161st Julian year. To Antoninus Pius the Greeks assign twenty years, whose beginning they take from the year 890 from the founding of the City, which falls in the 182nd Julian year. But the Egyptians begin the reign of Antoninus Pius from Thoth of the Nabonassar era 885, which fell on the twentieth day of July, in the 182nd Julian year. From this it appears for what reason Ptolemy and Censorinus differ from the other historians in reckoning the years of the Roman emperors. This must be noted carefully, lest we think that Ptolemy and Censorinus handed down a faulty connection of years, as some do who dream of it, being ignorant of the hypotheses.

units.la: Hisce omnibus præmissis facilius nobis erit osté-dere, Christum salvatorem nostrum passum esse anno decimo octavo Tiberii, cū baptizatus fuisset sub principium anni decimi quinti Tiberii,pro ut Roma-ni secundum Dionem numerant annos imperii Au-gusti Octaviani & Tiberii Cæsaris. Christum bap-tizatum esse in Iordane ante diem sextum Iduum No-vembris,in consulatu duorum Geminorum, hoc est, C.Rubellii,& C.Rufii,quorum uterq; Gemini cogno-mentū habebat, ut refert Tacitus lib. v, testis locu-pletissimus est D. Epiphanius. Quod autem consu-latus duorum Geminorum inciderit in annum Urbis conditæ septingentesimum octogesimum secundum, pulcherpul[?]herrimè ex antiquitatibus Romanis eruit Onu-frius Panuinius: ex quo colligitur, cum annus Vrbis condita 781 inciderit in annum Iulianum 74; annū decimum quintum Tiberii coepisse die decima nona Augusti, currete eodem anno Iuliano septuagesimo quarto, quod etiam prius indicauimus cumq; secundum hypothesin Epiphanii Christus sit baptizatus ante diem sextū Iduum Nouembris; sequitur Tibe-rium Caesarem ex anno decimo quinto aetatis transe-gisse duos menses & viginti dies, cum Christus baptizaretur a Ioanne in Iordane. Sequitur etiam Christum tunc nondum copleuisse annum vigesimum nonum aetatis suae, hoc est annum vigesimum nonum ab usita-ta aera Christi inchoatum, cuius principium incidit in kal. Ianuarias anni 46 Iuliani; vel si exi-stimemus Christum natum esse circa principiū anni 45 Iuliani, sequi-tur eum nodum compleuisse annum trigesimū aeta-tis suae, cum sacrum lauacrum suscipieret. Sane Lucas Euangelista scribit in principio tertii capitis, anno decimo quinto imperii Tiberii Caesaris Christum ve-nisse in omne regionē Iordanis, & praedicasse bapti-smū poenitentiae in remissionē peccatorum, eodēq; anno fuisse a Ioanne baptizatum: quod etiā in chro-nica sua retulit Eusebius Caesariensis. Hoc fundamē-tum est, a quo nullo modo est discedendum. Quod vero apud Lucam additur, καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος, vel vt D. Epiphanius citat, ἦν δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, rectè est interpretandum: non enim vult Euangelista Christum, cum baptizaretur, primum iniisse annum trigesimum aetatis, tunc enim non opus fuisset adiicere particulam ὡσεί, id est, quasi, vel fere: sed vult Christum baptizatum & praedicantem poenitentiam fere excessisse annum trigefimum ætatis: quamobrem vox ἀρχόμενος fiue præce-dat fiue subsequatur, non est construenda cum ἑτῶν τεσσαράκοντα, quasi inceperit annum trigesimum, sed absolutè est accipienda, quòd scilicet Christus baptizatus fuerit fere annorum triginta, incipiens, hoc est, cùm incepisset prædicare. Hanc interpretationem, quæ optima est, affert Epiphanius, cùm inquit, φησὶ δὲ πρὸς τὴν Ἰωάννην[?] καὶ ἐβαπτίσθη ἐν τῷ Ἰορδάνῃ ποταμῷ[?] τὰ τεσσαρακοστὰ τῆς ἡλικίας[?] ἐνσάρκως[?] scilicet secundum Ægyptios die duodecima Athyr, ante diem sextum Iduum Nouembris. Dico autem quòd circa decimum mensem, venerit (Christus) ad Ioannem, & baptizatus fuerit in Iordane fluuio anno trigesimo natiuitatis suæ, scilicet secundum Ægyptios die duodecima Athyr, ante diem sextum Iduum Nouembris. Ex quibus apparet, fi Christum statuamus natum esse in principio anni quadragesimi quinti Iuliani, eum tempore baptismi, qui incidit circa principium Nouembris, currente anno Iuliano septuagesimo quarto, tranfegifle annos viginti nouem & decem menses, hoc est, expleuisse fere annos triginta, quibus tantum deerant duo menses: atque hoc est, quod scriptura sacra refert, Iesum tunc fuisse filium fere triginta annorum: vt etiam hinc liceat videre, hypothefin Epiphanii, qua asserit Christum natum esse in principio anni quadragesimi quinti Iuliani, hoc est, circa medium quadragesimum fecundum annum ab imperio Augusti, sacris literis magis esse consentaneam, quàm eam quæ statuit Christum natum esse circa finem anni quadragesimi quinti Iuliani, die videlicet vigefima quinta Decembris: nam fecundum hanc hypothefin Christus baptizatus nondum compleuisset annum vigesimū nonū ætatis, quod repugnat histo- riæ Euangelicæ. Porrò Christum passum esse circa tempus vernum currente anno decimo octauo im- perii Tiberii, euidenter probat Eusebius Cæsari- ensis ab admiranda illa circa passionem Dominicam eclipsi solis, quæ in commentariis Ethnicorum dili- genter fuit consignata. is ait, Secundùm prophetias quæ de Deo fuerant prælocutæ, ad passionem ve- nit anno Tiberii XVIII. quo tempore & in aliis Ethni- corum commentariis hæc ad verbum scripta repe- rimus. Solis facta defectio, & tenebræ super vni- uersam terram. Bithynia terræ motu concussa, & in vrbe Nicæna ædes plurimæ corruerunt: quæ o- mnia his congruunt, quæ in passione Saluatoris ac- ciderunt. Scripsit verò super his & Phlegon, qui Olympiadum egregius supputator est, in decimo quarto libro ita dicens: Quarto autem anno du- centesimæ secundæ Olympiadis, magna & excel- lens inter omnes, quæ ante eam acciderant, defe- ctio solis est facta. dies hora sexta ita in tenebro- sam noctem versus, vt stellæ cœlo visæ sint, ter- ræque motus in Bithynia Nicænæ vrbis multas æ- des subuerterit. Hæc supra dictus vir. Argumentum autem huius rei, quòd Saluator isto anno passus sit, Euangelium præbet Ioannis, in quo scribitur, post quintum decimum annum Tiberii Cæsaris tribus annis Dominum prædicasse. Annus quartus Olym- piadis ducentesimæ secundæ, hoc est, annus Olym- piadicus octingentesimus octauus, cœpit à solsti- tio, labente anno Iuliano septuagesimo septimo: itaque passio Dominica subsequente vere incurrit in annum Iulianum septuagesimum octauum, hoc est, in annum decimum octauum Tiberii Caesaris, cuius principiu sumitur a die decima nona Augusti, currente anno Iuliano leptuagesimo leptimo. Sic latis confstat Christum passum esse anno quarto Olympiadis ducentesimae secundae: neq; concedendum est in eorum sententiam, qui autoritatem Phlegontis eludunt, & mendum aliquod in codice ipsius esse suspicantur, quasi pro anno quarto Olympiadis ducentesimae secundae, scribendum sit, anno primo Olympiadis ducentesimae tertiae: hoc enim ideo ab illis dicitur, vt passionem Dominicam referant ad annum subsequentem Iulianum 79, & inter baptismum & passionem Christi probent quatuor pafchata intercefiffe. Nos vero statuimus Christum baptizatum esse ante diem sextum Iduum Nouembris, currente anno Iuliano 74, & paf-chum verno tempore, currente anno Iuliano 78 :itaq; inter baptismum & passionem Christi agnoscimus tria tantum pafchata intercefiffe, quemadmodum Eusebius & Epiphanius testantur: quod etiam non coacte ex historia Euangelica probari potest. Hic vero quaeritur an annus septuagesimus octauus luliánus, in quem passionem Dominicam incidere dixi-mus, fit annus aetatis Christi trigesimus tertius, quemadmodum sensit Ioannes Lucidus cum aliis plerisque, vel fit annus aetatis Christi trigesimus quartus, sicut nonnulli exiftimarunt? Non est dubium, quin annus 78 Iulianus fit trigesimus tertius aetatis Christianae, fiue annorum Christi vsitatorum: an vero fit trigesimus tertius, vel trigesimus quartus aetatis, responderi nö potest nili per distinctionem: quatenus enim ex hypothesi Dionysii Abbatis Romani Christus natus putatur 25 Decebris, ad fine currente anno 45 luliano, eatenus ann° 78 Iulianus est annus aetatis Christi trigesimus tertius, quemadmodum sensit Ioannes Lucidus cum Paulo Burgensi[?], Lyrano, & aliis quos supra nominauimus: illi enim omnes ponunt eosdem esse annos aerae Christianae, & ætatis Christi, vt nativitas Christi intelligatur octiduo tantum præcedere principium annorum Christi vsitatorum.
units.tr: Having set all this out, it will be easier for us to show that Christ our Saviour suffered in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, since he was baptized near the beginning of the fifteenth year of Tiberius, reckoning the years of the reigns of Augustus Octavianus and Tiberius Caesar as the Romans do, following Dio. That Christ was baptized in the Jordan before the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of the two Gemini, that is, of C. Rubellius and C. Rufius, both of whom bore the surname Geminus, as Tacitus reports in book 5, is attested by the very full testimony of St Epiphanius. That the consulship of the two Gemini fell in the year of the city 782 is most ably drawn from the Roman antiquities by Onuphrius Panvinius. From this it follows that, since the year of the city 781 fell in the Julian year 74, the fifteenth year of Tiberius began on the nineteenth day of August, in the same Julian year 74, as we have already noted. And since, according to Epiphanius's hypothesis, Christ was baptized before the sixth day before the Ides of November, it follows that Tiberius Caesar had passed two months and twenty days of his fifteenth year when Christ was baptized by John in the Jordan. It follows also that Christ had not yet completed his twenty-ninth year of age, that is, the twenty-ninth year counted from the usual Christian era, whose beginning falls on 1 January of the Julian year 46. Or, if we think Christ was born about the beginning of the Julian year 45, it follows that he had completed his thirtieth year of age when he received the holy washing. Indeed, the evangelist Luke writes at the beginning of the third chapter that in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Christ came into all the region of the Jordan and preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, and that in the same year he was baptized by John. Eusebius of Caesarea also reports this in his Chronicle. This is the foundation, from which we must in no way depart. As for what is added in Luke, καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος [and Jesus himself was about thirty years old, beginning], or as St Epiphanius cites it, ἦν δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα [Jesus was beginning, about thirty years old], it must be interpreted correctly. For the evangelist does not mean that Christ, when he was baptized, had just entered his thirtieth year; in that case there would have been no need to add the particle ὡσεί, that is, "as if" or "about". Rather he means that Christ, when baptized and preaching repentance, had about passed his thirtieth year of age. Therefore the word ἀρχόμενος [beginning], whether it comes before or after, is not to be construed with ἑτῶν τριάκοντα [thirty years], as if he had begun his thirtieth year, but must be taken absolutely: that Christ was baptized at about thirty years of age, beginning, that is, when he had begun to preach. Epiphanius gives this interpretation, which is the best, when he says: "He says that to John he was baptized in the river Jordan at the fortieth of his age in the flesh" [the text here is corrupt], namely, according to the Egyptians, on the twelfth day of Athyr, before the sixth day before the Ides of November. I say moreover that about the tenth month Christ came to John and was baptized in the river Jordan in the thirtieth year of his birth, namely, according to the Egyptians on the twelfth day of Athyr, before the sixth day before the Ides of November. From these things it appears that, if we set Christ's birth at the beginning of the Julian year 45, then at the time of his baptism, which fell about the beginning of November in the Julian year 74, he had passed twenty-nine years and ten months, that is, had nearly completed thirty years, lacking only two months. And this is what Holy Scripture reports, that Jesus was then about thirty years old. From this one may also see that the hypothesis of Epiphanius, which asserts that Christ was born at the beginning of the Julian year 45, that is, about the middle of the forty-second year from the reign of Augustus, is more in agreement with the sacred writings than the view which holds that Christ was born near the end of the Julian year 45, namely on 25 December. For according to this latter hypothesis Christ, when baptized, had not yet completed his twenty-ninth year of age, which is inconsistent with the Gospel history. Moreover, that Christ suffered in the spring during the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius is clearly proved by Eusebius of Caesarea from that wonderful eclipse of the sun at the time of the Lord's passion, which was carefully recorded in the commentaries of the pagans. He says: "According to the prophecies that had been spoken about God, he came to the passion in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, at which time we have also found these things written word for word in other commentaries of the pagans: a defect of the sun occurred, and darkness over the whole earth; Bithynia was shaken by an earthquake, and in the city of Nicaea many buildings collapsed. All these things agree with what happened at the passion of the Saviour." Phlegon, an excellent reckoner of the Olympiads, also wrote about these things, in the fourteenth book, saying thus: "In the fourth year of the two hundred and second Olympiad, a great and excellent eclipse of the sun occurred, greater than all those that had happened before. The day was turned at the sixth hour into so dark a night that the stars were seen in the sky, and an earthquake in Bithynia overthrew many buildings in the city of Nicaea." So far the man quoted. The proof that the Saviour suffered in that year is given by the Gospel of John, in which it is written that the Lord preached for three years after the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. The fourth year of the two hundred and second Olympiad, that is, the eight hundred and eighth Olympiad year, began at the solstice in the Julian year 77 as it was running out. So the Lord's passion, which came in the following spring, truly falls in the Julian year 78, that is, in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, whose beginning is taken from the nineteenth day of August in the Julian year 77. Thus it is established that Christ suffered in the fourth year of the two hundred and second Olympiad. Nor should we agree with those who make light of the authority of Phlegon and suspect some error in his text, as if instead of the fourth year of the two hundred and second Olympiad it should be written the first year of the two hundred and third Olympiad. They say this so that they may refer the Lord's passion to the following Julian year 79, and prove that four Passovers intervened between Christ's baptism and passion. But we hold that Christ was baptized before the sixth day before the Ides of November in the Julian year 74, and suffered at the Passover in spring in the Julian year 78. Thus between the baptism and the passion of Christ we acknowledge that only three Passovers intervened, as Eusebius and Epiphanius testify; and this can be proved, not forcedly, from the Gospel history as well. Here, however, the question arises whether the Julian year 78, in which I have said the Lord's passion fell, is the thirty-third year of Christ's age, as John Lucidus and many others have thought, or the thirty-fourth year of his age, as some have judged. There is no doubt that the Julian year 78 is the thirty-third year of the Christian era, or of the usual years of Christ. But whether it is the thirty-third or the thirty-fourth year of his age cannot be answered except by a distinction. For insofar as, on the hypothesis of Dionysius the Roman Abbot, Christ is thought to have been born on 25 December at the end of the Julian year 45, to that extent the Julian year 78 is the thirty-third year of Christ's age, as John Lucidus held with Paul of Burgos, Nicholas of Lyra, and the others we named above. For all of these hold that the years of the Christian era and the years of Christ's age are the same, so that his birth is understood to precede the beginning of the usual years of Christ by only eight days.

units.la: Quatenus vero ex hypothesi Epiphanij statuitur, Christum natum esse circa principium anni Iuliani 45: eatenus annus 78 Iulianus, est trigesimus quartus ætatis Christi: vt mirandum sit, quare aliqui scribant Christum natum esse anno Iuliano 44, scilicet circa brumam labente anno Actiacæ victoriæ secundum Romanos vigesimo septimo, anno Nabonasari 747, anno Iphiti Olympiadico 775, & tamen volunt Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum filium Dei passum esse anno Iuliano 79, Aprilis 23, anno primo Olympiadis 205 currente, anno Nabonasari 781, pachon XII, anno Actiaco Augustali LXII. quasi annus 79 Iulianus fuerit annus ætatis Christi trigesimus quartus, cum tamen ex ipsorum hypothesi necessario sequatur, annum 79 Iulianum esse trigesimum quintum ætatis Christi, quemadmodum idem ostendit hypothesis Epiphanij: quare agnoscant se [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: As far as the hypothesis of Epiphanius establishes that Christ was born about the beginning of the Julian year 45, so far the Julian year 78 is the thirty-fourth year of Christ's age. So it is surprising that some write that Christ was born in the Julian year 44, namely about the winter solstice, in the twenty-seventh year after the Actian victory according to the Romans, Nabonassar year 747, Iphitus' Olympiad year 775. Yet these same writers want our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to have suffered in the Julian year 79, on April 23, in the first year of the 205th Olympiad, Nabonassar year 781, Pachon 12, Augustan Actian year 62, as if the Julian year 79 were the thirty-fourth year of Christ's age. Yet from their own hypothesis it necessarily follows that the Julian year 79 is the thirty-fifth year of Christ's age, as the hypothesis of Epiphanius also shows. Therefore let them acknowledge that they [illegible, ~12 letters]

units.la: Verum quidem est, annum 79 Iulianum esse annum Christi XXXIIII, & annum ætatis Christi secundum Dionysium 34: at secundum Epiphanium est annus ætatis Christi trigesimus quintus. Quare anni æræ Christi, minime sunt confundendi cum annis ætatis Christi: etsi enim varia sit opinio historicorum de anno, tempore anni, & die nativitatis Christi; æra tamen Christi, hoc est, principium annorum Christi vsitatorum est vnum idemque, quod ab omnibus agnoscitur.
units.tr: It is true that the Julian year 79 is the year 34 of Christ, and the thirty-fourth year of Christ's age according to Dionysius; but according to Epiphanius it is the thirty-fifth year of Christ's age. Hence the years of the era of Christ are by no means to be confused with the years of the age of Christ. For although historians differ in their opinions about the year, the season of the year, and the day of Christ's nativity, the era of Christ, that is, the beginning of the customary years of Christ, is one and the same and is acknowledged by all.

units.la: Quo mense & die Christus sit passus, non omnes[?] historici conveniunt: Epiphanius statuit eum pas-sum esse, cum ab Epiphaniis, hoc est, a quinta Januarij currentis anni Juliani 46, qui est principium anno-rum Christi usitatorum, transcgillet[?] annos triginta duos, & septuaginta quatuor dies: quia vult eum passum esse anno Juliano 78, die 13 kalend. Aprilis, hoc est, die 20 Martij, feria sexta, & resurrexisse 11 kal. Aprilis, ipso scilicet die aequinoctij verni, hoc est, die 22 Martij, feria prima. Quod autem haec sit mens Epiphanij ex illo constat, cum Christum passum ait anno trigesimo tertio aetatis, hoc est, anno Christi usitato trigesimo tertio, qui revera erat annus aetatis Christi trigesimus quartus, & annus Tiberij decimus octavus. Huc etiam accedit, quod plerique statuerint Christum incarnatum, hoc est conceptum fuisse circa aequinoctium vernum, die 25[?] Martij, qua acceperit Maria salutationem Angeli, & passum fuisse eadem die circa aequinoctium vernum, quasi Christus ab incarnatione sive conceptione usque ad pas-sionem suam compleverit annos triginta tres, ut sub initium anni trigesimi quarti ab incarnatione passus esse intelligatur. Sane anno Juliano septuagesimo octavo novilunium incidit in diem vigesimum Martij, ut ex enneadecaeteride Juliana evidenter probari potest, erat autem istud novilunium mensis Nisan, cum esset proximum aequinoctio verno, currente anno Judaico a conditu mundi 3793, qui erat annus communis, sine mense intercalari, & secundus cycli Metonici seu enneadecaeterici ab aera Alexandri Dhilkarnain continuati, quemadmodum osten-dimus in calendario Syriaco: itaque non potuit pascha Judaicum incidere in vigesimam Martij, sed incurrit in tertiam diem Aprilis, qua erat plenilunium, die decima quinta Nisan: quod etiam eleganter commonstravit Ioannes Lucidus in appendice chronologiae suae capite duodecimo, quem eo libentius sequimur, quod passionem Dominicam conferat in annum quartum Olympiadis 202. Quod autem Eusebius ait fuisse circa passionem Dominicam eclipsin solis, recte est accipiendum: non enim historia Evangelica asserit solem in plenilunio defecisse, sed interdiu tenebras densissimas obortas esse testatur, etiamsi noctu luna pleno orbe fulserit, quo indicaretur pascha Iudaicum instare. Nomen eclipseos siue de sole, siue de luna dicatur, non semper proprie accipitur apud autores, sed interdum quascunque tenebras siue prodigia circa solem & lunam visa significat, etiamsi nulla luminarium secundum calculum astronomicum sit obscuratio: hoc nos docet Xiphilinus in epitome Dionis de Vitellio, vbi sic ait, ὡς ἐν τούτῳ τῷ χρόνῳ πολλῆς ταραχῆς γενομένης ἐν τῷ στρατοπέδῳ τοῦ Βιτελλίου, [?] ἐπηύξησεν αὐτὴν ἡ σελήνη τῆς νυκτὸς ὀκλιποῦσα, ὥστε ὅτι καὶ ἱσχυ-ὰς [?] (καίπερ τοῖς θορυβουμένοις καὶ τὰ πάντα φοβούμενοις φόβον φέρει) ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι καὶ αἱματώδης καὶ μέλαινα, ἄλλα τινὰ χρώματα φοβερὰ ἀ-φιέναι ὡφέλει. hoc est, Cum eo tempore perturbatio multa esset in Vitellij exercitu, adauxit eam luna no-cte eclipsin patiens, non quod etiam fuerit obscura-ta, (quamuis turbatis etiam haec metum incutiant) sed quod & sanguinolenta & nigra apparuerit, a-liosque colores terribiles oftentarit. Quamobrem insigniter decipiuntur, qui ex solo nomine eclipseos, coniunctionem aut oppositionem luminarium conficiunt, nulla habita ratione enneadecaeteridis, vel etiam veram obscurationem solis & lunae circa caput & caudam Draconis contigisse existimant, nulla habita ratione calculi astronomici,qui iusto interuallo tem-poris congruit. Sic quo tempore mortuus est Augustus,scilicet die decima nona Augusti,currente anno Iuliano sexagesimo, scribit Dio contigisse maximam solis eclipfin: atqui tuc plenilunium fuit, sicut ex en-neadecaeteride Iuliana apparet. quippe annus sexagesimus Iulianus aureum numerum habuit III. qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur addiem quintum Iduum Ianuarij,&fecundum lunationes recurrit die quarta Augusti, vbi nouilunium indicat: hinc fi quindecim dies deorsum numerentur, peruenitur ad decimam nonam Augusti, in qua Augustus decessit,ipso plenilunio:quo tempore non potuit esse vera eclipsis solis, sed tantum insolita quaedam prodigia acciderunt, vt etiam fanguinoletus folinterdiu cofpiceretur. Hactenus nos a proposito auocauit historia baptismi & passionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quae necessario fuit declaranda: nunc redeamus ad conexionem annorum Iulianorum cum annis Christi & Nabonafari,vt quae deinceps sunt obseruanda, legitima metho-do acferie intelligamus. Substitimus autem in anno Iuliano 1 3 8,litera Dominicali existente F.qui est annus aerae Christianae 93, in quem incurrit Thoth Nabonafari 841, die 3 1 Iulij, feria quarta: quare ad annos sequentes progrediamur.
