units.tr: Historians do not agree on the month and day of Christ's passion. Epiphanius holds that he suffered when, counting from the Epiphany, that is, from January 5 of the current Julian year 46, which is the beginning of the customary years of Christ, thirty-two years and seventy-four days had passed. He holds that Christ suffered in the Julian year 78, on the 13th day before the Kalends of April, that is March 20, a Friday, and rose on the 11th day before the Kalends of April, namely on the very day of the vernal equinox, that is March 22, a Sunday. That this is Epiphanius' view is clear from the fact that he says Christ suffered in the thirty-third year of his age, that is, in the customary thirty-third year of Christ, which was really the thirty-fourth year of Christ's age, and the eighteenth year of Tiberius. To this must be added that many have held that Christ was incarnate, that is, conceived, about the vernal equinox, on March 25, when Mary received the angel's greeting, and that he suffered on the same day about the vernal equinox, as if Christ completed thirty-three years from his incarnation or conception until his passion, so that he is understood to have suffered at the beginning of the thirty-fourth year from the incarnation. Indeed, in the Julian year 78 the new moon fell on March 20, as can clearly be proved from the Julian enneadecaeteris. That new moon was in the month Nisan, since it was the nearest to the equinox, in the current Jewish year 3793 from the creation of the world, which was a common year without an intercalary month, and the second year of the Metonic or enneadecaeteric cycle continued from the era of Alexander Dhilkarnain, as we showed in the Syriac calendar. So the Jewish Passover could not fall on March 20, but fell on April 3, when there was a full moon, on the fifteenth day of Nisan. John Lucidus also showed this elegantly in the appendix to his chronology, chapter twelve, which we follow all the more gladly because he places the Lord's passion in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad. As for Eusebius' statement that there was an eclipse of the sun around the Lord's passion, it must be understood correctly: the Gospel history does not assert that the sun was eclipsed at full moon, but testifies that very dense darkness arose during the day, even though at night the moon shone with a full disc, which indicated that the Jewish Passover was at hand. The name "eclipse," whether it is said of the sun or of the moon, is not always taken in its proper sense by authors, but sometimes signifies any darkness or portents seen around the sun and moon, even when there is no obscuration of the luminaries according to astronomical calculation. Xiphilinus teaches us this in his epitome of Dio, on Vitellius, where he says: "since at that time great confusion arose in the camp of Vitellius, the moon, suffering an eclipse at night, increased it; not that it was really darkened (although such things strike fear into the troubled and those who fear everything), but that it appeared bloody and black and showed other terrible colors." Greek original as printed. The Latin rendering is: when at that time there was great confusion in Vitellius' army, the moon, eclipsing at night, increased it, not because it was obscured (though this strikes fear into the disturbed), but because it appeared bloody and black and displayed other frightful colors. Therefore those are greatly mistaken who, from the bare name of eclipse, conclude a conjunction or opposition of the luminaries, without regard to the enneadecaeteris, or who think that a true obscuration of the sun and moon occurred near the head and tail of the Dragon, without regard to the astronomical calculation, which agrees with the proper interval of time. Thus, at the time when Augustus died, namely on August 19 in the Julian year 60, Dio writes that a total eclipse of the sun occurred; yet it was then full moon, as appears from the Julian enneadecaeteris. For the Julian year 60 had the golden number 3, which in the Julian calendar is placed on the fifth day before the Ides of January, and recurs by lunations on August 4, where it indicates the new moon. Hence, if fifteen days are counted backward, one arrives at August 19, the day on which Augustus died, at the full moon itself. At that time there cannot have been a true eclipse of the sun, but only certain unusual portents occurred, so that even the sun was seen bloody during the day. Thus far the history of the baptism and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ has drawn us away from our purpose, though it had to be explained. Now let us return to the connection of the Julian years with the years of Christ and of Nabonassar, so that we may understand, by a sound method and sequence, what is to be observed henceforth. We stopped at the Julian year 138, with the dominical letter F, which is the year 93 of the Christian era, in which Thoth of Nabonassar year 841 falls on July 31, a Wednesday. Therefore let us proceed to the following years.

units.la: * Thoth Nabonasari 84 5[?] fecundum Ægyptios principium est imperij Traiani: is incidit in diem 3 o. Iulij, currente anno Iuliano centesimo secundo & quadragesimo. Ptolemæus lib. 7 Almagesti cap. 3, dicit Menelaum Geometram, quem Arabes Milæum appellarunt, Romæ obseruasse spicam Virginis, anno primo Traiani, qui fuerit annus Nabonasari 84 5[?], a meridie, 15 mensis Mechir elapsis horis decem: quod scilicet spica a luna per visibilem coniunctionem fuerit obscurata. Si a trigesimo Iulij die numeremus menses quinque Ægyptios, & 15 dies e mense Mechir, peruenimus ad 10 Ianuarij diem, anno labente Iuliano 143, & Christi 98, existente litera Dominicali G: ergo Menelai consideratio fuit nocte quæ secuta est 10 Ianuarij diem, feriam Mercurij.
units.tr: * Thoth of Nabonassar 84 5[?] is, according to the Egyptians, the beginning of the reign of Trajan. It falls on 3 July, in the Julian year 142. Ptolemy, in book 7 of the Almagest, chapter 3, says that Menelaus the geometer, whom the Arabs called Milaeus, observed the Spica of Virgo at Rome in the first year of Trajan, which was Nabonassar 84 5[?], at noon, when 15 days of the month Mechir had passed and ten hours more had elapsed. This was evidently because the Spica was obscured by the Moon through a visible conjunction. If we count five Egyptian months from 30 July and 15 days from the month Mechir, we arrive at 10 January, in the Julian year 143 and the year of Christ 98, when the Dominical letter was G. So Menelaus's observation took place in the night following 10 January, a Wednesday.

units.la: b Thoth Nabonasari 864 fecundum Ægyptios est principium regni Adriani, vt ex Ptolemæo & scri-pto Hebræi de æris temporum colligere licet: incur-rit ille Thoth in annum centesimum sexagesimum primum Iulianum, die 25 Iulij, feria sexta.
units.tr: Thoth of Nabonassar 864 is, according to the Egyptians, the beginning of the reign of Hadrian, as may be gathered from Ptolemy and from the Hebrew writing on the computation of times. That Thoth falls in the 161st Julian year, on 25 July, a Friday.

units.la: c Anno labente Nabonasari 880, qui incidit in annum 17 Adriani Imperatoris, hora secunda post meridiem, die 7 mensis Athyr, Ptolemæus accuratissimè obseruauit incidisse æquinoctium autumnale, vt ipse testatur lib. 3 Almagesti cap. 8. Thoth Nabonasari 880, qui incurrit in annum Iulianum 177, & Christi 132, vigesimo primo Julij, coepit die solis: quare si a 11 Julij inclusiue numeremus duos menses Aegyptios, nimirum Thoth & Paophi, & addamus 7 dies ex mense Athyr, descendimus in vigesimum quintum Septembris, diem Mercurij, a cuius meridie elapsis duabus horis Ptolemaeus obseruauit aequinoctiu incidisse. Quamobrem recte scripsit Joannes Stofle-rus in calendario Romano, propositione 38: Ptolemaeus anno 17 Adriani Imperatoris, qui fuit annus Nabuchodonosoris 880, Christi autem 132, inuenit solis ingressum in punctum aequinoctij autumnalis, die 25 mensis Septembris, horis 2 post meridiem: ex quo ingressu fecundum astrologorum doctrinam in promptu ingressus solis in punctum aequinoctij verni elicitur, die videlicet 22 Martij, horis 2 post meridiem. fuit igitur iuxta observationem Ptolemaei verissimam aequinoctium vernum die vigesima secunda Martij.
units.tr: In the year of Nabonassar 880, which corresponds to the 17th year of the Emperor Hadrian, at two o'clock in the afternoon, on the 7th day of the month Athyr, Ptolemy observed most accurately that the autumnal equinox had occurred, as he himself attests in book 3 of the Almagest, chapter 8. Thoth of Nabonassar 880, which falls in the Julian year 177 and of Christ 132, began on a Sunday, 21 July. So if we count inclusively from 11 July two Egyptian months, namely Thoth and Paophi, and add 7 days from the month Athyr, we come down to 25 September, a Wednesday. Two hours after noon on that day, Ptolemy observed that the equinox had occurred. Therefore John Stoflerus rightly wrote in his Roman calendar, proposition 38: Ptolemy, in the 17th year of the Emperor Hadrian, which was the year 880 of Nabuchodonosor, and of Christ 132, found the entry of the sun into the point of the autumnal equinox on 25 September, at two hours after noon. From this entry, according to the teaching of the astrologers, the entry of the sun into the point of the vernal equinox is readily derived, namely on 22 March at two hours after noon. Therefore, according to Ptolemy's most accurate observation, the vernal equinox fell on 22 March.

units.la: Thoth Nabonasari 885 fecundum Aegyptios est principium regni Antonini Pij: is autem incidit in annum Julianum 182, die vigesima Julij, feria sexta.
units.tr: Thoth of Nabonassar 885 is, according to the Egyptians, the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Pius. It falls in the Julian year 182, on 20 July, a Friday.

units.la: Thoth Nabonasari 886, recte Censorino incidit in annum secundum Antonini Pij Imperatoris: & in 13 kal. Augusti, hoc est in 20 Julij diem, feriam septimam: ut exactè demonstrat. Thoth Nabonasari 986, qui tempore Censorini incidit in diem septimum kal. Julij, h.e. in 25 Junij diem, feriam secundam: ut suo loco dicemus. Cum enim Censorinus ita scribit: Sed horum initia semper a primo die mensis eius summuntur, cui apud Aegyptios nomen est Thoth: quo hoc anno (scilicet Juliano 283) fuit ante diem septimum kal. Julij, cum abhinc annos centum Imperatore Antonino Pio II, Vlpio & Brutio Praesente Coss. Romae idem diesfuerint ante diem duodecimum kal. Augusti, quo tempore solet canicula in Ægypto facere exortum non ita accipiendum est, quasi Cenforinus afferat anno fecundo Antonini Pij Thoth Nabonafari 886 fuif-fein12 [?] kal. Augusti, sed initium dierum canicularium incidisse circa 12 kal. Aug. vt tunc sol in leonem transitum fecerit, caniculæ ortu iam imminente. Ergo cum annis centum Iulianis Thoth Ægyptiorum per 15 dies recesserit: siquidem singulis quadrienniis Iulianis diem vnum anteuertit: fatis constat anno Iuliano 183, qui fuit annus Christi 138, incurrisse Thoth Nabonafari 886, feria septima, ad 20 Iulij diem, litera dominicali existente F. Quod autem inciderit Thoth Nabonafari 886 in annum fecundum Antonini Pij, probari quoque potest ex Ptolemaeo, qui anno Nabonafari 886, hoc est, a morte Alexandri 462, nona die mensis Pharmuthi, circa solis occasum obseruauit cor leonis, quem situm respectu solis haberet: vt re-statur lib. 7 Almagesti cap. 2, vbi scribit expresse annum illum fuisse secundum Antonini: & lib. 9 Almagesti cap. 10 in obseruatione Mercurij dicit annum Nabonafari 886 incidere in secundum annum Antonini. Sed lib. 5 Almagesti cap. 1, annum tertium Antonini dicit esse à morte Alexandri 463, & lib. 10 Almagesti cap. 4 dicit Ptolemaeus ante imperium Antonini elapsos esse annos Nabonafari 884: vnde colligitur Thoth Nabonafari 885 incidere in annum primum Antonini Pij: quare euidens est annum Nabonafari 886, qui est à morte Alexandri 462 incurrere in annum secundum Antonini Pij, quod etiam recensuit Cenforinus. Si desideras tempus Ptolemaicæ obseruationis conferre cum anno Iuliano, repetendum est, Thoth Nabonafari 886 coepisse die sabbati, vt ostendit examen feriarum, & incurrisse in 20 Iulii diem, labentlabente anno Christi 138 : numerentur iraq;[?] septem menses Ægyptij,& adiiciantur 9 dies ex mense Phar-muthi,descenditur in 23 Februarij diem,feriam solis, anno currente Iuliano 184. Christi autem 139, sub literis dominicalibus E D. Ad hunc calculum proxi-mè accessit Copernicus lib.2 Reuolutionum cap.14, quando ait,hanc Ptolemæi in Basilisco stella obser-uationem factam fuisse anno Christi 139,die 24 Fe-bruarij: itaque à nobis differt vno tantum die. Quod autem necessario obseruatio Ptolemæi inciderit in diem solis, ostendit examen feriarum: nam septem menses Ægyptij cum 9 diebus summam faciunt 219 dierum, qui fi per septem diuidantur, in residuo re-linquitur binarius, qui indicium est nonu diem men-fis Pharmuthi esse fecundum à die illo, quo Thoth coeperat: coepit autem Thoth Nabonafari 886 die fabbathi: quare nona dies mensis Pharmuthi est dies solis, quæ incurrit in 23 Februarij anno Christi labé-te 139. Atqui 23 Februarij fecundum ordinem lite-rarum hebdomadicum notatur litera E, quæ index est diei dominici: quod sanè fieri non posset, nisi an-nus Christi 139 intercalaris effet, literas habens do-minicales ED:quarum prior more solito à kal.Ianua-riis vsque ad 24 Februarij diem index est Dominica-lis:posterior autem à 24 Februarij vfq; ad finem anni diem solis indicat. Quare ex hac Ptolemæi obserua-tione, quod inprimis notandum est, apparet annum Iulianum 184 intercalarem fuisse, sub literis domini-calibus ED:iuxta cyclum hebdomadicü 28 annorum solarium,à bisexto Augustali inchoatum:eandem fe-riarum leriem demonstrat Thoth Cenforini 986: idem probat æra Diocletiani, & anni ab ea vsque ad æram Persicam extensi idem docent: eundem feriarum ordinem probat æra Arabica & Perfica, de quibus omnibus deinceps dicemus. Porro æquino ctij autumnalis per Ptolemæu obferuatio, quæ facta eft anno Chrifti 132, vigefima quinta Septembris, die Mercurij, horafecuda poft meridiê, litera Dominicali exiftete F:cerrifllmu fuppeditat argumentu nos annos Nabonafari cu annis Iulianis & Chrifti recte coiunxifle. Fatetur enim Ptolemæus à Nabonafaro vfq; ad cósideratione fua trafiifle annos Ægyptios 879, & 66 dies cu duabus horis, h.e. diesin vniuerfu 320901, & duas horas: quare die labente 320902 obferuauit: fi numerus dieru 320902 diuidatur per 7; in refiduo relinquitur vnitas, quæ indicat diem, qua Ptolemæus obferuauit, fuiffe primam ab æra Nabonafari, hoc eft, diem Mercurij, vt etiá paulo ante oftendimus. Quod autem ante hanc Ptolemæi obferuationem elapfi fuerint anni Ægyptij 879, & 66 dies cum duabus horis, hoc modo probat Ptolemæus: à Nabonafaro vf-que ad mortem Alexandri elapfi fuerunt 424 anni Ægyptij: à morte Alexadri vfque ad Augufti monarchiam, hoc eft, vfque ad Thoth Augufti Actiacum tranfierunt anni Ægyptij 294, quod etiam fcribit vetus Chronologus apud Clementem, cum ait, Ἀλεξ[?]άνδρου [?]πλευτῆς ἐπὶ τὴν Αὐγούστου νίκην, ὅτι Ἀντώνιος ἑαυτὸν ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ, ἐπὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] πατρ[?] hoc eft, A morte Alexandri vfque ad Augufti victoriam, quando Antonius feipfum iugulauit Alexan-driæ, funt anni ducenti & nonaginta quatuor: àmonarchia autem Augufti vfq; ad obferuationem Ptolemæi elapfi funt anni Ægyptij 161, & 66 dies cum duabus horis: quamobrem recte infert Ptolemæus à Nabonafaro vfque ad confiderationem fuam effluxiffe annos Ægyptios 879, & 66 dies cum duabus ho-ris: ris: vt videre licet lib.3 Almagesti cap.8. Ex quibus intelligitur ante epocham Augusti Actiacam a Nabonasaro elapsos esse annos Aegyptios 718: si enim 294 addantur ad annos 424, consurgit summa 718 annorum: itaque Thoth anni Nabonasari 719 incurrit in Actiacam Augusti victoriam: quae iuxta Censorinum incidit in annum Iulianum decimum sextum, 29 mensis Sextilis: quatenus anno Iuliano 283 Thoth Nabonasari 986 incurrit in 25 die Iunij. Seda Thoth Actiaco vsque ad kal.Ianuarias anni Iuliani 46, unde principium est annorum Christi vsitatorum, elapsi sunt anni Aegyptij 29, & 132 dies: quatenus a meridie kal.Ian. more astronomorum supputamus epocham Christi, annorumque Iulianorum, prout tunc currebant, obseruamus dispositionem. Quod sane interuallum optime est notandum, cum fundamentum sit & indissolubile vinculum totius chronologiae nostrae: proinde si ad annos 718 Aegyptios, qui a Nabonasaro vsque ad victoriam Augusti Actiacam sunt elapsi, adiiciantur anni Aegyptij 29, & 132 dies, qui transierunt a Thoth Actiaco vsq; ad principium annorum Christi vsitatorum, consurgit summa 747 annorum Aegyptiorum, & 132 dierum: quot supra ostendimus praeteriisse a Nabonasaro, vsque ad epocham Christi. Hinc patet a principio vero annorum Christi vsque ad Ptolemaei obseruationem elapsos esse annos Aegyptios 131, & dies 299 cum duabus horis, hoc est, in vniuersum praeteriisse 48114 dies cum duabus horis: vt die labente 4811 s, Ptolemaeus obseruationem aequinoctij autumnalis instituerit, quod examen feriarum comprobat. Si enim dies 4811 s diuidantur per 7: in residuo relinquuntur quatuor,quod indicium est die quarto ab æra Christi inclusiuè sumto, hoc est die Mercurij obseruatio-nem Ptolemæi incidisse: quandoquidem vera epocha Christi cœpit die solis. Quod autem ad fixam Christi æram attinet, qua ponitur principium annorum Christi incidisse in meridiem sabbati, kal. Ian. anni 46 Iuliani, diximus antea eam diem sabbati re-ipsa conuenire cum die solis: cùm astronomi posuerint annum tertium Christi fuisse intercalarem, qui tamen fuit simplex, vt apparet ex vera annorum Iulianorum dispositione: hinc factum est, vt dies, quam visi sunt in epocha Christi anticipasse, in suum locum sit restituta: & interualla omnia iusta habeatur. Quare mendum est in epitome Regiomontani lib. 3 Almagesti propof. 21, quando scribitur cõsiderationem Ptolemæi fuisse post principium annorum Christi interiectis annis Ægyptiis 131, diebus 301, cum horis duabus. units.tr: Thoth of Nabonassar 886 (rightly, as Censorinus has it) fell in the second year of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, that is, on 20 July, a Saturday [feria septima], as I shall demonstrate exactly. Thoth of Nabonassar 986, which in Censorinus' time fell on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, that is on 25 June, a Monday [feria secunda], as we shall say in its place. For when Censorinus writes "But the beginnings of these are always taken from the first day of the month, which among the Egyptians is called Thoth. In this year (namely Julian 283) it was before the seventh day before the Kalends of July, when a hundred years ago, in the second year of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, with Ulpius and Brutius Praesens as consuls, the same day was before the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, when the dog star usually rises in Egypt", this is not to be taken as if Censorinus were asserting that in the second year of Antoninus Pius Thoth of Nabonassar 886 fell on the twelfth [?] day before the Kalends of August. Rather, the beginning of the dog days fell about the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, when the sun then passed into Leo and the rising of the dog star was already imminent. Therefore, since in a hundred Julian years the Egyptian Thoth had receded by fifteen days (for it moves one day earlier every four Julian years), it is certain that in Julian year 183, which was the year of Christ 138, Thoth of Nabonassar 886 fell on a Saturday, on 20 July, with the dominical letter F. That Thoth of Nabonassar 886 fell in the second year of Antoninus Pius can also be proved from Ptolemy. In the year of Nabonassar 886, that is 462 years from the death of Alexander, on the ninth day of the month Pharmuthi, near sunset, he observed the Heart of the Lion, to see what position it held relative to the sun. This is recorded in Almagest book 7, chapter 2, where he expressly writes that that year was the second of Antoninus. And in Almagest book 9, chapter 10, in his observation of Mercury, he says that the year Nabonassar 886 falls in the second year of Antoninus. But in Almagest book 5, chapter 1, he says that the third year of Antoninus is 463 years from the death of Alexander, and in Almagest book 10, chapter 4, Ptolemy says that before the reign of Antoninus the years of Nabonassar 884 had elapsed. From this it is gathered that Thoth of Nabonassar 885 fell in the first year of Antoninus Pius. Hence it is evident that the year Nabonassar 886, which is 462 years from the death of Alexander, falls in the second year of Antoninus Pius, as Censorinus also records. If you wish to compare the time of Ptolemy's observation with a Julian year, it must be recalled that Thoth of Nabonassar 886 began on a Saturday, as the reckoning of the weekdays shows, and fell on 20 July in the year of Christ 138 as it slipped by. Then, if one counts seven Egyptian months and adds nine days from the month Pharmuthi, one comes down to 23 February, a Sunday, in Julian year 184, the year of Christ 139, under the dominical letters E D. Copernicus, in Revolutions book 2, chapter 14, came very close to this calculation when he says that this observation of Ptolemy's star in Basiliscus was made in the year of Christ 139 on 24 February. So he differs from us by only one day. That Ptolemy's observation necessarily fell on a Sunday is shown by the reckoning of the weekdays. For seven Egyptian months with nine days make a sum of 219 days, and when these are divided by seven, a remainder of two is left. This indicates that the ninth day of the month Pharmuthi is the second day counting from the day on which Thoth began. Thoth of Nabonassar 886 began on a Saturday; therefore the ninth day of Pharmuthi is a Sunday, which falls on 23 February in the slipping year of Christ 139. But 23 February, in the weekly sequence of letters, is marked with the letter E, which is the sign of the Lord's day. This could not happen unless the year of Christ 139 were a leap year, having the dominical letters E D. Of these, the first, as usual from the Kalends of January to 24 February, indicates the Lord's day, while the latter, from 24 February to the end of the year, indicates Sunday. Hence from this observation of Ptolemy, which must be noted first of all, it appears that Julian year 184 was a leap year under the dominical letters E D, according to the 28-year weekly cycle of solar years, which begins with the Augustan bissextile. Thoth of Censorinus, 986, shows the same order of weekdays. The era of Diocletian proves the same, and the years extended from it to the Persian era teach the same. The Arabic and Persian eras also prove the same order of weekdays, and of all these we shall speak hereafter. Moreover, the autumnal equinox observed by Ptolemy, which was made in the year of Christ 132 on 25 September, a Wednesday, at the second hour after noon, the dominical letter being F, supplies a most certain argument that we have rightly joined the years of Nabonassar with the Julian and Christian years. For Ptolemy admits that from Nabonassar up to his own consideration 879 Egyptian years and 66 days with two hours had passed, that is, in all 320,901 days and two hours. Hence, with the day elapsing, he observed on 320,902. If the number of days, 320,902, is divided by 7, a remainder of one is left, which indicates that the day on which Ptolemy observed was the first day of the era of Nabonassar, that is, a Wednesday, as we showed a little earlier. That 879 Egyptian years and 66 days with two hours had elapsed before this observation of Ptolemy, he proves as follows. From Nabonassar to the death of Alexander, 424 Egyptian years elapsed. From the death of Alexander to the monarchy of Augustus, that is, to the Thoth of Augustus' Actian victory, 294 Egyptian years passed. The old chronologist cited by Clement also writes this, when he says [Ἀλεξάνδρου ... νίκην]: that is, "From the death of Alexander to Augustus' victory, when Antony slew himself at Alexandria, there are 294 years." From the monarchy of Augustus up to Ptolemy's observation, 161 Egyptian years and 66 days with two hours have elapsed. Therefore Ptolemy rightly infers that from Nabonassar up to his consideration 879 Egyptian years and 66 days with two hours had passed, as may be seen in Almagest book 3, chapter 8. From these figures it is understood that before the Actian epoch of Augustus, 718 Egyptian years had elapsed from Nabonassar. For if 294 are added to 424 years, the sum is 718 years. Thus Thoth of the year 719 of Nabonassar falls on Augustus' Actian victory, which according to Censorinus fell in the sixteenth Julian year, on the twenty-ninth day of the month Sextilis. Hence, as Julian year 283 corresponds to Thoth of Nabonassar 986, it falls on 25 June. From Thoth of Actium to the Kalends of January of Julian year 46, whence the commonly used beginning of the years of Christ is taken, 29 Egyptian years and 132 days have elapsed. For, following the astronomers, we reckon the epoch of Christ from noon of the Kalends of January, and we observe the arrangement of the Julian years as they then ran. This interval is certainly to be carefully noted, since it is the foundation and indissoluble bond of our whole chronology. Therefore, if to the 718 Egyptian years which elapsed from Nabonassar to Augustus' Actian victory we add the 29 Egyptian years and 132 days which passed from Thoth of Actium to the beginning of the commonly used years of Christ, the sum comes to 747 Egyptian years and 132 days. This is just what we showed above had passed from Nabonassar to the epoch of Christ. Hence it is clear that from the true beginning of the years of Christ up to Ptolemy's observation, 131 Egyptian years and 299 days with two hours had elapsed. That is, in all 48,114 days with two hours had passed, so that, with the day elapsing, Ptolemy began his observation of the autumnal equinox on 4,811 s. The reckoning of the weekdays confirms this. For if the days, 4,811 s, are divided by 7, four remain, which indicates the fourth day counted inclusively from the era of Christ, that is, Ptolemy's observation fell on a Wednesday, since the true epoch of Christ began on a Sunday. As for the fixed era of Christ, in which the beginning of the years of Christ is placed at noon on a Saturday, the Kalends of January of Julian year 46, we said before that this Saturday really agrees with Sunday. Astronomers have taken the third year of Christ to be a leap year, though it was in fact a common year, as appears from the true arrangement of the Julian years. Hence it came about that the day which they seem to have anticipated in the epoch of Christ has been restored to its place, and all the intervals are held to be correct. Hence there is an error in the epitome of Regiomontanus, Almagest book 3, proposition 21, where it is written that Ptolemy's consideration came after the beginning of the years of Christ, with 131 Egyptian years, 301 days and two hours intervening. units.la: {a} Hoc anno Nabonasari 887, qui fuit annus tertius Antonini Pij, & a morte Alexandri 463, nona die mensis Athyr prima hora post solis ortum, Alexandriæ Ptolemæus accuratissimè observauit incidisse æquinoctium autumnale: vt testatur libro tertio Almagesti capite primo. Thoth Nabonasari 887 incidit in decimam nonam Iulij, feriam primam, currente anno Iuliano 184, qui est annus Christi 139: ergo nona dies mensis Athyr respondit 25 Septembris, eiusdem anni Iuliani 184, quo tempore Ptolemæus observauit incidisse æquinoctium autumnale. Atque hæc obseruatio prorsus conuenit cum illa quā Ptolemæus habuit anno Nabonasari 880, die 7 mesis Athyr: vt illi plurimum fallantur, qui putant Ptolemæum insignem artificem per sua <bl>χείκωτα μηχανή-ματα</bl> deceptum fuisse, & sibi in obseruationibus suis non constare, neq; proportionem temporis ab Hipparcho elapsi confiderafle. Etenim Hipparchus deprehendit autumnale æquinoctium in 26 Septembris, Ptolemæus autem illud notauit die 25 [?] Septembris: itaque anticipatio æquinoctiorum intra annos fere 150 per vnum diem & horas aliquot est animaduersa: etsi enim vulgo putaretur æquinoctia singulis centenis annis diem vnum ascendere, tamen motus quidam trepidationis incognitus hoc interuallum temporis subinde mutabat.
units.tr: In this year of Nabonassar 887, which was the third year of Antoninus Pius and the 463rd from the death of Alexander, on the ninth day of the month Athyr, one hour after sunrise, Ptolemy at Alexandria observed most accurately that the autumnal equinox had fallen; as he testifies in the first chapter of the third book of the Almagest. Thoth of Nabonassar 887 fell on 19 July, a Sunday, in the current Julian year 184, which is the year of Christ 139. Therefore the ninth day of the month Athyr corresponded to 25 September of that same Julian year 184, when Ptolemy observed that the autumnal equinox had fallen. And this observation agrees exactly with the one Ptolemy made in the year of Nabonassar 880, on the 7th day of the month Athyr. Those are greatly mistaken who think that Ptolemy, that famous craftsman, was deceived by his own [cheikota mechanemata] contrivances, and that his observations did not agree with each other, or that he did not consider the interval of time elapsed since Hipparchus. For Hipparchus found the autumnal equinox on 26 September, while Ptolemy noted it on the 25th [?] of September. Thus an advance of the equinoxes by about one day and some hours was observed within about 150 years. For although it was commonly thought that the equinoxes moved forward by one day every hundred years, nevertheless a certain unknown motion of trepidation kept altering this interval of time from time to time.

units.la: Hoc anno Iuliano 185 [?], qui est annus à natiuitate Christi 238 [?] Censorinus scripsit præclarissimum suum libellum de die natali ad Q. Cærellium: in quo præter alia multa scitu dignißima ostendit, quæ fuerit ordinatio Diui C. Iulij Cæsaris in calendario Romano condendo, & quomodo anni Iuliani cum annis Nabonasari, à morte Alexandri, à Roma condita, Olympiadicis & Augustalibus sint connectendi. Præsupponit autem annum Iulianum 183 quasi fundamentum cæterorum omnium, & quasi certissimum temporum vehiculum: eumque lucidissimis notis signat, quod nimirum in illum incurrat Thoth Nabonasari 986, & in diem septimum kal. Iulij, hoc est, in 25 lunij: quod tunc consummati fuerint anni ab excessu Alexandri Magni quingenti sexaginta duo, hoc est, quod annus Nabonasari 986 fuerit à morte Alexandri quingentesimus sexagesimus secundus: si enim annos Ægyptios 424 qui à Nabonasaro vsque ad mortem morte Alexandri fluxerūt, adiicias ad annū à morte Alexandri quingentesimū sexagesimum secundum, prodit annus Nabonasari nongentesimus octogesi-mus sextus. Praeterea in annum Iulianum 285 Cen-sorinus ait incidere annum à Roma condita nongen-tesimum nonagesimum primum: à principio Olym-piadum millesimum & quartum decimum: à victo-ria Augusti Actiaca ducentesimum sexagesimum sep-timū: à triumpho Augustali ducentesimum sexagesi-mum quintum. Verba Censorini haec sunt: Hic an-nus, cuius velut index & titulus quidam est Vlpij & Pontiani consulatus, ab Olympiade prima millesi-mus est & quartus decimus, ex diebus duntaxat aesti-uis, quibus agon Olympicus celebratur. à Roma au-tem condita nongentesimus nonagesimus primus, & quidem ex Parilibus, unde vrbis anni numerantur. eorum vero annorum, quibus Iulianis nomen est, ducentesimus octogesimus tertius, sed ex die kal. Ian. vnde Iulius Caesar anni à se constituti fecit principium. at eorum qui vocantur anni Augustorum, ducentesimus sexagesimus quintus, perinde ex kal. Ian. quam-uis ex ante diem decimum sextum kal. Februarij Im-perator Caesar Diui filius, sententia L. Munacij Plan-ci à senatu caeterisque ciuibus Augustus appellatus est, se septimum & M. Vipsanio Agrippa III Coss. sed Aegyptij, quod biennio ante in poteltatem ditio-nemque populi Romani venerunt, habent hunc Au-gustorum annum ducentesimum sexagesimum septimum. nam vt à noltris, ita ab Aegyptiis quidam anni in literas relati sunt, vt quos Nabonasaru nominant, quod à primo imperij eius anno cōsurgunt: quorum hic nongentesimus octogesimus sextus est. item Phi-lippi, qui ab exceflu Alexandri Magni numerantur: & ad hunc usque perducti[?], annos quingentos sexa-ginta duos consummant. Sed horum initia semper à primo die mensis eius sumuntur, cui apud Ægyptios nomen est Thoth: quique hoc anno fuit ante diem septimum kal. Iulij, cum abhinc annos centum Impe-ratore Antonino Pio II, Vlpio & Brutio Præsente Coss. Romæ iidem dies fuerunt ante diem 12[?] kal. Augusti, quo tempore solet canicula in Ægypto fa-cere exortum. Dignissima hæc sunt consideratione, & aureis literis notanda: quæ Cesorini[?] ingenium vere historicum arguunt, & nobis ad annorum conne-xionem intelligendam prorsus sunt necessaria. Vult Censorinus Thoth Nabonasari 986[?] incurrisse in annum Iulianum 183, & in diem 25 lunij: quod certissimum esse feriæ hebdomadicæ à Nabonasaro usque ad nostram ætatem continuatæ, evidentissime monstrant: annus enim Iulianus 285 ex cyclo solis Augustali litera dominicalem habet G. & annus Nabonasari 986 cœpit die lunæ: quare 15 Iunij recte incidit in diem lunæ, ut nos in tabulis indicavimus. Huic etiam respondet Thoth Adiacus, qui incurrit in 29 mensis Sextilis, anno labente Iuliano decimo sexto: huic etiam congruit Thoth Iezdagirdicus, qui incurrit in annum Iulianum 677, decimum octavum diem Martij, feriam quartam, ut non dubium sit hæc omnia consentire. Cum autem annus Iulianus 283 fundamentum sit Censorini, cui omnem chronologiam superstruit: non immerito quæri potest, qua metho-do constet, annum 283 Iulianum recte comparari cum anno Christi 138.Id nos docet continuatio annorum Nabonasari usq; ad hæc tempora: nam Censorinus cum centum tantum annis elapsis post Ptolemæum hæc scripsisset, ignorare non potuit, quo in loco caledarij Romani effet Thoth Nabonasari 986. Deinde venerunt Persae, & ostenderunt Thoth Nabonasari 1380 incidere in diem 18 Martij, currente anno Christi 632. neque aberrare potuerunt in applicatione annorum Nabonasari ad annos Christi, cum iam per centum annos aera Christiana ex traditione Dionysij Abbatis Romani in vsu fuisset. Postea secutus est Muhamedes Aractenfis, qui ostendit Thoth Nabonasari 1630 incidere in diem decimam quintam Ianuarij, currente anno Christi 882. Deinde anno Christi millesimo cetefimo nonagesimo primo Hebraeus quidam venit, qui de aeris & interuallis temporum scripsit, &oftedit Thoth Nabonasari 1940 incidere in 30 Octobris, feriam quartam. Tandem accessit Alfonfus rex Hispaniarum, qui de sententia optimorum mathematicorum & historicorum pronunciauit Thoth Nabonasari bis millesimum incurrisse in decima quinta Octobris, feriam primam, currente anno Christi 1251, ita vt ad aeram Alfonfina, quae coepit kal. Iunij, labente anno Christi 1252 elapsi fuerint anni Aegyptiorum aequabiles a Nabonasaro 1999, & 230 dies. Inde ad nostra tempora certissimo calculo supputatur & continuantur anni Nabonasari: ad quos omnes reliquas aeras copulamus. Quamobrem li annos Nabonasari spectemus, dubium non est, quin annus Iulianus 283 sit annus Christi ducentesimus trigesimus octavus: quod etiam ex annis Antiochenis & Actiacis euidenter probari poterit. Etsi autem anni Christi apud Romanos ante Dionysium Abbatem in vsu non fuerint, apud Graecos tamen patres fuerunt notissimi, sicut apparet ex Chronicis Eusebij. Haec summa est connexionis chronologiae nostrae: quam nisi quis diligenter expedat, scopum nullum historiarum videbit, & instar caeci in tenebris oberrabit.
units.tr: In the Julian year 185 [?], which is the year 238 [?] from the birth of Christ, Censorinus wrote his most distinguished little book, On the Birthday, addressed to Q. Cærellius. In it, among many other things most worth knowing, he shows what arrangement the divine Gaius Julius Caesar made in establishing the Roman calendar, and how the Julian years are to be connected with the years of Nabonassar, with the years from the death of Alexander, with the years from the founding of Rome, with the Olympiads, and with the Augustan years. He takes the Julian year 283 as the foundation of all the rest and as the most reliable vehicle of dates, and he marks it with very clear indications: namely, that the first of Thoth in Nabonassar year 986 falls on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, that is, on 25 June. At that time 562 years had been completed since the departure of Alexander the Great; that is, the year 986 of Nabonassar was the five hundred and sixty-second year from the death of Alexander. For if you add the 424 Egyptian years that ran from Nabonassar to the death of Alexander to the five hundred and sixty-second year from the death of Alexander, you get the year 986 of Nabonassar. Moreover, Censorinus says that in the Julian year 285 there falls the year 991 from the founding of Rome; the 1014th from the beginning of the Olympiads; the 277th from the Actian victory of Augustus; and the 265th from the Augustan triumph. Censorinus' words are these: "This year, of which the consulship of Ulpius and Pontianus is as it were the index and title, is the 1014th from the first Olympiad, counting only the summer days on which the Olympic games are celebrated; from the founding of Rome it is the 991st, namely from the Parilia, from which the years of the city are counted. Of those years which bear the Julian name, it is the 283rd, but counted from the first of January, from which Julius Caesar made the beginning of the years he established. But of those years called the years of the Augusti, it is the 265th, likewise from the first of January, although Caesar, son of the divine one, was named Augustus by the senate and the other citizens, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, by the opinion of Lucius Munatius Plancus, in the seventh consulship of himself and the third consulship of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa. But the Egyptians, since they came under the power and dominion of the Roman people two years earlier, have this year of Augustus as the 267th. For just as some of our years have been recorded in writing, so also among the Egyptians there are some years which they call the years of Nabonassar, because they begin from the first year of his reign; of these, this is the 986th. Likewise there are the years of Philip, which are counted from the death of Alexander the Great, and which, brought down to this day, complete 562 years." But the beginnings of these are always taken from the first day of the month which the Egyptians call Thoth; and this year it fell on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, when a hundred years ago, in the second consulship of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, with Ulpius and Brutius Praesens as consuls, the same days at Rome fell on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, the time when the Dog Star usually rises in Egypt. These matters are most worthy of consideration and should be marked in golden letters: they show the truly historical mind of Censorinus, and they are absolutely necessary for us to understand the connection of the years. Censorinus wishes the first of Thoth of Nabonassar 986 to have fallen on the Julian year 283, and on 25 June. That this is certain, the weekly feast days continued from Nabonassar down to our own age most clearly show: for the Julian year 285, by the Augustan solar cycle, has the dominical letter G, and the year 986 of Nabonassar began on a Monday; hence 15 June rightly falls on a Monday, as we have indicated in the tables. The first of Thoth of Adiacus also agrees with this, which falls on the 29th day of the month of Sextilis in the sixteenth year of the Julian cycle; the first of Thoth of Yazdegerd also agrees, which falls on the eighteenth day of March in the Julian year 677, on a Wednesday, so that there is no doubt that all these agree. But since the Julian year 283 is the foundation of Censorinus, on which he builds all chronology, it may not unreasonably be asked by what method it is established that the Julian year 283 is rightly compared with the year 138 of Christ. The continuation of the years of Nabonassar down to these times teaches us this: for Censorinus, writing these things only a hundred years after Ptolemy, could not have been ignorant of where in the Roman calendar the year 986 of Nabonassar fell. Then the Persians came, and showed that the first of Thoth of Nabonassar 1380 fell on 18 March in the year 632 of Christ. Nor could they have gone astray in applying the years of Nabonassar to the years of Christ, since the Christian era had already been in use for a hundred years, through the tradition of Dionysius the Roman Abbot. After this came Muhammad of Aractes, who showed that the first of Thoth of Nabonassar 1630 fell on the fifteenth day of January in the year 882 of Christ. Then, in the year 1091 of Christ, a certain Hebrew came, who wrote about the eras and intervals of time, and showed that the first of Thoth of Nabonassar 1940 fell on 30 October, a Wednesday. At last came Alfonso, king of the Spains, who, following the opinion of the best mathematicians and historians, declared that the first of Thoth of Nabonassar, the two-thousandth, fell on the fifteenth day of October, a Sunday, in the year 1251 of Christ; so that, by the Alfonsine era, which began on the Kalends of June, when the year 1252 of Christ had elapsed, the even years of the Egyptians from Nabonassar amounted to 1999 years and 230 days. From this point down to our own times the years of Nabonassar are reckoned and continued by a most certain calculation, and to them we join all the other eras. Therefore, if we look to the years of Nabonassar, there is no doubt that the Julian year 283 is the year 238 of Christ; which can also be clearly proved from the Antiochene and Actian years. Although the years of Christ were not in use among the Romans before Dionysius the Abbot, they were nevertheless very well known among the Greek Fathers, as appears from the Chronicles of Eusebius. This is the sum of the connection of our chronology; unless someone works this out carefully, he will see no aim of histories, and will wander like a blind man in the dark.

units.la: * Hoc anno Iuliano trecetefimo vigefimo nono, qui fuit annus a natiuitate Chrifti ducentefimus octogefimus quartus, coepit imperare Diocletianus, 29 menfis Augusti,die Veneris, litera dominicali iuxta cyclum Auguftalem exiftete E:quado Thoth Nabonafari millefimus trigefimus fecundus erat in decima tertia lunij,feria fexta. Itaq; æra Diocletiani incurrit in 18 Athyr currête anno Nabonafari 1032. Etsi aute incertus autor Panegyrici fcribat Diocletianum imperium fuscepiffe ipfis Parilibus, id eft, XI kal. Maij: tamen Ægyptij Coptitæ æram Diocletiani traduxerunt ad 29 Augufti,vt refpoderet Thoth Adiaco,qui &ipfe incurrit in 29 Augufti,iuxta deprauatam rationem calendarij Romani, currente anno Iuliano decimo fexto. Hanc fixam æram Diocletiani a recentioribus Ægyptiis, qui Coptitæ appellantur, introduftam, hiftorici & aftronomi diligenter confignarunt, & æram Martyrum feu martyrij Sanctorum frequenter appellarunt: vt pofteri intelligerent, Diocletianum fummam tyrannidem aduerfus Chriftianos exercuiffe. Etsi enim ab anno decimo nono Diocletiani maxima fuerit perfecutio Chriftianorum, vt Eufebius in hiftoria ecclefiaftica teftatur; Coptitæ tamen in notationibus annorum fuorum initium perfecutionis Sanctorum fumunt a principio imperij Diocletiani: vt æra Diocletiani eadem fit cum æra martyrum Sanctorum, quod fuo loco ex Abul Hassumo[?] aliisque historicis comprobabo. Incidera autem æram Diocletiani in diem 29 Augusti, labente anno Christi 184. docent obseruationes Diui Am-brofij. idem tradit Maximus monachus in computo, idem scribit Alfonfus in canone ærarum: idem testatur Saracenus, cum inquit, Ægyptiorum autem æra initium (scilicet à Diocletiano) est a primo die Veneris, hoc est a primo die mensis Thoth: & ab isto die, scilicet a primo die mensis Thoth, usque ad diem Veneris, primum æra Arabum, sunt centum viginti tria millia & quadringenti & decem dies. Æram Diocletiani Alfraganus hisce verbis describit, Dies primus anni Coptitarum incepit a primo die Thoth, qui incidit in 29 Ab. hoc est, Augusti: ibi enim per Coptitas, recentiores Ægyptios intelligit, qui a die imperij Diocletiani cœperunt vsurpare annos Syros & Romanos, vt quarto quouis anno bisextum intercalarint. Vbi obseruandum est, abrogatâ Coptitas veteré sedem Thoth Nabonasari, & ad æram Diocletiani suum Thoth fixit: hinc factum est, vt 29 Augusti primum die mensis Thoth appellarint. Sed Persæ anno Christi labente 632 Thoth Nabonasari ad suum locum reuocarunt, idem fecit Albategnius circa annum Christi 882, & Alfonsus circa annum Christi 1252: a quo tempore ad nostram ætatem habemus certam annorum Ægyptiorum historiam. Neque hoc silentio est prætereundum, autores quosdam ex propria hypothesi menses Diocletiani extendere in annos quamplurimos præcedentes, vt opus sit considerare discrimen inter menses Diocletiani & Nabonasari: vt cum dicitur apud Eusebium in historia ecclesiastica lib.7, c.30. Anatolium Episcopum Laodicensem, qui tempore Diocletiani vixit, obseruasse æquinoctium autumnale die 26 Phamenoth mensis Ægyptiorum, hoc est, XI kal. Aprilis: satis intelligitur eum loqui de Phamenoth Diocletiani. Sic quādo Nicephorus Archiepiscopus Constantinopolitanus in Chronologia suarefert [?] Christum natum esse anno 42 imperij Augusti, die 29 Chiac, hoc est, 25 Decembris; intelligit Chiac Diocletiani, non autem Nabonasari: & quan-do Epiphanius scribit Christum natum esse anno 42 ab imperio Augusti, die vndecima Tybi secundum Ægyptios, qui fuit secundum Romanos ante diem octauum Iduum Ianuarij, manifestum est eum loqui de Tybi Diocletiani.
units.tr: In this year, the 329th of the Diocletian era, which was the 284th year from the birth of Christ, Diocletian began to reign on 29 August, a Friday; the dominical letter according to the Augustan cycle was E. Thoth of Nabonassar, the 1032nd year, fell on the 13th of June, a Friday. Therefore the era of Diocletian begins on 18 Athyr, in the year 1032 of Nabonassar. Although the unknown author of the Panegyric writes that Diocletian took up the empire on the Parilia itself, that is, on 21 April, nevertheless the Coptic Egyptians shifted the era of Diocletian to 29 August, so that Thoth would correspond to Athyr; this also fell on 29 August, according to the corrupted reckoning of the Roman calendar, in the sixteenth Julian year. The more recent historians and astronomers who are called Copts diligently recorded this fixed era of Diocletian, introduced by the recent Egyptians, and frequently called it the era of the Martyrs or of the martyrdom of the saints, so that posterity would understand that Diocletian exercised the greatest tyranny against the Christians. For although the greatest persecution of the Christians came in the nineteenth year of Diocletian, as Eusebius attests in his Ecclesiastical History, the Copts nevertheless, in marking the years of their own reckoning, take the beginning of the persecution of the saints from the beginning of Diocletian's reign, so that the era of Diocletian is the same as the era of the holy martyrs. I will prove this in its place from Abul Hassumo[?] and other historians. The era of Diocletian falls on 29 August, in the year 184 of Christ's era, as the observations of St Ambrose show. Maximus the monk likewise gives this in his computus, Alfonsus likewise writes it in his canon of eras, and Saracenus also bears witness, when he says: The era of the Egyptians (namely from Diocletian) begins on the first day of the week, that is, on the first day of the month Thoth; and from that day, namely the first day of the month Thoth, to the first day of the Arab era, there are 123,410 days. Alfraganus describes the era of Diocletian in these words: The first day of the year of the Copts began on the first day of Thoth, which fell on 29 Ab, that is, August; for there by "Copts" he means the more recent Egyptians, who from the day of Diocletian's reign began to use the Syrian and Roman years, intercalating a leap year every fourth year. Here it must be observed that, with the old seat of Thoth of Nabonassar abolished, the Copts fixed their own Thoth to the era of Diocletian; hence it came about that they called 29 August the first day of the month Thoth. But the Persians, in the year of Christ 632, restored Thoth of Nabonassar to its own place; Albategnius did the same about the year of Christ 882, and Alfonsus about the year of Christ 1252; from that time to our age we have a certain history of the Egyptian years. Nor should it be passed over in silence that certain authors, on their own hypothesis, extend the months of Diocletian back over very many preceding years, so that it is necessary to consider the difference between the months of Diocletian and of Nabonassar. Thus when Eusebius says in his Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 30, that Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, who lived in the time of Diocletian, observed the autumnal equinox on the 26th of Phamenoth, the month of the Egyptians, that is, 21 March, it is sufficiently clear that he speaks of the Phamenoth of Diocletian. So too when Nicephorus, archbishop of Constantinople, writes in his Chronology that Christ was born in the 42nd year of the reign of Augustus, on the 29th of Chiac, that is, 25 December, he means the Chiac of Diocletian, not that of Nabonassar; and when Epiphanius writes that Christ was born in the 42nd year from the empire of Augustus, on the eleventh day of Tybi according to the Egyptians, which was, according to the Romans, the day before the eighth of the Ides of January, it is plain that he speaks of the Tybi of Diocletian.

units.la: Vt autem rectè percipiatur, quibus diebus calendarij Iuliani respondeat dies Coptitarum, totum annum hac ratione conferre oportet: quod etiam fecit Episcopus Forofempronienis.
units.tr: To understand correctly which days of the Julian calendar correspond to the days of the Copts, one must compare the whole year in this way, as the Bishop of Forum Sempronii also did.
The fixed calendar of the Egyptians, or of Diocletian.

units.la: Huiusmodi est calendarium Ægyptiorum Coptitarum, qui respiciūt æram Diocletiani, & annis utuntur Romanis: horum enim Thoth perpetuò est in 29 Augusti, & prima dierum appendicum semper incurrit in 24 Augusti. Annis communibus ad Mesori postremum mensem adiiciunt quinque dies appendices: annis autem intercalaribus sex addunt: illamque sextam iniiciunt inter 28 & 29 Augusti: idcirco geminatur litera B. sicut in nostro calendario Iuliano litera F geminatur, quando bisextum inseritur inter 23 & 24 Februarij diem. Quod autem hic locus destinatus sit intercalationi apud recentiores Ægyptios, Saracenus euidenter ostendit, cum ait, Et menses eorum omnes sunt ex triginta diebus, nisi mensis Mesori eorum postremus: ipsi enim addunt infine eius quinque dies remanentes ex diebus anni: quare ex triginta quinque diebus constat: & cum est annus bisextilis, componunt eum ex triginta sex diebus. Scribit idem Saracenus annum secundum æræ Diocletiani, sextum, item decimum, decimum quartum, &c. bisextiles esse: ex quo intelligitur, si ad datos annos Diocletiani binariusadiiciatur, & fummaper 4 diuidatur, forevt an-nus is bisextilis habeatur, qui nihil in residuo relinquit post peractam diuisionem. Neque difficile est ex datis annis Iulianis & Christi, eruere annos respondentes Diocletiani: cum enim æra Diocletiani incurrat in 19 Augusti, labente anno Christi 284, intelligitur tunc elapsos fuisse annos Christi 283, qui fi subtrahantur ab annis subsequentibus Christi, prodit annus Diocletiani, cuius principium est a 19 Augusti: exempli gratia, annus fundationis Cafimiriani est annus Christi 1588. à quo anni 283 subtracti, relinquut[?] annum Diocletiani 1305, cuius principium incurrit in 19 Augusti, labente anno Christi 1588. Sic vitæ versa fi dentur anni Diocletiani, & ad eos adiiciantur anni 185, prodeunt anni Christi, in quos incidunt principia annorum Diocletiani ad diem 29 Augusti. Hoc insuper notandum est, propter diuersum situm intercalationis Coptitarum, in examine feriarum, diei vnius differentiam sæpenumero esse: quod ex E-piphanio colligere licet. is enim ait Christum natum esse ante diem octauum Iduum Ianuarij, hoc est, die quinta mensis Ianuarij fecundum Romanos, quam dicit fuisse sextam diem Syrograecorum ex mese Audinæo. Vt enim Syri diem auspicantur ab ortu solis, Romani autem a media nocte, quod tempus ipsis ex ante diem appellatur, ideoque Romani præueniunt, Syri autem subsequuntur: ita vndecima dies mensis Tybi Coptitarum, quæ iuxta Romanam confuetu-dinem respondet quinto Ianuarij, iuxta Syrogræcos applicari potest ad diem sextum Ianuarij, vel saltem eo recidit propter diuersum situm intercalationis.
units.tr: Such is the calendar of the Egyptian Copts, who reckon from the era of Diocletian and use the Roman years. For with them Thoth always falls on 29 August, and the first of the appended days always falls on 24 August. In common years they add five appended days to the end of the last month, Mesori; in leap years they add six, and they insert that sixth day between 28 and 29 August. Hence the letter B is doubled, just as in our Julian calendar the letter F is doubled when the leap day is inserted between 23 and 24 February. That this place was set aside for intercalation among the more recent Egyptians, Saracenus clearly shows when he says: "All their months consist of thirty days, except Mesori, their last month. For they add to its end the five days left over from the days of the year, so that it consists of thirty-five days. And when the year is a leap year, they make it up to thirty-six days." The same Saracenus writes that the sixth, tenth, fourteenth, and so on years of the era of Diocletian are leap years. From this it is understood that if 2 is added to a given year of Diocletian and the sum is divided by 4, that year is a leap year when nothing remains after the division. Nor is it difficult to work out the years of Diocletian corresponding to given Julian and Christian years. For since the era of Diocletian begins on 19 August in the year 284 of Christ, it is understood that the years 283 of Christ had then elapsed. If these are subtracted from the later years of Christ, the year of Diocletian results, whose beginning falls on 19 August. For example, the year of the foundation of Casimirian is the year 1588 of Christ. Subtracting 283 from it leaves the year 1305 of Diocletian, whose beginning falls on 19 August in the year 1588 of Christ. Thus, conversely, if the years of Diocletian are given and 185 is added to them, the years of Christ result, in which the beginnings of the years of Diocletian fall on 29 August. Moreover, it must be noted that, because of the differing placement of the Coptic intercalation, a difference of one day often arises in the calculation of the weekdays, as can be gathered from Epiphanius. For he says that Christ was born before the eighth day before the Ides of January, that is, on the fifth day of January according to the Romans, which he says was the sixth day of the Syrogreeks in the month Audynaeus. For as the Syrians begin the day at sunrise, but the Romans begin it at midnight, a time which they call ante diem, the Romans anticipate and the Syrians follow. So the eleventh day of the month Tybi of the Copts, which according to Roman custom corresponds to 5 January, can according to the Syrogreeks be applied to 6 January, or at least falls back on that day because of the differing placement of the intercalation.

units.la: {a} Hoc anno Christi trecentesimo duodecimo, mense Septembri, quinquennalia dedit Constantinus Magnus, postquam quadriennium absolutum ef-set ab ipsius Encaeniis, quae peractae fuerant anno Christi 308, VIII kal. Octobris. A primorum igitur quinquennalium panegyri, & quidem ex ante diem VIII kal. Octobris, labente anno Iuliano 357, & Christi 312 incipiunt Indictiones Constantinianae, quando Constantinus & Licinius Augg. secundum consulatum gesserunt, sicut etiam annotarunt Fasti Graeci, quos citat Onufrius, hisce verbis, Ἰνδικτιώνων Κωνσταντινιακῶν ἐντεῦθεν ἀρχή[?], id est, hinc Indictionum Constanti-niananianarū[?] exordiū. Sed quæ causa est, cur periodus annorum quindecim in vnaquaque Indictione coeperit vlurpari? quia scilicet anno quintodecimo à Quinquennalibus Constantinianis peracto, anno Christi 328, quo Vicennalia dedit Constantinus suorum[?] Encæniorum, teste Eusebio, dimissum est sacrofan-ctum Concilium Nicænum, anno tertio postquam convocatum fuisset à Constantino, accedente auctoritate Pontificis Sylvestri. Quamobrem interuallum Quinquennaliorum & Vicennaliorum Constantini fuerunt anni XV, quod postea institutum est temporibus notandis, ut nobis certo constaret de tempore & actis concilij Nicæni. Sed anni Indictionis cu-iusque diligenter ad nostra vsque tempora sunt continuati: licet Imperatores & Pontifices non adiecerint, quota esset Indictio, neque etiam expresserint, a quo mense & die annorum Indictionalium principia essent sumenda: hæc enim ex aliis temporum circumstantiis facile intelliguntur. Ponimus nos principium anni primi Indictionis primæ ad kal. Ianuarias anni Christi trecentesimi decimi tertij, secundum consuetudinem Pontificum Romanorum, licet ex institutione Constantini Magni, & sequentium aliquot Imperatorum comprobatione, Indictiones initium sumant à præcedenti Septembri: quamobrem si in datis annis Christi velimus cognoscere Indictionem, auferimus annos 312, & reliduum diuidimus per XV, hinc prouenit annus Indictionis, & quota sit currens Indictio, indicatur. Exempli gratia, si ab anno fundationis Cafimiriani, qui est annus Christi 1588, auferamus annos 312, remanent anni 1276, qui per quindecim diuisi in quotiente suggerunt 85[?] indictiones elapsas, & in reliduo relinquunt vnitatem quod indicium est annum Christi 1 ‹88 esse primum Indictionis Constantinianæ octogesimæ sextæ labé-tis. Est autem inuentum Indictionum vtilissimum notādis temporibus: quippe cius beneficio multi errores tolluntur, qui admissi [?] sunt ab autoribus in connexione annorum. Quare Iustinianus Imperator edicto præcepit, vt Indictionum annis[?] publicis inscrerentur, quemadmodum in nouellis constitutionibus authentica 47 videre licet. Cuius mandato non tantum tabelliones & publici notarij, verum etiam ecclesiastici calendarij computatores paruerunt: vnde factum est, vt ad nostram vsque ætatem salua & incolumis manserit Indictionum continuatio.
units.tr: {a} In this year of Christ 312, in September, Constantine the Great gave the quinquennial games, four years after his Encaenia, which had been celebrated in the year of Christ 308 on the 8th day before the Kalends of October. From the first quinquennial festival, namely from the 8th day before the Kalends of October in the Julian year 357, which is the year of Christ 312, the Constantinian indictions begin, when Constantine and Licinius, the Augusti, held their second consulship. The Greek Fasti, which Onufrius cites, note this in these words: [Ἰνδικτιώνων Κωνσταντινιακῶν ἐντεῦθεν ἀρχή], that is, "hence the beginning of the Constantinian indictions." But why did the period of fifteen years begin to be used in each indiction? Because in the fifteenth year after the Constantinian quinquennalia, in the year of Christ 328, when Constantine gave his Vicennalia, that is, the celebration of his Encaenia, according to Eusebius, the holy Council of Nicaea was dismissed, in the third year after it had been convened by Constantine, with the authority of Pope Sylvester added. Therefore the interval between the quinquennalia and vicennalia of Constantine was fifteen years, which was afterwards adopted for marking dates, so that we could be certain of the time and acts of the Council of Nicaea. But the years of each indiction have been carefully continued down to our own times, although the emperors and popes did not add which indiction it was, nor state from which month and day the years of the indictions were to be reckoned, for these are easily understood from other circumstances of the time. We take the beginning of the first year of the first indiction to be the Kalends of January in the year of Christ 313, according to the custom of the Roman pontiffs, although by the institution of Constantine the Great and the confirmation of several later emperors, the indictions take their beginning from the preceding September. Therefore, if in the given years of Christ we wish to learn the indiction, we subtract 312 years, divide the remainder by 15, and the result gives the year of the indiction, and the remainder indicates which indiction is current. For example, if from the year of the foundation of Casimirus, which is the year of Christ 1588, we subtract 312 years, 1276 years remain; divided by fifteen these give 85 elapsed indictions in the quotient, and leave a remainder of one, which shows that the year of Christ 1588 is the first year of the eighty-sixth indiction of the Constantinian cycle that has run its course. The invention of the indictions is very useful for marking times, for by its help many errors are removed which the authors admitted in the connection of years. Therefore the Emperor Justinian by edict ordered that the years of the indictions be inscribed in public documents, as may be seen in the Novels, Authentica 47. By his command not only notaries and public scribes, but also the computists of the ecclesiastical calendar obeyed, and so it came about that the continuity of the indictions has remained safe and intact down to our own age.

units.la: Hoc anno Christi trecentesimo vigesimo tertio, qui fuit annus Iulianus 368, litteris dominicalibus existentibus FE, die 23 Martij, feria prima, Patres ecclesiarum orientalium inierunt cneadecaeteridem [?] à neomenia proxima æquinoctio verno, quod obseruarunt confici die 21 Martij. Et sanciuerunt iidem patres, deinceps in sacro Pascha celebrando, perpetuo respiciendum esse ad neomeniam proximam æquinoctio verno, vt circa plenilunium illius lunationis festum paschionis [?] & resurrectionis Dominicæ peragatur: quod deinceps deretum [?] post coprobatum est per Episcopos trecentos & octodecim, qui concilio Nicæno præfuerunt, teste Epiphanio [?]. Itaq; annus Christi 323 est primus cycli eneadecaeteridis, quem hactenus ecclesia est secuta [?]: vnde intelligitur, quomodo in subsequentibus annis aureus numerus sit invenstigandus [?]. Cùm enim ante annum Christi 323 elapsi fuerint anni 322, à datis annis Christi auferantur anni 322 & reliquum diuidatur in 19: si nihil superfuerit, erit aureus numerus: vel illud ipsum quod supersupererit indicabit aureum numerum. Exempli gra-tia, cupio scire, quis sit aureus numerus anno Christi 360, quo Diuus Ambrosius scribit celebratam dominicam passionis ad 23 Aprilis: si ab anno Christi 360, auferantur anni 322, relinquuntur anni 38, qui si in 19 distribuantur, nihil superest: quare annus Christi 360 habet aureu numerum XIX. Ita si ab anno fundationis Casimiriani, qui est annus Christi 1588, subtrahantur anni 322, remanent anni 1266, qui per 19 diuisi, in residuo relinquunt 12 qui est aureus numerus anni Christi 1588, iuxta ordinationem ecclesiasticam. Quòd autem anno Christi 323 neomenia Paschalis inciderit in 23 Martij, euidenter probat enneadecaeteris Iuliana: nam annus Iulianus 368 numerum aureum habet VII, qui ponitur in calendario Iuliano ad 8 kalend. Aprilis: at quia luna ab ordinatione Iuliana vsque ad hoc tempus fere biduum anticipauit, neomenia coelestis fuit die 10 kalend. Aprilis, hoc est, 23 Martij. Hanc neomeniam Patres orientales & Nicaeni fecerunt initium cycli decennouennalis: ideo ad 23 Martij apposuerunt notam vnitatis, & cuique lunationi modo 30, modo 29 dies concesserunt, vt fieri solet in enneadecaeteride. Ex quo intelligitur numerum aureum ecclesiae receptum, initium suum habere a neomenia Paschali, quae proxima est aequinoctio verno, & extendi vsque ad subsequentem neomeniam Paschalem: quamobrem licet nos in Ephemeridibus vulgatis statim ad kalend. Ianuarias aureum numerum assignemus, is tamen semper a neomenia sequenti Paschali est inchoandus, sicut prima ecclesiae enneadecaeteris non ab ipsis kalend. Ianuariis anni Christi 323, sed a subsequenti neomenia Paschali, quae incurrit in 23 Martij, fuit inchoata. Quia vero Pascha celebrari solet mense Martio & Aprili, satis est ut aureū numerū in hisce duobus mensib. adscribamus, & quę si-tum tepore concilij Nicæni habuerit, consideremus.
units.tr: In this year of Christ 323, which was the Julian year 368, with the dominical letters being FE, on 23 March, the first day of the week, the Fathers of the Eastern churches began the nineteen-year cycle from the new moon nearest to the vernal equinox, which they observed as falling on 21 March. And the same Fathers decreed that thereafter, in celebrating the holy Passover, one must always look to the new moon nearest the vernal equinox, so that the feast of the Passover and the Lord's resurrection is held around the full moon of that lunation. This was afterwards confirmed by the three hundred and eighteen bishops who presided at the Council of Nicaea, according to Epiphanius. Thus the year of Christ 323 is the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, which the Church has followed up to now, and from this it is understood how the golden number is to be found in the following years. For since 322 years had elapsed before the year of Christ 323, subtract 322 from the given year of Christ and divide the remainder by 19: if nothing is left over, that is the golden number; or the very remainder left over will indicate the golden number. For example, I wish to know what the golden number is in the year of Christ 360, in which Saint Ambrose writes that the Lord's Day of the Passion was celebrated on 23 April. If from the year of Christ 360 we subtract 322 years, 38 years remain, which, divided by 19, leave nothing over; therefore the year of Christ 360 has the golden number XIX. Likewise, if from the year of the foundation of Casimirus, which is the year of Christ 1588, we subtract 322 years, 1266 years remain, which, divided by 19, leave 12 as remainder; this is the golden number of the year of Christ 1588, according to ecclesiastical ordinance. That the new moon of Easter fell on 23 March in the year of Christ 323 is clearly proved by the Julian nineteen-year cycle: for the Julian year 368 has the golden number VII, which is placed in the Julian calendar at 8 days before the Kalends of April; but since the moon had advanced by nearly two days from the Julian arrangement up to this time, the heavenly new moon fell on 10 days before the Kalends of April, that is, on 23 March. The Fathers of the East and the Nicene Fathers made this new moon the beginning of the cycle, and therefore they placed the mark of unity against 23 March and assigned to each lunation now 30 days, now 29 days, as is usually done in the nineteen-year cycle. From this it is understood that the golden number accepted by the Church has its beginning from the Paschal new moon which is nearest the vernal equinox, and extends to the following Paschal new moon. Therefore, although in the common ephemerides we assign the golden number at once at the Kalends of January, it must always be reckoned from the next Paschal new moon, just as the first cycle of the Church was begun not from the Kalends of January in the year of Christ 323, but from the following Paschal new moon, which fell on 23 March. But since Easter is usually celebrated in March and April, it is enough to ascribe the golden number in these two months, and to consider what position it had at the time of the Council of Nicaea.

Exempli gratia, fi aureus numerus fit XIX, ponitur is ad 5 Martij & 4 Aprilis: sed qui ponitur ad 4 Aprilis fine omni controuersia propinquior est æquinoctio verno, quod figitur in 21 Martij: ergo neomenia incurres in 4 Aprilis basis est proxime futuri Pafchatis celebrandi. Si aureus numerus fit XII, ponitur is ad 22 Martij,& 20 Aprilis: sed qui ponitur ad 22 Martij proximus est æquinoctio, quare ab illa neomenia lumendum est exordium Pafchatis celebrandi. Si contingat vtriusque mensis aureum numerum æque distare ab æquinoctio, tunc posterior habetur pro indice neomeniæ Paschalis. Neomenia Paschali inuenta, ab ea numerentur inclusiue dies XIIII, & perueneritur ad plenilunium, in quo Iudæi & Christiani Iudaizantes [illegible, ~20 letters] fiue Quartadecimani appellati, Pascha celebrat, quæcunque fit dies septimanæ. Quia vero ex Patrum constitutione festum Paschatis nobis celebrandum est fem-per die Dominica, qua Dominus & Saluator noster à mortuis resurrexit; fit vt die Dominica post XIIII lunam Paschalem trafigamus festum resurrectionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi: & fi contingat XIIII lu-nam incurrere in diem Dominicum, tunc post octi-duum demum celebramus Pascha,ne cum Iudæis aut Quartadecimanis conueniamus. Iuxta hunc canonem à Patribus & concilio Nicæno præscriptum vsque ad nostram ætatem folennitates Paschales celebrantur ab iis, qui nullam adhuc admiserunt æquinoctij verni aut cycli lunaris restitutionem: quasi adhuc æquinoctium vernum hæreat in 21 Martij, & quasi situs aurei numeri adhuc veras nouiluniorum sedes demonstret. Exempli gratia, hoc anno Christi 1589 [?] aureus numerus est XIII, qui in tabella Nicæna ponitur ad diem vndecimum Martij, à quo nos secundum stilum veterem & mendosum neomeniam Paschalem incipimus, cum tamen quinto die ante incideret neomenia cœlestis, vt experientia nos docuit, & Ephemerides astronomorum prædixerunt: à die vndecima Martij inclusiue numerantes XIIII dies, peruenimus ad 14 Martij, vbi plenilunium constituimus, quod tamen quarto die ante præcessit. itaq; sequenti die dominica, h.e. 30 Martij Pascha celebrauimus, quod tamen iuxta anticipationem æquinoctij verni & cycli lunaris emendationem fuisset celebrandum die 23 Martij. De hac deprauata Paschatis celebratione coquefti sunt viri eruditissimi, vt Robertus Linconiensis, Episcopus Cameracensis, Regiomontanus & Stoflerus: & in emendationem consenserat Ioannes XXIII Pontifex tempore concilij Constantiensis, sed nihil effectum est, donec Gregorius XIII ex calendario Romano decem dies eximeret, quo æquinoctium vernum rediret ad 21 Martij, cui tempore concilij Nicæni hærebat. Quemadmodum autem per exemtionem decem dierum æquinoctium vernum restitutum est ad priscam sedem concilij Nicæni: ita etiam per exemtionem quatuor dierum, quos luna suo motu à tempore concilij Nicæni anticipauit, aureus numerus ad vera nouilunia restitui potest, vt nimirum vnitas quæ à Patribus Nicænis collocata erat ad 23 Martij, retrahatur ad 19 Martij, & binarius qui erat positus ad 12 Martij figatur ad 8 Martij, & sic de aliis omnibus. Si enim ex tabella Nicæna velimus nostro seculo sedem nouilu-niorum cœlestium scrutari, inuentum aureum numerum cuiusque anni oportet in quintum diem prae-cedentem reiicere: ut hoc anno Christi 1589 aureus numerus currit XIII, quiin[?] tabella Nicaena ponitur ad undecimum diem Martij. quod si ergo in quin-tum diem praecederetem reiiciatur, neomeniam often-dit die 7 Martij, secundum medium motum vel pha-sin lunarem, ut in Ephemeridibus cernere licet. Haec neomenia proxima est verno aequinoctio, quod no-stro tempore conficitur in 10 & 11 Martij secundum stilum veterem: quam obrem si inde numeretur dies XIIII, descenditur ad 21 Martij, in quo plenilunium haeret: cum autem ea dies sit Veneiis[?],qui celebrari non potest festum resurrectionis Dominicae, utiq; Pascha reiiciendum est in subsequentem diem Dominicam, videlicet in 23 Martij, quae fuit 2 Aprilis secundum stilum Gregorianum. Hac ratione intelligitur, quomodo secundum nostri seculi aequinoctiu vernum neome-nia Paschalis indagari debeat, saluo manente cyclo decennouennali. Quaobrem miratur nonnulli, qua-re Gregorius XIII, aurei numeri quidem continuatio-nem conseruanda, illius autem usum abrogandu esse censuerit, & pro inuestigatione nouiluniorum Paschalium cyclum 30 Epactarum considerandum esse voluerit.
