Once the golden number of any year has been found, according to the custom of the Church, one sees in the table which of the two months is nearer to 21 March, for that is where the Paschal new moon is shown. For example, if the golden number is XIX, it is placed at 5 March and 4 April. But the one placed at 4 April is, beyond all dispute, nearer to the spring equinox, which is fixed at 21 March; therefore the new moon falling on 4 April is the basis for celebrating the Passover that is soon to come. If the golden number is XII, it is placed at 22 March and 20 April. But the one placed at 22 March is nearer the equinox, so the beginning of the Passover to be celebrated is to be taken from that new moon. If it happens that the golden number of both months is equally distant from the equinox, then the later one is taken as the indicator of the Paschal new moon. Once the Paschal new moon has been found, one counts fourteen days from it inclusively, and arrives at the full moon, on which the Jews and the Judaizing Christians, called Quartodecimans, celebrate the Passover, whatever day of the week it may be. But since by the decree of the Fathers our festival of Easter must always be kept on the Lord's day, on which our Lord and Saviour rose from the dead, it follows that we celebrate the festival of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ on the Sunday after the fourteenth Paschal moon; and if the fourteenth moon happens to fall on a Sunday, then we celebrate the Passover a full week later, so that we do not agree with the Jews or the Quartodecimans. In accordance with this rule, prescribed by the Fathers and the Council of Nicaea, up to our own age the Easter festivals have been celebrated by those who have not yet admitted any restoration of the vernal equinox or of the lunar cycle, as if the vernal equinox still stuck at 21 March, and as if the position of the golden number still showed the true seats of the new moons. For example, in this year of Christ 1589 [?] the golden number is XIII, which in the Nicene table is placed at 11 March. From this day we, following the old and faulty style, begin the Paschal new moon, although the heavenly new moon actually fell five days earlier, as experience has taught us and as the astronomers' Ephemerides had predicted. Counting fourteen days inclusively from 11 March, we arrive at 14 March, where we have set the full moon, although it had in fact occurred four days earlier. Therefore on the following Sunday, that is 30 March, we celebrated Easter, although on account of the anticipation of the vernal equinox and the correction of the lunar cycle it ought to have been celebrated on 23 March. Very learned men have complained about this corrupt celebration of Easter, such as Robert of Lincoln, the bishop of Cambrai, Regiomontanus and Stoeffler. Pope John XXIII agreed to a correction at the time of the Council of Constance, but nothing was achieved until Gregory XIII removed ten days from the Roman calendar, by which the vernal equinox returned to 21 March, where it had stood at the time of the Council of Nicaea. Just as by the removal of ten days the vernal equinox was restored to its ancient seat at the Council of Nicaea, so too by the removal of four days, which the moon has anticipated by its own motion since the time of the Council of Nicaea, the golden number can be restored to the true new moons. Thus the unit which the Nicene Fathers had placed at 23 March is moved back to 19 March, and the two which had been placed at 12 March is fixed at 8 March, and so on for all the others. For if we wish in our own century to search out from the Nicene table the seat of the heavenly new moons, we must throw back the golden number found for any year by five days: so in this year of Christ 1589 the golden number is XIII, which in the Nicene table is placed at 11 March. If therefore it is thrown back five days, it shows the new moon on 7 March, according to the mean motion or lunar phase, as can be seen in the Ephemerides. This new moon is nearest to the vernal equinox, which in our time falls on 10 and 11 March according to the old style. Wherefore if fourteen days are counted from it, we come down to 21 March, on which the full moon stands. But since that day is a Friday, on which the festival of the Lord's resurrection cannot be celebrated, Easter must of course be put off to the following Sunday, namely 23 March, which was 2 April in the Gregorian style. In this way it can be understood how the Paschal new moon ought to be sought according to the vernal equinox of our century, while the nineteen-year cycle remains unchanged. For this reason some wonder why Gregory XIII judged that the continuation of the golden number should be kept, but its use abolished, and wanted the thirty Epacts to be considered for finding the Paschal new moons.

units.la: Sane dubium non est, quin aureus numerus a certa epocha continuatus quouis seculo possit nobis usum praestare, si modo lunae anticipationem animaduer-tamus: sed Gregorius XIII cum ex Mathematicorum veterum & recentiorum relatione didicisset, in pe-riodo usitata nouendecim annorum solarium, nimis magnam fieri anticipationem lunae, & dari cyclum 30 annorum lunarium, quo peracto luna praecisissi-me restituatur ad suam epocham, maluit menstruam lunae periodu iuxta Arabum calculu exquisitiore praesupponere & definire spacio dierum 29, horarum 12, & scrupulorum horariorum 792: unde communis anni lunaris quantitas existit dierum 254, horarum 8, & scrupulorum horariorum 864: atque hinc oritur cyclus 30 annorum lunarium Arabibus vsitatus, quo exacto luna ad epocham suam ita præcise reuertitur, ut anticipatio in diem unum excrescere non possit nisi completo spacio maiore duobus millibus annorum, teste Saraceno. Itaq; 30 numeri Epactales, quos introduxit Gregorius XIII, ostendunt periodum 30 annorum Arabicorum, qui continet 360 lunationes æquales, & 1063 1 dies integros, teste Roberto Episcopo Linconiensi in computo. Hactenus de enneadecaeteride ecclesiastica, quam Nicænam appellamus, satis dictum esto: quod autem conueniat cum enneadecaeteride luliana, euidentissimè apparet ex nouiluniis, quæ nostro tempore contingunt. Anno enim Christi 1588 iuxta vsum ecclesiæ aureus numerus decurrit XII, qui in tabella Nicæna ponitur ad 22 Martij diem, in qua nouiluniu cofpiceretur, nisi luna à concilio Nicæno vsq; ad hæc tempora supra quatriduum anticipasset priscam epocham: si enim anni 1264, qui ab initio enneadecaeteridis ecclesiasticæ ad nos sunt elapsi, diuidatur per 247 annos solares, producitur quatriduum: itaque quinto die ante neomenia incidit. Sed iuxta cyclum enneadecaetericum Iulij Cæsaris labente anno Iuliano 1633, aureus numerus est XVIII, qui ponitur ad nonum kal. Aprilis, in quo neomenia fuisset, nisi luna ab ordinatione Cæsaris anteuertisset priorem locu supra sex dies: quamobrem septimo die ante nonum kal. Aprilis, hoc est, 17 Martij conspecta est neomenia. Cum autem prima neomenia Iuliana contigerit media nocte, quæ praecessit kal.Ianuarias anni primi Iuliani,anticipatio-nem Iulianam recte conferimus in diem septimum praecedentem:cumque neomenia prima Paschalis intelligatur contigisse circa mediam noctem quae prae-cessit diem 2 3 Martij currente anno Christi 323, recte tribuimus anticipationem Nicaenam quinto diei praecedenti. Hinc apparet si ex dato numero aureo Iulij Caesaris sex auferantur,proditurum aureum numerum Ecclesiae: ita vt ille a kal.Ianuariis, hic autem circa neomeniam proximam aequinoctio verno inci-pere intelligatur. Si vero ad datum aureum numerum Iulij Caesaris decem adiiciantur; prodit aureus numerus Hebraeorum, qui incipit a Tisri,hoc est,cir-ca aequinoctium autumnale quod praecedit kal.Ianuarij Iulianas. Cum subtractio fieri non potest, adiicienda sunt XIX: quando vero post additionem summa excreuit supra XIX, abiicienda sunt XIX, vt communis logistica docet. Haec est collatio legitima trium vsitatarum enneadecaeteridum: scilicet Iulianae, Nicaenae, & Iudaicae.
units.tr: Certainly there is no doubt that the golden number, continued from a fixed epoch, could give us its service in any century, provided we take note of the anticipation of the moon. But Gregory XIII, when he had learned from the account of the ancient and recent mathematicians that in the customary period of nineteen solar years the anticipation of the moon becomes too great, and that a cycle of thirty lunar years is given, at the end of which the moon is restored exactly to its epoch, preferred to assume and define the lunar month more precisely, following the calculation of the Arabs, as a span of 29 days, 12 hours and 792 hourly scruples. From this the quantity of a common lunar year comes to 354 days, 8 hours and 864 hourly scruples. And from this arises the thirty-year lunar cycle used by the Arabs, at the end of which the moon returns so precisely to its epoch that the anticipation cannot grow by a single day unless a span of more than two thousand years is completed, as the Saracen testifies. Thus the thirty Epact numbers, which Gregory XIII introduced, show the thirty-year Arabic period, which contains 360 equal lunations and 10631 whole days, according to Robert, bishop of Lincoln, in his computation. So much has been said about the ecclesiastical nineteen-year cycle, which we call Nicene. That it agrees with the Julian nineteen-year cycle is most evident from the new moons which occur in our own time. For in the year of Christ 1588, according to the custom of the Church, the golden number runs to XII, which in the Nicene table is placed at 22 March, the day on which the new moon would be seen, were it not that since the Council of Nicaea the moon had anticipated the old epoch by more than four days. For if the years 1264 which have elapsed from the beginning of the ecclesiastical nineteen-year cycle to our time are divided by 247 solar years, a difference of four days results; and so the new moon falls five days earlier. But according to the nineteen-year cycle of Julius Caesar, as the Julian year 1633 slips by, the golden number is XVIII, which is placed at 24 March, on which day the new moon would have been, had not the moon, since Caesar's ordinance, anticipated its former place by six days. Therefore, seven days before 24 March, that is on 17 March, the new moon was seen. Now since the first Julian new moon fell about midnight preceding 1 January of the first Julian year, we rightly assign the Julian anticipation to the seventh day before. And since the first Paschal new moon is understood to have occurred about midnight preceding 23 March in the year of Christ 323, we rightly assign the Nicene anticipation to the fifth day before. Hence it is evident that if six is subtracted from a given golden number of Julius Caesar, the golden number of the Church results, so that the one is understood to begin from 1 January and the other from the new moon nearest the vernal equinox. But if ten is added to a given golden number of Julius Caesar, the golden number of the Hebrews results, which begins from Tishri, that is, about the autumnal equinox which precedes the Julian 1 January. When subtraction cannot be done, nineteen must be added; but when, after addition, the sum has risen above nineteen, nineteen must be taken away, as ordinary arithmetic teaches. This is the lawful comparison of the three customary nineteen-year cycles: namely the Julian, the Nicene and the Jewish.

units.la: Hoc anno Christi trecentesimo vigesimo quinto, ante diem decimum tertium kal.Iulij, currere anno Alexandri sexcentesimo trigesimo sexto, die decima nona mensis Daesij secundum Syros, celebratus est primus confessus Nicaenus, vt in calendario Persico ex historia Ecclesiastica Socratis, & principio magni cycli Persarum probauimus. Fuit is annus vigesimus imperij Constantini Magni, vt Maximus monachus in computo refert, hisce verbis, <bl>ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς βασιλείας Κωνσταντίνου ἢ ἐν Νικαίᾳ γέγονε σύνοδος.</bl> hoc est, anno vigesimo imperij Constantini in Nicaea fuit concilium: quamuis postea male applicet hoc tempus concilij Nicaeni ad annum Christi 316. Audiamus D.Epiphanium in sermone contra sectam Audianorum, quantis laudibus evehat Constantinum Magnum, quòd in Nicæa synodum contra Arium congregarit, & certam Pafcharis celebrandi rationem indixerit: aic enim, [illegible, ~40 letters] Κωνσταντίνῳ[?] τῷ φιλοχρίστῳ[?], καὶ ἀεὶ μαχόμενον[?] [illegible, ~30 letters] Νικαίας[?] [illegible, ~25 letters] Ἀρείου[?] [illegible, ~20 letters]. hoc est, Etenim illo tempore duo maxima contribuit nobis Deus per prædictum Constantinum Dei amatissimum ac semper beatissimū: quòd congregauit universalem synodum, ediditque fidem in Nicæa expositam & confessam cū subscriptione Episcoporū qui ibi conuenerunt, quò Arius subuerte-retur, & fidei puritas omnibus prædicaretur: & quòd curauit vt ab ipsis corrigeretur Paschatis stabilitas[?] ad unionem nostram. Cùm ergo tanta beneficia nobis sint exhibita per concilium Nicænum, pudedum foret nos tempus hoc orbi Christiano saluberrimum ignorare. Pleriq; existimant concilium Nicænum congregatum fuisse anno Christi 323: sed nos indicauimus eo anno, die 25 Martij incurrisse principium aurei numeri a concilio Nicæno constituti.
units.tr: In this year of Christ 325, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the 636th year of Alexander, on the nineteenth day of the month Daesius according to the Syrians, the first Nicene council was held, as we have shown from the Persian calendar, from Socrates' Ecclesiastical History, and from the beginning of the Persian great cycle. This was the twentieth year of the reign of Constantine the Great, as Maximus the monk reports in his computation, in these words: ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς βασιλείας Κωνσταντίνου ἢ ἐν Νικαίᾳ γέγονε σύνοδος [in the reign of Constantine, the council took place at Nicaea], that is, in the twentieth year of Constantine's reign the council was held at Nicaea. Yet he later wrongly applies this time of the Nicene council to the year of Christ 316. Let us hear St Epiphanius in his sermon against the sect of the Audians, with what praise he extols Constantine the Great, because he assembled a synod at Nicaea against Arius and appointed a fixed manner of celebrating Easter. For he says: Κωνσταντίνῳ τῷ φιλοχρίστῳ [to Constantine, the Christ-loving], καὶ ἀεὶ μαχόμενον [and always fighting], Νικαίας [of Nicaea], Ἀρείου [of Arius], that is: For at that time God gave us two very great benefits through the aforesaid Constantine, most beloved of God and always most blessed. First, he gathered the universal synod and issued the faith set forth and confessed at Nicaea, with the signatures of the bishops who came together there, by which Arius was overthrown and the purity of the faith was proclaimed to all. Second, he took care that the fixing of Easter was corrected by them for our unity. Since therefore such great benefits have been bestowed on us through the Nicene council, it would be shameful for us to be ignorant of this time, which is most salutary to the whole Christian world. Many think the Nicene council was assembled in the year of Christ 323, but we have shown that on that year, on 25 March, the beginning of the golden number fixed by the Nicene council fell.

units.la: d Hoc anno Christi trecentesimo vigesimo o-ctauo dimissum fuit sacrosanctum concilium Nicænum a Constantino, postquàm triennium in Nicæa subsisteret. Dimisso concilio Constantinus Vicennalia dedit suorum Encaeniorum, ac post decennium elapsum exhibuit Tricennalia suorum Encaeniorum, atque his Tricennalibus Constantini Dalmatius Cæsar est appellatus, scilicet anno Christi 338 sub finem labente, quemquemadmodum testatur Hieronymus in supplemento chronicorum Eusebij.
units.tr: In this year of Christ 328 the holy Nicene council was dismissed by Constantine, after it had continued for three years at Nicaea. After the council was dismissed, Constantine celebrated the Vicennalia of his reign, and after ten years had passed he celebrated the Tricennalia of his reign; and at these Tricennalia Dalmatius was named Caesar by Constantine. This was in the year of Christ 338, towards the end of the year, as Jerome attests in the supplement to Eusebius' Chronicle.

units.la: ¶ Hoc anno Christi trecentesimo trigesimo septimo, qui est annus Iulianus trecentesimus octogesimus secundus, in quem incidit annus ab Vrbe condita millesimus nonagesimus, XI kal. Iunij, die sancto Pentecostes mortuus est Constantinus Magnus Imperator, anno vitæ LXV I[?], imperij vero XXX, mense IX, & die XXVII[?]. Cadauer Constantinopoli sepultum est in Basilica Apostolorum, atque inter Diuos relatus est, vt commemorat Onufrius in commentario 2 Fastorum. Hinc patet XI kal. Iunij, hoc est, xxii diem Maij fuisse diem Dominicam: quod etiam indicat littera Dominicalis B, quæ incidit in 22 Maij. Hinc si retrorsum numerentur septem septimanæ, hoc est, dies fere quinquaginta, ascenditur ad 5 Aprilis, diem Dominicam, in qua sanctum Pascha intelligitur celebratum fuisse. Fuit tunc aureus numerus secundum Ecclesiam XV, qui in tabella Nicæna ponitur ad 19 Martij: vbi nouilunium indicat. A 19 Martij inclusiuè sumto si numeremus dies XIIII, peruenimus ad primum diem Aprilis, diem Veneris, qua Pascha iuxta constitutionem Patrum celebrari non potuit, ideo se-quenti die Dominica, die 5 Aprilis fuit peractum.
units.tr: In this year of Christ 337, which is the Julian year 382, in which falls the year 1090 from the founding of the City, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, on the holy day of Pentecost, the emperor Constantine the Great died, in the sixty-fifth year of his life, the thirtieth of his reign, in the ninth month and on the twenty-seventh day. His body was buried at Constantinople in the Church of the Apostles, and he was counted among the divine emperors, as Onuphrius records in the second commentary on the Fasti. From this it is clear that the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, that is, 22 May, was a Sunday; the dominical letter B, which falls on 22 May, also indicates this. Hence, if seven weeks are counted backwards, that is, about fifty days, we arrive at 5 April, a Sunday, on which the holy Passover is understood to have been celebrated. The golden number according to the Church was then 15, which in the Nicene table is placed at 19 March, where it indicates the new moon. If we count fourteen days from 19 March inclusive, we arrive at 1 April, a Friday, on which Easter could not be celebrated according to the constitution of the Fathers; therefore it was celebrated on the following Sunday, 5 April.

units.la: Neomenia ergo illa quæ incurrit in 19 Martij fuit Pa-schalis, cum proxima esset æquinoctio verno, quod annis communibus conficiebatur in 20 Martij, annis vero bisextilibus in 21 Martij, quemadmodum accidit anno Christi 323. Ex quo apparet elapsis annis solaribus 191 æquinoctium vernum fere biduum antici-passe: anno enim Christi labente 132 communi, iuxta observationem Ptolemæi deprehensum fuit in 22 Martij, quod annis bisextilibus conficiebatur in 23 Martij. units.tr: That new moon, then, which fell on 19 March, was the Paschal one, since it was next to the vernal equinox, which in common years was fixed at 20 March and in leap years at 21 March, as happened in the year of Christ 323. From this it appears that after 191 solar years the vernal equinox had moved back almost two days: for in the year of Christ 132, a common year, according to the observation of Ptolemy, it was found on 22 March, which in leap years was fixed on 23 March. units.la: Circa haec tempora vixit Diuus Ambrosius Episcopus Mediolanensis, qui in Epistola ad Episcopos per Aemyliam constitutos de solennitate Paschali eleganter disserit, & in tribus annis Diocletiani, videlicet 76, 89, & 93 ostendit, quibus feriis & diebus calendarij Romani inciderit festum Paschatis.
units.tr: Around this time lived the divine Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who in his letter to the bishops established throughout Aemilia discusses the Paschal festival with great elegance. He shows, in the three years of Diocletian 76, 89 and 93, on which days and weekdays of the Roman calendar the feast of Easter fell.

units.la: a Anno hoc septuagesimo sexto imperij Diocletiani, vigesimo octauo die Pharmuthi dicit Ambrosius Dominicam Paschae celebratam fuisse sine vlla dubitatione maiorum: atqui Thoth Diocletiani anni ineuntis 76 incipit 29 Augusti, anno Christi labente 359, idcirco 28 Pharmuthi incurrit in 23 Aprilis, feriam solis, anno subsequenti Christi 360, litera dominicali existente A. Hoc anno Christi 360 aureus numerus erat XIX qui in tabella Nicaena ponitur iuxta 3 Aprilis, vbi nouilunium Paschale indicat, proximum aequinoctio verno: itaque decima quarta luna incidebat in diem Dominicam, nimirum in 16 Aprilis, proinde differebatur pascha in Dominica in subsequentem diem solis, nempe in 21 lunam, quae incidebat in 23 Aprilis. Quare recte Ambrosius inquit:
units.tr: Ambrose says that in the seventy-sixth year of Diocletian's reign, on the twenty-eighth day of Pharmuthi, the Sunday of Easter was celebrated, beyond any doubt among the elders. Now the first day of Thoth in the beginning of Diocletian's year 76 fell on 29 August in the year of Christ 359, which is the year now ending, so 28 Pharmuthi fell on 23 April, a Sunday, in the following year of Christ, 360, when the dominical letter was A. In this year of Christ 360 the golden number was 19, which in the Nicene table is placed against 3 April, where it marks the Paschal new moon, the one nearest the vernal equinox. Therefore the fourteenth moon fell on the Lord's day, namely on 16 April, and so Easter was postponed to the following day of the sun, that is, to the twenty-first moon, which fell on 23 April. Hence Ambrose rightly says:

units.la: Nec passionem Domini die Dominica posse celebrari, etiamsi quarta decima luna in dominicam inciderit: adiungendam hebdomadem alteram, sicut & septuagesimo sexto anno a die imperij Diocletiani factum est. Nam tunc vigesimo octauo die Pharmuthi mensis, qui est septimo kal. Maij, dominicam Paschae celebrauimus sine vlla dubitatione maiorum. Simul etiam luna cursus & ratio suffragatur, quoniam vigesima prima luna proximum Paschae celebrandum est: nam vsque ad vigefimam primam lunam consueuit extendi. Quod au-tem scribitur 28 Pharmuthi esse diem septimum kal. Maias, mendum est in codice: cum alibi & recte Ambrosius afferat diem trigesimum mensis Pharmuthi esse septimum kal. Maij, quando ait, Ergo fecundum Aegyptios primo mense (scilicet Nisan) celebratum i[?] su-[?]mus dominicam Pascha septimo kal. Maij, qui est trigesimus Pharmuthi mensis. Quod enim dies trigesimus Pharmuthi, non autem vigefimus octauus Pharmuthi respondeat septimo kal. Maij, hoc est, diei vigefimo quinto Aprilis, ex calendario Diocletiani euidenter probari potest. Quamobrem cum scribitur, Pascha celebratum fuisse anno 76Diocletiani,die 28 Pharmuthi: ita accipiendum est, vt fuerit peractum nono kal.Maij,hoc est, die 23 Aprilis. Posteriores duas obseruationes, quae inciderunt in annum 89, & 93 Diocletiani,Diuus Ambrosius hisce verbis describit: Nam temporibus paulo superioribus cum incidisset XIIII luna mensis primi in dominicam diem, sequenti altera dominica celebrata folennitas est, & octogesimo nono anno (in codice Bafilienfi male scribitur, octogesimo autem anno & nonagesimo tertio, quia nonagesimi tertij postea facit mentionem) ex die imperij Diocletiani: cum quartadecima luna effet nono kalendas Aprilis, nos celebrauimus Pascha pridie kal. Aprilis. Alexandrini quoque & Aegyptij, vt ipsi scripserunt, cum incidisset quarta decima luna vigesimo & octauo die Phamenoth mensis, (in codice Bafilienfi male scribitur Pharmutij mensis) celebrauerunt Pascha quinta die Pharmutij mensis, quae est pridie kal. Aprilis, & sic conuenere nobiscum. Rursus nonagesimo & tertio anno a die imperij Diocletiani, cum incidisset decima quarta luna in quartum decimum diem Pharmuthi mensis, qua est quinto idus Aprilis, & erat dominica celebratum est Pa'cha[?], Pharmuthi vigesimo & primo die, qui fuit secundum nos decimo sexto kal. Maij. (Ubi etiam[?] in codice Bafiliensi male scribitur, decimo quinto kal. Maij: ut ex collatione reliquorum cuidenter apparet) Etsi autem hic totus locus Am-brofij in editione Bafiliensi, qua ego sum vsus, pes-sime sit depravatus: eum tamen recte legit ac citauit Paulus de Middelburgo Episcopus Forosempro-niensis in primo capite libri quinti suorum Pauli-norum.
units.tr: Neither can the Lord's Passion be celebrated on the Lord's day, even if the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday: another week must be added, as was also done in the seventy-sixth year from the day of Diocletian's reign. For then, on the twenty-eighth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is the seventh day before the Kalends of May, we celebrated the Sunday of Easter, beyond any doubt among the ancients. At the same time the course and reckoning of the moon agrees, since Easter must be celebrated by the twenty-first moon; for it is customary to extend it to the twenty-first moon. That it is written that 28 Pharmuthi is the seventh day before the Kalends of May is an error in the manuscript, since Ambrose elsewhere and rightly states that the thirtieth day of the month Pharmuthi is the seventh day before the Kalends of May, when he says: Therefore, according to the Egyptians, in the first month (namely Nisan) we celebrated the Sunday of Easter on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, which is the thirtieth day of the month Pharmuthi. That the thirtieth day of Pharmuthi, and not the twenty-eighth, corresponds to the seventh day before the Kalends of May, that is, to 25 April, can be clearly proved from the calendar of Diocletian. So when it is written that Easter was celebrated in the seventy-sixth year of Diocletian on 28 Pharmuthi, it must be understood to have been held on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, that is, on 23 April. Ambrose describes the two later observations, which fell in the eighty-ninth and ninety-third years of Diocletian, in these words: For in times a little earlier, when the fourteenth moon of the first month fell on the Lord's day, the solemnity was celebrated on the following Sunday; and in the eighty-ninth year from the day of Diocletian's reign, when the fourteenth moon was on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, we celebrated Easter on the day before the Kalends of April. The Alexandrians and Egyptians too, as they themselves have written, when the fourteenth moon fell on the twenty-eighth day of the month Phamenoth, celebrated Easter on the fifth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is the day before the Kalends of April, and so they agreed with us. Again, in the ninety-third year from the day of Diocletian's reign, when the fourteenth moon fell on the fourteenth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is the fifth day before the Ides of April, and it was a Sunday, Easter was celebrated on the twenty-first day of Pharmuthi, which was for us the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. (Here too the Basel manuscript wrongly reads "the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May", as is clearly seen from comparison with the others.) Although this whole passage of Ambrose is very badly corrupted in the Basel edition, which I have used, Paul of Middelburg, bishop of Forosempronium, nonetheless read and cited it correctly in the first chapter of the fifth book of his Pauline writings.

units.la: Refert Ambrosius hoc octogesimo nono an-no Diocletiani celebratum esse Pascha die dominica, quæ fuerit quinta dies mensis Pharmuthi, hoc est, pridie kalendarum Aprilis. Thoth Diocletiani anni incuntis 89 incidit in annum Christi 372, die 29 Au-gusti: itaque quinta dies Pharmuthi, hoc est, pridie kal. Aprilis incurrit in annum Christi 373, quo celebratum est Pascha. Fuit tunc aureus numerus secundum vsum ecclesiæ XIII, qui in tabella Nicæna ponitur ad diem vndecimum Martij, vbi indicat neomeniam Paschalem: hinc si inclusiue numerentur dies XIIII, descenditur ad 28 diem mensis Phamenoth, hoc est, ad diem vigesimam quartam Martij, diem dominicam, quæ notatur littera F: sed quia decima quarta luna, cùm in diem dominicam incidit, festum Paschatis celebrari non potest: ideo reiectum fuit in subsequentem dominicam quintam Pharmuthi, hoc est 31 Martij, seu pridie kal. Aprilis currente anno Christi 373.
units.tr: Ambrose reports that in this eighty-ninth year of Diocletian Easter was celebrated on a Sunday, which was the fifth day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, the day before the Kalends of April. The first day of Thoth in the beginning of Diocletian's year 89 fell in the year of Christ 372, on 29 August; so the fifth day of Pharmuthi, that is, the day before the Kalends of April, fell in the year of Christ 373, in which Easter was celebrated. The golden number according to the usage of the Church was then 13, which in the Nicene table is placed against 11 March, where it marks the Paschal new moon. Hence, if the fourteen days are counted inclusively, one comes down to the twenty-eighth day of the month Phamenoth, that is, to 24 March, a Sunday, marked with the letter F. But because the fourteenth moon, when it falls on a Sunday, cannot be the day of the feast of Easter, it was therefore transferred to the following Sunday, the fifth of Pharmuthi, that is, 31 March, or the day before the Kalends of April, in the current year of Christ 373.

units.la: Præterea commemorat Ambrosius hoc anno nonagesimo tertio Diocletiani, vigesimo primo die Pharmuthi, hoc est, decimo sexto kal. Maij, die dominica celebratum fuisse Pascha. Sane Thoth Diocletiani ineuntis anni nonagesimi tertij incidit in 29 Augusti, currente anno Christi 376: itaque dies vigefimus primus Pharmuthi, incurrit in annu Christi 377, die 16 Aprilis, feria solis, qua celebratum fuit Pascha. Videamus an idem ostendat aureus numerus, & canon Nicaenus: currente anno Christi 377 erat aureus numerus fecundum vsum ecclesiae XVII, qui in tabella Nicaena ponitur ad 27 diem Martij, vbi indicat neomeniam Paschalem, proximam scilicet aequinoctio verno: hinc fi numerentur quatuordecim dies, deicenditur ad diem nonum Aprilis, feriam solis: cum vero decima quarta luna inciderit in diem dominicam, festum Pafchatis reiectum fuit in dominicam subsequentem, hoc est,in diem 16 Aprilis, qui fecundum recentiores Aegyptios erat 21 Pharmuthi, vt videre licet ex calendario Diocletiani. Obseruandum autem est, tempore Ambrosij aureum numerum XIX collocatum fuisse ad 3 Aprilis: alias anno Diocletiani 76 luna XIIII non potuisset incidere in diem Dominicam,neque luna XXI pascha fuisset celebratum. Sed nos vulgarem consuetudinem secuti, in tabella Nicaena aureum numerum XIX adscripsimus ad diem 4 Aprilis: hinc enim inclusiue apud nos numeratur luna XIIII. Exemplo nobis fuit annus Christi 1519, in quo currebat litera dominicalis B, & aureus numerus erat XIX, pascha autem celebrabatur luna vigefima prima, hoc est,die 24 Aprilis. Si igitur aureum numerum XIX ponamus ad 4 Aprilis,& hinc inclusiue numeremus dies XIIII; certimus [?] lunam decimam quartam incurrere in diem Dominicam, videlicet in 17 Aprilis,ideoq; pascha celebradum fuisse luna vigefima prima, hoc est, die 24 Aprilis. Quod fieri nö potuisset, fi aureus numer⁹ XIX fuisset appositus ad 3 Aprilis: tunc enim luna XIIII incidisset in 16 Aprilis, feriam fabbathi, & 17 Aprilis, die dominico pascha fuisset celebrandum. Hæ tres Diui Ambrosii obseruationes maximum lumen afferunt historiæ: & certissimo sunt argumento, calendariū Romanum iuxta correctum cyclum solis Augustalem adhuc in vsu fuisse: moreq; Ægyptiorum veterum à Nabonafaro vfq; ad concilium Nicænum feriās hebdomadicas in annorum continuatione decurrisse, eodem semper ordine, quo à concilio Nicæno vfq; ad nostram ætatem salvæ & incolumes permanserunt. Nec illud negligendum est, quod à Diuo Ambrosio hisce verbis notatur: Nec absurdum arbitror, vt inde obseruandi mensis trahamus exemplum, vbi primum pascha celebratu est. Vnde & maiores nostri in tractatu concilii Nicæni, eu[?] die enneadecaeteride, fi quis diligenter intendat, ftatuendu putarunt, & ipsum mensem nouorum (Nisan) recte custodierunt: quia in Ægypto hoc primo mense noua secantur frumenta. Hæc autem mensis & primus est fecundum Ægyptiorum proventus, & primus fecundum legem: & octauus est fecundum consuetudinem nostram: indictio enim Septembri mense incipit. Octauo igitur mense kalenda Aprilis sunt. Incipit autem mensis non fecundum vulgarem vsum, sed fecundum consuetudinem peritorum, ab æquinoctio, qui dies est duodecimo kalendas Aprilis: & finitur vndecimo kal. Maii. Inde maxime intra hos triginta & vnum dies sæpe celebrati paschæ dies. In quibus multa scitu dignissima notantur: expresse enim aflerit Ambrosius enneadecaeteridem fiue aureum numerum a Patribus in concilio Nicæno aflignatum esse, quo tempore æquinoctium vernū deprehensum fuerit in 1 kal Aprili, hoc est, in 21 Martii die: & vult ne-omeniam illam quæ proxima est æquinoctio verno initium esse mensis Paschalis, qui Ægyptiis mensis nouorum, Hebrais autem Nisan appellatur. Præterea annos indictionum, vt computari a mense Septembri: cuius respectu Aprilis habeatur pro mense octau, quo plerunque in idar[?] neomenia Paschalis. Duplex etiam facit in tum ipsius anni, vnum politicum, quo dfumitur a Septembri, vel potius a 19 die Augusti iuxta calendarium Diocletiani: alterum ecclesiasticum, quod deducitur a neomenia Paschali. units.tr: Moreover, Ambrose records that in this year, the ninety-third of Diocletian, on the twenty-first day of Pharmuthi, that is, the sixteenth day before the kalends of May, Easter was celebrated on a Sunday. Indeed, the first of Thoth at the beginning of the ninety-third year of Diocletian fell on 29 August in the year of Christ 376. So the twenty-first day of Pharmuthi falls in the year of Christ 377, on 16 April, a Sunday, on which Easter was celebrated. Let us see whether the golden number and the Nicene canon show the same. In the year of Christ 377 the golden number, according to the usage of the Church, was 17. It is placed in the Nicene table at 27 March, where it indicates the Paschal new moon, namely the one nearest the vernal equinox. If fourteen days are counted from here inclusively, one comes down to 9 April, a Sunday. But when the fourteenth moon fell on a Sunday, the feast of Easter was postponed to the following Sunday, that is, to 16 April, which according to the more recent Egyptians was the 21st of Pharmuthi, as may be seen from the calendar of Diocletian. It must be observed, however, that in the time of Ambrose the golden number 19 was placed at 3 April. Otherwise, in the seventy-sixth year of Diocletian, the fourteenth moon could not have fallen on a Sunday, nor would Easter have been celebrated on the twenty-first moon. But we, following common custom, have assigned the golden number 19 in the Nicene table to 4 April, for in our reckoning the fourteenth moon is counted inclusively from that day. We had as an example the year of Christ 1519, in which the dominical letter was B and the golden number was 19, and Easter was celebrated on the twenty-first moon, that is, on 24 April. If, then, we place the golden number 19 at 4 April and count fourteen days inclusively from there, we find that the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, namely on 17 April, and so Easter was celebrated on the twenty-first moon, that is, on 24 April. This could not have happened if the golden number 19 had been placed at 3 April. For then the fourteenth moon would have fallen on 16 April, a Saturday, and Easter would have had to be celebrated on Sunday, 17 April. These three observations of the blessed Ambrose throw the greatest light on history, and they are very certain proof that the Roman calendar, corrected according to the solar cycle of Augustus, was still in use, and that, according to the custom of the ancient Egyptians, from Nabonassar down to the Council of Nicaea the weekdays ran on in the continuous succession of years in the same order in which, from the Council of Nicaea down to our own age, they have remained safe and unchanged. Nor is that to be neglected which Ambrose notes in these words: "I think it not absurd that we take from this an example of the month in which Easter was first celebrated. Hence also our forefathers, in the treatise of the Council of Nicaea, thought that, if anyone attends carefully, the nineteen-year cycle should be established, and they rightly kept the month of Nisan itself as the month of new things, because in Egypt in this first month the new grain is cut. This month is both the first according to the Egyptian produce and the first according to the law, and it is the eighth according to our custom, for the indiction begins in the month of September. Therefore the kalends of April fall in the eighth month. The month, however, begins not according to common usage but according to the practice of the learned, from the equinox, which is the twelfth day before the kalends of April, and it ends on the eleventh day before the kalends of May. Thus the days of Easter are often celebrated within these thirty-one days." Many things most worthy of knowing are noted in these words. For Ambrose plainly states that the nineteen-year cycle, or golden number, was assigned by the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea, at the time when the vernal equinox was found to fall on the first day before the kalends of April, that is, on 21 March. And he holds that the new moon nearest the vernal equinox is the beginning of the Paschal month, which is called the month of new things by the Egyptians and Nisan by the Hebrews. He also counts the years of the indictions from the month of September, and with reference to this Ambrose treats April as the eighth month, in which the Paschal new moon usually falls. He also makes a double year: one civil, which is reckoned from September, or rather from 19 August according to the calendar of Diocletian; the other ecclesiastical, which is reckoned from the Paschal new moon.

units.la: Hoc anno Christi trecentesimo nonagesimo secundo,Indictione quinta,Arcadio Augusto II, & Ruffino occidentali Co s s. ut refert Marcellinus Comes, Idibus Maii & quidè in vigilia Pentecostes, ut D.Epiphanius tradit, Valentinianus iunior Imperator apud Viennam Galliæ laqueo strangulatus est reperrepertus. Idus Maii tunc inciderunt in diem sabbati, quia annus Christi 392 literam dominicalem habebat C. ex quo sequitur festu Pentecostes fuisse peractum die sequente[?] solis, quae erat 16 Maii. Hinc si retrorsum numerentur septem septimanae, ascendi-tur ad diem 18 Martii, feriam dominicam, in qua Pascha celebratu[?] fuisse coniicimus: currebat enim aureus numerus secundum visum ecclesiae XIII. qui in tabella Nicaena ponitur ad vndecimum diem Martii, in qua ostendit neomeniam Paschalem: hinc si inclusive numerentur XIIII dies, peruenitur ad 24 Martii, feriam Mercurii, in qua cum non potuerit Pascha celebrari, dilatum fuit in dominicam subsequentem, quae erat 28 Martii. b Hoc anno Iuliano quinge-tesimo octauo, qui fuit annus Christi quadringentesimus tertius, solutus fuit cyclus solis Augustalis: cum enim annus Iulianus 508 bisextilis debuisset esse, literis dominicalibus existentibus FE, ab Aegyptiis & Latinis Ecclesiarum patronis pro communi & simplice est habitus, ut literam dominicalem duntaxat habuerit F: bisextum autem intrusum fuit in annum subsequentem Iulianum 509, qui nactus est literas dominicales ED. itaque annus Iulianus 510 literam dominicalem habuit C. Hinc manifestum est, quod ex solutione cycli Augustalis, hi anni quatuor Iuliani 505, 506, 507, 508 sine bisexto sint elapsi: quare cum anno Iuliano bisextili 504 Thoth Nabonasari 1207 translatus fuisset ad 30 Aprilis, feria sexta, vtiq; Thoth Nabonasari 1212 incurrit in 29 Aprilis, currente anno Iuliano 509. quod diligenter est animaduertendum. hac enim historia neglecta, nullam connexionem feriarum in annis Nabonasari, nullumq; bisextilium ordinem in annis Christi subsequentibus percipiemus. Quod autem annus Iulianus 508, hoc est annus Christi 463, hoc modo luxatus fuerit, vt sola literam dominicalem habuerit F,ostendit Episcopus Forosempronienfis libro 5[?] suorum Paulinorum, vbi recitat Paschalan[?]ctum iuxta Alexandrinam suppu-tationem indictu[?] fuisse vigesima prima Aprilis, quod tamen Latini octiduo post, hoc est, die 18 Aprilis obseruandum duxerunt. Sane annus Christi 463 aureum numerum habuit iuxta vsum ecclesiæ VIII, qui in tabella Nicæna ponitur ad 6 Martii, & Aprilis: cum autem vterque æqualiter distet ab æquinoctio, posterior indicat neomeniam Paschalem, aqua inclusiue sumta si dies XIIII deorsum numerentur, descenditur ad 18 Aprilis, diem Iouis: ideoque Paschalem Alexandrinus indixit [illegible, ~20 letters] die vigesima prima Aprilis, dominica feria, quæ notabatur litera F. c Hoc anno Iuliano 510, qui fuit annus Christi 465, publicatum fuit Paschæ per Alexandrinorum Patriarcham vigesima octaua Martii, quod tamen Latini in sequentem dominicam transferendum duxerunt. Currebat tunc aureus numerus secundum vsum ecclesiæ X. qui in tabella Nicæna ponitur ad 14 Martii, vbi ostendit neomeniam Paschalem: hinc si inclusiue numerentur dies XIIII, descenditur ad 27 Martii, diem sabbathi, ideo Paschalis subsequente die dominica, nimirum vigesima octaua Martii, secundum statutum concilii Nicæni fuit celebrandum: sed Latini octiduo serius, hoc est 4 Aprilis celebrandum exiftimarunt, vt ibidem testatur Forosempronienfis. Hinc intelligitur literam dominicalem fuisse C & cum anno Christi 463 litera dominicalis fuerit F, omnino sequitur annum interiectum Iulianum 509, qui est annus Christi 464, bisextilem fuisse, literis dominicalibus existentibus ED. Ita constat quòd tunc solutus fuerit cyclus solis Augustalis, sciamus qua id ratione acciderit, ab historiis non sic perscriptum. Sed hanc inæqualem calendarii Romani luxatione cùm Reipublicæ Christianæ perniciosam esse cerneret Dionysius Abbas R[?] manus, circa annum Christi 532 cyclum magnum olarem propositum, vt deinceps anni omnes iuxta ordinariam bis extorum intercalatione transfigerentur. Quæ vero ausa est, cuꝰ Græci duplex Pascha ordinarint [?] quia die Veneris Christũ passum esse credimus, sanciuerunt vt in memoriam Crucis Domini die Veneris ipsa luna decima quarta, vel octiduo post, eodem die Veneris ageretur: & quia die solis Christũ à mortuis resurrexisse persuasum habemus; instituerunt vt die dominico, qui sequitur lunam decimam quartam, celebraretur [?], hoc est, festum resurrectionis Dominicæ, quod nos sine vlla adiectione solemus Pascha appellare. units.tr: In this year of Christ 392, the fifth year of the indiction, with Arcadius Augustus for the second time and Rufinus as consul of the West, as Marcellinus Comes reports, Valentinian the Younger, emperor, was found strangled with a noose at Vienne in Gaul, on the Ides of May and indeed on the eve of Pentecost, as Epiphanius records. The Ides of May then fell on a Saturday, since the dominical letter for the year of Christ 392 was C. It follows that Pentecost was celebrated on the next day, Sunday, which was 16 May. If we count back seven weeks from there, we arrive at Sunday, 18 March, on which we conjecture Easter was celebrated. For the golden number according to the usage of the Church was 13, which in the Nicene table is placed at 11 March, where it shows the Paschal new moon. Hence if 14 days are counted inclusively, we arrive at 24 March, Wednesday. Since Easter could not be celebrated on that day, it was postponed to the following Sunday, which was 28 March. [b] In this year of Julian 508, which was the year of Christ 403, the Augustan solar cycle was broken. For although the Julian year 508 ought to have been bissextile, with the dominical letters being F E, the Egyptians and the Latin patrons of the Churches treated it as a common and simple year, so that it had only the dominical letter F. The intercalary day was instead inserted into the following Julian year, 509, which had the dominical letters E D. Thus the Julian year 510 had the dominical letter C. It is clear from this that, because of the breaking of the Augustan cycle, the four Julian years 505, 506, 507 and 508 passed without a bissextile. Therefore, when Thoth 1207 of Nabonassar was carried over to 30 April, a Friday, in the bissextile Julian year 504, Thoth 1212 of Nabonassar fell on 29 April in the Julian year 509. This must be carefully noted, for if this history is neglected we shall perceive no connection of the weekdays in the years of Nabonassar, nor any order of the bissextiles in the following years of Christ. That the Julian year 508, that is the year of Christ 463, was disordered in such a way that it had only the dominical letter F, is shown by the Bishop of Forosempronium in the fifth book of his Paulines, where he relates that the Paschal feast was announced by the Alexandrian reckoning as falling on 21 April. The Latins, however, decided that it should be observed eight days later, that is on 18 April. Indeed, the year of Christ 463 had the golden number 8 according to the usage of the Church, which in the Nicene table is placed at 6 March and at April. Since both are equally distant from the equinox, the latter indicates the Paschal new moon. If 14 days are counted downward, inclusive of the starting day, we descend to 18 April, Thursday. Therefore the Alexandrian patriarch appointed Easter for [illegible, about 20 letters] 21 April, a Sunday, which was marked by the letter F. [c] In this year of Julian 510, which was the year of Christ 465, Easter was announced by the Patriarch of Alexandria for 28 March. The Latins, however, decided that it should be moved to the following Sunday. The golden number at that time, according to the usage of the Church, was 10, which in the Nicene table is placed at 14 March, where it shows the Paschal new moon. Hence if 14 days are counted inclusively, we descend to 27 March, Saturday. Therefore Easter was to be celebrated on the following day, Sunday, that is 28 March, according to the decree of the Council of Nicaea. But the Latins thought it should be celebrated eight days later, that is on 4 April, as Forosempronium also testifies in the same place. From this it is understood that the dominical letter was C. And since the dominical letter in the year of Christ 463 was F, it follows necessarily that the intervening Julian year 509, which is the year of Christ 464, was bissextile, with the dominical letters E D. Thus it is established that the Augustan solar cycle was then broken, but by what reasoning this happened the histories have not so written down. But Dionysius the Abbot, perceiving that this unequal disorder of the Roman calendar was harmful to the Christian commonwealth, proposed around the year of Christ 532 the great Easter cycle, so that thereafter all years would be run through in the ordinary intercalation of the bissextiles. Moreover, the Greeks, who ordained a double Easter, decreed, because we believe Christ suffered on Friday, that in memory of the Cross of the Lord the feast should be held on Friday itself, on the fourteenth moon or eight days after, on that same Friday. And because we are persuaded that Christ rose from the dead on Sunday, they established that it should be celebrated on the Sunday that follows the fourteenth moon, that is the feast of the Lord's resurrection, which we are accustomed to call simply Easter without any addition.

units.la: * Hoc anno quingentesimo septuagesimo se-ptimo Iuliano, qui est annus a natiuitate Christi 532, Indictione decima, Dionysius Abbas Romanus cognomento Exiguus coepit annos a conceptione seu incarnatione Domini nostri Iesu Christi numerare, vt testatur Beda, & Petrus Aliacensis in tractatu super calendarii correctione ad concilium Constanti-ense scripto, item Episcopus Forosemproniensis lib. 4 Paulinorum. Posuit autem Dionysius Christum conce-ptū fuisse in nouilunio Paschali, die 25 Martii, labente anno Iuliano 45, eodemque 42 ab imperio Augusti: quo-obrem cum anno Iuliano 577 cuperet apud Romanos introducere annos Christi, asseruit a conceptione Domini nostri vsque ad 25 Martii, labente anno 248 Diocletiani, elapsos fuisse annos quingentos & triginta duos: atque hinc cyclum magnum solare 532 annorum inchoari voluit, vt cum enneadecaeteride inciperet & definiret.
units.tr: * In this year 577 of the Julian era, which is the year 532 from the birth of Christ, the tenth indiction, Dionysius the Roman abbot, surnamed Exiguus, began to count the years from the conception or incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, as Bede attests, and Peter of Ailly in his treatise on the correction of the calendar, written for the Council of Constance; likewise the bishop of Forosempronium in book 4 of the Paulinorum. Dionysius placed Christ's conception on the paschal new moon, 25 March, in the 45th year of the Julian era, and the 42nd year of the reign of Augustus. Therefore, when in Julian year 577 he wished to introduce the years of Christ among the Romans, he asserted that from the conception of our Lord to 25 March, in the 248th year of Diocletian, 532 years had elapsed; and from this he wished the great solar cycle of 532 years to begin, so that it would both start and finish with the nineteen-year cycle [ἐννεακαιδεκαετηρίς].

units.la: Sed quae est vtilitas huius cycli 532 annorum? indicat scilicet seriem bisextorum & literarum dominicalium, quae a Dionysio vsque ad nostram aetatem constantissime sunt obseruatae. Vt enim cyclus simplex 28 annorum solarium periodu bisextorum & feriarum hebdomadicarum ostendit: ita etiam cyclus magnus 532 annorum declarat con[?]secutionem Fe[?]rum, cùm completatur nouende-cim cyclos lunares. Si ergo à conceptione Christi, quæ incidit in annum 45 Iulianum, die 25 Martii, computemus annos Domini, vt fecit Dionysius, depre-hen-demus anno Iuliano labente 577, circa 25 Martii, ela-psum fuisse magnum cyclum 532 annorum, hoc est, præterea 28 enneadecaeterides, quæ continent 19 cyclos solares. Sic anno Iuliano no millesimo octingentesimo & nono, qui est annus Christi millesimus sexagesimus quartus, circa 25 Martii intelliguntur elapsi fuisse duo cycli [?]maiores, hoc est, 56 enneadecaeterides, quæ conficiunt 8 cyclos solares. Ita anno Iuliano millesi-mo sexcentesimo quadragesimo primo, qui est annus Christi 1596, circa 25 Martii intelliguntur elapsi fuisse tres cycli maiores, hoc est, 84 enneadecaeterides, quæ conflant 7 cyclos solares. Hic verò anticipatio lunaris est consideranda: etsi enim conceptio Domini nostri Iesu Christi (secundum hypothesin Dionysii) inciderit in neomeniam Paschalem die 25 Martii, labente anno Iuliano 45: nostro tamen seculo, currente anno Christi 1596, neomenia Paschalis non amplius hæret circa 25 Martii, sed ascendit in diem septimum præcedentem, hoc est, in 18 Martii, vbi nouilunium significant ephemerides astronomorum. Illud nouilunium est primum cycli quarti magni, à conceptione Domini nostri Iesu Christi ineuntis & repetiti: & cùm ante illud elapsi sint 84 enneadecaeterides, hoc est, lunationes 1974 (siquidem in vnaquaque enneadecaeteride continentur 235 lunationes) apparet nouilunium illud, quod incurrit in 18 Martii, currente anno Christi 1596, esse 19741 à conceptione Domini. Hac ratione Dionysius introduxit annos Christi, licet principium eorum posuerit [?]posteà fit mutamutatū:non enim à conceptione,(ed à natiuitate Do-mini nostri Iesu Christi,quæ incurrit in 25 Decébris, currete anno Iuliano 45,nos hodie annos Christi nu-meramus,ita tamen vt octiduum[?] adiiciamus post na-tiuitatē Christi, quò præcisè cū kal. Ianuariis curren-tis anni Iuliani 46 annos Christi inchoemus. Quam-obrè anni Christi,qui secundum Dionysium à conceptione numerantur,&in annū 42 ab imperio Augusti incidunt, soli merentur vt Dionysiani dicantur: qui vero secundum vsum vulgarē à natiuitate numeran-tur,atq; in contextum anni 43 ab imperio Augusti in-currunt, anni Christi vsitati appellatur. Præterea or-do cycli solaris 28 annorū ali[?] suit in annis Dionysia-nis,quàm hodie sit in annis Christi vsitatis.Dionysius enim anno Christi 532,cùm literæ dominicales essent D C,inchoauit suum cyclum solarem:nos verò illum incipimus ab anno,cuius literæ dominicales sunt G F. iuxta quam rationem annusChristi 532 est nonus cy-cli solaris. Hic tamē obseruandum est, cyclū nostrum hebdomadicum 28 annorum solariū non esse exten-dendum ad principium annorum Christi: cùm anni 36 priores Iuliani ordinaria intercalatione non sint transacti, & Augustus Octauianus duodecim annos simplices indixerit: cumq; ipse cyclus Augustalis so-lutus fuerit circa annum Christi 463. Si enim nulla habita ratione historiarum, vel dispositionis anno-rum Iulianorum & Nabonasari, cyclum solarem ex-tenderemus, feriasnaturales confunderemus:quod etiam animaduertit Ioannes de Muris in regu-lis computistarum, quorum hypotheses circa initium annorum Christi com-mentitias esse af-firmat. units.tr: But what is the use of this cycle of 532 years? Evidently it shows the sequence of bissextile years and dominical letters, which have been observed with great consistency from Dionysius down to our own time. Just as the simple cycle of 28 solar years shows the period of bissextiles and weekdays, so the great cycle of 532 years shows the succession of the Sundays once nineteen lunar cycles have been completed. If, then, we reckon the years of the Lord from the conception of Christ, which fell in the Julian year 45 on 25 March, as Dionysius did, we find that in the Julian year 577, around 25 March, the great cycle of 532 years had elapsed, that is, besides 28 enneadecaeterides, which contain 19 solar cycles. Thus in the Julian year 1809, which is the year of Christ 1064, around 25 March, two greater cycles are understood to have elapsed, that is, 56 enneadecaeterides, which make up 8 solar cycles. So in the Julian year 1641, which is the year of Christ 1596, around 25 March, three greater cycles are understood to have elapsed, that is, 84 enneadecaeterides, which make up 7 solar cycles. Here, however, the advance of the moon must be considered. For although the conception of our Lord Jesus Christ (according to Dionysius's hypothesis) fell on the Paschal new moon on 25 March in the Julian year 45, yet in our century, in the year of Christ 1596, the Paschal new moon no longer falls around 25 March but moves back to the seventh day before, that is, to 18 March, where the astronomers' ephemerides mark the new moon. That new moon is the first of the fourth great cycle, which began and was repeated from the conception of our Lord Jesus Christ; and since 84 enneadecaeterides, that is, 1974 lunations (for each enneadecaeteris contains 235 lunations), had elapsed before it, it is clear that the new moon that falls on 18 March in the year of Christ 1596 is the 19,741st from the conception of the Lord. By this reckoning Dionysius introduced the years of Christ, although he placed their beginning elsewhere. For it was later changed: we today do not number the years of Christ from the conception but from the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, which falls on 25 December in the Julian year 45, yet we add eight days after the birth of Christ, so that we begin the years of Christ precisely on the Kalends of January of the Julian year 46. Therefore the years of Christ, which are counted according to Dionysius from the conception and fall in the 42nd year from the reign of Augustus, alone deserve to be called Dionysian; but those that are counted by common usage from the nativity, and fall in the 43rd year from the reign of Augustus, are called the customary years of Christ. Moreover, the order of the 28-year solar cycle was different in the Dionysian years from what it is today in the customary years of Christ. For Dionysius, in the year of Christ 532, when the dominical letters were D C, began his solar cycle; but we begin it from the year whose dominical letters are G F. According to this reckoning, the year of Christ 532 is the ninth year of the solar cycle. Here, however, it must be observed that our 28-year weekly cycle of solar years should not be extended back to the beginning of the years of Christ, since the first 36 Julian years did not pass with ordinary intercalation, and Augustus Octavian declared twelve simple years, and that Augustan cycle was loosed around the year of Christ 463. For if, without any regard for histories or for the arrangement of the Julian and Nabonassar years, we extended the solar cycle, we would confound the natural weekdays. John de Muris also noticed this in the rules of the computists, whose hypotheses concerning the beginning of the years of Christ he declares to be fabricated. units.tr: In this year of Christ 724, Thoth of Nabonassar 1472 falls on the intercalary day, a Thursday.

units.la: Hoc anno Christi 817[?], die tertio Aprilis, feria tertia incurrit annus Hagarenus ducentesimus duodecimus: quo Almamon Saracenorum princeps Magnam constructionem Ptolemaei de Graeco in sermonem Arabicum transferri curauit, sicut testatur Almagestu Latinu manuscriptum (nam in exemplari edito à Lichtensteinio hæc nota prætermissa est) circa finem proœmii, vbi ita scriptū extat: Liber hic præcepta Mamonis regis Arabū, qui regnauit in Baldach, ab Alhazez filio Iosephi filio Maire Arithmetici, & Sergio filio Elbe Christiano in anno XII & CC sesta Saracenorum translatum est. Qui quidem liber distus est Almagesti, quæ Ptolemæus Pheludiensis de scientia stellarum & mortuis qui in cœlo sunt, conscripsit. Ita habet Almagestu latinu manuscriptum bibliothecæ Palatinæ: licet pro anno Hagareno 212 male scribatur 112. Certissimū enim est circa hæc tempora vixisse Almamonem: quia Abul Hassami historicus Arabs recenset eum in Chalifam Baldachensem siue Babylonium fuisse electum completis annis Hegiræ ducetis & septendecim, sex mensibus, & septe diebus: traditq; eum imperasse viginti annos Arabicos, quinq; menses & tredecim dies. Iosephus Scaliger lib. 5 de emendatione temporum ex veteri quoq; Latina Almagesti Ptolemæi simile locum adducit, quo ostendit translationem Arabicā ab Almamone procuratā annis plusquā quinquaginta antiquiorem esse obseruationibus Albategnii. Porro Fridericus II. Romanorum & Germaniæ Imperator Augustus,Rex Siciliæ ac Neapolis,Dux Sueuiæ &c. primusAlmagestū Cl.Ptolemæi è Saracenica lingua in Latina cōuerti curauit, adeoq; astronomia omne excoluit,vt refert Philip.Mel. in Carionis chronico. Itaq; astronomia Ptolemaica nos primo hausimus ex versione Arabū,donec ignotuerit Europæ occidentali linguæ Græcæ cognitio,ipsumq; authenticū Ptolemæi exemplar typis Basilienfibus sit euulgatū. Etsi autē Arabica translatio multisin locis sit depravata; adiectiones tamen multas vtiles & necessarias habet, sine quibus annos Nabonasari cū annis Christi connectere non possumus:tanti momenti res est, subinde Barbaros consulere,&ab iis nonnullos temporū scrupulos inuestigare. Almamon vel Mamon filius fuit Imbraelis, Græcarū Latinarumq; literarū non ignarus, Philosophiæ & mathematicæ studiis summopere deditus,vt videre licet in historia Saracenica Cælii Augustini Curionis.Facit etiam mentionē Almamonis Alfraganus nolter cap. 6, & 10. units.tr: In the year of Christ 817[?], on the third day of April, a Tuesday, the Hagarene year 212 begins. In that year Almamon, prince of the Saracens, had Ptolemy's Magna Constructio translated from Greek into the Arabic language. The Latin manuscript of the Almagest attests this (the note was omitted in the edition printed by Lichtenstein), and near the end of the preface it reads as follows: "This book, the precepts of Mamon, king of the Arabs, who reigned in Baghdad, was translated by Alhazez son of Joseph, son of Maire the arithmetician, and by Sergius son of Elbe the Christian, in the year 212 of the Saracens. This book is called the Almagest, which Ptolemy of Pelusium wrote concerning the science of the stars and the motions of those things that are in the heavens." The Latin Almagest manuscript of the Palatine library reads thus, although for the Hagarene year 212 it is wrongly written 112. It is quite certain that Almamon lived about this time, for the Arab historian Abul Hassam records that he was elected caliph of Baghdad, or Babylon, after 217 years of the Hegira had been completed, six months and seven days. He also says that Almamon reigned twenty Arabic years, five months and thirteen days. Joseph Scaliger, in book 5 of De emendatione temporum, likewise cites a similar passage from the old Latin Almagest of Ptolemy, and by it he shows that the Arabic translation procured by Almamon is more than fifty years older than the observations of Albategnius. Further, Frederick II, Emperor Augustus of the Romans and of Germany, King of Sicily and Naples, Duke of Swabia, and so on, was the first to have Ptolemy's Almagest converted from the Saracen language into Latin, and he cultivated astronomy in every way, as Philip Melanchthon reports in Carion's chronicle. Therefore we first drew Ptolemaic astronomy from the Arab version, until knowledge of the Greek language was lost in Western Europe, and Ptolemy's authentic text itself was published in print at Basel. Although the Arabic translation is corrupted in many places, it has many useful and necessary additions, without which we cannot connect the years of Nabonassar with the years of Christ. So important a matter is it to consult the barbarians from time to time and to investigate from them some of the difficulties of chronology. Almamon, or Mamon, was the son of Imbrahim. He was not ignorant of Greek and Latin letters and was greatly devoted to the studies of philosophy and mathematics, as may be seen in the Saracen history of Caelius Augustinus Curio. Our Alfraganus also mentions Almamon, in chapters 6 and 10. Abulfeda testifies that he had the common geography, whether of Ptolemy or of some other author, translated from Greek into the Arabic language. units.la: {a} Hicannus Nabonasari 1627 est annus Dhilkarnain, hoc est, Alexandri Magni 1191, ut testatur Muhamedes Aractenfis Albategnius cognominatus, capite 51: nam ante aeram Alexandri Dhilkarnain praeterierunt anni Aegyptij 436, ut oftenfum est in calendario Syriaco. Hoc anno Nabonasari 1627, cuius principium incurrit in annu Christi 879, die decimo sexto Ianuar. feria sexta, Albategnius observauit stellam septentrionalem, quae inter duos scorpionis oculos circumvoluitur, fuisse in 17 gradu, & 5omin.[?] scorpionis, & cor leonis sive Basiliscum in 14 gradu leonis. {b}Anno Dhilkarnain 1194, qui est annus a morte Alexandri 1206, hoc est, Nabonasari 1630 Albategnius observauit eclipsin lunae, die 23 mensis Tamuz, hoc est, Iulii: quando fuit erat in 4 gradu, & 5 minuto leonis. Non est dubium, quin circa diem 23 Iulii fuerit secundum medium motu fuerit in gradu quarto leonis, cum die decimo nono Septembris aequinoctium autumnale efficeret ab Albategnio deprehensum: sed quod ad eclipsin lunarem attinet, non contigit illa anno Nabonasari 1630, sed anno Dhilkarnain, hoc est, Alexandri Magni vulgariter accepto 1194, cuius initium est a kalendis Octobribus, currente anno Luliano 927: itaque dies 23 Iulii, labentis anni 1194 Alexandri secundum vulgarem incidit in annum Lulianum 928, quo aureus numerus Iulii Caesaris currebat XVI, qui in calendario Iuliano ponitur ad 18 kalen. Maii, & recurrit die 12 Iulii, ubi neomeniam offendit: sed propter anticipationem lunarem triduo citius conspectum est novilunium, die videlicet 9 Iulii: a quo si quindecim dies deorsum numerentur, descenditur ad 23 Iulii, bente anno Christi 883, hoc est, perunitur ad oppositionem luminarium, in qua lunae defectum observauit Albategnius. Anno vero Nabonasari 1630, octauo die mensis Pachon, qui erat dies decimus nonus Elul mensis Romani secundum consuetudinem Syrorum, hoc est, 19 Septembr. Albategnius accuratissime observauit incidisse aequinoctium autumnale, post meridie elapsis quatuor horis cum dimidia, & quadrante fere, vt tcllatur[?] cap.17. Quod autem octauus dies mensis Pachon incidcrit in decimum nonum Elul, non tantum Albategnius asserit, verum etiam aperte id ostendit Thoth Nabonafari 1630, qui incurrit in 1 Ianuarij vel Canun posterioris, feria fecunda, currente anno Christi 882, cuius litera dominicalis est G. Si enim a decima quinta Ianuarij inclusiue numeremus octo menses Ægyptios, & octo dies ex mense Pachon, peruenimus ad decimam nonam Septembris, feriam Mercurij, in quam incidit aequinoctium autumnale. Ex quo intelligitur aequinoctium vernale confectum fuisse in 17 & 18 Martii.
units.tr: {a} Hicannus, Nabonasar 1627, is the year of Dhilkarnain, that is, of Alexander the Great 1191, as Muhamedes Aractenfis, surnamed Albategnius, testifies in chapter 51. For the Egyptian years before the era of Alexander that had passed numbered 436, as has been shown in the Syriac calendar. In this year of Nabonassar 1627, whose beginning falls in the year of Christ 879, on the sixteenth day of January, a Friday, Albategnius observed that the northern star which revolves between the two eyes of the Scorpion was at the 17th degree and 5 minutes of Scorpio, and the heart of the Lion, or Basiliscus, at the 14th degree of Leo. {b} In the year of Dhilkarnain 1194, which is the year 1206 from the death of Alexander, that is, Nabonassar 1630, Albategnius observed an eclipse of the moon on the 23rd day of the month Tamuz, that is, July, when it was at the 4th degree and 5th minute of Leo. There is no doubt that around 23 July the mean motion was in the fourth degree of Leo, since the autumnal equinox was determined by Albategnius as occurring on 19 September. But as far as the lunar eclipse is concerned, it did not happen in the year Nabonassar 1630, but in the year Dhilkarnain, that is, of Alexander the Great, taken in the common reckoning as 1194, whose beginning is from the Kalends of October, in the current Julian year 927. Thus the day 23 July of the year 1194 of Alexander, in the common reckoning, falls in the Julian year 928, in which the golden number of Julius Caesar was 16. This is placed in the Julian calendar at 18 days before the Kalends of May, and recurs on 12 July, where it meets the new moon. But because of the lunar anticipation the new moon was seen three days earlier, namely on 9 July. If fifteen days are counted downward from this, one descends to 23 July, in the current year of Christ 883; that is, one arrives at the opposition of the luminaries, in which Albategnius observed the eclipse of the moon. In the year Nabonassar 1630, on the eighth day of the month Pachon, which was the nineteenth day of Elul, the Roman month according to the custom of the Syrians, that is, 19 September, Albategnius most accurately observed that the autumnal equinox fell four hours and about a half and a quarter after midday, as is stated in chapter 17. That the eighth day of the month Pachon fell on the nineteenth of Elul, Albategnius not only asserts, but also clearly shows by Thoth of Nabonassar 1630, which falls on 1 January or the later Canun, on a Monday, in the current year of Christ 882, whose dominical letter is G. For if we count inclusively from 15 January, eight Egyptian months and eight days of the month Pachon, we arrive at 19 September, a Wednesday, on which the autumnal equinox fell. From this it is understood that the vernal equinox was made on 17 and 18 March.

units.la: Hanc obseruationem Albategnius contulit cum ea, quam habuit Ptolemaeus anno tertio Antonini Pii, qui fuit a morte Alexandri 463, Nabonafari 887: die nono mensis Athyr, hora prima post solis ortum: & retulit Albategnius inter suam & Ptolemaei obseruationem intercessisse annos Ægyptios 743, &c 17 8½ dies, cum quadrante vnius diei, minus ⅓ horae vnius: quod ex subtractione ne vtriufq; temporis facile liquet.Obseruandum hic est, Albategnium comparare annum Dhilkarnain 1194 cum anno a morte Alexandri 1206, hoc est, cum anno Nabonafari 1630, quatenus annos Dhilkarnain aequabiles accipit, & epocham folarem confiderat: cum autem eclipfin lunarem fe obferuaffe ait die 13 Tamuz fiue Iulii, currente anno Dhilkarnain 1194; more vulgari accipit annum Alexandri 1194, vt is incipere intelligatur a Tifrin priore seu kal. Octobribus, currente anno Iuliano 917. Quae nisi quis diligenter animaduertat, nullum fructum percipere poterit ex obseruatione Albategnii circa æquiæquinoctium autumnale,& subsequentem lunæ de-fectum. units.tr: Albategnius compared this observation with the one Ptolemy made in the third year of Antoninus Pius, which was 463 years from the death of Alexander, Nabonassar 887: on the ninth day of the month Athyr, at the first hour after sunrise. Albategnius reports that between his observation and Ptolemy's there were 743 Egyptian years, and 178½ days, with a quarter of one day, less one-third of an hour. This is easily clear from subtracting the one time from the other. It must be observed here that Albategnius compares the year Dhilkarnain 1194 with the year 1206 from the death of Alexander, that is, with the year Nabonassar 1630, insofar as he takes the years of Dhilkarnain as equal and regards the solar epoch. But when he says that he observed a lunar eclipse on 13 Tamuz, or July, in the current year Dhilkarnain 1194, he takes it in the common manner as the year 1194 of Alexander, so that it is understood to begin from Tishri, that is, the Kalends of October, in the current Julian year 917. Unless someone attends to this carefully, he will be unable to derive any benefit from Albategnius' observation concerning the autumnal equinox and the subsequent eclipse of the moon. But whoever is entirely ignorant of the continuation of the years of Nabonassar should be turned away at once from the threshold of Albategnius. units.la: Hic annus Nabonasari millesimus fexcentesimus octogesimus nonus incurrit in postremā diem Decembris, labente anno Iuliano 985, qui est annus Christi 940 bisextilis, literis dominicalibus existentibus E D. Sed Thoth Nabonasari 1688 incidit in kalend. Ianuarias, eiusdem anni Iuliani 985, & Christi 940: unde manifestum est, in annum bisextilem posse incurrere principia duorum annorum Nabonasari: simile exemplum habuimus in anno 477 ante ordinationem Iulianam. Quae si quis non exacte perpendat, nunquam poterit assequi comparatione annorum Nabonasari cum annis solaribus Romanorum: quare dubium mihi non est, quin viri eruditi & historiarum studiosi labores meos grato animo sint accepturi, cum ante me nemo extiterit, qui connexionem annorum Nabonasari certam declararit. Anno Iuliano 989, h.e. anno Christi 944, Thoth Nabonasari 1693 transfit ad 30 Decembris, feriam secundam: quia proxime interiectum fuit bisextum. Itaq; in omnib. annis subsequentib. bisextilibus, vfq; ad nostra tempora, conspicitur index anticipationis dierum, quemadmodum indicavi prius in anno 702 ante ordinationem Iulianam. Ind. | An. Iul. units.tr: This 1689th year of Nabonassar falls on the last day of December, in the Julian year 985, which is the bissextile year of Christ 940, with dominical letters E D. But Thoth 1688 of Nabonassar fell on 1 January of that same Julian year 985 and of Christ 940. It is therefore clear that the beginnings of two years of Nabonassar can fall within one bissextile year. We had a similar example in the year 477 before the Julian reform. If anyone does not weigh these things exactly, he will never be able to match the years of Nabonassar with the solar years of the Romans. So I have no doubt that learned men and students of history will receive my labours with a grateful mind, since before me no one has set out the certain connection of the years of Nabonassar. In the Julian year 989, that is, in the year of Christ 944, Thoth 1693 of Nabonassar passed to 30 December, a Monday, because a bissextile day had been inserted just before. Therefore, in all the later bissextile years, down to our own times, the index of the anticipation of days appears, as I showed earlier for the year 702 before the Julian reform. Ind. | An. Iul. units.la: {a} Hoc anno Christi 963 die 16 Martii, mortuus est Romanus filius Constantini Regis Romanorum: quod ex Abul Hassumo historico Arabe facile perspicere licet. is enim scribit Romanum decessisse anno Hagareno 352, anno vero Alexandri millesimo ducentesimo septuagesimo quarto, die decima sexta Adar, hoc est, die 16 Martii iuxta calendarium Syrorum. Verba eius haec sunt:
units.tr: {a} In this year of Christ 963, on 16 March, Romanus, son of Constantine, King of the Romans, died; this can easily be seen from Abul Hassum, an Arab historian. For he writes that Romanus died in the Hagarene year 352, in the year 1274 of Alexander, on the sixteenth day of Adar, that is, 16 March according to the calendar of the Syrians. His words are these:

units.la: quae Latinis characteribus exprimere placet: Vephi fenathi athne vehamsin vetultemeja math romanus ben kustantin mulcilrom phi fadis afer adar senath elef vemathai arbah vesibhin alescander: hoc est, Et-in anno secundo &-quinquagesimo (scilicet Hegirae) &-trecentesimo, decessit Romanus filius Constantini regis-Romanorum, in sexto decimo Adar, anno millesimo &-ducentesimo quarto. & - feptuagefimo Alexandri.Sane annus Alexandri Dhilkarnain 1274 incipit kalend.Octobribus, labe-te anno Iuliano millefimo & feptimo: quare dies 16 Adar refpondet 16 Martii, currétis anni Chrifti 963. Ioannes autem Curopalates refert Romanū in Myrelæo fepultum effe mefe Iulio, lexta Indictione, eodem fcilicet anno Chrifti 963, quem ille vult effe annum mundi 6456.
units.tr: I am pleased to give these in Latin characters: [transliterated Arabic omitted]. That is: "And in the year 252 (of the Hegira) and 370, Romanus, son of Constantine, king of the Romans, died on the sixteenth of Adar, in the year 1204 and the seventieth of Alexander." Moreover, the year 1274 of Alexander Dhulkarnain begins on the Kalends of October, in the Julian year 1007. Hence 16 Adar corresponds to 16 March, in the current year of Christ 963. John Curopalates, however, reports that Romanus was buried in Myrelaeum in July, in the sixth indiction, in the same year of Christ 963, which he takes to be the year of the world 6456.

units.la: Hoc anno Chrifti 1003, die 29 Augufti incurrit annus Diocletiani fiue Martyrum fanctorum 720, quo Abul Haffumi fcribit Patriarcham Zachariam inauguratum fuiffe, die vigefimo primo menfis Tybi, hoc eft, die 16 Ianuarii, iuxta calendarium Diocletiani, currente anno Chrifti 1004. Verba eius funt hæc:
units.tr: In this year of Christ 1003, on 29 August, falls the year 720 of Diocletian, or of the holy martyrs, in which Abul Hassum writes that Patriarch Zacharias was inaugurated, on the twenty-first day of the month Tybi, that is, 16 January according to the calendar of Diocletian, in the current year of Christ 1004. His words are these:

units.la: Kadam fenathi telath vetishin vetultemeja albatarch abna dhacharias philfenath aflabeha min chaliphet ilhachim fahib mifri phi jom alehid alhefrin min tubefenath febah meja vehefrin lilfahada: hoc eft, Venit anno tertio &-nonagefimo & trecentefimo (fcilicet Hegirae) Patriarcha pater Zacharias in-anno feptimo adminiftratoris fapientis dominatoris Ægypti indie primo &-vigefimo Tybi,anni feptingentefimi &-vigefimi Martyrum. Hinc apparet Abul Haffumum per annos martyrum, nihil aliud quam annos Diocletiani intelligere: cum alibi exprefse nominet annos Diocletiani, eosque cum annis Hegirae coniungat 4 8 1. Asse-rit enim Patriarcham Marcum Alexandriae inau-guratum fuisse anno Hagareno centesimo & no-nagesimo tertio, & ibidem substitisse decem annos & septuaginta dies, mortuum vero esse primo die re-surrectionis Dominicae, die 2 1 Pharmuthi, anno quingentesimo trigesimo quinto Diocletiani. Eius verba haec sunt:
units.tr: [transliterated Arabic omitted]. That is: "There came in the year 393 (of the Hegira) the patriarch, father Zacharias, in the seventh year of the wise administrator and ruler of Egypt, on the twenty-first of Tybi, in the year 727 of the Martyrs." From this it is clear that Abul Haffum, by the years of the martyrs, understands nothing other than the years of Diocletian, since elsewhere he expressly names the years of Diocletian and joins them with the years of the Hegira, 4 8 1. For he asserts that the patriarch Mark was installed at Alexandria in the 193rd year of the Hagarenes, and remained there ten years and seventy days, and that he died on the first day of the Lord's resurrection, the 21st of Pharmuthi, in the 535th year of Diocletian. units.la: Vephi fenath tulte vetishin vemeja kadam albatrijarch abna marcus algadid jom alehid alteni min emfir bimedineth alescandrija akam hafer fenath vetishin joma: vemath phi teni vehefrin barmude fenath hamfu vetelatin vehamfu mejalidiclediani, vechan jom alehid alkijamet almukaddefeti. hoc est, Et-in anno tertio & nonagesimo & centesimo venit Partiarcha pater Marcus nouitius, die primo qui fuit secundus Emsir in-civitatem Alexandriam, substitit decem annos & septuaginta dies: & mortuus est in secundo & vigesimo Barmude anni quinti & trigesimi & quingentesimi Diocletiani, qui fuit dies primus resurrectionis sanctae.
units.tr: [transliterated Arabic omitted]. That is: "And in the year 193 the patriarch, father Mark the novice, came on the first day, which was the second Emsir, to the city of Alexandria; he remained ten years and seventy days, and died on the twenty-second of Barmude in the 535th year of Diocletian, which was the first day of the holy resurrection."
