units.la: Albategnius gradui vni cœlesti tribuit iter bidui 41: tradit stellas fixas progredi in 66 annis gradum vnum 78: quid suo tempore obseruarit 475.
units.tr: Albategnius assigns two days' journey to one celestial degree 41; he records that the fixed stars advance one degree in 66 years 78; what he observed in his own time 475.

units.la: Albategnius obseruationem suam de æquinoctio autumnali, conferet cū obseruatione Ptolemæi, quam instituit anno tertio Antonini Pii, hoc est, anno Nabonasari 887, die 9 mensis Athyr 476. Albategnius annos Alexandri Dhilkarnain modo facit æquabiles, modo Romanos folares 476
units.tr: Albategnius compares his observation of the autumnal equinox with the observation of Ptolemy, which Ptolemy made in the third year of Antoninus Pius, that is, in the year 887 of Nabonassar, on the 9th day of the month Athyr 476. Albategnius sometimes makes the years of Alexander Dhilkarnain equal, and sometimes uses the Roman solar years 476.

units.la: Alchethi ale rechabateh, hoc est, procidens in genu suum, Arabibus dicitur Hercules 107
units.tr: Alchethi ale rechabateh, that is, falling on his knees, is what the Arabs call Hercules 107.
The Arabs call Aldebaran the eye of the bull 100.

units.la: Alexander Magnus Arabibus appellatur Dhilkarnain, hoc est, habens duo cornua 15: curita dictus sit 56, 311. Alexander non dicitur Ailkarnain, id est, aries bicornis 310, 311. Alexander Magnus mortuus est in Babylone an-no XXXIII ætatis suæ 307 à morte Alexandri vsque ad principium regni Chaldæorum Ptolemæus statuit elapsos annos tredecim Ægyptios 313.
units.tr: The Arabs call Alexander the Great Dhilkarnain, that is, having two horns 15; why he was so named 56, 311. Alexander is not called Ailkarnain, that is, the two-horned ram 310, 311. Alexander the Great died at Babylon in the thirty-third year of his age 307. From the death of Alexander to the beginning of the Chaldean kingdom, Ptolemy reckons thirteen years of the Egyptians as having elapsed 313.

units.la: Alexandrū Dhilkarnain, & Seleucum Nicanore Arabes agnoscunt pro primis Reipubl. Romanæ monarchis 152.
units.tr: The Arabs acknowledge Alexander Dhilkarnain and Seleucus Nicanor as the first monarchs of the Roman republic 152.

units.la: Alexandro Mamaeæ filio imperante historiam suam Romanam finiuit Dio 390
units.tr: Dio ended his Roman history in the reign of Alexander, son of Mamaea 390.

units.la: Alexandriæ longitudo secundum Ptolemæum quanta sit. quæ item secundum Abilfeideam 49. Alexandriæ longitudo confertur cum longitudine Cordubæ 53
units.tr: How great the longitude of Alexandria is according to Ptolemy, and likewise according to Abulfeda 49. The longitude of Alexandria is compared with the longitude of Cordoba 53.

units.la: Alfarkatan sunt duæ stellæ lucidiores in corpore vrsæ minoris 107
units.tr: Alfarkatan are two brighter stars in the body of the Little Bear. 107

units.la: Alfonsus in canone æraru tradit diem 21 Pharmuthi, currete anno Nabonasari 1000, incidisse in kal. Iunias, labete anno Christi 1252 528
units.tr: Alfonsus, in the Canon of Eras, records that the 21st day of Pharmuthi, when the year of Nabonassar was 1000, fell on the Kalends of June in the year of Christ 1252. 528

units.la: Alfraganus nomen est autoris & libri 4. Alfraganus à Fragana patria sic dictus 4: p-prio nomine dictus fuit Muhamed 4: vixit circa annum Domini 950. 5 & 124: post Almamonem & Albategnium floruit 27: eruditissimus suum libellum de principiis astronomiæ Arabicè conscripsit 5: opusculum suum distinxit in 30 cap. sed Hebræus interpres recensuit 32 capita 7. Alfraganus in contextum nulla ichemata inseruit,neq; illa habentur in Hebraea & Latina bibl.Palatinae versio-ne 7z
units.tr: Alfraganus is the name of the author and of the book. 4. He was called Alfraganus from his homeland, Fragana; by his proper name he was called Muhamed. 4. He lived around the year of the Lord 950. 5 & 124. He flourished after Almamon and Albategnius. 27. The most learned man wrote his little book on the principles of astronomy in Arabic. 5. He divided his small work into 30 chapters, but the Hebrew translator arranged it into 32 chapters. 7. Alfraganus inserted no figures into the text, and they are not found in the Hebrew or the Latin Palatine library version. 7

units.la: Alfragani versio Latina multo melior & pfectior, quàm sit vulgata Ioannis Hispalensis, manuscripta extat in bibliotheca Palatina, incerto autore 5. Alfragani caput primum in versione vulgata Hispalensis mutilum, restituitur ex Hebraea translatione & versione Latina m.f.bibliothecae Pal.13: necin Alfragani vulgatis editionib. necin Latina bibl. Pal. versione exstant, quae multa inferuntur ab interprete Hebraeo 18,&19
units.tr: Alfraganus' Latin version, much better and more perfect than the printed one by John of Seville, survives in manuscript in the Palatine library, author unknown. 5. The first chapter of Alfraganus, defective in the printed Seville version, is restored from the Hebrew translation and the Latin manuscript in the Palatine library (m.f.). 13. Neither the printed editions of Alfraganus nor the Latin Palatine version contain it; much is inserted by the Hebrew translator. 18 & 19

units.la: Alfraganus pleraq; defumfit ex Muhamede Aradenfi Albategnio 5: chronologiam suam pertexit vsq; ad aeram Persicam, vnde extendenda est ad nostra tempora 15,464. Scriptit tractatum de obseruanda maxima solis declinatione, qui tamen non peruenit ad manus nostras 27: post Almamone & Albategnium maximam solis declinationem posuit 23 grad. &35min. 27: per annos & menses Persicos declarat periodos planetarum 90: primi climatis medium statuit in illis locis, vbi prolixior dies est tredecim horarum 43; proposuit ordinem & interualla quinq; vsitatissimarū aerarum 15. Alfraganus tribus lignis oftedit, Sohel esse stellam Canobum 101: cur attribuerit singulis mansionibus lunaribus tredecim dies 114: cum vulgo Arabum existimat aeram Persicam ceptisse a regno Iezdaicerris: sed illa incepit a morte Iezdaicerris 14: quinq; Almageftu etia appellat Canonem Ptolemaicum 5: ex Syris Christianis didicit natiuitatem Christi incurrisse in noctem, quae praecessit diem 1 5 Canun prioris, hoc est, Decembris 14.
units.tr: Alfraganus mostly borrowed from Muhammad of Aradin, Albategnius. 5. He carried his chronology down to the Persian era, from which it must be extended to our times. 15, 464. He wrote a treatise on observing the greatest declination of the sun, which nevertheless has not come into our hands. 27. After Almamon and Albategnius, he put the greatest declination of the sun at 23 degrees and 35 minutes. 27. He expresses the periods of the planets in Persian years and months. 90. He placed the middle of the first clime in those places where the longest day is thirteen hours. 43. He set out the order and intervals of the five most commonly used eras. 15. Alfraganus showed by three proofs that Sohel is the star Canopus. 101. Why he assigned thirteen days to each lunar mansion. 114. He holds, with the common opinion of the Arabs, that the Persian era began with the reign of Yazdegerd; but it began with the death of Yazdegerd. 14. He also calls the Ptolemaic Canon the Almagest. 5. From Syrian Christians he learned that the birth of Christ fell on the night preceding the 1st day of Kanun the former, that is, December. 14

units.la: Alfraganu publice praelegit Regiomontanus in Academia Patauina 5
units.tr: Alfraganus was publicly lectured on by Regiomontanus at the University of Padua. 5

units.la: Algedi dicitur capricornus, quod nomen confusum est ab interprete Hebraeo cum Alchethi, quod Herculem significat 107
units.tr: Algedi is the name for Capricorn; this name was confused by the Hebrew translator with Alchethi, which means Hercules. 107
Algol is called Medusa by the Arabs. 107

units.la: Almageftum Arabes vocant astronomiam Ptolemaei, quasi dicas, opus [?]. Almageftum Latinum m.f.in bibliotheca Palatina 326. Almagefti Arabici epitome docet stellas fixas in 70 annis progredi gradum vnum 78
units.tr: The Arabs call the astronomy of Ptolemy "Almagest," as if you were to say "the work [?]". The Latin Almagest is in the Palatine library. 326. An Arabic epitome of the Almagest teaches that the fixed stars advance one degree in 70 years. 78

units.la: Almamon rex Arabum mathematum studiosissimus paulo ante Albategnium vixit,
units.tr: Almamon, king of the Arabs, a most diligent student of mathematics, lived shortly before Albategnius,

units.la: vel illi Fuit coçtaneus 151. Almamon corrupte Almehon appellatur 27. Almamon imperauit viginti annos Arabicos,quinq; menfes,& tredecim dies 471. Almamon Saracenorum princeps Magnam conftructionem Ptolemaei de Graeco in fermonem Arabicum tranfferri curauit anno 112 Hagareno 471: Geographia vulgarem fiue Ptolemaei lit,fiue alius autoris, de Graeco in fermonem arabicum curauit transferri, vt teftatur Abilfedea 472: maxima folis declinationem inuenit 23 grad. & 35 min. 17 Almamonis mentionem facit Alfraganus cap. 6, & 10, 472
units.tr: or was his contemporary. 151. Almamon is corruptly called Almehon. 27. Almamon, king of the Arabs and Babylonian caliph, was called Amir al-mu'minin, that is, commander of the faithful. 41. When he was elected caliph of Babylon is recorded from the Arab historian Abulfeda. 471. Almamon reigned twenty Arabic years, five months and thirteen days. 471. Almamon, prince of the Saracens, had the Great Construction of Ptolemy translated from Greek into Arabic in the year 112 of the Hegira. 471. He had the Geography, whether of Ptolemy or of another author, translated from Greek into Arabic, as Abulfeda testifies. 472. He found the greatest declination of the sun to be 23 degrees and 35 minutes. 17. Alfraganus makes mention of Almamon in chapters 6 and 10. 472

units.la: Almenkeb Arabib. dicitur humerus dexter Pegafi | 107
units.tr: Almenkeb is called the right shoulder of Pegasus by the Arabs. 107
Alramech is called Arcturus by the Arabs. 101
Altayr is called the vulture by the Arabs. 107
Alvakah is called the lyre by the Arabs. 107

units.la: Ambrofius Epifcopus Mediolanenfis quando vixerit 445. Ambrofius in tribus annis Diocletiani feftum Pafchatis indicat 445: afferit enneadecaeteridem fiue aureu numerum a patrib.in concilio Nicaeno affignatu fuiffe 449: duplex facit initiu anni, vnum politicum a menfe Septembri,alterum ecclefiafticum a neomenia Paichali 450: teftatur,tempore concilii Nicaeni aequinoctium vernum haefiffe in 12 kal. Aprilis, hoc eft, in 21 Martii 449,450: annos Indictionu computat a menfe Septembri 450. Ambrofii obferuationes tres dePafchate celebrato confirmant cyclum folis Auguftalem 449
units.tr: When Ambrose, bishop of Milan, lived. 445. Ambrose indicates the feast of Passover in the third year of Diocletian. 445. He asserts that the enneadecaeteris, or golden number, was assigned by the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea. 449. He makes a double beginning of the year: one civil, from the month of September, the other ecclesiastical, from the new moon of Passover. 450. He testifies that at the time of the Council of Nicaea the vernal equinox fell on the 12th day before the Kalends of April, that is, on 21 March. 449, 450. He reckons the indictions from the month of September. 450. Three of Ambrose's observations on the celebration of Passover confirm the Augustan solar cycle. 449

units.la: Anni Christi, qui a natiuitate vel circucifione numeranTUR, anni Christi vsitati appellantur 459. Anni Christi a natiuitate numerati, oCTIDUO praecedunt eos, qui a circumcisione numerantur 178. Anni aerae Christi, minime sunt confundendi cum annis aetatis Christi 401.
units.tr: The years of Christ which are counted from the nativity or the circumcision are called the customary years of Christ. 459. The years of Christ counted from the nativity precede by eight days those counted from the circumcision. 178. The years of the era of Christ must by no means be confused with the years of Christ's age. 401

units.la: Anni Christi, qui a conceptione numerantur, vocantur anni Dionyfiani 459. Anni Christi, apud Romanos in vsu non fuerunt ante Dionysium Abbatem, sed apud Graecos fuerut notissimi 419.
units.tr: The years of Christ counted from the conception are called Dionysian years. 459. The years of Christ were not in use among the Romans before Dionysius the Abbot, but were very well known among the Greeks. 419

units.la: Anni Christi centesimi aliqui fuerunt simplices, aliqui bisextiles 529. Anni Christi & Alexandri in bisexto conuenire coeperunt circa annum 509 Iulianum 229. An-
units.tr: Some centuries of Christ were common, some bissextile. 529. The years of Christ and of Alexander began to coincide in the bissextile year around the Julian year 509. 229. An-

units.la: ni Christi connectendi sunt cum annis Iulianis 174. Annus natiuitatis Christi, est annus 45 Iulianus 367. Annus primus aerae Christianae, est 46 Iulianus 367. Annus primus Christi incurrit in annum mundi Iudaicu 3761. 232
units.tr: ni Christi are to be connected with the Julian years. 174. The year of Christ's nativity is the 45th Julian year. 367. The first year of the Christian era is the 46th Julian year. 367. The first year of Christ falls in the Jewish year of the world 3761. 232

units.la: Anno natiuitatis Christi, hoc est, anno Iuliano 45 bruma haesit circa 25 & 24 Decembris 346. Anno Christi 337, Pascha fuit celebratu 3 Aprilis 443. Anno Christi 819, die 17 Aprilis celebratu esse sanctum Pascha, probatur ex Abul Haffumo 486.
units.tr: In the year of Christ's nativity, that is, Julian year 45, the winter solstice fell around 25 and 24 December. 346. In the year of Christ 337, Easter was celebrated on 3 April. 443. In the year of Christ 819, on 17 April, holy Easter was celebrated, as proved from Abulfeda. 486.

units.la: Anno Christi 879, die 16 Ianuarii, feria sexta, Albategnius obseruauit stellam septentrionalem, quae inter duos scorpionis oculos circumuoluitur, fuisse in 17 gradu, & 50 minuto scorpionis 475. Anno Christi 883, die vigefima tertia Iulii Albategnius obseruauit lunae defectum 475.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 879, on 16 January, a Friday, Albategnius observed that the northern star which revolves between the two eyes of the Scorpion was at the 17th degree and 50th minute of Scorpio. 475. In the year of Christ 883, on the 23rd day of July, Albategnius observed an eclipse of the moon. 475.

units.la: Anno Christi 940, Thoth Nabonafari 1688 incurrit in kal. Ianuarias, & Thoth Nabonafari 1689 incidit in diem vltimam Decembris 479

units.la: Anno Christi 1589 pascha celebrauimus iuxta veterem stilum, die 30 Martii 438
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1589 we celebrated Easter according to the old style, on 30 March. 438

units.la: ante Annum Christi 1700 differentia veteris & novi calendarii est decem dierum 527.
units.tr: Before the year of Christ 1700 the difference between the old and new calendars is ten days. 527

units.la: Anno Christi 1700, die 24 Iunii, iuxta stilum veterem, incurrit dies 18 Tamuz, labente anno aerae Iudaicae 5460. 525: eodem anno, die itidem 24 Iunii, incurrit dies 18 menses Muharam, labente anno Hagareno 1112. 526.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1700, on 24 June, old style, falls the 18th day of Tammuz, in the year 5460 of the Jewish era. 525. In the same year, on the same 24 June, falls the 18th day of Muharram, in the year 1112 of the Hegira. 526.

units.la: eodem Anno Christi 1700, die 7 Iunii, stilo veteri, & 18 Iunii stilo novo incidit novilunium, quod probatur ex aureo num. & Epacta Gregoriana IX. 526.
units.tr: In the same year of Christ 1700, on 7 June Old Style, which is 18 June New Style, the new moon falls. This is shown from the golden number and the Gregorian epact. 526.

units.la: Anno Christi 1700, post 23 Februarii diem, differentia veteris & novi calendarii incipit esse vndecim dierum, vsq; ad annum Christi 1800. 528.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1700, after 23 February, the difference between the old and new calendars becomes eleven days, until the year of Christ 1800. 528.

units.la: Anno Christi 1800, post 23 Februarii, differentia veteris & novi calendarii incipit esse duodecim dierum, vsque ad annum Christi 1900. 528.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1800, after 23 February, the difference between the old and new calendars becomes twelve days, until the year of Christ 1900. 528.

units.la: Anno Christi 1900, post 23 Februarii, differentia veteris & novi calendarii incipit esse tredecim dierum, vsq; ad an-
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1900, after 23 February, the difference between the old and new calendars becomes thirteen days, until the year of Christ 2100. 528.

units.la: num Christi 2100. 528. Anno Christi 2100, excidet vigesimum septimum bisextum, iuxta ordinationem Gregorianam 528.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 2100, the twenty-seventh leap year is dropped, according to the Gregorian ordinance. 528.

units.la: Anno Christi 2100, dies 24 Februarii, iuxta stilum veterem, respondebit diei 18 Ianuarii, iuxta stilum nouum 528
units.tr: In the year of Christ 2100, 24 February Old Style will correspond to 18 January New Style. 528.

units.la: Annum coelestem quomodo describat Varro de re rustica 317
units.tr: How Varro, in De re rustica, describes the heavenly year. 317.

units.la: Annus communis & deficiens apud Hebraeos continet trecentos & quinquaginta tres dies 235.
units.tr: The common and deficient year among the Hebrews contains 353 days. 235.

units.la: Annus communis & ordinarius apud Hebraeos constat trecentis & quinquaginta quatuor diebus 235.
units.tr: The common and ordinary year among the Hebrews consists of 354 days. 235.

units.la: Annus communis & plenus siue abundans apud Hebraeos continet trecentos & quinquaginta quinque dies 235.
units.tr: The common and full, or abundant, year among the Hebrews contains 355 days. 235.

units.la: Annos communes, Hebraei appellat annos Alexandri Dhilkarnain 492.
units.tr: The Hebrews call common years the years of Alexander Dhilkarnain. 492.

units.la: Annus confusionis fuit tertius consulatus Caesaris 167. coepit die 14 Octobris, labente anno secundo ante ordinationem Iulianam 350.
units.tr: The year of confusion was the third consulship of Caesar. It began on 14 October, in the second year before the Julian ordinance. 167, 350.

units.la: habuit quindecim menses, seu dies 445, teste Cenforino & Suetonio 165, 350
units.tr: It had fifteen months, or 445 days, according to Censorinus and Suetonius. 165, 350.

units.la: Annum magnum Cynicum, seu periodum annorum Aegyptiorum 1460 obseruant Persae 218
units.tr: The Persians observe the great Cynic year, or period of the Egyptian years, of 1460 years. 218.

units.la: Anni Diocletiani apud Aegyptios, Arabes, Persas aliosq; populos orientales, usq; ad nostram ætatem costantissimè obseruatur 464. Anni Diocletiani quomodo comparandi sint cum annis Christi 430
units.tr: The era of Diocletian is most constantly observed among the Egyptians, Arabs, Persians and other eastern peoples down to our own time. 464. How the years of Diocletian are to be compared with the years of Christ. 430.

units.la: Annos Hebræorum vsitatos male aliqui extendunt ad principium mundi 259,260.
units.tr: Some wrongly extend the customary years of the Hebrews back to the beginning of the world. 259, 260.

units.la: Anni Hebræorum à certa epocha elegantissimè deducuntur in contextum annorum Iulianorum vsitatû & æquabilem 260. Annorum Hebræorum dispositio quomodo sit inuestigada 250
units.tr: The years of the Hebrews are most elegantly deduced from a fixed epoch into the customary and regular sequence of Julian years. 260. How the arrangement of the Hebrew years is to be investigated. 250.

units.la: Anni Hegiræ ab interprete Auerrhois appellantur anni a prædicatione Muhamedis 204

units.tr: The Julian years are the vehicle of the wandering years of Nabonassar. 192. The first year before the Julian ordinance was confused, and had 445 days. 530. The Arabs hold that the first year before the Julian ordinance was a bissextile year and had 366 days. 530. The first Julian year was a simple year, consisting of 365 days. 167. The fourth Julian year, immediately after the triumvirate of Augustus, is held to be the first year of the reign of Augustus. 177. units.la: Annus 45 Iul. est 28 Augustorum seu Actiacae victoriae secundum Romanos 179,180.
units.tr: The 45th Julian year is the 28th Augustan year, or the year of the Actian victory, according to the Romans. 179, 180.

units.la: Ann° 45 Iul. est 41 imperii Augusti, quo Christum natum esse asserit Eusebius 177.
units.tr: The 45th Julian year is the 41st year of the reign of Augustus, in which Eusebius asserts that Christ was born. 177.

units.la: Annus 45 Iulianus, quo Christus conceptus & natus est, litera dominicalem habuit B. 529.
units.tr: The 45th Julian year, in which Christ was conceived and born, had the dominical letter B. 529.

units.la: Anno 45 Iuliano circa aequinoctium vernum incipit annus vrbis conditae 753. 180.
units.tr: In the 45th Julian year, about the vernal equinox, the year of the founding of the city, 753, begins. 180.

units.la: Anno 45 Iuliano circa solstitium aestiuum incipit annus Olympiadicus 776.180.
units.tr: In the 45th Julian year, about the summer solstice, the Olympiad year 776 begins. 180.

units.la: Annus 46 Iulianus est principium annorum Christi vsitatorum, quatenus illi a circumcisione Domini suppu-

and this is proved by various arguments. 181.

units.la: Annus 52 Iulianus accepit primum bisextu Augustale 529.
units.tr: The 52nd Julian year received the first Augustan bissextile. 529.

units.la: Annus 78 Iulianus est anno trigesimus tertius aerae Christianae, & 33 aetatis Christi secundum Dionysium Abbatem, & 34 aetatis Christi secundum Epiphanium 46 r.
units.tr: The 78th Julian year is the thirty-third year of the Christian era, and the 33rd year of Christ's age according to Dionysius Exiguus, and the 34th year of Christ's age according to Epiphanius. 46 r.

units.la: Annis Iulianis elapsis 133,134, & 135 diem vnum anticipant aequinoctia & solstitia 179.

units.tr: An indiction is a period of fifteen years: 433. The Constantinian indictions begin from the festival of the first quinquennalia, eight days before the Kalends of October, in the year of Christ 312, 432: when they began, see ibid. There are two beginnings of indictions: one from the institution of Constantine the Great, from September, or 8 days before the Kalends of October; the other from the institution of the Pontiffs, from the Kalends of January: 433. The invention of indictions is very useful for dating times: 434. The start of the year among the Syrians is taken from the earlier Tishri, or from Elul: 227. The Arabs call the Fortunate Isles Paradise, and the west of the middle world: 54. Intercalary years: see Year. How the intercalation of the Syrians differs from that of the ancient Romans: 228. Ptolemy puts the interval between the era of Domitian and that of Trajan at sixteen Egyptian years: 395. The Arabs put the interval between the first Julian year and the first year of the era of Christ at 45 years: 361. The interval between the epoch of Christ and the first observation of the autumnal equinox, instituted by Ptolemy, is 131 Egyptian years and 199 days with two hours: 411. The interval between Nabonassar and the epoch of Christ is 747 Egyptian years and 132 days: 411. What the interval of the periodic month is: 89. The interval between the quinquennalia and vicennalia of Constantine was fifteen years, and this was the beginning of the periodic indictions: 433. The interval between Thoth Actiacus and the era of Christ is 29 Egyptian years and 132 days: 411. The interval between the Fortunate Isles and the shore of the western ocean is ten degrees: 50; it is not always the same: 53. John XXIII, pope at the time of the Council of Constance, agreed to a correction of the calendar: 438; he issued a decree for correcting the Roman calendar: 505. John Kouropalates reports that a Roman was buried in the Myrelaion in the month of July, in the sixth indiction, in the year of Christ 963, which he wants to be the year of the world 6456: 484. John of Seville, around the year of the Lord 1142, translated Alfraganus into Latin: 5. John of Seville's astrological epitome: 111. John Lucidus rightly places the Lord's Passion on 3 April, in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad: 403. John of Sacrobosco drew his doctrine of the primum mobile from Alfraganus: 5.

Ptolemy and Censorinus handed down the true connection of the years according to the hypotheses of the Greeks and Egyptians 396.
